Government Admin Simulator 1982.
Or, that is how it would be if this game weren't addictive, engrossing and filled with misery everywhere you look.
You are a lowly citizen given the opportunity to admit people into the country. You need to be alert for any problems with their documents, a typo here, the height of the person, anything can be wrong, and you need a sharp eye.
Having worked in admin before make me realise it's easier when you've done this kind of focused examination of documents to ensure the people have everything they need.
Pre-scripted events like terrorism, bombs, a secret government organisation, bribes from applicants, favours from officials appear to make you question the orders you receive from above, along with potential opportunities to give your family a better home. And yes, you do have a family, though you don't see them, you need to inspect enough people each day to earn money for rent, food, heat, and medicine etc when needed.
Multiple endings, so plenty of chances to get it wrong or right. Overall, a very well made game which harkens back to the era of the fall of the Soviet union, East and West Germany and the breakup of Yugoslavia.

Karl Marx once said that alienation from your labor was one of the reasons for unhappiness and Papers, Please by indie developer Lucas Pope sure shows us why. In Papers, Please you play an citizen of the communist state of Arstotzka. One morning you recieve a note saying you now work in the new border checkpoint and it is your job to approve or deny those who would like to enter the country. You will have to examine increasingly numerous and complex documents and decide if the applicants will be allowed into Arstotzka.
While the game's concept would appear boring and unappealing, good writing and occasional moral decisions keep you interested throughout the game. Will you accept the bribe to let the smuggler through in order you feed your family? Will you carry out jobs for the Arstotzkan Revolutionaries? How will you feed your family? Through these decisions the game will humanize everyone whom you are involved with in the game. The game also has brilliant art and music. While Lucas Pope claims that this art style just happened, it sets the mood for the entire game. Bleak, dark, and lifeless.
The game suffers from some monotony, but that is clearly the point. There's some artistic value in how it forces you to carry on, stamping passport after passport to feed your family. The game itself is only 10 dollars (USD), just right for what comes out to be about a 5 hour title.
Papers, Please is an example of what can come out of a brilliant indie developer when they put their mind to it. It takes what would seem like a poor game idea and turns it into an enjoyable 5 hour experience which will make you question the morality of your actions and the state of the world.

While you wouldn't expect a game about border control and passport stamping to be fun, Papers, Please has a unique method of storytelling that doesn't get old. The pressure to be correct and the urge to help those who don't have the proper documentation gives Papers, Please an interesting storyline and gameplay.

Now, I just recently beat "Papers, Please" and thoroughly enjoyed myself.
In this game, you live in the made-up Communist nation of Arstotzka and your name has been drawn in a "labor lottery" which I have never heard of before, but I imagine is similar to jury duty in America. The particular job you have been given (regardless of whether you want it, because hey, it's communism) is to be a border checkpoint worker. Your family is given a house to live in, but you must provide enough money to keep them safe and sound.
This game starts off quite linear and intriguing as you admit or decline people based on their paperwork and the rules you are issued everyday before starting. As time goes on however, events happen and more rules are added into your book to help ensure the safety of Arstotzka. Each day, you only have so much time to process people and that puts a lot of pressure on you because you have a family you have to pay the bills for.
This game presents you with many choices throughout. Some of these are moral choices or opportunities to make some money. Not all the opportunities are legal though...How much are you willing to do to compromise the nation's security to make sure you have food on the table? There are twenty different endings and the game makes you feel like your decisions actually matter.
As far as gameplay alone goes during the process of admitting applicants, it is actually exhilarating. You know you need to do a good job of examing their paperwork so that you don't lose money or even your job, but you also just want to work as fast as possible to get more money for your son's medication, or to pay the heat bill, or whatever the game throws at you. The rules constantly change and evolve with the times and it makes gameplay an enthusiastic struggle of work ethics, money, and guilt.
I cannot say how thoroughly impressed I am that one man alone made this game. It is definitely worth playing. 10/10.

Recipe for Ferrero Rocher
Ingredients
1 packet nestle dark chocolate melts
25 g Copha
nutella
20 unsalted hazelnuts or 20 almonds
crushed nuts
Directions
Melt copha and chocolate together.
Pour a little into ice cube trays.
Refrigerate/freeze to set.
Spoon a bit of nutella into the centre of each chocolate.
Place nut in the centre of each chocolate.
Top with remaining chocolate.
Sprinkle with chopped nuts.
Place in freezer for 15-20 mins.

Mount and Blade was Sid Meier's Pirates refashioned as medieval warbands, Blood and Gold Caribbean is Sid Meier's Pirates fashioned as medieval warbands fashioned back into piracy. It loses and gains something from the transition.
For starters, this is the only M&B "mod" I've tried that actually feels like a different game at its core. Outside of maybe Viking Conquest which did some clever combat rebalancing, almost every M&B mod just felt like the base game only with more spreadsheets, troop trees, piles of pointless management and economic fiddle for a game that was mostly "combat and stuff between combat." Every mod just felt like an average Doom WAD: new map, same core. And the M&B core is fun but it ain't Doom.
Blood and Gold shakes all this up wonderfully. Ship combat, ship boarding combat, piles of gold to upgrade, reload, rehire troops, and  of course deck you and your heroes out in nice gear. Guns that are actually fun to use... perks to aim for when leveling your character... the entire gameflow feels similar but actually like it dances to a new beat. A few scripted story quests break up the M&B-ish boredom too, that can lead you to intrigue and even romance.
The management aspects are a little overblown, giving you three full pages of buildings to build in various towns, to manage a dozen different resources, with the addition to throw spare ships around to set up your own convoys.
In addition, "crew" and "soldiers" are two separate resources, which need to be refilled periodically through two very different processes, a design choice sop to the M&B core gameplay, where a 350 crew ship isn't going to have 350 nord huscarls in your party without being a mess (And multiply that by 6 ships if you really are going nuts.).
Factions are here. Conquest is here. Building your own faction is an option. But unlike M&B, just being a pirate and building up an armada, piles of gold, and an economic engine across the Caribbean is its own reward, whereas in M&B you basically play fetch quest until you can get in good with a faction and start having some fun. It's a side dish here when the core gameplay is still strong.
All in all, B&G is a fine pirate game, if you don't mind the innate jankiness of it being an M&B mod writ large. The ambition is unmatched in all the M&B mods I've sampled.

Don't listen to these other salty sailors who think this is a bad game. They're the kind of people who are on the bottom deck alone eating dried fish instead of up on deck drinking rum and wine with the crew.
Blood & Gold: Caribbean! can be judged as two things: A pirate game, and a mount & blade game. And it fits both those boots perfectly, without having some awkward walk while wearing them. It combines the features and engine of mount & blade games, the awesome firearm warfare that we were first introduced to in With Fire And Sword, and the thrill of being a fearsome pistol & sword-toting PIRATE! Or you can be a privateer under the crown of the Netherlands, England, France, or, my personal favorite, Spain!
The game has a lot of the features that previous mount & blade games did, yet 50% of Blood & Gold: Caribbean! is all new features and metagames, including but not limited to things like naval combat and raiding sea fortresses from your ship, to exploring Inca & Aztec temples for treasure and, well, killin' people with new toys! If you've ever played other great pirate games like Sid Meier's Pirates!, Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag, or Sea Dogs: To Each His Own, you WOULD have fun with this game. Blood & Gold: Caribbean! is an amazing pirate game, easily making its place into my top 10, and also an amazing mount & blade game, easily tieing or even better than Warband and With Fire And Sword. I could go on and on about how great of a game this is, but this is a steam review and not an HBO special. I'll let you go here, since I know your finger is already itching to scroll up and buy it or add it to your wishlist -- and if it's not, enjoy your dried fish for one on the bottom deck!

I was completely new to the Homeworld Universe before purchasing this product, unlike many who had played the non-remastered versions of this game. I must say though, it is absolutely wonderful.
Pros:
-Beautiful Soundtrack. I've played countless strategy games, but this one captures the essence of the mood by certain evants.
-Great graphics. I run this on a non-gaming laptop, yet at a great FPS on higher settings. Space has never looked so good.
-The ships actually have some interesting roles and there isn't that "one unit" that is the end-all-be-all. This allows for a variety of ships in your fleet. Also adds to action trying to handle the vast array of fleets to fight your enemy.
-Story. It isn't pretentious nor too simple. They really nailed on this one.
-It is a good challenge to play through the story against CPU or friends. You don't feel overwhelmed with a million functions that are all cluttered like other games. This allows you to actually play rather than trying to micromanage a medium-sized fleet.
-Tutorial is actually useful.
-Soundtrack.
-Did I say soundtrack again? Yeah, it's that good.
Cons:
-Wouldn't say this a con, more like a desire, but it'd be great to have a master campaign. One where you can actually expand your domain in  real time.
-I really wish there were much more 1v1 maps that were much larger. I love the game, but it'd be much more fun if the maps were large and maybe even a moon here and there would be nice to utilize. Like a base or something.
If you liked the original homeworld (and that's probably why you clicked on the icon), you'll love this.  Why are you still reading this? Go on! Buy it!

Borderlands 2 is an amazing game for the right moment. That is the best statement to summarize the entire experience you will recieve with this purchase. If you are a fan of the Borderlands universe and love wacky-yeat delightful banter as you experience a sudo-RPG like gameplay than look no further than making this your next game addition to your Steam Library.
Borderlands 2 can best be discribed as a unique experience for the first playthough only. After completing the main storyline and a few sidequests here and there for leveling and a few good loot spots, the game becomes repetitive in an old fashion RPG grindfest. Only after you trudge through the second playthrough do you unlock the actual game in terms of gameplay. Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode pits you against all of the elements that thrive on Pandora and gives you the best possible loot adjacent to your level. My experience both solo and in a party have given plenty of highs and lows, but all in all I will have to say that the enjoyment I experienced in this game has been matched by no other on Steam.
Oh, and don't think that playing alone in the Borderlands is a chore or an impossible task just from the trailer! Solo play is hand crafted to make sure your bosses are brutal and your journey is full of fun detours. But to say co-op deminishes the fun from the storyline would be a bold face lie! Having a companion actually doubles the fun and adds more spontainous action into the mix. Definately a game that can be shared with buddies who need a mostly cheerful romp through a bloodfilled FPS.
Overall I would say that the ammount of time I have spent in this game, pre and post-DLC and across multiple platforms is a good justification on my positive review of this game. Definately pick this game up!
Final Verdict:
Solo: 8/10
Co-op: 9/10

The short version?  If you like The Elder Scrolls, and you at least don't mind MMORPGs, go ahead and pick this one up.  If you actively dislike MMOs, give it a skip and wait for the next mainstream entry in the franchise.
Slightly longer version: Straight up front, this is not The Elder Scrolls VI.  If you're looking for the next Skyrim, or Oblivion, or Morrowind, and nothing else will do, move along.  This is what happens when an awesome franchise puts out a game that takes one step to the right.  It looks like an Elder Scrolls game, it sounds like an Elder Scrolls game, and it feels like one, too.  But it's not the next Skyrim.
Your quest, while still epic, will not feel as epic simply because of all the other people in the world doing the same thing.  The world won't change as much at your actions, though it does change more at them than I've seen in other MMOs.  Your engagement with the NPCs and the world will probably not feel as deep.  Large chunks of it are comfortably familiar, though - your leveling and skill improvement system, for example (use skills and get better at them), as well as the Alchemy system are taken straight from the other games.  There are Ayleid ruins, familiar friends and enemies, the lore is all there, you have to hock your stolen goods at a fence, etc.
But there are some things it does better, too - the crafting system is the best I've seen in any TES game, and among the best I've seen in any MMO; it's deep and flexible, offering you lots of options, but being really user-friendly and accessible at the same time.  I'm drawn in by the Enchanting crafting too, the search for runes in the ruins and wild places of the world, then combining them into glyphs, rather than just taking a soul gem and glomming a spell onto an item.  And crafting writs are an elegant solution to a classic MMO problem - I want to improve my skill so I can make cool stuff, but grinding out iron daggers and selling them is boring and slow.  Enter writs, where by crafting specific items and turning them in, you make some money and a big chunk of experience at your trade.
Character creation and development are the most flexible and open-ended I've ever seen them - you want to be a stealthy mage wearing heavy armor and carrying an axe?  Go for it.  Now, are some builds more optimal than others?  Of course.  But there are very few artificial barriers in the way of player choice, and if you put the effort into it, you can make anything work.  The familiar refrain in the world chat logs when some veteran of other online games asks "what's the best?" is "just play however you want."  And you really can.
The Elder Scrolls Online really occupies this sort of odd space between its Elder Scrolls parts and its Online parts.  I haven't been super impressed with the community, but it's no worse than any other MMO (or other place occupied by People On The Internet).  And honestly, you can safely ignore they're even there most of the time, which is what I mean by the odd space; you're in this online game with a lot of other people, but a lot of the time I don't really notice or care that they're there.  Now, if you want to group up and be social and do lots of group content, there's plenty there for you - but if you just want to strike out on your own and explore the world, there's plenty for you, too, and the vast majority of the content can be enjoyed either way.  So if you don't mind other people running around the hub town in your Elder Scrolls game, give this one a go.

If you are looking for a cute and relaxing game to kill boredom, I recommend The Cat Games, especially if you love cats!

Now, I just recently beat "Papers, Please" and thoroughly enjoyed myself.
In this game, you live in the made-up Communist nation of Arstotzka and your name has been drawn in a "labor lottery" which I have never heard of before, but I imagine is similar to jury duty in America. The particular job you have been given (regardless of whether you want it, because hey, it's communism) is to be a border checkpoint worker. Your family is given a house to live in, but you must provide enough money to keep them safe and sound.
This game starts off quite linear and intriguing as you admit or decline people based on their paperwork and the rules you are issued everyday before starting. As time goes on however, events happen and more rules are added into your book to help ensure the safety of Arstotzka. Each day, you only have so much time to process people and that puts a lot of pressure on you because you have a family you have to pay the bills for.
This game presents you with many choices throughout. Some of these are moral choices or opportunities to make some money. Not all the opportunities are legal though...How much are you willing to do to compromise the nation's security to make sure you have food on the table? There are twenty different endings and the game makes you feel like your decisions actually matter.
As far as gameplay alone goes during the process of admitting applicants, it is actually exhilarating. You know you need to do a good job of examing their paperwork so that you don't lose money or even your job, but you also just want to work as fast as possible to get more money for your son's medication, or to pay the heat bill, or whatever the game throws at you. The rules constantly change and evolve with the times and it makes gameplay an enthusiastic struggle of work ethics, money, and guilt.
I cannot say how thoroughly impressed I am that one man alone made this game. It is definitely worth playing. 10/10.

Papers, Please is one of the most innovating and impressive games from this year. Being a sort of point-and-click game, Papers, Please excels in the way it uses it.
You take the role of an Arstotzkan border controller who regulates the border checkpoint in Grestin, Arstotzka.
You must earn money by doing your job accordingly and with as few errors as possible in order to feed and protect your family, as well as keeping them healthy and living under a roof.
The game focuses on the basic mechanics of point-and-click, but uses this mechanic in a very different way by allowing the player to check entrees' passports as they attempt to enter the country of Arstotzka. Your duty, as border controll, is to make sure that only people with valid documents enter the country.
If you make any errors, small amounts of your salary will be held back, and you may even allow in a terrorist if the person that you allowed entrance carried a bomb and you forgot to x-ray them because they had expired documents, for example.
The game has a very simple art direction, as well as a very simple sound design. Lucas Pope, the creator of the game, really nailed it with Papers, Please, as he created something inspiring, entertaining, and very different.
Papers, Please is one of its kind, and is one of those rare indie games that you should defnitely try out.
The only complaint I have is that the main story is too short, but even so, the game has a freemode and so you can continue to play on without focusing on the main story, even though the main story is crafted in a specific way and has its own events, the freemode is very fun too.
No more needs to be said.
Glory to Arstotzka.

This is the single most terrifying game I have ever played, and one of the most striking I have ever experienced. The sense of isolation, of total fear, is unmatched by anything except perhaps if you played System Shock as a child. A gun will keep you alive, but it cannot defend you from the anomalies, the radiation, the hunger. It cannot penetrate the darkness for you. It cannot be a friend, a confidant, or an ally. Coupled with mods to alleviate the worst of the bugs (and what game of ambition and vision has been anything but buggy?), I rate this as one of the most compelling experiences I've ever had in gaming memory, even six years after its release.

Alien Isolation is a great survival horror game that is beautifully designed. Every single little screen,knob and button has been faithfully recreated with amazing detail. The space station you explore during the game gives you the same awe and wonder that you may experience in Bioshock. The particle effects range from little sparks, to embers to, oxygen pumping into a rooms -- it's all really well done.
In terms of gameplay, it moves quite slowly. Depending on what difficulty you play on, there will be more severe concequences for being detected by an enemy. Enemies include hostile humans, synths, aliens and face huggers. The game relies on saving stations that are very random in placement -- sometimes they are close to another sometimes they are far apart. When they are far though, you get this massive sense of relief from saving.
You'll also be relieved to know that you can kill most of these enemies with a hit of your trusty wrench. The alien, however is invincible and will stalk you throughout most of the game. You'll have to hide from it in a variety of vents, closets, cabinets and even under desks and tables.
After 15 hours in those vents playing hide-and-go-seek with the alien for FAR too long, I was ready to put the game down but I felt this obligation to finish the story and save the character I was playing as from this nightmare.
I'd pick it up while it's on sale. It's definitely worth it just to experience the beautifully crafted environment and for some good scares.

I know it will say that I have very little (if any) time in the game up above, but I poured hundreds of hours into this game during early early access (when you could only get this game from their website).
I'm an English guy. I deal with words and phrases and ideas. I have a hard time with math, and I have an even worse time dealing in 3-D concepts like "Put this here, then there, then connect this," blah blah blah. Engineering/math/computer science as careers are far beyond me.
If you're like me, don't let that keep you from playing this game. It is intuitive once you get the hang of it, and it'll seem intimidating at times at the sheer complexity once you get into end game stuff, but the feeling of finally getting a train running and off-loading into your smelters, which in turn feed into a main bus that will eventually get you enough solar panels to power the whole damn thing and keep those biters off your back for a few more expansions, is like crack.
There is very little story, and even less hand-holding. You can spend hours googling to find the best set-ups and the best mods and the best everything. Or you can just play, and figure it out as you go, and go to Google after your first successful factory to see how other people have done it. Either way, this game is that special type of complex that might look out of your depth, but is very much within your grasp.

I am part of a DevOps team at work and we have dedicated this as our group game. It is a good way to exercise your intuitive grasp of the theory of constraints.
It does such a good job of simulating automation and it's ever increasing levels of complexity that it could actually improve your efficiency at work.
I highly recommend this game for it's intellectual depth and hours of fun that it packs!
P.S. The quality of this game is way above the typical steam early access game.

For me indie games offer a way to tell immersive and emotionally engaging stories in ways that are inaccessible in any other medium. I can easily say that Papers, Please is the most emotionally heart-wrenching game I have ever played. By far. I would go so far as to say that this is a perfect game. The gameplay itself is stressful and difficult, which may sound off-putting but that really is the point. You deal with the stress and paranoia because the game gives you reasons to do so. Throughout the game you make seriously difficult decisions which will always have consequences. In my first playthrough I took something that I knew I shouldn't, but I was scared that if I didn't my son would starve. That wasn't  a fabricated choice the game threw at me. It was the result of my gameplay affecting the story in a way that I had to make these difficult decisions. This is perhaps the only game I've played where your decisions truly affect the story. And not just for 'good' or 'bad' endings. Everything is grey and unclear.
Papers, Please is an masterpiece with one of the most immersive stories I've ever played. This is all an attempt to say that I like it very much.
Simple yet deep, it will challenge you as a brain game while testing your moral compass. With a couple dozen possible endings and an infinity mode there's some replayability here.

One of the more fairly interesting games that I've played. I didn't honestly know what to expect from this but it is actually one of the more morally ambigious games I've played in recent memory (aside from The Last of Us and Fallout New Vegas), you are tasked with being an immigration officer in a fictional communist country in the 80's. It's surprisingly tense with the fact that while you have to let certain people through and send certain people the other way, choices are presented to you from time to time, such as if you should let a certain person through even if they don't have the right paperwork. Do you let a girl's family through but not the girl due to her having the wrong papers? Can you make that choice and live with the consequences? Can you afford to do this as if you get to many citations against you then your pay can be docked which you surely need to support your family who suck up all of your money at the end of the day. It really makes you question your own morality and what you would do in that situation. Sometimes when you feel like you have made the right choice something ends up happening that you didn't expect. They could have been completly lying to you the entire time but you won't know until the end. With multiple endings and an endless mode available this is definitely a must buy if everything I have just talked about interests you. I definitely give it a big recommendation and I think you should totally buy this.
It's unique, interesting, and worth a look. There's nothing quite like it out there.

One of my all-time favorite games; played both the originals when they came out.  The persistence from level to level is novel and really ties the single player campaign together: build early, build often, move it all cautiously, and zoom in after you issue orders to take in the massive battles.
Word of warning, though: you can't capture Vagyr capitals in HW2.  Doing so just disables them.  Still useful, but won't net you +1 capital ship.

Gearbox has done an excellent job updating a classic space RTS, one of my favourite games ever made. The original Homeworld was excellent for its rich atmosphere and lore, which was supported by a fantastic art style and amazing sound production. Gearbox has kept the same nostalgic atmosphere while adding massive improvements and quality-of-life improvements to the game. On top of that, they've been very active in the community, responding to issues quickly and effectively, releasing new patches that have fixed minor issues.

Homeworlds 1 and 2 are among the best games ever made for PC. This "Remastered" version does a good job of preserving that legacy and also adds increased graphic fidelity and performance. The single player missions are engaging, the original's voice acting and artwork remain haunting and first class, the storyline is compelling. If you love science fiction and don't get goose bumps at least once, there is something wrong with you. My sole complaint is that for a game which championed free movement in three dimensional space, that element of strategy is often overlooked in the campaign: like Kahn, your enemies suffer from two-dimensional thinking. But if you've never played Homeworld and you see this game on sale, don't hesitate.
Meanwhile multiplayer remains a shabby amateur mess with horrific balance issues, even after a one year wait for patches, and the bulk of the "community" is toxic beyond belief, but this is Gearbox and Steam, so you already knew that.

Preamble:
I played HW1 a long time ago when I was too young to really appreciate it. I only had vague memories of it coming in.
Homeworld 1:
A simple game that still manages to make a great impact thanks to it's beautiful presentation. You really do feel like you're leading a group of nomadic exiles in search of their new home, and all the bizarre scenarios they find them selves in.
I love the idea of being able to take everything with you to the next mission, although it did create some really nasty situations, especially during the Nebula missions, and the last few missions feel like a cakewalk if you over-prepared (Not that it makes the last mission any more beautifully done).
Homeworld 2:
Will play soon.

An extremely good game that makes me dream about conveyor belts and robo arms, the first night after playing this i actually dreamed it. It's great fun to automate everything, especially the automatic tech unlocking which is especially complex and especially impressive when completed.
The main reason this is so good is because you take a simple concept- mining, smelting, crafting, etc.- and then you make it complex by adding machines, wiring, automatic crafters, and conveyor belts. Unlike other games which are complicated, but once you have the rules understood it's simple, this game is simple, but once you get deeper in it becomes complicated. And don't confuse complicated with hard, this game is fairly easy. And don't confuse easy with boring, it's extremely addicting and fun. this game can be described as a puzzle game, survival game, city builder, or just a game where you have to make stuff fit in a small space.
Example:
I decide not to make 100 bottles to unlock a new tech, so I automate red bottles...
Green bottles now required, so I grumble to myself and go make turrets, then I decide to automate the green bottles.
BLUE bottles now required, so I grumble to myself and quit the game, next day I spend a few hours automating the blue ones.
PURPLE BOTTLES now required... I realised how easy purple bottles can be made so I set up a train system, just because they're cool and more complicated.
Also a fun and overlooked part: TANKS just load up a bunch of cannon shells, hop in a tank, and spend a day blowing up the nests around your base. sooo satisfying to watch all that purple blood spew everywhere, and watch the nests flatten out as they die. *note* Not a very bloody game.
Also, definitely worth $20.00, 11/10 -- the only reason it's not 10/10 is because it's $20.00, not $19.99

OK after playing quite a lot of M&B, I decided I needed to write again this review and replace the more
with a more serious one.
As other users have mentioned, be it they thumb this game up or down, the game is quite glitchy. I personally felt that the M&B engine worked wonderfully with this game, but sadly I can't really comment how much of an improvement it was compared to the first release, since I never played that.
It all comes down to how much a person gets affected by minor glitches and bugs, along with lag. Whatever the changes under the hood are in B&G, the game is quite a bit more laggy and it has some battlefields that it lags for no particular reason. You actually can experience the same kind of lag even in mods of M&B so I am feeling there is something in the actual native engine that causes the problems.
These though battles can be mostly ignored, since at least I did not do that many battles on land and in sea I did not experience bad lag. Where though the lag is real, is sieges. I only done one land siege and the rest were all sea sieges, so I can't really comment on the land ones. Sea sieges though will make you lag like crazy. The main reason is that the battle is actually all of your troops against all the troops of the enemy at once. There are no controlled waves that depending you computer you can make larger or smaller. I am on a C2Quad @3.2GHz and a ATI R9 280X 3GB and the battle would reach as low as 6-8 FPS while the ships are heading towards the fortress, before any battle starts. Obviously as the battle starts and enemies and allies die, the FPS slowly gets better, but no matter what the lag is bad. Keep in mind I am not saying that the only reason the lag is so bad is the huge battles, but also even normal battles do not feel as smooth as M&Bs.
Obviously there are quite some other glitches and problems, some that can break immersion for some people. For me the main things that are missing are more ship models, which I can understand why they are hard to be implemented.
The game is quite unrefined, but for loved of Pirate games that could enjoy a mediocre game running on the M&B engine, I am sure you will love it as much as me. I enjoyed it and easily would replay.
Now something a bit off topic, is that when I read reviews on here, I feel people are comparing B&G with all the awesome free community modules that people can get in M&B. The reason is that they make M&B Warband sound so highly sophisticated and perfect, but maybe because I have played so many of its community mods, I find M&B:W a really nice game, but not all that perfect. Obviously if you compare its huge gamma of modules you can get on it with just a game that feels like a module itself, it will not hold a candle to it.
At least as far as I know, there are no other modules with Naval battles like B&G. Viking Conquest/Brytenwalda naval battles do not feel anything like B&G's and at least I do not know any mods that does anything close to it. Definitely a diamond in the rough that I am hoping it will be polished. Honestly though, I bought it on a sale and the 130 or so hours I put into it have already earned more than I payed.

Homeworlds 1 and 2 are among the best games ever made for PC. This "Remastered" version does a good job of preserving that legacy and also adds increased graphic fidelity and performance. The single player missions are engaging, the original's voice acting and artwork remain haunting and first class, the storyline is compelling. If you love science fiction and don't get goose bumps at least once, there is something wrong with you. My sole complaint is that for a game which championed free movement in three dimensional space, that element of strategy is often overlooked in the campaign: like Kahn, your enemies suffer from two-dimensional thinking. But if you've never played Homeworld and you see this game on sale, don't hesitate.
Meanwhile multiplayer remains a shabby amateur mess with horrific balance issues, even after a one year wait for patches, and the bulk of the "community" is toxic beyond belief, but this is Gearbox and Steam, so you already knew that.

As I have never played the original Homeworld series before, my comments made here are based on my feelings playing this game as a new player, and not on whether this is a good remake of the original series.
In this game, basically what the player needs to do is pretty much like all the other RTS games, such as harvesting the resource, creating a fleet, researching new technology, defending the mothership, and destroying all enemy spaceships, etc.
The differences between this game and other RTS games include:
1) There is only one type of resource in this game. It's simple but quite boring.
2) The battlefield is in the outer space; there is no topographic features of any kind in this game. That is, no roads, no lakes, no mountains, no nothing to speed up or slow down the moving speed of your units. Futhermore, you can't hide behind anything to dodge fire; you can't plan ambush; and you can't make a detour or anything. You just go directly toward the enemy then fight, and so is the enemy.
3) When you assign multiple units in a fleet, you can specify its formation. However, there is no tutorial or hints to tell you what are the advantages and disadvantages of each formation. In fact, after several hours of play, I still have no idea at all whether the selection of formation will affect the attacking or defending ability of the fleet or not.
4) Although the player can command a specfic unit to attack a selected enemy, normally you won't have time to do so, as you cannot pause the game and there are simply too many enemy to target and you got so many spaceships to control. As a matter of fact, the program always hung up whenever I continuously move my units around the map. I'm not sure whether it's the problem of my computer (which I bought around a year ago to perform some computationally intensive numerical simulation) or there actually is a bug in this program. As a result, all I did in this game was to produce spaceships, group them as a fleet, assign them to attack, then they will move straightforward to the enemy to kill or get killed.
5) The strength of your enemy in each mission is scaled to match the strength of your army at the end of previous mission. You are triumphant to have won a tremendous victory in a mission? You probably won't laugh for long because in the next mission a much stronger enemy is waiting to greet you.
6) The research is boring too. There is no such thing as tech tree in this game. Basically you just click on the research tab whenever the game tells you that there is a new tech available for you to research. And in maybe 30 seconds, the system informs you that the research is completed, and then, you are done. Oh, I almost forget to mention that they didn't even bother to design the icons for the technologies. It's just a text box; you click on the box whenever the system reminds you to do new research.
Of course there are some nice features that enable the game to have received an overwhelmingly good review from the players. However, if I were to know those game settings/features as listed above, I would not waste my time or money on this remastered game.

Buggy, yet quite unique take on the tower defense genre. Unfortunately, it left Early Access too soon and seems more-or-less abandoned at this point, as if the devs had decided to prioritize other titles instead. Scumbag move! But if this game works for you and the bugs aren't too distracting, like the lack of music in-game, then it's hard to put down. The units are all awesome, and you can take direct control of ALL of them, and then of some other extra air and ground units at your disposal, so you can take matter on your own hands if things get to hectic, like a F-14 Tomcat, an Apache helicopter, WWI era tanks or the Red Baron's own aircraft just to mention some. From WWI to the Cold War, there's lots of content here and factions, all DLCs for both games are already included, so lots of hours of fun.
Quite strategic in its use of units and upgrades, since every upgrade comes with side effects, like longer reloading times for WWI era artillery, or with different effects in the case of modern American artillery -spread instead of direct ammo/howitzer with precise munitions vs barrage of MLRS- or a mortar emplacement with bio-chemical ammo that later can be turned into a flamethrower and then into a regular mortar with napalm effects, each with their own pluses and cons. To add variety to an already varied game, you can make use of random special powers, abilities and you can also take control of a hero, but it's not really necessary, and that's only if you manage to obtain them by killing enemy units directly in a combo. The bosses are awesome, they're these humongous machines that dwarf any other units so they're always fun and interesting to fight.
Having said that, I would give this game a neutral rating due to the Early Access blunder and amount of bugs, and the lack of in-game music really pisses me off. But this being Steam, it's either a thumbs down a thumbs up, so I'm going with a positive rating overall since I did indeed enjoy my time with Toy Soldiers: Complete.

The Cat Games is a very casual, easygoing game that's intended for cat lovers. If you are not a cat person, you would not enjoy The Cat Games.
The game is controlled entirely with the mouse, except for the computer puzzle code which requires a text input. There are three main games to play; Indoor Racing, Swim Challenge and Cat Breed Billards, as well as several other minigames involving napping, leaping at birds outside the window, and viewing cat pictures on a computer.
Indoor Racing isn't necessarily a
game per-se, but a randomly generated obstacle course that you guide a cat through. Swim Challenge requires you to click on various objects being flung in the cat's direction as to not knock the cat into the bathtub. Cat Breed Billards is a billards game where you have to sink the cat ball corresponding to the breed you're given; you don't get penalized for sinking the wrong cats, but you get a large point bonus if you sink the correct cat breed first.
Ultimately, The Cat Games is rather short, simple and sweet; I managed to obtain all the achievements in about an hour of gameplay. I would recommend The Cat Games for casual gamers who love cats. Having said that, you may not enjoy this game if you're a serious gamer, or you don't necessarily like cats.

The Zone. A barren wasteland that has been surrounding the Chernobyl Nuclair Power Plant since it's disaster in 1986. Many venture into the Zone, looking for strange artifacts, objects of mystery and value. A lot goes on in the Zone and you're not alone. Other Stalkers (scavengers, trespassers, adventurers, loners, killers, explorers and robbers) search for fortune as well, everyone has their own goal and it's every man to himself (barring certain factions).
There's only a few enemies all stalkers share: the horribly mutated creatures of the zone, ranging from blinded dogs and mutated pigs to bloodsuckers and controllers. A stalker must be aware of such dangers at any time, since behind every corner death may wait for you,unless you can outsmart death. Sneaking, awareness, precision and tactics come into play when you're taking on entire groups of enemies, and when they're all finally dead, it feels very satisfying.
The Zone is, with all it's dangers, a large place to explore. The A-Life engine makes it feel as if everyone and everything isn't just there because they're programmed to, they feel as if they were doing something, and you happen to bump into them. Sometimes this might result in a gunfight, sometimes they will greet you or help you. Also guitars and campfires.
As for the combat mechanics, they're probably some of the fairest mechanics I've seen to date. When just starting the game, enemies may seem like bullet sponges. And sure, some do seem to take a ton of bullets, but then you realise what mechanics are behind them. Bulletproof vests reduce damage take from gunfire, bullet drop makes your shots miss if you don't aim well, and hipfire will also hit jack♥♥♥♥♥♥ To take down enemies, you'll have to be precise and accurate. Shooting the head of an enemy that isn't wearing head protection will result in it's immediate death. Such mechanics make the game feel both realistic and rewarding. Landing that perfect headshot from a silenced weapon to see a tough guy go down without the rest of his gang knowing what is going on just feels good.
9.5/10

This game, right here, is fantastic. Set around 15 years after the original film, it puts us in the shoes of Ellen Ripley's daughter, Amanda, seeking closure about her mother destiny's after she learns the Nostromo flight recorder was recovered.
This is practically my first experience with the Alien franchise, as I'll have to admit I've never seen an Alien film in its entirety, only parts of them (that's something I should fix ASAP); although I do know the plot of the first film. And I must say that if you're in the same situation as me, then this is a great opportunity to get into the franchise. The aesthethic is retro-futuristic; it seems they aimed to recapture the feeling of the original film, and they did a fantastic job; Sevastopol is an amazing space station, full of areas to explore, and to hide. As far as the soundtrack goes, it's excellent. It really sets the tone of tension during several moments.
As far as gameplay goes, this isn't a run and gun. And this isn't a "hide in a corner and wait until the enemy goes away/learn the movement patters" stealth game. No, this is a stealth game about movement, survival, and adaptation. This game will punish you if you stick to the same tactics; the Alien will learn, and so you must learn as well. It's not just about hiding in a corner, it's about outsmarting a much stronger and faster enemy. And even then, the Alien isn't the only threat; there are other people on the station, who will do anything to survive; and then there's the Working Joes, those unsettling androids, who might not look like much of a threat with their slow movement, but can really take you by surprise.
At times, it might seem there are huge difficulty spikes, but this is not true; it's part of the challenge. Sometimes you'll find yourself stuck in an area, getting spotted and dying time and time again, and then, when you go back again, you'll find it wasn't as difficult as you originally thought; that happened to me several times. It's all about paying attention to your surroundings, and making the best use of the tools you have available.
The story, as I mentioned in the first paragraph, is about Amanda looking to get some closure on her mother's fate. When going to the station that was holding the Nostromo flight recorder, things aren't as smooth as they should, and soon you're trapped in this huge station with an Alien on your back. I don't want to give any more details, as something that adds to the experience are the surprises you'll find aboard Sevastopol.
Well, I don't think there's much more to add. I could write a thousand more words, but I don't feel I would make this game any justice. It's just something that you need to experience by yourself.

While the concept is really cool and the core game is pretty damn fun; the controls and camera views really drag the enjoyment factor down. For some God-awful reason they used a turn-based strategy control scheme in an RTS tower\defense game; it makes absolutely no sense.
I was constantly fighting to put the camera where I need it to see wtf is going on. For some reason the camera doesn't pan vertically, so you're stuck with a very narrow view of the battlefield which has enemies coming from all angles. There is a top-down view that shows much more of the battlefield, but it's probably the most boring way to play the game.
With the tilt\pan camera, you have to constanlty be scrolling over the battlefield because the view is so restricted. But that leads to another annoying issue when the scrolling will pause if the mouse cursor passes over emplacements. There's absolutely no reason for it other than to make scrolling around even more difficult.
The unit menus have a radial-type menu where you select upgrades and actions. However, once a unit has been highlighted, left-clicking ANYWHERE else on the screen will complete the highlighted action; even if your mouse pointer is nowhere near the button. Again, it makes no sense and is annoying if you just want to click on another unit.
Controlling units (mainly aircraft) can be difficult because of the forced mouse accelleration. Control can act anywhere from sluggsh to super twitchy\sensitive, absolutely no consistancy. One second you're doing Immelmans, the next you're stuck in a turn and can't pull out fast enough. There is no rudder control, and using the "roll" controls didn't seem to work for me.
Maybe it plays better with a gamepad since it is a console port; but dear god...if you don't like to constantly get frustrated by ♥♥♥♥♥♥ camera angles and♥♥♥♥♥♥poor controls then avoid at all costs.
The controls are my only real complaint in this otherwise fun and addicting game; I'd only recommend when it's on a steep sale and you have some extra patience.

In Papers Please you are a customs official, responsible for approving or rejecting entry of immigrants. Gameplay involves checking documents for inconsistencies, like when a name or number doesnt match or documents are missing. There are also story specific rules like denying entry to all people from a specific country. Its surprisingly complex, but the game does a great job of gradually teaching the player new rules. I'm going to start out by saying I love Toy Soldiers. I played 75+ hours of the original's console version both on and off-line. It had a unique charm to it that felt like the developer's really took time in crafting a unique IP into a full fleshed out and realized game. If you have the chance to play the original I'd highly recommend it. It has its own unique sense of quirkiness and has a lot of twists on the Tower Defense Genre of games that make the level enjoyable to play over and over again. Part of the original's charm too was that the levels were challenging, but if you mastered those twists on the gameplay mechanics, and did well enough in the early rounds you could gradually build a fortress of defensive lines no one could penetrate.
All of that makes what I am about to say that much harder. I can't recommend this game to nearly anyone in its current condition. The game has an excessive number of bugs for me which is odd considering that it runs fine with only a few frame rate drops sporadically. Units will fall through the map constantly for me to the point where some entire waves of enemies may as well not have spawned because they didn't even come into line of my forward gun positions. At the time of writing this I have beat every campaign and DLC in the game, except for the original Toy Soldier's main German campaign, and I have won literally every boss battle since the tutorial by the boss spawning, and then immediately dropping through the map only to despawn and be considered destroyed. Then a message pops up telling me congratulations your victory, though I never fired a shot. The game will also crash randomly on me during map loading or when a new wave spawns. Other times heat seeking missiles will just decide that they are not locked on and stop tracking the target half way through their flight. This is honestly astounding to me considering how much the original impressed me. I haven't been able to find anything on message boards saying that this is unique to a specific build or version, but I know that this is happening fairly frequently to others as well.
Even when the game is not being a bug parade, the balancing is very messed up. There are some enemies that are capable of sustaining multiple direct hits from max upgraded artillery. This is fine on its own. In small batches it is a fun challenge to try and crush these bullet sponges as they drive up to your front line. The issue is when the developer has built a wave of these enemies that has 15 of these storming at you full speed, and the map only has two places to set artillery pieces it. Any other gun placement can barely touch these enemy types, and they will routinely break your lines causing you to leave the fun of building your base/ piloting a vehicle to turn around and mop up the remnants. In addition to this, the buildup of challenge is more of a cliff face than a traditional learning curve. Enemy waves start out with low armor and low numbers, but in the last five waves will ramp up to dozens of layered enemy types that are bullet sponges, some of whom can also just run over emplacements, destroying them in the process. The game at this point quickly becomes a test of how quickly can you spend money to get your gun emplacements back before the next wave, and this becomes tedious at best.
In its current version I would go so far as to say the game is unplayable. To me that is a tremendous shame. The original brought me many hours of enjoyment with friends and by replaying the campaigns for their challenges to unlock various war memorabilia (another feature stripped from this version). This feels like a game that has lost any care that was originally placed into its IP. It comes across as a hollowed shell of a concept, filled with half-finished gameplay mechanics that was slapped together and never tested before release. Seeing as it has been out for a while not, and from what I can tell there have been little efforts to address these issues, I would say Signal Studios has given up on this project entirely. I emphatically do not recommend this game to fans of the genre and would recommend either trying to find a copy of the original for console or to look elsewhere if you are interested in something like this game, because what we were given can barely count as one.
Buy now. Not later.

Papers, Please is a fantastic little indie game set in a fictional Eastern European country called Arstotzka in the fall of 1982.  You play as an Immigration Officer at a check point into Arstotzka. The gameplay compromises checking passports and other required documentation in determining if they can enter the country.  Even though the game play sounds simple, it very quickly becomes complicated by adding more and more rules and requirements to allow people entry.  Depending on how you play, how well you play, and which story line you follow, the game offers a variety of endings.  If you can get past having to stamp passports for gameplay, Papers, Please offers a great gaming experience.
Although simplistic on its face, this game shows a hidden depth and is strangely compelling.

I really wanted to like this game.  I'm a big fan of M&B and open world conecept games in general.  The game has several good ideas going, even if they've become tropes by now, and for the most part the personal combat system works great.
Sadly, however, that seems to be the
thing that works great.  Yes, the first-person combat is everything you'd expect from the M&B engine, but everything else ranks from "meh" to "poor" in comparison.  The towns are lag-filled messes, with every one of them functionally identical.  It borrows the resource model from Port Royal, which is a shame because Port Royal's resource model is a disaster, and then somehow managed to make it even worse with fixed pricing and even more shallow economics that, somehow, someway, manages to be even more dreary & less intutive than its progenitor.  Economics in this game are, simply put, horribly broken and pricing on both goods & equipment are basically darts thrown at a wall of numbers during an LSD binge.
Ship combat is... there, I guess.  Another mash of tropes, it's the same formula we've seen used in ever wooden-ship navy combat minigame we've seen in the last twenty years or so.  Not that it's a bad formula - after all it worked in Sid Meier's Pirates - but at the same time nothing new is really brought to the table except for first person boarding combat.  While this does seem new & exciting it doesn't take long to realize that the number of goons you bring & the number of goons you fight against rarely has anything do with the actual numbers claimed to be on board the ships.  It's also buggy movement-wise, and one wrong pixel can toss you overboard or clip you into something & freeze you into place.
There's a few missions, too, all buggy to one degree or another.  You can toss torches at ships and watch them do nothing, accidentally exit temple ruins too soon simply by facing the wrong way, get weird dialog pop-ups out of nowhere from characters you've never met, and generally run around wondering what you're supposed to be doing because there is no real in-game guides that actually, y'know, teach you anything.
Overall I'd say the general problem is that they took the solid M&B combat engine and then tried adding lots of stuff to it that it was never really meant to do in the first place, and then spent the next several years trying to bugfix the resulting mess.  The result is a game with one great strength followed by a long list of ever increasing weaknesses.  The ship combat barely works.  The economic game doesn't work at all.  The scripted stories... I can't even tell if they're working.  The strategic map is a mess that still has pathfinding issues to this day.
Saddest of all is that you know a game has reached the end of its development life when they try to sell you it's soundtrack for extra cash (y'know, the same soundtrack that's already included in the game you already own?).  Therefore I don't see any of these problems ever getting fixed, which is a shame.
The
are good.  We've needed a pirate game with more first person combat for a long time.  It's the
that was lacking, because they used a engine that's good for first person combat and not much else, and it's that not much else that brings the game down.  I don't blame the developers for the limitations of the game engine.  I'm sure they did the best with what they had to work with.  The problem is mostly just the inadequacy of the tools.

TL;DR: It’s like Dishonored 1, but 2. But you've probably already heard that. The difference is now it feels like luxury, because locations are unspeakably beautiful. Do you know how they used to make games with just a few locations while the gameplay screamed for an openworld, but these locations were really detailed and had a developer’s heart imprinted in them? Well, this is it. DH2 is a short game, and it feels almost like half time shorter than DH1, and when you realize that - you can’t help feeling disappointed and frustrated. But when you settle down and play it - you see that quality of the content is making it up for everything else.
And the quality is so damn high you can pause the game at any time and make a screenshot, and it will look like a painting. It is achieved by both artistic and technological endeavors. You’ve got an excellent art design, tons of objects and detailed models, which have no interaction with the gameplay whatsoever and exist only for the sake of the hot visuals. And it makes a really big difference for you to feel that the world is alive. You may rush the levels to the objective or you may wander around and look under every rock, but the pleasuring aesthetic feeling of traveling in a detailed world will strike you all the same.
However, everything else regarding gameplay is left exactly the same as DH1, meaning the game itself is very easy to finish. As before, it features a quite intricate level design, leaving you with decisions of how do you want to traverse it. But the amount of things that can actually stop you from finishing your mission is close to nothing. It becomes hard and challenging if you try to beat the game completely stealthily, but if you deal with the enemies as you go, then there is no need to be creative. You can still try to play with finesse to your own amusement, and reload if there was no grace in the actions you performed, and I did exactly that, but I’ve always wanted it to be “do it gracefully or fail” type of gameplay.
The same goes for exploring the world. While searching rooms for loot in DH2 is not completely pointless – it is very close. You don’t need money because you don’t need items, and you don’t need upgrades because most of them are useless. You don’t need incendiary bolts to blow up a nest because you can simply walk to it and break it with your sword and you won’t take damage (I was doing it like that on hard difficulty all the time). And that’s how most of the gadgets work in this game – it's there, it works, but you have absolutely no need for it. You can amuse yourself by trying it several times, but that’s it. And while you can’t downright blame the game for it, you can’t say anything good about it either.
Nevertheless, DH2 is completely worth it’s time. You may finish it several times, try different play styles and unlock every possible path, or you could just play it once and enjoy it’s arguably quite short, but generously stuffed with top quality content play time. It’s up to you, like anything else you do in this game. And it’s great.
P.S. I bought this by the time every issue regarding poor performance was successfully fixed. In fact, I played it on a 100$ video card from 2016, in 1080p, with everything set to HIGH, and it ran much smoother than on PS4. And the price was great. I think I made myself clear.

Easily as addictive as Civ 5. I never write reviews but doing this to give suggestions for devs. Stellar game as everyone else has pointed out.
Criticisms as of 3/7/16  (I only have two):
-Not sure if done deliberately but the most annoying thing is how you can't have perpendicular pipelines. So this basically requires my refinery operations to be exactly aligned to a body of water if I need to transport water. It is however rewarding to figure out an efficient configuration for liquids
-You guys should fully flesh out the campaign. I really enjoyed it and I feel like it wouldn't be difficulllt to make perhaps 8-10 more missions that walk players through the tech tree and different scenarios. Another improvement would be to add some touches to the existing campaign such as actually being able to drive down the coordinates you found in mission 2, or actually flying the airplane in mission 4.
-I read your website for possible changes in the future. A cool idea might be having corporations that manufacture industrial or consumer products that are sold to markets. It could be competitive in that there might be other player/AI corporations competing with you for a short period of time, so this really necessitates maximising efficiency (just like in manufacturing IRL) whereas in the normal mode sometimes there's a lack of pressure.
For more RTS elements as you discussed in your site, you could have buildings that produce fighting robots that head towards a rally point. If you have other players, it kind of becomes a passive Supreme Commander but with a greatly fleshed out macroeconomic/production system that, again, necessitates efficiency due to the competitive element.
Anyways, like everyone else says, tons of variety, full control over the production configurations you want to design, deep tech tree, lots of logistical elements that nearly all strategy games skimp on, and more. The spine of the game is there with factory designing/logistics - I just really hope that more variety of game modes comes out by the time this game is fully released, with a more fleshed out combat mechanic.

This game takes management to a whole other level and to be honest this game makes it so that there will never need to be another management game ever, Let me explain.
We have here the most complicated management game ever in reality. You may say that there are some other games that are similar and other things that come close (some minecraft mods come to mind instantly) however this game is unique in the fact that you can spend 10,000 hours on it and still be thinking about a faster way to get...I don't know lets say electricity. It challenges your ability to multitask and understand the importance of every single thing you put down. You will constantly be second guessing as you try to comprehend faster and faster ways of producing things.
For being in early access this game is ingenious and seems mostly complete. The only real cons are the lack of challenging enemies in super late game, no dedicated servers, as well as the fact that you will waste all your time managing a factory and forget to manage your own life....
That being said this game features full mod support somthing that is amazing in it's own right and there are some amazing modders from what I've seen that have already began to mod extensively.
All in all I rate it as such:

Story:None:None
Gameplay:5/5:Must Keep Playing!!!!
Replay Value:HIGH:

The M&B engine may be old, but to me, it offers some unique experiences.  For example, the chaoic crush of sailors and soldiers during a boarding in this game is one of the more interesting takes on boarding actions that I've seen in a game.  Even a high level character with great equipment must take care not to be surrounded.  Sure, naval combat might seem a bit simplistic, and the graphics are indeed dated, but it has a moderate and satisfying learning curve that has translated into an immersive and enjoyable experience for me.  Also, the devs seems to be supporting it well with updates from time to time.
So, if you like the M&B experience and pirates, I'd suggest it.  While other reviewers have mentioned technical issues, I've had none in over thirty hours in game on a Windows 8.1 laptop with a 980m.

Dark Souls 2...
Dark Souls 2 takes you 'the player' into a story where you don't really need to follow that to be able to play this game to the end. If you are looking for a story, you can find that by reading item descriptions and talking with NPC's you find in the game.
You will not find any missions or quests, apart from these two: Get 4 powerful souls to open an area. Find a way to kill the final boss in the game.
How you are going to get these souls is up to you, how you are going to find a way to kill the final boss in the game is up to you.
If you have played Demon's and Dark Souls, you may find this one a little easy. Don't get me wrong, the game gets (a lot) more difficult when you progress to journey 2,3,4 and beyond. Just like the NG+ NG++ NG+++ etc. modes from the previous title (Dark Souls)
On a side note: You can burn bonfire astetics into any bonfire you find and then that bonfire will rise in level and diffuculty as if you were on journey 2,3,4 and beyond for every bonfire astetic burnt. (so if it's too easy, just chug one or two of these into that bonfire and then... good luck..)
Everything else you would expect from a dark souls game is there. Some controls have been tweaked and you can now get more control with some additional settings you can tinker with for your keyboard or controller, visuals, way of combat etc. ( I would recommend playing this with an x-box controller, if you have another pc controller you may need additional software and/or pc setting tweaks to get everything working correctly. )

I was especially enchanted by the way they really captured that Age of Sail feeling by making the ships lightning-fast and nimble, and how the game tracks ammunition but doesn't have a way of reflecting whether or not your shots hit.
Like my cannonades, this one's a bad miss.

I've played this game a fair amount offline as well, as a fan of older Total War titles and in this time period itself.
Just don't buy the game.
The only advances CA has made to the TW series have seem to be just Graphical in nature.
You could see it as a trend from Empire an Shogun, that the AI just wasn't able to cope, the difference is that the package is far tighter. So whereas it was noticeable, it didn't detract from the experience.
Death moves are the only way units die, what's the point of having 200 men against 200 men when only a few die at any given time due to some perversion for Homeric style combat instead of actual battles and their respective battle lines being fought across (Force upon the playing, ironically by the new focus on graphical improvements and motion capture.)
Units have no weight, a charging mass of cavalry or elephants has no real impact on the units they are charging.
If you want a better Rome Total war experience, stick to R:TW or M:TW with a mod to emulate the Classical era.

I would say the subtitle of 'dystopian document thriller' is partly correct.  The setting and mechanics in this game are fairly unique I think, where you play a border agent in a country with an oppressive government.
The gameplay itself is actually fairly routine, and can be summarized as rule memorization and observation skills.  This is fine, as it works and makes sense within the story.  The sound design and aesthetic lend to this very well.  There were no performance issues.
I don't think there is that much replayability to the story despite the variety of endings.  There is an unlockable endless mode, which could make this fun as a pastime too  Still, I'd reccomend this game for its unique experience.  Its really not something you see every day.

As with all the COD games after BO2 and MW3, this one too suffers the same backlash, part true and part rediculous. The SP campaign is fantastic, as with most the later games, Great graphics and great modes for BOT use. An important mechanic considering "online games" in which the money spent is an investment, without bots that investment is totally reliant on a "playerbase number". In such an oversaturated market the idea that a game in this genre will maintain a large playerbase past the 6 month mark is ludicrous. Devolving then into a sect of fanbois and "vets" who know the game so well that noobs have little to no chance of maintaining interest, and those "vets" have no patience or desire to deal with them. In such a situation, the lack of bots = you've just wasted your money (see Verdun, Rising Storm 2, ect) whos playability will last only as long as a large playerbase remains to provide the diversity, which is pretty much moot in this day and age in the long run.
So, once again, you have a COD game, extremely overpriced and with a horrible DLC pricepoint making the game hugely expensive which despite it at least being a permanent game you can always play due to bots. This of course = massive negative reviews beause "the MP is dead"...well NO♥♥♥♥♥♥sherlock. 99% of all these games will end up that way, yet still, digbats will lay out 60-150 bucks and then scream foul because they couldn't wait a year to get it for a prioce that won't make them angry when "the mp IS DEAD".  If you get the base game for under 10 or the full package for under, let's say 25, then you'll be fine. The SP campaign is VERY fun, nice graphics, nice mechanics and will not leave you PO'd about what you spent vs what you get in the "playable" department. I got this for 5.99$ @ cdkeys dot com. And just like when I got COD Ghosts (The full package) for 22$ I've enjoyed greatly both games. If you browse the reviews you'll see this pattern and how the majority of negatives revolve around "dead". And if you paid 60$ for the base game I can certainly understand, but I also think you're an idiot and your review reflects that fact in doing what you should have known BETTER than to do.
Get it for a reasonable price and you'll be fine, stop being fools and paying so much and then screeching "SP is great, graphics are great, mechanics are great, but MP is dead so imma slap a negative"...as if you didn't already know and were a total fool for paying more than you should = your reviews are tainted. imo.

Thought it would be a god-awful paid version of the M&B mod Nova Aetas, actually a swashbuckling adventure with landings that work and did I mention that trading is a viable profession and piracy can be a means to that ends?
So a pro/con list seems to be a good idea.
PROS:
It's mount and blade engine, bring on the mods (there are already mods lol)
Trading is the regular old buy low, sell high except you can effect production postively/negatively through your own business and raids as well as doing trade missions.
Fairly simple controls, it's not too well explained but once you figure it all out it's fairly easy to manage your ships/crew/business/finances
Town quest board, great improvement over regular M&B systems and there are more unqiue/generic quests in general.
Gun combat is more fun/fluid than say Napoleonic wars.
Titles/ranks system that adds a sense of progression to the game so you have other goals to work towards.
And there are many more.
Cons
Been in EA a fair while, but it's had a free DLC so I guess that makes up for it a bit.
First person view in the ship seems to be buggy and you can't rotate your camera from what I seen to see where the other ships are, although when doing regular cannon fights it's better to use the minimap.
Path finding is kinda bad for your ship, often times it will go back to port if the most direct route is directyly in line with your clicked destination.
Sometimes your own ships like to ram you in battle, although this is generally when deadstopping and turning so kinda your fault lol.
Has the feeling of an expansion to M&B but the polish of a mod atm.
If you wanted mount and blade warband with pirates, then this is for you but be warned it's still developing.
For using the Mount&Blade engine/format along, I want to recommend this. Maybe with a little more polish and fixes, it'll deserve a thumbs up.

While this is a fun game, sadly I would feel bad giving this a positive review. I love Warband and simply picked it up because it ran on the same engine. It's not a horrible game, it can be fun and it's very low on bugs. But that's where it stops. The more you play the game, the more you realise that this isn't worth the price. The game gets old, fast. Even compared to something like With Fire and Sword, its very boring and repetitive stuff. Some of the radiant quests you get from the man in the tavern are fun, but even then there're very few types, and many are just straight up boring or broken. (IE, stand behind a wall for 5 minutes to take over a mine, still never fixed the good 'ol M&B AI). This game just feels like a polished mod for Warband. It's not a complete broken mess and most of the content is there, but just not enough. Plus, even when I can get great frames in Warband, this game will lag my PC, so there are also some optimization problems as well. But then again, this game has one major feature that none of the other Mount and Blade games don't : Boobs. So if you like to waste $200 to disappoint some random prostÍtute after slaughtering some Frenchmen, then this is for you.
Jokes aside, I would skip this game until there're more opportunities for fun gameplay like in the other games, or until there's a more active modding community to give this game some content.

Homeworld Remastered was released in February of 2015. In spite of being a Homeworld fan, I decided to wait for the reviews; and I was glad that I did. While the game was not short of impressing people for its new visual enhancements + the merging of both games units and assets for a unified game, the developers neglected some very important details on the game that we all love. The formations in Homeworld Remastered were screwed up. In the Original Homeworld, people remember the fact that formations assigned to groups of units actually impacted their ability to effectively and efficiently dispose enemies.
As explained in details by one of the reviewers: that whole aspect was stripped away as a different method for damage calculation was done on ship to ship combat. The problem was, individual ships didn't feel individual anymore, the formations did not chew up hostile ships like they were supposed to; and that right there frusterated me, which believe it or not: deterred me from buying this game. It was only over a year after in the fine month of June 2016, that the game developers decided to release a patch which RESTORED this crucial gameplay aspect. The formations are back and are effective again! The only complaint is you can't make larger formations (large spheres would be nice).
Two hours into the game, I have been satisfied with my conclusion that the game is now fixed, and the good old mechanics have returned! Coupled with the new visuals, multiplayer support, mod support and Homeworld 1 and 2 content merge; I would say this is a rather spectacular title that is worth grabbing. The 2.0 patch really did it a good number, and even though I have my doubts about Gearbox; I am honestly surprised. If you like Space RTS games with 3-dimensional movement, formations, tactics and fleet battles; I highly recommend this game. Originally made by Relic; Homeworld was and still is a one of a kind RTS game to me.
Pros:
+Unit formations work.
+Content merge of HW1 and HW2 for interesting battles.
+Very nice visuals.
+Multiplayer support.
+Mod support.
+Modern OS support.
+Everything that made Homeworld great.
Cons:
-There is no way to save custom paint schemes, preview for ships allows no rotation for viewing models.
Overall: This game is worth it now, kudos to a company for listening to its critics and fixing something, rather than ignoring them altogether. There may be hope for gaming.

I know it will say that I have very little (if any) time in the game up above, but I poured hundreds of hours into this game during early early access (when you could only get this game from their website).
I'm an English guy. I deal with words and phrases and ideas. I have a hard time with math, and I have an even worse time dealing in 3-D concepts like "Put this here, then there, then connect this," blah blah blah. Engineering/math/computer science as careers are far beyond me.
If you're like me, don't let that keep you from playing this game. It is intuitive once you get the hang of it, and it'll seem intimidating at times at the sheer complexity once you get into end game stuff, but the feeling of finally getting a train running and off-loading into your smelters, which in turn feed into a main bus that will eventually get you enough solar panels to power the whole damn thing and keep those biters off your back for a few more expansions, is like crack.
There is very little story, and even less hand-holding. You can spend hours googling to find the best set-ups and the best mods and the best everything. Or you can just play, and figure it out as you go, and go to Google after your first successful factory to see how other people have done it. Either way, this game is that special type of complex that might look out of your depth, but is very much within your grasp.

I am part of a DevOps team at work and we have dedicated this as our group game. It is a good way to exercise your intuitive grasp of the theory of constraints.
It does such a good job of simulating automation and it's ever increasing levels of complexity that it could actually improve your efficiency at work.
I highly recommend this game for it's intellectual depth and hours of fun that it packs!
P.S. The quality of this game is way above the typical steam early access game.
