My Early Access Launch Day Impressions Video:
Okay, for the second time now, this is a game that has completely reversed my review from an original 'two thumbs down' review that I posted on it's early access to a positive 'two thumbs up' review just a couple of days later.
Why?
Well, I admitted in my original review that I loved almost everything about this game from the graphics, crafting and even the Kings castle how who controlled the kings throne could set their own tax rate and collect that percentage of taxes on all other players collected resouces.  My problem came with the core of this game on that first day, about my first two hours of game time where the combat experience was laggy and suffered from extremely slow framerates.
Since then and about 20 hours of game time later..  I'm sold that this game is not only a two thumbs up, but the most fun, best multiplayer survival sandbox game out now.  It's incredibly fun, period.  Yes it has bugs and glitches and things that make you scratch your head like deer that run from you and fly through the air against logic and physics.  It doesn't matter.  This game is so much fun that it's easy to overlook these little problems and glitches that make no sense.
Granted, I havent put all those hours in myself, as my son's best friend has been using my account to play with my son these past couple of days.  But both of them agree that this game is loads of fun after going on a five hour adventure in the game just this afternoon.
I will be posting videos on this game soon, because covering everything fun and great about what these developers have created with this would make an insanely long wall of text that few would read.  Let's just say though that if you are an existing fan of similar games like Rust, Seven Days To Die, and the Forest, then you will probably love this game.  I have over 500 hours into Rust, and this game so far offers deeper gameplay, better graphics, and more fun then Rust.
It's not perfect, but it IS a helluva lot of fun, and these developers (who completely missed with StarForge) have both surprised and impressed me with RoK.  My biggest fear and reason to tell people to hold back is my fear that cheaters and hackers might take over and ruin this great game.  But it also might be a good reason to tell people to jump in NOW before that happens and experience all the fun it offers while it lasts.  Maybe the developers will continue to impress me and actually support and make this game even better and be able to control the cheaters and hackers.  {crosses my fingers}
With over 40 hours of game time in already between my son and I, this game has already been worth it's purchase price, and I suspect there are hundreds of hours to come.  The medeival style crafting in this game is already about 10 times that of what Rust 2.0 offers now, and we've only crafted about 15% of everything possible with all the hours we've already played.  ..Awesome.
Any serious fans of Rust should not pass on this one right now.  For Rust fans particularly, this game is a definite and serious "MUST-BUY".  Wait, unless you are one of those weasel cheating, hack-using losers from Rust... then you should sat far, far away!  :-))

The STALKER series, and especially SoC are flawed gems. Buggy, glitchy, poorly optimized, SoC realistically *requires* you to play modded for a better experience. And yet, a gem.
What SoC does right, and why I think it's amazing, is atmosphere and immersion. SoC will make you feel like you're in someplace beautiful, and lonely, and strange. There are few other games that have made me feel compelled to seek shelter because of a thunderstorm.
This goes hand in hand with the other feature of SoC, which is that it hates you. It dares you to try and get it running smoothly. It has no use for a hand holding, danger free first mission. Your weapons throw spitballs, a wrong step will kill you, with mods the very air will turn into deadly blowouts. Maybe there's intent there, maybe its all misforture, but the zone wants you dead. In short, it's Fun, ala Dwarf Fortress.
SoC is flawed. But just try and not get sucked in.

ProTip: QuickSave OFTEN, there will be many times you step around a corner and get insta-killed (yes, even on Easy) by some prick with a shotgun that you didn't know was there. The game is frustrating at first because your pistol is very underpowered, it will often take many bullets to drop someone with it, especially from range, you may empty several clips trying to hit someone. ProTip: headshots ftw. It gets easier once you get better weapons, but the opening bit is quite difficult because of your limited arsenal. A few of my friends never got past the first hour (and they like hard games) because of the stupidity of how underpowered the starting pistol is, if that tells you anything.
I did actually complete the game, but the last two rooms were so frustrating because of the save game bug. When you quicksave and reload, enemies won't always be in the same place they were when you saved it - sometimes, they'll be right behind you, or in your face ready to blast you when you saved it with them in another room. Be aware of that, try to quicksave as far from enemies as possible, especially when you're indoors or underground.
Do recommend though, if you can get past the first hour or so, it's a pretty solid game, just a very difficult one.

There's a great game in here, but it's held back by horrible performance.
I'm a huge fan of Dishonored 1, completed it about 5 or so times. I was aware of the issues this game had initially, but with it being a year since then, and there being Overwhelmingly Positive recent reviews, I thought it'd been fixed at least decently. Sadly this is not the case.
In the prologue, the performance varies from okay to good, but once you get into the first expansive city things get really bad. I have 4790K + GTX 1080ti and I get drops to 34fps at only 1080p, with my gpu usage going to as low as 25%. That's just a horrendus waste of my GPU power. Even at Very Low settings it only raises that fps drop to 45-50fps.
For reference,  I can run The Witcher 3 at 144fps on Ultra settings pretty much constant in any area  with the lowest drop I've ever seen being 108fps. If I put that game to the lowest settings my fps will skyrocket to 250-300.
It's really a shame, becase the game is good, I love the custom difficulty and the gameplay feels like an improved Dishonored 1, and the levels feel much more expansive with many more routes to take.
If you can deal with the performance then I'd say give this a try, if not, don't even bother. It really sucks that the because game ran so well and this one is the polar opposite. They should have just used the Unreal Engine again, don't know why they tried to make an in-house new engine, it really turned out badly. Wish I could give the game a thumbs up but the performance 2 thumbs down.

Note: theHunter is a NICHE game. It's a wonderful niche game, don't get me wrong. But other than the gameplay itself, I have nothing but issues with it. Compare this game to the big name games out there... CoD, Bioshock, Farcry, Skyrim and so forth... ignore the genre. Production value and sales are what I'm comparing here. In all of these big name games have one thing in common. You buy the game, you can play it. All of it. You unlock gear and items as you play through. You don't have to buy additional junk just to complete missions/progress through the game. Occasionally you will have expansions or add-ons, more DLC that you can buy that will in most cases extend the gameplay, but in all cases will at least net you more content of some kind. So, I'll take CoD, one of the best known, most loved, and highest selling franchises in the gaming industry. I think I paid $60 when it first came out. That was it, for the whole game, all equipment, all levels and weapons attainable for that $60. Oh, I forgot to mention that you OWN the game at that point, you don't have to buy a membership to enjoy all of the games content.
Now, theHunter. Free to Play? No, it's not mistitled. It's deceptively titled. The F2P portion conains one rifle, one scope, a bleat call, a camera, a GPS and binoculars. Oh, That's fine and all, but you only get to hunt ONE animal (Mule deer) on ONE reserve. If anything, it's a free demo. If you expect to see the rich content in this game, forget it. This "demo" is nothing more than a snapshot. Ok,... so that's what you've gotten for free. Let's spend $60 on this game, like we would any other, and see where it gets us. $45 for one year basic, and another $15 for three more months. That's it. That's what you get. I would love to say that you get more, but you don't. You get 15 months, with no additional gear, no additional weapons. Oh, you DO get the option to hunt on all the reserves. You also gt the licences to hunt all of these animals. But you still CAN'T because you haven't bought the proper weapons, proper ammo, proper equipment.... So you have to shell out more money just to take advantage of the fact you just shelled out $60 for 15 months of play time. What's that? Did I just hear someone squeak the words World of Warcraft? Denied. WoW at least gave you access to all of it's content after you've paid your subscription. And no, I'm not going to complain about the subscription, as WoW is/was an MMO. Gotta maintain those servers. Yeah, I know theHunter has multiplayer. Big deal. Out of the 20 people who enjoy multiplayer, theHunter could loose all 20 of them and still be a perfectly great game as single player only.
You guys want to make more money? Add the cottontails and a crappy shot gun to the "Free to Play" version, and call it a free demo. Sell the game for $30, and monthly membership of $5. Make gear and weapons unlockable. Get rid of the microtransaction garbage. I would buy this game for $30. I would pay a $5 subscription, IF I had access to all of the games content after I made those purchases. That's at LEAST $35 you guys would have made from my first month. $5 and maybe even more a month after for my continues subscription. However, due to the way you guys have decided to sell this game, I've spent $15 for the subscription, had my fill becasue I refuse to spend more money on trivial, and temporary purchases, and that's it. You've made $15 from me, and you won't make any more.
I don't recommend this game. Sure, download it, shoot a few mule deer, and call it quits. For the price you'll be paying to make anything in this game available for use and the fact that these are only temporary purchases, (subscription/consumables)  this game isn't worth the disk space it occupies. Even with WoW, purchased when it was released, and played for the first year at about $180 is still cheaper than this. You want a good hunting game? Play CoD, or FarCry, or Bioshock. You get to hunt people and monsters, you get tons of weapons to choose from, you don't have to pay a monthly subscription, and your purchases are yours to keep!! DON'T SPEND A DIME ON THIS GAME.

Soon, however, this nasty group of creatures showed up.  Looking like a cross between shrimp, pill bugs, and armadillos these nasty things made short work of my wonderful constructions.  I was able to put the nasty bugs to rest finally, but soon more of their friends showed up to wreak more havok. Highly recommend.

Dwarfs is a small strategy game, where you control hordes of curious dwarfs who just can't resist digging after gold, often leading you to watch your dwarfs doom your entire village with enemies, lava or floods.
A game where dwarfs are so drunk, they voluntarily walk into lava, and no Deus Ex Machina can help!
As a standard, you need to reach a certain amount of gold to win. But there exist many more gamemodes in the paid version.
You get skirmish mode – which gives you sandbox, so you can create your own map. Rush mode where they just continuously breed like hamsters, but you can only let 200 die.
Dark mode – where every unexplored part of the map is dark, and you blindly send your dwarfs to explore.
Difficulty – so you can play from casual to crazy hardcore mode. Since it includes Hardcore & Tedi Hardcore mode.
Endless mode – So you can play until you’ve dug every nook & cranny.
summer carnival – where you throw axes at goblins
Base defend pack – Like a tower defence mode and yet so much different, like you dig the routes and defend with your dwarves.
It’s a fun game where every map is randomly generated – of course the game modes doesn’t change, but there’s still some good replay-value.
You get to unlock an axe for Killing Floor 1, which is good at killing Fleshpounds.
You transfer your achievements from the free version, so you don’t have to grind all over again.
More modes and higher difficulty than the free version. – It gets challenging.
You will hate your suicidal dwarves for literally trying to die in every way, possible.
All the times you start over because suddenly… Lava.
Be aware of the spider-queen, if you dislike spiders.
A few bugs can occur in getting the achievements, but I didn't see any bugs in the game. - Verify integrity of game files.
A small yet frustrating and yet strangely fun game.
Try out the free version and then decide from there. – No reason to buy it if there’s a chance of disliking it, however it’s worth saving in your library and return to occasionally for a map.

Alien: Isolation is clearly the best Alien-Game ever and also a great Surivival Game. It manages what very few Horror-Games manage to: It scares you without even showing you anything scary, just with sound and imagination what could show up behind the next corner.
You really can't fight the Alien for the most part of the Game, which is clearly the best part of it. When you get the Flame-Thrower it makes it definitely easier and less scary, because its your Security-Net if you get spotted.
Another great thing is the very detailed Alien-Atmosphere. You really feel like in the Movie, everything has this 70s/80s High-Tech look.
The visuals are stunning if you can handle the Aliasing. I playeyd it in 2880x1620, so they mostly eliminated the Aliasing and Shimmering. Overall the Game ran very well.
The only real flaw of this Game is: The Save-System! It feels like you crawl from Savestation to Savestation. I don't know if that was the best design-decision, it definitly makes it more thrilling but if you miss a SaveStation it can end in 30+minutes lost if you die. I had my problems with it, especially in the early stages until I figured out how the Alien works. But you get used to it and there are enough Stations, if find them all.

I first played a cracked version of this game, simply to try out, as i often do, an uncommon looking game, for the purpose of experiencing different the different things this medium can offer. At that moment i was not expecting Papers, Please to be one of the most absorbing and exciting games i've had the pleasure of playing, after my first play through of about 2 hours, i rushed to buy this game, as it simply wouldn't have been fair from my part not to.
The fact that the gameplay, which can basically be summed up as spot the differences, ends up being as engaging as it is, is truly a testament of the ability this game has draw you into the world and it's ambient. And for me personally I found this to be one of the most engaging experiences I've had with entertainment(including movies, books, etc), there were moments of moral decisions which call out to the best of mankind, at the cost of your 'score' in the game, which i find great since it makes us think more of what it is we are doing while playing a game, since it presents us with either the path to move the game forward and the cost of our morals, or stick to our beliefs despite the consequences, and i truly appreciate when a game makes us go that far.
I haven't been able to play all the games i've wanted to this year, however from the ones i've played, and from what i've seen and heard of the others, this is unapologetically my game of the year of 2013.
p.s. Apologies for any orthography errors, i did this kinda in a rush, since i'm at the end of the semester and i really should be studying :(.

Well after a rough start at launch, I have to say I can say that this game is at last enjoyable in my opinion. Even though most players would argue that some mechanics are at their worst than previous titles. Having played previous Total War titles for hundreds of hours, I can say that this game has the best AI and Diplomacy than previous titles. Even though they have some issues at times, it still does not hide the fact that older TW games have it worse. It's weakest part is the political system. This is what prevents you from triggering a civil war on your empire. This system does it's job to prevent you from a civil war or allowing it depending on your management of it, but it fails to deliver depth to the game by limiting the options you have on your Dilemmas and Intrigues as the game progresses, and being the game mechanic with the least explanations and tooltips leaving it for vague reasons of why that happened or how that happened. At first, I saw it as a better successor for the Family Tree present in previous titles, that it would bring better depth if that's why they removed it. But it fails to do this, leaving fans with the desire for a better in-depth political system or a Family Tree.
+ Gorgeous large campaign map. (Probably the largest before Attila)
+ Over 100 factions present in the campaign map (About 12 are playable without DLCs)
+ The new army traditions mechanic
+ Open ended Sandbox experience
+ Tooltip galore
+ Beautiful graphics and environments
+ Epic classical era battles and variations of battle maps
+ Attention to dynamic conversations between soldiers (i,e: A soldier panicking as an elephant unit approaches in)
+ AAA High Quality sound effects, Metal clashing, bodies falling, shield bashing, all heard individually as the battle rages on
+ Realistic motion captured animations for each individual soldier fighting to their death
+ Large amount of options to set your custom battles
+Campaign Coop up to 2 players
- Somewhat shallow Politics system
- AI doing odd things at times and odd decisions during campaign play
- Bland UI
- Lack of historical battles
- Not a rewarding multiplayer, no profile stats
- Obnoxious voice acting in few instances
- No city exchanging during Diplomacy unlike previous titles.
- Passive AI at certain circumstances
- Lack of proper Anti-Aliasing

After 5 hours I'm more than satisfied with Dark Souls 2. I never played DS1, but spent dozens of hours on Demon Soul. Compared to Demon Soul I find Dark Souls more forgiving and linear, as there are less open paths for player to find his/hers death.
As for PC conversion... well, it's Namco... Everything is presented with "Press A / X / Y for this and that", rather than showing binded key. This can be extremely frustrating at beginning. Also accepting configurations on menu is puzzle by itself, as every change in option is canceled if you press ESC to return to previous menu... who would have though you have to press BACKSPACE in order to accept changes!? So yes, do play with controller if possible, as WASD isn't encouraged, nor preferred way to play.
Still, game looks good. It's not Crysis, but has that simplistic and plain Demon Soul / Dark Soul atmosphere... and it plays solid 60 FPS on high-settings and with older hardware (GTX 670).
It's evil, It's rewarding... and it's fun! I wonder if this is going to get more play hours than my Far Cry 3 did (~100h).

At first, I had apprehensions about DS2.
I quickly ovecame these.
This game is incredibly well made, with some of the richest lore i have ever seen, and incredible combat. This series captures the essence of an RPG, focusing on how important leveling is. If you spend all points on strength, you won't live long enough to use your weapon. If you Don't put enough points into specialization trees, you will be much weaker, and it will be harder to catch up. I love that they implemented the respec system, due to the fact that sometimes I get tired of the same playstyle, and wish to change my character without grinding again.
At first i was concerned because DS1 had an occult following, and there was almost no margin for error.
With that said, From Software definitely came through.
One qualm I do have is the torch system. It was such a novel idea, but they spoiled it by making all areas (excluding one of course ;] )
Final rating: 8.75/10
Would buy again. Super high replayability.

At first, I was not pleased with this game. It was very buggy and frustrating, with numerous other issues like HUGE pathing problems, stupid ai and automation problems (Several harvesters waiting to get to a single asteroid to harvest when they're surrounded by unnoccupied other ones). However, the largest problems lay in the fact that "Homeworld 1 remastered" was essentially just homeworld 2 with homeworld 1 ships, because a lot of mechanics which gave the original tactical depth had to be removed so it could fit into homeworld 2's engine. This meant that the whole collection was a buggy, broken, imbalanced shadow of the originals.
This update (in my experience so far) fixed everything that was wrong. It has fixed formations, ballistics, tactics, pathing (mostly), targeting priorities, balance, and all general bugs (that i've experienced so far).
I can now safely say that:
Overall a great experience and a very solid recommendation after the update.

If you had asked me to review this Remastered version of Homeworld back when it released.  I wouldn't have rated it very positively.  The big problem I had with the game then was that the Homeworld 1 assets and campaign were superimposed on the mechanics and engine of the 2nd game.  Unfortunately Homeworld 2 changed the way fighters were built and controlled from the first game.  This creates a game-breaking problem in the Homeworld 1 campaign (which is worth playing on the original release).
The latest 2.0 update to Homeworld: Remastered has largely fixed those issues.  Fighter formations and behaviors for Homeworld 1 fighters have returned which is crucial to success in the campaign.  I have yet to try this in Multiplayer to see how this affects balance.  That being said, I'm very happy with the update Gearbox has made to this game with regards to the single player campaign and I look very much forward to completing it again in the remastered edition.

You play the role of a shipwrecked astronaut, freshly marooned on an alien planet.  All you have is your wits and knowledge of supply-chain management to keep you alive.  For people who love logistics, this game is for you.  Your job is to bend the planet to your will, and automate the heck out of each step in the process.
At first, all you can do is build small mining machines which gather resources for you.  Soon, you unlock the ability to build furnaces to process the resources.  You then manually transfer the materials from one machine to the other.  Before long, you gain the ability to construct conveyor belts to automate the process of moving the materials around.  This seems to be the heart of the game; figure out how to automate the process of whatever you’ve just done manually.  Make the machines do the work for you.
Eventually, you wind up with several conveyor belts, robotic arms, furnaces, mining platforms, all working towards generating the raw materials you need for more complex constructions.
It’s not all just fun and games with the factory building.  Eventually, the natives of the planet take notice of your resource consumption and come tell you to stop.  Unfortunately for you, they want to coerce you by killing you.  Unfortunately for them, you’re armed, and not going to take their demands lightly.  In other words, your assembly area will soon be littered with the bodies of your overly aggressive hosts.
In a game of escalating difficulty and complexity, you soon learn how to build better defenses to combat the increasing number of enemies trying to convince you to cease operations.  Machine guns, automated gun turrets, and pistols are available for your protection, and you’ll need them to fend off the never-ending waves of native creatures.
Eventually, I built up quite a production facility.  I had several different types of resources being mined, processed, and stored automatically.  I then was given the goal of building radar dishes to locate the wreckage of my mothership.  These radar dishes consume quite a bit of electricity, so production had to scale with demand.  Several electricity generating boilers were constructed to feed the power hungry devices.
While playing the game, the comparison came to me that this game was a little like building Redstone contraptions in Minecraft.  If you’ve ever built anything interesting with Redstone, this game might be up your alley.
I’ve seen some videos on the Steam store that show just how complex these mega-factories can become.  Trains convey materials long-distance, conveyor belts going every direction to process materials; it’s like giant Rube Goldberg machines.  My meager facility didn’t come close to the potential complexity of this game.
What I liked:  The premise is fresh and unique.  The interface took a few minutes to get used to, but eventually I found it was quite good for manipulating your factories.  The graphics are detailed and well done.
What I didn’t like:  Having to stop playing and come write this review. :)  I really can’t think of anything I didn’t like.  Wait, I think I found a typo in a description, if that counts.
This one is well worth a look if you like building games.  It’s certainly worth watching the videos out there just to see the game in action.  Pictures just don’t do it justice.
Thanks for reading.

Consider this a recommendation for the entire STALKER series so far (latest as of this being Call of Pripyat). The STALKER games are FPS/Survival Horror/RPG hybrids where the emphasis is on the FPS gunplay and the survival elements.
You can get thirsty or hungry or need sleep and have to manage those needs alongside that of the deteriorating conditions of your weapons and armors. Ammunition, food, and drink needed to survive are scarce, but can be traded for with almost anyone if you have the right amount of goods or money to sacrifice for it. The game has large maps you can travel between like a sandbox game, and the gunplay is some of the tightest I've seen with really good gun physics. The games also have a wildlife simulation system similar to the one in place in FarCry 3 in a way; animals and mutants will run around and do their own thing after they spawn and kill each other (and maybe you) for survival or food.
Despite the large amount of freedom these games afford you to carve your own path, they feel very focused and are best approached with a strategic mindset.

Dwarfs!? Yes you heard correctly. Anyways, the game is a strategic tower defense game where you direct and control dwarves to collect minerals and explore caves.
Gameplay:
The main goal of the game is to defend your outpost, which is the center of the diggers, and explore as much as possible. Diggers will slowly come out and start digging in random areas. You can let them go loose, or direct them on where to dig. Each time they dig, you earn gold. Gold can be used to make more outposts, hire more warriors, or convert an outpost to have more digger dwarves come out. Warriors and Diggers can be directed to go a certain direction. However, the arrows will stay, which can direct wandering Diggers and Warriors to the same path.
Each map has three main things to pay attention to: minerals, caves, and of course your outpost. Minerals are what rake the money in. Caves could contain treasure, but can also be full of danger, which is lava, water, minions, and even boss battles. It is important to defend your outpost from these obstacles, otherwise, it's game over.
There are a couple of gamemodes: skirmish, base defense, campaign, and the basic arcade mode. There's a bit of variety in this game, but with a common goal.
Controls:
Controls are a slight hit-and-miss. The reason being is sometimes the clicks do not register when trying to set up dynamite and outposts. Another problem is that sometimes dwarves will ignore your commands on where to go. Just be sure to pay attention and make sure things are going through.
Music:
If you're used to medieval tones, then this is the type of music it has. It's a bit upbeat and relaxing...well...contrast to the higher difficulties you end up playing.
Graphics:
The graphics compare to a typical flash game that caters to a cartoony look. The game is overhead, but the art is still detailed with medieval tones.
Story:
Not much of a story, lad. But I think yer gonna enjoy the witty dwarf who guides ye through the nooks n crannies. What every dwarf loves is killin monsters, ale, and of course gold...the thing that ties the whole thing togetha. Keep everythin in order, kid, and ye'll have the thickest beard known to every dwarf!
Overall:
Dwarfs!? is a casual or challenging(depends on how you want it to look or play) tower defense game that could mean hours of fun to earn your medals and get the highest possible score. While the controls are a bit off, the gameplay is still fun and simple. Collect money and explore with many different gamemodes. With a classic medieval tone and dwarves that stay true to their heritage, this game can be enjoyed by people of all ages.
Pros:
-Relaxing Music
-Simple game, but with many possible obstacles.
-Variety of difficulties.
-Variety of gamemodes.
Cons:
-Controls are a bit stiff sometimes.

Toy soldiers is an enjoyable merger of tower defense strategy and arcade action. Not a deep game, but good light entertainment. As a kid, I loved to play with plastic toy soldiers and this game may be thought of as seeing those childhood games come to life, including the embellishments of a child's imagination. In contrast to some other reviewers, I found the Cold War missions to be generally bug free and stable. There is the very occasional crash to desktop, but otherwise Toy Soldiers functions well. For those of you who have played the original Toy Soldiers, the Great War missions in this version are similar, but not exactly the same. The ability to earn barrages (one-shot area effect attacks) is a nice addition, but I think that the balance is off on some of the missions compared to the original. One difficulty that affects both the Great War and Cold War parts of the game is that control of fixed-aircraft almost requires a gamepad or joystick. The original Toy Soldiers worked just fine with keyboard and mouse, but this version does not use keyboard input, making planes almost unplayable with a mouse only. I found it possible to complete the missions without using the jets or biplanes. Helicopters work just fine.

Toy Soldiers does what it wants to do: It wants to provide nice quirky fun, from anywhere to experienced players, to casual players.
PROS:
art style
It is fun
steam achievements and trading cards
a lot of options
Invasion mode
CONS:
-The final level in the campaign is a major jump in difficulty. It has to be 90% impossible. I think you have to set everything up just right.
-A few levels make you have to position everything 'just right'.
If you want to have a cheap game that'll provide hours of fun - get it. If you like strategy games, what are you waiting for!?

Well after a rough start at launch, I have to say I can say that this game is at last enjoyable in my opinion. Even though most players would argue that some mechanics are at their worst than previous titles. Having played previous Total War titles for hundreds of hours, I can say that this game has the best AI and Diplomacy than previous titles. Even though they have some issues at times, it still does not hide the fact that older TW games have it worse. It's weakest part is the political system. This is what prevents you from triggering a civil war on your empire. This system does it's job to prevent you from a civil war or allowing it depending on your management of it, but it fails to deliver depth to the game by limiting the options you have on your Dilemmas and Intrigues as the game progresses, and being the game mechanic with the least explanations and tooltips leaving it for vague reasons of why that happened or how that happened. At first, I saw it as a better successor for the Family Tree present in previous titles, that it would bring better depth if that's why they removed it. A visual novel like game with multiple choices of answers for every response of your character. Heavily inspired by the old days with AOL Instant Messanger, you follow the story of 'Yourself' and a girl named Emily. You go through 5 chapters that span 5 years (each real conversation is a chapter/year) and the tale of 2 friends from high school growing up. Now as the game progresses you can view certain people's profiles throughout the chapters to expand the world of friends that you live in.
Without spoiling anything as that's for the bottom because someone knows I need to release my feelings for this great title, it's definitely worth playing/reading through one time with straight up honest decisions. If you want to have some emotional or heart break type of moments or in general are an experimental type, I'd definitely re-read with a different mindset at all times.
--Finally, half-spoilerish (not really), I truly haven't made a grammar mistake in the review, even though it may seem as such--
**************SPOILERS AHEAD, STAY AWAY UNTIL YOU'VE PLAYED THE GAME ONCE*************
Such an interesting tale of 2 friends growing apart, and while in the review I may have sounded like I had alot on my mind, I really don't. I'd only like to close out this review or my thoughts on this title with a very depressing or 'philisophical' sort of observation. After a week of playing the game here is my review of the experiences I've had so far. I'm a completely new player, but I have experience with Elder Scrolls games.
If you love the Elder Scrolls universe, this game is must buy for you. As many have said before, this is not Skyrim with friends and don't expect it to be. This is an Elder Scrolls game set in the same universe as Skyrim/Oblivion/Morrowind etc. is. There is something here for casual and hardcore players alike, but I feel that the end game meta doesn't really allow the freedom of choice in terms of builds.
PVE is mediocre but it is very accessible. There is a huge amount of quests, and you can visit 2/3 of Tamriel, which is awesome if you love the lore of the previous games. Although I really suck at it, PVP is a blast! The veteran players will crush you of course, but you'll be still having fun. just make sure to always group up while you're in the PVP zone (Cyrodiil).
You'll be playing on one mega server, so you don't have to worry about server population, you only have to decide between North America or the Europe server and you're ready to go. Most of the people you come across are friendly/helpful, haven't run into any toxic people yet. Guilds are also plenty and welcoming for new players.
The game has an extensive crafting system, which I absolutely love. Just give a try, you won't be disappointed!
Sadly, unlike its predecessors, this game is not really for the roleplaying audience. The available classes are bit lackluster, and there are only four of them. Also, pretty much all four does the same just in a different way. But this is my own opinion, you might actually like it.
Currently, my biggest issue with the game is inventory space. My god, it is horrible. If you enjoy crafting like I am, then you're in for some really-really-really annoying times. Even if you're just starting out, your inventory will fill up in a matter of hours. There are so many crafting items, that there is simply no way to start a decent stock of everything you might need later because you'll constantly run out of inventory space. There are options to buy more inventory space, but these too will become filled very quickly, and prices will skyrocket after a few upgrades. It is such a chore that it is constantly taking the player out of the immersion and it's just annoying. Now there is a fairly convenient remedy to this: the crafting bag. Naturally, it is only available if you're a subscriber (note: you just bought an almost full priced game) and in my opinion, paying EUR 13 monthly so I don't have to constantly fiddle around in my inventory just feels too free-to-play (and not the good kind) to me.
Now to the pros and cons:

If you love The Elder Scrolls, and enjoy MMO's then this game is right up your alley.
*Edit - Be wary if you decide to purchase the Gold Edition. You can play any race EXCEPT the Imperial. Which is weird because the Gold Edition comes with Imperial DLC... In order to create an Imperial charecter you have to fork out another 2100 crowns to upgrade. Shady business...

Disclaimer: I was in the beta back in 2014
I bought Elder Scrolls Online during the recent free play weekend after having waited over two years for the price to drop enough during a sale. This strategy was due to the impression I got during the beta, at the end of which I was unsure how the game would do.  I wasn't willing to pay much for it because I didn't have high hopes, but I did want to own it eventually as an avid Elder Scrolls fan.
My, how things have changed. With the still fairly-recent One Tamriel update the amount of accessible content for a single character increased significantly, along with the ability to interact with a wider range of players (based on the three factions). I really like the idea of the Champion system, although I'm obviously not level 50 yet.
As for what I can comment on directly, the game is very well populated with interesting quests and material gathering sources. The combat system feels quite fluid, but I may be biased since I'm having way too much fun playing an agile dual-wielding Khajiit. There are skill lines for pretty much everything, making skill choices tough (in a good way) but allowing plenty of customization. The crafting system's use of traits, deconstruction, and research isn't entirely non-standard, but is flexible enough to make crafting rather fun. Being able to craft enchantments of varying potency and effect is a nice touch. Crafting "buff food" is also included as "provisioning". The world feels quite large, with many places to travel, even though only about half of Tamriel is accessible. Rare treasure maps can also be found that show a sketch of a location where treasure is hidden, encouraging exploration of new areas.
So far, the main story has been quite interesting. I'm not very far, so I can't comment too much, but it certainly has an Elder Scrolls feel. Outside of the main story, each area has its own set of quests that tell the story of events happening in the area, and often place tough decisions in your hands. This makes many quests feel much heavier than the usual dull "get A of B", "kill X of Y", etc. This tendency, along with the pure density of "things to do" in any given area, creates an impressive sense of immersion. The beatiful visuals also contribute nicely.
For the collectors among us (of which I am one), Elder Scrolls Online provides no shortage of collectibles in the form of special hats, costumes, skins, personalities (animation sets, basically), polymorphs (character appearances), pets of various usefulness and cuteness, and a wide variety of mounts (horses, lion, bear, camel, wolf, etc). There are also a plethora of built-in achievements covering practically every subject, many of which give rewards such as dyes.
For those who appreciate customization, armor pieces have three dye slots that are mapped to different parts of the item, allowing trims and highlights to be set. I personally find this allows a fantastic level of visual customization that goes beyond most MMORPGs I've played, although I certainly don't claim it's unique. As for characters themselves, there is an appreciable selection of faces, hair styles, facial markings, and plenty of sliders. And if, for some reason, you feel like being a skeleton or a Draugr for a while, you can do that too (if you acquire the Polymorphs).
I may have only logged 50 hours so far, but I've already subbed because Zenimax (and Bethesda) have taken Elder Scrolls Online a long ways since the beta. It's certainly worth checking out, especially if you're an Elder Scrolls fan. Especially at ~$15 (for now) with no subscription. I can't think of a better deal on an MMORPG with this level of content.

Consider this a recommendation for the entire STALKER series so far (latest as of this being Call of Pripyat). The STALKER games are FPS/Survival Horror/RPG hybrids where the emphasis is on the FPS gunplay and the survival elements.
You can get thirsty or hungry or need sleep and have to manage those needs alongside that of the deteriorating conditions of your weapons and armors. Ammunition, food, and drink needed to survive are scarce, but can be traded for with almost anyone if you have the right amount of goods or money to sacrifice for it. The game has large maps you can travel between like a sandbox game, and the gunplay is some of the tightest I've seen with really good gun physics. The games also have a wildlife simulation system similar to the one in place in FarCry 3 in a way; animals and mutants will run around and do their own thing after they spawn and kill each other (and maybe you) for survival or food.
Despite the large amount of freedom these games afford you to carve your own path, they feel very focused and are best approached with a strategic mindset.

Hi Guys, I aboslute Love this game to bits, I have since on the old consoles, but i have ran into a prob that  I seem to not be able to fix, There are missing textures on all ships, no matter how much i delete and re-download the game, textures still missing, But apart from that, the game is just awesome.

I cannot in good conscience recommend this "remaster" of Homeworld 1 & 2. The new graphics are fantastic (when they aren't glitching out) but the game takes a step backwards in almost every other regard.
Fuel consumption is gone, which while convenient, almost entirely negates the necessity of support frigates and carriers. Fighter screens now break formation at the first sign of enemy contact, and tactical stances are seemingly nonexistent.
Some aesthetic flourishes from the original have been removed, things only a vet would notice. Research stations no longer rotate idly. The game automatically collects all resources between missions, which bugs the heck out of me. One of my favorite atmospheric touches in the original was the time spent quietly and patiently gathering minerals after a fight. The sluggishness of this process gave you time to reflect on the story, made you admire the beautiful outer space vistas and felt like something a real life space commander would have to endure. It was cool. Now the game just slurps everything up after it's too late to make any use of it.
The song "Homeworld" by Yes has also been removed from the credits, due to legal reasons. Give me a break.
What bothers me the most, however, is the complete removal of title cards for in-game speech. A nifty rectangular box with a character portrait used to pop up whenever someone talked to you. Now it's just a boring line of floating text.
Some of the in-game triggers no longer function. In the last mission, Captain Elson never showed up with his relief fleet and I was left to attack the enemy flagship on my own.
And before I forget: Every other time I played the game I'd be greeted with flickering textures or see-through ships. No matter how many graphical options I switched on or off, raised or lowered, nothing could be done. It was distracting. Unacceptable for a release priding itself on its updated graphics.
Lastly, the game just feels dumbed-down and generally easier.
Basically, Gearbox just "upgraded" every design aspect of Homeworld 1 to that of Homeworld 2, a game which, despite the graphical overhall, inspired ship designs and stellar soundtrack, always failed to capture my imagination. The lack of manual Hyperspace is ultimately what killed it for me.
Perhaps the most grievous sin in this "remaster" is the absense of the best game in the Homeworld series: Cataclysm. Yes, I understand they've "lost" the source code. How hard would it be to rip a copy off the disc and include it in the download? If you haven't played Cataclysm, you are missing out. It is one of the best real-time strategy games ever made, and probably the only title in the genre to fall under the unique label, "horror-RTS".
If you have never played a Homeworld game then this is a must buy, as classic versions of both 1 & 2 are included. If you were already a fan, like me, skip it or wait for a proper patch.

This collection is amazing. First about the collection itself, the collection has a whole bunch of content that at the time of writing I haven't even got to yet. Not only do they have the original homeworld 1 and 2, but also the re-mastered version which clearly had a lot of love put into them.
Now, I know some people will call this blasphemous, but I haven't played the original versions, and I'll give a review for each game in the collection. There may be changes in the originals and remasters like the UI and apparently some unit balancing issues? Again, the changes seem small and don't seem to impact the gameplay for the casual or moderate homeworld fan.
Anyway, onto the review, I'll go in order of Homeworld and Homeworld 2 had to be cut short due to me running out of characters. [grumble grumble]
Homeworld was an amazing experience to go through, and gave me a feeling a game hasn't given me in awhile. This is a sense of mystery and the feeling of being a small speck in the midst of outer space. An insignificant spec, just managing to survive. But as you go along, the largest foe opposing you who seem like an unstoppable force that will wipe you out in the blink of an eye. But you just bite at the small, weak appendages of this large creature until you (hopefully) become large enough to stand a chance.
But as the game goes along, and you realise you're hatred of this foe is not alone, you end up becoming stronger, as you gain more and more victories, and you become something greater than what you started, you don't feel weak against your foe, you end up feeling like you can just make it.
Now, for the gameplay of the game, the gameplay is very strategic, much more strategic than what I was expecting. You can't just throw your mighty battleships at the enemy and expect to win, because since you may of destroyed their first offensive, you're heavily crippled, and it just so happens that there are, admittedly smaller, but far scarier foes awaiting just outside the range of your sensors, and they are hungry. I find myself later in the game attempting to break off their fleet in chasing something small, but leading them where my ships lay, and I have the advantage by planning the whole thing in advance. Your experience might be different but I had a blast.
Now for some memorable moments from my playthrough of the game, some spoilers.
The first moment I can think of is the first attack on the foe (completely forgot their name, some federation). When we warp in, my battle relay guy(?) notifies me that the hostile fleet is right ahead. Here, I'm a bit scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because I saw what they can do, and even though its weakened, they still have a substantial fleet. He gave the order to exterminate the fleet. At this moment of time, I still see that fleat as an unstoppable force, and they had battlecruisers and I didn't. Did I mention I was scared? Anyway, I mass produced these vehicle extraction units (forgot the name) which basically steals ships in hopes of capturing one of the ships. However, it turned out that I overestimated the foe (which is what I always do, it's better to overestimate and crush your foe with overwhelming force them to not be prepared for a superior force) and I ended up destroying most of their ships, except for one. I then got this evil grin on my face as this carrier was trying to escape from me, I ordered my ships to shoot out the engines, and I sent in the extractors. I ended up stealing their carrier as a trophy, a claim of "I annihilated your force and now I'm using your ship against you" sort of fashion. That ship eventually became invaluable to the fleet, acting as a medical station for the smaller ships and as a transport bay for them as well. Protection from attack.
The second moment I'll share is this moment when you enter a nebula and there is deadly radiation flooding the area. You had to plan your moves carefully to not have your ship's be dissolved in the radiation (a bit unrealistic but it's a videogame so I'll let it slide) I'm moving through this cloud and I spot a minelayer. This is the first one I encountered one, I quickly destroy it and think to myself, "Job well done, no mines! Onwards to glory!" but a little bit later, I found the mine field it set up, it crippled some of my most powerful ships, and when I'm getting my repair frigates ready, I spot 2 destroyers peek out from the nebula. At this point in time, I had about 3 destroyers, the carrier (the one I stole earlier) and a fleet of frigates. "Piece of cake" I thought to myself. Bad mistake, because with them, they had missile frigates that were staying JUST out of sight, but firing on my ships nonetheless. And whatever the hell that destroyer was made from, my whole fleet of 25 ish ships was completely and utterly obliterated by 5 ships and a few mines. Then I started planning out my path for the target, and I had an escort, and everything, finding small bands of these ships and crushing them under suprise.
The third, and final moment I can share is the junkyard. During this level, you enter a creepy junkyard, with a bunch of gun platforms dotting the place, protecting...something...still don't know what it was. No biggy I thought, but something didn't feel right, so I sent my capital ships in with caution, and to obliterate the gun platform obviously. But after I sent them out, I started doing some micromanaging at base, when I heard "one of your ships have gone missing". "What do you mean, 'one of your ships have gone missing'? How the hell can you lose a capital ship?" I'm thinking to myself. then I look over, and I see the missing ship warp back into view, but it was hostile. I had no idea what was going on until I saw this one small-ish ship coming in, only known as the Junkyard Dog, and it was barreling straight for one of the capital ships. The it just snatches it and warped out at a becon. I was stunned, but also very♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥so I restarted the level. After about 3 ish restarts, I got very♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at this dog and after my attempts of sending small ships through the junkyard failed miserably, I got♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and made ships that could freeze it. I had like 5 of them, so the dog couldn't escape. I had my whole fleet waiting nervously for any signs of the dog. And when my guard was low, it came within 1 km from one of my ships! I know, 1 kilometer seems far, but remember, these ships are several kilometers in length so that was WAY too close for comfort. I froze it and with all the might of my fleet, and about 10 minutes of continuous fire from all ships, I finally killed the dog. I was never so happy to kill a dog until now.

STALKER's mostly built on the side quests that lead to exploring the large areas. Since the narrative is so weak, I'd go so far as to say that the game didn't need a plot. There's plenty of enjoyment in taking on an endless (literally) supply of missions for people, hoarding cash, and replacing your broken armor and weapons while hunting down artifacts to strengthen your character. You can actually ignore the main game past a point and just do side quests. In fact, you'd be ignoring a lot of the sights and areas of the overworld if you just did the main game.
If you've played Borderlands, you've already experienced something similar to this. An open-world game where you take on quests from various different people and groups while looting corpses and finding stashes that force you to inventory manage since you have limited bp space. There's negatives and positives to the comparison: Borderlands has a better narrative, outright looks superior (graphically), lacks the glitches and other misc issues STALKER has, and generally feels more like a finished product with no ideas left behind due to time constraints. Yet Stalker has a greater complexity to both the weapons and character management, and a more interesting world and storyline.
A few remaining notes: this game doesn't need mods to be playable; STALKER complete makes the game easier and is better for a 2nd playthrough; don't pick up every weapon as you will be weighed down.

When I first came across this game way before it was on Steam, I was actually looking for a hunting game to buy.  I read around the net, and lots of people recommended this one, so I downloaded it, and began playing the free version.  As most people are complaining about the free version is basically a demo, but to say you "can't" unlock things without paying money is a lie.  You can earn em$ in various ways.  You can also purchase a lot of things by simply doing the equivilent of quests in the game, and earning gm$.  If you look through the reviews you'll see that most people writing bad reviews and giving a thumbs down have played the game less than a couple of hours.  I'm assuming thats why I have yet to see a review that mentions those things.
Getting past all the complaining about "free to play" whiners, every game that is free to play is still trying to make money, and this one is no exception.  I would highly recommend the "Trailrunner Starter Bundle" which is the $50 starter membership.  This gives you access to hunt all reserves, all animals, and gives you several guns+items+ammo, and allows you to host multiplayer games.  You will find that with this bundle you will actually have all the weapons to hunt all game as well.  This is a one year membership that renews for $35 a year after the initial purchase.
After I bought my membership, a couple months later I went ahead and bought $20 worth of in game currency, em$.  I now have every item I really want, and love this game to death.
I'm not complaining about the price, because you can't buy a better hunting game than this, there isn't one on the market anywhere.  Not one person in these reviews has said "someothergame" is better.  If one ever comes out, guess what?  It's going to cost $50-$60.
As for gameplay, this is the best simulator I've ever played, and I've hunted IRL for over 20 years.  You can stalk or still hunt, you can call, you can bait, you can do all the things in this game just like a real hunt, and the AI isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  I personally love predator hunting, and this game doesn't disappoint.

Love this game already. As you can see from my playtime, I'm playing this exclusively since it came out. This is my 4th edit, editting it each day of alpha. TL;DR - Yes the game is very much worth your time, and at 20 dollars it's a steal. I would recommend it up to 40 dollars tbh.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
MOST IMPORTANT IMO - SANDBOX FACTOR: Obscenely high! Everyone wants to make a sandbox game these days, and almost all of them fall short of the most important thing: something to DO that feels meaningful. With these other titles, you start the game, you make your fortress/grind out top end crafting, and you're done. The game is over. If PVP is a thing you defend it, but it's live or die and respawn.
In this game, you have a king who constantly taxes you. That guy is the worst. All of your activities as a little islander peasant are constantly accompanied by a sense of something more: either you're working towards gearing up to take on the king, or you're working towards making your little shack in the woods to gank people at, or you're building an impenetrable fortress to house your max level crafting tables and hoard of materials.
There's no other way to put it: with the perma death, loot loss, always-existing (when you log out you're just laying there in the game, asleep and vulnerable)  and the options for imprisoning and such, the game feels meaningful, and not like another empty sandbox.
As far as gankfest goes: On a server with a large popualtion of new players, the "spawning beach" rapidly devolves into a Rust-style "beat people with sticks senselessly" idiot-fest. However, on servers with stable populations, people ratehr quickly evovle past that. Ocne you get some armor on, I woul say 1 out of every 5 or so people you encoutner will kill on sight. Most are just trying to build their little home and don't wanna fight to the death over some berries.
Which brings us to the real glory of this game. The sandbox is so real. remember how ArcheAge offered us player housing? Remember Star Wars Galaxies, where you built wherever and made it home? This game has what you want. Build a structure and hang a crest on the wall, and no one can build within a certain radius unless they breach your walls (which requires siege equipment at higehr tiers, and a double thick wood wall would take 45 minutes to break a one-tile hole through) and take out the crest. No one can minecraft-style build a little bridge and hop your wall if you have a creat up and you build intelligently. You can absolutely have your own fort... and once the server grows, everyone is eyeballing their neighbor and thinknig about what some siege equipment would be like...
COMBAT: Intuitive but currently not that deep. I think it needs a man-at-arms dodge a la Chivalry and that alone will add 90% of the needed depth. I say this because the combat currently boils down to attack and block, since there's no quick-step and overhead/jab do not alter the damage you deal. Very promising, but not quite there yet. Ranged is where it's at, mostly because the melle is definitely not at a Chivalry level of depth, but since they're aiming to model after Chivalry, I have high hopes here.
CRAFTING: Incredible. Upgrade workbenches to unlock better/more complex items to craft. Resources are scattered and scarce enough that it's not as easy as making a little fort and investing time to unlock everything. You're going to have to wander out and find where each thing spawns, gather and come back, it's that simple. Adds to the meaningful sandbox feel.
SURVIVAL: Food and water are a thing, but this isn't Project Zomboid levels of survivalism. The primary risk is players/wild animals, which is how I feel it should be. The hunger/thirst are tuned in such a way that you can spend 80+% of your game time doing things other than gathering food/water, which I feel is a great balance.
PRICE POINT: It's 20 bucks man. That's dirt cheap, and considering that the game feels like a full game already, 5 hours into launch, I think it's an extremely solid investment. Updating now on day 3, and I would gladly have paid 40 dollars for this game as-is now. I'll be very surprised if the price doesn't go up as the game develops, as I can see this being a big hit.
---Updated for Day 3 of Alpha release--
No wipes, and there have been patches. Devs are actively working on this title. According to McDuderstein in the comments, the devs are posting on the RoK Facebook page when they are taking servers down for testing, which is great.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Bugs I've Heard of:
I've heard that sometiems doors will be closed client side, but register as still being open server side. I've never experiecned it, but I recommend building multiple doors at your entrance just in case.
Bugs I've experienced:
Sometimes you'll try to itneract with a workbench, or attack, and nothing will happen. Logging otu and back in usually resolves, if not close the client and re-open.
Sometimes you'll attack an enemy and not see any damage markers, they won't die, etc. You're probably de-synced; again, close the client and re-launch and it should resolve. It's a good idea to whack an animal every so often to check for this: I had a 30 minute excursion of gathering earlier, attacked a werewolf on the way back, didn't do damage and realized I was bugged. when I re-logged, I was back at the base, and my whole excursion had taken place in de-sync land, meaning it never happened. Not too brutal, but a bit of a waste of time.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Those are the only bugs I've experienced! Again, I think at 20 dollars the game is a steal, and I would feel perfectly fine if I'd paid 30. Highly recommend the game, and the only things I see needing improvement are combat depths, server stability, and lag (you get serverwide lag spikes every so often when the server is close to full). Server stabiltiy seems to be their primary focus right now, which is quite alright with me!

I pre-ordered the game through Amazon and did not play it for some time after it shipped to delay gratification as motivation during college. Ultimately the code had already been used by the time I got the game so I didn't end up playing it for some time later until Rome II was on sale here. As such I never experienced any of the alleged balance or performance issues experienced immediately following release.
Rome II is a massive improvement over the other TW titles I've played (the most recent being Empire). The living campaign map, which features factions for each independent tribe rather than a catch-all rebel faction, was a huge draw for me. The game has also been rebalanced to require more thoughtful diplomacy and campaigning. Hard caps on armies and agents mean that the computer can no longer "cheat" 20 stacks into existence or simply overpower you with its tolerance for tedious management activities. Open field battles are now actually meaningful, and no longer just an inconvenient delay on your way to capturing the settlement. Economic management requires meaningful choices as the player cannot simply build everything - food and resource dynamics are great, but trade is less fleshed out than in Empire. The map is huge, beautiful, and diverse.
Perhaps I am not the most critical gamer but I immensely enjoyed Rome II and hope others come to see that many design choices derided as "streamlining" or the bro-ing of Total War add a great deal of depth to the series. In my view, these changes have eliminated bad, tedious complexity and replaced it with interesting, fun complexity.

Been playing this game recently after a hiatus because of other commitments and finally got around to writing a real review rather than a useless 1 line quip.  As much as I flat out love this game/series it does have some bad/good qualities to it.
The Bad:  The level design doesn't feel as unique or as meshed as well as Dark Souls 1 did.  The areas feel more seperated, which works only by the fact that you can teleport between bonfires from the start.  Online interaction with others can vary widely, but a lot of frustrating lag will have you get killed by invaders before you know what's happening.  A couple of the areas are really bland and don't really add the experience.  Some of the bosses really phone it in and don't feel very "Dark Soul"ish.  LOOKING AT YOU DRAGONRIDER!
The Good: The graphics are more polished and the frame rate is really nice.  There's never any stuttering from areas (oh god Blighttown why), and little to no visual lag.  There's a ton of various armors and weapons to use, each with their own pros and cons, so it really feels you like you can do whatever you want with your character.  Network this time is not stupid crappy GFWL and has dedicated servers.  Makes co-op and invasions a lot more stable and fun.  Some of the bosses are really unique and challenging with interesting mechanics.
Overall this is a great game.  Please keep in mind I haven't done the DLC content yet, but I hear it's mostly better than the main game. This is one of my favorite game series out there. After finding the origional Toy solider back on the Xbox marketplace, I was immediately taken in by the perfect balance between tower defense, RTS, and a bit of some 3rd person shooting elements. The WWI theme was well executed and the "fiction" aspects, such as the rare tanks and bosses, only further developed the theme.
The series continues by extending into the Cold War. Just like before, the mixture of gameplay styles blend well together and the theme is noticeable. However, despite the "raw fun" gameplay; there are some issues. The user interface isn't as intuitive as before; as switching/selecting units can be difficult at times, due to some wonky hit boxes and camera angles. There are also their far share of bugs, ranging from hilarious to game breaking. On one hand, the game froze but was quick to recover to a good auto-save system; on the other hand, two bosses fell threw the stage and were killed near immediately. This left me more disappointed than anything else, as I really do enjoy the creative boss fights.
Overall, the polish isn't there but it is clear that the dev team made an effort to create a fun/unique experience that builds of the previous game.

I was so excited for this game.  I loved Just Cause 2 and knew for sure its sequel was going to be a hit.
I was very wrong.
The pros:
Updated physics and graphics, better grapple/parachute mechanics, the wingsuit, awesome explosions and destruction.  An overall beautiful game that has so much potential.
The cons:
-Performance is very poor especially for those on PC (unless you have certain Nvidia cards I believe).  The game was created as a console game and was not ported over very well.
-Memory Leaks.
-Gameplay is constantly interrupted when there's a disconnect with the server.
-Devs don't appear to actively support or fix these issues.
-No minimap
-Car and motorcycle handling is absolutely atrocious.  They seem to have been made for just console controllers and wheels, then directly ported to PC.  The lag is huge between pressing a button to turn on the keyboard and the vehicle actually turning, to the point that you'll fall off cliffs, hit buildings, and spin out of control because there's no sensible way to make the vehicles do what you want.  It's not just a learning curve, or something to get used to - it's a design flaw, because the only way to control a vehicle is to possess Jedi abilities to see what's coming before it happens.  Only then will you have time to press the key and keep it pressed long enough for the car to respond in time.  I can't even get in vehicles in JC3.  I'm belaboring this point because vehicle chases and combat were such a huge part of JC2, and they're completely ruined by these shoddy mechanics that the devs still stand by.  They should, at the very least, give the option to revert to JC2 mechanics.
The list goes on.  It hurts me to say, but don't buy it.

"What the ♥♥♥♥ are you playing?" is what you will hear from behind you, and, quite seriously but with a wry smile on your face, you will say, "A game where I'm a border control agent in a fake ex-Soviet dictatorship that's just reopened it's borders to its neighbors." This game is amazing. You are just a border guard stamping papers to either allow or deny people trying to enter Arstotzka (so basically it's a country under the soviet control in the cold war era). I'm not sure where I begin to explain why this game is awesome, wait, actually I do. The music. It is amazing. There is one theme to this game, and it's so bloody effective and perfectly captures the mood of the game; it is bleak, desolate, depressing and oppressive and I love it. The gameplay is deceptively simple and engaging, and considering how mundane the task of what you are doing it is hard to pull away. The game can be quite harsh to the player while asking you to make you to make decisions and the effects are not always clear right away. This game is the perfect marriage of theme and mechanics and is a masterpiece.

Do you let in the human trafficker or a child molester. Will you let people get killed by turning them back to their hostile homeland. Do you help an underground organization doing their missions. Definately recommended.

I'm going to put all the developers past issues of other releases aside before I critique this game. I do however recommend you do your research on ANY developer before personally supporting them in an Early Access title. If their past issues put a huge red flag up for you I do not blame you and I recommend you look elsewhere regardless of the games current state.
That being said let's critque the actual current build of the game. I am writing this on 3/11/2015 and have had press access for around a week now.
Crafting: Crafting is really well done and the amount of things you can craft right now is honestly amazing for an early access title. Pretty much everything you see in the world alive/dead can be used for some sort of recipe. There is siege weapons, torture weapons, and a decent selection of major building blocks for castle/house creation. Another HUGE plus is that crafting stations like fireplaces and benches are able to be picked up which makes moving very easy.
The World: Although quite small the world does feel well thought out. There is some absolutely beautiful scenery in this game and I find certain parts of the world hold rarer resources (for example one side of the map may have an abundance of rocks but no flax to be found). I like that it makes moving pretty much needed.
Combat: Having only tested combat once I am definitely not a guru on this subject but it did feel quite decent, latency definitely affects projectiles quite drastically and might be an issue for some people expecting super smooth combat. Overall with melee I had no major complaints but it can be improved.
Building: Building just fine, my only complaint is if you misplace a block theres no delete option and you have to sit there for 5 minutes whacking it to get rid of it so take you time placing them. This would also make rearranging a nightmare.
Politics: Politics atleast right now seem very basic with one king ruler who can impose a tax and claim the land name. You also get a crown and very decent sword. I did not see any way to form a guild so I cannot mention much about that now.
Gathering: Gathering in this game is very well done. Upgraded or gathering-focused weapons yield more per hit and the way trees fall and break is very rewarding, you visually can see how much is left in a resource and it makes gathering kind of enjoyable.
Survival: This is where I think this game went a little wrong. I don't see the need for survival mechanics personally. It is very hard at the start unless you have a good spawn point with an abundance of berries. I would rather see future developement focus on political warfare and creation aspects, I feel survival will feel more like a nuisance than fun for most casual players.
Sever Size: Currently the server size is EXTREMELY small to keep with the map size I assume (I think it's 28 players). This is a huge downside to me, when it comes to medieval warfare you want huge battles with 100's of people. I definitely hope they plan on expanding the map and increasing the server size in the future.
Overall I really enjoyed my time and I think this game had great potential but it's very hard to judge in it's current state how it will play out as a political controlling type game. I do recommend this title but I warn of the risks associtated with this companies past games.

The total war franchise is one of my most favorite and Rome 2 emperors edition my most played on steam.Creative Assembly is one of the most reliable manufacturers in the game industry but Rome 2 had many problems.Problems that made a but impression in the community and produced a black sheep on their accomplishments.

Rome 2 had plenty of bugs and glitches ,bad optimization and a very slow performance.All of that combined to the dlcs that constantly come out on a price made a bad start up for the game.Thankfully all of this belong in the past.Creative Assembly after many updates make it work and offer us the emperors edition of the game that includes all the updates and patches and the Imperator Augustus Campaign pack dlc.

As the name precedes players starts their campaign in the era of Rome. If you expect a game similair to more mainstream fare like Age of Empires, you will be out of your comfort zone here. I know I was. Honestly, it is an incredibly complicated game to excel at, but it is impossible for it to be any other way. You have complete control over every unit, with 360' movement in space. This is important because every unit has a different defenses and attacks, with some only being effective from certain angles, allowing a cunning opponent to take out your forces with surgical precision if you are not careful.
The sound design is incredible, with the music and voices taking a backseat to the gameplay, but complementing it wonderfully. I can't claim to be a writer or a composer, but the atmosphere of the first few missions is nearly unsurpassed.
The launch of the game was rather rocky, with many of the Remastered's features and changes being buggy and incomplete, but the untouched original versions are also included in the purchase so there was an alternative during the early days before these issues were patched.
I have no nostalgic history with this game, and as of yet I have only played the remastered versions, so this is not an exhaustive review, but after playing what I have I can say that anyone looking for a more nuanced strategy game will likely be pleasently surprised.

I loved the first Dishonored. I played through the story and every story DLC, in both low and high chaos. When I saw this game announced, I was excited because the first Dishonored was a great open sandbox, truly allowing you to approach obstacles in almost any way you could imagine with an interesting plot and polished world.
Dishonored 2 did not disappoint me. The level design was much like the first game, allowing multiple approaches to your objectives. There were often times I would approach sections and find multiple different ways to approach them, some not always obvious until you explore. You can choose to also use supernatural powers like teleports, blinks, possession, bend time, dark vision, and more as well as an arsenal of weapons and gadgets including swords, pistols, crossbows, mines and grenades. Or completely ignore them altogether and play the entire game passively. Movement and combat both feel great.
The game takes place 15 years after the events of the first game. While the first game took place entirely in the city of Dunwall, much of the second game takes place in the city of Karnaca, south of Dunwall, with a few missions returning to Dunwall. If you did play Dishonored 1 or the DLCs, you may recognize some familiar faces and names from the original game, while at the same time meeting a new cast of interesting characters. I thoroughly enjoyed the setting and locations of Dishonored 2, particularly one mission called The Clockwork Mansion.
There are two playable characters, Corvo Attano, the protagonist of the first game, or his daughter, Empress Emily Kaldwin, who rose to power and claimed the throne following the events of the first game, only to be unjustly and unfairly overthrown 15 years later at the start of Dishonored 2. You'll be exploring the world and eliminating or neutralizing targets with either character as you work to restore order and take back your rightful position as Empress. Both have unique powers and dialogue within the world that will change depending on which character you choose. This made my second playthrough just as enjoyable as my first. I did two playthroughs: one in low chaos with no supernatural powers with Emily, and one in high chaos with all supernatural powers with Corvo. If you're looking for a challenge, definitely try a playthrough with no powers. Without the ability to simply blink through areas I appreciated the environments and level design much more.
There are side missions scattered throughout the main story, so be sure to explore. Enemies will often have idle chatter that may provide the location of secret items, alternate routes through levels, or alternate ways of dealing with your targets. The notes, journals, diaries, etc. are all worth listening to because they provide quite a bit of background on the characters, and the reasons for their motives, as well as hints on alternate paths and actions for many of your main objectives. Much of the story is a continuation of Dishonored 1 and its DLCs. The backstory is explained in Dishonored 2 through still cutscene flashbacks, so it's not necessarily vital to have played the first game, but I would highly recommend playing the first game and its DLCs before starting this game, as the entire story arc across both games is enjoyable, with likeable characters and a great designed world.
