Chaos, explosions and total dhamaal, is the best way to describe Just Cause 3. Wait isn’t that the same that can be said of Just Cause 2? Of course, it wouldn’t be Just Cause without it.
The plot (yes there is a plot) revolves around our older and grizzlier protagonist Rico Rodriguez, who’s altruistically concerned about liberating the people of Medici from Sebastiano Di Ravello's military dictatorship…basically a setup for the player to go “I want more boom boom”  but not in the Hot Coffee mod way ;D
Just Cause 3’s island of Medici map is HHHUUUUGEEEE over 400 square miles as per the developer. This might sound bigger than their previous game’s map but it isn’t, it’s around same size, however it is prettier and denser. In other words, you have more things to go BOOM!
Avalanche studio has made Just Cause 3 characters a lot more likable, Rico himself is warmer, he has a lot more engaging presence than Just Cause 2.The supporting characters add a fun likable flavour, and the entire game has a unique sense of ridiculousness to it, like a silly 80’s action comedy flick.
The grappling hook♥♥♥♥♥wing suit has been upgraded, it can now shoot farther, tie several things together (such as vehicles), and act as your primary means of getting around the island if you are so talented. This is a nod to the amazingly fun grappling hook mod of Just Cause 2 which allowed all of this.
Just Cause 3 throws the player (literally) into the heat of the action without nudging or showing you the way. Basically here are your new weapons, it makes things go BOOM, and this is where you need to go. That’s it, everything else you figure out. Fly around to take a sports car, shoot everyone in the face, get to the attack chopper, shoot everyone in the face and make things go BOOM, go to objectives, double BOOM BOOM, jump out, for some ground battle, shoot everyone in the face and the♥♥♥♥♥♥twice over. Oh and don’t forget…make things go BOOM again! While this is no different from its predecessor Just Cause 2, it does have the same flaw,too much repetition, and no real staying power.
Just Cause 3 needs a lot of muscle to run, you cannot throw a mid range 4GB rig at it, it WILL be unplayable. When the developers say minimum 6GB system RAM, they mean it. Ensure that you are somewhere above the minimum mark and you should be good to play the game. Despite the performance bugs that have been ironed out since its launch, expect the game to slow down occasionally or worse crash even.
All in all, you don’t want to miss this dhamaal of a game. It isn’t GTA V and it doesn’t pretend to be. It is a junk food game that lacks the richness and depth but is good at one thing– Making you have a blast till it lasts. Suddenly I feel hungry for Mc Donald’s fries!

You play the role of a shipwrecked astronaut, freshly marooned on an alien planet.  All you have is your wits and knowledge of supply-chain management to keep you alive.  For people who love logistics, this game is for you.  Your job is to bend the planet to your will, and automate the heck out of each step in the process.
At first, all you can do is build small mining machines which gather resources for you.  Soon, you unlock the ability to build furnaces to process the resources.  You then manually transfer the materials from one machine to the other.  Before long, you gain the ability to construct conveyor belts to automate the process of moving the materials around.  This seems to be the heart of the game; figure out how to automate the process of whatever you’ve just done manually.  Make the machines do the work for you.
Eventually, you wind up with several conveyor belts, robotic arms, furnaces, mining platforms, all working towards generating the raw materials you need for more complex constructions.
It’s not all just fun and games with the factory building.  Eventually, the natives of the planet take notice of your resource consumption and come tell you to stop.  Unfortunately for you, they want to coerce you by killing you.  Unfortunately for them, you’re armed, and not going to take their demands lightly.  In other words, your assembly area will soon be littered with the bodies of your overly aggressive hosts.
In a game of escalating difficulty and complexity, you soon learn how to build better defenses to combat the increasing number of enemies trying to convince you to cease operations.  Machine guns, automated gun turrets, and pistols are available for your protection, and you’ll need them to fend off the never-ending waves of native creatures.
Eventually, I built up quite a production facility.  I had several different types of resources being mined, processed, and stored automatically.  I then was given the goal of building radar dishes to locate the wreckage of my mothership.  These radar dishes consume quite a bit of electricity, so production had to scale with demand.  Several electricity generating boilers were constructed to feed the power hungry devices.
While playing the game, the comparison came to me that this game was a little like building Redstone contraptions in Minecraft.  If you’ve ever built anything interesting with Redstone, this game might be up your alley.
I’ve seen some videos on the Steam store that show just how complex these mega-factories can become.  Trains convey materials long-distance, conveyor belts going every direction to process materials; it’s like giant Rube Goldberg machines.  My meager facility didn’t come close to the potential complexity of this game.
What I liked:  The premise is fresh and unique.  The interface took a few minutes to get used to, but eventually I found it was quite good for manipulating your factories.  The graphics are detailed and well done.
What I didn’t like:  Having to stop playing and come write this review. :)  I really can’t think of anything I didn’t like.  Wait, I think I found a typo in a description, if that counts.
This one is well worth a look if you like building games.  It’s certainly worth watching the videos out there just to see the game in action.  Pictures just don’t do it justice.
Thanks for reading.

I really enjoyed the first Dishonored. I have a lot of games to play through, but it pulled me back in to play it to completion three times to date, and the world and its characters encouraged me to play through non-lethally and to use stealth at all times. I never wanted to "finish already" in an area in that game, and loved combing over every inch of the city for hidden upgrade items and incapacitating people. The inn which comes between each mission serves as a means of strengthening the story, not only informing the player of the next objective, but giving insight into the personalities of the various resistance members and subtler developments with Corvo and Emily, and even carrying a bit of that over into a mission. I had a blast with Dishonored, and I feel certain that I'll play through it again someday, since I've already done it thrice and am smiling just thinking back on it for this review.
I'm not here to review the first Dishonored, though. I think it's great, and I'm simply wanting to point out that stealthy and  non-lethal gameplay in immersive environments with an art style I like and a pleasant (even if simple) story with pacing that I thought was great, and an enjoyable set of powers, are absolutely "my jam." It's for some of these reasons that I enjoyed Deus Ex Human Revolution and Vampire the Masquerade Bloodlines SO, so much. But then there's Dishonored 2...
While this sequel has the visual splendor of its predecessor with improved graphics, stealthy and non-lethal gameplay with a few improvements like non-lethal drop takedowns, I rarely felt that the game was immersive in the way that the first one was. You see, until Dishonored 2, I never really appreciated the inn which came between missions in the first game, because I didn't understand that it is the humanizing element of the game. It is where virtually all character development, foreshadowing, and significant story developments occur. WIth Dishonored 2, that is gone, and you will find yourself on a boat with just 1 NPC (eventually 2 after 10 or 20 hours or so of gametime, depending on how you play), and the NPCs on the boat never felt very compelling to me and did not make me care more about the game world or my mission.
That's what it all boils down to: sheer apathy. I just can't care about this game, other than to frown and say that I'm disappointed that I didn't enjoy it. My heart goes out to the folks who had/have performance issues. Although I had none myself, I have been unable to find the willpower - for several months now - to even start this game up again. The story is so similar to the first game (Home Alone 2 had more plot variance than these two games do from what I've seen) that I absolutely don't care what happens. There are so few persistent characters in the sequel's storyline, and those characters appeal so little to me that, hypothetically, if every character in the game died at the end, it simply wouldn't bother me, even though that would bum me out in almost any other game.
The only complaints I have about the actual gameplay are that it seemed like the density of guard population was ramped up, if only to create additional busy work, because knocking them all out and hiding their bodies in Dishonored 2 felt like busy work because it took so long to clear everything, whereas in the original, I enjoyed the process and it didn't take forever. My other complaint is that I simply do not enjoy Emily's powers at all, and had already invested far too many hours for me to be willing to restart as Corvo. His powers were pretty perfect in the first game, and although I loved the sound of Emily's and having some variety, I disliked all of her powers when I finally played the game and used them.
I have very little problems with the gameplay. My issues with it stem this being a franchise designed with a strong visual aesthetic and immersion factors, requiring that I really get into the setting, its story, its characters, and that I feel motivated by these things to press on and feel enthralled by the game, just elated to be there...but instead, I want to be playing any number of Steam shovelware games instead that I haven't tried before, because Dishonored 2 instills such bottomless apathy in me toward it. I can't even get angry or sad about not enjoying the game, and drawing up the motivation to even review it has been taxing and sigh-inducing for me.
Before Dishonored 2, I was a "shut up and take my money" kinda guy when it came to the Dishonored franchise, generally speaking. After playing this game for more than 20 hours and getting a little over half done, judging by a walkthrough chapter list I just Googled, I now have almost no interest in the franchise going forward. It would take some serious news and changes in the franchise to make me consider purchasing future titles in it, even at $4.99 deep Steam discounts. Hopefully you find this sequel more enjoyable than I did, but I sincerely suspect I will never touch it again, because it leaves me listless and dissatisfied at almost every turn.

Dark Souls II has brutally set itself securely on the top of my all time favorite gaming experiences in my life; and this is from a guy who started playing games in the early eighties.
As with the predecessor Dark Souls (1) I started out with the game on xbox 360 (offline) to go and buy it for the ps3 to get online - just to also buy it on Steam to get mods and better coop support etc. All in all I have easily over a thousand hours in these two masterpieces, and as it feels now I got a thousand more just waiting to be played...
The Souls series has the chunkiest and weightiest combat controls I've yet to experience anywhere else, and in contrary to popular belief the game isn't hard in the sense it most often means. Other games often push the difficulty with more numbers of enemies, ai x-ray sight, taking ten headshots without falling etc. But not Dark Souls, oh no!
The enemies in Dark Souls 1&2 are meant to be respected, they are there for you to duel with. If you run in head first screaming Leeeeroy they will throw your head out the way it came - laughing at the fool storming through the door... But if you take it easy, be aware of your surroundings and keep your shield up all the while being paranoid of ambushes you will most definitely survive longer and longer. After dying over and over and over in the starting areas of the previous game I thought this was going to be a crazily difficult game.
But suddenly something clicked. Something about respecting the opponents, taking the time to wait for an opportunity to strike and backing up to take a breath before going back into the fights - that made things instantly smoother. I started running through the same area in a fraction of the time I did earlier only because I finally understood how it all worked.
After pushing through the initial learning curve, you just might find that you've stumbled upon a promise of the holy grail of gaming.
Perfect controls, amazing atmosphere, dark humor, fascinating lore, loot in droves and frankly amazing looking gear that gives the fashionista in you an ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic experience.
One of the very best games ever made, and is only matched by its predecessor.
I cannot give enough praise to this gemstone of an experience, I am in absolute love of this entire IP and can't wait to experience the last two DLCs.

The One Tamriel update changes everything.
I played ESO when it first came out, and I played it a year after it came out, both times I tried to give it my best shot and invested a good number of hours trying to get into it. But gee, there were so many problems with the game back then, I could never stay when the negatives quite outweighed the positives, as much as I wanted to.
Now, however, the "One Tamriel" update has been released, completely overhauling the entire game for the better. No more traditional zones that you must level in, no more being unable to interact with players from different alliances, no more soul destroyingly bad Veteran ranks.
You can travel anywhere you like in the world of Tamriel, fight anything you desire, quest in whatever land you wish and group up with other players regardless of Alliance or character level. In addition, dueling has been brought in to the game, brand new ultimate abilities have been added and special seasonal/holiday events are in (important to a strong community feel).
It took them two years, but holy moly, this is finally a game woth playing, and a game woth loving.
With how cheap you can pick this game up for these days, I see no reason anymore not to give this a try.
And remember! Even on a brand new character you can go wherever you like! You are not restricted into grinding until "end-game" to start whatever fun content you desire. Just go for it : )

Elder Scrolls Online (ESO) is a hit-and-slash based MMORPG game based on the Elder Scrolls (duh) universe made by Zenimax Online (Thanks for the correction, Oni, metareaper, and flobish). Players will explore Tamriel and do quests given by NPCs across Tamriel. This game is focused both on PvE and PvP, each requires a lot of time to master and grind. Similar to its offline relative, TES V: Skyrim, ESO has a massive content in it and you can expect thousands of hours of gameplay.  Quest's style is also similar to Skyrim. Instead of 'Kill 50 monsters' or 'Collect 100 chicken feets' like in other MMORPGs, ESO offers various kinds of immersive Skyrim-like tasks. Like 'Tail Dar'Van to the secret place' or 'Change A or B's sword with a flawed sword' or 'Assassinate Lord Quintus Jarol in his estate'. These quests involves stealth, lockpicking, pickpocketing, assassination, choice-driven outcome, and many other elements. In short, ESO is a story-driven MMORPG with rich content that offers the player a new way to interact with the game.
1. Pay To Win?
Definitely not. Purchasing 'Crowns' - ESO's premium currency - will only cut down your grinding time. If you have the time to grind and enjoys the grinding process, there is really no benefit you can get from Crowns. ESO Plus members only gain a crafting bag, all DLCs, and 10% bonus XP. In my opinion, membership is quite useless if you have the Gold Edition. Crowns will also unlock special cosmetics like special mounts and pets. But again, they are just cosmetics. They have no advantage over the free items. However, I always encourage everyone to purchase premium currency and DLCs to support the developers. Purchasing Crowns is not completely useless. You can browse around the store to see what kind of benefit it offers over non-paying users.
2. Is this Skyrim Online?
No. This is set exactly 948 years (Thanks for the correction, Mr. Cracktus Jack!) before the events in TES V: Skyrim. This is the 2nd Era and even Talos has not been born yet, moreover the Dragonborn. A lot of people keep asking in-game "WHERE IS THE DRAGONBORN?! Or are we all dragonborns?". If you pay attention to the in-game calendar, it's 2E (Second Era). Skyrim is set on 4E (Fourth Era). This is definitely not Skyrim Online, but it is set on the Elder Scrolls Universe. You will still meet or hear familiar characters like Akatosh, Mara, Thieves Guild, The Dark Brotherhood, etc but this is not set in the same time with Skyrim. Expect MMORPG-compatible quests and storyline instead of complete similarity with Skyrim's gameplay.
1. Rich content. Tons of story, side-quests, items to unlock, hidden collectibles, crafting system, skills, characters, etc. Side-quests are mostly a bit cliche but that's compeletely understandable. You can't expect them to write thousands of well-written story. I do, however, have to give them credits for the great main quest's storyline.
2. Active and friendly community. As expected from a pay to play game, the community does not have a lot of toxic players and they are very helpful to new players.
3. Very large map. This means there are tons of exploration bonuses and sights to see.
4. Better fighting animations. Compared to Skyrim, it is not as crude. Not as smooth as Warframe but it is still better than Skyrim.
5. Not the best and latest graphics but it looks awesome and up-to-expectations from a 2014 game.
6. Almost no trollers. This is gold for a MMORPG. I can enjoy online play without the presence of people who intentionally ruin the gameplay.
7. Definitely fun to play with friends. This is not one of those solo-focused MMORPGs. Having 1-3 friends to play with will be very beneficial to your ESO gaming experience.
8. Helpful Add-Ons will cut down your grinding time
9. Grinding process is not boring. Again, they are not like those 'Kill 100 headcrabs' MMORPG.
10. Emotions made the social interactions very alive. I spent a lot of hours just messing around the city with various emotions (/kowtow, /lute, /bucketsplash, etc). People around me are surprisingly very supportive in creating a mutually entertaining random fun (e.g. flash mob, orchestra, mass-play-dead, etc)
11. If you're into Role-Playing (RP), there are a lot of RP guilds in ESO. I'm not into RP myself but I saw one of them in action once and I can say their dedication is amazing.
12. You can create up to 8 characters and you can share the items & money between them. IMO, this is another golden point. ESO offers a massive room for improvisations, practice, and testing. Devs did their best to balance out everything so you can try out every class/alliance/race in-game without having to pay a single dime. Grinding new characters will not be as difficult if you already have one well-off 'main' character.
1. Musics are not as epic as Skyrim and mostly 'meh' quality. This might not be important for some people but IMO this is a huge letdown, considering the fact that this has relation with Skyrim.
2. Very expensive crown store items. Want those cool-looking armors? Be prepared to pay ~$50 for each style. However, you can get them for free if you are patient in farming for the motifs.
3. A bit confusing for new players. There are way too many elements to learn and it takes a long time to know your way around. ESO needs a better tutorial system.
4. IMO, I agree with others that Bows are a bit underpowered. I have seen numerous discussions about underpowered bows in various zone chats so this seems as an issue that devs should address.
5. Stealth kills are a bit weird. You can only insta-kill using Dark Brotherhood's special Blade. Stealth damage should have more value. However, I agree with Oni that stealth wasn't meant to be a huge element in the game. Stealth system exists but it's just not well made.
6. Gathering resources seem to be severely under-rewarding. Stealing items from town markets and deconstructing them will give a lot more resources faster.
7. No Asia server.
8. Combat with same-level enemies takes way too long and this is the very first thing my fellow gamers noticed whenever they watch me play. It seems that I'm not the only one who thinks that the enemies are too tanky.
9. Crafting system lacks explanation. I had to watch kevduit's video on YouTube first before fully understanding it.
10. Kills mid-low spec PC. My friends have a laptop with specs above the minimum requirements, but they can barely play smoothly (2 - 30 fps). I understand this is a heavy-load game, but it would be great if they have more optimization options.
ESO is definitely a MMORPG to look at. I am not a huge fan of MMORPG myself since most of them are pay-to-win or have similar patterns of gameplay. ESO is unique. It looks awesome, it has worth-reading stories, and abundant content. I believe this is definitely worth trying. I am still not that far into the game when I write this review so I may update this review again one day. I hope this review can be helpful for you. Thank you for reading!

On the other side if you are in mobas for the competitive nature, and expect a decent amount of balance and absence of bugs this game is not what you want to play. This game has a multitude of problems.
To start with, this game has bug issues. Several characters and items have bugs that either are reappearing or persist throughout the entire game's lifetime. Some of which have the potential to change an entire game result because of things like collision errors that make you stuck in walls. While these are semi rare and the majority of bugs are fixed in 1-2 weeks there is still an above average amount of bugs in Smite, which changes the experience. When confronted with this, in order of frequency, Hirez: A- Ignores them outright. B- Says they are working on the bug(s) even though in some cases it has been litteral years since the bug showed up. C- Say the bug is intended even though it is obvious this is a lie.
Hirez also has community managment issues. There are way too many cases of people who are known by the entire community for breaking rules by: harrassment, trolling ( to an unacceptable level), Targeted attacks on players, exc. Nothing happens to these people more often than not. On the other side of the coin, Hirez has been proven to show favorites to personalities/ friends of people who work there, and WILL ban people on the word of those people reguarless of if any rules have been broken or not.

This is also the company that was/is in charge of tribes. Those of you who are familiar with that particular game will know that, this does not allow them for much trust.
Overall, because of the things listed here, it is impossible for me to recomend this game. There are too many good games, with merit to waste your time on this one in my opinion.
As of early 2017 I came back to see if the game got better on a competitive level. It did not. The meta has been stale for months upon months, and it takes Hirez to fix things so bad that lesser companies wouldn't even concider because it's such a bad idea. 'Homeworld Remasted Collection' is a package that includes the remastered version of Homeworld, a game from 1999, as well as the remastered version of Homeworld 2, that was released in 2003. Additionally the package includes the classic version of both games. Although Homeworld and Homeworld 2 are both very similar real-time strategy games, they both play and feel very different.
The discovery of an ancient stone plate showing an engraved course through the galaxy, triggers your people on a journey through space to find your original home world. As expected this journey comes with many obstacles and as commander of fleet it is your task to overcome them. In other words, you have to fight. Think of Battlestar Galactica and you get the idea.
The concept of the game is really cool and takes you on an intense science fiction journey that feels very unique. Every hyper-jump brings you to a new level in the game. Your remaining fleet arrives centred around your mother-ship. The mother-ship is capable of constructing all kind of different ships. Frigates, cruisers, corvettes, fighters or destroyers, you name it. Additionally you can research new technologies to upgrade your equipment. In order to build new ships you need to collect resources. Resources can be found in asteroid fields and shipwrecks.
As for Homeworld 1 most levels are slow paced. Most of the time you are not attacked unless you engage the enemy. This allows you to take your time, which is a wonderful thing. You can drink a cup of tea or relax with a glass of whisky, harvest nearby resources, explore your surroundings and plan your strategy. In this way Homeworld 1 almost feels like a game of chess.
Homeworld 2 is the complete opposite. In Homeworld 2 you are constantly put under pressure by never-ending scripting events that force you to permanently fight for survival. Additionally the amount of enemies seems endless at times because the developers implemented a variable AI that automatically adjusts to your fleet size and makes sure it's stronger than yours. The relaxing atmosphere from Homeworld 1 is diminished to a few isolated occasions in Homeworld 2, which makes both games two very different experiences.
Both games are generally considered to be hard games. And while I really had to struggle with some levels in Homeworld 1 I was always able to manage them by re-trying one way or the other. This is not necessarily the case for Homeworld 2. The achievement statistic on Steams shop page shows that many players gave up on Homeworld 2. This impression is mirrored in the forums. Homeworld 2 is an extremely difficult game and can be very frustrating at times.
Pros: (both games)
- beautiful graphics, still not like games from today but considering the age of the games the developers did a great job
- tutorials
- good keyboard interface
- very good music
- good voice acting, well designed ship communications
- option to manually save at any time, very important!
- addictive, after failing to complete a level I went to bed and woke up at three o'clock at night, re-tried and made it :-)
- interesting story
- very good cutscenes with regard to contents
Pros: (Homeworld 1)
- relaxing, great atmosphere
- difficulty is well balanced, rather easy in the beginning and pretty hard in the end (but still not as hard as every single level in Homeworld 2)
- freedom to self-initiate the hyper-jump to the next level
Pros: (Homeworld 2)
- resource collectors and repair ships are now combined in one unit
- more ship upgrade options
- Cons: (both games)
- games come without manual. Thankfully players provided links to the manuals in the forums that left me with four documents of 173 pages, nice
- if you end up finishing a level with a remaining fleet that is unfit to beat the next level you need to replay the last level to make sure your remaining fleet is prepared for the upcoming challenge
- one achievement asks you to play the tutorial of the classic game. Unfortunately this is not possible because the classic version keeps crashing. Forums are full of players with this problem. Adding this kind of achievement was a really dumb move from the devs.
- Cons: (Homeworld 1)
- last level seemed a little to hard
- Cons: (Homeworld 2)
- stressful most of the time
- can be frustrating at times
- too difficult
- if your last main objective has been completed the game automatically hyper-jumps into the next level. This can be a huge problem if your fleet is diminished after a lengthy fight and you jump right into the next fight. In order to prepare your fleet before jumping you have to wait before completing the final main objective
- salvage corvettes make no more sense because they have become far to expensive to justify the risk
- maximum number of ships in a group is restricted. In Homeworld 1 you can exceed the maximum number by capturing enemy ships.
- stuttering cutscenes
All in all I really enjoyed both games. They offer a very unique atmosphere. I don't know any other game with a similar mood. Homeworld 1 deserves a 100% recommendation while Homeworld 2 deserves a recommendation for the hard core fans but probably not for everybody.

Checking passports might sound easy enough but as the tasks you have to perform get harder you also discover that doing things by the books might not always be the right thing after all.
All in all this little game really makes you think about the society we live in, especially about immigration and how sometimes seemingly arbitrarily rules can define one person's whole life. That being said, the game also has a lot of genuinely funny moments.
As you can see I can't recommend this game enough.

The Good:
I've been playing the Total War series since the original Shogun came out fifteen years ago, I've played every incarnation except Attila, and I have to say the series just keeps getting better and better. Rome II definitely has the feel of a massive campaign, with massive armies and massive empires battling against each other. I've only racked up 20 hours as of writing this review but I can see that this is one that's going to eat into a lot of my time.
Graphically, it's a very beautiful game. Unfortunately my system won't run it on anything approaching ultra settings, though even on a mix of High and Very High it still looks heaps better than (for example) Medieval 2 on its highest settings. I know I'm going to need a system upgrade at some point in the not too distant future, but for now it looks like CA have done a decent job of optimising this game for lower-end systems. (For those who need to know, I tried running the benchmark on Ultra settings across the board and got <5 fps. o.O)
Having said all that, as with most games, there are bad points to this one as well as good.
The Bad:
As a few other reviewers have said, this is one of those situations where you buy the base game, and can have a lot of fun with it, but to really get the most out of it you have to then buy a literal metiric f**k-ton of DLCs. The core game is thirty quid, and then all of the DLC is another sixty quid on top of that, and this is a good year or so after the game was released. Now, I appreciate that game developers have to make their money, and I don't have anything against DLC in particular, but I think three new campaigns (at a tenner each), four new culture packs (at six quid each), two new unit packs (at two quid each) and the blood and gore add-on (also two quid) is maybe going at bit far?
And The Rest:
I love this series, and despite my whining over the cost of all the DLC I will probably end up buying it all at some point. I'll also end up getting Attila (plus all the DLC), as well as Warhammer (plus DLC) when that comes out. I'd like to hope that somewhere along the way CA and their publishers make a few changes to their business model as far as DLC is concerned, but I'm not going to hold my breath. I also hope that the series continues to push the envelope on what can be achieved graphically and technically with the games. As long as they keep doing that, I'll keep playing 'em.

Elder Scrolls Online (ESO) is a hit-and-slash based MMORPG game based on the Elder Scrolls (duh) universe made by Zenimax Online (Thanks for the correction, Oni, metareaper, and flobish). Players will explore Tamriel and do quests given by NPCs across Tamriel. This game is focused both on PvE and PvP, each requires a lot of time to master and grind. Similar to its offline relative, TES V: Skyrim, ESO has a massive content in it and you can expect thousands of hours of gameplay.  Quest's style is also similar to Skyrim. Instead of 'Kill 50 monsters' or 'Collect 100 chicken feets' like in other MMORPGs, ESO offers various kinds of immersive Skyrim-like tasks. Like 'Tail Dar'Van to the secret place' or 'Change A or B's sword with a flawed sword' or 'Assassinate Lord Quintus Jarol in his estate'. These quests involves stealth, lockpicking, pickpocketing, assassination, choice-driven outcome, and many other elements. In short, ESO is a story-driven MMORPG with rich content that offers the player a new way to interact with the game.
1. Pay To Win?
Definitely not. Purchasing 'Crowns' - ESO's premium currency - will only cut down your grinding time. If you have the time to grind and enjoys the grinding process, there is really no benefit you can get from Crowns. ESO Plus members only gain a crafting bag, all DLCs, and 10% bonus XP. In my opinion, membership is quite useless if you have the Gold Edition. Crowns will also unlock special cosmetics like special mounts and pets. But again, they are just cosmetics. They have no advantage over the free items. However, I always encourage everyone to purchase premium currency and DLCs to support the developers. Purchasing Crowns is not completely useless. You can browse around the store to see what kind of benefit it offers over non-paying users.
2. Is this Skyrim Online?
No. This is set exactly 948 years (Thanks for the correction, Mr. Cracktus Jack!) before the events in TES V: Skyrim. This is the 2nd Era and even Talos has not been born yet, moreover the Dragonborn. A lot of people keep asking in-game "WHERE IS THE DRAGONBORN?! Or are we all dragonborns?". If you pay attention to the in-game calendar, it's 2E (Second Era). Skyrim is set on 4E (Fourth Era). This is definitely not Skyrim Online, but it is set on the Elder Scrolls Universe. You will still meet or hear familiar characters like Akatosh, Mara, Thieves Guild, The Dark Brotherhood, etc but this is not set in the same time with Skyrim. Expect MMORPG-compatible quests and storyline instead of complete similarity with Skyrim's gameplay.
1. Rich content. Tons of story, side-quests, items to unlock, hidden collectibles, crafting system, skills, characters, etc. Side-quests are mostly a bit cliche but that's compeletely understandable. You can't expect them to write thousands of well-written story. I do, however, have to give them credits for the great main quest's storyline.
2. Active and friendly community. As expected from a pay to play game, the community does not have a lot of toxic players and they are very helpful to new players.
3. Very large map. This means there are tons of exploration bonuses and sights to see.
4. Better fighting animations. Compared to Skyrim, it is not as crude. Not as smooth as Warframe but it is still better than Skyrim.
5. Not the best and latest graphics but it looks awesome and up-to-expectations from a 2014 game.
6. Almost no trollers. This is gold for a MMORPG. I can enjoy online play without the presence of people who intentionally ruin the gameplay.
7. Definitely fun to play with friends. This is not one of those solo-focused MMORPGs. Having 1-3 friends to play with will be very beneficial to your ESO gaming experience.
8. Helpful Add-Ons will cut down your grinding time
9. Grinding process is not boring. Again, they are not like those 'Kill 100 headcrabs' MMORPG.
10. Emotions made the social interactions very alive. I spent a lot of hours just messing around the city with various emotions (/kowtow, /lute, /bucketsplash, etc). People around me are surprisingly very supportive in creating a mutually entertaining random fun (e.g. flash mob, orchestra, mass-play-dead, etc)
11. If you're into Role-Playing (RP), there are a lot of RP guilds in ESO. I'm not into RP myself but I saw one of them in action once and I can say their dedication is amazing.
12. You can create up to 8 characters and you can share the items & money between them. IMO, this is another golden point. ESO offers a massive room for improvisations, practice, and testing. Devs did their best to balance out everything so you can try out every class/alliance/race in-game without having to pay a single dime. Grinding new characters will not be as difficult if you already have one well-off 'main' character.
1. Musics are not as epic as Skyrim and mostly 'meh' quality. This might not be important for some people but IMO this is a huge letdown, considering the fact that this has relation with Skyrim.
2. Very expensive crown store items. Want those cool-looking armors? Be prepared to pay ~$50 for each style. However, you can get them for free if you are patient in farming for the motifs.
3. A bit confusing for new players. There are way too many elements to learn and it takes a long time to know your way around. ESO needs a better tutorial system.
4. IMO, I agree with others that Bows are a bit underpowered. I have seen numerous discussions about underpowered bows in various zone chats so this seems as an issue that devs should address.
5. Stealth kills are a bit weird. You can only insta-kill using Dark Brotherhood's special Blade. Stealth damage should have more value. However, I agree with Oni that stealth wasn't meant to be a huge element in the game. Stealth system exists but it's just not well made.
6. Gathering resources seem to be severely under-rewarding. Stealing items from town markets and deconstructing them will give a lot more resources faster.
7. No Asia server.
8. Combat with same-level enemies takes way too long and this is the very first thing my fellow gamers noticed whenever they watch me play. It seems that I'm not the only one who thinks that the enemies are too tanky.
9. Crafting system lacks explanation. I had to watch kevduit's video on YouTube first before fully understanding it.
10. Kills mid-low spec PC. My friends have a laptop with specs above the minimum requirements, but they can barely play smoothly (2 - 30 fps). I understand this is a heavy-load game, but it would be great if they have more optimization options.
ESO is definitely a MMORPG to look at. I am not a huge fan of MMORPG myself since most of them are pay-to-win or have similar patterns of gameplay. ESO is unique. It looks awesome, it has worth-reading stories, and abundant content. I believe this is definitely worth trying. I am still not that far into the game when I write this review so I may update this review again one day. I hope this review can be helpful for you. Thank you for reading!

At the time I wrote this I had finished Deserts of Kharak, the original homeworld and then 4 missions in to Homeworld 2 before I had to take a breal and play something else.
I wrote this review because Homeworld was probably the actual first game that turned me into a hardcore gamer.  I religiously played the original, cataclysm and homeworld 2.
I would give this a 7.5 out of 10 for the following reasons:
- Buggy, formations simply do not work as they are supposed to.  In homeworld 1 the rounds actually had trajectory and a path.  So if the round didn't hit, then no damage was sustained.  They have taken the hit mechanics of 2 (random number generator) and grafted it on to the orignal, which screws everything up.  In the original strike craft, if used correctly, could still be a force to be reckoned with.  However the current build has taken out the evasive, agressive neutral, options which limit the use of strike craft.  Also the enemy AI is buggy with formations attacking piece meal instead of a coordinated assault.  In some attacks my forces were completely ignored for the scout I had scouting out their formation.  They completely ignored the 3 Battlecruisers and 8 destroyers i had letting me slaughter them.
- Ion cannon issues? In the original I remember long battles that allowed you to outmaneuver the enemy, however this seems to be another homeworld 2 aspect added to the original. I do not remember capital ships "melting" that quickly in the orignal homeworld. Battles seem to last a quarter of the time it took in the original.
-  Excellent graphical update.
- Great story told in graphic art form
- good voice acting, In my real life job I enjoy hearing the radio chatter going about.  It adds a sense of realism.
- Gameplay is still the same old homeworld.
-Homeworld 2 seems the same gameplay wise.
Bottom Line: I finsished Homeworld 1 despite the bugginess/Homeworld 2 engine grafted to the game.  I would definately recommend it to people who never had a chance to play it when it came out.  However, I would recommmend to everyone playing (especially veterans of the series) that you wait until it is patched. (WHich I have heard there is a massive one coming soon) before playing.  It is not the same homeworld.

I didn't like this as much as I thought I would.  I never played the original version, so I'm just now experiencing Homeworld in the Remastered Collection.
It does seem to be a good 3D RTS engine and watching the ships in combat is amazing.  The storyline and plot is also interesting, at least as far as I played.
Is probably a game worth looking into or trying at least once, if its on sale.  But I think in today's RTS world, its a bit behind, even with the updated graphics.  I stopped playing at about the 6th mission for several reasons:
1.  Even playing normal difficulty, the AI is brutal throwing in larger ships like Frigates and even Destroyers very soon in the game, I think about the 4th or 5th mission.  Before you have even had a chance to build more than a few of them.  So unless you have researched and crank out some serious frigates, you will be toast.  I think its the I've read some walkthroughs and you can "cheese" your way through these missions by capturing with salvage frigates, but that seems cheesy and more like an exploit, then winning with combat.
2.  Resources are limited and always seem to be on the same place in the map,  A group of asteroids or a cloud of interstellar gas - always in about the same places.   it makes it kind of boring and also makes the game a bit unforgiving, if you mess up and lose to many ships or make a mistake, the campaign mission is pretty much over, or the next campaign mission will be impossible because you don't have enough resources to build new ships or do research.
3.  I got bored with the space theme.  It looks beautiful flying around for a while and watching ship combat, but then after a bit its boring to me, compared to land based RTS games.  In the land based ones, you can use the terrain to your advantage in attacking and setting up bases, and building defenses.  But in Homeworld, you are pretty much thrown into a system with your unmovable base ship stuck in one place.  With tons of empty space around you.  I just found that the combat got kind of boring because its mostly scrambling around to send groups of ships to certain places, without much strategy or base defense building involved.

You play the role of a shipwrecked astronaut, freshly marooned on an alien planet.  All you have is your wits and knowledge of supply-chain management to keep you alive.  For people who love logistics, this game is for you.  Your job is to bend the planet to your will, and automate the heck out of each step in the process.
At first, all you can do is build small mining machines which gather resources for you.  Soon, you unlock the ability to build furnaces to process the resources.  You then manually transfer the materials from one machine to the other.  Before long, you gain the ability to construct conveyor belts to automate the process of moving the materials around.  This seems to be the heart of the game; figure out how to automate the process of whatever you’ve just done manually.  Make the machines do the work for you.
Eventually, you wind up with several conveyor belts, robotic arms, furnaces, mining platforms, all working towards generating the raw materials you need for more complex constructions.
It’s not all just fun and games with the factory building.  Eventually, the natives of the planet take notice of your resource consumption and come tell you to stop.  Unfortunately for you, they want to coerce you by killing you.  Unfortunately for them, you’re armed, and not going to take their demands lightly.  In other words, your assembly area will soon be littered with the bodies of your overly aggressive hosts.
In a game of escalating difficulty and complexity, you soon learn how to build better defenses to combat the increasing number of enemies trying to convince you to cease operations.  Machine guns, automated gun turrets, and pistols are available for your protection, and you’ll need them to fend off the never-ending waves of native creatures.
Eventually, I built up quite a production facility.  I had several different types of resources being mined, processed, and stored automatically.  I then was given the goal of building radar dishes to locate the wreckage of my mothership.  These radar dishes consume quite a bit of electricity, so production had to scale with demand.  Several electricity generating boilers were constructed to feed the power hungry devices.
While playing the game, the comparison came to me that this game was a little like building Redstone contraptions in Minecraft.  If you’ve ever built anything interesting with Redstone, this game might be up your alley.
I’ve seen some videos on the Steam store that show just how complex these mega-factories can become.  Trains convey materials long-distance, conveyor belts going every direction to process materials; it’s like giant Rube Goldberg machines.  My meager facility didn’t come close to the potential complexity of this game.
What I liked:  The premise is fresh and unique.  The interface took a few minutes to get used to, but eventually I found it was quite good for manipulating your factories.  The graphics are detailed and well done.
What I didn’t like:  Having to stop playing and come write this review. :)  I really can’t think of anything I didn’t like.  Wait, I think I found a typo in a description, if that counts.
This one is well worth a look if you like building games.  It’s certainly worth watching the videos out there just to see the game in action.  Pictures just don’t do it justice.
Thanks for reading.

Alien: Isolation is one of my most favorite Games. First of all I am a huge Fan of the Alien franchise.
That being said, I think this game is one of the best the horror genre had to offer in recent years, and this is not because it is an Alien game.
. The game is well paced, and parts of high intensity and stress are followed by parts were there is nothing ... or is there? Sometimes it takes a while before you come across the next threat, but you never really know when it will happen. This suspense is a key element of the games atmosphere.
Also the AI of the Alien helps to make it believable that it is in fact looking for you. Not the most comfortable thought to be honest. This feeling ist underlined by the fact that you are not at the top of the food chain, and even as you progress through the game, you don't get there.
For me this is an important point, because there often is a point in a horror game when you reach this top spot of the food chain and it kills the horror aspect. You stop being afraid, and you take the role of the hunter. There may be stress left but no horror (if this makes any sense to you).
When comparing the game to the movie installments of Alien, I think it best compares to the first, and third part. If you expect something like the second movie for instance you will be disapointed. There are weapons but you won't run through corridors with your pulse rifle or a smart gun ... ever.
However you will have moments were you think you are safe, but the Alien gets you. When this happens you most likely became to uncautious (and I for my part usually need a minute or two to gather myself, before resuming to play).
and you and your cardiovascular system can handle the feeling of desperation while fighting for "your" life,

Emily is Away is an experimental game, simulating the AOL messaging app present in computers during the era of Windows XP. It follows the relationship of Emily and the protagonist, whom you name, throughout their college years up until senior year. The following review is heavily laden with SPOILERS, so if you do not want to have the game ruined for you, I advice that you walk away now.
***SPOILERS***
The game takes place over the course of 5 years. Senior year of high school all the way to senior year of college, segmented into 5 chapters, one for each year, obviously. You play the role of Emily's hopelessly in love best friend, who somewhat keeps in touch with her over their careers. As the years go by, you slowly drift apart until eventually you just stop talking altogether. The writing here is very solid. The characters use improper grammar, misspell things, you see the protagonist delete incorrectly typed things and even things that you wouldn't want to say to your crush. The dialogue seems like it could easily been written by two college students at the time. But that's not why we're here, now is it? We're here because of the touted story, and the choices you make in the game affecting what happens at the end. Let me tell you right now that this is, in fact, a lie. You do not change what happens at the end of the game. You can change the events that lead up to the ending, but you do not affect a single thing about the ending itself. But, before you immediately write this off as ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, let me explain in detail what happens. In senior year of high school, she talks to a young man from the high school named Brad on AIM. He confesses that he has a crush on her, and they start dating. Whether or not you say to ignore him is irrelevant. Your freshman year of college, you talk to her, and she says that she and Brad are kinda happy, fighting occasionally, but happy nonetheless. Whether or not you tell her to break up with him is irrelevant. Sophomore year of college, she tells you that they broke up and asks if you guys can hang out. Here's the "big" choice in the game. If you say no, she becomes even more lonely and sad. If you say yes, she visits and you hook up, regardless of any outlier, such as alcohol or activity. Junior year, she talks to you, asking why you hooked up with her or why you didn't want to hang out with her that day. She is upset at either result and leaves. Everything you say to confort her is irrelevant. Senior year, she messages you one last time, saying hi, talking a bit, and briefly mentioning offhandedly that she got back together with Brad, that she is sad about the way things went, and you say goodbye for the last time. Anything that can be done here is irrelevant. Throughout those five years, you form your own friendships, groups, and have your own life as well. However, by the end of it, any sort of friend that you have at the end is irrelevant. Are you noticing a pattern here? You can change the little details here and there, but nothing you do will affect the outcome. Everything you say and do will mean nothing in the end. And I feel that this idea is brilliant. Why? Because I've never believed in human agency. I've always said that those who do not believe in victims of circumstance have never been one. I've always known that we are victims to fate, to be tossed into the wind and followed on the fickle whims of the current of luck, only to fall to our position in life, regardless of what we have said and done up to that point. And I know that I'm not alone on this. However, I also know that I am not alone when I say that while I believe this, that defeats the purpose of playing a video game at all. The complete and total lack of a happy ending for anyone involved invalidates the entire journey to begin with. I know that some people will like this game because of this design choice. And I can easily see why. It's a very risky move, one that deserves some credit. And I also know that there are those who will like the game because it's artsy and nothing else. And they have the right to do that. But it's one that ultimately leaves the player feeling emotionally unsatisfied in the end. A little bit wiser, which is most certainly good, but nonetheless unsatisfied. So, take my opinion with a grain of salt, if you want. Odds are you aren't even going to read this all the way through. You'll just see the thumbs down and move on. If you did read this all the way through, congrats. However, it was still irrelevant.

Decent Total War title, unplayable in the beginning but has since been made playable.
I recommend it for anyone who likes strategy.

The Good:
I've been playing the Total War series since the original Shogun came out fifteen years ago, I've played every incarnation except Attila, and I have to say the series just keeps getting better and better. Rome II definitely has the feel of a massive campaign, with massive armies and massive empires battling against each other. I've only racked up 20 hours as of writing this review but I can see that this is one that's going to eat into a lot of my time.
Graphically, it's a very beautiful game. Unfortunately my system won't run it on anything approaching ultra settings, though even on a mix of High and Very High it still looks heaps better than (for example) Medieval 2 on its highest settings. I know I'm going to need a system upgrade at some point in the not too distant future, but for now it looks like CA have done a decent job of optimising this game for lower-end systems. (For those who need to know, I tried running the benchmark on Ultra settings across the board and got <5 fps. o.O)
Having said all that, as with most games, there are bad points to this one as well as good.
The Bad:
As a few other reviewers have said, this is one of those situations where you buy the base game, and can have a lot of fun with it, but to really get the most out of it you have to then buy a literal metiric f**k-ton of DLCs. The core game is thirty quid, and then all of the DLC is another sixty quid on top of that, and this is a good year or so after the game was released. Now, I appreciate that game developers have to make their money, and I don't have anything against DLC in particular, but I think three new campaigns (at a tenner each), four new culture packs (at six quid each), two new unit packs (at two quid each) and the blood and gore add-on (also two quid) is maybe going at bit far?
And The Rest:
I love this series, and despite my whining over the cost of all the DLC I will probably end up buying it all at some point. I'll also end up getting Attila (plus all the DLC), as well as Warhammer (plus DLC) when that comes out. I'd like to hope that somewhere along the way CA and their publishers make a few changes to their business model as far as DLC is concerned, but I'm not going to hold my breath. I also hope that the series continues to push the envelope on what can be achieved graphically and technically with the games. As long as they keep doing that, I'll keep playing 'em.

Dark Souls 2 is forgettable. Demon’s Souls and Dark Souls weren’t. On paper Dark Souls 2 improves on many problems in the first two games. But at the same time it fails to capture the most important aspects that made everyone love the other games.
Everyone gets hung up on the difficulty of the Souls games. As if that’s the only thing that makes them good. They’re more than that. There’s plenty of bone hard games out there, but none have the same devoted fanbase as the Souls games. There’s more going on here than the marketing or even the fans would want you to think. And that’s where Dark Souls 2 goes wrong. On the surface this is the same as the other two. But when you dig deep you notice there’s nothing there. Dark Souls and Demon’s Souls were rich. This isn’t.
Here’s a comprehensive list of what the sequel gets right. The multiplayer is reliable. In Dark Souls 1 it’s a borderline unusable mess. You can now run the game at any resolution, and the performance is good. That’s the end of the list.
It’s clear that the developers of Dark Souls 2 aimed too high. They tried to outdo the original game, with a team that was unqualified to even dream of doing so. They made a new engine with an improved lighting engine. In trailers it almost looked like a next-gen game! Unfortunately it was so slow they scrapped it before release. What you’re left with is a game that looks worse than its predecessors. There’s almost no contrast, the lighting is mostly flat, the art direction confusing. Words you wouldn’t use to describe the other Souls games.
More importantly though there’s no cohesion to the world. The transitions between environments is nonsensical. There’s far too many locations, and they’re all too small. There’s no way anyone could live in this world. In the other Souls games the worlds were plausible. You saw the remnants of great civilizations, and you could believe in them. There’s maybe a couple exceptions to the rule in Dark Souls 2, but they’re in the minority. Almost every environment you pass through you reach the end and think “oh, that’s it? Ok..”.
The DLC packs do their best to redeem the game. They’re an admirable effort, easily outdoing anything the main game did. There’s hope yet for this team. But after finishing the DLCs and returning to the normal areas one last time I’m not wistful or nostalgic for anything that happened during my journey. I look at the world and all I see is meaningless maps. This isn’t a world with history, where I connected with characters and went on a journey that I’ll remember. It’s just a game. A Souls game should be more than that.
I’m split. Dark Souls 2 isn’t “bad” by any regular metric. But the more I play it the more disappointed I am in it. At some point I’ll replay Demon’s Souls and Dark Souls. I never want to play Dark Souls 2 again.

Alien: Isolation is one of my most favorite Games. First of all I am a huge Fan of the Alien franchise.
That being said, I think this game is one of the best the horror genre had to offer in recent years, and this is not because it is an Alien game.
. The game is well paced, and parts of high intensity and stress are followed by parts were there is nothing ... or is there? Sometimes it takes a while before you come across the next threat, but you never really know when it will happen. This suspense is a key element of the games atmosphere.
Also the AI of the Alien helps to make it believable that it is in fact looking for you. Not the most comfortable thought to be honest. This feeling ist underlined by the fact that you are not at the top of the food chain, and even as you progress through the game, you don't get there.
For me this is an important point, because there often is a point in a horror game when you reach this top spot of the food chain and it kills the horror aspect. You stop being afraid, and you take the role of the hunter. There may be stress left but no horror (if this makes any sense to you).
When comparing the game to the movie installments of Alien, I think it best compares to the first, and third part. If you expect something like the second movie for instance you will be disapointed. There are weapons but you won't run through corridors with your pulse rifle or a smart gun ... ever.
However you will have moments were you think you are safe, but the Alien gets you. When this happens you most likely became to uncautious (and I for my part usually need a minute or two to gather myself, before resuming to play).
and you and your cardiovascular system can handle the feeling of desperation while fighting for "your" life,

I have been a lover of Pirate genre games since Sid Meier released the first iteration of pirate based sandbox games in 1987 with Pirates!  The first time I played that game my age barely hit double digits and I was hooked from the moment I slipped in the disc on my Commodore64 and began playing.  The pirate game sandbox open world genre has had its ups and downs, and those years where it was practically absent from the gaming market with no or very few titles being released.  However, in the recent decade us open world pirate game genre lovers have had their fair share and shake of titles available on Steam and through other mediums offering some degree of selection.
What makes this game special and entertaining as a pirate sandbox game? Well, if you have played Mount and Blade, then you will have an idea of the style and functionality of this game, which is essentially a very extensive paid mod of the original Mount and Blade title.  It uses the same engine and graphics, but places the landscape in the Caribbean and thus introduces ships along with land combat as you as the player traverses through both environments.
While there are quests that are offered by people that are independent, are allies, or may join you as you discover and meet them during your travels, the game plays more like an open world, do what you want, anything goes, type of game than a story driven game built through a chain of quests, as most sandbox RPGs are designed.  The intent of game play is to amass power, stength and infamy through your conquest in the new world.   Will you become a factions greastest leader, its most feared adversary, a traitor, or a notorious loner pirate with no love for anyone but a vicious streak to amass power and gold?  That is the game... anything goes and be whatever and whoever you want to be making the replay value as good as it can get in this type of game.
To break down the game into its simplist structure, you start with a ship and you begin your conquest as you rampage through the caribbean.  Obviously, and like all other RPGs, you start with very little, or just enough to get you going.  You can attack by sea on your ship, which changes the screen to a battle area where the controls of the ship have more of an arcade feel than a simulation - so more like Sid Meier Pirates! than the Sea Dogs or Age of Pirates titles.  You can also embark on land and engage in land battles where you command your troops against the enemy real time, which of course is the epitomy of this game since it was built with the guts of the title, Mount and Blade.
As you gain momentum through victories both land and sea your notoriety steadily increases and the "powers that be", the factions, start having an opinion over your actions, for better or worse.  Your actions can even result in independent faction captains forming an opinion over your behavior for better or worse.  This is represented by a plus/negative point system to gauge your relations with the major factions and their respective captains who traverse the map looking for fame and fortune just like you but in the name of their faction.  You can join any one of the powers or simply accept a letter of marque authorizing you to unilaterally attack their enemies.  If you decide to attack without authority by any one faction your acts are branded as piracy and you gain a negative appeal from all factions regardless of whether they are at war with the faction you attacked or not.  There are also the factionless, Pirates, Picaroons, Smugglers, who sail with no allegiance that if attacked and destroyed you will gain positive notoriety with all factions, so that balance is present in the game mechanics.
Your character and the characters that you find to join you and ultimately sail a ship of your fleet, all gain experience and level.  Your sailors and your soldiers also level through daily automatic training and through your battles and crusades.  While your sailors and soldiers experience simple leveling with automatic point increases in their skills/attributes and combat prowess, whereby you don't manually increase their respective skill traits and attributes, you and your catains are an entirely different story.  You as well as your captains level up as you/they gain experience, and you receive a series of points to apply to respectively to your attributes, skills, combat skills and traits... yes, there are actually four components to leveling your character and your captains.  Attributes will determine the maximum skill value you can accumulate by skill related to the respective and applicable attribute, skills enhance your combat abilities, tracking, sail and ship proficiency and a lot more, while you also increase your combat skills based on your preference, for example two handed weapons, firearms, cannons and or one handed weapons, even bows that you can find on the natives.  You also gain trait points that afford bonuses to your various skills and or abilities.  The greater your attributes the higher you can increase their relative skills that are dependent upon those attributes, which also has a bearing on combat skills.
In addition to the leveling of your character by numeric values on your character sheet, you also gain what is called, "Renown".  Each action and or reaction in game equates to Renown that you gain through victorious endeavors battling other faction vessels and armies.  As you increase your Renown you gain a greater posterity represented by military officer positions, i.e. Ensign, Captain, Commodore and like names.  This will enable you to own plantations and engage in commerce and trade between your holdings in different colonies throughout the caribbean, purchase larger ships, have more soldiers, and other various but similar overall benefits to your gameplay.
The game truly lets you follow your own destiny.  If you join a faction and take over a warring faction's colony you can request to become its governor.  If you are selected, you control that town, as well as its defense, city buildings and production resources.  If you conquest a town as an independent captain successfully and assume control of that town, you can name your faction and become an independent faction within the caribbean, one that you can wage war against the other factions, Spain, France, Dutch or the Pirate faction, or can establish trading pacts with other factions.
The game has the flavor of Sid Meier Pirates! but with the execution of Mount and Blade gameplay and corresponding tactics, and although the feel of game play may be arcadish rather than simulation, there is greater depth with each interaction by combat in game.  You want to take that town, then you have to beseige the town.  If the town can withstand a seige for days on end then you either scale the walls with your troops or take the battle to the fort by sea with your ship to weaken its defenses then take the battle to the shores.  Land battles are real time and while you can only position your soldiers on the map and provide simple orders during combat, you are also dropped into the middle of battle fighting side by side with your contingent.  Sea battles start with your ship, but can end on the deck of the other ship fighting along side your men to eliminate the enemy soldiers and sailors to succesfully take the ship as your prize. You can modify your ship making it more combat resilient, or carry more tonnage for trading or loot, and purchase larger or smaller cannons on the various decks depending upon the type of ship.
Although the graphics are a bit dated for a game released in 2015, this game is more substance over style, and if you love the open world sand box pirate genre and can accept a game with charisma and depth but may not be all too pretty then this game offers a unique perspective to its gameplay for this genre.

By god someone made Sid Meier's Pirates 2! Except with mount and blade battles and the ability to walk around towns!
Is it polished? God no! Is it bug free? Hell no.
It IS however, a much more enjoyable and accessible game than the entire Age of Pirates series. If you have finished Black Flag, and are tired of replaying Sid Meier's Pirates! Pick this up. Its feature complete, and a hell of a lot of fun. A little knowledge of the Mount and Blade Engine goes a LOOONG way, as that game isn't particularly user friendly either. (hint F does everything from boarding to swinging on a rope. :P)
Its also not very well optimized,  You definitely should be using a mid-to-high range rig for the bigger fleet fights.
If you have never played Pirates! You are a captain of a small vessel, and you sail around the caribbean accepting missions, joining factions, trading, committing piracy, or whatever your heart desires. Buying ships, building a fleet, and one day starting your own faction is all possible.
Combat is typical mount and blade combat, with an arcadey Pirates! style ship combat. Boarding reverts to M&B combat which allows for some really fun fencing and shooting of mens with muskets. Ive won a few fights by hiding in the highest mast and shooting my foes.
Overall this is a really great game if you are looking for Sid Meier's Pirates 2 and love mount and Blade. Worth every penny on sale, and I don't regret buying this game at full price. What else is a pirate to do after watching Black Sails?

This was one of the very first space RTS games I have ever played back in my early teens. With the remastered edition, graphics are slightly updated and everything (especially UI) is given a better polish. For it's age (and update), it can still hold value for space fans.
I haven't completed the first Homeworld but have the second (and am still sort of unfamiliar with the story). Basically, you play as this race called the Hiigarans. The game starts with the Hiigarans attempting to finish constructing their mothership but are quickly interrupted by attacking Vaygr enemies. From what I understood from the first game, there are 3 ancient power cores in the universe that if all three are collected by the wrong people, "end times" can ensue.
The
follows a somewhat unique sequence. There is no base to build. There are no supply depots. There are no factories. There is only the mothership! The mothership is capable of building resource collectors, battle units from interceptor to capitol ship size and mobile resource centers. It is the headquarters that will provide everything necessary and will take your leftover units to the next level. Capitol ships and space stations are also units that can create more units. The issue here is that certain units require certain modules to build. A capitol ship cannot build frigates unless a frigate module has been built. Same concept applies with the space station. The challenge here is trying to balance out the fleet while being conservative with resources. The RTS factor to the game is unique in the sense that most of the crafts you build come in squadrons (except for the larger units like frigates). The space in which you can tell the units to move is on a 3D plane (the Z axis positioning can be modified by holding shift and the right mouse button). This adds some substance to the game as you can ambush your opponent in 3D! Having the right setup and formation can really bolster defense. Choosing units isn't too much of a hassle. If you find that your selecting repair units as well as military units, there is a special setting within the options to prioritize selection of military units. This is a good way to keep your peon units out of fights. There can be a lot going on at times and it can be hard to keep track of units. Pressing space will allow the player to zoom out and see the ENTIRE battlefield. This is a good way to manage your units. To make the camera go up and down for a better view, simply press insert or delete.
There are a few categories of units : strike craft, utility class, capital and frigate. Strike crafts usually come in groups (of 3 to 5) and consist of interceptors, bombers and corvettes. Bombers are more or less meant to strike larger ships and structures. Corvettes are quite slower than interceptors but pack more of a punch in their armor and weapons. Frigate classes have the ability to heal themselves but quite slowly. There are two types of frigates, marine and flak. Flak is meant to deal some heavy damage to structures and larger ships while marine frigates are meant to invade and seize control of structures or even opposing ships. Capital ships consists of carriers (which can build ships) and two battle focused units : destroyers and battle-cruisers. The mothership is the only ship capable of creating such behemoths. Destroyers are quite obvious and are meant to be like boulders rolling from afar but battle-cruisers are definitely devastators. They are able to have 5 strike crafts docked with them and give an additional 2 module slots. These guys are definitely the bad boys of the game.
Resources are harvested by specialty units called resource collectors. Resource collectors need to be told where to go in order to start their operation. They may stop in their tracks when there are no more resources left in an area and will most likely have to be told to move on to somewhere else. A mobile resource center can be created to cover more area and allow your resource collectors to submit their resources there instead of going all the way back to the mothership. Resource collectors are also able to repair units and structures but require additional research to unlock this ability. Research upgrades are available for a lot of units to improve their defense, mobility or offense. New unit types also have to be unlocked through research. Additionally, a few units will have special abilities available to unlock (such as corvettes laying out mines).
The
are pretty good. Definitely an upgrade from the original. The
are good and provide a decent atmosphere. The explosions sound varied as well as the weapons. The dialogue is as intriguing as the story line. Honestly, going from the old graphics to this is really enjoyable. I feel though you could have done just a bit more to make it that much more appealing to the eyes.
Overall, a good game. The ability to fight in three dimensions coupled with it's unique approach to creating units makes the game poke it's head from the crowd. I found the price to be a bit steep and bought this game off a humble bundle. I think if it's for sale under $15 and you're a real space fan, you'll like it. If you're looking for ground breaking space RTS/battle simulator, this isn't it.
RATING : 7.35/10

Who knew a realistic bureaucracy simulator could be so fun. In “Papers, Please” you play an immigration officer in a fake communist country in 1982. You stamp passports, ask for documents, and check every detail from the dates on forms, to the height and weight of the person. The game gets progressively harder adding more details to cross-reference. The person might look a bit different from their passport photo so you fingerprint them and compare it to their record, or if the person’s stated gender doesn't match their appearance you take a scan of them and check their junk. But the best part of the game is the hard moral choices you have to make along the way. You have a family and have to pay for things like rent, heat, food, and medicine. You earn money for each passport you approve or deny but get fined if you make more than 2 mistakes per day. If you suck you might have to take kickbacks form the guards, or even take bribes from terrorist, just to feed your family. If you’re good you can afford to give your kid a gift for Christmas or even move into a better apartment. This game is truly brilliant. It takes what sounds like the worst premise for a game and turns it into one of the most well-executed and bizarrely addictive games I've played in a long time.

Dark Souls 2 is forgettable. Demon’s Souls and Dark Souls weren’t. On paper Dark Souls 2 improves on many problems in the first two games. But at the same time it fails to capture the most important aspects that made everyone love the other games.
Everyone gets hung up on the difficulty of the Souls games. As if that’s the only thing that makes them good. They’re more than that. There’s plenty of bone hard games out there, but none have the same devoted fanbase as the Souls games. There’s more going on here than the marketing or even the fans would want you to think. And that’s where Dark Souls 2 goes wrong. On the surface this is the same as the other two. But when you dig deep you notice there’s nothing there. Dark Souls and Demon’s Souls were rich. This isn’t.
Here’s a comprehensive list of what the sequel gets right. The multiplayer is reliable. In Dark Souls 1 it’s a borderline unusable mess. You can now run the game at any resolution, and the performance is good. That’s the end of the list.
It’s clear that the developers of Dark Souls 2 aimed too high. They tried to outdo the original game, with a team that was unqualified to even dream of doing so. They made a new engine with an improved lighting engine. In trailers it almost looked like a next-gen game! Unfortunately it was so slow they scrapped it before release. What you’re left with is a game that looks worse than its predecessors. There’s almost no contrast, the lighting is mostly flat, the art direction confusing. Words you wouldn’t use to describe the other Souls games.
More importantly though there’s no cohesion to the world. The transitions between environments is nonsensical. There’s far too many locations, and they’re all too small. There’s no way anyone could live in this world. In the other Souls games the worlds were plausible. You saw the remnants of great civilizations, and you could believe in them. There’s maybe a couple exceptions to the rule in Dark Souls 2, but they’re in the minority. Almost every environment you pass through you reach the end and think “oh, that’s it? Ok..”.
The DLC packs do their best to redeem the game. They’re an admirable effort, easily outdoing anything the main game did. There’s hope yet for this team. But after finishing the DLCs and returning to the normal areas one last time I’m not wistful or nostalgic for anything that happened during my journey. I look at the world and all I see is meaningless maps. This isn’t a world with history, where I connected with characters and went on a journey that I’ll remember. It’s just a game. A Souls game should be more than that.
I’m split. Dark Souls 2 isn’t “bad” by any regular metric. But the more I play it the more disappointed I am in it. At some point I’ll replay Demon’s Souls and Dark Souls. I never want to play Dark Souls 2 again.
