Toy Soliders Complete is the original Toy Soldiers tower defense game along with its 2 expansions and the Cold War stand-alone with it's two expansions.
Tower Defense, eh?
The basic game loop:
- You can place turrets in specific locations. Certain turrets (like ani-air and artillery) require larger spaces. Upgrade turrets and fend off the invading forces.
## The main difference here is that you can both directly control any turret giving you more accuracy and better kill counts, as well as using various level-specific vehicles which run on batteries.
Pros:
- Great aesthetic. Love the fact that all the levels are like in a kids room.
- Level design is generally good. Sometimes i was able to place down turrets and then sit back for a round or two and let them go to down on stuff. Other times, there were bosses that would instant kill my turrets. But overall, I feel it was well done.
-Lots of levels.
- Survival and vs modes (didnt play vs),
The Bad
- Over the course of the game, I ran into 2 hard crashes to desktop and one instance where an enemy soldier didnt move and I had to hunt him down after the level was basically over. Over the course of 15 hours this doesnt seem like a huge deal.
- I literally cant play the last mission of the main cold war campaign because it hard crashes to desktop on the loading screen. So thats annoying. Beat everything else though with no simialr issues,
Overall:
While this is still in early access, it generally feels like a finished game with a few annoying bugs, Gameplay-wise I say it is worth it. I am a bit annoyed I cant play one level, but thats one in a lot, so whatever. I do hope they fix it.

In order to survive the player will have to find planets where to recover fuel, oxygen and ore in order to repair possible damages to the ship hull. On our way to the new colony we will need to recover important key resources, that will be needed to create are new colony, and possibly also find other survivors, that will help us repopulate our race!

THERE ARE SPOILERS IN THIS REVIEW, SO TL;DR IT'S DEFINITELY WORTH 96% ON STEAM, GET IT NOW!
I recieved this game as a gift back in January 2015. Played it a little, went back to sweating on TF2.
Tried it again on September 2016, and after 3 days of playing I was hooked, and I still am to the day of writing this review.
It's an extremely fun game. It's far better with friends of course, but I've been playing it alone mostly whilst I've had it, and I still find it to be one of the best games I've ever played.
It fits in perfectly with a mashup of RPG and FPS. Collecting a whole range of new guns and other equipment whilst going along a story I could've never thought of in my dreams! (I mean that in a good way.)
Many people say that this game doesn't have as good of a story or atmosphere as the first in the series. And I can see why they think that. The first game's story was much less dialogue and more freeloading around as a mercenary on the hunt for a vault in a desert wasteland. This game's story has more of a Hollywood-esque style, as you constantly hear from and know about your main villain, with his jackassy tone of voice and his lovable dark comedy. You know in the end you'll kill him, and it feels more like a movie. This can be either better or worse depending on what your preferences are.
Comparing it to the first game, this game is a lot better in terms of gameplay. Holding down crouch is a lot more practical that pressing it and pressing it again to stop crouching, in my opinion, plus in this game you don't lose sprint speed whilst jumping. Also, last game didn't have a minimap, which was a pain.
The 4 non-DLC protagonists in the game are similar to the 4 in the last game. You have your army man with a turret, your siren with magic powers, your tall sniper guy and your muscular man who likes guns and punching. However, the skills are much different, with the exception of Axton. Maya's phaselock puts enemies in the air for a short time, Salvador's gunzerking lets you hold two of your guns in a furious rampage and Zer0's decepti0n lets you go invisible whilst creating a clone, letting you be able to play in a much different way than just sniping. This lets players relate to their favourite classes back in the first game, aswell as giving them a new taste of skills.
The atmosphere in this game is one of the best I've seen, and fits perfectly with the choice of soundtrack. Each track is made to perfectly represent the atmosphere in the area, some of the best being the Southern Shelf, Caustic Caverns and Sawtooth Cauldron.
So, overall, a great game! Definitely deserves its ratings. Get it now!

Woo! I finished Blood & Gold: Caribbean. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥was this game fun.
TL;DR I recommend this game if you played Sid Meyers Pirates and wished it was alot deeper, or played Mount and Blade: Warband until the King phase but couldn’t finish it. Otherwise, it’s too buggy and difficult to be an entry into Warband, and too deep and complicated compared to Sid Meyers Pirates.
I think the people who considered this a spiritual Sequel to Sid Meyers: Pirates! were right on the money. While the engine is Warband, and the mechanics of town management, trading, and combat are identical to Warband. I really feel like the flow of the story is completely the same as Pirates!.
Warband had no story, it was basically mechanics in a medieval setting. But Sid Meyers’s entire focus was attempting to re-unite your family and kill of an evil Spaniard. Blood & Gold ramps this up to 11 by giving you a love interest, more than 2 evil spaniards, and basically a completely conquerable world. It’s alot deeper and more enjoyable than Sid Meyers Pirates! and it takes some of the best parts of Warband and applies it to a pirate game.
But that combination is the biggest hurdle of wether or not you should play this game. Warband's engine means this game comes with alot of jank. Fallout 3 jank doesn’t even come close. The horse races look like they came right out of Far Cry 2′s map editor. Sometimes if a musketeer didn’t move after his wall fell, he’d be floating in space like Wile-E-Coyote. I played a bunch of ship battles were my entire crew was just getting knocked out by something. You can’t designate compaions as non-combatants so every battle had a Treasurer, secretary of state, and my food shopping guy going in with the battle hardened veterans. Also when I sold my slaves to the slave dealer, he’d teleport out after one batch, when he normally would stay in town for a week. Also the tutorial Text didn’t stay on screen long enough for me to read every one of them, so there is a couple game concepts I’m not completely clear on. I think they should stay up until you click accept, and then have an option to disable tutorials later.
But dude. I had so much fun. I had fun pretending to be the danish queen to steal territory from my fellow captains. I had fun using ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to bring captains over to my faction. Every sea battle was amazing. Each of the weird quests is worth doing at least once. I loved doing Ann’s weirdly sadistic quest line. I thought the end game was amazing. I liked firing the blunderbuss. I liked swinging the Axe-pistol. I liked defending and attacking in sieges. I liked how your cabinet of officials ride on the boat with you so you can do business outside of towns.
I think my favorite memory of this game will be when my ship was broadside with another ship. I had just switched from grapeshot to soild balls. (Grapeshot by the way, is designed to eliminate crew without damaging the sails or hull. Solid balls damage the hell out of the hull.) All the cannons were loaded, I said the order to fire. Just complete carnage. I didn’t realize 42lb cannons could do so much damage.
The raw time it took me to finish the game was about 2-3 weeks, 41 hours in total. That’s from start to credits with my prior knowledge being 300 hours in warband and 30-40 hours in Sid Meyers.

This game is like a beautiful graceful wolf in sheeps clothes.
It looks astounding, the graphics are really good, seen the size of the world you can explore (with no loading screens, except when you jump into the game, of course). The game is at times so detailed, your mouth will drop from astonishment. I mean, they put in details you tought were extinct in the modern day videogames. (e.g. when a player executes an action, when for example he's reloading his rifle, you can see this in great detail. Or the AI behaves very realisticly. etc.) This game feels so alive, you will wander around in it's world, feeling as if you're actually hunting.
Then comes along, the business model. Here is the only, and game-breaking problem I have with the game. The business model is god awful. It claims it's a F2P game, wich it is, to a very small degree. If you want to be able to hunt more than one type of animal, with more than one gun, you will have to pay. A lot. When you just want to be able to hunt all types of game, you will pay $35 a year. But you can't hunt any type of animal with the same starters gun. No no, when you want to hunt birds, you'll need a different gun. When you hunt big game, you need a different gun. They use this system on everything. You'll pay at least $60 A YEAR, just to be able to play the 'full game'. Take that with a grain of salt, because upon purchasing this package, you get all types of hunting licenses, "full acces to all hunting grounds" (this is an actual feature of the package, even tough you can roam around everywhere without this package.), and about 7 guns. You'll need to pay aditionally, when you want extra items, wich are particularly usefull , such as a game-specific caller (attracts the game you are hunting.). Etc.
They claim this is a F2P game, but you get a rather meagre demo, instead of an actual F2P game. When you want to play the actual game, you'll pay a lot of money. Unfortunately, there is no other alternative, than to pay. They force you to pay, because you can't play the game without opening your wallet.
A missed opportunity, in my eyes, as the business model kicks this otherwise great game in the nuts, over, and over, and over..

So I'm not going to lie, I've never heard of this game prior to a few days ago on its steam release, which is a shame really because I am normally quite happy to support some indie games from the start if they show promise, obviously taking advantage of getting the game for a cheap price would have been nice to but I can happily say now after taking the £15 steam plunge I am very happy with my purchase.
To start this review as an example, I started playing at 6pm, I stopped playing at 4am.
I started out by doing the first 3 tutorials thanks to watching the space engineer’s chief playing it on twitch I wanted to know what it was all about.
I stopped playing that to go straight to playing the game with a friend that I convinced to buy it also, I changed the default port to the 'Minecraft' port to avoid another setting on the port forwarding on my router, this is a practice I do all the time along with most people I know now to make everything easier, it’s almost like it’s become the default 'Gaming Port'.
We both spawned in, right next to some materials with little to know idea what they are for, a quick 3 minutes floating around the menu system and I've got the controls down with no issue. I even re-binding the talk key to the `¬¦ key next to 1 as I find this to be my default 'console' key since the burnt orange golden days of 'Half-Life', I am to yet use the console but now I have the facility to add commands if I need to fix the game or edit something beyond my control, which is a nice feature to debug any game rather than just give up.
The base game is "Gather X, Smelt in Y, Create Z, Repeat" until you have basic systems in place, needless to say getting these systems up and running take a while but once you do its very therapeutic having it all work while you sit back and wait for your tech tree research (Default T) to trickle down the timer to unlock the next challenge to learn.
The learning curve at the start is very high, but in reality its literally just building blocks over the base items, i.e. Faster loading arms, special task arms, faster loading belts, underground belts, electric over fuel burning furnaces etc.
Once you have conquered that base knowledge you will be well on your way to conquering the rest of the game and getting smashed by the 'Zerg' like aliens that are attracted to your base by the pollution you create.
The graphics? Old school Starcraft / Fallout 1 style, an art type I can appreciate for years when done well in the mix of fluid animations such as a the steam and fire.
Gameplay? Loving it, totally addicted but I can already foresee it not being for everyone that enjoys micro system management.
Value for money? 100%, I believe any game that can hold my attention for large blocks of time and that can give myself equal to double hour per £/$ is worth it, if you pay £1 per play of 'Time Crisis' or any other popular arcade games for 15 minutes tops then its totally worth 1hr - £/$1. This game has already drawn in 11 hours for its £15 purchase and that’s after one play through.
Fun element? Very, I vastly believe however that the game is / will be more fun when playing with other people just like most of these games like 'Space Engineers', 'Minecraft' or 'Terraria' etc, again the fun element depends on the learning ability of your team and what you each like to specialize in.
I'd say I would give this game a solid 8.5/10 so far, that I could see going up, as I have not fully explored it as of the time of writing this review, giving it some form of steam workshop modding compatibility will vastly further the life of the game I feel like 'Space Engineers' has done.
If I was to give this game a review in one sentence, I would finish it off with:- "A game where you manage your management and lose your evenings with OCD overload."

+ Brings back what we liked about the original; combat, a variety of cool enemies to get destroyed by, etc.
+ Patches bring balance to weapons/armor - That OP build you hate? Got nerfed. Want to use that obscure weird and unpopular weapon? It's probably viable.
+ Light shafts are absolutely gorgeous and give you all the more reason to praise the sun
+ Wind. Cloth and the like with actively react to the wind, and show that that passage has quite the gust going through it without resorting to having a bunch of leaves show you that the wind exists.
+ Difficulty - Not any more infuriating, nor casual than the first.
+ NG+ does more than adjust enemy health and damage to a higher level - it adds new/more enemies, and upgraded or new rewards.
+ Pretty damn well optimized - a moderate PC will achieve 60fps/1080p without drops on max settings.
- As with the first, some areas are badly made (graphics-wise), and more than a casual glance will reveal crappy textures, and graphical shortcuts.
- PvP is still laggy. A majority of fights will be well tolerable, but dying to a swordpoint that's 2 feet away from touching you is infuriating, and this game will give you that experience more than most every modern PvP game. That being said, most lag is able to be adapted to.
- Katanas are still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Gameplay 9/10 - Fun to play, create your own style, with fun and unique encounters. Only held back by online hiccups, and the occasional badly designed enemy/frustrating encounter.
Sound 6/10 - Retains the musical style as the first game, with a large amount of silence countered by "epic" boss music, and the occasional peaceful peace for the safe area. What's missing are the boss themes that don't feel like generic.
Graphics 7/10 - In a tech sense this game is graphically out of date, retaining a Demon's Souls (circa 2009) level of graphics. That being said, despite the out of date tech, the game does look great, sunbeams and wind effects are a very good touch, but graphical shortcuts are still evident.
Overall a solid 8/10 - Does some things better than the first, some worse, but is still Dark Souls and still a lot of fun.

You like Dark Souls? You like dying repeatedly in quest for gear and currency? If so there's a big chance you won't be let down by the successor of one of modern gamings most nerve-wrecking, most unforgiving titles.
Dark Souls 2 tries hard to go above and beyond the first one to the point where it becomes almost self-aware. Why settle for less enemies when you can have more? Why not place an extra trap for the heck of it? You'll almost hear the game asking itself these types of questions as you journey the dark, varied and still beautifully realized environments that only a 'Souls' game seems to offer.  You will quickly learn that the game speaks to you in visuals rather than  blatant exposition. You need to look very deep in order to find any kind of narrative. I understand that some will find this lazy or downright irritating. I, for one, feel that it is one of the games positives, giving the experience a constant sense of mystery and motivation.
Other than that, the game keeps most of its gameplay mechanics intact. You've still got the Souls, functioning as both experience and currency. You've still got a slow, tense (and oftentimes clunky) combat-system in place. And there are still many, many ways to die, some being clever whilst others being downright cheap.
The game runs at a steady 60fps (unlike its technically inferior console counterparts) and holds up in both visual quality and the outlandish gameplay that the game so heavily thrives on. Do not expect to be blown away as you might have been with previous installments, but the game holds up more than enough to merit a recommendation.

A longtime Mac user, I've wanted to play the Homeworld series for years, but I also wanted to start with the original. With the release of Homeworld: Remastered on SteamPlay, I had an opportunity to experience the story from the beginning; an opportunity I seized upon.
But even with updated graphics, the original has NOT aged well. I didn't encounter any of the bugs that others have complained about, but the game is sorely missing a modern feature of any major RTS: speed control. Jump in, analyze the objectives, formulate a response... and then wait 20 minutes while your ships move around the map. Messed up the strategy? Wait another 20 minutes while your next battle group traverses the map. Really messed up? Start the mission from scratch.
While speed control was apparently added in Homeworld 2, playing the original without it is nothing less than a painful waste of time. What's more, the game sorely needs some light in-game training on how best to deploy new ships and technologies, things which instead are thrown at you with only minimal explanation as to their use.
I wanted to enjoy Homeworld very badly, but the shortcomings of the original have made that impossible. The amount of time the game eats up also meant I was well-past the 2 hours of gameplay refund-cutoff by the time I realized I couldn't play it anymore.

I was torn on whether to give a positive or negative vote to this game. While I did have good fun, it only lasted for the hour or so it took me to complete the first 4 maps, which are pretty similar to each other. The other 2 hours of gameplay  were from trying over and over, and repeatedly failing, to complete the game's fifth and last map, which is absolutely frustrating.
The difficulty curve in this game is so ♥♥♥♥ed up you might as well call it non-existent. The first level is a bit hard because you're still figuring out how to properly land. After you learn that, it's a walk in the park for the next 3 levels. On the fifth and last, however, the game basically becomes Dark Souls, only more unforgiving. You're being constantly chased by ships which fire lasers and guided missiles at you, with no way to fight back. When you do manage to shake them off, you're already low on oxygen and fuel and need to land on a planet to restock. Problem is, almost every time you land, the game's God punishes your insolence by summoning a bunch of asteroids that get attracted by the planet surface and rain upon it, meaning you have to quickly leave before you become space milkshake. When it's not the asteroids, it's more enemy ships coming from absolutely out of the blue already firing at you. There's no way to avoid drawing the attention of these ships, as your field of view is very narrow. By the time you're able to notice them, they're already firing at you.
With all that, you end up not having time to get enough resources, and you eventually die of suffocation or lack of fuel. Thus, I decided not to recommend a game with such a poorly thought out difficulty curve.

The first Toy Soldiers is one of my all time favorite games. The fact that this has the original Toy Soldiers and all of its DLC AND the second Toy Soldier and all of ITS DLC for $10 is amazing. I grew up playing countless tower defense flash games and this game is by far the best in the tower defense genre I have played. The selling-point mechanic that sets this game apart from other tower defense games is that you can take control of your various towers and vehicles on the map to fight the waves of enemies head on. While controlling a tower the game will give it bonus abilities, for example an AI mortar tower will fire one round then aim and fire again; when the play controls that same tower they can now fire three mortars in quick succession or take control of one fired shell, altering its course slightly and speed dramatically. However you can play the entire game without touching a vehicle or controlling a tower and play it as any other tower defense game, the vehicles and tower control will just give you that extra edge when things get tense and enemies slip through the lines.
This game is beautifully themed and designed, all the soldiers, vehicles, towers, and environments are in the style of an old war diorama model kit. The vehicles are all wind up, the soldiers are all display figures, the towers are all little glued together models, and the maps all take place in open model terrain cases, complete with painted cardboard sky and cloud borders on maps that give you a plane.
One of my favorite parts of the game is the ability to pause it at any time and enter "Tilt-Shift mode" which brings the depth of field and focal point really close up and drops the camera to near the ground so you can take some awesome screenshots, check out my Toy Soldiers screenshots on my profile for some examples.
The maps offer a fair bit of challenge to them but you can always make it harder by playing on a harder difficultly. There are other gamemodes like Survival and with this complete pack there's even multiplayer, but I haven't tried that out yet.
A final note is that the music and sound design is superb, Signal has really made a great game, I consider this my 'perfect game' for this genre.

Minecraft is in 3D; Terraria in 2D sidewise; Factorio is in birds-eye view. However, the gameplay feels very different from either of these experiences. This game is all about supply chain management and logistics micro-management. If you liked Anno 1404 or 2070, you will fall in love with this game.

Start from using your hands to collect ore and finish by having complicated logistics networks that involve multiple conveyor belts, pipes with different liquids of various temperatures, trains and drones, and do so on massive scales.
Tech tree, variety of resources, vehicles, evolving combat and having an actual end goal – build a spacecraft to leave the planet, make it feel simply perfect. It feels like one of those games that I will play all weekends long, never touch it for a few months, play another weekend from start to end, repeat.
Overall, this game should serve as a Golden Standard of how Early Access Games should work (seen only 1 bug from 11 hours of play), and not what some of us have experienced… Looking at you, developers of Spacebase DF-9.

Note: This review was originally written prior to the 2.0 rebalance patch.  While the 2.0 patch gets the game to much better state, the original version of Homeworld 1 still remains better playing than the Remastered version; I have to stand by my thumbs down.
---
Homeworld 1 is in my opinion the far better of the two games and is unfortunately not well maintained in the Remastered version.
Homeworld 1 was a game of relatively slow naval battles.  There was time to plan meaningful maneuvers, and the game has a certain grace many other RTSes lack as a result.  Carefully managing the units you had was in many ways more important than simply building a large number of units or even always matching units against their appropriate counter-units in fights.
Homeworld 2 was headed by a new lead designer who decided to throw out most of what made HW1 feel unique and just make a Starcraft clone.  Rock-paper-scissors balance taken to extremes; huge fleets that could be wiped out in seconds; a game won more by clicks-per-second and sheer numbers than strategy.  It lost much of its grace and was a massive disappointment for me.  On top of that, another of its problems was a very poorly implemented dynamic difficulty system that scaled the number of enemies you'd face on some missions based on your fleet size and resources at the start of the mission.  On paper it's an ok idea, but in practice it punishes you for keeping your fleet alive and wasn't well tested or balanced so that sometimes you would face an unreasonable number of enemies.
Homeworld Remastered puts the first game in the second's engine, and it is unfortunately rebalanced to be more like the second - complete with poorly implemented dynamic difficulty scaling.  Version 1.0 was nearly unplayable due to the balance being so bad.  The 2.0 patch pushes balance a bit closer back to true Homeworld 1 and reigns in the unreasonable difficulty scaling, but it still doesn't feel right.  Fleets that were viable with careful management in the original game still get wiped out too quickly.  Strike craft aren't as effective as they should be.  Plus there are AI problems with the units not engaging enemies the way they should.
This isn't just a matter of me wanting the game to exactly duplicate Homeworld 1 due to nostalgia goggles.  I replayed the original recently and I still think it's a better balanced, more entertaining game than the compromised version of it they crammed into the Remastered engine. It's an incredible shame because the updated graphics of the Remastered version are great.
I'll grant that building essentially two Remastered versions from scratch (one based on HW1's engine and another based on HW2) would be a bit too much to ask, and I'm thankful that they included the original versions in this package.  However, given that the Remastered version is a fairly big departure from the original, it is disappointing that they couldn't then do a very bare minimum of work to make the original versions more easily playable on modern systems.  Specifically, it's always been possible to configure HW1 to run in modern widescreen resolutions but it requires a registry edit to do so - not too hard for a savvy user, but still annoying.  Would it really have been that hard for them to do minimal things like update the options menu to be able to directly select modern resolutions?

This is repetitive but really fun. It's a casual 2D strategy Indie game which includes a bonus Tower Defense game-mode, and more. This game is more of a game where you run in the background whilst doing other things in the non-virtual world. For example: I love to paint my Games Workshop miniatures, so I play this game in the background, listening to calm, enjoyable music while i'm painting my miniatures. If my Dwarfs need help or require micro-managing so they won't release Doom, I pause my painting and micro-manage them. When it's all safe, I return to painting.
The main game-play or game-mode is the, 'Arcade mode'. This is where you select a difficulty a time limit, so a random generated underworld spawns. Your Dwarfs will go mining anywhere they like, although you can set them paths to mine for a bit of gold. Caves will spawn in the map which can contain good or bad things or nothing for your Dwarfs. It could be an empty cave, it could filled with water of lava that will spread killing anything in it's path until contained or until it reaches and destroys your town. It could be filled with goblins, or even a boss goblin; 'Shaman'. It could be filled with treasure or with rich minerals to mine. Minerals will spawn around the map to be mined so it can be turned into gold.
The 'Campaign' are basically challenges as well as a tutorial.
The 'Skirmish' are basically bonus game-modes. The first one is 'Sandbox'. This is basically where you can play around with the underworld. Spawn in everything you like and mess around with the settings of things like: water or lava speed. You can make the world for your dwarfs to thrive, or just die. It's basically arcade mode but instead of a random generated world, you get to create the world before or during when your dwarfs mine, with no time limit.
Rush mode is basically Arcade mode but with one difficulty and no time limit. The catch is however, new Dwarfs spawn all the time and you have 200 lives (so if 200 dwarfs die, you die/loose).
Dark mode is like Arcade mode but there is only one difficulty and no time limit. However the catch is, everything that isn't mined is hidden. So you don't know where the minerals are or the caves.
Endless mode is basically Arcade mode but you decide how big the map is as well as there is no-time limit.
Carnival game mode is basically a bonus game mode. You are a dwarf and you have throw axes at moving targets. You can move within a small area but you only have 10 axes. This game-mode is fun to compete with friends to see who can get the highest score.
The last game-mode is called 'Base defence.' This basically tower defence but with a twist. You get to create your own paths with digger Dwarfs. Whenever a portal spawns, just before the goblins spawn, a digger dwarfs spawns. He'll try to dig to your village the quickest way possible, but you can always create him your own paths, for some money. Whenever you kill a goblin, you get money. And like any other tower defence game, you can buy towers and then upgrade them.
Overall I think this game is great and fun to play. It's worth getting this game if you like casual games.

Lemmings meets tunnels and dwarves.
Dwarfs!? is top down 2d strategy game developed by Tripwire Interactive. You play as an overseer whose goal is to manage the dwarve's mining operations and make sure things go smoothly.
As an overseer you have to control the safety of your mine through moving units, dealing with environmental hazards and building new structures. Gold is the main currency in the game. It is obtained by simply letting miners detroy blocks on the map. Miners will go off on their own detroying blocks and earning gold and aren't all directly controlled by the player. However, the direction the dwaf is moving in can be manipulated by selecting them and draging  (which creates a path) in a direction to make them move somewhere else. This can't be done sparringly however as it costs gold and the further the direction you send the dwarf, the more it costs. That is why it is best to let the dwarves do their own thing and simply resolve problems when they arise (like lemmings). There are also traps such as water and lava (which floods the mine). When they reach your town hall, the game ends. To deal with this, you have to block the entrance with walls. Lava will break down walls over time, so you have to set explosives to create holes for lava to fall into. Further hazards are enemies such as goblins, spiders, skeletons etc which can be found within the mines. To help deal with these foes you can recruit soldiers. All units gain experience as they complete their tasks, which makes them perform better when they level up. Besides building walls and dynamite, you can also build outposts. Outposts can be used to train your soldiers which increase health and damage. Training takes time and the more time it takes, the more gold it costs.
There are plenty of game modes to play. Campaign involves completing challenges which range between getting a certain score, number of units or defeating foes with limited troops. There is also a tower defence mode, where you have to defend your town hall against waves of foes through clever tunnel and tower placement. Arcade mode has you explore a massive map in timed game, trying to get the highest score. Skirmish includes a variety of different modes including a carnival game (where you have to hit the targets) and endless mode (play a 60 minute game). With all theses game modes available, there is plenty of replayability.
Audio is decent. The music is alright and gives a somewhat light-hearted medieval feel. Voice acting from the tutorial guy is decent as well.
Graphics are dated. Textures don't have alot of detail to them and the models are basic.
If you enjoy games where you can sit back and let your workers do most of the work, and solve issues when they occur, as well as having plenty of game modes, this game is for you.

Concept: Last Horizon is a minimalistic space exploration and action game where the objective is to save the human race following the destruction of earth. In order to do this you will have to discover a habitable planet, colonize it and redevelop your civilization. Throughout this journey you will be required to accomplish mini objectives that come in the form of discovering, mining and collecting life and resources from other planets in order to terraform your new base planet. Throughout your journey you will come across other survivors.
Minimalistic presentation: In staying true to the concept of the game everything featured within Last Horizon is kept to the bare minimum. In this regard we are talking graphics, sound, game play mechanics, the whole kit and caboodle. You may think that being so simplistic that it would subtract from the experience but it is a strong positive in the game. Everything is present when and where you need it to be and when you don’t you really are given the sensation that you are exploring an expansive universe. It’s an intelligent aesthetic that helps create a more immersive environment. Had Pixeljam gone the other way it would not have meshed nearly as well as what it does.
Insane difficulty starting out (for average gamers): In my first few attempts at playing I felt like a space pinata or pinball. I was bouncing off of planets left and right. Apparently this is the experience that most players have. I didn’t feel as though there were nearly enough tutorial information in the game and while the developers may explain that it’s part of the basic nature of the game the information that is provided isn’t enough to to avoid early frustrations with the game. Certainly, once you have taught yourself how to play the game gets easier – yet obviously more rewarding – it’s a steep learning curve that will frustrate many gamers to the point of quitting before the game sucks them into its web.
No native controller: In my opinion Last Horizon is dying to be played by using a controller. It makes the game play so much easier and feels a lot more natural than when playing without it. However, disappointingly there is is no native controller support in the game. You’ll have to use a controller companion in order to play using one. This is, by far, the most grievous mistake in judgment that Pixeljam have made in the development of the game.
Not a lot of content: If truth is told there isn’t a lot of content within Last Horizon. Once you learn how to play and become competent at the basic game play you may get a further hour or two tops out of the game. Learning how to play properly will likely be the most time consuming part of the title. It’s a good little game but you’re not going to get much mileage out of it. That’s not necessarily a bad thing but those of you seeking a longer game should look elsewhere. However, those of you looking for a more casual title who would like to spend an evening – or part thereof – with a good solid title will find this satisfying their need.
Last Horizon is a very reasonable minimalist space exploration title that will provide you with a few hours of steady game play. In regards to a price-quality equation it’s about right.

This is a strategy game that focuses heavily on micromanagement...
...and that's about the only thing I can nail down about this game...
It has so many elements from other titles but it's managed to not only merge all these obscure niche gameplay elements but also improve on a lot of existing elements.  For instance crafting exists similar to other titles like Minecraft but they've eliminated most of the tedious parts of crafting in general, then they add onto it by allowing the player to automate crafting very early on.
It also has a combat system, but it's simplified enough to not require shooting skills while trying to focus more on the micro-management style of the game.  Even the micromanagement seems pretty streamlined and intuitive.  One of the biggest issues most factory style management games have is restrictive access on imputting and outputing items from a machine but Factorio has impressed me so far in that respect.
Although in my opinion the depth displayed thus far is what's impressed me most.  I remember when the Buildcraft and Industrial Craft mods for Minecraft were new and I followed their development into Tekkit and eventually FTB, those mods made that open world survival game special for me, Factorio fills that same itch that those mods once scratched, but I feel Factorio just seems much more focused though.
All in all Factorio is still a niche game and will only appeal to specific gamers, if you like this style of game then you really can't go wrong by picking this title up.  Even in it's current early access form it's still very playable.

Initially I played this game for a few hours and hit pretty much every problem you could possibly hit. I wrote it off as poorly designed with terrible AI.
Then, some weeks later, I went back to it. And I loved it.
Pros
-----
- The old school low-fi sci-fi art aesthetic is just fantastic.
- Amanda Ripley is a great (almost Freeman-esque) protagonist who thinks (not shoots) her out of problems.
- The voice acting is excellent.
- Two of the enemy types (no spoilers here) have fantastic AI and are terrifying opponents.
Cons
-----
- The human enemies are dire. Their AI is awful and really breaks the immersion of the game. It would have been infinitely better if they had been removed and the only other humans you heard/saw were through glass or on the radio. Honestly I've had moments where I'd sprint right up to 'bad guys' and it takes them 15-20 seconds to react when I'm 3 inches from their face. Randomly some of them don't even acknowledge you at all.
- There is basically nothing in the way of tutorials. Even after trying to Google the purpose of the Rewire functions most people online seem unsure or conflicted about what they actually do. A lot of the items and more nuanced mechanics are only explained if you happen to glimpse the right Tool Tip on the loading screen...
Summary
----------
There's nothing out there really like this game and although CA tripped up with a few things you can't argue it's a fantastic bit of stealth gaming, a good story and abrilliant homage to Ridley Scott's movie.
Recommendations
-----------------------
- Play it on HARD! The difficulty below that is just dull.
- If you get frustrated that you've done the same bit too many times, QUIT! Honestly, come back to it another time and you'll probably breeze through it, this game rewards patience.

Last Horizon:
~~~~~~~~~~
Earth is no longer habitable and your mission is find another suitable planet where mankind can re-establish itself. So, my dear astronauts - take control of your spaceship and find our next home!
Last Horizon is an action/exploration game where you take control of a spaceship which has the capability to terraform ecosystems so when you reach your new home you will have all necessary resources for the human race. However, before you get there you will need to make sure you keep the fundamental resources you and your vessel needs to successfully reach your destination.
Your spacecraft does not have any weapons whatsoever, all you have is fuel, oxygen and a hull (structure of your craft). As you take off and start your journey through space, you will very quickly see grey arrows coming up around the screen. These arrows will show you the planets that are in that direction.  You will use fuel and oxygen, and will without doubt have a few close encounters with meteors, shooting stars or even natural satellites, which will damage your hull; the only way to re-fill your gauges of fuel and oxygen as well as repairing your hull is to land safely and gently on those planets. Each landing will be rewarded by points; the best landing will give you 2000 points. Just a couple of hints for you: do not land in the water or anything pointy….Not a good idea! White arrows will tell you where to land your vessel to collect resources or rescue another human colonies.  Purple arrows are really fun - just go right at them and you will receive a warm welcome from an alien race who have firepower on their planet and also on their vessels. One of the best ways to get rid of these little pests is to lead them into a field of asteroids…. BOOM! Keep an eye on your fuel and oxygen for me or you will get Boomed too!
A couple of other things you have to be careful of: black holes and suns - get to close to them and you will die!
I really enjoy this game, play even if it can be quite frustrating at times (especially with these Alien pests), and for the control, I have absolutely no issues playing this game with the keyboard. I like the gravity feel when you reach a planet’s atmosphere - it is fun! Difficulty seems to double each time you beat a level. Nice 2D graphics and the game is really well priced.

Positives:
~~~~~~~~

-	Fun and challenging game
-	Nice 2D graphics
-	Easy to control
-	Four flights to beat
-	Achievements
Negative:
~~~~~~~
-	No weapons to defend yourself against the aliens
-	A bit repetitive
I really enjoy this game and I thoroughly recommend it!
9/10

Last Horizon is an entertaining little roguelite that lives up to the Dino Run legacy of Pixeljam. The game is fun, and features very good visual and sound design with a hypnotizing space ambient soundtrack. The only downside is the game's miniature size.
The core Lunar Lander style gameplay is a lot of fun - the gravity mechanics and a solid control scheme make navigating the depths of space interesting even after hundreds of successful landings. Seeing a 'PERFECT' pop up after an especially smooth descent to a planet's surface is very satisfying, expecially if you've done it with minimal fuel. The resource management is very simple, and it is very difficult to kill yourself by running out of fuel or oxygen. I'd like a little more of a challenging strategic experience on that front, but if you're not the type to get off on crushing diffculty and howling curses at the RNG, you'll probably enjoy that. Death usually comes at the hands of a Spelunky-style Rube Goldberg machine: bounce off a fast-orbiting moon into an astroid field, then ricochet into the waiting surface guns of a hostile alien world for the lose.
I also think that the look and feel of the game deserves a call out - space, its denizens and its planets are all very minimal and a bit cute, along with the very well done but sometimes cartoony sound design. The music is invaluable as well, the haunting soundtrack really sets the mood for a lonely journey through deep space.
My only complaints are with the size of the game: The four available missions are slowly ramp up difficulty, adding aliens, massive asteroid belts and orbital debris around planets, but they make me long for an endless mode of some kind - after playing all four missions the only replay value really comes from playing the last mission over and over again. I'd also love an optional difficulty setting -reduce resources to an amount that encourages real conservation and risky moments.
Overall a great game for $5.

Most of the combat happens on ships, which are too confined and claustrophobic to do any of the fun Mount and Blade stuff like ride your horse through ranks of archers.  This is a more unpleasant shortcoming than it might sound like, because tons of seemingly cool ideas like the ability to climb up riggings to the crow\'s nests just turns into unmanageable blocking and failed swings in the elbow-room-ranges you constantly find yourself in.  Even the handguns aren\'t that great because you really have to be careful not to hit your own troops.  (The ship-to-ship combat is fun enough--but also way too similar to the Sid Meier\'s Pirates remake.)
So, a thumbs down and I\'m sad to say it. As of May 27, 2016 (the release of the campaign DLC), the game is still riddled with [obvious] bugs that make the game almost unplayable.
Since the game uses Mount & Blade's engine, you can imagine how most infantry combat works: you've played it on big open fields in the other games and the AI seems somewhat capable. You see them trying to scale cliffs and they run through rivers to get to you, but it's no biggie, right? Nothing a few arrows can't handle to deal with it.
In this game, however, the maps are highly intricate and have a feeling of verticality to them. There's multiple story structures; debris on the ground... TL;DR there's a TON of stuff for the AI to get stuck on. And what's worse, sometimes they spawn in areas even you can't get to, thus making battles and missions sometimes utterly pointless.
There's a lot of issues with this game. I've only played it for roughly three hours--enough time to amass a fleet and capture/govern my own little corner of the carribean, but in those three hours I've had to alt-f4 and/or replay missions so many times just to get anything done.

Last week I stepped on an ant pile. Thousands of little ants came crawling out of the dirt. This game manages to still have more bugs than that ant pile. Game breaking issues have plagued my first few attempts at starting a new adventure. The overall Game actually wasn't too bad, but like it's been mentioned already, this game is essentially a warband mod...with guns...it's a fire and sword mod actually. Not to mention load times are painful (although this maybe my machine, however the times stay equally long no matter what quality I set the game too). If you get this game make sure to save often, even if the bugs don't get you, the penalties for being defeated are dreadful.

Where do I begin? If this game had a "you buy it, you get everything, all guns/licenses/reserves/etc for a flat $50.00" (which is a new release AAA price), I probably would've done it. But the nickle-and-diming ridiculousness of their membership plans is something I won't accept. Even most MMORPG's have a hard time maintaining a monthly subscription, yet theHunter thinks that people will keep doling out the money to retain to their guns/licenses/access to certain parts of the game.
What if I don't want to play for the full 3 months? It makes the customer feel like they're flushing money down the drain. I'd rather hand over a big chunk up front, get my entire game, and be able to pick it up when I feel like it. Not, oh 5 months down the road I think about trying it again, and they want even more money.
The real trick is that if they do sucker you into paying for a membership, at the end of that time, you suddenly realize... I'm going to lose all my access, but I've got all this progress I want to keep working on, I don't want to lose it and should pay more to keep going! That's how they'll hook you and keep the cash flowing in endlessly, as opposed to simply letting people buy the full game normally and be done with it.
As to the actual gameplay... The animals are few and far between, and most of the time when you find a track, it's frequently not going to be the kind you're allowed to hunt. Which is pretty much only mule deer, and you have one gun. So every time annoying pheasants or whitetail deer pops up on the Huntermate tracking device, you get reminded to either fork over the money or you're blocked from certain content. It's irritating.
The game world itself is gorgeous, and the tracking system is uniquely detailed -- but that's not nearly enough to make me overlook the above issues. I would be a customer, if it weren't for their greedy scheme.
The other hysterical part is that they actually asked their fans to leave positive reviews, because they think all the bad reviews "create a distorted picture of the community's feelings." How about you stop trying to cover up people's genuine reactions to your greediness? The majority are voicing their complaints that this is a bad business model.

Basically what is free is that you can walk around the levels (which are beautiful) and try and track 1 of the 2 animals you are allowed to hunt. Firstly this is depressing because there are around 14 animals currently in the game to hunt, which you can still track even though you can't hunt them. Secondly because the 2nd animal (the rabbit) you can't even hunt because the rifle you started with is too strong (hence all your kills are disqualified).
For those of you thinking, that's fine I can work my way up - well you can't. The only way to earn in game credits is by completing challenges, which award you with so few credits you can't even unlock a single animal lisense for 1 day. You can't buy guns with the in-game currency and if you do manage to complete the challenges there are only a limited number and you have to pay to reset them.
This game does have the potential to be great, but the business model at the minute is rubbish. A much better system might be to have a reward of in-game currency (endless) for trophies. But alas you will have to pay to enjoy anything much past an hour or two's enjoyment.

I've changed my mind, this is not actually a worthy successor to the first game. Nonetheless, I do recommend it.
It feels as though a significant delay has been added to every animation. Your character reacts more slowly, and is trapped within an animation for longer. Fights aren't fun and snappy anymore. They are slow and painful, and it doesn't feel like it's your fault when you end up dying for these slow response times.
The plot isn't mysterious like in Dks1, it's just incredibly vague. Item descriptions used to come with detailed story descriptions, now they usually say something along the lines of "this sword might have belonged to a king who may have done something bad."
The "connected world" feeling is also virtually gone. Because bonfire warping is available from the beginning so you never find shortcuts anymore, and you have to go to Majula for every level up, and also because bad world design.
It still gets my recommendation, though. Because we don't get to have many games like this. No objective beacons, no minimaps, no regenerating health. Those things don't just ruin a game, they're lazy game design. Dks2 design cuts corners, but it's still pretty solid and I wouldn't have put so many hours into it if I wasn't having a good time.

So I'm not going to lie, I've never heard of this game prior to a few days ago on its steam release, which is a shame really because I am normally quite happy to support some indie games from the start if they show promise, obviously taking advantage of getting the game for a cheap price would have been nice to but I can happily say now after taking the £15 steam plunge I am very happy with my purchase.
To start this review as an example, I started playing at 6pm, I stopped playing at 4am.
I started out by doing the first 3 tutorials thanks to watching the space engineer’s chief playing it on twitch I wanted to know what it was all about.
I stopped playing that to go straight to playing the game with a friend that I convinced to buy it also, I changed the default port to the 'Minecraft' port to avoid another setting on the port forwarding on my router, this is a practice I do all the time along with most people I know now to make everything easier, it’s almost like it’s become the default 'Gaming Port'.
We both spawned in, right next to some materials with little to know idea what they are for, a quick 3 minutes floating around the menu system and I've got the controls down with no issue. I even re-binding the talk key to the `¬¦ key next to 1 as I find this to be my default 'console' key since the burnt orange golden days of 'Half-Life', I am to yet use the console but now I have the facility to add commands if I need to fix the game or edit something beyond my control, which is a nice feature to debug any game rather than just give up.
The base game is "Gather X, Smelt in Y, Create Z, Repeat" until you have basic systems in place, needless to say getting these systems up and running take a while but once you do its very therapeutic having it all work while you sit back and wait for your tech tree research (Default T) to trickle down the timer to unlock the next challenge to learn.
The learning curve at the start is very high, but in reality its literally just building blocks over the base items, i.e. Faster loading arms, special task arms, faster loading belts, underground belts, electric over fuel burning furnaces etc.
Once you have conquered that base knowledge you will be well on your way to conquering the rest of the game and getting smashed by the 'Zerg' like aliens that are attracted to your base by the pollution you create.
The graphics? Old school Starcraft / Fallout 1 style, an art type I can appreciate for years when done well in the mix of fluid animations such as a the steam and fire.
Gameplay? Loving it, totally addicted but I can already foresee it not being for everyone that enjoys micro system management.
Value for money? 100%, I believe any game that can hold my attention for large blocks of time and that can give myself equal to double hour per £/$ is worth it, if you pay £1 per play of 'Time Crisis' or any other popular arcade games for 15 minutes tops then its totally worth 1hr - £/$1. This game has already drawn in 11 hours for its £15 purchase and that’s after one play through.
Fun element? Very, I vastly believe however that the game is / will be more fun when playing with other people just like most of these games like 'Space Engineers', 'Minecraft' or 'Terraria' etc, again the fun element depends on the learning ability of your team and what you each like to specialize in.
I'd say I would give this game a solid 8.5/10 so far, that I could see going up, as I have not fully explored it as of the time of writing this review, giving it some form of steam workshop modding compatibility will vastly further the life of the game I feel like 'Space Engineers' has done.
If I was to give this game a review in one sentence, I would finish it off with:- "A game where you manage your management and lose your evenings with OCD overload."

Initially I played this game for a few hours and hit pretty much every problem you could possibly hit. I wrote it off as poorly designed with terrible AI.
Then, some weeks later, I went back to it. And I loved it.
Pros
-----
- The old school low-fi sci-fi art aesthetic is just fantastic.
- Amanda Ripley is a great (almost Freeman-esque) protagonist who thinks (not shoots) her out of problems.
- The voice acting is excellent.
- Two of the enemy types (no spoilers here) have fantastic AI and are terrifying opponents.
Cons
-----
- The human enemies are dire. Their AI is awful and really breaks the immersion of the game. It would have been infinitely better if they had been removed and the only other humans you heard/saw were through glass or on the radio. Honestly I've had moments where I'd sprint right up to 'bad guys' and it takes them 15-20 seconds to react when I'm 3 inches from their face. Randomly some of them don't even acknowledge you at all.
- There is basically nothing in the way of tutorials. Even after trying to Google the purpose of the Rewire functions most people online seem unsure or conflicted about what they actually do. A lot of the items and more nuanced mechanics are only explained if you happen to glimpse the right Tool Tip on the loading screen...
Summary
----------
There's nothing out there really like this game and although CA tripped up with a few things you can't argue it's a fantastic bit of stealth gaming, a good story and abrilliant homage to Ridley Scott's movie.
Recommendations
-----------------------
- Play it on HARD! The difficulty below that is just dull.
- If you get frustrated that you've done the same bit too many times, QUIT! Honestly, come back to it another time and you'll probably breeze through it, this game rewards patience.

Pitch: this is the future soldier! 2054 to be exact. Exo armor and other high tech gadgets have come to the battlefield. You are Scott Mitchell, a US marine to whom Atlas, a mega military corporation is giving a second chance. You'll embark into a worldwide conflict full of actions and thrill.
Now COD Advanced warfare leaves me with a mixed feeling. On one hand, the game delivers its promises with tons of high paced actions. a really good narrative for the solo campaign (with actors delivering a good screenplay) and this unique COD feeling.
But on the other hand, it feels like an unpolished game: the gameplay is chaotic, you don't have that many weapons choice, the graphic engine, while pleasant, feels really heavy at time and we can feel that despite the official claim that the engine was rewritten from scratch, well, they took huge chunks of the old one. AND, many missions feels like a reskin of previous COD ones.
AND, AND, the biggest drawback of this game is the AI. I mean, WTF! Your teammates in missions are completely useless! So many times I found them sitting right next to the ennemies and they don't do anything. They just watch and enjoy the show. From all the COD I played, this one is by far the worst to this regard.
So in the end, I can't say that this game is bad, or that I wouldn't recoomend it, but it's definetely not my preferred COD, but hey, if you get it on sale, why not, you'll get a 10h interactive action movie that will let you taste the future warfare!

Last Horizon is a space action/exploration game where it’s your job to save the human race! Earth has somehow been destroyed and you and your ship are all that’s left. Your job is to find another, hospitable planet and re-establish the human race there. Along the way you’ll need to stop on barren planets to collect fuel as well as collect life from other planets to terraform your new home. Perhaps you’ll even find some other survivors along the way.
Last Horizon is very basic in its presentation throughout but that’s not a bad thing, in fact the minimalist design really suits the game. It’s rather colourful and while all of the models are fairly basic they all look good. The UI is out of your way for the most part but it when it is there it gets the job done without getting in your way. The only issue I had with the presentation is a minor one, the mouse cursor stays visible when you’re playing. Those of you who have read my other reviews will know that this is one of my biggest pet peeves when it comes to gaming and Last Horizon will not escape my wrath! Seeing as you never need the mouse during gameplay (even the menu doesn’t require the mouse) it seems completely stupid, and distracting, to have the mouse cursor visible. But like I said, not a major issue (though the time spent on complaining about it might suggest otherwise).
Last Horizon’s gameplay is again fairly basic (that seems to be a running theme does it not?). You begin one of four missions on what remains on Earth and then you’ll blast off, in search of your new home. Other planets will be pointed out to you in the form of arrows at the edges of your screen. A blank arrow means a barren planet. An arrow filled with white means a planet with some form of life on it. A coloured arrow means a planet with sentient life on it. You’ll need to stop at the first of these two to collect resources and you’ll probably want to avoid the last one.
Speaking of resources, there are three:
Stopping on a planet with life on it will allow you to collect the life from it to be used on your own planet. Taking half will give you a fair amount of points while allowing the planet to survive and taking all of the planet’s life will give you more points but kill off the planet, unless you really care about planets made of particles I’d suggest taking it all to maximise your points.
Back to those missions I mentioned earlier. The first mission is the most basic and therefore easiest. Each mission after that adds a new gameplay element which makes the mission slightly harder than the last. I honestly didn’t notice a huge difference in difficulty between the four different missions so it’s effectively playing the same mission again with some slight variation.
Lost Horizon may not have a huge amount of content, but what’s there is a lot of fun to play. It looks good. It feels good. It sounds good. If you’re unsure, hold out for a discount but if you’re a fan of space exploration games then I’d suggest you pick this one up.

Last Horizon is a fun if brief space exploration game with some very fun uses of gravity. Your world has been destroyed and you need to move to a new planet hopefully picking up life forms, other surviving humans, and avoid hostile aliens along the way.
Unfortunately your fragile ship doesnt have the fuel or oxygen to do so and your forced to make many pit stops on random planets along the way. All have different gravitational pulls so landing can frequently be a bit hair raising especially when landing between two mountains, while avoiding a lava sea, while asteroids and comets slam into the surface around you...
Did I mention their are black holes and aliens who want to blast you to man pulp?
My only criticism is the game is rather short and while its procedurally generated each time having only 4 different game modes each with an increased difficulty means you've probably got 2 - 4 hours of gameplay before you beat the game.
There is a leaderboard if becoming the "best" in the world is your thing and the game is priced nicely at $5 so in my opinion for the cost of about half the price of a movie you get a few hours of hair raising fun.

TL;DR: Casual lemming manager. Once you get over the tutorial it's a quite okay managing strategy game.
Hi mate! Do you like Lemmings? Because that's what Dwarfs basically are, mindless, gold digging lemmings. Get in here and you'll get to be their over
seer! For good measure, in the tutorial missions you'll also get a grain of rowdy men (or dwarves) talking a bit like pirates or woodchucks, or that's how I imagine people like that would speak. Voice acting sounds horrible. Tutorial's fine otherwise, and the game turns out not too bad either.
In Dwarfs!? you control the mindless horde of dwarves on their quest for digging gold and minerals while protecting your base from monsters and natural hazards. Of course, you could just slack off because handing out orders costs precious gold. The dwarves will work independently and bring gold into your coffers. To direct them just makes them go where you want.
So why bother? The mine is full of unknown caves and precious minerals. Minerals bring lots of gold and dwarves will only occasionally find them independently. Also, caves contain either treasure or hazard in the form of monsters or sources of rapidly flowing water or lava. All will destroy your base if you don't stop them. So you got to be ready for some overseeing.
For monsters you need to send in warriors: you can either build a fort near or send a team in with a catapult. How that works is beyond me, but the warrior dwarves seem unaffected by the flight. For water or lava you got to seal the passage before it overflows your base. Unfortunately (and that's the point) the dwarves are mindless and they
eventually open up more holes for the flows. Your walls and wall sealing techniques will counter these, but usually you need a dwarf to go over there and go all kamikaze with a dynamite to finish the job. Tens or even hundreds of dwarves die each game.
Annoyingly, when something (usually bad) happens, you'd of course want to go there immediately. There's usually an icon showing you where it happens and clicking it will get you there instantly. However, there's no button to get back to where you were and if you don't click it fast enough, you'll have to go find it yourself. If it was water or lava, you're probably screwed for that mine.
Several game modes will keep you busy: arcade is the classic mode with several difficulty levels that affect the action costs and the frequency of hazardous caves. The hardest setting is actually very difficult indeed requiring loads of overseering to survive. There's also a sort of tower defense mode, a mode with super fast spawning dwarves, a dark mode where you can't see the caves or minerals (very difficult) and a couple of achievement yielding challenges. Plus a meager mini game where you shoot moving boards like in the games of de olde.
Curiously this one and the F2P version are considered different games: still, the achievements are transferrable between the two versions so you get 2 perfect games if you can ace this one. F2P version does not contain the most difficult settings and the silly mini game so that's basically what you're paying for. Top Leaderboards are a joke though, as it seems someone has acquired a ludicrous and curiously regular amounts of points in all of them.
I recommend it for casual game sessions because I generally enjoyed hoarding the achievements. I'd recommend getting it on sale though, 50 % discount or better. However, if someone asks you to Dwarf in their mine, just don't: the job safety is just not cut for it.

+Atmosphere - playing this at night in a dark room really is scary and I've jumped back in my seat more times than I care to think of. It's so, so tense at times.
+Graphics - they've captured the feel of the 1979 movie perfectly
+Difficulty - this is not an easy game, which is good and bad. It's a hugely rewarding and relieving feeling to finish an area, but also frustrating because...
-Console save points - I really like the in-game implementation, pushing a keycard into a slot etc. I really don't like having to save at specific points. Firstly because it always asks if you want to overwrite which breaks immersion and secondly because the game's so hard you can easily play for 30 minutes and lose all that progress because there's so few save points, or find yourself navigating away from your objective in order to stop yourself losing all the progress up to then. It's the one reason I haven't completed the game as it's just too frustrating to have to re-do long segments over and over because of the difficulty.
I still recommend the game because it has some excellent features and it's often on sale for a reasonable price but if someone can make a quicksave mod it'd be perfect.

(I only recommend this game for the included Classic version of Homeworld.)
Homeworld Remastered:
This is not a remaster! A truer statement is that this is an official Homeworld mod for Homeworld 2. Nothing works the same as it did in the original game. Imagine any other game you like, say Starcraft, but with all the behaviour and stats of all the units changed and many core mecanics changed or simply not working. It really isn't nearly as good a game as the original Homeworld was. The _only_ reason to play the remaster is to experience Homeworld with modern graphics (which will give you an appreciation of what it felt like for those who played the original game when it came out).
Homeworld II Remastered:
A well made remaster. However, Homeworld II is a far inferior game to Homeworld. It takes liberties with the story and the universe which are (to me) comparable to those that Star Wars I: Phantom Menace took with respect to the original trilogy.
Closing Statement:
Homeworld is my favourite game of all time. This remaster is unfortunate as it will give new players a much worse experience than the original game did.
I still recommend this collection purely because it includes the original game (the "Classic" version) which is not sold separately on Steam. Be warned that the Classic version seems to crash on the first mission for many players.

This game is incredible.  It has replay value of the same order as Kerbal Space Program.
For me the story goes a bit like this.  I downloaded the demo sometime in 2014, just to try the game out for 15 minutes.  After the first 5 minutes of thinking "what?!," I started to really become absorbed in the game.  So much so that I bought the alpha within the hour.  Fast forward 2 years and I now use a whiteboard to plan out factory segments and ensure that they will work.
You can have endless fun building and then rearranging and tweaking logistical and production systems.  Want that mining operation to run at full capacity all the time?  Set up a buffer system.  Only ever want to have 100 transport belts produced at once?  Limit the output.
There's no one correct way to play.  You can build as big, brash and loud as you like, or you can take a different approach and be minimal - only producing what's necessary.  But, your actions have consequences.  So, if you build that big stinking factory and create a huge pollution cloud, you'd better be ready to defend yourself from the angry bugs that will come to destroy you and your factory.  The good news there is that you can make gun turrets and automatically build and ship ammo to them.  The bad news is that the bugs get tougher.
I must have hundreds of hours of playtime on this game and I've not completed a playthrough yet.  To me, that says a lot about how much fun the midgame is.  Besides, once you get to the midgame, you can build train networks which realistically opens you up to having remote facilities.  Like the look of that huge copper deposit that's 25 screens away?  Not a problem - run a train line up there and set up a mining operation, perhaps with its own dedicated power supply and defense system.
This game is for anyone who enjoys a sense of order.  I've already managed to persuade 2 other guys to buy it and I'm working on a third (he's a bit of a graphics freak though, so it's difficult).
Now a couple of words for the developers.  They are fantastic.  There is a detailed update on their website every friday where they discuss their plans for the future, give a taste of upcoming features and say what they've been doing over the last week or so.  The game also gets a bugfix update every week or two.  The devs openly support mods and there's an active modding community with many excellent mods already available.
Factorio is an absolute blast and a steal at the price.  People like playing it - at the time of writing this review, there are over 3,000 positive reviews.  And if you're still not sure, there's always the demo that you can try out - just please allow yourself some time to properly understand what's going on.

Ah, SMITE. When I think of SMITE, I think of the perfect MOBA. Now hear me out, we all now that the MOBA genre is a very delicate subject in gaming nowadays, some hate it, some love it. Me personally, until I found this game, I was still in the toxic jungle known as the League of Legends community. Thank the Lord I decided to give this game a try, cuz sweet baby Jesus, where has this game been all my life?!
1.THE LEAST TOXIC COMMUNITY. I've just been informed by a friend of mine while writing this review that they have just encountered a player who reported them for a God choice. Though such an event is a rarity, just like in any game, it's still possible. Not every game has a perfect community, but SMITE has the least chances that you'll stumble upon a grumpy cat.
2. You think the Isometric Projection of LoL or DOTA just aren't your cup of tea? Well look no further, for SMITE comes in with a fast-paced gameplay in THIRD PERSON. This way, you have a better view of your God, and the action feels much more intense and fluid. This way, you'll be moving with the WASD keys and attacking with your left click. This means, as a ranged character, you will have to aim your attacks, not just click on the target.
3. Graphically speaking, this game is impressive. I cranked it up to max, and found no hit in the FPS departament whatsoever. Performance is well worked upon, and the design of the Gods is fantastic.
4. And let's not miss the most important aspect of this game: YOU ARE PLAYING GOD. We all love mythologies, and seeing your favourite God fill in the role of either Mage, Hunter, Warrior, Support or Guardian is impressive to say the least. I myself remember making a project about my favourite God, Hades, for school. As soon as I got into this game and noticed the wide variety of Gods, I immediately searched up Hades, and to my surprise, he looked AMAZING and PLAYED amazingly. And if for some reason, you don't like the default skin for your favourite God, thankfully, you can earn gems to buy alternative skins or avatars for your profile. (Keep in mind, some skins can also be bought with Favour, the main currency, though you will have to gain mastery and be proficient with the God first).
Overall, SMITE is not your typical MOBA. Anything you hated about MOBAs up until now, this game will fix it for you. Without a doubt, I'd highly recommend you give this game a try. There is NO P2W system, and literally ANYTHING can be bought with enough effort.

I'll start this brief review with two points.  First is the acknowledgement that, for someone who is accustomed to the Mount & Blade engine, it may be a completely different experience.  Second is the fact that, like all of us, I've been playing games for years now and generally know how they work.
Ok, so on to my experience.  So I start playing this game, and all seems well aside from the fairly steep learning curve.  I get a mission to relieve a besieged fort, which seems pretty basic at least in outline: go in, figure out how to kill the natives, and as an added bonus try not to die while doing it.
That's when things get bizarre.  First, there doesn't seem to be any way to control anything but my character.   That's fine, I think; given time I can figure out how that works.  There have to be tutorials somewhere, right?  Maybe there even are, but I didn't get that far because I got knocked unconscious by some native or other who was probably feeling slightly resentful about everything that was going on.
Know what happens next?  Nothing.  That's right, nothing, unless I had a stroke (which was unlikely since there was no smell of toast or facial numbness, but I still mention anyway in the interest of fairness).  I sat there and watched nothing because the battle moved on.  I controlled nothing because I was unconscious.  Unconsciousness implied the thoroughly mistaken hope that one day I would regain consciousness and maybe rejoin the battle, but that didn't happen either.
Then it got even better.  There's no way to reload the game in battle... unless it's just THIS battle, which would put me square into the "get cancer twice then struck by lightning" unlucky zone.  Fine, hardcore whatever... but there's also no way to stop the game.  Seriously, there's no end game button, no return to main menu, no quit to desktop, no accessible game menu that changes anything but video/audio options,
Please, think about that for a second.  Your character is lying there.  There's no way to take control of anything else (I even employed desperation measures, which means looking at the keybind list one by one and seeing what each button does), no way to do anything at all in game, and no way to get out of the game except the nuclear option  of task manager.
The event was frustrating.  Google didn't help, nor did checking the official forums.  For me, it was a game breaking experience... although as always your mileage may vary... and one I don't care to repeat.
The game has a lot of potential, a very interesting premise, and for other people it sounds like it can be pretty fun.  For me, though, as soon as I hit post I'm heading to the hospital just to make sure it wasn't a stroke, because this seems like a pretty significant design flaw.

I've been playing MMO's since UO launched back in the 90s, but I had sat out ESO when it launched due it having a high purchase price and subscription fee, but no free trial system. I wasn't willing to do a blind buy-in.
The game has since dropped the subscription fee (it's optional now), lowered the purchase price, and recently offered a free weekend. Finally having the opportunity to try it out I did just that, and the very next day I purchased the Gold Edition.
This isn't your regular MMO. This is a MMO that rewards Explorer-type players, rather than focusing solely on dungeon treadmills and min/maxing for PvP.
As with other Elder Scroll games, the game is filled with lore for you to discover. NPC dialogue trees frequently contain branches that exist solely to flesh out backstories or lore events. Books you can read are all over the place, as are notes and letters (including quest-related ones).
The main storyline quests will lead you from one area to the next, but by leaving the path you will discover even more places and quests. These optional side quests are done very well, generally to the same quality as the main storyline.
To give an example, for 3 days now I've been trying to complete a particular quest where I need to find two Fighter's Guild NPCs.
On the first day I got sidetracked by quests taking place around town. I solved some corruption in the town watch, was sent to a Daedra realm, and got certified for crafting.
On the second day I got sidetracked by finding players taking part in a boss event, then found a shrine with a bunch of monkeys and bananas, ran into a handful of vampires, then got wrangled into stopping a pirate invasion on the beach.
The third day I swore that I would finally complete that Fighter's Guild quest, but along the way I found a mine which obviously I had to see what was inside. I wind up clearing the place and defeating the boss at the end, earning an achievement for clearing it.
Maybe tomorrow I'll get around to completing the Fighter's Guild quest?
Contributing to the encouragement to explore is that you don't see any levels on enemies. Instead, it appears that encounters are scaled to your current character's range. Even drops from enemies and in chests will be for your level. This lets you go where you want to go when you feel like going there. There are plenty of chests, barrels, crates, and dressers for thieves to seek out, along with locked houses you can break in to loot. The thievery/sneak system plays like straight out of the singleplayer Elder Scrolls.
I can't say what the game is like once you've completed all the quests, since I'm still relatively low. But given how long working through the game is taking me, this title is well worth the price - especially with the current sale. The amount of entertainment you'll get out of it will translate to paying pennies per hour.
