I am in love with this franchise.  The indirect method of story telling, the combat, the feeling of conquering a difficult challenge; Souls provides.  The graphics are much improved from the first game and the combat feels faster and more responsive.  The story remains similar to the first game.  Find the king, that's all you're told.  But along the way you begin to uncover the secrets of the world and what happened to the kingdom and characters of old.   Multiplayer remains a unique experience that is often both rewarding and frustrating all at once.  From Soft included more NPC summons this time though, so playing the game offline to avoid unwelcome invasions while still getting the help of summons is an option.
There are some irksome elements that I found to the game.  Parrying is much more difficult with the frame window being drastically reduced on many weapons.  Hit boxes can be inconsistent, especially with downward smash attacks.  The NPC summons are often game breaking in their power (Jester Thomas will solo his boss for you), but again that is a choice for the player to make.  The game lacks a truly memorable boss fight.  Where the original game had Orns and Smough, Manus, the Dark Dragon, this game struggles to find a boss that has interesting mechanics while also being a challenge (though Sin in the DLC and Fume Knight have certainly made an impact on me).
Pick it up if you're a Souls fan.  Some elements may disappoint you but through and through this is still Souls.  If you're on the fence about the previous game I would still recommend giving this sequel a try as it eases the player into the mechanics better and provides more help along the way.

After having enjoyed Dishonored 1 (qv: my review and reasons for waiting) and then seeing the art direction for Dishonored 2 was radically different, I knew I would fall into this story and world once more. I was NOT wrong.
Where D1's plot was virtually nonexistent unless you played Daud's DLC, D2's is very much apparent and available to the main character with plentiful lore - but also if you choose to ignore books and journals, or not bother to overhear conversations, it's still an easily taken-in story. There is so much more going on in this world than D1 actually showed - and the character development in the intervening years between games has been marvelous.
Literally everything about this game is wonderful - except the engine it's on. More on that later I guess.
The artistry of Dishonored 2 is among the best I've ever seen, in not just games, but art in general. Architecturally gorgeous locations, lived-in and vibrant cityscapes, and far more variety in visuals than its Dunwall counterpart, Karnaca is sheer beauty. Subtle hints and nudges about the deeper story and plot abound. The music... Oh how I am sad that Daniel Licht has passed away, because this soundtrack is absolutely stunning. The dialog and variety of characters populating the city far surpass the original game.
The game play itself is terrific. A smoother feel than D1's, for whatever reason, perhaps more responsive. Smoothly moving between magic or item use and combat, good venues for all the stealth and up front combat you'd want. I really do hope that we get a dlc that allows us to hunt or stealth our ways through these maps, like the Dunwall trials.
So many choices: at bare minimum there are six ways to go through the game - Corvo/Emily, High/Low Chaos, and Powers/No Powers. But that being said, there are individual missions which provide a stunning array of options as well. Some of them are canon, others not so much. But the replayability of the game is both obvious and amazing.
The real downside is the atrocious engine choice. I notice that Death of the Outsider lacks the 'powered by idtech' statement on its load screen - and that may be a telling point, because DotO is far smoother in performance, and didn't have the vast array of issues that D2 had on launch. If the game could be redone in the newer or better id6 engine, rather than 5, that would be lovely. I'm not holding my breath. But then I've completed this game so many times the engine is not really a problem for me.
Overall, if you liked the stealth or combat approach of Dishonored 1, if you are interested in the actual world and fleshing out the story behind what Corvo never learned in that game, Dishonored 2 is a must-play. Download the demo first, to make sure your computer can handle it, because some just cannot. I was pleasantly surprised by my 2g video card actually running it well, so your mileage may vary there. Otherwise, all my thumbs up for this game.

The first Dishonored title was, and still is one of my favorite stealth games, and the sequel does nothing but improve on it in every single way imaginable. When I completed the original Dishonored along with all of it's accompanying DLC, I was still itching for more, and hoped that a sequel would soon arise. A couple months after it's release, I quickly picked up a copy while it was on sale and never looked back.
I don't know how Arcane Studios did it, but they managed to make the parkour and combat even more streamlined and seamless than it already was. The combination of the refined parkour, combat, and powers opens up the possibilities to how you approach a situation
than it already had previously established.
The storyline in Dishonored 2 is a continuation from the original, and builds on the notes system so well that it greatly intensifies and reinforces what the city's thoughts and opinions can reveal about certain plot elements and characters.
For the first time in the Dishonored series, you have a choice of either playing as Corvo, continuing your story and journey from Dunwall, or playing as his daughter Emily; this forges a new point of view of the world and incorporates powers exclusive to her that really makes her stand out as her own unique character.
Overall, Dishonored 2 is a worthy sequel that does not fail to disappoint even the most hardcore fans like myself. I have completed the game twice so far, which has allowed me to experience the rich and diverse playstyles you get to chose from. If you are looking for a fresh, new incorporation of Dishonored with a new storyline, characters, abilities, and the emphasis of replayability, I could not accentuate my recommendation enough.

"Papers, Please" is self described as "A dystopian document thriller." I couldn't give it a better description than that.  Time is money, and you need to process as many passports as possible before the day ends.  The more passports you process, the more money you can make, which keeps your family from suffering.  The whole process of examing passports for correct data starts out easy at first, but gets tougher every day with more complex bureaucracy.  If it wasn't tough enough to suffer through a hard day's work, you also may find your day ending short with a possible terrorist attack.  Although this all sounds masochistic, that is where the true beauty of the game shines.  The two problems I have with this game is the short amount of time they give you for each day (frantic indeed), and the fact that it retails at $10.  I usually don't have a problem with the price of a game, but even at $10, it is a very simple game that could just as easily have been released as a Flash game on Newgrounds.  If you love high stress puzzle games, or ever had the dream of working at your local DMV, you definitely need to check this out.

Toy Soldiers is a great game, that being said it doesn't seem that the developers feel this way. Let me explain, this game is still missing content, that content being many multiplayer maps. Aside from this, the multiplayer itself has issues. Local multiplayer has some serious bugs (one example is having to jump before being able to sprint) and the online multiplayer is non existant, something the community has been asking to be fixed I'd imagine since the game was released on early access in 2014. I love Toy Soldiers, although if you are looking to play the game, I'd reccomend just waiting for the War Chest sequel because this game is honestly a waste of money, and as much as I'd like to say that it is a waste of money "for now" I don't think the devs care enough to update the game. With over a year in early acess and little word about updates, bug fixes, or an offical release date, your money would be better spent being thrown into a sinkhole.

If you don't care about co-op, ignore my review and read someone elses.  My  review is aimed at people who really care about co-op.
As a solo experience, Toy Soldiers is great.  However, If you're like me and thought about buying Toy Soldiers to play with friends, WAIT UNTIL THE MULTIPLAYER BUGS ARE FIXED.  I really can't stress that enough.  This game currently has desynchronization problems that make it unplayable for many people.  You may go several levels without the problem, but often your connection will sever and you'll both drop from the game.  As far as I can tell, retrying over and over will not "luck" your way past the bug.  Once you encounter it, its a wall you can't get past.  It's extremely frustrating and it's been an issue for months.  I realize this game is Early Access, but it deserves criticism as a standalone product if money is involved.  So consider yourself warned.
Toy Soldiers is a great game on Xbox Live (good enough to buy it again on the PC) and I hope to one day see it fully operational on the PC, but until this game-breaking issue is resolved, I can't recommend it as a co-op experience.

The Gatherers from Amnesia scared you? Well, they just got smarter.
Alien: Isolation really stands out being played by movie enthusiast such as myself, making you smirk at every retro console and flicker of the videotape filters. We don't frown at noticable practical effect-ingenuity, we embrace and appluade it. The fantastic vision and style of the Alien movie really shines through in this game, and I think it's safe to say that this is the one we were waiting for; The game to light the way for all future "Alien" games.
"You are my lucky star. You... Lucky, lucky, lucky, lucky, lucky."
I would recommend you to play on hard difficulty, no doubt. It gives the narrative much more credit, and unless you aren't used to controlling PC first person games, you should be able to work your way between savingpoints just fine. Take your time with it.
"That's amazing. What is it?"
My personal favorite xenomorph will always lean towards what H.R. Giger intended it to be: a tall, skinny, biological machine twisting around itself, confusing the human eye and creating something terrible as if spawned from his Necronomicon. The original Alien (in my opinion) was never meant to be Cameron's dime a dozen fiend the action 80's "Aliens" brought us (which was a great film in its own right), and this game really highlights how powerless a human being is against such a nightmarish creature.
"It's a robot. Ash is a god damn robot."
Yeah... Expect to see alot of robots called working Joes. They most of the time feel like placeholders to not over-use our alien friend, and it gets annoying sometimes sneaking around them. To their credit they do help in the pacing of the game, and the developers couldn't have made them more menacing, calmly walking towards you in a determined manner. I would have preferred to have more and interesting ways of taking them out, but most of the time you don't even need to.
"Final report of the commercial starship Nostromo"
Is it perfect? No. Did I play it with rose-tinted glasses? Probably. Should you buy it? Definitely.
If you like horror game titles such as Amnesia and Outlast you will be amazed at how well this game performs. Now if you're also someone who is a fan of the Alien Franchise, you will get your every pennies worth; and more out of it. Just the atmosphere and design faithfully crafted in the image of the original Alien movie will put a wide smile on your face. A must have in your PC game collection.

Nope. Not even close to ten out of ten. "How do we keep our cash cow franchise fresh and new?" the developers thought. By adding
Now if you do think this would feel fresh and new, don't bother. Advanced Warfare is more of the same in comparison of the older games. And
- I said the same thing for Black Ops 2 and I sure as hell will say it for Advanced Warfare. Because this game is just as bad, if not, WORSE than Black Ops 2. In my review, I will do my best to cover everything this game has to offer here on the PC platform, Campaign and the non existant multiplayer. Let's begin.
Is it me, or does Advanced Warfare try really hard to out perform previous Call of Duty campaigns with increasingly preposterous scenarios set to an orgy of explosions that would make even Michael Bay blush. Loud, dumb, and full of... fun, I'll admit it- the single player campaign is mostly a wild ride. Being the first Call of Duty fully fledged by Sledgehammer games, it's pretty well done. Throwing us 45 years into the future, giving us exo skeleton suits that turn us into super soldiers. It immediately helps explain what you can do in a way no Call of Duty really has, it fits. But it tries to fool you, making you think an exo suit makes you survive longer-NOPE. The time to kill is the same as every previous Call of Duty, making the exo suits seem rather muted during the experience. At times, almost like they're not even there if it weren't for the jetpack ability. Especially when at one point in the game, a main character gets her @$% kicked while wearing one against a single exoless enemy when they just made a point how one exo suit can take on five exoless dudes at once.
You are Jack Mitchell, really good friend of Will Irons, though you wouldn't really know that as the opening seems like you met with him for the first time. North Korea has invaded Seoul, and somehow has better technology-

And your friend, Will Irorns will inevitably die for his country and your left arm will become amputated.
It turns out that Will was the son of a famous CEO who controls a massive private military corporation, Jonathan Irons, played by Kevin Spacey. This is what really sets the story in motion once he selects you for his crew, and I honestly LOVE Spacey's performence in this game; he absolutely nails it. If this game didn't have Spacey, it would have been more generic and bland.
However, the rest of the campaign is painfully cliched, and the worst part is what you think is going to happen from the start... completely happens. Seriously, you can see the plot twist coming from a mile away; there is absolutly no clever thought or interesting twist, or try to blur the line between hero and villain- NOPE. Once Kevin Spacey gets accepted in the United Nations, he just decides to declare war on the entire world because..
It's the very same directed linear shooting gallary, anytime something cool happens, it's just a simpe button press, contextual. But there are a couple cool sections in Advanced Warfare, a hovercycle escape, a boat escape, where you can submerge underwater for a few seconds to avoid obsticles. There's a few missions where you use a grapple hook and scale buildings like spiderman. But all of these cool things that happen feel very automatic even though you are in control; you don't feel like you're contributing a whole lot to the action that is happening in these sequences. But there are many fun sequences and a ton of variety and I do appreciate this. The campaign is good enough to keep you going to the end. But for some reason, there is no 'exit to main menu' option in between missions
The ending, I don't know why It's so hard for a billion dollar franchise to have a GODDAMN SATISFYING ENDING, with a massive cliffhanger sequel bait ending, once Activision runs out of ideas, boom, Advanced Warfare 2, and all this talk how "This is just the beginning" and "The war against the Atlas Corporation goes on".
BUT NO. There is no war.
This game is incredible. Combined with nastalgia, and the quality of appearance and mechanics of this game, Homeworld remastered really provides that satisfactory gameplay I am looking for.

The overall "Homeworld" experience is really fantastic. The games got all the mechanical and artistic elements right, from the way the gameplay and GUI interact, to the music, to the story, to the artwork - the series is legenday for good reason.
There is a pretty big "YMMV" point when you play it again, though.
See, when you play the games the first time, you're awed by the experience as a whole. The artistry of it all just kind of overwhelms you. However, when you come back to the games (especially "Homeworld 2") after a good long while, a bit of disappointment does creep in. You're no longer gaping in amazement at the setting, and so the macro-structure of the gameplay becomes more noticeable.
The "Homeworld" series - at least to me - takes the unfortunate route of melding a single-solution puzzle with the RTS genre. You can't really find your own groove. Instead, you end up having to figure out "the one magic trick" that gets you through the mission. To me, that's an unwelcome subversion of the strategy element. The player's choices seem frustratingly constrained at times, whether it's from a lack of available resources or from the scenario requiring a very specific fleet structure.
The achievement that is the "Homeworld" saga is, in the end, dimmed only slightly by this problem. I still see the series as THE Gold Standard for this kind of game. This remaster is 100% worth picking up; I just think it's also worth mentioning that certain choices regarding the gameplay might not be everybody's cup of tea.

I've been playing this game for about a week (though I haven't been active in this game for a few days). My experience was a decent one. While the game claims it is "Free to play", that is about the extent of it's F2P model. Loading the game for the first time, I'm only given a "Guest" License, which only allows me to hunt Mule Deer, and Cottontail Rabbits. I also get the basic weapon (.243 Nosler Rifle) as well as a Deer "Bleat" Caller, Binos, and a Digital Camera as well as the HunterMate (a PDA of sorts). Very basic stuff. To be expected when starting for the first time. I spent hours learning the game, walking around, taking in the sights (which were majestic, by the way), and trying to locate my first prey. It really didn't take long despite others' claims that there were no animals. It just took some patience and careful movement, as well as some time sitting around waiting for my prey to come to me when I used the caller. The game does have tutorials, and they weren't hard to find, and they explained pretty much the basics on how to find animals and how to use the items you're given.
Spending some more time in this game, I decided to take a look at the store to see what I could purchase. Well, turns out you need gm$. Pretty much your in-game currency which can be obtained through running missions. The missions weren't hard. It's just that you need to do quite a number of them to be able to purchase some of the items in the store. But not all. Most items (and I mean MOST) require you to use em$, which is obtained through spending actual money. I ended up spending $20 to buy a few things and also purchased some ammo with the gm$ that I accumulated while running missions. Not too bad, though I wish the real money I spent was better spent for more than what I got. Still, I was happy with what I purchased and moved on. I wasn't expecting to have everything this game has to offer while only spending $20.
I'm still having fun in this game and I find it to be enjoyable. However, I'm not too keen on the way the game is tagged as "Free to Play" when it's clear that most items can only be purchased with real money. I can see why the developers need to make some money, but this is pretty fraudulent. Most F2P games allow you to purchase ALL items in the store using in-game currency (gm$) but at an extended length of time. This is NOT the case. While it is a fun game to play, I cannot recommend it at this time because it really is NOT Free to Play. It is more like a demo. It's free to only hunt 2 animals, use 1 weapon and use only 1 caller. To get other weapons and other, more useful items, as well as having to purchase the licenses needed to hunt other animals, you WILL HAVE to spend real money. Being able to spend in-game currency on some items is a plus, but there's just not enough items to do this with to justify a true F2P game.
Overall, a good game. But if you want to do more in this game other than hunt Mule Deer and Cottontail Rabbits, and/or just walk around taking in the sights, you will have to open up your wallet.

I've been playing MMO's since UO launched back in the 90s, but I had sat out ESO when it launched due it having a high purchase price and subscription fee, but no free trial system. I wasn't willing to do a blind buy-in.
The game has since dropped the subscription fee (it's optional now), lowered the purchase price, and recently offered a free weekend. Finally having the opportunity to try it out I did just that, and the very next day I purchased the Gold Edition.
This isn't your regular MMO. This is a MMO that rewards Explorer-type players, rather than focusing solely on dungeon treadmills and min/maxing for PvP.
As with other Elder Scroll games, the game is filled with lore for you to discover. NPC dialogue trees frequently contain branches that exist solely to flesh out backstories or lore events. Books you can read are all over the place, as are notes and letters (including quest-related ones).
The main storyline quests will lead you from one area to the next, but by leaving the path you will discover even more places and quests. These optional side quests are done very well, generally to the same quality as the main storyline.
To give an example, for 3 days now I've been trying to complete a particular quest where I need to find two Fighter's Guild NPCs.
On the first day I got sidetracked by quests taking place around town. I solved some corruption in the town watch, was sent to a Daedra realm, and got certified for crafting.
On the second day I got sidetracked by finding players taking part in a boss event, then found a shrine with a bunch of monkeys and bananas, ran into a handful of vampires, then got wrangled into stopping a pirate invasion on the beach.
The third day I swore that I would finally complete that Fighter's Guild quest, but along the way I found a mine which obviously I had to see what was inside. I wind up clearing the place and defeating the boss at the end, earning an achievement for clearing it.
Maybe tomorrow I'll get around to completing the Fighter's Guild quest?
Contributing to the encouragement to explore is that you don't see any levels on enemies. Instead, it appears that encounters are scaled to your current character's range. Even drops from enemies and in chests will be for your level. This lets you go where you want to go when you feel like going there. There are plenty of chests, barrels, crates, and dressers for thieves to seek out, along with locked houses you can break in to loot. The thievery/sneak system plays like straight out of the singleplayer Elder Scrolls.
I can't say what the game is like once you've completed all the quests, since I'm still relatively low. But given how long working through the game is taking me, this title is well worth the price - especially with the current sale. The amount of entertainment you'll get out of it will translate to paying pennies per hour.

If you enjoyed the first games youll enjoy these about equally, the LUA based programming system made a multitude of mods available to the community long before the remakes. If you like slow paced intense RTS style games this title is definately worth a playthrough.

A fun strategy/management game that can keep you occupied for minutes or hours.
You are a babysitter to dwarfs. You use arrows, walls and dynamite to guide them towards treasures and away from danger. The dangers that await the dwarfs are lava, water and nasty creatures like goblins and spiders. And the dwarfs love looking for treasure, so much so that they will dig into a lava pit to find some. Fortunately you are given the tools to prevent this from hapening. You get guide arrows to switch their direction, dynamite to create holes for water and lava to flow in and walls to block the flow of water and slow the flow of lava. You can also seal up areas permanently by hardening rock, but this can cost a lot of gold (especially in the harder difficulties).
With the game's multiple mode, difficulty and time settings you can enjoy a nice long high score game, or go for a quick 5 minute hardcore challenge. There is also an alternate game, akin to a carnival shooting gallery (throwing axes/shooting at side scrolling targets), which can be fun for a bit.
For the achievement & perfect game collectors, this game offers a 2 for 1. Any achievement you get in the paid version will also be unlocked if you play the free version. The achievements themselves are fairly easy to get within a few hours. The only issue is that some of the achievements will not register in the paid version, unless you unlock them in the free version (you can meet the criteria in the paid version and not need to buy the dlc).
Overall a nice game, 7/10. Definitely worth picking up in a sale.
I wouldn't buy it out of sale (£7.99 / $9.99), but it may be worth it to some, so try the free version first.

This top down casual strategy game seems pretty crude at first. And it is. There isn't much to it. The UI and unit control is clunky and difficult to work with. It's a bit buggy and it's not much to look at. However... it's pretty addictive.
The poor UI seems to be part of the difficulty of the game. When you are trying to cope with a river of Lava consuming your tunnel network, two Giant Spider Queens infesting your mine with hundreds of spiders, a flood, and all the while trying to mine gold to fund your efforts, things get pretty frantic and desperate.
You may find it very annoying in fact, as often the game will give you virtually no time to react. There is a slow time ability on a long cooldown, but even with this often it is impossible to stop a lava flow in time for example.
You have no direct control over the dwarves. Instead you can choose to spend money to force them to walk and dig in a particular direction. This makes every decision difficult if you are trying to conserve money, which you will need for military units, and for blocking off fatal sections of the mine, or forcing your miners to commit suicide to block off a tunnel.
The gameplay kind of reminds me of Dungeon Keeper (i'm sure there are better examples though) and makes me wonder if this game doesn't have a better approach to unit control. After all, you wouldn't expect to be able to rapidly redeploy your forces and execute manoeuvres underground.
There are a few random mini games thrown in, a few different play modes, even a tower defence for some reason. But the main game is where it's at. Try it on Normal mode for an hour and see if you can last that long! Definitely worth a look if you are interested in strat or managment games.

Haunting and... well, "memorable" in a good way, too -- STALKER is a game that needed to happen. It's a great twist on the traditional horror shooter, even more so than Half Life. You awake with a PDA that will come to motivate the character as much as it motivates the player. And it's a mystery -- er, well... there's a whole deus ex machina (...almost literally) aspect to the ending. It's addressed by the other two titles in the series, which I also recommend.
It's got a bit of a learning curve, but there's more than a bit to see and do once you get your bearings -- I trudged through it blindly twice, motivated less by the story and more by the need for better weapons and more ammo. But once I got comfortable, I realized I was missing half the game by refusing to revisit older zones. *Actual* game content, not just side quests.
Make sure to download and install "STALKER Complete" (available for each of the 3 STALKER games) for a drastically improved (read: more realistic = harder + more engaging) experience. Know your quicksave key, and keep exploring.
The sudden and confusing ending... well... the *actual* ending (there are three fakes ones -- seriously, go back to older zones) is handled well in the third game, "STALKER: Call of Pripyat" (probably the best of the series). "STALKER: Clear Sky" is a decent attempt at a prequel that overhauls several aspects of game play for a... well... it's a little different, but worth it.

Dishonored 2 is a solid fun game that stays true to the roots of what made Dishonored 1 a great experience. The levels design, puzzles, graphics, and power usage allows almost infinite replayability and the New Game plus is done so that you can have all powers available in your second playthrough. Just remember to break apart all your bonecharms and turn them into runes.
The story and characters are also functional and the tone and voice-acting works well when it tries. None of this would matter of course if the gameplay wasn't fun, and it really is. The powers are a blast to use and it was clever of them to allow both Emily and Corvo to access multiple areas with their respective powers so that you don't feel restricted while playing as one versus the other (ex: shadow walk can allow you to enter grates without possession).
The game flows well and does it what it sets out to do. Dishonored 2 is a solid experience that delivers on what it promises. The story isn't groundbreaking, but it's functional enough to keep the game on its feet while riding off its great presentation and amazing gameplay.

Last Horizon is a graceful 2D arcade game with gentle resource management strategy. It's simple and repetitive, but in a way that's compulsive - like the better arcade games of the 80s.
As you head to your new home, you consume fuel, oxygen and (if you keep bashing into things) hull integrity. To replace these resources, you find a planet and land on it anywhere safe.
But the planet's resources are finite and allocated at random, so you might not be able to fill all three things to the top. Your scanner will let you know what's available before you land - but it's rare this makes much of a strategic difference given the sheer number of planets. Provided you aren't continually coming in on fumes, you won't come a cropper.
Gameplay video:
There are planets that hold special resources (ie colonies and terraforming gubs) that mainly exist to boost your score if you complete the level, but they also help steer the story and atmosphere. I was hoping these resources would have more of a gameplay effect, really.
So the strategy element isn't that challenging, but the arcadey bit is. The mechanics are based on Thrust, so landing on a planet is a case of carefully letting gravity guide you in as you reverse onto a clear patch of planet surface. If you're in a panic and come in too hot, it's easy to side-swipe a mountain and kill yourself.
The rest of space can be tricky, too. Asteroids collide with moons and send them hurtling into the nearest planet. Black holes appear at the last moment. Binary star systems can inspire both awe and terror as you thread the needle of two suns' gravity wells.
There are also alien ships and planets. They start off benign, but later aliens begin to resent your presence and you may not be able to linger in some areas of space very long. You can land on their planets to refuel, but you'd better be quick before the missiles arrive!
All these moments tends to be exciting rather than a source of frustration. There's not much more stuff to discover beyond them, though.
There are a small handful of unlockable levels in the version I played. The first few (Flights A, B and C) are essentially not random, as far as I could tell. All planets are in the same fixed location with only their resources changing from game to game. So it's not really a rogue-lite exploration game, more Thrust without borders.
But then you unlock Flight X, and the game becomes a lot less predictable. Each run is now different, and the level is much longer than the earlier ones. There are some VAST areas of space with no resources available, so you'll actually need to plot an intelligent course instead of heading vertically upwards and hoping for the best. This is the best way to play it - it's challenging, epic and forces you to consider your resources far more - consigning the first levels to quick practice modes.
Last Horizon is a game of moments. It can be both funny and frustrating as you get tonked by an orbiting moon or swiped by a passing comet (swoooosh!). Like fellow ambient space exploration game RymdResa, it's a game that pretends to be calming, while repeatedly hurling rocks at you and sucking you across an event horizon. The main thing is that it's replayable enough for the price - but also feels like it misses a few opportunities to add the depth that would keep you playing for a long time to come.

This game is pretty cool, but I feel like it was rushed out and poorly thought through.
The gameplay is fluent and easy to learn.
But it lacks a replay-/keep-factor.
You will eventually let it rest in your library.
Why?
There is plenty of tracks, AI is challenging and the game is pretty awesome. But that's it.
Tracks get repetetive. You have to race everyone of them four times. 2 Races, Twice in the Cup.
MX1 and MX2 don't really differ, apart from speeds and velocity and some other high-math boopdidoo.
This is why I think it has been rushed out; there is no changing weather, no track variation, no customizing of your bike.
You just race, race, race, jump and change teams from time to time.
The "Social Media" ingame is pathetic. You get clearly thought-up usernames with 7 variations of props, threats or some other junk.
Even if it is a fairly new game, the graphics are relatively bad. The track and biker are what feels like HD, but everything else: mushy, misty and 2D textures. If you really look at it, it makes you cringe and gives you that feeling of "uh-oh I guess I wasted some money, oh well"
Nevertheless, the tracks are cool as mentioned, there are some pretty crazy jumps and you can always get a good giggle at how your driver crashes sometimes.
Overall: If you are a MX fan, and you got some time on your hands, get this on sale, MAYBE.

Haunting and... well, "memorable" in a good way, too -- STALKER is a game that needed to happen. It's a great twist on the traditional horror shooter, even more so than Half Life. You awake with a PDA that will come to motivate the character as much as it motivates the player. And it's a mystery -- er, well... there's a whole deus ex machina (...almost literally) aspect to the ending. It's addressed by the other two titles in the series, which I also recommend.
It's got a bit of a learning curve, but there's more than a bit to see and do once you get your bearings -- I trudged through it blindly twice, motivated less by the story and more by the need for better weapons and more ammo. But once I got comfortable, I realized I was missing half the game by refusing to revisit older zones. *Actual* game content, not just side quests.
Make sure to download and install "STALKER Complete" (available for each of the 3 STALKER games) for a drastically improved (read: more realistic = harder + more engaging) experience. Know your quicksave key, and keep exploring.
The sudden and confusing ending... well... the *actual* ending (there are three fakes ones -- seriously, go back to older zones) is handled well in the third game, "STALKER: Call of Pripyat" (probably the best of the series). "STALKER: Clear Sky" is a decent attempt at a prequel that overhauls several aspects of game play for a... well... it's a little different, but worth it.

I'm still playing with semi-auto rider controls because I just don't care that much, but it's fun.
There is quite a bit of variety in the tracks, both in their layouts (flat, very hilly, fast or technical, and so on) and in the surface. I came across tracks where I could not get a decent lap time until I changed things in the bike set-up, which speaks well for that. The surface of the track in this can look kind of janky at times (frequently the ruts don't render until they're behind you) and the engine sounds could be a lot better, but I'm really enjoying it and I think it's very much worth buying on sale.

My all time favorite series of all time, the Souls series. Even dating back to Demon's Souls, when most people were turned off by its difficulty. Then when Dark Souls launched, it generated this huge fanbase and community. And it's crazy to see how big and popular these games have gotten. But it's only because they're so good. It doesn't matter how new you are, or how big of a veteran you are; you're still going to die. A lot. I've completed all sorts of weird, silly, or difficult playthroughs throughout all of these games. And it never gets old. I still love making a new character, using a new build, still discovering things after 100+ completions. It's a game that immerses you in more than the gameplay. The storytelling (or lack there of) really intrigues you. You want to know more about this strange world, and you learn more by figuring it out. They don't cram narrative down your throat, or tell you directly where to go or what to do. That's for you to figure out. There's so many things that this game trains you to notice. This game is incredible.  It has replay value of the same order as Kerbal Space Program.
For me the story goes a bit like this.  I downloaded the demo sometime in 2014, just to try the game out for 15 minutes.  After the first 5 minutes of thinking "what?!," I started to really become absorbed in the game.  So much so that I bought the alpha within the hour.  Fast forward 2 years and I now use a whiteboard to plan out factory segments and ensure that they will work.
You can have endless fun building and then rearranging and tweaking logistical and production systems.  Want that mining operation to run at full capacity all the time?  Set up a buffer system.  Only ever want to have 100 transport belts produced at once?  Limit the output.
There's no one correct way to play.  You can build as big, brash and loud as you like, or you can take a different approach and be minimal - only producing what's necessary.  But, your actions have consequences.  So, if you build that big stinking factory and create a huge pollution cloud, you'd better be ready to defend yourself from the angry bugs that will come to destroy you and your factory.  The good news there is that you can make gun turrets and automatically build and ship ammo to them.  The bad news is that the bugs get tougher.
I must have hundreds of hours of playtime on this game and I've not completed a playthrough yet.  To me, that says a lot about how much fun the midgame is.  Besides, once you get to the midgame, you can build train networks which realistically opens you up to having remote facilities.  Like the look of that huge copper deposit that's 25 screens away?  Not a problem - run a train line up there and set up a mining operation, perhaps with its own dedicated power supply and defense system.
This game is for anyone who enjoys a sense of order.  I've already managed to persuade 2 other guys to buy it and I'm working on a third (he's a bit of a graphics freak though, so it's difficult).
Now a couple of words for the developers.  They are fantastic.  There is a detailed update on their website every friday where they discuss their plans for the future, give a taste of upcoming features and say what they've been doing over the last week or so.  The game also gets a bugfix update every week or two.  The devs openly support mods and there's an active modding community with many excellent mods already available.
Factorio is an absolute blast and a steal at the price.  People like playing it - at the time of writing this review, there are over 3,000 positive reviews.  And if you're still not sure, there's always the demo that you can try out - just please allow yourself some time to properly understand what's going on.

A Journey worth fighting for. What is the journey? The end? The beginning? Perhaps just the middle. Such is the way of life. Such is the way all cycles come to be: Life or death. Patience & impatience, Strength and weakness. And so on and so forth. The cycle continues. The days go by, and we remember fondly of memories of once upon time long forgotten. Years go by, decades pass, kingdoms rise and fall and what remains thereafter?
Sigh, Dark Souls II(DSII); What to think of such a game... Last time to the previous installment I discussed my feelings with the prequel to the soul series, so lets try something different. DSII; is utterly, madness to the limit with a slice of pain and two bread slices of masochism in there. Or is it sadism? to Die and die and die once more, only to be reborn again and again and again! to understand Dark Souls you need to die(virtually! and live once more) for example:
In games we die many times, falling off cliffs, running out of "X" amount of life, losing hp from an enemy and etc. However with the soul series it's something different, something unique. Yes you die as in any other game, but for some reason you go back up, to finish the one last fight before stopping in the night, to venture into the unknown and strike at riches before you, it's similar in the case of the real world except we only get 1 life (or 2+ if someone saves us) We grow, we have dreams, ambitions, goals, but we stumble along the way, we catch a drifting diamond in the horizon and sometimes we forget our goal. Here and now, we forget.
It's the same with Dark souls I and II, we get lost, we die, and live once again. However what is reoccurring is the drive, this will, or motivation to succeed, this human ability that allows to go beyond our limits and achieve something great. That is only a small part of what is in store for you in the soul series.
To be honest and in my personal opinion I have no clue how I survived my trek through DSII, for starters I died CONSTANTLY (and I absolutely hated it), because I lose my money(which is used to buy equipment and lvl up). In this case I would then be SUPER cautious of wherever I went even mimic chests, every door i went through, a shield was in front to protect me, every turn lead to a steady 1 hit ko Death back to the checkpoint (With losing your own $$), and with every encounter with an enemy I had to stay cool and not arrogant in my belief. For instance:
Granted that kind of encounter doesn't happen often, but the sense of paranoia and cautiousness saved me countless times throughout the whole game. Sure, favoring one class over the other may have great Advantages, but it's all useless if you can't even incorporate said strategy into the combat and survival. Mage, Cleric, Pyro, Dark Mage, Beserker, Bow + Arrow classes and etc. are all great to try out and mix and match, never straying far into one build only (like me with only melee, pyro, cleric, heavy ultra great-sword user). Its a delicate balance to become w/e you want to be! (provided you have the $ to lvl up lol).
Nevertheless the point is: you can't be prepared for a game such as this, it will shock and amaze you at times as well as frustrate you to no end like a gadfly. And for some unfathomable reason there will be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bags (Trolls) in the game who will invade you and make your life a living hell, the best advice I can give you is just stay cool, and coordinate some form of surprise on your own enemy, be it summoning for help or whipping out a whip to whip them out of your world.
It wouldn’t be Dark Souls without any invasions, and it only spices your sense of caution to remain online again, to venture forward into the unknown for riches and risk being attacked by a wayward traveler? Or quit while your ahead and take a break? Decisions, choices, and paths are up to you!
The difference, I found between the two games (my analysis at least) that differs from it’s prequel is the hp reduction that occurs every time you die, an more than enough bonfire location, recycled boss attack patterns from first with new combos in, new equipment, spells, characters, classes, mechanics, and story-wise. It’s enough essentially to distinguish the prequel to the sequel.
Although, I couldn’t help but notice how I continued to have the thought in my head “How unique areas in the game were.” Compared to the prequel, in terms of memorable aesthetic and artistic creativity. It felt underwhelming, to me at least, I still very much appreciate the areas, but it felt hollow in a sense. In the first the connected areas would be open to you and you could go about them where you please, with different challenges and unique enemy types at every area, along with a long dungeon to explore
But, with DSII there were some places that were too quick to pass through, (I believe this is due to accessibility the developers were talking about by making it  more accessible to everyone, not easy for that wouldn’t be Dark Souls). I think this might be due to the hp reduction upon death and more bonfires (checkpoints) in every area to mitigate further stress and frustration. However by doing so they have lessened some quality in a sense to the atmosphere of an area.
Despite, the small feeling above, I still very much appreciate the areas that were pretty distinct within DSII like
All those areas I thought, were done pretty well done in terms of structure in the area, balance of enemies and challenges, as well as a unique atmosphere to play through. Compared to the first, there Is more areas that were unique that I had immense fun and joy to play-through. By no means do I hate one small aspect of DSII, it’s just a nagging feeling of comparison imo.
Fear and death are constant companions in the treacherous path to moving forward, Just as strength and life are partners with you in the afterlife and in the living. Perseverance the shield of your tenacity, the sword, my everlasting courage to strike true, and my armor to bear witness countless act of my will.
The trial awaits, oh young naïve wanderer, with but self and will you have. Does your soul have what it takes to brace for the dark? In the coming of days…

Before I start, let me say that the only thing I don’t like about this game is how short the story is. With just 9 missions coming in at around 90 min each, you don’t get that much time out of one play through. HOWEVER this game has more replayablilty potential then something like Skyrim imo. The two charecters you can play with different abilities, voices, interactions etc give you at least two play throughs. I played the original Homeworld and loved it for many reasons, one of those reasons was having no unit limits.  When I purchased HW:RC I played Homeworld 2 first and was disappointed with the unreasonably small unit limit on the smaller craft.  After finishing Homeworld 2 Remasterd and played Homeworld 1 remastered I was happy to see that at least the unit cap was set to 70 for the light craft.

With amazing continued support from Gearbox, and mod capabilities far beyond the original games, Homeworld Remastered has revitalized the franchise in a way we could have scarcely imagined less than five years ago. Homeworld lives again in glorious HD, and the remastered ship models and backgrounds are second to none.

It's almost as if they said to themselves, "Let's make homeworld look twice as good, but play half as well".
I can't say much about homeworld 2: remastered since I haven't played the original too many times  but homeworld 1: remastered is a tragic disappointment when compared to the original. I wish I'd read the reviews before buying. It's baffling that they haven't ironed out such major bugs in such a long time.
Bottom Line:
I can't recommend this game to new comers with all of the broken elements that made the original so good. You will be left wondering what all the fuss is about with such a mediocre game.
I definitely can't recommend this game to veterans who've already tasted the goodness of the original. You will go 'Wow' when you see the graphics on level 1, and then you'll be mounting frustration as you discover one broken feature after the other.
Details:
- Formations: Don't work. Ships break formation as soon as they engage enemies which defeats the purpose entirely. Battles are basically a free for all. This occurs in hw2 as well.
- Tactics: Don't work. There is no discernible difference between the 3 tactics. The buttons are just eye/ear candy.
- Tactical map: Homeworld 1 allowed you to specify a 'move to' point, then hold the shift key to lock that point while panning with rmb to adjust elevation. This is no longer possible, and you have to specify both the 'move to' location and the elevation from a single angle. Not possible, not impressed. Also applies to hw2.
- Salvaging: It's nice that they've made it possible to salvage those standard and missle corvettes in the early missions (without painful scuttle tactics).  It's NOT nice that the 6 assault frigates from mission 3 simply disappear when captured (and are down to 4 for some reason).
- Resourcing: Nerfed to 500 RU's per load (down from 600) for no apparent reason. Takes an eternity to collect resources. Also there's a whole lot more resources available in each level, severely hurting the fine tuned balance of the original game. But I guess that was an easier fix than trying to fix the balance.
- Balance: Downright terrible. Battles that should be over in a flash take forever and with unacceptible losses. An army of 21 interceptors, 7 heavy corvettes and 4 assault frigates should suffer no losses when facing 5 interceptors + 2 corvettes. Neither should they take more than 5 minutes. But that's not homeworld "remastered".
- Interface: I, for one, preferred the original build manager to the homeworld 2 multi page build manager since it's easier building everything from a single page.
If it ain't broke, don't make a half-a!$@d attempt at 'remastering' the game.

i started playing after getting home from work one day. 7 hours later it was 1 AM, i had a factory setup that looked like a microchip, and the planet was slowly starting to die of polution. i think im starting to like the hell out of this. better scale, and better gameplay than most triple A games. id pay 60$ for it, much less 20. well worth every penny.
However, this game lacks an end game, and is quite repatative once youve finished the tech tree. dont play this expecting minecraft with automation, this is a model train set (quite literally most of the time). once youre 8 hours in, youve done everything. thats it, its just a matter of finding more efficient ways to do♥♥♥♥♥♥ or setting stupid chalanges for yourself. or trying to survive extreme biter mode. (ps, never play this game on easier modes its so unbelievably boring without antagonists). all these issues will probably be sorted out by the full release. and with mods, so dont worry about it if the model rail sets and being really creative and puzzle solvey is fun for you.
Now, id just like to point out how ♥♥♥♥ing genius the devs are. the  way the game mechanics are designed, so that even with seemingly little content, there is SO MUCH to do, and the perfect, and i mean PERFECT scalling system they have. what with the pollution system, how research works, and so on. let me explain that a bit;
Pollution: its the thing burning♥♥♥♥♥♥and oil drilling adds to the air. it agros biters, and causes you problems, however, the game is desinged so that while pollution is a big thing and something to watch, once you get the mid-end game, controlling it becomes quite easy and not much of an inconvinience. by the time you get to the mid/ end game, biter attacks are no longer something to worry much about. even behemoth waves can be fell with the proper turret research and ammo/energy production isnt hard or expensive. the biters only stop your expansion at that point, and thats where the game play comes in, by the mid/end game pollution is no longer an intresting mechanic, and just a hassle. so they give you ways to solve that hassle, both adding to gameplay/ incuraging advancement while keeping their mechanics from getting in the way of gameplay progression.
Research: in every game you need to start off by moving up the research tree. however, research is designed to scale. unlike most games where research is done by throwing cash or base materials at a thing, research in Factorio very much encurages mass production centers, and forces you to make use of new technologies as they become availible if you want to keep progressing. it also scales very well, while first technologies can be completed by a single center in a couple minutes, the mid/end game ones would take hours with a single center. this keeps a player from having technology that they dont have the means to mass produce, and puts in a very nice progression scale. where an experianced player can finish most the base tech stuff in an hour or so, a new player will take 10. this keeps a very nice pace no matter the setting or player experiance, you always feel like youre moving forward at the best pace for you.
material production: most people wont notice this, but how the more advanced things are made (ex advanced circuts) are designed to encurage certian actions or setups, and as there is a puzzle game hidden under the skin in factorio, and its genius. when playing the game, look at whats required to make a thing, and how the map auto spawns where things end up, and youll see what i mean. its designed to make you think, and encurage clever player actions that result in a sense of acomplishment, and also a really god damn cool looking factory.
tl/dr: really smart design added to a fun base concept. its well worth it as is, and will probably only get better from here. cant wait to see what the devs do in the future, theyve more than proven they are quite savy chaps.

I've played this game a bit now, and I suppose it deserves a review.
Pros:
-In my opinion, the most visually pleasing moba in existence
-Design work put into aesthetics is truly astounding
-Fairly large character pools, with diverse enough abilities to keep the games varied and interesting.
-The devs are actually rather attentive. and balance (and break) the game constantly, making for a very fluid metagame
-Mechanics are just... satistfying. The abilities feel very smooth and the skill cap is very high
-Relatively easy to get good at, but perilously difficult to be come great.
-A good "beginners moba", if such a thing exists, even though the tutorials blow.
Cons:
-Ranked system (and matchmaking as a whole) is rather poor due to semi-low playerbase.
-Punishments for disconnections and harassment are nearly nonexistent.
-Playerbase can be toxic, but less so in my experience than that of DotA or Lol for example.
-Tutorial poorly prepares players for pvp action.
-Roles are called on a first come first serve basis, which can lead to fighting in lobby.
-Rather lackluster pro scene
Overall:
This is my favorite moba, and despite its flaws, it has a ton of potential and room to grow, and it is up to the team at HiRez to follow through.

In this game you play as a character who is essentially Zyzz in an alternate universe where he didn't begin to feign confidence or eventually forfeit his life while on the journey for optimal aesthetics. The complete anithesis to all that Zyzz came to stand for upon his unfortunate, early demise.
As Zyzz, while you can't seek gains, eat chicken for protein or shred like you might expect, you can actually talk to a woman online. Now, this is where the game really picks up.
The game allows you to enter a screenname and your real first name. This is a cool little mechanic because at a glance it doesn't seem like much, but Emily will refer to you as your real name occasionally which is great for immerson. Unless you're like me and made your real name 'largecock'. Still, it was heartwarming when she said that I would "...always be largecock. =]" nonetheless. There are also nice references in the form of the display picture you choose which change depending on the chapter, which are good for a bit of a nostalgia-induced smile.
It's a simple game but the attention to detail is there. Sometimes you'll misspell words and have to correct them, sometimes the discussion becomes so contentious that you'll feel the need to rephrase. It's these little things that really reinforce the feeling that Zyzz is trying his hardest to kindle something between the two of them, albeit relatively unsuccessfuly throughout.
Simple text-based games designed to evoke emotion are by no means new but for my money this is one of the better ones. Zyzz might be a bit of a beta (especially toward the end) and Emily might arbitrarily hold on to menial events for quite long but in the immortal words of Linkin Park which are, for me, intrinsically entwined with that Windows XP wallpaper and IM messengers which would now be considered ancient (yahoo 4 lyf add me on friendster) "In the end, it doesn't even matter," and in the end this game is a worthwhile for a playthrough at the least.
Also the steam screenshots on this game's page are pretty funny so that's cool.

I actually liked Caribbean, and the general thrust of the gameplay which was focused on trade and world domination, with a side of mount and blade style simulated combat.  Although it runs rather slow on potato systems, the graphics are a great improvement over Mount and Blade.
If Caribbean was getting some mount and blade in Port Royale, this iteration is getting more mount and blade in Port Royale.  Tons of missions, more sandbox features like blackjack and barroom brawls.  There are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s if you're into micro♥♥♥♥♥♥♥style roleplay.  And there are guns and swords.  Really big ones.
The mission varieties here are much greater than the original game, with more mount and blade styled quests.  But to call them Mount and Bladeish quests is doing this game somewhat of a disservice.  It's still weird as you're completely unable to swim (Mount and Blade's engine is to blame for that, I'm afraid.), but they've pulled off some interesting missions here.
In short, if you didn't like Caribbean, you may not change your mind for this game.  Watch let's plays, look at other reviews and the feature list to decide if this game is for you before buying.  And ignore the minimum specs listed, the game may not run so well on them.  I can run it just barely at a steady 13 fps on my potato, but I don't know, your mileage may vary.  I wouldn't recommend this game as an impulse buy, as many pirate-styled games can be.  But it has been fun for me.

Short Review:
The developers of this game nailed the trailer, the intricate and delicate systems that work together, the level of depth in the gathering; crafting; automation and monsters/combat, and the programming of the actual game itself, netcode and prediction algorithms included. I look forward to seeing what more they do with this game.
Long Review:
When I watched the first trailer, I thought it would be more like a city builder, but with a factory theme. The description made it sound interesting with automating your factories. The trailer definitely showed a lot going on and I was interested, especially with the monsters and turrets shooting at them.
I didn't watch any other videos and I didn't look up any other information. (Steam refunds let you safely do less research on games and more playing)
When I got in the game and played the tutorial, I was surprised to see that I controlled a character in the game. This really wasn't shown in the first trailer on Steam. I notice now that the second trailer does show this.
I found that I could harvest wood, stone, and other resources.
Then I could use them to craft.
Then I could automate the harvesting using the things I crafted.
Then I could automate the transport of the automated harvested items.
Then I could automate...
The depth that this "Early Access" game has is insane. There are so many different systems in play. Harvesting, crafting, energy/power usage, automation, pollution, monsters, combat, etc. Then there are tons of things you can research to let you do more.
When I eventually went to quit for the night, I noticed it had a multiplayer menu option. An "Early Access" game with online co-op. All these different systems and you can mess with all of them with your friends online. As of version 0.12.0, they have an early dedicated server that runs without the graphical overhead. This worked really well for myself and 2 others at a later date. We didn't encounter any lag or disconnects. With all the automation going on, it's amazing that there was no lag or disconnects. It is a direct connect system, requiring IP address and port, and is peer-to-peer.
(Edit: Someone was having major connection issues and it did affect the others, so it isn't perfect. Hopefully they fix it so that not everyone has to suffer from one person's connection.) It sounds like a server browser system is coming soon. While text chat is possible, I would heavily suggest using a voice chat program to communicate with one another, due to all the things that are going on in game.
There also seems to be mod support already. I haven't even come close to experiencing all of what this game has to give, but mods can only extend the life of this already great game.

Game has some flaws, but aside from that it is an experience I wouldn't want to miss.
-The graphics.
Altough they are a bit outdated, I think they hold up pretty well if you put them on high. Also, because the graphics aren't the best older computers can run this game more stable.
-The zombies.
Although they are a giant unstoppable horde at first, once you learn the game you will get trough the waves of undead without a problem. The zombies look fine, but behave amazing. The zombies are mostly slow shambling people who won't surprise you when you turn your back on them. The number of zombies, combined with some crawlers and runners makes it really challenging to survive though.
A zombie can grab you and kill you in a matter of seconds if you don't react quickly. This game is like the dark souls of zombie games (in a good way).
-The controls.
Although slightly confusing at first, a quick look trough the options menu will both inform you of the buttons to press aswell as to give you the option to change them. They aren't that complicated, but give some realism to the game.
Example: I walk down a dark hallway, but don't have a flashlight. Instead of bringing out said flashlight my characters pulls out a small lighter. I have to click a couple of times before it works, and the light isn't that great, but it helps.
Example: I want to check how much ammo I have in my magazine. Instead of looking at a counter that is always on the screen like in most games, I have to hold R to make my character actually pull the magaine out of the weapon, check the bullets (you can choose to let him either say how much he has, show it for a second in numbers, or both), and put the magazine back in after i'm done. It might be slow at first, but it really adds immersion.
-The community.
Yes, it is toxic. Yes, it is annoying. But it also is amazing. If you happen to find a server with good ping, no modifications, and a steady numbers of players, you can hit the jackpot. In most of my games I have had at least one person being helpful, using (voice)chat and explaining the game to noobs that ask for help. If you wanna change the community, try to start with yourself. Try to help the noobs you see. It will pay off in the long run.
I recommend this game, as it is hard but rewarding, and great to play (with friends).

This game is really fun. MX-style racing adds so much to the racing genre I really wish it was more represented. Here is my breakdown of this game.
Pretty good, even in 2016. I think mxGP2 looks quite a bit better, especially the dirt/environment, but this game is good enough. Bikes and animation looks fluid and natural for the most part. Dirt flings everywhere, adding to the immersion.
Aesthetically the sound is bad, but funtionally it's pretty good. Importantly, the engine sounds are consistent with the RPM range, so you know when to shift up or down by sound alone. Also, you'll know when you land awkwardly as the game will make a distant thud -- indicating that you've lost momentum and you probably need to shift down. This audio-visual feedback is really great.
You can certainly feel the bike in this game. The game is a constant balance of pushing your bike to the max without going out of control, which is a blast. In the meanwhile, bumps in the track will move your bike around so you are constantly adusting. Hitting the ruts and berms correctly are important for optimal speed. I recommend playing with manual transmission -- it makes you "feel" the engine and forces you to make more real-time decisions on when to shift to maintain momentum of the bike.
AI is really bad and not consistent across tracks. The demo probably has the best AI you'll see, but most other tracks have significantly worse AI. I usually give them a 7 second head start, which makes the game more challenging.
I plan to get mxpg2 eventually, but I wasn't impressed by the demo. The bikes feel fundamentally different than in mxgp1, and I'm not sure it's for the best.

I'm 40 years old.
I've been a Total War fan since my early 20s when Shogun: TW came out and have played every single TW game that ever came out since, and enjoyed most. I even grew to love Empire where the Naval combat was truly EPIC.
This particular offering, is a total fail on the part of CA and please, before you unleash the dogs, understand that this is just one man's opinion.
It seems to me that Creative Assembly, like many companies before it, made the decision, or rather made the mistake, of trying to appeal to a larger segment of the population at the expense of it's core base and it's own principles.
Bear with me while I relate a story.
Once upon a time I played a great mmofps called "World War 2 online" it had a small, but successful, loyal and growing fan base. The company was doing great. The reason their game was successful was because it stood apart. It was a really REALLY great combat simulation. You spawned in the rear, had to assemble with other players on trucks, took at least 15 minutes before you even GOT to where the action was, and then, because getting to the front line was such a pain in the butt, took your time and worked in teams to take the objective. Tanks, planes, platoons of players working together made the game a gem, and a truly unique experience.
Then the developers decided to go in a different direction. They added mobile spawns that spawned you directly into the battle zone. This attracted a bunch of new players, who spawned in rushed into combat and died, then they rinsed and repeated that process until all the infantry and tank and plane supplies ran out. Oh did I mention that battlefield supplies were limited? They were. Teamwork among players started degrading, then fell apart, there was no real reason to work together when you could just spawn in and shoot.
The older fan base asked the developers to work on better maps, eliminate the spawn point system, streamline command and control to enable the players to get back and to improve the old system. The developers listened carefully, then worked on improving graphics, added a mini map and a HUD, and, by the time they were done they had "Battlefield 1942" which, unfortunately for them, EA already created and I already owned.
I, and thousands of other who already owned BF 1942, stopped playing, and World War 2 online is all but dead today, at least compared to to what it used to be.
SO, what does this have anything to do with Rome 2?
Well, once upon a time there was a unique game called Shogun Total War. It was made by a company that provided a unique experience. A historically accurate (at least as historically accurate as our Intel 486 processors could provide) recreation of strategies and battles. The company philosophy at the time was "Lets recreate the world of Medieval Japan, the battles, the epic scale of an ancient civilization"
This concept, of staying true to history, and to provide a unique experience, was improved on in the Rome, and especially the Medieval Series. The battles got more realistic, the maps more refined and bigger. The diplomacy... well let's face it, the diplomacy was never CA's strong suite, but at least they tried.
Even with Empire TW, they stayed true to the concept of "History first". That game had problems not because of game speeds, or flawed concept, but because the technology they used to build the game with was just not up to the task, and you know what? That was OK, they had sold me awesome, unique products for (at that time) 15 years, they were entitled to a lemon.
Then came Shogun 2, and the direction the company was taking started to shift. The combat was sped up, not because the Japanese were super fast killers historically, but because they needed shorter battles to cater to Online mode. It was the only thing that was wrong, in an otherwise flawless offering, and it went unnoticed by many but a few of the die hard fans, but it was a sign of things to come. I enjoyed Shogun 2 and, frankly, the fall of the Samurai went a long way to fix the speed issue.
Then came Rome 2.
I can well imagine that the decisions that were made by CA made perfect sense to them:
We can make more money by appealing to a wider audience. We will appeal to a wider audience by making this game simpler. Simpler empire management, faster, online friendly battles, cool exploits like "flaming Javelins" and "Whistling arrows", will attract that younger demographic group. Furthermore, with a simplified interface we can migrate the game to the console platform and double our profit margin.
Now we don't want to lose our core base though, so let's keep up a good front and release historically thrilling Demos, like for example Rome storming Carthage. Make it good. They will love the final product in any case because so many new players will be playing.
OK guys, let's get busy.
Nowhere in their thought process was even remotely concerned with historical accuracy, or recreating anything. The vision that made the company successful, that vision of staying true to History, of creating that epic, untouchable, grand strategy and battle simulation game, was gone.
And now we have Starcraft 2 Total War. Unfortunately, I already had that one.
Needless to say, my days of preordering anything from CA are over.
I hope they find their way back, or like World World 2 online, they will become for me another nice memory.

You know when you play a first-person shooter that claims to be about “how far you’re willing to go to protect the ones you love,” or “the true cost of a life,” or “moral ambiguity,” but the gameplay actually consists of shooting hundreds of dudes in the face? And you know how in the back of your mind, you wonder, “I wonder what it’d be like if a game actually designed its gameplay around those concepts rather than just duct-taping them on through noninteractive story?”
Papers, Please is that game. It manages to ask (and importantly, not answer) questions of duty, safety, privacy, family, self-interest, and morality through an incredibly simple, focused set of mechanics based around checking transit papers and stamping passports.
And it’s spectacular.

EDIT:
This review still stands for this game on it's own, but if recent news is to be believed, the upcoming "Remake" of Dark Souls II with all of the graphics, sound, online play and design improvements will NOT be a patch for the existing game, as such, I would NOT recommend buying this game now. Just don't. While you will get some new content, you will not be getting the definitive version of the game. Every owner of this game has just been swept down.
Again, DON'T buy this game unless news arrives that this disgusting business move will be changed for PC owners. Feel free to read up on what I've said about the game in it's current state though.
---------
When it comes to mechanics, the overall game feel and flow of Dark Souls II is twice the game Dark Souls could ever be. From movement, to stats, HUD, Visual and gameplay design balance and performance, this game has all you could ever want. However in it's learning curve and overall story and progression, it is half of what Dark Souls' world had to offer. In terms of content, it is still massive in scale but less non-linear level structures and a shorter focus on exploration and secrets brings it down a notch from the full experience the first game came to offer.
Compare Dark Souls II's many areas to your average level in a platform game. Multi-tiered but with all directions being fairly obvious in order, required skill level and all eventually leading to the same place. Dark Souls in comparison was more like one large level which was ripe for exploring, and was interconnected and layed out more cleverly, giving sharp players an edge over others and providing a sense of adventure as well as a little intimidation when you found yourself suddenly rushing into a very difficult area.
You could almost say this game is desinged to be enjoyed in the same way. Dark Souls II feels like a journey you make piece-by-piece, taking stops at your main town in between each little segment. This is aided by the fact going back to the main town of the game is the only way to improve your stats, each part of the game ecourages you to take it all in one bite and then let it rest. The first game on the other hand was very hard to put down, for better or worse.
Because of this change in pace and flow, it's understandable that die-hard fans of Dark Souls continue to this day, to play that game instead of this one. But is this game bad, or heck, worse than the first game? Heck no.
Dark Souls II is one of the most satisfying, most responsive and overall good games I've played in a very long time. Compared to the slightly clunky nature of the first game, this game feels smooth as butter without losing the slow, weighted feel of a Souls game. And the RPG is strong too, the story is light on the surface but insanely deep below, and forging your own story, as well as building your own character is better than ever, with practically any kind of weapon or ability viable in some way.
Of course, everything else is honestly standard fare at this point. While there are some changes to balancing and matchmaking, the skills you carry forward from the previous games are in full use here, with minor changes serving to freshen the adventure rather than cripple it.  Whether you enjoy it is up to if you don't mind the quickened pace the game offers, this game is definitely more about forward motion.
Now here's where Dark Souls II shines the most above it's predecessor if nowhere else- the PC port. While far from the PC gamer's dream you will find this game running at any framerate you want and practically any resolution your heart desires hassle-free and without mod intervention. Not only that, it'll stay consistent with any mid-low to high range rig- a 60FPS, 1080p target is hard to miss. The environment also feels more natural and fittingly dark with the option to use SSAO and other such effects at a very low performance cost. It serves to improve upon what already looks like a great game with some good environments and good lighting effects, textures and character models.
Overall, Dark Souls II is a very polarising game to the community.. but I think it's an absolutely fantastic piece of software. Yes, I recommend it. And I'd certainly recommend it even at it's full price. It's highly welcoming to new players, very replayable, challenging, fun and full of content and looks good too. A good game to close out the 7th Generation in Action-RPG games and an adventure to stand among the top games of the last few years.
Go ahead, give it a try.

I am writing this review only from what I've played in the original HW remaster, as that's the only reason I bought the game. This version of this game is ok. I only recommend it if you are a diehard Homeworld fan and want to see the ships in HD awesomeness. Other than that, it is actually a huge let down.
The main point of this review is to list a few things that are different(in a bad way) between this and the original Homeworld.
-Strike craft no longer have finite fuel and do not require refuels
-Resource collectors must be constantly told to harvest, as they will stall and idle if not near any resources
-You cannot capture assault frigates and use them in your fleet in the third mission. They are converted to RU's instead.
-Sphere formation when guarding is laughable. Your ships form a small sphere to the side of your guarded ship, rather than encircling the ship as a sphere with the guarded ship the origin.
-Strike Craft will downright LEAVE a ship they are guarding leaving it open for other craft
-There are many MANY small bugs throughout what I've played so far that are just downright silly. Two examples of this, are in the second mission, it is possible that if your first salvage corvette is destroyed after salving the wreckage, any corvette afterwards will be unable to salvage. Additionally, salvage corvettes get really glitchy when capturing big ships, and when you have distraction fighters dropping like flies, time is of the essence, but when the salvage corvettes are glitching out and wasting time, it ruins a nicely executed plan.
-Many ships have had their attributes changed. The Assault Frigate (not the best frigate, but still) now is much weaker than the original Homeworld.
Fortunately, this release comes with the original version of Homeworld. But this game suffers from a lack of passionate programmers ensuring the underlying code works properly and is faithful to the original gameplay. It really feels like this game was outsourced by Gearbox, similar to Aliens: Colonial Marines.
I'm starting to believe that if it's not Borderlands, don't buy it from Gearbox.
