After playing Fallout 2 a long time ago I wondered what a post apocalyptic game would be like from the Russian side. Well, heres the answer. Its got a seriousness that the Fallout series does not, and a darker, more brooding atmosphere. Much like Shadowrun you cannot take a lot of gunfire,
forcing  you to think through your firefights and play in a less run-and-gun style. That being said, once you get used to crouching and aiming then moving to a new position, you can take on fairly large groups of enemies. The only downside to this game is the long load times, but heres a fix...start the game with -noprefetch and, ironically, it runs smoother and faster and  loads quickly. My guess is that the game is too agressive with the prefetching and if you tell it to cut that out it fetches as needed instead of
all at once. Also, you have to really focus on what you want to accomplish, its easy to get mission overload here. Choose one or two  and run with them before doing another.

In the grimdark near future of the russian landscape surrounding the ruined city of Chernobyl EVERYTHING IS TRYING TO KILL YOU.
That's actually a pretty good summary of this game, a dark, (oftentimes terrifying) shooter, which pits an amnesiac protagonist against a variety of thugs, mutants, and bizarre supernatural phenomenon as he tries to find the truth about his past and what is actually occuring with the ZONE.
Progress through the game is accomplished by completing the main objectives, as well as a number of optional sidequests assigned by an angry fat man, offering various rewards, though this usually isn't as lucrative as simple murdering groups of bandits and taking and selling their things.
The game is very grim, and even without the spooky story, I had a lot of fun just roaming around and trying to keep my Stalker fed, armed, and relatively radiation free.  The graphics and voice acting are pretty sub-par, but these are ignorable gripes.
I highly recommend this game.

Before I tell my little story I have to say right away that this game is really quite enjoyable despite its inperfections (including an unintentionally hillarious climbing animation), and if you can tolerate the unintuitiveness of mount and blade you'll do fine with this.
So my story starts off with the daughter of a pirate whom I lovingly named "No-Beard". Newly captained and ready for anything she sets off, and is instantly attacked by pirates. Now, of course this is no issue for No-Beard, and she quickly managed to board the ship and get instantly knocked out by a musketeer. Luckily her crew was slightly less bullet-prone and captured the ship without her help.
This happened a few more times and she gained quite a bit of money, so she decided to put it into the bank... because that sounded like a good idea, and she spent the money that wasn't in the bank on repairs for the ships. Upon leaving the city for the open ocean, No-Beard spotted a group of smugglers, and that's pretty easy money. This time, however, something seemed off. The cannons weren't loading for some reason; I can't imagine why... Oh wait! I have no crew! How did that happen? Maybe all that grape shot.
Obviously, it's difficult to kill the entire crew by yourself without a counter button, so No-Beard is captured by the smugglers and sold into slavery on a plantation, which sorta sucks. Naturally she attempts to escape by herself, and is run over by a horse. After she convinces evey other slave to join her escape, two at a time, she sucesfully manages to escape with only twenty of the slaves being killed by the guards.
Pennieless and without a ship, she carefully heads back to a city to look for a job to make enough money to buy another ship, but the only job available is helping the french army cause panic for an excuse to wipe out the indigenous peoples. Meh, I have no morals. What I wasn't told is that the village me and an army will need to terrorize is on a different island, which sort of ruins my plan to use the money from the quest to buy a ship. But I have a bank account, don't I? Thank goodness I trusted most of my money with this random person I just met! Unfortunately I'm still about a hundred dollars short, so I end up literally selling the clothes off my back in order to afford the cheapest ship there is.
After setting off and avoiding contact with every other ship like a navy run by reddit, No-Beard makes it to the camp near the village to prepare for a not-even-slightly morally grey murder romp. Fully prepped and dressed in a grass dress, I realize that they probably wanted me to bring the army myself to take out the town, considering I'm the only one there. Well I suppose I can just run awa... oh, I was shot.♥♥♥♥♥♥
Apparantly, getting nearly killed made my realtionship with the♥♥♥♥♥♥who gave me the job go way down. Naturally I'm on another ship on the way to another plantation, and either luckily, or un, Windows decided that this would be a great time to tell me to activate my key, and crash the unsaved game.
I'd like to think I grew as a person from this experience, and being a slave gave me a new perspective on pixelated life. Hopefully the next pirate persona I decide to adopt has a better chance in life, and manages to not get enslaved twice.

After 40 hours and one play though defeating the Brotherhood and capturing all of their bases and half a dozen from the Spanish (cheating heavily by exporting my main character, giving her "lots" more money, and then importing her back into the game):
Pros:
- If you like the mount and blade games and you like pirate games, you will like this game.
- It plays very solidly on Windows 10 OS.
- Don't let the Cons below sway you, as I said this is a very good game on the verge of becoming a great game with another update or two.
Cons (listed for the developers):
- Major bug, I just went to start a new game and the Start new Game option is greyed out. I deleted saved games, checked integrity of files, but can't seem to fix it.  Help! [I just changed my review to negative based on this bug until it is fixed and I can play the game again.]
- All the major pieces are here, however there are some pieces left out from Warband, such as sieging cities/forts, you can only assault them.
- The menus get a bit tideous at times, e.g., it would be nice to be able to move troops you purchase from the garrison directly to the fort and not have to transport them back and forth through the main character's company.
- I have to redistribute crews before reaching port and I can fill my ships from the other ships easily. I understand there should be a certain minium sized prize crew to sail a ship (one is laughable, but you allow it), but the others I should be able to more easily move to my depleted crews on my core ships.
- the little plus sign doesn't show up on the list of crew when you click their button on the Party screen, this is annoying, having to search through each to find which ones advanced during battles, and who is the screen so small? Why not just use the regular crew/party screen?
- Another item basic to all mount and blade games that is missing is that you can't choose which "captives" you freed to bring into your company, it automatically chooses the weakest captives, from what I can tell. I could understand certain nationalities based on faction not joining, but... this sucks as it currently stands.
- If you play as a pirate it would be fun after sea battles to be able to recruit sailors from defeated crews) or impress them if you are British, etc.).
- The sea battles seem a little simplistic, they never seem to vary from head on encounters. And there is no way to command your other ships other than to anchor them. Needs work.
- There is a very minor bug that caused a crash right after start up before I did anything (happened twice, no negative effect either time).
- The game seems to be a little laggier than latest Warband.

Homeworld is an RTS in true 3D with a fantastic art style. Visually it looks like a 1970s/1980s sci-fi, like old-school Battle Star Galactica and Star Wars. Check out the artist Chris Foss if you like the visuals in Homeworld - it's very reminiscent of Foss's work. The art stye is also reminiscent of those old Usborne Books of the Future I used to read as kid.
Much like a classic book, Homeworld seems timeless. I cannot believe that I was playing this game 16(!) years ago and yet here I am playing it today with gameplay that's still just as good, just as fun as it was so many years ago.
I'd gladly pay $40 each for both Homeworld and Homeworld 2, but here you're getting both, remastered for same price. In fact, I only paid $20 since the game was on sale for 50% off.  Great value! Both games have a decent single player campaign, skirmish modes and multiplayer. Even if you have just the smallest desire to play an RTS, check out Homeworld.

Played this game with a few friends online and then again with my son on local. Both times were quite enjoyable. It is very much a game about mastering chaos and then chuckling a little bit at one joke taken to an absurd extreme.  For as tiring as the 'Bro' themeing gets, the game remains enjoyable and actually does eventually benefit from mastery as you learn to recognize the exploding enemies from the firing ones.
Overall, game plays like a high intensity Contra, but instead of getting different guns for two generic gues, the entire cast of characters (and there are a LOT of characters) are all 'Bro' versions of action heroes from film.  BRO-bocop, RamBRO, TimeBRO, etc.  There are even a few 'BRO' versions of female heroes (Ripley from Alien, the Bride from Kill Bill, etc) Everyone has over the top muscles but, again, while it is a simple and somewhat immature theme, the game fully executes on it with great graphics, excellent gameplay, and a few chuckles at the next purile height the game takes it's macho image to.
There is a 'story' mode... which really isn't much of a story, but that's fine. The story is not why you'd play this game.
I imagine the game would be fairly dull without a friend, though, so the multiplayer aspect is not just a feature, it's essentially a requirement.  Pick up the 4 pack and get your fiends to play, they'll thank you.

After playing Fallout 2 a long time ago I wondered what a post apocalyptic game would be like from the Russian side. Well, heres the answer. Its got a seriousness that the Fallout series does not, and a darker, more brooding atmosphere. Much like Shadowrun you cannot take a lot of gunfire,
forcing  you to think through your firefights and play in a less run-and-gun style. That being said, once you get used to crouching and aiming then moving to a new position, you can take on fairly large groups of enemies. The only downside to this game is the long load times, but heres a fix...start the game with -noprefetch and, ironically, it runs smoother and faster and  loads quickly. My guess is that the game is too agressive with the prefetching and if you tell it to cut that out it fetches as needed instead of

"A third person, character-locked camera," I thought, "That might make playing this genre easier." So I tried SMITE, since it's free and I already had a Hi-Rez account.
The note of a mandatory tutorial from another review was accurate, but I felt fine taking some time to re-acquaint myself with the genre and the camera system of SMITE.
After a first level cumulating in a markedly unnecessary, scantly clad character, I continued the tutorial. Level two passed without note, same for the third level. The simple, single-lane map worked and I got along fine with the controls. Then the unique mode of arena 5v5 tutorial happened:
I'm done.
P.S. if the trailer didn't tip you off that this was basically a League of Legends rip-off, playing any characters and looking at basically *any* of the UI elements of the game interface will show you a remarkable similarity...

PROS
- Tower defence with fully 3D environments, creeps and weapon behaviors
- Turrets are varied and use ballistics, as well as AI aiming, instead of automatic guaranteed damage outputs
- Player can control fully fleshed out turrets or vehicles to take part in the defence, not just a gimmick
- GI Joe/Cold War 1980s trimmings, with historical weapons and creeps and a good amount of tongue-in-cheek
- Visuals and sound are excellent (for a game from 2011) Players can also joyfully destroy most level features, leaving levels looking war torn.
CONS
- World War 1 content, whilst expanded, is inferior to the original Toy Soldiers game. Game breaking bugs etc
- Multiplayer issues - DO NOT EXPECT ONLINE MULTIPLAYER TO WORK, split screen is great fun
- Will not appeal to those fond of tower defence games full of numbers and fixed variables, or players who don't find the "random and whacky" nature of AI aiming and projectile physics to be enjoyable.

If you're a tower defense fan but tired of strict grid-and-number affairs, give Toy Soldiers a try. If you've got any interest in 20th century military history, give Toy Soldiers a try.
Instead of coldly precise towers on a grid issuing 10 points of damage every 2.5 seconds to the nearest creep, Toy Soldiers has machine guns snaking lead around the heads of Russian troops, or surface-to-air missiles casting smoky trails as they home in on supersonic US Tomcat jets. A proper realtime game with physics and 3D projectiles instead of simply disguised dice rolls hitting HP sponges.
As opposed to weighing up number based tower upgrades, area-of-effects and watching hundreds of creeps marching in a static laneway Toy Soldiers brings real time chaos and player controlled action to the mix. Build your turrets and watch their various attacks interact with the environment and enemy waves without the spreadsheet-precision of regular TD games. Take control of turrets yourself and chain up combos to unleash powerful player controlled call-ins, or hop into a vacant helicopter or tank to sweep the battlefield clean of enemies yourself.
Oozing with charm and  great "modelling diorama" asthetics Toy Soldiers is a breakout from the tower defense mould. Containing both the grim madness of the WW1 Western Front as well as the over-the-top 1980s Cold War, Toy Soldiers is a delightful mix of historical homage and video game fun. Contains the best representation of WW1 in a game I've seen, though perhaps the original, un-tweaked Toy Soldiers game nails it better. Only time will tell if TS:C improves or degrades the WW1 content.
[UPDATE - Sadly it seems that the World War 1 content is doomed to be buggy and generally inferior to the original, but such is the effect of porting an older game into a newer game engine. Still, the very well polished Cold War aspect of the game is extremely worth the purchase.]

There is a lot of bugs and the game does crash ocasionally, but this is in Early Access so what do you expect? This a defenite buy here."
No, it's not a defenite buy. Take a look at my new review for this game:
Toy Soldiers Complete....what can I say about it. Well I can say  it's only half of a good game.  Cold War is awesome, it has explosions, easy to learn mechanics, and overall good gameplay (and the DLC is free!).  There are a few issues in Cold War but are not very noticeable. TS1 in this game....sucks.  There are so many problems with TS1 in this game.  I own the original Toy Soldiers, so when I bought TS:C I expected TS1 to be an exact port, but I was wrong.  SO MANY GLITCHES can be found in TS1 in this game, and even after a new update comes out some glitches still remain unfixed (and continuously remain unfixed even after constant updates).  Signal Studios tried to combine what they did in Cold War in their "remastered" version of TS1,  by adding Turbo Charge, Barrages, and other things, but these additions only reduced the quality of the game.  The barrages in the TS:C version of TS1 are just the Cold War barrages but polished to look different, and I'm pretty sure World War I nor Toy Soldiers 1 had an orbital laser, it's just madness!   Signal Studios should've just stuck to their guns, but they just
to add something new.  I get that Signal Studios wanted to balance the games so in VS. mode one team couldn't have a higher advantage over the other, but what they did here was just terrible. Here is a list of 10 glitches and inaccuracies in this version of TS1 included in this game:
1) Whenever the Chemical Level 3 is used, it leaves behind the gas cloud and it loops over and over.
2) Whenever the Machine Gun Level 3 is used, the muzzle can be quite blinding.
3) Some enemy units are overpowered and have way too much health.
4) The Anti-Air guns have this annoying gravity bullet velocity that forces you to shoot higher and due to this renders the Anti-Air gun's AI to be completely useless.
5) The Anti-Tank guns are just the models of the Level 3 Anti-Infantry guns taken from the original TS1.
6) TS1 bosses have a bit too little health.
7) The Machine Gun models are also taken from TS1, which is ok, but the models are from the wrong parts of the game.
8) The Sniper Tower is really just a Machine Gun Level 2 but modified.
9) The Mortars have the same effects from Cold War.
10) The sounds for the Chemicals Levels 1 and 2 are swapped.
There's plenty more glitches and inaccuracies in this version of TS1.  If you want Cold War on PC,  go ahead, buy this acursed thing. If you don't have TS1 and instead buy this game thinking it has the original TS1, you'll be very disappointed.  The only thing that's worth buying in this game is Cold War, but that's about it. This game is only half good and half completed. Cold War is ok; but TS1 in this game sucks. If I were you, I wouldn't buy it. Instead I'd wait for Toy Soldiers: War Chest to come out and then buy the original, 100% authentic, no doubt about it, not sheet TS1 on PC. The original TS1 does have Windows Live Arcade and it forces you to play online, but just deal with it, be glad it has SteamWorks at least.
Thank goodness Ubisoft is making the next Toy Soldiers, because I think they will do a whole lot better job than Signal Studios ever did with this damn game.  I know this game is still in Early Access, but this is just lousy.

Ok, so my review is basically a bug list that needs fixing from the devs:
Crashes when trying to retreat during special missions. Being able to see the battle play out is ok, but your maps often mess up the pathing, and then it can take forever. There's no way back to the menu screen then.
Not being able to control your men during special missions. If you ask me to do a 31 v 31 skirmish with native gear against armed enemies, then letting me use the basic mount and blade commands would be nice
The command and control system has gotten worse from Warband era Mount and Blade, I haven't played enough Fire and Sword to comment. There's a map, but it's unintuitive, didn't work for me while trying to move units, and it plays out in real time. I used to just ride my horse towards the nearest high point and tell infantry and archers to stay there. Now I have to sit on my horse and wait for them to get there. Not good.
Horseman are worthless. Don't pick up any Harquesibiers if you plan on fighting on the land. You'll bury them the next day. If you get them to follow you, and make sure they hold off, and play a retreating action with them you can inflict some casualites, but they have really, really low survivability, even if you don't let them get mobbed. Often I'll steamroll an enemy, but lose most of my stupid horse gunners.
Armour is key, but doesn't seem to scale up nicely. I'm still on a fairly easy difficulty, and the armour is tissue paper. Especially to guns. Taking 27p damage in a 32 head protection helmet when I can't even kill regular troops on every hit with a high end gun is infuriating. I guess it doesn't matter so much since the armour costs nothing once you start raiding convoys, but still.
You can't do anything to avoid a boarding. If the AI thinks it will win a boarding, it will charge you, if not, it will sail in circles firing it's cannons. It's really obvious, really quick. So if the enemy boat comes at you, fire on it with a broadside and run away. Use your chainshot and it'll stop. It's fine for now, but it's going to get old soon, which brings me to the next point.
Boarding combat is really damn stupid. I don't seem to have any way of knowing how many men I'll field, how many combat troops I have on each boat, or assigning them, I can't order my men to stand grand, so if I'm outnumbered, there goes picking them off and using a local numerical advantage to inflict some casualties.
Taverns are just annoying. Fix the layout. I don't want to climb stairs to do anything.
Every menu takes forever to load.
Your ship will automatically land if it bumps into a port. This will cost you tax, and take a while, loading, more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Sometimes pathing will do this for no reason.
Multiple ship boardings aren't possible.
I do really like this game. It shows a lot of promise, and a lot of people asked for it. But it needs serious patching, and probably some content updates. I just can't recommend it to you if you aren't willing to put up with the bugs. It's mount and blade on ships, and yeah, for the most part it works, even with the clunky, dated engine and combat limiting the boarding action. Like Mount and Blade, you can fall into a rhythm of progress and have a lot of fun. Just, look up a tutorial first. Recruiting is dumb, and you need to recruit heavily. There's a message board in towns for it. You advance a lot quicker in this game than the originals, or maybe I'm just better. The combat feels harder, and I played on fairly hard difficulties, full damage, full speed, full size, etc in Warband, which is good and bad. Getting better ships is based on "Rank" which is based on your reputation, which lags far behind what you can do combat wise. It's easier to steal better ships than buy them, which becomes more of a problem as you start looking at attacking Captains for their ships.  I've got a fleet of Light Galleons, still chasing down a medium or an even better ship and the best I can buy is a brig.
Upgrading ships is expensive. Don't do it until you have a decent ship, otherwise you're wasting time. Don't be scared to sell ships and upgrade.

Alright. I might rustle some jimmies by not being on the bandwagon, but I really can't recommend this title. The TL,DR version is if you're looking for a good horror expereince, try the Amnesia line instead.
= Basics
The game is put together well. Graphics are tight, sound design is fairly excellent with surround sound headphones.
= Mechanics problems
Controls are usually good but there are some clunky aspects. Whenever you interact with certain object types (save points, rewiring panels, terminals) you wind up locked into a multi-second animation from which you cannot cancel. If something comes up behind you it's either going to score free hits (synthetics and humans) or an insta-kill (alien).
Gameplay breaks out to combat (very limited, and usually feels anti-climactic), walking, and occasional mini-games. Mini-games take the form of "open this panel", "pull this lever", and "hack this interface", with several variations on each. Opening a panel, for example, might require hitting A -> Left Trigger -> down on the Left Stick, or it might be A -> both triggers -> down on both sticks, or it might be just A (to slap a button), or you might have to cut a panel off the front first. But it's still only variations on opening a door, and conveys all the thrill you think it should.
After a couple of hours these tasks all start to feel like filler. The variety feels a bit forced, as though the devs know they shouldn't repeat /too/ much but they only have a stable of 3 tricks to pull from for any given type of action. Wanna complicate things? Let's make the player spin up a generator before they can actually open the door! This is neither fun nor was it engaging to me.
= Pacing problems
A:I alternates between "stressful" moments (with appropriate music), "stealth" moments (where you have time to spot enemies and plan your approach), and long sections where the game becomes a walking simulator.
Sequences without the Alien feel kind of dry. Human enemies are frightening the first time you encounter them, but once you start getting weapons, they're easy to handle. For that matter, whenever there's Alien/Human overlap, dispatching human enemies is as simple as calling in your ever-present guardian devil. A simple Noisemaker will clear untold hordes of humans from a room. I mean, the Alien actually does the clearing work, but you get how this goes already.
Stretches of the game where you're fighting synthetics is alternately frustrating (early, when you're under-armed) and boring (later, when you've got some stun baton charges, EMPs, a shotgun or bolt gun, etc). The synthetics do not move fast, are easy to avoid, and have no way to pursue you into vents.
The bits where the Alien is on site are sometimes stressful, sometimes goofy (crouching behind a box is enough to avoid detection, and this thing rarely looks under desks for some reason), but as a direct confrontation with the Alien is an instant-death scenario, you'll wind up spending much of the early game appreciating the undersides of office furniture or the insides of lockers. The Alien likes to hang out extra-long at times, leaving you trapped with nothing to do and no way to progress.
The game as a whole suffers from having very long corridors with generally slow motion (fast running is possible but draws too much attention to be recommended). Some parts of the game (any work in a space suit) prevents you from running or using weapons, so you already know that you're either not going to encounter enemy resistance or any you find will be handled through the game's version of quicktime events (leading to a loss of player agency).
There are /many/ long hallways, and there are quite a few areas of forced backtracking (with none of the new-mechanics thrill that metroidvania titles bring). While I appreciate taking your time to build up a sense of scale, grandeur, or impact, making me spend 3 minutes doing nothing but walking up a long♥♥♥♥♥staircase in a spacesuit isn't fun.
= Story
The story is generally good though it's told in a fragmented way through terminal notes, audio logs, and brief updates from other characters you encounter.
The last 2-3 hours of the game didn't land well in my opinion. We reach a point where I (the player) am entirely good with letting things end, but there's no choice presented, so my character moves on with a bone-headed decision that artificially extends an ending I /knew/ had to be coming. Then we go through a few long-winded sequences where "stress" is a product of music and bright lights rather than any real feeling of terror in the player -- scenes where the game is telling me "Hurry! Hurry!" but I know damn well I could sit and watch things burn for another six hours if I wanted as all the logic is scripted. The game can tell me "you need to be frightened!" every few minutes and blare alarms all it wants; the impact wasn't there, and the glacial end-game pacing left me feeling like I was never really getting anywhere.
I even found the twists boring. "Ho hum, almost made it, - oh no! something happened! Now we get to do another lengthy mission of filler tasks where we'll probably cut through a panel or two, hack some♥♥♥♥♥♥ and press A a few dozen more times. weee."
The ending of this game didn't suit me at all. I found the conclusion transparent and the ending cinematic unfulfilling.
= Overall
I'd give this a 3/5. There were very few technical faults to speak of (some clipping issues, a rare driver crash - nothing major). This title is put together well. But I didn't feel the experience is worth the $50 asking price at all, and the prevailing memory I have of this game is feeling kind of bored at how things went. This one winds up in my "meh" folder.

Dark Souls 2 is a sequel to Dark Souls, and between the two, I personally like it better than the first game. Dark Souls 2 has expanded on the mechanics of the first game and improved them considerably, and the game's story is rich and, while considerably more vague than the first, is still great to speculate and put its pieces together. Unlike the wicked thing that was the first game's PC port, Dark Souls 2 runs smoothly even on low-end PCs at full 60 frames per second, and while the game did suffer from a graphical downgrade during development, it is still beautiful and gorgeous at times. The backstab-centric Player versus Player of the first game is gone, making it far more varied and entertaining and co-op is also improved upon, being more rewarding and encouraged while still being loads of fun. The soundtrack is among jaw-dropping at times.
That's not to say the game is lacking in flaws, though. The game lacks the first installment's charismatic characters, it relies on pitting the player against hordes of enemies too often for the sake of difficulty, and there is also terribly implemented mechanics such as Soul Memory and bugs which cause weapons to lose their durability twice faster on PC due to the game running at 60 fps.
The three DLCs, the Lost Crowns Trilogy, is a must-get for those who like the Souls series. Similar to Artorias of the Abyss in the first game, the Lost Crowns possesses some of the best atmosphere and level design in the game, at times surpassing the core game itself, expanding on the world and adding a great level of depth at seemingly minor details in the game's lore. My personal favorite among them would be Crown of the Old Iron King, which holds what is in my opinion the best bosses in the game, while Crown of the Ivory King is the weakest. While it is still a definitely must-play experience, it also holds what is in my opinion the worst area in any Souls game. Yes, even worse than Lost Izalith.
If you liked Dark Souls 1, you will also enjoy Dark Souls 2. Good luck, and don't give up, skeleton!

My play time is split between the PC and a console.
I really wanted to like this game. I loved the other two Souls games. I loved the Kings Field games. I would be happy if the only video games I ever owned were Dark Souls and Demons' Souls.
This game, though, feels dead and empty in not-an-evocative kind of way.
Part of this has to do with streamlining mechanics and part of it has to do with getting rid of the more arcane game elements (like Demons' Souls light world/dark world thing).
I think the majority of what made Dark Souls 2 unenjoyable is down to two things: the level design in particular and the level design more broadly construed.
Broad level design: Dark Souls in particular did a great job of stitching together very different, but distinct areas. Here, there is much less of a sense of purpose to the broad composition of the map(s). Many of the maps also suffer from a general bland-ness. In Dark Souls and Demons Souls (and Kings Field) if there was a castle or castle-like structure it mattered both in terms of story and in terms of architecture. Too many of the maps feel as if stone is thrown in to provide a break from forest or vice versa.
Level design in the particulars: Demons' Souls and Kings Field(s) do a lovely job of marrying the level design with the enemy design and their placement. There is a strong sort of ambience that feels wierdly lacking in DS2. Sort of like they just threw things in one section or the other. The preceding games also generally worked by introducing you to one or two of an enemy type and then adding a few more in novel combinations, using the level design to advantage (smaller units hiding, rats luring you into pits, zombies waiting in ambush, etc.). In DS2, its enemy -> more enemy -> even more enemies.
The maps are also generally larger and the falls less frequent, meaning that the shabby, path-bound, easy-to-cheese AI from the game's predecessors is back but is much easier to exploit (and this is a huge contributor to that empty feeling I get in the maps. I got the sense in Kings Field and Dark Souls, especially Dark Souls, that there were _exactly_ as many enemies in a place as there needed to be. Here, there is just way too much space for the enemies provided). Which isn't to say that this is totally fumbled, just that it felt as if space and enemy density and lighting, etc were constantly considered in previous games to create a fraut, nail-biting experience, and there are still places where the level design feels inspired (early on, I think the most obvious example is that pirate cove place).
I mean the rest of it is pretty good, but the rest of it is more or less on offer in Dark Souls and Demons' Souls and those two are, I imagine, a lot less money to buy.

In 1999 I played a game that would forever impress me
When I opened the box I was presented with a beautiful manual/lore book full of information and background for the game I was playing.
It was beautiful
Then I loaded the game up.
I was stunned by the gorgeousness of the graphics
I marvelled at how times had come along so much that this piece of art was now in my possession
When I played the game the intricacies of the strategy and the challenge of keeping your fleet in one piece and seeing it grow, remembering that old ion array frigate in the last mission that you acquired in the third mission, the epic story as you fought for the right to regain your homeworld and I thought it couldn’t get any better.
I was wrong
A year later Cataclysm was released, a standalone expansion from the original, it used the same engine but it was altered in a way that changed the rules, following a story set 15 years after landfall on the homeworld, you follow a family of miners who uncover a dark secret and a parasitic virus and you must race to stop it. Again it expanded on the visuals, tactics and story, again I thought it could not get better, and again I was wrong…
Homeworld 2 was released in 2003, and with it a rewritten engine, stunning visuals that reminded me of the opening scene from revenge of the sith, and a slightly retconned but no less epic story.
100 years after reclaiming your homeworld, the old enemy have arisen under a new leader. Using the artefact of an ancient super powerful hyperspace engine, But you have one too, and there are legends of a third. To reclaim your homeworld once again, you must liberate the second core, find the third and unite the cores to end the threat once and for all.
Can it get better?
Yes, Homeworld remastered is all of these games (with the exception of cataclysm, which I hope they add at some point) with updated engines and even better stunning hi definition visuals. It’s an epic experience. If you have played the original and loved them, buy it. If you’re a fan of epic sci fi, buy it. If you like strategy games, buy it.
Just buy it, go on click add to cart and put your money where it belongs.

Not a remastered edition but a rehashed one. If you've played the original, don't try this - keep your money, memories and old copy intact. If you haven't played Homeworld and can't handle anything but the latest graphics then this is the one for you.
Alot of the other reviews sum it up perfectly, some particular points that require ephasis though:
-Formations are broken and do not work.
-Completely different unit balances compared to the original (especially frigates. They are now just lumps of RUs that specialise in sploding real good).
-HW1 remastered hit system is all based on a system of probabilities of hitting a target (like HW2) instead of an actual hit is a hit. As HW1 was designed on an actual hit system, this mucks up the gameplay. Adding to this is HW2's specialisation system coming into play (eg assault frigates are good vs fighters, so if you tell them to attack corvettes, a slower and larger target, all their shots will still miss as they are not a unit "good vs corvettes"). It is basically a port of HW1 into HW2 therefore if you want to play using the remastered graphics but the orginal gameplay style (of HW1), you can't (defeats the purpose of buying remastered)
-Units behave differently than the original Homeworlds (eg corvettes circling an enemy now only use half their guns) - above explains part of this too.
-Complete lie when they say you will get the original games - they've fondled all LAN and multiplayer options out of them which is so substantial a change that they can't be considered as original verisons. Therefore you can't play multiplayer with the classics - a key feature which THE CLASSICS HAD (and it wasn't a multiplayer beta strap on like this "remastered" edition has. That's right people, when the original Homeworld came out, multiplayer in the Homeworld universe was not in beta - it was already COMPLETE)
Given this is a "mastering" of a classic, of which all they had to do was improve the graphics, its a very poor show and blatant cash grab leveraging on Homeworld's reputation established so long ago.
Will have to consider greatly before buying anything from Gearbox Software

Ok so the only reason I ever played this game to start with was to get an item in Killing Floor lol. But as it just so happens to be, this isn't a bad little game. It's simple enough in design but can yield a nice challenge.
Between the lava rushes and floods, mother nature can be one hateful ♥♥♥♥♥ in this game. You may think having only two environmental hazards would quickly become stale, but I didn't find that to be the case. They can be unforgiving.
There are several modes in Dwarfs?! but for the most part your goal is to mine as much of the map as you can, without your base being overcome before the time runs out.
In each game you'll have ups and downs contained within caves of unknown content until entrance that could either hold Gold, a Boss, mini-hoard, lava, or water.
You can spend in game currency to use blocks that block off cave systems and prevent your workers from breaching the containment area but be warned, if you block off the entire system without first discovering it's contents there will be a penalty in the form of a deduction from your gold... an important item I may add. One tactic you may want to try is blocking off all but 1 square then send in 2 workers with dynamite equipped in case it's lava or water. In that event it's best to sacrifice a worker to make a drainage hole in the earth and completely sealing that hazard, which will give you a bonus.
Along the way you may construct outposts with your gold and train warriors and workers. Good thing they put this in because the map is rather large and this will cut down on travel time during combat or intervention.
In the harder modes controlling your workers becomes extremely important. There are more hazards to be found and they flow faster so having 2 or 3 workers tap into separate conduits will be a quick death for you.
So that's the general idea, I'll let you explore the rest of the game for yourself :)
Oh yeah, don't forget about the Killing Floor award, whatever it was. Happy gaming!

This game is probably closer to an RTS than anything, but has its own take on ordering your minions about to maximize beneficial outcomes.  I ended up really enjoying the gameplay, learning how to efficiently collect resources and defeat the various bosses.  A lot of how each game plays out is up to chance (map generation), so sometimes even the best orders don't work out the way you expect. You've gone underground to narrowly avoid a military assault on a complex. All you hear is your own breathing and the whirling of an old emergency light that would have died years ago if it didn't require so little energy. You double check your Makarov and newly acquired AK74, making sure they're both filled on ammo as you slowly walk down the dark hallway. You peer into a large, open, room, and see nothing besides pipes, containers, and a corpse. You flick your flashlight on before moving to check the corpse, grabbing some bread, vodka, and ammo. As you take another peek around, a monstorous roar makes you jump. Heavy breathing is heard in the distance, not your own, from foreign lungs. No man breathes like that. You pull out your AK, looking where the noise is coming from but see nothing. And then a second roar, and as you turn to check behind you, the bloodsucker has already wrapped its tentacles around your head.

I only started launching this game through Steam sometime in the past year, so my logged hours should really be well above 3000. I've been playing this game since open Beta and I've seen it undergo many transformations; from the early days of bug-ridden quests at launch, to the unfortunate decision of going f2p, to the latest social integration of removing faction restrictions for PvE, this game has changed in many ways. Like any MMO, it will likely never be perfect and there will always be people who criticise one aspect of the game or another. As much as I've had my gripes with it however, it stands at a sweet spot today, and if you're into MMOs, and particularly TES lore, you should definitely give this a try. It is a beautiful game, with fantastic graphics, engaging questlines, fun easter eggs, great characters, and most importantly, an amazing community. As much as ZOS has screwed up in many ways, they have, for the most part, kept to their schedule on regularly released updates, and although they're not always particularly great, they keep the game bustling with players from all walks of life. If you are looking for a hardcore endgame/raiding formula with ample variety, this may not be your best bet, but if you enjoy challenging PvP and fun PvE, you won't be disappointed. I can't stress this enough: the community in this game is GREAT. Join a guild (or five) as soon as you come in, and your experience will be that much better.

This is one of the best free to play games i ever played.So im going to write the review in colums:
Graphics-Pretty much half life 2. The source engine is capable to produce pretty good visuals even to this day.So expect good graphics.
Gameplay-Team Work is key here.Try alone and your chances of completing a map are pretty low unless you know what you are doing and played the maps over and over.You got melee and firearms to protect yourself.Melees are pretty useful throughout the game but when you stack up on ammo you will want to use your firearm because you will find ammo throughout the map if you search that is.A little complain is that the actions you do are a little bit slow but nothing game breaking.There is a inventory system which allows you to carry a limited number of resources so managing them with teammates to carry as much as possible is crucial.Although you cant carry 2 of the same items like medkits at the same time.Zombies vary from walkers to crawlers to kids.The melee system may feel awkward at first but mastering the shove command you will have an easier time staying alive.The real deal comes down when you get infected. You can also bleed but being infected has a really big impact on the player.Put it like this:you get bitten and see vains in your screen. Those vains continue to grow and vision gets darker meaning you are turning.You can only postpone this by eating the pills but the only way to get a cure is through the gene therapy(which is pretty rare and sometimes doesnt spawn at all).If you cant find pills you can shoot yourself to avoid turning into a zombie.
Multiplayer:This game requires teamwork to be completed.Sadly this is hard to achive if you play with total randoms.Dont forget!This is a free to play game meaning that everyone can play it so expect find a lot of Aholes in this game.Team voice chat is recomended.The game offers 8 players coop which is nice.Unless you know the guys you are playing with or you are sure that those guys can play then go ahead but if you enter a public server you will most likely end up wasting your time.Most of the maps can be completed with 2-3 players and sometimes that way its even easier.Being with 7 other people in a post apocalyptic world where supplies are scarce is not such a good situation to be in as you though it would be.The smaller the group the easier is to manage your resources. i suggest 2-3 players in a server.Get a friend or your brother or sister to have the full effect.
Ambience:It does a great job at making you feel like you are in a zombie infested city.The visuals,the music and the voice acting does a great job.Firstly you encounter normal zombies but later you will find runners and crawlers and even kids (which would be controversial but i think that the director of the game did a great job putting them in for added realism).There are dark areas where you need your flashlight to see.Or you can let other people shine the light for you as you kill zombies to clear the way.As i previously mention being infected leads you to multiple choices if you wanna tell the group or hide it.It does a great job at making you feel hopeless.There are other survivors here and there but they are mostly inside vehicles meaning you cant see them only hear them.
Overall:This is not your average free to play game. This game doesnt have microtransitions AT ALL!You heard me! This is one of those few games which doesnt contain a single in game purchase.The only thing this game will cost you is the bandwith you will use to download it. The game is beautifully crafted,designed and its really enjoyable for a free to play game.The maps have high replay value,the sounds are spot on,graphics are great,gameplay is adrenaline filled and when all of these combine the right way you will have a total blast.I strongly suggest this game and if you havent played yet go ahead and do it! You wont regret it.This game gets a solid 10/10 without a single doubt!

Toy Soldiers: Complete is in early access, so at the present time only Cold War is available to play. Keep that in mind for the review, but if it's any consolation, I've also played both on Xbox 360.
Toy Soldiers is a tower defense game where the player can control turrets to take more control (or use special turret functions), use vehicles or call powers down upon the enemy. This is the all-inclusive Toy Soldiers package; both games and all of the DLC are included. Toy Soldiers is World War I themed while Cold War is 80's action movie interpretations of the cold war.
The game is easy to jump in to. The only thing to keep in mind is that turrets sometimes change a lot when upgrading. For example: level 2 anti-tank turrets lose their shell cams, which is useful for targeting long distance enemies. The rest is simple: defend your toy box (base) from enemies.
There's a campaign mode and two mini campaigns (previously DLC) along with versus, survival and minigames. The game also supports coop, but I haven't tried it on PC yet. Toy Soldiers has plenty to offer at the moment, as it's well polished, funny and most of all: fun. In it's current state it's well worth $10, but once it make it out of early access (and includes the original Toy Soldiers) it'll be a steal.

There are no shallows. We all know that shallows were very important for the pirates as they were one of the ways that they could escape from warships. The sloops, especially the bigger ones, are underestimated. Sloops were the primary ships of pirates, and the way they are represented in the game, unless you have a sloop yourself or a cutter, you have nothing to fear as a merchant from the pirates with that kind of ship in this game. Sloops are fast, maneuverable, have decent amount of cannons for their size and are quite dangerous in the hands of pirates. Also, they can go where no warships can go making it easy for them to sail away.
When you are boarding a ship or you are being boarded, the ships should be a bit bigger, and the amount of masts you have on each ships should reflect the amount of mast you have on each ship, not a default arena where people kill each other. If my ship has only one big mast, then there should be only one big mast. There is lots of work to be done here. Also, I want the ships to be as big as the ship I am boarding with, if I am using a sloop, then it is as big as a sloop with one mast, if I am boarding with a trimast corvette or three-decker then three mast plus big deck. I also want to have my entire load of men to attack not just a dozen or twenty. If I have a 100 men on board, I want a 100 men to assault the other ship. Otherwise I lose men uselessly by doing that silly 20 vs 20. I want a gauge like in Mount & Blade that tells the game how many guys I want on the map for each side.
Taking the Mount & Blade system into the Carribean is a good idea, but the designers should have put more time into research of the period and what made a pirate good at what he does as well as putting more time into coding. Graphics are unimportant as you have seen in Mount & Blade. M&B's graphics were ordinary, but the game was awesome. So build on that.
Oh yeah, add shallows where warships cannot enter without taking damage.
Also, I've noticed that no matter what the shape of your ships are in your fleet, you do not slow down on the world map. Sorry but that makes no sense. I captured a ship that had basically no masts or sails left and I was still moving at top speed on the the world map. In reality, a fleet moves at the speed of the slowest ship you have in it.
Another thing, when you sell a ship you should be able to keep and transfer its crew to your remaining ships, it's silly to always buy the damn guys over and over again because you sent some onto ships you have captured for sailing it back to port.
Trading is possible, although there should be like a logbook that your character writes into when he finds a milk run so that you can remember easily. But you would need to discover it. Like buy rum in town A and sell it in town E. Or maybe some guy in port that you can pay and he tells you where you can sell for a profit the merchandise found in this town. Or do like the old Mount & Blade and assess the market by using time instead of money and it would be evaluated according to your merchant skill.
I like the game, and recommend buying it for people who likes pirate/sea games and Mount & Blade. But it requires lots of tweaking still.

Homeworld is a legendary PC game and I'd love to be able to recommend this Remastered Collection.  At first glance it's everything it was promised to be: a rebuilt version of Homeworld 1 & 2 (no HW:Cataclysm unfortunately) using an updated engine to make the games much prettier, fix many compatibility issues, and address various long-standing bugs.
The reason I can't give that recommendation is that the new engine shared by Homeworld 1&2 in this remake is based on Homeworld 2's engine, and it's a fundamentally different game from Homeworld 1.  Many of the issues this causes are cosmetic but others make the game borderline unplayable.  The two most egregious flaws introduced are to do with the "formation" and "tactics" systems.
Formations are theoretically still in the game but ships now break formation for almost any reason.  This frequently reduces the core of the game's combat system to little more than "have more ships at the fight than your opponent".  You used to be able to do things like attack from multiple directions while keeping your ships in effective groupings, put your ships into a wall formation to bring more firepower to bear at once, put them in a sphere formation to guard a weaker ship, and so on - none of this works anymore.  You can still take advantage of weaker armor in different areas of your enemy's ships, but it's a disorganized mess.
The tactics system, which previously made the difference between your ships focusing on maneuverability or firepower, has been stripped out altogether.  This used to be a very valuable game mechanic, allowing you to press your advantage in one-sided battle to quickly end it before enemy reinforcements arrived, or use maneuverable mode to escape unfavorable situations.  The tactics system is now the same as Homeworld 2's, and basically every other RTS: aggressive (attack on sight), defensive (attack if attacked), and passive (ignore enemies).  This might not sound like a big deal if you've never played Homeworld before, but it was one of the most unique aspects of the game, and it functioned extremely well in combination with smart formation choices.
Lesser but still important issues are to do with changes to the game's interface and how various ships function.
The game's main user interface has been replaced with one inspired by Homeworld 2, which had much simpler "rock-paper-scissors" ship balancing and all that really mattered was "this ship is good against this ship".  Homeworld 1 was more complex than this though and its UI gave you appropriately more complex information, including things like fire arc coverage - a major differentiating factor between different ship types.  This is vital information, removed in service of making the game more accessible, but it has the opposite effect: new players won't know what the real advantages between different ships really are, and this is a game that severely punishes choosing the wrong fleet composition.
As for the functional issues with various ships, unfortunately there's not much I can say.  I threw up my hands in disgust long before I had the opportunity to experience more than the first five or so missions and a bit of the multiplayer, so there's a lot of stuff I only know about based on what I've heard others say, like how repair ships are apparently broken in some way.  One thing I know about is that the concept of fuel has been removed, and this has huge gameplay implications.  I don't like this change, it's like if Valve added regenerating health and cover mechanics to Half-Life.  I recognize that it's a technical limitation and would require a lot of work to fix, and it's not nearly as big of an issue as formations and tactics being removed though, so it's something I can overlook.  Worrying about fuel did become a hassle at times.
edit: One thing I forgot to mention is that Homeworld used a weapon system where projectiles/beams were fired and whether they hit or not depended on... well, whether they actually hit or not.  The bullets were physical objects which could be dodged.  Everything in Homeworld 2's combat is based on accuracy percentages, and this is how Homeworld's combat now works due to it being based on HW2's engine.  This isn't game-breaking but it does make the game feel less... I don't know how to describe it... less real?  Less dynamic?  The results of combat are predictable.  [X] always beats [Y] in [Z] scenario.  The real-world effect of this change is often only cosmetic but I think it does detract from the original game's gameplay feel.
-----
Gearbox has been vaguely promising a patch to solve at least the formation and tactics problem for almost a year now.  Maybe it'll come out eventually, who knows.  It's hard to forgive that they shipped the game in this state.  It's beginning to look like Homeworld Remastered Collection is just the latest in Gearbox's series of recent acquisitions followed by cynical cash-grabs, which began with Duke Nukem Forever and Aliens Colonial Marines.  With all three of these titles, Gearbox did a big song and dance about how they were huge fans of the franchise and "wanted to do right by the fans", then released a broken mess.  At least the had the decency to not add DLC or resource bonus microtransactions.
Of the three titles, only Homeworld Remastered Collection was received favorably (mainly by critics and customers who'd never played the original), and it's the only one that's received a follow-up.  You know, it's funny, I don't remember Randy Pitchford sending out any cocky tweets about pre-order numbers for Deserts of Kharak like he did for Homeworld Remastered Collection.  I can't imagine why.

This is a fun little Arcade/Sim/Strategy game. You start out with a base, which is constantly generating miners which will go out and mine on there on, usually in the general direction of minerals. You can also set down a path that the Dwarf, and any other Dwarf that steps on the path will follow. This is great for getting them to go mine the good stuff. Eventually it gets to the point where there's simply too many miners to micro manage, which is fine and part of the fun. They'll eventually, whether purposely or accidentally  mine into a water reservoir. You have to quickly wall it off and mark the tiles surrounding it as a "don't mine this!" warning, else it'll drown everyone. They'll eventually also mine into lava, which acts almost the same, except it'll burn through your man-made walls, so you have to make a hole in the floor, using dynamite and a Dwarf sacrifice, then mark the walls with a no-mine warning. You have to be quick though, since Dwarfs move slow and the lava needs to be secured before it burns through all your walls.
It's fun just mining around, then suddenly one of your Dwarfs off screen will tunnel into lava, then you have to rush to fix it.
It's a fun game, though perhaps a bit overpriced at $10. I recommend playing the F2P version, and if you like that, buy the paid version, which offers much more. Though try to get that on sale also.

TL;DR: If you like MMOs, but are tired of the same ole' formula, give this a shot. If you like TES, you'll love it.
I only started launching this game through Steam sometime in the past year, so my logged hours should really be well above 3000. I've been playing this game since open Beta and I've seen it undergo many transformations; from the early days of bug-ridden quests at launch, to the unfortunate decision of going f2p, to the latest social integration of removing faction restrictions for PvE, this game has changed in many ways. Like any MMO, it will likely never be perfect and there will always be people who criticise one aspect of the game or another. As much as I've had my gripes with it however, it stands at a sweet spot today, and if you're into MMOs, and particularly TES lore, you should definitely give this a try. It is a beautiful game, with fantastic graphics, engaging questlines, fun easter eggs, great characters, and most importantly, an amazing community. As much as ZOS has screwed up in many ways, they have, for the most part, kept to their schedule on regularly released updates, and although they're not always particularly great, they keep the game bustling with players from all walks of life. If you are looking for a hardcore endgame/raiding formula with ample variety, this may not be your best bet, but if you enjoy challenging PvP and fun PvE, you won't be disappointed. I can't stress this enough: the community in this game is GREAT. Join a guild (or five) as soon as you come in, and your experience will be that much better.

I have wanted to write a review about this game for a long time, and now that I have beaten the main game AND all the dlc's, I think I'm finally ready to do it.As you may or may not know, I love the Souls games. They might even be my favorite game series of all time, and that is exactly why I'm going to be pretty critical and nitpicky in this review. So without further ado, let's get this review started.
When I first heard that this game is comming out, my hype meter pretty much exploded.I said to myself: A Sequel to Dark souls, 1 of the best games I've played and which in my opinion was also a large improvement from Demon's souls? Oh golly gee willikers this must be my lucky day.
So when this game was finally realeased on pc, I was quite disappointed to see the downgraded graphics and the lack of some gameplay elements from the original demo that was shown. However, this did not ruin the game for me, so I ventured forth into the land of Drangleic.
1 of the key differences between this game and Dark souls 1 is the movement. Everything feels a bit different, and I actually liked this new feel of the game. However, I can see why someone would not enjoy this. For example, parries and backstabs both work a bit differently now, jumping and rolling are not the same as they used to be and so on. I personally like most of these new changes, and I'd say that the gameplay in DaS2 is an improvement from DaS1.
Because of these new elements, even veteran players will have to learn something new before they can go destroy all of the bosses.
Speaking of bosses, there are plenty of those for you to kill, 1 could even argue that there are few too many. Some of these fights are either super easy, poorly made or total copies of other fights from the series. Even the dlc's did not avoid this. However, even thought the level of quality in the boss fights is not as high as in the previous game, there are still some great fights to be had, like Sir Alonne, The Looking glass knight and Executioners chariot. Some people complained that the amount of humanoid bosses is too high but honestly, that never reall bothered me. Sure, I'd like to see more variety, but as long as the fight is fun, challenging and well made, I'm ok with it. Some of the normal enemies are also pretty badly made, like those mace wielders at Dragon Shrine, however, many of dem enemies have been nefred.
Another element of the game that has been improved are the online features. You can actually summon people now without getting the Summoning failed message 95% of the ♥♥♥♥ing time. Also, it seems that the amount of lag in co-op and pvp is also far less than what it was in the older games. I have encountered far less lag stabbing for example. I think that the PVP works much better in this than it did in the older games. Sure, hackers and other cheaters are still around, but getting rid of those ain't exactly easy. Some people just don't know how to git gud right?
Ok, I have been mostly positive so far, but now it's time to get critical. First of all, remember the world of Dark souls 1? How it was all connected, and how the layout made sense? Well that is pretty much dead now. Areas are placed all over the ♥♥♥♥ing place, and they are barely connected anymore. A Volcano city on top of a windmill? How does that make any  sense!? The DLC did a good job fixing this, and they do not share the same problem as the main game. Another thing that the DLC fixed really well, is the level desing. Many of the levels in Dark Souls 2 are quite linear compared to the other games. Demon's Souls had some huge levels to explore, and this game doesn't even get close to those, which is a shame.
Hitboxes are another thing that are seriously messed up in this game, when you compare this to the older games. You can get smashed even though the enemy hit about 2 metres  away from you. Some enemies do this more often than others and yes, I'm looking at you the Last giant and Smelter Demon. I did already mention that plenty of old bosses get repeated, but I didn't talk about this other issue in many of the boss fights, random minions. Adding a bunch of enemies into the boss fight doesn't make it challenging, it makes it cheap. Also, putting 2 bosses that you have seen before in the same room is not good game desing either.They repeat these trick WAY too many times, and I really hope that Bloodborne won't have a lot of this stuff.
But what about the story and the lore? The lore has always been a key element in the Souls games. It's interesting stuff to look into, and I suggest that all players try to do so. Dark souls 2 makes the mistake of having a few too many connections to the first game. They reference things from the first game way too much, and it simply turns into huge fanservice. Another problem with the story and the lore is that a lot of things are not explained properly. Sure, they want people to make their own theories, but shouldn't there be an actual truth hidden there somewhere? The Ending is a great example of this.
I think I have said pretty much everything by now. I know that plenty of people have already made some great critiques about this game, but I simply wanted to tell my side of the story. Even with all these complaints, I still think that the all things considered even the base game is a pretty amazing package on it's own, however compared to the rest of the Souls games it simply doesn't hold up for me. But now that I have played the DLC's, my opinions towards the game as a whole have gotten a lot more positive. The level of quality in those is higher than in the main game, and I STRONGLY recommend that you get those if you intend to give this game a shot. They are worth every penny. I can't wait for Bloodborne to come out, all aboard the hype train!
Edit: Well Bloodborne is my favorite game of all time now so getting on that hype train was worth it

This is my first ever MX game, of any kind. I bought MX vs ATV Encore, but got a refund through Steam, as my controller (a Logitech dual) didn't work, so I never got to play that.
I know nothing about the MXGP circuit, so I wasn't sure if I should get it, but all the positive reviews here changed my mind.
Now my review, again coming from a "virgin" of the series:
It's great! I started on the easiest AI mode to get a feel for it. After qualifying pole and winning every race through the first 6 in career, I bumped up to hard AI. Now at least, I get a challenge from the AI.
Tracks look superb, and the bikes do as well. I find myself having a blast as I jump, slide into corners, and run flat out on straightaways.  Overall, the fun factor is a 10/10.
Of course, as with any game, there are some bugs. Namely, bike disappears in the pit after running practice, qualifying, and usually Race 1. Also, the sound cuts out to the point I have to back out and restart the game. And, I get a temporary freeze in the action during a race that can get annoying.
Overall, this game is nicely done, and I'm going to start watching the real MXGP circuit on TV to judge how realistic the game is. From what I've seen thus far, it seems to be as real as a video game can be! I love watching replays of my races. The attention to detail can really be seen here; from the lighting, to the tracks, to the dirt on the bikes and riders, it gives a realistic appearance of a race.
I recommend this game for anyone who, like me,  wants something different from F1 or "left turn only" Nascar games.

Review of #Factorio:
In short - This game is the kind of game you can't stop playing, there's always one more thing you want to do and by the time you stop you realise it's been a few hours since you started.
When you're Sent from your home planet to find a new planet to mine resources from or colonize And the ship you're on  crashes on what you think is a deserted planet You find yourself with very little tools to start with.
Now it's your mission to start mining those resources that the planet has to rebuild your ability to send a satellite into space to communicate with your home planet in order to be rescued. you need to start by harvesting  wood and mining iron and copper smelt them into usable plates and crafts tools and machines to help you achieve that goal. along the way you will engage in research enabling you to improve your existing tools, craft new ones and more.
But, in contrast to what you were led to believe, the planet is inhabited by native alien life forms and the pollution you create with your technology and machines make them become aggressive towards you and you’re factories.So now you need to survive and to do that you craft weapons and other measures to fight back and hold them off.
When resources become scarce you are forced to forge a  railroad  and use trains with loading and unloading mechanisms to bring resources from far away areas called outposts. you also need to defend those outposts and maintain them.
This game is a combination of simulation / RTS/ building / management  / tower defense  genre game. it can be played as a single player game or a multiplayer game. it is an  angled above view, resembling games like Sim City, (Transport) tycoon games, minecraft (with Tekkit mod mod), Anno series,  dwarf fortress, Prison architect, Big Pharma. it has a demo with 3 missions and shows basic game concepts ( highly recommended) and it is very friendly to the modding community ( using  Lua). it also has an in-game map editor + Lua scripting and a dedicated server.
All in all it is recommended by me to anyone that likes this kind of games -  I have logged hundreds of hours playing this game since a very early release (0.10.8 alpha)  back in August 2014 and have not stopped playing it since.

Excellent game overall -- I'm enjoying the unique construction dynamics and the focus on player-built assembly lines. The one criticism I have is that in the main campaign the 3rd level (the one with virtually no resources where you must destroy all the colonies with what weapons you have) seems really high in difficulty even on 'normal' mode. Maybe I'm just not a hardcore gamer, but truth be told I couldn't beat that one without cheating (and believe you me, I tried).
I have a suggestion, actually. It struck me that with the story setting -- that you're a marrooned space traveler building his/her way back into space -- something very basic was missing. Shelter. Productivity's all well and good but even if you've got an infinite supply of freeze-dried space rations you're still going to want somewhere to spend the night or sit down after a while (speaking in-character, of course). I'd suggest a three-tier "housing" solution:
-A low-tech wood and stone 'shack' that can be entered like a vehicle. While inside, the player's health regenerates more quickly (useful for recovering after enemy encounters).
-A medium-tech 'bunker' that has a radar as one of it's ingredients. Better health regeneration than the shack, plus a large "sensor zone" around it that will pre-emptively alert the player when enemies are detected (serving as an early warning system for attacks). Needs to be hooked up to the power grid to function.
-A high-tech 'command center' that is basically the bunker on steroids. Very high armor and a built-in weapon system. Independently powered (batteries and other power tech items would be ingredients) with high player health regen bonus, command centers are ideal for staking out new resource claims in dangerous territories. Could also have storage capacity to further enhance its usefulness.
Hope you like the idea!

Original Review: Addictive little arcade game about dwarves, not to be confused with that other more trendy game about establishing dwarven settlements. After a while, if you're careful, it just comes down to juggling things until time runs out.... then the replayability fades somewhat, though to be honest, I haven't even tried all the game modes. There's a tower defense mode a shooting gallery, and more. Get it on sale if you think you might enjoy it and give it a try. For the day I've spent playing the game (24.1 hours), if I had to make the decision again, I'd spend $2.50 on it.
Okay, that's a bit snarky, admittedly. It's simple, but fun. I recommend it for kids, young and old, who don't mind playing a game with older-looking graphics. Buy it on sale.
P.S. Developer appears to have taken note of my complaint regarding monitor resolution issues and made it easier for me to get to options and reset the settings to something that works better for me. That or the game fixed itself. That or I imagined the whole thing. Nah... the dev stood by his product and that makes it worth something more in my opinion.

A fun, cute, casual game.  At its core this game is like a very basic version of pacman meets minecraft.  Dwarfs spawn continously and move about the mine map on their own.  You guide them and coax them to do your bidding to explore, gain money/increase score.  As more dwarfs spawn the harder it is to control them.
There are no complicated elements to distract you from the main aim of the game which is to guide your dwarfs as they mine the map uncovering resources or caves with rewards or dangers.  You can build outposts with guards to fight off monsters, use dynamite to cut-off dangerous traps or turn earth to concetre to block of sections you dont want your miners to explore.  These simple mechanics mean you can get into the game very, very quickly.  However just because it is simple to play does not mean it is easy to master...
The game has a lot of depth with several game modes including a set of campaign challenges which plays like a tutorial that gets harder and encourages you to develop your technique.  These will become vital in the Arcade mode or the Skirmish challenges.  Gameplay remains the same throughout with the difficultly and the achievements being the driver for you to take on harder and harder challenges.
Overall I found this fun if the last few challenges a little frustrating but, its great to start up if you just want some quick frantic fun for an hour or so.  It is repetitive with only the randomly drawn maps changing from game to game.  Though for what it costs its value for money.  Just dont expect AAA graphics.

There is a single reason i cannot reccomend this game. Dynamic difficulty. What is that?
You have ships of total power 5, the next encounter has enemy ships of 7 power. You have total power 7? The encounter will be of power 9. You have 10 power? You go against enemy power 13. And so on. You always deal with a supreme force. A fleet equal to yours and somewhat better to counter the human brain superiority against CPU AI.
The main supportive idea behind that is that you cannot focus on build a massive fleet and win by numbers. You have to use 'real strategy' and 'real tactics' to win. At least that is what they majority of fans are saying.
Well i disagree. And the reason is simple. Firstly, i beat the game and without any save-load-try again stuff. Not a big deal, most players can do, if not they need some retries and that is all. Really, since when load and retry is a deep strategy and tactic?!?!
On top of that, why build a lot of ships? The game does not count your stored resources for adjusting difficulty. You go with few ships, face few ships, build a few more and keep going. If that is strategy and tactic i am Napoleon.
Not to mention the salvage corvette thing. Two corvette class ships can disable and salvage a frigate (and larger classes) but 2 combet class corvettes cannot take down a frigate. The salvage class ships would make sence if they salvage disabled or heavy damaged ships. This looks like a cheat to me and not a tactic.
To make a long story short, do not build many ships, have 2-4-6 and so on salvage corvs, build few ships after the encounter has spawned and you are good for the entire game. Do not use your resources to build ships in advance before you hyperspace. 'To be prepared' obviously is not this game's motto. 'Play dead' is more like it.
Nice experience from a view, i do not rememeber any other RTS punishing the hard prepared folks.
