tries hard to satisfy fans on the franchise by 'innovating' (in respect to within its own style) gameplay and attempting to rectify for the mess of the
storyline by hiring famous actor Kevin Spacey  who does an exceptional job trying carry the plotline by himself but is so desperately alone.
Before I get into actually reviewing the game I must mention the various technical issues that plagued the game from its release 3 years ago. There's plenty of threads in various hardware/gaming forums and even steam discussions, where users mentioned the myriad of issues with Advanced Warfare. Unfortunately I also had issues with the game and seeing that several others users did/do too, this is a warning to prospective buyers to be aware that there's a good chance your game will be crushing several times. I finally managed to find the root of my issues was the game not liking my X.M.P RAM profile (OC ram) but once I manage to underclock, it worked fine for the most part.
Now visually the game is absolutely superb. It's a 3 year old game and still looks like it was made yesterday. On ultra/extra quality textures and post-processing effects, Advanced Warfare looks and runs beautifully with very few occasional hitches on specific areas. The animations especially during the cutscenes are fantastic and for a few moments I thought that the real Kevin Spacey was actually talking to me! Credit where credit is due, the eye candy alone is a great positive aspect of the entire game.
Now lets jump into the gameplay and say that I'm glad we saw some changes in the overall Call of Duty style mechanics. You still have your quick time events, shooting galleries, vehicular combat but regular gameplay now includes the use of the futuristic exo suit. The exo suit has 3 'powers' each depending on the mission you play (unfortunately you cannot pre-choose which power to use in the mission) which did manage to heavily increase the fun factor. Powers include a 'bullet time' ability, a protective riot-style shield, sonic waves which confuses enemies, stim packs, cloaking devices and a few movement affecting ones like dodging moves, wall climbing and grappling hooks. There are specific occasions and mission where use of these powers is mandatory to progress but some of the combat ones will be available for all missions. These powers run on a battery system so you need to choose carefully where and how to use them.
There's also a specific challenges during the course of the game, limited to kill, headshot kills, grenade kills and finding intel. Completing a milestone in each of the categories grants you an exo suit upgrade point which you can use to upgrade you exo suit by increasing your max health, reduce recoil, increase battery life for you powers and a few more. These sort of pseudo-RPG elements, make for a nice little added feature although in the grand scheme of things, they won't make a huge impact on normal difficulty. It's still is good to focus on some though for some little extra power during the campaign.
The game also includes heavily futuristic weaponry and gadgets which actually made Advanced Warfare a lot more enjoyable compared to other CoD titles. Weapons resemble modern firearms but also draw inspiration from cyberpunk style themes, including some special grenades who paint enemies, EMP charges, friend of foe identifier scopes and many more.
The features mentioned above actually make Advanced Warfare seem more... advanced! There's a nice spirit of what the future of warfare might look like a few decades from now and the developers did a good job trying to convey that atmosphere throughout the game. There's all sorts of technological progress appearing in the various places you'll be visiting in the campaign, from flying cars, hovercycles, weaponized drones to even keypads on people's wooden doors which made for an interesting contrast.
Storywise, the game managed to keep me quite interested for the first half. Kevin Spacey's mannerisms and voice acting are captured exquisitely in the cutscenes and despite his character falling into the standard 'disillusioned idealist gone mad' trope that Call of Duty's bad guys are designed, for the most part his character portrays more qualities than the ones you're used to on a regular antagonist. There's a nice pace and flow in the gameplay regarding the story and it's actually pretty well done, for the most part, sort of reminiscent of the blockbuster-esque
saga.
However the last act falls and feels pretty short with a very anticlimactic and abrupt ending which let me completely unsatisfied. There's a pretty decent buildup until the ending, but the way the whole thing goes down is pretty lackluster.
The missions are quite interesting but that's doesn't mean much; even Ghosts had interesting missions but it failed to deliver on the story.
So is this a worthy title in the Call of Duty franchise? Well it certainly is a huge step up from Ghosts although Ghosts did set the bar pretty low. There's an air of the much more successful Modern Warfare captured in Advanced Warfare and in some subtle ways you can see it. There's a few touching moments which are ruined by otherwise gameplay elements and in particular I wanted to mention about the whole 'Press F to pay respects'.
While it's relatively early in the story and you have only exposition regarding your relationship with the person who died, it's still a kinda somber moment in the game. The scene is actually pretty well crafted until that stupid prompt appears in the center of the screen and breaks any immersion that might have been made. And isn't that one of the most Call of Duty-est things you ever seen? A game notorious for holding your hand with prompts, a game which is the definition of linear, to actually force the player to push a button so you can say farewell to a person you met 20 minutes ago in the game's lore is your best friend.
That's what Call of Duty is all about. A 6 hour trip in which you 'supersoldier' your way through all those who threaten civilization. You fight for justice/liberty/honor but
if you press the right buttons at the right time. Sometimes great characters and stories hide in that repetitive gameplay and sometimes their qualities will shine through the stagnant gameplay. That's what I love about Call of Duty. It's a cheesy, 6 hour interactive movie where you get a false sense of empowerment by defeating everything that represents evil; and when the antagonists in their final hours declare their misguided sense of righteousness, when they make that gloating arrogant villain speech, you might be lucky enough if you become emotionally invested and defy him both in the game and in your mind.
Call of Duty®: Advanced Warfare, is actually quite decent for an FPS and Call of Duty title but it's not without its flaws that exist in the core of the franchise which spun over the last 14 years. I was quite torn if this game deserved a thumbs up or a thumbs down. As a die hard fan of the franchise this satisfied me but also disappointed me. I'm giving this a very, very, very reluctant thumbs up, despite the abrupt final act and some technical issues I had. This is only recommended for hardcore fans of the singleplayer campaigns that Call of Duty has to offer, as I cannot make any critique on the multiplayer aspect of the game. Even from a pure FPS standpoint, it's actually quite decent albeit short so spend your money accordingly should you wish so.

I started as a small time pirate looting unfortunate enough small boats. Then I went on a quest in the far, far away town to find out governor's source of income. Plan was to seduce governor's daughter so she can tell me the dirty secret. She was reserved, but after few nice gestures and the night out in the inn, she opened up. Her father was arrested, but then we fell in love. so I became the new governor and formed my own faction. Suffice to say, England, my former ally, was bitter because of that.
I tried to manage all this state affairs, but it wasn't easy. Economy was weak so I decided to go pirating and gather some cash. Few moment later, I spotted ongoing battle between my allies and new enemy, England. It was rather huge battle for me at the moment - lots of galleons while I had meager one-deck-of cannons boat. I said what the heck and went straight into the battle. I waited until both parties were exhausted, then grape-shoted one galleon and boarded it. Melee fight started, my heroes and well trained boarding party fought well. We got the ship!
Now, after owning heavy galleon I started intercepting English trade convoys. I established my own trade routes. Money was flowing. My reputation grew. Then one day, while passing near the Spanish city, I saw huge English navy besieging the city. I could see fiercest ships - 1st,  2nd, 3rd ships of the line. And the Spanish city fell. So it was time for me to get hell out of there. But then I was small group of ships - 2nd and 3rd ship of line, breaking from rest of the attack force. It was time to do my vulture tactics again!
I went into the battle - and there where two ships sailing straight into me. I started damaging the sails of the first ship, while cornering so second enemy ship didn't have the clear shot - first one was blocking her view. Then I switched to grapes, and decimated first ship's crew. Turned out tactic was good - crew count fell from 550 down to 50! Then I made a sharp turn and boarded the ship. After a quick battle one of the biggest ships were mine. I didn't have enough crew to sink the other enemy, so I managed to retreat. Some of my crew weren't happy, but hey, we won the jackpot!
I wasn't home for quite some time. My relationship with my wife began to deteriorate. Meanwhile, she was fighting natives and protecting the land. So I headed to my land. In was at that moment I saw several English ship of the line convoys following me. They wanted a revenge. But hey, I can outrun then, right? So I was sailing across the Caribbean, while enemy was behind my feet. They were relentless. I reached my city, but the didn't stop. I went inland by foot, by they also did that!♥♥♥♥♥♥ this was going to be bad. But then, I could somehow cover my tracks so they lost me. I returned to the town, got my wife, and boarded my new ship. I left the garrison in the city because enemy was still there somewhere. Maybe my only city will fall and I will lose my faction. Who knows?

I had high hopes when I bought this game, as I really like the Alien movies.
And I am very happy they delivered this on Linux on which I played it.
The main game concept is that you hide and sneak past enemies, to reach the goals that are set in a linear storyline. You can't kill the Alien.. and kiling the humans and robots can be hard too.
This means the game really forces you to be very careful and sometimes you really feel you are in the Alien movie experiencing everything that Ripley has experienced.. which is great.
To put myself to more suspense I started and finished the main game in "hard" mode, which was ok to do if you are careful and save regulary. I only got stuck a few times in which I needed to repeat the same scenario multiple times to get further. I now restart the game in nightmare.. which also seems doable, so maybe you can try starting in that mode too.
When I started the game the first few levels I was not really sure I would recommend it.
The game has some flaws, like:
- in the first level you can look down and see your legs.. however the walking animation is terrible.
- in later levels your body is removed.. this also means you dont have a shadow in contrast to another character.
- level design has much detail.. many lights/textures/shadows/objects.. however many times I see the exact same 3D object next to eachother.. (eg in the first level the same document is placed twice next to eachother on the wall). Many rooms and complete areas are identical.. except from minor details. And the reflection seen in the astronaut helmet is the same in every location. I believe the designer did not do enough effort here to let you feel emerged into the enviroment.
- also the physics does not seem right at some moments.. if you turn you might hit some object (eg carbage can)  behind you, making a lot of noise.. it would seem you might have a tail to cause something like that.
- the alien should be attracted to sound.. as it can hear you running/breathing/etc.. however louder noises if you open doors, turn on generators,  alarms. etc.. doesn't attract the alien. This does not make sense.
- many events (including the alien spawning and movements) are heavily scripted and when you noticed that, the thrill of a real alien hunting you is gone. There are moments that I first crouch and I am scared the alien notices me, until I understand the alien wont spawn at all.. at that moment you can make as much noise as you can. Also there are situations where the alien repeats a certain pattern and you must simply change your pattern to get further.
- the robots and other humans will mostly try to hurt you when they notice you, but you can easily run away from the robots and the humans are easy target with your flame thrower (although you should preserve that to scare the alien).
- And last.. the alien is simply guided to your location, so SPOILER ALERT: in almost many cases if you simply walk to your goal and you never stop to hide then the alien will mostly spawn behind you and you finish each level without much effort.. but I feel this is lame and spoils the experience of the gameplay.
All in all.. I feel the game developers could have made a better game with some few improvements.
So maybe they had problems reaching their deadline or budget concerns to make those last fixes.
With all above negative remarks I would still recommend this game.
Simply because if you play the game as though the alien or any other enemy could be around each corner, you need to crawl and sneak past enemies.. which makes it a lot harder to explore all rooms on all levels and will get you a thrill you wll not easily forget. ;)
Also the game lets you use and build several weapons, but I noticed I would use only:
- stun baton to stun humans and normal robots without alerting the alien
- pipe bomb and emp mine to kill/stun the normal robots (when the alien is not near)
- the flamethrower to scare the alien
- bolt gun to kill the advanced robots
The other stuff I basically did not use.. either because it seemed to loud.. attract the alien
or do little or no damage.

People complain a lot about the price model for this game which honestly is the first of any free-to-play where I've thought the model made sense. Let's say they charged the normal price of $50-60 on this game. Then only if you really thought this game was interesting would you go out and purchase it. With the actual in-game purchase model, you decide if you are interested with what is actually quite a fair free version. You can hunt anything you want, you just don't get "points" (who cares) for them. But if you want other guns, you have to pay. So what I did was start out at $15 to unlock all licenses and then purchased a shotugn with slugs for $5 more to be able to kill almost anything in game. Then I decided to try more and more guns and gear until I found I had everything I wanted. By that time I had spent ~$50-$60. I have around a hundred hours in game (including non-Steam play) at ths point and it seemed well worth it. Had I decided at $20 that I didn't like the game, I wouldn't have had to spend any more. How can you complain about that?
It's a very enjoyable game and is quite relaxing and beautiful. If you like the outdoors but like to play video games too, this is a great activity for nights and after work when you are beat. It is really an experience like no other and actually motivated me to get my hunting license and begin learning about the real world of hunting! Pretty cool when a game can do that! Can't say enough how much I enjoy a game like this.

I am a big fan of dwarf fortress and was very excited about picking this up. I had read about it before hand so I didn't feel disapointed about it being completely different, I think one of the developers said "don't think DF, think lemmings" (or maybe it was totalbiscuit, can't remember I'm afraid). Like lemmings, your dwarfs will happily walk to their doom or do something that screws up your entire game. This is where the majority of the challenge comes from and I think the game suffers for that a little. In order to help with that you can change the direction that your dwarf is digging with arrows, make an infintiely deep hole by sacrificing your dwarf (this will allow you to pour water/lava away) and hardening the walls which makes it impossible to dig through. These tools cost you a lot of money so its important to be smart about how you are spending. Yes, those rare crystals would be faster to get to using an arrow but if a dwarf uncovers lava in an open area then you are in real trouble. As the game goes on you will gain more dwarfs which will make earning money much quicker but also opens up problematic areas more quickly too.
The nice things about it is that there are a lot of difficulty levels and it requires a lot of concentration. If you enjoy being challenged, you will find that itch scratched in this game. Another nice feature is that you set a time limit before you go in, great if you have a specific amount of time to burn. The graphics and music are nice too.
Theres quite a lot of comedy here too. The narrator is voiced by one of the yogscast youtube starts. I'm not too into the yogscast myself but I know it has a lot of fans and some people will just eat that up! The acheivements are fun to get too and its very self aware in its humour.
I give it 5/10, to me that's an average game. This doesn't mean I say you should completely ignore it, it's fine and it may turn out that you love it. I think I will pick it up from time to time as it does have an entertaining value to it, but unless its on a steam sale you might want to pass up on this one. I can imagine that people who don't like the "hands off" simulation game like dwarf fortress or dungeon keeper then the on purpose dumb AI could drive them absolutely mad. Personally I think that if you watched a gameplay video of this and you think it looks fun, then you will find it fun. I feel a little bad giving it an average score as there are a lot of fun nice little things here there just isn't too much of it, but what is here is very well polished.
I'd love to hear what other players think.

The game features both single player and multiplayer adventures where a designed character takes to the seas in search of riches. The campaign maps includes all of the important towns in the Caribbean, where different factions vie for supremacy. Each city includes a tavern where subordinate leaders can be recruited, a shipbuilder for purchasing or repairing ships, a market for trade, a mansion for missions, and a town hall to purchase and manage factories. Party members gain experience and earn upgrades through combat, which can take place both on land and in the sea. Terrestrial battles mirror those found in Mount & Blade, while naval combat is fairly traditional: movement using the wind to position cannons towards the enemy, with different types of shot available and boarding actions once crews have been diminished. Blood & Gold: Caribbean! feels and plays like a somewhat substantial modification of Mount & Blade (which it is), with all of the pluses (freeform living world) and minuses (many rough edges) that particular game engine entails.

This game is what Sid Meier's Pirates! was meant to be when it grew up (and drank too much rum).  I love the boarding party battles and watching people fall from the crow's nest.  I swear, I say 'wheeee! splat!' every time.  There are some little things that need tweaking but a great pirate game.

ORIGINAL REVIEW Fairly good game, I got it for free since I had originally owned Caribbean! which I had a coupon for at some point for some reason. I haven't read into it, but I'm pretty sure this is the game they care about now, and sort of just left Caribbean! in a dumpster after the prom.
If you have played Mount and Blade, it'll feel familiar, due to it using the same engine and whatever, so thats fun. The naval combat is comparable to Sid Meier's: Pirates!, though a little more blocky, and sometimes I don't quite get where my cannons are supposed to be firing, though overall its pretty good. The boarding party, ship-to-ship, trench combat is not the best. If you have a big crew/party, buckle up, especially if you or your enemy has a small ship, it gets very cramped very quick. Pretty certain I've killed more of my crew than the enemy has. If you and your foe have a big ship and big crews, it can be fun. Now for land battles, I haven't gotten far in that aspect. In Caribbean! I had cannons and the whole shabang, and that was great and all, though the mechanics were weird, and there was no friendly fire from cannon. I don't know if cannons work the same in this, but land battles are still fun, positioning units can be a little rough, but the maps are decent sized. I have helped siege a town, and those are gruesome. The enemy, in the city I attacked, had little cannons on the wall, shooting out at you as you stormed the beach. They said they would make sieging difficult, and they delivered, so well done there. The town only had 300 or so, and the people I was helping, and myself, had about 500-600 and we ended up limping away with 300 give or take. This was also near the beginning of the game, so elite troops were scarce, but even so.
The quest system is pretty neat, there is a variety of things you can do, from blowing up a mine, defending a mine, or even lighting ships on fire. The only downside to these is that you only have a finite number of troops, like 7 or so, and the enemy has 7 or so waves, consisting of 7 or so guys each. Just have to find a corner and let them come to you.

It's worth playing through once; it retains enough of the Dark Souls magic to be an enjoyable experience. I was really hoping that this game would just be Dark Souls with functioning online, but unfortunately, they felt the need to screw it up in various ways.
The biggest way they ruined this game was with Soul Memory. With Soul Memory, invasions aren't determined by soul level; good players with high-soul-level characters will frequently invade weak players with low-soul-level characters. In their attempt to stop people from twinking and ganking low-level players, they made it even easier to twink and gank. Finally, they ruined end-game PVP, as there's no level cap anymore. Everyone's a level 700 Hex user wearing Havel's. Good ♥♥♥♥ing job, From Software! That was a really good idea. Bravo.
They made invasion items too much of a chore to get. This is reflected in the fact that invasions are rare in this game; most PVP is done by red soapstone. There's also an invasion time limit, which allows the invaded to simply turtle up and wait for the invader to leave. The whole reason that invasions are fun is because there's a new threat with a human intelligence in your world; on a pure, PVP combat level, the Souls series is woefully deficient. Also, the soundtrack is awful, and that's by Souls series standards.
7/10 play it once but don't expect it to be as good as Demon's Souls or Dark Souls and don't expect to get any fun at all out of PVP

This is a good game and I recommend it if you liked the first dishonored. I will be talking about cons:
- If you have a realtively weak pc, you will spend a good deal of time trying to find the perfect adaptive resolution settings. The trick that did it for me is set adaptivity to performance and then enable the best antialiasing possible. That way even when the game lowers resolution, it wont look aweful.
- One thing that you will notice in this game is that the levels are now bigger and have more stuff to do. While theoratically that sounds like a good thing, sometimes I found myself getting frustrated because the map does not really guide your experience very well. You can get to your objective in so many different ways. In some maps this is a good thing. In others, truly frustrating.
- The AI. The AI in this game is really confusing. Sometimes you will be surprised by how smart the NPCs are whereas sometimes they are outright stupid. This makes AI unpredictable and so you will find yourself saving and loading back many many times if you are trying to go for an undected run.
- This last con is purely subjective. When I finished the first map, I was shown that I killed and was detected by enemies with two big red Xes. Being someone who likes to aim for achievments, I wanted to complete my first playthrough undetected and with no kills.  So I restarted the game just for that. As the game went on, it truly felt frustrating trying to keep this playstyle as the maps get even bigger and more complex. I kinda wish I just played the game normally as now I cannot got back mid playthrough. This closely related to the maps con that I mentioned. Trying to go for a no detection run will be a real pain and I cant wait for my second playthrough where I eliminate each and every NPC. Thats what they get for being annoying as hell.

I have only played Homeworld 2 Remastered so far and my review is based on this game only and not the Homeworld 1 Remastered. Also this is my first game in this franchise and space RTS games.
Homeworld 2 Remastered doesn't have a very high learning curve as this is one of the reasons I have always stayed away from space RTS games. I don't have the time and energy to sit through hours of guides and tutorials to learn how to play a space game (looking at Eve online). After 10 minutes of basic tutorials, the game put you right in the campaign and you start building your gunships, etc and within 5 minutes you have a battle on your hands...
I didn't have any issues getting into the game other than getting used to the 3.5 dimension view. I am more familiar with RTS games such as C&C, rise of nation, dawn of wars, original world of war craft RTS, company of heros, etc and having a new Z dimension to deal with is a bit frustrating at times, so I try to ignore it for now or not use it (which so far I haven't really needed to use the Z dimension for anything).
Overall Homeworld 2 Remastered is a great game with nice graphics and lots of details. However I wish I could zoom in more to the ships during the battles to fully experience the destructions, but I can't expect total war depth of view in a large space ship gun battle from a remastred game.
This game is a great entry to space RTS games if you willing to put the time to actually play it and learn the basics. Last but not least the game has an excellent voice acting and story.

Watch the video review here!
History & Overview
-Released in 2014
-Developed and published by Milestone and distributed by Bandai Namco Games
-Released on PC, PS3, PS4, PS VITA, and Xbox360
-Standard Racing Affair
In MXGP it's your typical standard racing affair but just with a lot more mud and dirt thrown in.
The game has a number of different standard modes to choose from, including an instant race mode which basically randomly selects a track and rider for you, and you simply race.
As well as a “Grand Prix” mode which let's you pick a rider or your own created one, a track, and race.
A “championship” mode which let's you pick a rider or your own, select tracks and make your customized season to race for and championship to win.
A time attack mode, which is pretty self explanatory that let's you race for the best time on any given track.
As well as online multiplayer, but as of this recording it's pretty much dead sadly, so this review will be based purely on the single player content of the game.
But the core aspect to the single player of the game itself  is the “Career mode” which let's you use a customized character of your very own, select a team to race for and represent, and build your very own fan-base.
Each time you compete in a race your rewarded with experience that unlocks you new gear as well as “fans” that comment on how you did on a race via a weird mock twitter thing...
But is any of this any good?
The Good
-Standard racing game with solid mechanics
-Real world mechanics, brands, and riders
-Decent controls with a bit of a learning curve
Growing up personally I was pretty fond of games such as the “MX vs ATV” series, so when I was offered the chance to review MXGP I jumped on the idea naturally because of this.
MXGP is brought to us by the same cats behind the “MotoGP” franchise and where as games such as MX vs ATV go for more of an arcade approach to off-road racing, MXGP aims for a much more grounded and pure racing focused approach with solid mechanics backing it.
Controlling your bike definitely has a learning curve to it, you'll need to know how to approach each jump, and you use both analog sticks to shift your weight with the bike as you ride and it feels really responsive once you wrap your head around the controls themselves, the first few times I raced I fell plenty of times not knowing I actually had to shift my weight and use both analog sticks.
I personally played on the default settings of the game with the default assisted control settings as I'm pretty rusty when it comes to off-road style racing games, but the game does offer the option to completely disable all the control assists and adjust them as you wish for all the purists out there.
What MXGP does best is that it offers a more real world approach to Motocross racing and with real world mechanics, everything from the physics of the bike itself and shifting your weight with it, to how you land from jumps, turn corners, to the tracks being being based off real world locations with plenty of different tracks to choose from, to the teams utilizing real world brands, and racing against real world drivers.
But sadly it doesn't do much in the way of standing out or being interesting for very long... So let's discuss why with...
The Bad
-No tricks?
-No real in-depth customization
-Not much variety and tons of game padding
One of the reasons why I loved games such as the MX vs ATV series was doing all the fantastic tricks that you could pull off, sadly MXGP features none of that.
The most trick related thing you'll even be doing in MXGP is whipping or scrubbing your bike to aim for a better landing in between slopes,  as I said previously MXGP aims for a more grounded and racing focused experience, which I guess is what the actual MXGP competition is, but none the less I was kinda disappointed by this.
Next up the game doesn't offer much in customization, when you're creating your character you basically pick a pre-created display picture for him who's probably just random developer, select a nationality, make a name, and pick a number...
That's really about it, but then again character customization in a racing game isn't a huge deal obviously, but this also extends to your bike as well, outside of adjusting the control assists or your bikes technical aspects, you have no real aesthetic customization to your bike itself which is also pretty disappointing.
But probably my biggest issue is the massive amounts of padding in the career mode itself, you basically go to your calender, select your next race, set up your settings, you can do a practice run to wrap your head around the track, then you can do qualifying race, all of this you can skip of course.
Then you finally race.... Then you race again... Maybe this is how it works in the actual MXGP but by the time you've done all this you've basically raced this same track a good 4 times and spent a good 15 to 20 minutes with it.
Then you come back to your garage-thing, read your email for potential teams or sponsors, and read your twitter thing.
Then you select your next race event and do it all over again.
By the end of it all after racing every event, the game then just simply tells you to do it all over again but with a different class of bikes and slightly improved AI, the exact same tracks, in the exact same order.
To which I just simply responded “No” after having already sunk 8 hours or so into this game.
But now let's discuss,
The Ugly
-Looks bland, nothing really impressive
-Muddy tracks being torn up as you race is kinda cool
-Locked at 30fps
-Clipping issues, bugs, and crashes
-No licensed music or soundtrack while racing
-Over all presentation is somewhat bland
Where we discuss the graphics, technical aspects, soundtrack, and general presentation of the game.
Over all MXGP is fairly bland looking considering this is a 2014 release and doesn't offer much in the way  of visuals nor will it be any bit taxing on your system by any means, the tracks themselves are based on real world locations and look decent enough and the track itself having the dirt torn up by bikes as you race is pretty neat to see.
However what's not so neat to see was my frame rate counter being locked at 30, I don't see any valid reason for a racing game of all things to be locked at 30fps, especially on PC.
The game also suffers from some clipping issues as you fall from your bike the odd time, as well as some other bugs and the odd rare crash I had happen once or twice during my 8 or so hours with it.
As for the soundtrack side of things, the game is completely devoid of any licensed music or soundtrack outside of the main menu music which is generic guitar stuff, so as your racing you'll basically just hear the wonderful sounds of dirt-bike engines.
And all over the presentation for MXGP is just extremely bland, everything from the lifeless career mode and fake twitter social media thing, to the lack of music as you race, the only thing that even stood out to me was the massive amounts of in-game Monster Energy advertisements.
Final Thoughts
Over all MXGP certainly feels like a budget title and doesn't do much to convince you otherwise.
It's a competent racing game with nice mechanics going for it but it doesn't do much in the way to stand out from the rest and I still ONLY recommend if it if you're big into MX racing or off-road racing games in general.

Factorio is a survival game which quickly turns into a heavy management and expansion game where you will ponder upon what kind of complex system to create. I will add a TL;DR at the end.
In Factorio you start off with nothing and expand into an empire of automation. The game starts simple and it allows itself to become more and more complex. This is a game that requires patience and the determination to make everything work. Factorio will have a time where it becomes more of a management game than a survival game until the natives decide to attack in a horde and destroy everything you have worked for, making you have to multitask between industrialization and defense from the locals. It has a huge amount of possible replayability.  Factorio has highly addicting gameplay which will leave you wanting to just finish one more supply line from your electric drill, to your furnace, to the assembly machine, into a chest. Oh wait my research finished? Well I guess I should put in my new robots. Oh wait the natives dared attack me? COMBAT ROBOTS ASSEMBLE. Well now the natives destroyed some of my automation so I should probably fix it. Overall Factorio is an impressively fun game, but it also is not something you can just pick up and easily play.
Don’t judge a book by it’s cover could be used to express this game as the graphics are not top-notch as other games, but the gameplay it comes with is luscious and immersive. There really is no music and the sounds of machinery will slowly take over.

We have a few automation chains running and are constantly expanding and trying to figure out an ideal production chain to gain the greatest efficiency of all our resources. So far I don’t see any signs of us dropping this game.
Factorio is not an easy game, you cannot simply pick it up and expect to know everything. PRELUDE: If you're mature and appreciate high quality games continue reading. The rating on the review is because of immature idiots who want everything for free - got nothing to do with the game. If you're a spoiled immature brat wanting more handouts to go with your welfare cheque, mark it down and ♥♥♥♥ off. Don't bother with entitlement whining in the comments, I'll just kill it.
..oo00oo..
Now, the game.
- GRAPHICS -
This is gorgeous. A 6.00am start at Redfeather had me mesmerised. There are some placing issues, grass and trees above ground etc. but it's really only aesthetics and does little to detract gameplay.
With my trusty 670gtx/i7/8Gb rig this game shines with only minor fan speedup when scene changing. A steady 60fps with only minor tearing (I haven't bothered changing the default yet so could probably be sorted easily enough).
Very easy to look at and the animalation (now there's a word) is very attractive. Slightly robotic at times but hey, if we had 500,000 vectors to plot per animal we couldn't play without a Cray.
- SOUND -
There could be a little more control over some of the ambients, eg: ocean waves, as sound is a critcal and tactile sense in this game and some of it gets over the top. Rain, wind etc. is good and animal calls, while lacking in some bearing seperation, is true to form.
And the guns? Wow. Crank it people. It might take 2 hours of tracking before you fire but I get great delight hearing the .308 reverb off the valley walls. My kids, avid fans all, bounce off their chair! The bang-ratchet-bang of the pump action while pheasant shooting is as sweet as.
(Err.... an 11.00pm .308 shot scored me some wife-wrath so headphones people!)
- GAMEPLAY -
If holding shift + W is your only way to get somewhere this is NOT your thing. If the destination is more important than the journey or you're expecting a gluttony of "shootables", DO NOT BUY.
This requires patience and lots of it, much of it is tedium. This is hunting. You are a hunter. Stealth. Cover. Shadows. Crouching. Camoflauge. Downwind. ALL of this comes into play.  I've even suggested on the forums that you need to move like YOU are the hunted for best results.
Animals, particularly those munched on by predators have an uncanny sense of smell and hearing. And it IS fascinating to watch animals through a scope pausing, sniffing and treading lightly. "Wary skittishness" has been modelled beautifully and really adds to the sense of the hunters plight... Let's face it, we're blundering lunkheads in natures true arena and you'll pay the price for it.
-Shooting.
In RL, I have probably loosed close to 10,000 rounds. Mostly night shooting for foxes and roos. As a staunch user of the .243 in that era I took great delight in how well this acts, sounds and plays like a .243 ingame. I can "feel" the shoulder kick and smell the powder. (I know, it's psychosomatic but you get what I'm saying....)
Scope tracking is well mimiced and looking downrange for a headshot @ 150m is frustratingly difficult. Zoom capabilities are also true-to-form in that higher zoom will produce greater scope movement. Nice work in this department. Note that there are many scopes, sizes and types, many aimed (yck yck) at quality shooting and range judgement.
- The shotty is divine albeit a rather blunt instrument.
- The .30 is popular and goes off like a firecracker on steroids.
- The Anshutz .308 -a spend money on it- gun has just entered my inventory and is a darling to use. I linked it up with a 9x50 and I'm REALLY loving this outfit.
I've made mention on the forums that I'm concerned that there is no score rewards based on target range despite the obvious (monetary) push to high-quality equipment. In my view this is wrong, both ingame and economically. My weapons and equipment need to be valuable to me but there is no reason to use anything other than a 12 gauge with the right ammo for the kill. Why charge up to $15 RL money for a gun and scope that counts towards.... nothing?
-Animal Tracking
I like the way this has been done. It's very difficult to mimic the senses from a 3D enviroment in a 2D rectangle and yet this gives a sense of tracking success with target sighting as the eventual reward. The kill itself does become secondary on the harder to track species and I've once or twice found myself shooting only a photo and simply walking away. Seriously.
-Competitions
Good fun and ultimately (at least for me) is the reason I play. Nope, I haven't won any as I write but I've got close. The planning and dedication required to win a trophy is high level stuff and really needs to be worked at. I'm loving them. Soon.......
- GENERAL -
In the interests of brevity I'm going to mention the words achievements (LOTS of them), missions, multiplayer, XP building all in the one sentence. The reasons will be quite obvious. You gotta pay to play, not a real lot, and it's worth every cent.
- UI -
In a sentence on the launcher windows. Messy. Clunky. Confusing. EW. Get someone on this. Rule of thumb, evaluate your UI on your grandmothers. If they're confused it's bad OK?  Even ingame I find some "habit formed clicking" breaks on some changes to equipment.
..oo00oo..
- SUMMARY -
CONS
Tedious at times with all that walking.
Could ultimately cost quite a bit.
UI.
Scoring is errr.... pointless. (pun intended)

Excellent game, excellent control scheme and a lot of content. Programming is a bit clunky at times (characters controllable after finishing level, some bosses having easy bypasses involving shooting or running through impenetrable barriers etc) and endgame is a let down in that the stages don't reopen (the only way to revisit a stage is to start from the beginning and play until you get there).
The game is divided in three phases, starting with basic terrorism, which continues through most of the game. Phase two starts gradually and the shift is done very well. Last phase on the other hand comes very abruptly and feels a bit glued on.
Most negative thing I can think of, is that some characters are hugely OP and the game at times requires the player to restrict themselves (if a gamebreakingly good character to the situation comes up) to get a challenge. A heavily weapon-laden boss is hardly a challenge if you have the means to keep them stunned until dead.
Overall, would recommend for everyone looking for nostalgia, fully destructible environment, platforming, fast-paced gameplay, sidescrollers and/or brojokes.

This game has a LOT of issues. Seeing as it's in the sale and there will be a lot of people considering buying it, I feel like I should outline the issues. TL;DR and specs at the bottom.
- Performance, it varies from person to person but personally I have a medium/high-end gaming rig and still get stuttering and frame drops. I get smoother framerates on games with more graphic fedelity. On consoles it's the same story, constant frame rate drops.
- There's a memory leak issue that is yet to be fixed. Instead of fixing the issue, the devs just raised the minimum RAM requirement from 8GB to 16GB and added a message for every time you boot up the game telling you that you have insufficient memory. Apparently getting more RAM actually fixes a lot of performance issues with the game, go figure.
- The car handling in this game is so, so, bad. People says that Just Cause 2's handling was bad, but that game is a shining light of glory compared to JC3's habdling. And then just wait until you try a motorbike. The turning is horrid, it feels like you have no control sometimes. You hold down the button or move the stick to turn and there's a delay of about 1 second until your bike actually starts turning.  It's so easy to make them spin out and / or flip. Again, when the devs were questioned about this, they literally said "We think it's fine!" (can't find the link to the tweet but I'm sure it's out there).
- There's no native way to change the FOV. There's mods that let you do so but then when you do change it a whole bunch of glitches appear, like terrain not rendering, animations ending, etc. I usually wouldn't mind, but the default FOV is so low to begin with, try driving a car, it's right up in your face and you can barely see past it.
- Missions are creative until you realise that a lot of them are the same being repeated multiple times. Story is boring, I ended up ignoring it and just ♥♥♥♥ing around. Plus, at least for me, destroying bases got boring after a while because there's so god damn many. Just Cause 2 did the whole "Chaos" thing better. When you destroyed military vehicles, killed personnel, destroyed bases, etc. you would gain Chaos and once you reached a certain point you would unlock new items and missions. This worked great because you would end up unlocking things just by ♥♥♥♥ing around. Just Cause 3 however makes you liberate towns and bases, which are mostly just the same thing over and over again. Destroy these buildings, shut down this surveillance system, open this door, free these prisoners, kill there people. Over and over. It's very repetitive. As for Chaos? It's just a meanless stat.
- The rebel drop system is stupid. In JC3 you have to collect flares from rebel bases, and then use those to call in a rebel drop. You have limited flares, but that's ok because you can just get whatever you want for free whenever you want. Right? Wrong, because there's ♥♥♥♥ing WAIT TIMERS. You sometimes have to wait up to 20 minutes before you can drop in a plane again. It's one of the most anti-fun things a developer can do and is often paired with micro transactions that let you reduce the wait, but JC3 doesn't even HAVE microtransactions so the decision makes no sense.
Those are my main issues, but while I'm at it:
- There's no minimap. Why is there no minimap. You can pause the game and look at the map from there to find things buy that's no reason not to have a mini map.
- There's no sprint button. It makes Rico feel really slow in combat because you can't make him run any faster. The devs said that they want you to "use Rico's other movement skills" or whatever but JC2's sprint button was super useful.
- Devs said they wanted to support modders but every patch completely broke most mod. I think there's still some mods that haven't been updated to the latest versions of the game.
- Speaking of patches, there hasn't been one in months. You know what the latest patch was? DLC release. No big fixes. These devs charged us heaps of money for lackluster DLC and the worst part is I was idiotic enough to buy the first one. I'll give them the fact that have a booster on my wingsuit is cool but maybe they could use the extra time spent on DLC fixing the huge bugs in the game? Wait, that doesn't earn them money. Whoops, lol
- WHY DID THEY RE-INVENT THE WHEEL AND BIND LEFT CTRL TO BACK. WHY NOT JUST USE ESC. YOU KNOW, LIKE EVERY OTHER PROGRAM AND GAME EVER PROGRAMMED LIKE EVER. WHY.
TL;DR: Is this game fun? Hell yeah, I have like 70 hours on it. Is it worth full price? ♥♥♥♥ no. Buy Just Cause 2 in the next sale for like $3 and then play it for three years until Just Cause 3 is a similar price. Just Cause 3 could have been great given another year of development. But it's just gonna forever be that game that could have been ♥♥♥♥ing awesome but instead blowed and probably killed the entire franchise. Good job, Avalanche. Next time give the game to a competent development team.
Rant over. Can you tell I'm still salty about a nearly 1 year old release?

EDIT 25 NOV:
This review got way more popular than I expected, so I thought I would fix a couple of things I said:
1. The developers didn't actually bump the minimum amount of ram to 16GB. I thought they did, but I guess I remembered wrong. However, if you don't have at least 16GB of RAM, you still get a pop-up when you start the game telling you that your RAM is insufficient.
2. I was wrong to call my rig high-end, I've changed that to medium/high-end. It's true that my i5 processor and 8GB RAM (the RAM particularly leading to the memory leak issue) aren't as good as an i7 or 16GB RAM, but my gpu, a GTX 970, was one of the best cards you could get when this game released.
I've noticed that the recommended CPU is actually an i7, but I feel like this further shows the performance issues with the game as you shouldn't need an i7 to run a game like this. Take, for example, GTA; a game that is arguably nicer looking and the recommended processor is an i5.
EDIT 25 OCT (2017):
The multiplayer mod is out and has been for quite some time, and I have to say, if you have a group of friends to play it with, it's a ton of fun. However, it still doesn't justify the price tag of the game, or aid any of the performance issues that still plague this release to this day.
My opinion has changed somewhat since I wrote this review nearly a year ago. If you have a high end graphics card, (1060 / 480 or better) have at LEAST 16GB of RAM (most important), and a decent CPU (preferably 6-core i5, i7 or ryzen 7) then I would recommend buying this game on sale, but for no more than say $15.
(I can't stress how important 16 gigs of RAM is.)
And I'm not exaggerating with those performance numbers, the game runs *that* badly. Look at the performance sastisfaction of nvidia and amd - 60% and 32% respectively. That's pretty bad.
Oh, and don't bother with any of the DLC, at least at their full price. Total rip-off. They're worth a couple bucks total at best. Plus, with the multiplayer mod, you get the wingsuit boost for free. Don't tell anyone I told you that tho. It can be our lil' secret.
So, conclusion. now that this game is nearly 2 years old:
Got friends? Got a beefed up rig? Got 16GB + of ram? Buy the game on sale. Otherwise don't

Borderlands 2 is one of my favorite games of all time and my favorite co-op shooter. However i will give the fairest review to this game, so ill exclude my bias opinions.

Artstyle/graphics
If you have seen gameplay/pictures of the borderland games, you will notice the unique artstyle to the game. This is cel shaded-style. This gives the game a more unique feel and it also suits the gamestyle, as its a not so serious game.

GAMEPLAY
The gameplay is excellent.I don't want to get into detail with the story, just to evade accidental spoilers, but you don't have to play the other borderlands to understand the story, the story is explained throughout the game, the story is  intriguing and very FUN! The rng system allows for TONS of weapons to be looted by you. According to Gearbox Software, there are over 17,750,000 different variations of weapons in Borderlands 2. Borderlands 2 uses a procedural process to generate its various guns in certain classes, such as handguns, shotguns, assault rifles, sniper rifles, and more, but with many variations of firing speed, reload speed, damage type and more. This means every gun is unique. However as you level up you will see that less guns become as valuable to use as they are outdamaged by many weapons. *cough* unkempt Harold *cough* This is because the game gets alot harder once you've beaten it. There is a mode called true vault hunter mode which includes the same story but with higher level and stronger enemies, but this allows you to progress your character more, allowing you to level up more and find better weapons. To level past 50 you will have to purchase some dlc, however it is not needed to enjoy the game.

I need to make it clear that I played this game with the Mechromancer.
I tried the other classes, but they lacked the charm and fun of the previous game. The Gunzerker was the most interesting but the others were pale compared to Borderlands 1.
The plot is much better this time around, though, and the environments much more varied. No longer do you spend countless hours wandering the same "desert junk yard" which mysteriously has occasional swamps. The huge variety of environments, enemies, and improved music all make for the game to be an over all more enjoyable experience. I rarely got bored with the sameness of anything as I did with the previous game.
The DLC are particularly interesting, and again, I found the arena (or arenas now) to be one of the more enjoyable aspects of the game.
The game tries to sell itself on replayability, like the past one did, but this isn't a feature which particularly interested me. Once I played through all of the content once, I wasn't too keen on doing it all over again just for "better guns." So if you're not big on that stuff either, I can assure you that the game does not rely on replaying content to be fun, like other games (such as Dragonbal Xenoverse) do. You don't have to do anything over and over again.
The villains are hit and miss, but the main badguy, Jack is extremely memorable. He is a very well written sociopath, and it takes you a while to realize exactly what he is because he is that manipulative with his words. Unlike the last game though, the final battle is not difficult in any way, so it's a good thing that the story and previous challenges were fulfilling. The ending is easily much more satisfying than the last game's, which angered more than a few people. That ending is explained and I can say I did genuinely enjoy playing this game with the Mechromancer.
The game does get harder with multiple people playing, and I reccomend this. It gets pretty chaotic and is a ton of fun.
I'd give this am 8.5 or maybe a 9 out of 10.

Damn dwarves, always digging too deep… Uh… Erm-ahem. Hi.
If you’re reading this, chances are you’re interested in Dwarfs!?. Maybe you think it could be your kind of game. I have to start by saying that if you’re looking for something remotely like Dwarf Fortress, this is not it. Dwarfs!? is a completely unrelated casual game.
With that out of the way, what is Dwarfs!?, really? Well, it’s a game about managing dwarves as they dig further and further from their home. If it doesn’t sound too hard, believe me, this job has a lot more excitement than you think.
As the dwarves dig deeper, you’ll want to direct them towards minerals and treasure caves, which boost your score. However, they may also find monsters, water veins, or worse, streams of lava. On that event, you have to try and seal that path before the whole level is flooded and/or your main base is destroyed. This requires an escalating amount of micromanagement, but hey, just try to not die.
And… that’s basically it, really. It comes with several modes, each of which has few different rules, but I’ll admit I spent most of my time with the default, arcade mode, which gives you a time limit (5, 15, 30 or 60 minutes) to explore the cave as far as you can and maximize your score. I could have stuck with the F2P version for that, but I don’t regret my purchase. It’s a pretty good casual game that I find myself coming back to every once in a while.
…it could have done without the obnoxious voice acting, though.

The Call of Duty franchise had its share of ups and downs over the course of time, attempting to innovate and come up with refreshing ideas every year in order to keep its fans entertained, but it's not every year that we see a change so drastic from the original Call of Duty formula. Advanced Warfare takes the biggest risks since the original Modern Warfare, taking the franchise to new battlegrounds as the story takes place in the year 2054, following Private Jack Mitchell, a soldier of the United States Marine Corps throughout a mission in Seoul which led to a terrible accident that earned him a military discharge.
The story opens up when Mitchell is offered to join the Atlas Corporation, the world's most powerful private military contractor, by CEO Jonathan Irons, father of Private Will Irons, who fought along Mitchell before he died in Seoul. It would be a huge disappointment if after one of the most action-packed and tense openings in Call of Duty history, the story would only fade out with typical action-games cliches, but Advanced Warfare is way better than that. After your first tour of Atlas, you will start to get an insight into the world's problems and how Atlas plans to solve them in the future, taking you on a dramatic journey that touches on some of the most sensitive matters of our age in a believable and authentic way, that feels almost scary when you realize how close we really are to all that happening in the near future. The drama and tension effect in the campaign's story is all courtesy of Kevin Spacey, who manages to bring Jonathan Irons' character to life with some powerful and motivating dialogue, making Advanced Warfare's story the most touching and dramatic one in any Call of Duty game to date.
Without spoiling anything, because this truly is one story that you have to experience for yourself, the 8 hour long campaign will take you to some of the most intriguing and breathtaking locations seen in a first person shooter, all while making you feel like a genuine part of the environment and giving you the power to control the game with your many gadgets and weapons. Maybe it does come naturally with the freedom of movement given to you by your exo-suit, but Advanced Warfare is the first game in the franchise that manages to make the players feel like a highly trained soldier without the use of cutscenes or quick time events, as the game constantly throws breathtaking and action-packed moments at you, all which makes perfect sense from a story perspective and without taking the control away from you too often.
The biggest change in multiplayer is the new freedom of movement granted by your exo-suit as you can now dash and boost into the air, opening up all sorts of new techniques and tactics that simply didn't exist before. In the games that came before it, the natural response to incoming fire was taking cover, but the exo-suit changed that strategy forever, making competitive multiplayer more fast-phased and action-packed than ever before. This is a mechanic that has been used in multiple games afterwards such as Titanfall 2, Halo 5 or Activision's own Call of Duty: Black Ops 3 and Call of Duty: Infinite Warfare only to name a few, but none of them came close to the smooth and fluid usage of this ability in the same way Advanced Warfare did, and they all have this game to look up to for bringing up the idea and refining it into a multiplayer environment.
Popular game modes such as Hardpoint and Capture the flag made a return from Black Ops II, adding to the traditional modes such as Team Deathmatch, Free for all or Kill Confirmed, along with the brand new mode Uplink, where you have to bring a satellite drone from the neutral central point of the match all the way to the enemy station located near their spawn point in order to score points, all while battling your way through the enemy base.
Advanced Warfare's response to Black Ops' Zombie mode is Exo Survival, even though this also turned into a zombie mode later on with the release of the "Havoc" DLC, but at its core it wasn't that much different from Zombies to begin with. Exo Survival puts you in team of four against different waves of enemies with different objectives per wave. What is different from the already popular Zombies mode is the objective-based waves, where you will have to complete different tasks such as collecting the dog tags of killed enemies, survive against drones or kill a given number of enemies within a time limit.
This is without doubt one of the best, if not the very best campaign in any Call of Duty game, as apart from the actually believable and logical story, it constantly throws action-packed moments at you without going too over the top and giving you freedom of movement and the ability to take decisions on which way you approach a situation like never before. The campaign is a great introduction to Advanced Warfare's new gadgets, weapons and the exo suit, which unfortunately won't be available to use until later on in the campaign to its full potential, but you will never feel the need to do so simply because there will always be a new toy for you to play with, and from a gameplay perspective the campaign gives you a great introduction to the brand new mechanic that changed first person shooters in the years to follow.
Even moments like controlling a drone or a helicopter never feel like the "necessary in any first person shooter" moments, simply because they are phased so well and always find brand new futuristic ways to make it more fun to watch and play. The same applies to weapons, as you are given a short introduction to the different types of guns that you can use, and after that the entire game opens up as your playground to try them out and see which one best suits your playstyle before jumping into multiplayer.
As Activision mentioned, this is the first Call of Duty game built from the ground up for the new generation of hardware and it looks simply astonishing, with beautiful landscapes that now have a sense of scale and freedom thanks to the exo-suit and detail put into every corner of every single map that you will visit. Motion capture has been used to bring the actors to life inside the game and performances by Kevin Spacey and Troy Baker along with many others make this game's story believable and dramatic in some scenes, which is truly a next-gen experience just looking at it.
The sound effects are what you would expect from a major triple A title, but that is not the star of the show here. The amazing dialogue combined with professional and experienced voice actors and a powerful soundtrack make Advanced Warfare an experience that you will remember for years to come. While Kevin Spacey and Troy Baker are obviously the starts of the show here, voicing Atlas CEO Jonathan Irons and your character Jack Mitchell respectively, other voice actors do just as an amazing job in both likeness and dialogue delivery, with special mentions for Angela Gots	as the voice and likeness of Ilona and Gideon Emery as the voice and likeness of Gideon.
Advanced Warfare is a brand new twist on the Call of Duty formula and a welcome one, as the exo-suit and futuristic theme gives plenty of new ways to play the game and its solid package of content will ensure you have something to do for weeks to come, all while keeping the competitive aspect, mastery and skill based first person shooter action that made the franchise popular in the first place.

MXGP, the official motocross videogame. This is a good simulation of the real motocross event and how the bike handles. You can play as the official riders and race on the real world motocross tracks. Also, you get bikes like KTM, Suzuki, Honda, Yamaha, Kawasaki and Tm (I don't remember the last manufacturer). In Career mode, you start as a wildcard rider and if you are good enough, you'll move up to the MX1 class. The riding physics are good, and it is somewhat newbie-friendly. It will take a while to get used to the handling of the bike, and the AI (on easy they can be a challenge if you are new to the game).
One drawback is you can't turn off the controller vibration. This is pretty annoying, especially for someone who doesn't like to play with vibration (like me). The multiplayer? There's almost no one playing there, but it doesn't bother me.
If you are planning to get this game, I suggest that you get a controller first. You'll have a hard time playing using the keyboard. If you like racing or sports games, I would recommend this game. It's a pretty fun game overall.

First, don't let the screen shots fool you into thinking they're only from a prerender cinematic. No, these are in game results that quickly grab your eyeballs and attempt to pull'em from your sockets!
Unlike most motorcycle racers out there, this one definately requires you to pay close attention to not only your speed while cornering, but the use of rider leaning plus turning the bike. Yes, you better let off that throttle else it's into the hay stacks, crowds, and trees.
Very, very different--and not made easy by default! Even with all driving assists enabled, and NPC racers AI set to basic, you will need some patience and determination to succeed at avoiding last place or DNF ranking in every race.
With that all said, I love this game. Although only scratching the surface thus far, it looks, sounds and feels as expected in a true racing sim. On paper, (no pun intended), this game has a pretty boring premise. See how much mind-numbing paperwork you can process in a day to make ends meet. It sounds like a level of enjoyment that can be achieved through the use of Microsft Excel. However, clever storytelling, surprising character development and a difficulty curve that increases as the layers of beaurocracy stack up, make this game intriguing and surprisingly addictive.
It is 1982 in a fictional slice of Eastern Europe. The player becomes a border control inspector in the nightmare totalitarian state of Arstotzka, turning away impoverish families into the cold because their visas are a few weeks out of date. Or maybe you want to play the good guy and let a few desperate people slip through the net? But you also have a family to feed, and in this communist society, your salary is paid based on how many people you process correctly in a day. Too many citations and you’ll be the one left out in the cold.
The simplistic graphics of this game are more than just nostalgia. They add to the impact when something shocking and unexpected happens. Like that guy with shifty-looking eyes strutting out of the ticket booth and shouting ‘GLORY TO KOLECHIA’, shortly before blowing himself up and redecorating the wall with the innards of your security guards.
Your moral choices can alter the stormy political atmosphere, re-unite friends and lovers and deliver justice in any way you see fit. For people don't just live in the country. They ARE the country. I think my only complaint about the game is that it feels dry, sinister and clinical. I know that it was designed to be this way, but it means I can't play for any more than a few minutes before I just feel ... dirty inside ... and want to play something brighter, more colourful and happy.
Nevertheless, Papers Please gets 9/10 from me. Glory to Arstotzka, komrade.

Factorio is currently the number one game based off of user reviews on steam, and thats not from some silly hype train!
I bought this game from their origional Indie Go Go campaign a few years ago when i was watching xisumavoid play it. The game has gone through several amazing updates bringing tools like the splitter and the power armors. I have more than 200 hours of non steam game time and have loved every minute of the 200+ hours.
About the game:
Factorio is a factory building game where you spend your time trying to acheive your own goals, unless you play in the campaign missions. You start off with coal powerd machines and work to acheive things like steam or solar powerd bases that can produce every thing you need. And you spend alot of time revising your plans for your factory untill you find the optimum setup for your assembly machines, oil pumps, or "smeting plants" to produce the right amount of resources for the rest of the base. And eventually you may aggress the neighboring natives and have to defend your base using machine guns, laser turrets, tanks, or firearms. And as you continue to grow and defend against the natives, they become more intellegent and begin to set up bases closer to your base while growing their smaller bases and will sometimes attack from multiple fronts at once untill they win or you destroy their bases.
Who would like this game?
first off anyone who enjoyed buildcraft/industrialcraft from minecraft mod packs.
people who enjoy trying to find the best solution to a problem they may have caused.
or people that strive to build things bigger and better than something else they have built.
Pros
The game runs on low end computers if you need that.
The graphics however simple they are, are very nice and satisfying to me
You get a huge sense of success as you progress through the game
The developers allow you to create custom scenarios, so you can make little missions.
The developers make the right decisions that AAA titles would never do
For example, since i bought this game before it was released on steam, i got a free steam key for it :>
They have never charged for unnescisary dlc's, expansions, or microtransactions.
And have always kept the Community's opinion in mind.
And you also are allowed to customize alot in how the world is generated.
Cons
.... cant think of anything lol
All in all the game is amazing, and if you have $20 and want the game it is definitely worth it in my opinion and 99.9% of the other people who have this game.

Here's my review the 'second expedition' to Rome.
When I first recieved the game last Christmas, I was (and still am as I write this review) playing on a crappy laptop. I managed to trun the graphics down, resolution downscaled, and overclock my computer to a decent but unsatisfactory rate. This does not make the game bad, I just needed a new machine with a bigger processor.
Historically speaking, all factions have existed and are within historical bounds of the timeframe of which the Roman Republic and the Empire existed. However, when you reach some of the more famous time periods like 70-60 B.C when Caesar arrives in your general candidates pool in the grand campaign, he can often be mismatched with different houses (e.g Gauis Julius Caesar belonging to the Houseof Junia).
The construction system is simple once you get the hang of it. Starting players might not get it at first which will affect their food supply and how to maintain it, but overall the system of town and city management is okay, depending on your strategic understanding of how to spend money you recieve or coerce others to give you through diplomacy or force.
The military system follows that closely of the Marian reforms later on in the first century B.C, and the unit structure (even if not playing as Rome) is very unique as is. When you subjugate another faction to yours, you are able to integrate their units into your auxiliary instead of just only paying for mercenaries like the old Rome: Total war, giving a sense of diversity and a close meaning to the client state or Roman Auxiliary armies.
Overall, to those who wrote a bad review on this game probably paid more attention to the force of elephant mounted units and simply the way everything looks. Regardless of the nit-picky people, I have to give this game two thumbs up.
9/10, great job CA & SEGA I'm looking forward to buying Attila, and playing Warhammer when it releases.
P.S When you play Rome in the start, attack Velathri, Alalia, THEN Ariminium. Unless you want the Etruscan League always at your back for the next 50 turns...

(March 05, 2016). The game's preview video shows what maximally complex factory and base look like, that you could build in-game. If the idea of building that from the ground up excites you (starting from nothing but a hand pick and some raw materials, then building things and researching technologies), then Factorio is definitely for you. Factorio executes brilliantly on the vision of a building and running a supply chain and factory, in a way that no other game has delivers (see "The Genre", below for related games).
Factorio performs well on Windows 10 in Ultra 4K HD, with UI scale-up. It advertises multiplayer co-op, though I haven't gotten an opportunity to try it.
The game includes a single player tutorial and campaign, following the story of a person who crash-landed on the planet. The beginning of the campaign is a tutorial that teaches you everything you need to know about the game, including UI overlays showing where to click, and what to process. You don't need to be intimidated about the complexity of getting started, since the Tutorial walks you thought it. I highly recommend that players of all skill levels play the tutorial. From there, the campaign proceeds to put the player into a number of scenarios: build a vehicle to search for survivors; recover and improve this abandoned base. The campaign has been a fun campanion to sandbox mode. I have only played a few missions in, so far, as of this review.
You control a single character in a top-down 2D world, who has health and that you must protect. You've crash landed on a planet, and have knowledge of advanced technology, but don't have the raw materials to rebuild yourship. Your character can also assemble machines. Your first step in the world is to harvest some resources yourself, by mining them with your pick or axe. With those basic resources, you assemble mining machines and vehicles to automate the process, as well as weapons to protect yourself.
In Factorio, you build increasingly sophisticated factories and assembly line operations. Initially, your mining machine might output its raw minerals to a crate, such that you ferry them over to the smelter yourself. You might operate that way for a while, until you've completed the research and have the raw materials to build conveyor belts. Then you can run a conveyor belt between the mining machine and your smelter! With the conveyor belt running to the smelter, you can only just begin to keep up with the increasing demands you'll have for increasingly-more-complex finished products. Throughout this time, you're running throughout your base putting coal into your machines by hand.
Eventually, you build an electricity grid to power all your machines from steam engines rather than coal, and increasingly advanced transportation systems for your raw products. There are several types of conveyor belts, going all the way up to trains; you can lay the trail for your supply trains to run alone, to ferry resources from remote locations into your processing plant.
The game arranges all of these processes to feel exciting, satisfying, and incremental. Each step as a meaningful, meaty improvement, that makes you glad for what you've done, but hungry for the next level (of automation, of materials, ...)
The game is not a pure sandbox, and that's a good thing. Your character has a health bar, and can die. (It automatically regenerates if you haven't taken damage for a while. The player has no food or other needs.)
There are other creatures on the planet with you, and they don't like the pollution that your factories produce. You need to defend yourself from them. When they attack, you defend from them largely in Tower Defense fashion. The game provides a variety of defenses, from surrounding yourself with fortified walls, to building automated gun-turrets, or constructing tank vehicles to drive around in. As you expand your operations, you'll be faced with increasingly storng waves of enemies to defend against. This creates some pressure and gives direction to your mining operation. Your goal is to assemble the materials to launch a space ship before being overwhelmed by the horde! Free play sandbox modes are also available. So far, combat appears to occur at just the right frequency to create some tension, but not frequently enough to stop me from relaxing and building too.
For many years I've sought a game that would allow me to build, manage, and update supply chains; to develop and upgrade factories and assembly lines. I tried robotic mining in
with mods and modpacks like
, but it wasn't really polished or a good enough experience to hold me.
is excellent, but it's as much about space flight and flight simulation as building. I've loved
, which is great fun, but it's early access and there's only so much you can do. I tried
, which has a similarly long supply chain, but it was difficult to figure out, and the "random events" made the game "fun" but derailed my construction projects.
is another beatiful and wonderfully fun game that relies on supply chains, but the replay value drops off after several playthroughs (I wish its author would add more content!). If you've enjoyed any of the games I listed above, then you'll probably enjoy Factorio.
I'm now approaching 60 hours playing Factorio, and I'd have to say that I've found my new favorite building game. After that much time, I feel like I've only explored a small piece of the game (in a good way). Factorio is an instant classic for me.

Thisi s a really great game. On the surface it looks pretty straight forward, but it gets more and more complicated - but not so complicated that it stops being fun. You are basically a border worker who checks documents on people immigrating over. Your job is to make sure they don't have false information, fake documents, bombs, etc... all while saving money to keep your family alive and comfortable. I learn something new with each passing day (each day is a 'level') and if you mess up you can go back to a previous day and start over. For example, I accepted a bribe on day 11 for $1000. A few days later I moved into a nicer apartment. My neighbors reported my 'new wealth' to the athorities and they took my bribe money and are investigating the situation. I haven't found out what is going to happen yet, but if i lose my job i'm going to revert back to the day before I took the bribe money and be sure not to take it again :) Anyway, great game and definitely something to take about with other people who have played.

First thing I noticed playing this game: Looking at my mouse move around the screen with an odd sense of nostalgia for the Oregon Trail days in Computer Class circa 1992, but with a twisted knowledge that this computer was not heaving with every swing of my mouse hand. The classic grinding sound of god knows what going on inside those tan trashcans as I try to figure out how much buffalo meat to carry missing now replaced with a commanding bassline of a soundtrack.
Papers, Please is without a doubt the most flawlessly executed game of it's style, in my experience. Nothing else has captured the tone, the feel, the sticking power of this game.
As it's core Papers, Please is nothing more than a simple timed puzzle game but at it's best it becomes a place to test your nerves, your wit, and your morals. The story progresses in increasingly diverse ways as days go by and family members die, nothing more than tones and words on the screen. You'd be surprised what one can do with an awkward or dulled color palette (see: Alan Moore's The Watchmen, Frank Miller's Ronin).
It also contains an "Endless" mode as well if you ever just want to, you know, feel like a communist paper-pusher.
All-in-all it's a $5 buy. Anything more is just tipping the artist.
