I want to preface this by stating that my play time is longer due to restarting the game while halfway through. If not for this, my play time would be about 3 hours.
Now, why do I feel that's important? Because in all honesty the game is exceedingly short. I do understand why this was done, as the game has multiple difficulty options to extend play time. The highest difficulty allows for no saving, so a longer game wouldn't be truly viable under such circumstances. That said, however, and again while I understand it, that doesn't excuse the short length.
Many of the achievements encourage you to replay the game, and while there are some different paths through the areas, the only major deviation is prior to the first boss. There are two different paths to take which lead to two different bosses, but this is the only time such a thing happens. It would have added much more replay value to the game if all of the bosses were like this, but sadly they aren't.
Major power ups are very limited and one is obtained in an order that makes it pointless. The armor, with its half damage reduction would have been highly useful mid-game, yet it's the last major upgrade gained, and by that time there's perhaps little more than perhaps twenty minutes left in the game, if that. None of the enemies ramp up the damage potential beyond this point, making its reduction moot. The bow, while it adds some range, is only useful for some puzzle sections due to its weak power compared to the upgraded sword and its powerful charge swing, plus its inability to be fired in any direction but forward. The shield should have been a basic item from the beginning as it deflects arrows and your character looks like he has a shield to begin with, yet lacks any projectile deflecting qualities.
The shop update, while it looks good on the surface, is a bit of a pointless addition. The ability to store power boosts, invincibility and attack items seems useful, however in every mode where shops are available, the game poses little significant threat to the player. The only time I even bothered to pop an invincibility item was the very last boss, and that made it such a cake walk that I felt bad for cheesing it. The attack items are extremely weak and are incapable of killing anything in a single hit, some not even in two to three uses. In the higher difficulties where items would be useful, there are no shops at all.
However, with all of this said, the game is extremely fun for what it is. The music is by no means a masterpiece, but there was no a single track that wore out its welcome. I personally wouldn't buy the soundtrack DLC, but that's in no way an accusation of poor quality.
The controls with a controller are tight and responsive, I didn't find myself fighting with them, nor was there any moment where I could look at the game and truly blame the controls for mistakes. When I screwed up it was my fault, not the game. I haven't tested the keyboard controls, mind you, which perhaps I should in the future, but for now 360 controller users can rejoice because there's no jank here.
The story... is, well, serviceable. This isn't an RPG, nor is the story very important, but as a framing device it services its purpose. Don't go in expecting more than just a bare bones reason as to why anything is happening or a minimum conclusion.
The game, to me at least, has a strong feeling of the NES and Game Boy Kid Icarus games to it, with perhaps a bit of Alex Kidd mixed in. The HUD is very clearly original Legend of Zelda inspired. It manages to blend all of this into a game that is fun and addicting for however long you can get out of it, and frankly I was left with wanting more. If there's ever a sequel, I can only hope that it's longer while retaining the same charm as this game managed to capture, because then I feel it'd be a truly amazing, must play game.

I've mentioned it before on my 8-Bit Boy post that I think too many indie devs get caught up in just mimicking that older visual aesthetic and forget that the reason we have nostalgia for those old games is that they were actually fun and not that they looked like they were old.
When they were new, we didn't know any better in terms of the aesthetic so we didn't really give all that much of a♥♥♥♥♥♥about how the game looked. And when we played a bad game back then we tried to suck it up and choke it down because we were dumb kids who just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥away our weekend game rental on something trashy like ♥♥♥♥in Beetlejuice on NES or Home Improvement on SNES. Now that we have choices and easy access to just absurd numbers of games, we don't have to put up with stupid garbage (unless you're a masochist like me) and we'll just move onto something different if the game is♥♥♥♥♥♥
I dunno. It's fun to think about, and I think the central and easy answer is that the gameplay in a modern retro platformer is the important thing because invoking that particular time period brings me back to that "who cares what it looks like" mindset. But there are a few other smaller things going on there, I'm pretty sure.

It's the year 2900 and you are a treasure hunter on a lawless Prison Planet full of mad criminals, violent aliens and murderous robots.
Nice soundtrack, pleasant gunplay, decently intelligent AI, optional 4 player coop and addictive gameplay with a potential up ro 100+ hours and more. Sadly, the Missions and level design gets somewhat same-ish, there is little to no difference in the gameplay of the (up to) 6 player classes, the overall product is riddled with paid DLC and the story is a load of pretentious bullshît garnered with bland, unlikeable bystanders. The exception being the antihero you fight, who is in itself quite excellent. On the other hand the female lead character is singlehandedly one of the most disgusting putrid cûnts I have seen in any piece of media to this day. Anthony Burch, the head writer for the storyline, is a fûcking marxist SJW cuck.
I bought the GOTY Edition and not even there was all DLC inclusive. What the fûck Gearbox? I even bought Duke Nukem Forever at full price back in the day from you. Dishonored 2 is very similar to its predecessor, in way of combat, and its overall aesthetic. It notably takes inspiration from Dishonored's two main DLC's, The Knife of Dunwall and the Brigmore Witches. The player characters--from which the player has the choice between Dishonored's protagonist Corvo Attano, or his daughter Empress Emily Kaldwin--are both voice acted (though this does not add much to the game, and often can come across rather stiff), and each have their own individual set of powers. These powers, unlike in Dishonored, have a corresponding skill tree, and can each be bought and upgraded through the use of runes found throughout the maps. The mechanics that made Dishonored 1 great are still there, though they have each been refined, and make the game considerably more enjoyable.
That being said, players who have not played (and completed) The Knife of Dunwall and The Brigmore Witches may find themselves not as invested in the plot of Dishonored 2. The antagonist of D2 is the atagonist of both of Dishonored's DLC's, that being Delilah Copperspoon, who is revealed within the first five of the minutes of the game to be the long-lost aunt of Emily Kaldwin.
For those who got to know Delilah in TKoD/TBW, and faced off against her as Daud, I daresay, will find themselves more motivated to take her down. Because of the fact that many players did not get to meet Delilah in D1, Arkane Studios almost throws exposition in the player's face in order to fill them in, which almost removes the exploratory plot in D1 which many players, including myself, were attracted to. Rather than having the player discover the plot on their own, Arkane leads the player by the hand, which can feel quite frustrating for experienced players.
Tl;dr Dishonored 2 is still a great game, though it doesn't quite live up the high standard of Dishonored 1. Would reccommend purchasing, and provides many hours of quality gameplay, in a living, breathing world.

What do I think of Dishonored 2... It's a really good, tentpole, AAA game. "Play it your way," is something of a cliche but Dishonored 2 really delivers. Violent vs pacifist, stealthy vs aggressive, magic powers vs all natural, two characters, dozens of paths through each level. On my second playthough I was constantly surprised at how many locations I hadn't seen, how many times I found multiple paths around that I missed the first time. I'm not at the place in life that I want to get hundreds of hours out of a game, but this is the type of game that I could imagine doing 8 or more run throughs, especiallly with the way they implemented a new game+.
If you are wondering about Dishonored 1 vs Dishonored 2.... it's hard to say. You could go either way. Dishonored 2 improves on almost every technical element of the first game, the graphics are better (but 1 isn't shabby), and the gameplay is technically better, the powers are more interesting (and fun to combine). The level design in Dishonored 2 is something else, really impressive. Dishonored 2 is WAY gorier than 1 (but 1 still felt brutal). But Dishonored 1 has a charm to it... the story is possibly better, and there is something in the simpler levels and style that is charming. They are both great.

This game was in development for about 7 years and came out of nowhere in 2007, GSC Game World's last game series and will probably be the only thing they are remembered for.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is a First-Person Shooter / Role-Playing / Survival Horror game set in a sci-fi alternate reality inside the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant and its Exclusion Zone. People risk their lives sneaking into "The Zone" in order to retrieve rare and precious artifacts to sell on the black market.
You play the role of The Marked One. After being rescued from a freak accident and suffering from amnesia, you're placed in a harsh world of bandits, anomalies, dangerous killer mutants and the Ukrainian military tasked with keeping people out of the Zone. People around the Zone dream of breaching the Zones inner defenses and as rumour has it, unlimited wealth and artifacts await the first person to do so.
The story involves you travelling to many places around the zone including abandoned warehouses, labratories, millitary baracks and power stations. The game swaps its pacing around fairly often; dealing with humans in hostile environments to having to infiltrate areas infested with deadly mutants that will tear you to shreds in seconds.
And they WILL tear you to bits. Most games cast you as some kind of bullet sponge able to survive multiple shotgun blasts to the face. You try running head first into a gun fight in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. and your insides will be decorating the scenery before you can pick out a target to shoot.
This vunerability of your character greatly enhances the fear and survival aspects to S.T.A.L.K.E.R.. You will need to think about eating and drinking on a regular basis to avoid death and keep your strength up. You'll need bandages to stop yourself bleeding to death, You'll need Vodka to flush radiation from your system and you'll need to really focus on aiming and timing shots as one shot to the head will finish both enemies and you off in no time.
The artifacts around the Zone will also help you. Most artifacts come with both positive and negative effects that can help you survive. Some rare artifacts only have good effects to them but you'll really have to keep an eye out for them. Artifact effects include health regeneration at a cost to being very vunerable to bleeding out when hit, protection from the numerous anomalies around that will kill you if you get too close and many more. You can mix and match artifacts as you see fit.
The game also tells you how visible you are to other enemies and even how much sound you're making when moving and reloading your guns. Enemies can hear you so reloading whilst right next to an unsuspecting bloodsucker might be the last move you make.
The game also has multiple endings but don't think that the ending you find right away is the... 'correct' one :)

I first became acuainted with this game back in April 2014, after having watched Quill18 play it for a little while. It seemed like a really interesting and deep game that focused heavily on logistics and planning, and I fell for it right away. In a way this game can be compared to Minecraft. It's an open world game where the gameplay itself is the real attraction and a purpose unto itself, rather than being driven by the actual stated goal of the game (The End in Minecraft, as of writing the rocket silo in this game, though that will probably be expanded upon in future updates). The actual play mechanics of it is beautiful, and if you were the person wanting to build complicated redstone machinery, this game is definitively for you.

Bought the game from the developer's website almost two years ago after seeing a let's play of it. Needless to say, I got addicted to it rather quickly...
I was pleasantly surprised how fleshed out the game already was back then and, in my opinion at least, it has only gotten better over time. The developers are great, giving status updates and sneak peeks about the things they are working on frequently. I'm seeing more and more devs doing this, involving the community more in the development process, which is awesome.
About the game itself, I never knew making complex production chains could be so much fun. Getting raw resources, refining them and then using those refined resources to make some end product, which, depending on what you are making, might be needed for yet another product. The game starts out simple, but grows in complexity as you need more and more things to make more and more stuff. In the late game, this can get very time consuming, unless you know exactly what you are doing. Whether this is good or bad, I suppose it depends on the person playing. I don't really mind the game being a big timesink, since I often find myself just staring at the production lines I've just made, mesmerised by the inserters moving tirelessly, only to snap back as a small, red icon next to the toolbar starts blinking and everything grinds to a halt. I realise biters are eating away at my power supply, just because I was too occupied with other things and I forgot to make defenses...
All in all, if you like building bases (or factories, in this case), figuring out the ratios to make everything work efficiently and defending all the stuff you make from those pesky aliens, then this game could be for you. If you don't mind spending hours upon hours perfecting your production chains, then this game could definitely be for you.

What is nice is just how the game does not hold the player's hand throughout the game. Adventure in the Tower of Flight is a hard game, but it offers a fair challenge, which is rare in games. Most of the time, challenge comes from artificial aspects such as check point starvation, limited continues, or beginners traps. There is none of this in Adventure in the Tower of Flight. Adventure in the Tower of Flight may look manageable from the outside looking in, but when played on one's own, it's not as easy as it looks.
I had a lot of fun with Adventure in the Tower of Flight, and it is definitely one of the few times I saw a retro throwback that nails everything about retro games perfectly, even more so than some retro games themselves. In addition to that, the game is just addictive and I found myself constantly in that “okay one more try” kind of mood every time I died until I finished the whole thing within the span of a few days.
It is highly recommended that you check out Adventure in the Tower of Flight, as it is quite the underrated game when it comes to Steam's library of retro “throwbacks” and it is the perfect thing to recommend to those who have been hoping to find something that doesn't miss the point of retro games, or that isn't exactly like them to a fault.

An interesting but slightly confusing platformer game.
Adventure in the Tower of Flight is a game where your character has the ability to fly from the start. While the game shows a lot of potential at first, it becomes repetitive and confusing soon as you fight the same enemies over and over while traversing through rooms that look similar to each other. Sometimes you're given a choice of a path to choose, but you have no way of knowing if you're going to the right direction or towards an optional area and sometimes you end up re-visiting the same areas.
In game, you'll collect both gold and feathers which can be used to purchase items, but there is not much to buy. The only thing worth buying with feathers is an instant revive potion (the Magic Feather grants 15 seconds of invulnerability, but it's used immediately and is very rarely useful). There are no significant upgrades to be purchases with either gold or feathers and, because of this, very soon there will be little encouragement for the player to even bother trying to pick them up or even to look for secrets, as secrets usually just lead to more gold and feathers and are therefore often meaningless.
Cons aside, it's a fun game nonetheless. It's neither too short or too long, has some very interesting boss fights and there are (meaningful) upgrades to be obtained along the way.

What do I think of Dishonored 2... It's a really good, tentpole, AAA game. "Play it your way," is something of a cliche but Dishonored 2 really delivers. Violent vs pacifist, stealthy vs aggressive, magic powers vs all natural, two characters, dozens of paths through each level. On my second playthough I was constantly surprised at how many locations I hadn't seen, how many times I found multiple paths around that I missed the first time. I'm not at the place in life that I want to get hundreds of hours out of a game, but this is the type of game that I could imagine doing 8 or more run throughs, especiallly with the way they implemented a new game+.
If you are wondering about Dishonored 1 vs Dishonored 2.... it's hard to say. You could go either way. Dishonored 2 improves on almost every technical element of the first game, the graphics are better (but 1 isn't shabby), and the gameplay is technically better, the powers are more interesting (and fun to combine). The level design in Dishonored 2 is something else, really impressive. Dishonored 2 is WAY gorier than 1 (but 1 still felt brutal). But Dishonored 1 has a charm to it... the story is possibly better, and there is something in the simpler levels and style that is charming. They are both great.

A nice vertically oriented platformer, with a pleasing aesthetic that seems to take equal inspiration from NES classics like
and early Apogee hits like
.  The ubiquitous jumping mechanic is replaced with flight:  a generous meter allows you to float almost freely about the lofty, linear stages as you suddenly strike out with a dash attack or charge up your blade for a power-swing.  The mostly deliberate speed of Wing's movements, together with the pacing of the levels themselves, gives the game a slightly foggy, meditative feeling -- as in a pleasant dream decorated with fleecy clouds and slowly billowing draperies that stretch up beyond the limit of sight.
When I was an NES-addicted kid, I had lots of dreams about playing games that didn't exist, mostly games set in towering castles with slow, low-G action; I know I must not be the only one, since somebody made a game like this, drawing undoubtedly from the collective unconscious that all 2D gamers share.  Throughout my playthrough I felt a warm buzz of everyday mysticality, like an amplification of the little thrill you sometimes get when you walk away from a radio mid-song, only to hear the end of the same song sounding from a parked car a couple minutes later.  There's nothing truly magical about everybody getting the same broadcast, but it's easy (and fun) to let part of yourself believe that there is.
(If you are a calloused veteran of old-school platformers, attain maximum enjoyment by cranking the difficulty up to MASTER -- but no higher!)

Although this game has a few flaws it's still the best motorcross game I've ever played. MXGP is not a game where you pull off insane tricks or jump off giant cliffs. MXGP is a recreation of real MX racing and it does this fairly well.
Pros:
+ There are multiple game types - Instant race, Grand Prix, Championship season, Career Mode and Time attack. It has  recreated tracks from real tracks on the MX tour. The tracks also have track deformation of the dirt and mud. There seams to be a lot of tracks as well. I'm not real far into it but the season I'm in has at least a dozen to complete.
+ Multiple difficulties that can be tweaked to make MXGP as easy/arcade or Hard/Simulation as you prefer.
+ The physics and handling of the motorcycles are done very well. No other MX game has gotten this close to the feeling of riding a real MX bike. (yes I have ridden on real MX bikes and street bikes as well)
+The replays look good and have multiple options like slow motion, pause and a free cam. You can get some nice screenshots.
+ Graphics are solid. The riders and the bikes look good and gather dirt and mud on them during the race. The tracks are pretty good too but could have been done better. I use SweetFX on this game and it makes it look better.
+You can remap the controls on the controller. I recommend you use a controller. I don't know of any racing game that work well with mouse and keyboard. At least not for me. I recommend that you change the lean forward and backwards to the same stick as steering left and right. It feels much more natural this way.
+You level up, unlock pictures, gear, bikes ect and you get more fans the better you do in each race. Also there is a simulated email and twitter type media in the game that makes tyou feel you are being watched by teams, fans and your manager. It's a nice touch to give a sense of progression and connection in the game.
Cons:
- The presentation is pretty bad. In between races I've had my bike disappear in the pits. The pit crew guy is working on an imaginary, invisible bike. Also before a race, during the intro scene, my rider was shaking around like he was have convultions. The pit crew and girl who holds the starting card all look and act like zombies. Why even put these in the game ?  Also, Some of the ground during races has pop in and loads textures too. The game needs a patch to fix these things.
- The sound is not very good either. The bikes just sound weak, why can't developers get this right ? Even if it's not realistic they need to alter the engine sounds to make them more rich and intense. Also, There is no option to play music during races, it would be nice to have. I noticed there is barely any sounds of the stadium surroundings happening. It would be great to have the crowd react to what is happening. Cheer when you overtake or respond to a big wreck. Make the game and the race feel exciting Milestone ! Enough with the barebones, boring presentation already !
Also a track announcer being heard over the PA system would add some immersion. Having your pit crew tell you your doing great or you have 1 lap to go would really add some interaction to the game. These things could have be easily added into the game and would make the game better. On my PC the sound cuts in and out during start videos but no real problem in game so far. I've seen that many people have had problems in game though. Patch these things into the game Milestone.
Overall the game just feels kind of bland. This happed in other games by Milestone. I loved the racing and handling in MotoGP 08 but it has the same barebones presentaion and sound as well. Milestone get the racing right, and that is what is most important, but they need to add some flavor and style into these games. As for now I will enjoy MXGP for what it is but there is definately room for improvement.

Thisi s a really great game. On the surface it looks pretty straight forward, but it gets more and more complicated - but not so complicated that it stops being fun. You are basically a border worker who checks documents on people immigrating over. Your job is to make sure they don't have false information, fake documents, bombs, etc... all while saving money to keep your family alive and comfortable. First thing I noticed playing this game: Looking at my mouse move around the screen with an odd sense of nostalgia for the Oregon Trail days in Computer Class circa 1992, but with a twisted knowledge that this computer was not heaving with every swing of my mouse hand. The classic grinding sound of god knows what going on inside those tan trashcans as I try to figure out how much buffalo meat to carry missing now replaced with a commanding bassline of a soundtrack.
Papers, Please is without a doubt the most flawlessly executed game of it's style, in my experience. Nothing else has captured the tone, the feel, the sticking power of this game.
As it's core Papers, Please is nothing more than a simple timed puzzle game but at it's best it becomes a place to test your nerves, your wit, and your morals. The story progresses in increasingly diverse ways as days go by and family members die, nothing more than tones and words on the screen. You'd be surprised what one can do with an awkward or dulled color palette (see: Alan Moore's The Watchmen, Frank Miller's Ronin).
It also contains an "Endless" mode as well if you ever just want to, you know, feel like a communist paper-pusher.
All-in-all it's a $5 buy. Anything more is just tipping the artist.

[NOTE: THIS REVIEW IS BY SOMEONE WHO HAS NEVER PLAYED THE CLASSIC HOMEWORLD SERIES, THEREFORE THIS REVIEW IS FROM MY EXPERIANCE]
Homeworld is an RTS game that is massivley popular with sci-fi fans. I have never played any of the classic Homeworld games but I can see why people love them. I myself, am an RTS fan. I remember once going round to a friends house many years ago and watched his dad play the origninal Homeworld, and to this very day, it is as cool as i thought.
The Homeworld story itself is fantastic. I have only played through two of the campaign missions, but i must say i'm impressed. One thing that i have found myself doing over the past two hours of game time is practicing my skills in the player vs CPU game mode. This game mode is great for new players to try out tactics and practice for online and campaign missions, espcecially when i hear that campaign missions are very hard as the story progresses. I put on the Star Wars soundtrack as i played this game, and for some reason, it feels more enjoyable and, if i must say, rather nostalgic.
The Gameplay is quite basic on the surface. Click on a unit and click on the map of where you want it to go, but under the surface is quite complex. Menues ranging from formations to attack or defensive positions really makes you want to experiment with your tactics in the game. Even one slip up can cause great danger to your units, it's quite punishing. But in order to get these ships you must harvest for RU Or Resource Points. To get these points you must send your Resource Ships to nearby asteroids to mine materials and bring them back to the Mothership. Ah the Mothership, probably the most badass ship i have ever seen, and a ship that has stuck in my mind. Its argubly the icon for the series.
I can't tell you much about the online as i haven't played it and i'm scared too becuase I know i'll get rekt, very hard. The soundtrack in this game is wonderful, very atmospehric and sets the scene in such away that it alone draws you in. The controls can get quite complex to start off with, but after you play the tutorial missions two or three times. then you get used to it. The Remastered Collection comes with Homeworld Remastered, Homeworld 2 Remastered and the un-remastered original Homeworld 1 & 2.
I do have a one criticism however, the camera can be a bit buggy. As you load up a mission your camera can get stuck and with force you to exit and re-enter the mission itself over and over.
I must say, this game is one that i'lll be coming back to for a long period of time. I do recommend the game, even if you do not have a clue what Homeworld is, then still get it and find out. I was abit sketchy towards this RTS game as I didn't know if i was going to enjoy it or not. Still, get it, no matter if your a fan or a newbie like me. Get it.
Overall: 9.5/10

This game has a LOT of issues. Seeing as it's in the sale and there will be a lot of people considering buying it, I feel like I should outline the issues. TL;DR and specs at the bottom.
- Performance, it varies from person to person but personally I have a medium/high-end gaming rig and still get stuttering and frame drops. I get smoother framerates on games with more graphic fedelity. On consoles it's the same story, constant frame rate drops.
- There's a memory leak issue that is yet to be fixed. Instead of fixing the issue, the devs just raised the minimum RAM requirement from 8GB to 16GB and added a message for every time you boot up the game telling you that you have insufficient memory. Apparently getting more RAM actually fixes a lot of performance issues with the game, go figure.
- The car handling in this game is so, so, bad. People says that Just Cause 2's handling was bad, but that game is a shining light of glory compared to JC3's habdling. And then just wait until you try a motorbike. The turning is horrid, it feels like you have no control sometimes. You hold down the button or move the stick to turn and there's a delay of about 1 second until your bike actually starts turning.  It's so easy to make them spin out and / or flip. Again, when the devs were questioned about this, they literally said "We think it's fine!" (can't find the link to the tweet but I'm sure it's out there).
- There's no native way to change the FOV. There's mods that let you do so but then when you do change it a whole bunch of glitches appear, like terrain not rendering, animations ending, etc. I usually wouldn't mind, but the default FOV is so low to begin with, try driving a car, it's right up in your face and you can barely see past it.
- Missions are creative until you realise that a lot of them are the same being repeated multiple times. Story is boring, I ended up ignoring it and just ♥♥♥♥ing around. Plus, at least for me, destroying bases got boring after a while because there's so god damn many. Just Cause 2 did the whole "Chaos" thing better. When you destroyed military vehicles, killed personnel, destroyed bases, etc. you would gain Chaos and once you reached a certain point you would unlock new items and missions. This worked great because you would end up unlocking things just by ♥♥♥♥ing around. Just Cause 3 however makes you liberate towns and bases, which are mostly just the same thing over and over again. Destroy these buildings, shut down this surveillance system, open this door, free these prisoners, kill there people. Over and over. It's very repetitive. As for Chaos? It's just a meanless stat.
- The rebel drop system is stupid. In JC3 you have to collect flares from rebel bases, and then use those to call in a rebel drop. You have limited flares, but that's ok because you can just get whatever you want for free whenever you want. Right? Wrong, because there's ♥♥♥♥ing WAIT TIMERS. You sometimes have to wait up to 20 minutes before you can drop in a plane again. It's one of the most anti-fun things a developer can do and is often paired with micro transactions that let you reduce the wait, but JC3 doesn't even HAVE microtransactions so the decision makes no sense.
Those are my main issues, but while I'm at it:
- There's no minimap. Why is there no minimap. You can pause the game and look at the map from there to find things buy that's no reason not to have a mini map.
- There's no sprint button. It makes Rico feel really slow in combat because you can't make him run any faster. The devs said that they want you to "use Rico's other movement skills" or whatever but JC2's sprint button was super useful.
- Devs said they wanted to support modders but every patch completely broke most mod. I think there's still some mods that haven't been updated to the latest versions of the game.
- Speaking of patches, there hasn't been one in months. You know what the latest patch was? DLC release. No big fixes. These devs charged us heaps of money for lackluster DLC and the worst part is I was idiotic enough to buy the first one. I'll give them the fact that have a booster on my wingsuit is cool but maybe they could use the extra time spent on DLC fixing the huge bugs in the game? Wait, that doesn't earn them money. Whoops, lol
- WHY DID THEY RE-INVENT THE WHEEL AND BIND LEFT CTRL TO BACK. WHY NOT JUST USE ESC. YOU KNOW, LIKE EVERY OTHER PROGRAM AND GAME EVER PROGRAMMED LIKE EVER. WHY.
TL;DR: Is this game fun? Hell yeah, I have like 70 hours on it. Is it worth full price? ♥♥♥♥ no. Buy Just Cause 2 in the next sale for like $3 and then play it for three years until Just Cause 3 is a similar price. Just Cause 3 could have been great given another year of development. But it's just gonna forever be that game that could have been ♥♥♥♥ing awesome but instead blowed and probably killed the entire franchise. Good job, Avalanche. Next time give the game to a competent development team.
Rant over. Can you tell I'm still salty about a nearly 1 year old release?

RE-TINKERED? Re-HASHED?
In the music industry when a work is re-mastered, it generally means that technologies unnavailable at the time of the original recording are used to clear away the audio artifacts of an analog mastering process and hopefully present a truer version of the artist's work. In other words, it's "cleaned up" and will sound better than it ever has - especially on the new higher fidelity systems available.
What Gearbox implies in their title is that they've done this with a game - whith higher resolution. Same work, by the same artists - just more enjoyable on modern systems.
That's not what happened.
What happened is more like a REMIX. The new artist can't help themselves and attempts to add to the original: to improve it or make it their own. And that's fine under two conditions:
1. The new artist is honest about what's going on
2. The new artist is talented enough to succeed
Neither is the case here.
What we have is a game that's somewhat better to look at, with a host of new bugs, newly broken mechanics, and at least one story breaking bug that stops progression several levels in and has you sitting there in deep space with nothing to do wishing it hand't cost you $34 dollars and many frustrating hours to get there.
I wish I had avoided this one. But the allure of Relic's artistry was too great. If you are reading this and considering the purchase out of a nostalgic memory of what once was I'll say this: playing Gearbox's version of Homeworld is like going back to your home town after four years away at colledge. Many things are familiar, many are jarringly not, and the Home(world) you remember exists only in the past.
It's too bad these hacks don't know their trade.

(March 05, 2016). The game's preview video shows what maximally complex factory and base look like, that you could build in-game. If the idea of building that from the ground up excites you (starting from nothing but a hand pick and some raw materials, then building things and researching technologies), then Factorio is definitely for you. Factorio executes brilliantly on the vision of a building and running a supply chain and factory, in a way that no other game has delivers (see "The Genre", below for related games).
Factorio performs well on Windows 10 in Ultra 4K HD, with UI scale-up. It advertises multiplayer co-op, though I haven't gotten an opportunity to try it.
The game includes a single player tutorial and campaign, following the story of a person who crash-landed on the planet. The beginning of the campaign is a tutorial that teaches you everything you need to know about the game, including UI overlays showing where to click, and what to process. You don't need to be intimidated about the complexity of getting started, since the Tutorial walks you thought it. I highly recommend that players of all skill levels play the tutorial. From there, the campaign proceeds to put the player into a number of scenarios: build a vehicle to search for survivors; recover and improve this abandoned base. The campaign has been a fun campanion to sandbox mode. I have only played a few missions in, so far, as of this review.
You control a single character in a top-down 2D world, who has health and that you must protect. You've crash landed on a planet, and have knowledge of advanced technology, but don't have the raw materials to rebuild yourship. Your character can also assemble machines. Your first step in the world is to harvest some resources yourself, by mining them with your pick or axe. With those basic resources, you assemble mining machines and vehicles to automate the process, as well as weapons to protect yourself.
In Factorio, you build increasingly sophisticated factories and assembly line operations. Initially, your mining machine might output its raw minerals to a crate, such that you ferry them over to the smelter yourself. You might operate that way for a while, until you've completed the research and have the raw materials to build conveyor belts. Then you can run a conveyor belt between the mining machine and your smelter! With the conveyor belt running to the smelter, you can only just begin to keep up with the increasing demands you'll have for increasingly-more-complex finished products. Throughout this time, you're running throughout your base putting coal into your machines by hand.
Eventually, you build an electricity grid to power all your machines from steam engines rather than coal, and increasingly advanced transportation systems for your raw products. There are several types of conveyor belts, going all the way up to trains; you can lay the trail for your supply trains to run alone, to ferry resources from remote locations into your processing plant.
The game arranges all of these processes to feel exciting, satisfying, and incremental. Each step as a meaningful, meaty improvement, that makes you glad for what you've done, but hungry for the next level (of automation, of materials, ...)
The game is not a pure sandbox, and that's a good thing. Your character has a health bar, and can die. (It automatically regenerates if you haven't taken damage for a while. The player has no food or other needs.)
There are other creatures on the planet with you, and they don't like the pollution that your factories produce. You need to defend yourself from them. When they attack, you defend from them largely in Tower Defense fashion. The game provides a variety of defenses, from surrounding yourself with fortified walls, to building automated gun-turrets, or constructing tank vehicles to drive around in. As you expand your operations, you'll be faced with increasingly storng waves of enemies to defend against. This creates some pressure and gives direction to your mining operation. Your goal is to assemble the materials to launch a space ship before being overwhelmed by the horde! Free play sandbox modes are also available. So far, combat appears to occur at just the right frequency to create some tension, but not frequently enough to stop me from relaxing and building too.
For many years I've sought a game that would allow me to build, manage, and update supply chains; to develop and upgrade factories and assembly lines. I tried robotic mining in
with mods and modpacks like
, but it wasn't really polished or a good enough experience to hold me.
is excellent, but it's as much about space flight and flight simulation as building. I've loved
, which is great fun, but it's early access and there's only so much you can do. I tried
, which has a similarly long supply chain, but it was difficult to figure out, and the "random events" made the game "fun" but derailed my construction projects.
is another beatiful and wonderfully fun game that relies on supply chains, but the replay value drops off after several playthroughs (I wish its author would add more content!). If you've enjoyed any of the games I listed above, then you'll probably enjoy Factorio.
I'm now approaching 60 hours playing Factorio, and I'd have to say that I've found my new favorite building game. After that much time, I feel like I've only explored a small piece of the game (in a good way). Factorio is an instant classic for me.

Bought the game from the developer's website almost two years ago after seeing a let's play of it. Needless to say, I got addicted to it rather quickly...
I was pleasantly surprised how fleshed out the game already was back then and, in my opinion at least, it has only gotten better over time. The developers are great, giving status updates and sneak peeks about the things they are working on frequently. I'm seeing more and more devs doing this, involving the community more in the development process, which is awesome.
About the game itself, I never knew making complex production chains could be so much fun. Getting raw resources, refining them and then using those refined resources to make some end product, which, depending on what you are making, might be needed for yet another product. The game starts out simple, but grows in complexity as you need more and more things to make more and more stuff. In the late game, this can get very time consuming, unless you know exactly what you are doing. Whether this is good or bad, I suppose it depends on the person playing. I don't really mind the game being a big timesink, since I often find myself just staring at the production lines I've just made, mesmerised by the inserters moving tirelessly, only to snap back as a small, red icon next to the toolbar starts blinking and everything grinds to a halt. I realise biters are eating away at my power supply, just because I was too occupied with other things and I forgot to make defenses...
All in all, if you like building bases (or factories, in this case), figuring out the ratios to make everything work efficiently and defending all the stuff you make from those pesky aliens, then this game could be for you. If you don't mind spending hours upon hours perfecting your production chains, then this game could definitely be for you.

Sadly it still suffers from trying to shoehorn a pirate game into the M&B engine, with little success. M&B handles land combat wonderfully, but the ship battles are still extremely lacking. I wanted nothing more than for this game to take the place of Age of Pirates 2 (which has it's own flaws) but even being given this "updated" version for free for buying the original, I still regret buying the original. More specifically:
Ship handling is just awkward and unsmooth. It works fine at speed, but when moving slow, the ships twitch and jerk while turning. Visual feedback during combat is lacking. Unless on top of the other ship, it is almost impossible to tell if the shots hit (except for when chain knocks down a sail.)
The ship interfaces are awkward at best and was clearly scabbed onto the existing M&B interface. The town overviews are a nice attempt, but are bland and generic.
As in the M&B games, the ground combat excels and is good fun. Unfortunately ship decks are extremely cramped. While it may be realistic, it leads to fairly frustrating battles of just watching the crews fight because there is no way to get through the mobs to actually do anything.
The overworld map again falls short. Trying to move between locations often left my ship travelling at right angles. Instead of travelling in a straight line to the target, the letter "L" became a common occurance. I haven't moved like that in a game since the old NES days. To make it worse, the times it happened seemed to be frequent and random, but not every time, making it difficult to navigate. On top of that, the overworld map is just ugly. It's stuck in between two worlds. One being a high resolution, high color map, the other being really low quality ship and town icons. They completely clash against the map and the clash is visually hard to stare at.
There are many other issues and the game is unfortunately just fundamentally flawed. I apprecaite their attempt at trying to correct some of the major issues with the original version, this one still isn't really an improvement. Caribbean should have been it's very own game and not built on top of an engine that simply was not designed for it.

WHAT IS THE HUNTER?
The hunter is a simulation game based on real life hunting, it requires patience and it's time consuming but rewarding in the end. there is something about that feeling of stalking your pray knowing that one simple sound may spooke the price buck, but if your quiet and careful a well place shot to a vital organ may kill it instantly and you go home with a trophy or you can miss and track him back again all depends how you aproach the sitation.The world is expansive, lot of walking but fear not aoutowalk option is availive!!, there are a big number of different variaty of animals from a simple mule deer to white tail,brown bears,moose,canadian goose among many others, not to mention weapons like hunting rifles (of course), bows, shotguns, revolvers, special rifles, as well as clothing and hunting tools. truly in an immersice world with a lot in your hands to choose and make your simulation a better experience.
IS IT FREE TO PLAY OR PAY TO WIN?
The game is free to play with its restrictions, currently you can can hunt two animals for free, mule deers and rabbits (male & female), you can roam and explore any map but the animals are restiricted to a membership or hunting permit found at this link.

The Hunter couples gorgeous graphics and immersive sound design to create vast environments that feel real when you step into them, something that other hunting games out there just don’t replicate.
Recent hunting games have been shoe-horning you down corridors while Ibex and Lions jump out onto your shotgun barrel. The Hunter gives you the opportunity to experience the journey, a complete hunting scenario: Listening out for calls, tracking, and observation, not just constantly providing a slurry of beautiful beasts to bludgeon.
I believe the game suffers when informing new comers. I’d recommend checking out the wiki before jumping in as there are some rules for Guest players who haven’t purchased a membership regarding what you can hunt and where. I have all confidence in the Dev team though! They are constantly active and seem to value and utilise feedback. New content is always on the horizon whether it is new gear, weapons, species or reserves to hunt. The game also boasts a strong community to hunt alongside or against in an interesting array of hunting challenges.

A very realistic zombie apocalypse simulator. You play as one of the selectable survivors. Every one of them has the same ability and status. There's no HUD in game so you must relied on your character behavior. He or she may gasp for air when they're low on stamina. The screen will cover with blood, which means you are terribly bleeding. You may notice orange vains start gathering around the screen, and your vision is getting darker and darker......You will become one of the abomination.........unless you got the cure or pills to last. The game featured two main game modes, objective and wave defense. Objective is similar to L4D story mechanic, but much more content. Wave defense let the player defense 1-3 key area in a map within certain amount of waves of enemy (1~11). No matter what the game mode is, finding items around the map and secret within them is the key to survival. Each map is also unique and provides some lore to what could have happen before.........

As a fan of Nintendo's NES Kid Icarus, the art and gameplay of Tower of Flight drew me in right away, as this is exactly the type of game I was hoping to play in the retro style. The flight and fun gameplay especially is appealing to me. Something that is very easy to get the hang up within a minute or less, but has plenty of adventure and fun elements to keep me playing as a fan of adventure action games. The controls are responsive and if I goof up, it's my lack of game play skill that's to blame most of the time. The graphics are nicely drawn sprites, with sharp sound and music.
Only VERY minor complaint in the entire game would be that when your health is near 0, the warning health chimes keep beeping till you get more health. Problem with that, much as in Assassin's Creed 1, is you might go for a long while before getting a health up, so it becomes part of the music and is an unnecessary sound, acting as a constant warning that the player is already likely aware of; get more health! But it's not a deal breaker and once you get your health up, it thankfully disappears. I don't think there's an option to turn it off, but not a big deal consider the rest of the game is great fun.
I wasn't sure how the game saves progress, but thankfully when you contact the winged spheres, once they fly up, you have saved your progress. There are Knights that give you tips if you need them also. To conclude, you gain new abilities and go through many castles and different underwater maps, facing all kinds of fun enemies from fish, butterflies to globs that spit, and more. If you're looking for a fun retro style adventure game, Tower of Flight is an excellent choice.  Really enjoying the game and do not regret my purchase.

RE-TINKERED? Re-HASHED?
In the music industry when a work is re-mastered, it generally means that technologies unnavailable at the time of the original recording are used to clear away the audio artifacts of an analog mastering process and hopefully present a truer version of the artist's work. In other words, it's "cleaned up" and will sound better than it ever has - especially on the new higher fidelity systems available.
What Gearbox implies in their title is that they've done this with a game - whith higher resolution. Same work, by the same artists - just more enjoyable on modern systems.
That's not what happened.
What happened is more like a REMIX. The new artist can't help themselves and attempts to add to the original: to improve it or make it their own. And that's fine under two conditions:
1. The new artist is honest about what's going on
2. The new artist is talented enough to succeed
Neither is the case here.
What we have is a game that's somewhat better to look at, with a host of new bugs, newly broken mechanics, and at least one story breaking bug that stops progression several levels in and has you sitting there in deep space with nothing to do wishing it hand't cost you $34 dollars and many frustrating hours to get there.

This game can be fun. It has a few different race options so you can do an instant race or a career mode. The game also has a multiplayer online that I have not tried out. The graphics look sort of dated. They do not look bad. However they do not have the wow factor either. That being said the tracks you race on are varied and a good mix. Some of the tracks have a lot of elevation and some are more flat with little hills scattered around the track. I also think the intro to each track is very well done. Live action video intermixed with game footage. It looks cool.
I have the game on easy and on easy as you would expect its super easy to come in first in every race. I find that to be a good thing because the handeling is a bit of mystery to me still. You control the bike with left stick and the rider with the right stick. In theory this should make it more interesting in practice I found it to be a mixed bag. My issue with the handeling of the bike is that the rider will sometimes fall for no reason at all. It can be annoying. A turn you think you can make if you lean to the right can cause you to wipe out. So if you do not lean at all you can easily take the corner perhaps because sometimes he will go nuts and crash for no reason. That is very annoying and really hurts the gameplay. It would help if they would have added a meter to let you know what caused the crash and how to avoid crashing in the turns. Something like what Forza and Grid 2 has.  A meter to let the player know if he is leaning to far left or right. It feels like a lot like luck when you can manage a turn.
My other nit pick besides the weird falling down is other riders hitting you and making you crash. Now this looks cool because it can also happen to other computer motorcycles. So that is cool. However the AI racers can be really agressive and can knock you off your bike while they get off scott free. Thats annoying. You can do it to other racers but again its mostly just luck if you pull it out.
My other nit pick is the sound. The game cut me off from sound into my next race and this appears to be a common complaint that just never got fixed. I have my audio settings for stero only. Also the game crashed on me one time however after having played a few more races it has yet to repeat this issue. The sound when it works is very good.
I feel like I should mention one more thing. The tracks have very little life to them. While the tracks look good and are varied their is not a lot that moves on them in the background. I wish the game had more background stuff that moved more. For an example in one race map their is a wind turbine and it looks good but it never moves. So its a mixed bag. If I was rating it I would give it a 7/10. The other thing is the price for $20 dollars I would never buy this as its to expensive for what you get. For the price of $5 to $10 dollars its a lot better looking at this price. I paid 5.
Also this is not an arcade game but more of a lite simulator. You cannot go full bore thru the corners as you will crash out. So you do have to watch the throttle also you can customize your bike for suspension and gear ratios.

TL;DR: great game === great gameplay === in-game graphics options not good and need to use settings in the GPU control panel === highly recommended.
I wasn't really expecting much from this game. I had seen the negative reviews on the "MotoGP 14" game (mainly things that said "stay away from this developer"). However, I chose to ignore this, and I am glad that I did as the game seems pretty good!
Don't use the vsync setting within the game as it will perform "vsync" to 30fps instead of 60fps. Instead, use the vsync settings on your GPU's control panel (remember to set Triple Buffering too for an even smoother vsync). In fact, you should set all of the graphics options (e.g. anti-aliasing) within the GPU control panel also. All of this is based on information provided directly by Milestone on the following Steam forum post:
I was able to set everything to the maximum level and I get smooth 60fps on a twin GTX 980M in SLI.
The beginner option offers a valid challenge for those new to that type of game. Since I am new to motorcycle games, I chose this option and I was pleased with it.
The career mode is reminiscent of Project Cars; the fake social media and the emails from the team. This is a nice touch.
I haven't tried the multiplayer options, so unfortunately I cannot comment.
Overall, I recommend this game wholeheartedly.
Enjoy!

So I wrote a short review of the previous version of this game (Caribbean). This review takes in account the changes to the former version.
That being said, although there were many new changes and additions, I still wouldn't recommend the game. Sure, I enjoy my time in this game, but you have got to be a huge M&B fan and get a hardon from pirates in order to like Blood and Gold.
There are a lot of new mechanics since the game changed its name. For example, setting up an enterprise is made easier and more detailed, going ashore now leaves your boat in the harbor, so you have to go back there to sail again and there are all new sorts of missions.
Still, even though there are many new additions, they all work as well as the main mechanics: not good! I wonder how this studio took everything M&B had, but made it worse. Really, the whole tactical part of battles is glitchy and some options are left out (like ordering your troops to stand closer to each other). Also, general performance, graphics, and small details in the item balance and economy are apparently downgraded. Not to mention the countless bugs.
But I can't stress enough how much fun this game is, if you're willing to look past the initial - mind I say, huge - flaws. It's M&B with pirates and a decent naval battlesystem, very surprising and diverse new missions and the overall feel of being a complete badass as a pirate.
Conclusion? This game or mod if you will, isn't worth twenty bugs due to all the downsides. Still, the mechanics are there and this game is promising. I just hope the developer keeps polishing the game and soon, I'll probably recommend it. For now, stay away from this game unless you know M&B and you know how crappy but incredibly fun the mods can be. Cheers!

Unfortunately Caribbean simply has too many issues to recommend and I'm requesting a refund.
*Frequently crashes and subject to numerous graphical glitches between menus and load screens.
*Load times are extremely long.
*Low frame rate on many maps
*Naval combat has fixed camera making it difficult to aim.
*Ship animations on map are jerky and poorly animated.
*Music often stops completely and there is no ambient sound on map.
There are many free M&B mods that run better, are more polished and simply are more fun than this game.

A very realistic zombie apocalypse simulator. You play as one of the selectable survivors. Every one of them has the same ability and status. There's no HUD in game so you must relied on your character behavior. He or she may gasp for air when they're low on stamina. The screen will cover with blood, which means you are terribly bleeding. You may notice orange vains start gathering around the screen, and your vision is getting darker and darker......You will become one of the abomination.........unless you got the cure or pills to last. The game featured two main game modes, objective and wave defense. Objective is similar to L4D story mechanic, but much more content. Wave defense let the player defense 1-3 key area in a map within certain amount of waves of enemy (1~11). No matter what the game mode is, finding items around the map and secret within them is the key to survival. Each map is also unique and provides some lore to what could have happen before.........
............This game is free.............There are servers with modded maps and more.......

when played on Nightmare difficulty and the best Stealth Horror game I have played so far.
I am a big fan of the very first Alien Movie and this game manages to capture a lot of the atmosphere the movie delivered.
I recommend playing it on the highest difficulty setting on your first play through. You get this feeling of helplessness that to me was core of my gaming experience and reflects what the Alien stands for - beeing the perfect killing machine.
The Gameplay is very solid and controls are easy to manage. The hiding mechanics are well made and a lot of fun to use.
Puzzles are nice and not to hard to solve. The door hacking mechanic is dull and boring on easy and normal difficulty setting but actually very thrilling on hard and nightmare because of the very small time windows you have between the Alien attacks.
The crafting system is a little confusing at first but ultimately not needed once to finish the game - you can easily complete the game without the use of healing items, noise makers or flashlight batteries once on any difficulty.
The story and design of the world fits into the Alien universe and does a very good job merging with the original movie. It is not the best story ever told but gets the job done and offers some cool parts. But do not expect to much.
Sound an leveldesign are flawless and to me the very best this videogame has to offer. Graphics are well made and the high level of detail put into making this game is very much appreciated.
If you get the game for less than 20$ you should definitively check it out you get a very good game for a fair price.
I would NOT recommend buying it for 30$ or more. It is arguable short and does not offer any replay value in my opionion so you are done with the game in 6-13 hours depending on how much you die.

With great pixel art and charming, 8 bit music, Adventure in the Tower of Flight hearkens back to the old school RPGs of yesteryear. Gameplay is decently challenging without becoming too annoying, the items and equipment are satisfying, and the story is enough to keep you interested. However, the story is my biggest criticism. There's not much there, and a bit more being added would make me like this a lot more. The ever-classic rescue of a damsel would have been a superb and fitting addition to this game, one which I would highly recommend adding in a patch to add more depth to the story. But, overall, it's a nostalgic, decently produced game that will take a few hours for a play through, definitely worth the sale price I paid for it, and a fair deal at the regular price, as well. Trading cards are also a huge plus. Recommended.

It's... okay.  If you're a fan of retro platformers, you'll probably like this game.  The problem is, though, that the genre is just oversaturated to the point where a retro platformer needs to really be execeptional or really unique to stand out.  Unfortunately, Adventure in the Tower of Flight doesn't really make itself stand out.
HOWEVER, that isn't to say that it is not fun.
The game is fun enough for what it is.  The two main differences here are 1, you can fly from the beginning and 2, you occasionally pick up upgrades as you go through the game.  It's almost like a metroidvania lite in that aspect, but you don't have an open world to explore like in a metroidvania.  Once you leave a room, the only way to go is forward.
There's also a shop, but it's kinda lame.  You save and you save and you don't get anything really interesting out of it.  Useful, sure, but not interesting.
It's not great but it's not bad, but I think it's better picked up on a sale.

First things first, I bought the game in high hopes. I followed the previous game "Caribbean" and hoped for a good release.
When I saw that Caribbean was gone from the shop, I found, that the game got re-released with a new name etc.
Reading the user reviews and the blog I thought "Lets give it a try". I love the pirate scenario and I loved M&B.
After some hours into the game I reconciled, that it is a bug infested, badly optimized and overpriced mod of the glorious game M&B:
- every time when you go from navigation map to town/fight it lags horrible.
- Often when trying to "go ashore" it crashed without a good explanation "Trying to find a solution".
- (Pathfinding) Most of my fights on land with some indians (outside of missions) ended in a stalemate, because all the indians run into the void (big river, 2 bridges) and my guys tried to shoot em and got speared. Imagine that, trowing a spear from 50m stright up and killing a armored spanish soldier...
- I dont know exactly how many music tracks this game has.. but I found it very repetitive and on other occasions the game was just mute.
- Apparently enemy ships without crew will still shoot at you, maybe the tracking system is a bit off, because when I boarded there was all the time atleast one person fighting me and my crew.
- When visiting a pirate town you get negative affection for a colonial power (very good spies perhaps?)
+ The battles from quests were fine but you cant order your soldiers to stay put or follow.
+ Naval fights were fun but I found my ships often shoot at ghost ships and you cant change ammunition of your fleet.
I refunded this game, because I could and I did not have fun playing. I would not have done that for a early access title!
Unfortunately the devs decided to release all the features without proper fixing, so I would say at the current stage it is a Beta version and not final. @Devs: Maybe take some time to fix all the problems, make adjustments and improvements.
tl:dr
Game is badly optimized, crashes alot, music stinks. Nice naval fights and quests.
Feels a bit unfinished, but its an enjoyable, addictive game. I recommend it!

MXGP - The Official Motocross Videogame is a motocross racing simulation game developed by Milestone S.r.l. In MXGP you start your career as a wildcard and work your way through MX2 and MX1 championships until you can rise to the top of the leaderboard. As you get better and perform well through the season you'll get offers from better teams and you'll have a much wider selection than the handful of teams you can pick as a wildcard. As well as the career mode there's also Instant Race, Grand Prix, Championship, Time Trial and Multiplayer game modes.
+Great graphics
+Realistic physics
+Interesting control scheme (Gamepad) where one stick is used to steer the bike while the other is used to control how your rider is leaning
+You compete against 15 other riders across 14 real tracks
+The 60 riders and 60 bikes featured in the game are all real
+Winning/competing earns you EXP which levels you up, levelling up unlocks new rider portraits and helmets
+In career mode you can skip stages you don't want to play, for example you can go straight to qualifying if you don't want to do any practice laps
+Quite a few different teams, each with their own bike livery and outfit
+Your team sets you goals which you have to complete in order to stay with said team which adds extra challenge to the game
+/-The multiplayer is pretty dead, personally I don't care since I only play Singleplayer in racing games but I know this is a big deal for a lot of people
-The game does not take kindly to Alt+Tab, it will always freeze the game if not your whole PC
-Not a major issue but the mouse can't be used to navigate the menus
-The tutorials only feature Gamepad bindings so they're useless if you wish to play with KB&M
-The KB&M controls are absolutely awful but that's to be expected from a racing game
-The bike sounds aren't great, i.e. they don't sound realistic
Verdict:
Worth Purchasing (7.5/10)
MXGP is a good motocross racing sim with great graphics, realistic physics, an interesting control scheme and licensed bikes, riders and tracks. If you're a fan of motocross or you're interested in getting into it you can't go wrong with this game.

Adventure in the Tower of Flight is a action packed 2D platformer. Your goal is to become the first man ever that climbed the top of the tower, and thus becoming the ruler of all known world. Along the way you will encounter countless monsters, collect thousands of coins and probably die dozens of times.
Developer clearly had a vision of making a true retro experience, and all aspects of the game (especially visuals and sounds) are in the right alignment with that retro vision.
Level design is top-notch and it is a real joy to soar through it. You will find yourself journeying through fire, snow, day and night, and even underwater. It is very diverse, colorful and all together easy on the eye. You can even find numerous hidden passages throughout the tower that will reward you dearly.
Sound is exactly in tune with other aspects of the game and will subtly accompany you through your adventure. Its neither to intense (as in many modern NES clones) nor it is to dim and unappealing.
There is only one thing in the Adventure in the Tower of Flight that is really inexplicably badly made, and that things are the boss fights, with their easy to master patterns and unapealing challanges.
15€ is a bit too much to ask for this game, but if you are a retro console fan, or platformer fan of any kind, you wouldn't want to miss out on this title.

A really well crafted retro platformer that gets right what so many miss when trying to emulate this type of game.  Tight controls and reasonable difficulty means that you want to keep coming back to try that area again and again and if you die, you know it's probably your fault.
This game has influences from several major titles, all of which were gems.  You have an overall feel of Kid Icarus in the level designs and setting.  A flight mechanic similar to Gargoyle's Quest which challenges you to constantly think about how you can squeeze just a little more flight power out of your character to make it to that treasure and sword play straight out of The Legend of Zelda.  Couple that with a spot on 8-bit graphic style and music and you have a game that really has the potential to launch a series of fun adventure platformers.
If you love these types of games, you can't go wrong with this one.  Worth every penny of the asking price.

Adventure in the Tower of Flight review
( Also on
)
In terms of video game releases, there’s usually a drought during the summer season, as publishers are prepping their triple-A titles for a fall/holiday release.
Oddly enough, that doesn’t seem to be case this year. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt eased us into the summer at the end of May; in June, The Elder Scrolls Online came to the PS4 and Xbox One, Final Fantasy XIV received its first major expansion with Heavensward, and finally, Batman: Arkham Knight headlined the month; nothing notable in July besides Deception IV: The Nightmare Princess, God of War III: Remastered, and N++; things pick up again in August with the pair of Sony exclusives Until Dawn and Everybody’s Gone to the Rapture.
With such a busy summer, it’s even stranger,  that I found myself playing Adventure in the Tower of Flight, a debut indie title from developer Pixel Barrage. But hey, just as my appetite for 2D action platformers was satiated with Shovel Knight, it’s been hollow ever since I completed it, and this looked as if it could fill the void.
What is it?
Adventure in the Tower of Flight is a retro-styled 2D action platformer. Assuming the role of Wing, you’re tasked with ascending a tower in search of five relics, with hopes of becoming “ruler of all known land”. Just as in the era of the games it emulates, the story here is bare bones and only serves as a means to get you into the action. Adventure in the Tower of Flight wears its inspirations on its sleeves, and it permeates every aspect of the game, from the visuals, sound, presentation, and most importantly gameplay.
The tower that you’re climbing is split up into different areas (essentially worlds), with their own thematic rooms. The level design is top-notch, as each room is impressively crafted, and makes use of all the screen real estate, both vertically and horizontally.
There are two types of currency (in the form of treasure) to collect throughout the game: gold, represented as coins and jewels, and magic feathers. Treasure may be found on the bodies of dead enemies or hidden behind destructible sections of the environment. The treasure can eventually be spent on a limited variety of items found in various shops scattered throughout the game, but unfortunately, these lack diversity, largely being made up of health refills, extra lives, instant revive bottles.
How does it play?
I’m happy to say, the movement is extremely tight; no momentum on your run speed or slipperiness. As far as jump trajectory, here’s where the main gameplay mechanic comes into play. Just as your name implies, you have the ability to hover in the air for a certain period of time. This is measured by a meter in the upper left corner of the screen; the longer you hold jump, the faster it will deplete. If your timing is impeccable, you’ll be able to remain airborne for as long as you like. With what could’ve been a mere gimmick, it’s used extensively throughout the game, as you are constantly ascending up this tower. Plenty of situations, with tricky platforms and devious enemies, require you to have a mastery of the mechanics in order to proceed.
How’s the presentation?
Out of all the retro-styled games I’ve played in the last few years, and there’s been a lot (far too many actually), Adventure in the Tower of Flight distinguishes itself from the competition, partially due to the restraint the developers show; it succeeds by not doing too much out of the ordinary, so if positioned alongside native NES titles, it wouldn’t look out of place. The models aren’t overdone, showing just the right amount of detail to provide personality and differentiate from each other. Similarly, a familiar palate of primary colors provides the backgrounds with the right blend of diversity and familiarity.
Just as the visuals were carefully created, the sound design is another aspect that harbors the essence of the era. Naturally, being in the constraints of its inspiration, there’s only so much they can do here without overstepping the boundaries they’ve set for themselves. With that being said, the sound design is great. There’s just the right amount of crunchiness and distortion to certain sound effects, and the music is wonderful. The melodies become infectious and each theme has enough breakdowns to never become repetitive.

What didn’t you like?
As my time with the Adventure in the Tower of Flight was thoroughly positive, when I did come across certain parts of the game that soured me, they were more prominent. My biggest issue with the game was the boss battles. For a game that’s so well designed, it was surprising that nearly every boss battle felt uninspired and brainless. Central to the problem was their lack of attack patterns; because of their predictability, they never posed a threat. The only enjoyable boss battle came at the end of the game; by constantly keeping you on the move without a moment of respite, the boss forced you to leverage all your moves in order to survive, resulting in a legitimately difficult and fun fight.
I also had an issue when the game tried to get out of its comfort zone and offer a bit of exploration; it’s very minor, as it only occupies a small percentage of the game, but still worth noting. There’s a point where you come across a small village half-way up the tower, but in order to progress, you need to obtain a key. The problem is that the NPCs are very vague in offering you information on the steps that follow, and there’s no indication of when you actually obtained the item. Yes, I understand that this might be in the same vein as “NES hard” platformers, but it was unnecessarily frustrating.
Unfortunately, retrieving keys to progress through locked doors comes up a few more times after this point, but it’s never as frustrating as it was in the village. When you encounter a locked door, several different rooms are available for you to search through for the key. My primary complaint is that there’s no easy way to determine which door leads to what room or where you’ll wind up exiting from. It seems like an idea that wasn’t fully realized, as if the developers wanted to offer some exploration, but decided against it to keep the game more action oriented. I would be all up for it, if they decided to go that route, but then a mini map would be a necessity.
Final Thoughts
If you need that retro styled 2D action platformer itch to be scratched, I can’t recommend many other games over Adventure in the Tower of Flight. Solid level design, tight controls, wrapped up in a faithful aesthetic and infectious soundtrack go a long way to solidify it as one of the best games in its genre released this year. Just as the era of games it wants to fit in with, its short length (I completed it in about three hours) and four difficulty modes, provide tons of replay value. I must warn you though, at its current price point of $15.00, some might not find the game to worth its price of admission.

After over a year of constant development and facing almost impossible odds, the developers managed to create a good game out of a buggy mess on release without screwing over the people who bought it way back when. They could have taken the money and run like so many independant developers have before them, but they stuck with it. This is clearly a point of passion for the devs and their perseverance should be enough to warrant a purchase.
We need to support good business practices in the games industry, this is an example of that.
Oh, and the game is fun albeit more difficult than Mount and Blade. This isn't artifical difficulty either, it's because Blood and Gold has things that Mount and Blade doesn't that makes a lot more sense in a roleplaying environment.
Example: You get captured by bandits, they take EVERYTHING (put your money in banks), then you have to manually escape by killing guards and making your way to the exit.
My main criticism would be that at the start of the game, there's very little direction. There's no merchant of Praven to set me on my first quest, showing me the extreme basics of the game. This can be offsetting for any new players to the Mount and Blade-style games.
Also, what happened to the pretty world map from the original release of Caribbean? The one that looked like a 17th century painted/drawn map.

It cannot be killed, can hear the slightest sound from half a mile away, and barrels down corridors like a freight train the moment it knows your location with certainty. Run when you should have walked, let your motion tracker beep a few times, or even forget to hold your breath while you hide inside a locker, and you may have sealed your fate.
I played this game on the recommended "Hard" mode. I have played Silent Hill, Resident Evil, and Dead Space, but I have never been this terrified of a game before. This is not a game to be played to relax at the end of the day. You will quit this game each evening feeling relieved that it's over and looking forward to work the next day.

This game is a really fun game, and I easily would recommend it to anyone who enjoys motocross/supercross/offroad racing. Though I do have some negatives too.
-There are not many tracks, and after a while it gets pretty boring.
-The same people win season mode every season... not very exciting.
-The game has reached a point for me where everything is very easy, as I can crash 10 times a race and still win.
-The AI are pretty dumb on some of the courses, or there are ways to cut the track.
-The PS4 version has 22 racers, while PC has 16 racers in one race?
Those are my negatives. Here are my positives.
+There is a actually a season mode, and then a customizable championship mode. This is something I love having in racing games.
+Graphics are nice. Runs perfectly smooth on my little GT 640.
+A much more realistic feel than MX vs ATV, which is something I wanted.
+Still, 16 racers is a lot. I just don't understand why PS4 has more tracks and racers. Some PC's could handle it.
