Before I get into the review I want to address the criticisms of the game's units. There's been a long standing criticism that the game's "rock, paper, scissors" gameplay, where everything has a counter. It appears some people are pretty irritated about that. Well, here's the thing: that's warfare. Look at modern militaries today. Everything has a counter. Infantry carry shoulder fired missile systems to destroy vehicles and hard points to remove those threats. Tanks carry both AP and HE rounds to deal with infantry and vehicles. Aircraft can be shot down like nothing by guided missile and surface to air missile systems. Everything has a counter. The game's system for units is actually the more realistic one, believe it or not. So, I don't understand the gripes about it. Just make sure you've got solid recon and you're fine. It's important to note though that even modern militaries have combined arms forces, so don't think that just because you've got the counter to something that you won't get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked. A well rounded, combined arms force, regardless of its composition, is still a big part of your overall fleet strategy. The next thing I want to address is a big gripe I've seen about fighter strategies. With the hindrance given to fighters in the remastered edition, interceptors no longer play a large role in the battle. They're weaker, and that's also realistic. One thing that should be understood is that air superiority and interceptor aircraft are made for a single purpose: to fight other aircraft. Unless a large ship has no support, there's really no reason why you should be using interceptors to attack a large vessel. The fact of the matter is that you're not going to make a dent in the hull of a ship with a massive superstructure, and a hull designed to both take weapons fire and the force of gravity, in the vacuum of space where a hull breach vents an entire compartment, and possibly an explosive decompression. It just isn't logical to believe that you can make that happen. Historically, the Japanese in world war 2 would run suicide kamikaze attack against a large ship, because that's really the only way a fighter can cause a severe amount of damage against something that big, unless it's carrying bombs. The same goes for any unit in the game, where every unit has a purpose, be it specialized attacks against certain kinds of unit or support for the important vessels in your fleet. But, I digress.
If you're looking for a deeply strategic and tactical space simulation with an excellent storyline and back story (seriously, it's fantastic!), then you've come to the right place. With mods being ported over to the Remastered collection, you won't have to wait long for your replay ability value to skyrocket. It's even better that, as I write this review, the game is discounted for the winter sales. You should already have this game in your steam library. As far as I'm concerned, it's blown games like Sins of a Solar Empire off the planet.

Where the game fails is in my opinion its writing. The writing is shallow, devoid of nuance, black and white and contains a lot of current social justice themes in a preachy way. Unlike in Dishonored 1, very little is left to one's imagination. What was once just an insinuation for the attentive player, is now said explicitly and repeated throughout the game (as the most obvious example the identity of the heart). Emily is a very promising character with no development whatsoever aside from "now I have seen the injustices I used to ignore and I will try to be better". Delilah's motivation as the wronged ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child doesn't work believably. The game can't decide whether she is cruel and sadistic (she is) or if she deserves our pity for being the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child (she does, at least according to the game). The same goes for another bad actor - the serial killer Hypatia. She suffers from a split personality and just like other bad women in the game is presented just as a victim of circumstances. What's more - after she (her sane part) learns about the killing, she has almost no reaction to it! The shallowness of the writing can be seen very well on Anton Sokolov. He lost all his nuance from the previous game. The writers imbued him with a new, interesting topic - old age. But all he does with it is moan how he aches and how he looks forward to dying.
There is also an unpleasant streak of current social justice themes that don't belong in the world and that weren't there in the first game. Emily is a bisexual, at least in English (in German, French and other languages with declined verbs the translators decided to make her a heterosexual). A rich silver baron loves the workers' union in his mines, fulfills their every request (thus precluding their raison d'etre at all) and at your last meeting demands that you strive to create "a more inclusive" society.
With Arkane being located in the USA and with Harvey Smith publicly praising Anita Sarkeesian, I guess this change of tone was inevitable. It makes me fear for their next projects. Arkane has some of the best level and gameplay designers in the world today, but I hope they won't hide their work behind preachy, shallow writing.
And last but not least among my criticism: The voice actors are much blander than in the first game. I loved the English voice acting of Piero Joplin and The Outsider. There is now no one as good as Joplin and The Outsider changed from melancholic to just a normal voice actor.
All in all Dishonored 2 is a good game with rich gameplay, amazing level design and some frustrating writing and voice acting. I recommend the game.

Firstly, it's important to state that this is a *really* fun game. You need to know that before I bring in my criticisms of it. Go through this with a buddy (or a couple of 'em!) and you're going to have a great time, as you plough through enemies and unlock all the different 'bros' along the way. It's a 2D side-scrolling game in the mold of something from the SNES or Megadrive, and you'll die a LOT. Be prepared for that. For a fun co-op experience, this will hit the spot.
Now, all of that being said, this game is incredibly buggy. It's loaded up with glitches galore; from spawning errors, to insta-deaths that aren't supposed to happen, to bosses not even dying properly. The game is littered with issues, and many of them seemed to affect the final two levels as myself and a friend approached the ending. Both of the final bosses died on one of our screens and not the other, glitching out and forcing us to tell each other what was happening on our end. I didn't even get to see the ending of the game, having been greeted with a black screen that simply wouldn't go away. Task manager sorted that problem out but, really, I'm disappointed.
There's such a gem of a game in here, and I absolutely recommend it, but be prepared for a bumpy ride along the way. There are many issues to fix, and the developer(s) does seem to be active on the forum and asking for bug reports, so there's hope for this. It just should be a much more polished experience, which I reckon another six months or so of patching might take it to. Again, recommend as a fun co-op game, but be ready for a wealth of issues to plague that experience.

Isolation successfully managed the one thing that every other Aliens game failed at since 1999, making the Alien a true and terrifying threat worthy of it's origin. And that is even not the only god-awful thing you'll be facing onboard the failing orbital station in your quest for survival.

A solid investment for the argument that "video games can be art." Papers, Please puts you into the shoes of a border patrol police officer tasked with turning up all the fakes trying to enter your glorious country. It's more than that though: you are faced with choices as to how to spend your money (your son gets sick a lot and needs medicine) and there are other factors at play here. The game is quite simple, and the gameplay I found actually quite annoying. How many times do I have to double, or even triple check this document to make sure I haven't made any mistakes? However, if you don't mind immersing yourself Papers, Please offers one of the highest watermarks in simulation stories. I've only scratched the surface since I only got four endings of the 20, but if you're looking for something a little different this is right up your alley.

While I've played document thrillers before like Presumed Guilty or Floor13, Lucas Pope created a quite unique experience with Papers, please!
You are a border checkpoint officer in the fictional pseudo-communist country Arstotzka. Your goal is to process as many entrants as possible per day to earn enough money, pay your bills and keep your family fed and healthy. And while you drown in paperwork the game constantly confronts you with moral dilemmas. It's your choice: will you strictly follow the rules given by a facist arbitrary bureaucracy or will you turn a blind eye to that poor refugee's expired passport? Will you accept bribes or even risk your family's lives by turning against the regime?
I'm not sure if Papers, please! is fun, but it is indeed a 'strangely absorbing experience' and it will make you think about individual responsibility.
One playthrough is about 4hrs... due to multiple endings and an unlockable endless-mode you can extend this time significantly.

Excerpt:
Around this time last year, Total War: Rome II stumbled out of the gate seemingly with its pants down. Despite our rather positive review, we felt that the game wasn't completed to the level we expected it to be: it was buggy, the AI was lackluster, and some advertised features were stripped from the game right before launch (I'm looking at you, defense deployment and political system). However, Creative Assembly has blessed us yet again with the game that should have been: Total War: Rome II - Emperor Edition.
To start out, not too much has changed between Rome II and Emperor Edition aside from the inclusion of a brand new Imperator Augustus campaign that puts you in the middle of the Second Triumvirate with Rome split into four factions vying for control. With the same scale of the original grand campaign, Imperator Augustus is bound to keep you on your toes with further threats of splintering (if you're Roman) and opportunistic wars (for everyone else).
Play as either Marc Antony, Lepidus, Octavian, or Pompey and bring peace to Rome. Or, if you'd like something a little less Latin, the Iceni, Marcomanni, Dacia, Egypt, Parthia, and Armenia are also available for you to enjoy (the last of which is now also available in the grand campaign, alongside Syracuse). With the political system now overhauled, civil war has become a significant factor in large empires--especially if you haven't been watching the generals of other houses closely. The more stable your faction's political situation, the better economic and military bonuses you receive. Finally, political intrigue is viable option, both within and without your fledgling country.
...
Overall, Emperor Edition has reinvigorated my love for Rome II, however much like Empire and Napoleon before it, it stands as a testament to how Creative Assembly should slow down and plug all the holes in their games before launching. I certainly hope they treat the upcoming Attila with the respect it deserves.

This game is a prime example of how not to make a platformer and brawling game. Every platform you can stand on is railroaded in with invisible walls that stop you from making mistakes and learning how to play the game properly - What's going to teach someone to stop mashing the jump button to try and make an "obvious" jump more? Falling to their death, or their character awkwardly stumbling at the edge as if they COULD jump, but won't?
The combat portion of the game is decent in a one-on-one situation or two-on-one situation - you can block, dodge and attack without having to constantly spam crowd control attacks to avoid being killed. Unfortunately, the game doesn't seem to know its own limits and will often throw you into fights with three enemies - or potentially even more. At that point it becomes a battle just to keep yourself alive and avoid bleeding health left right and centre as you're completely surrounded and forced to constantly knock back enemies rather than perform useful attacks.
Another example of terrible battle design is the first boss of the game, at the end of chapter 2 - he has clearly telegraphed attacks, which is good, but if you dodge too early he swivels on the spot to hit you as you get up again. There is no clear point at which it is safe to dodge - which is absurd! Being aimbotted by the AI while they appear to be locked into an animation feels and looks terrible.
Many of the issues with this game can be overcome if you mould yourself into the kind of gamer it wants - one who looks for the next flashing, shiny metal pole or handhold and who doesn't try to explore or try new things, and one who's willing to put in the effort to learn specific attack timings and perfect attacking and dodging even when vastly outnumbered and battling a camera system that often obscures nearly everything useful from view.
I can't imagine there are many gamers out there who are going to be able to fill both shoes at once, and so I find it difficult to think anyone could enjoy this game in its entirety - many will simply persevere for the story.

Brilliant side-scrolling shooter best summarized as "Metal Slug with destructible terrain", and improves on that series in every way other than quality of sprites.
But even that glowing recommendation does not do the game justice: rescuing captives in Metal Slug is of relatively little import, but in Broforce each one is both an extra life and a change of character: hilarious 80s-90s action heroes with pumped up machismo, including "Rambro", "Brominator", "Brolander", etc.
Each Bro plays very differently, as might be expected when they range from a the sword-wielding Bronan to Tank Girl knockoff Tank Bro, who comes with, yes, a tank. As it happens, one of the very few criticisms I have for the game is that some of the bros play so differently that it can be frustrating being forced to change at every death -- it's difficult to practice.
The comedy doesn't end with the bros, either; the story-mode plot is a delightfully pitch-perfect parody of action movie stereotypes.
The strongest recommendation I can give is that when the most recent update was made I thought I'd play a few levels just to see the new characters and I ended up playing through the full game again. It's that good.

If you want an action-packed, fast paced, comical and super epic game, Broforce is the entertainment product for you. A pure shoot 'em up that heavily revolves around strategy so you don't blow yourself up ((which without strategy you will do a lot)) is enough to get your blood pumping, and your brain working. And let's not forget the constant references to classic action movies ranging from Rambo all the way to The Professional, this is the pure action homage. This game will get your epicosity fuel burning and your intelligence level rising as you destroy countless enemies with both constant explosions and well thought out warfare. If you want none of this, you truly are not a Bro.

Honestly, It's been so long since I played Just Cause 2, but even after all these years I still feel like I'm playing the same game, just with prettier explosions, and with a lot of brand new cons:
- Driving controls are terrible, I just forgoed driving completely, especially since wingsuiting is faster.
- Upgrades are locked behind tedious challange missions, the better you do the challange, the more upgrade points you unlock. I absolutely hated this. I wanted to unlock a basic upgrade for my grenades, and in order to do that I had to do these painfully unfun challanges that just frustrated me.
- No dodge-roll or sprinting mechanics. This is one of my biggest issues with this game. You CANNOT just drop sprinting and rolling in a 3rd person action game, especially in one where there's a ton of explosions and gunplay. I can't count how many times I've found myself in a situation where I just instinctively wanted to dodge roll or to sprint, only to find that I didn't even have the option to do so. I suppose the devs wanted us to focus more on using the grappling hook, but that's just such a tedious thing to do when all I want to do is cover a short distance in a quick, cool way. The lack of these two mechanics makes gunplay really boring and awkward.
- Waiting for this game to boot up is a damn chore. The DRM has me waiting at the main menu for about 30-40 seconds, until a window opens up where the game attempts to connect to the servers and verify the files. This discourages me from even starting the game.
- The gameplay just gets repetitive and boring way too quickly. You can only blow up so many choppers and structures before it loses its charm. I haven't even discovered half of the map and I already feel like I'm done playing.
It's a shame, been really looking forward to playing this.
I will say one thing though. Hearing Ezio Auditore's voice actor come back and do the voice of the main protagonist again is just awesome.

Factorio is a wonderful game.  Most games I move on once I've "figured them out", often before fully completing them.  This one has held my attention for much much longer.  Why?
1) It's about building!
2) It's about automating!
Those two are usually enough to get going, but not to stay so long :)
What keeps it going is
1) The right amount of flexilbiity that your factory never turns out the same, even if you use similar patterns.
2) There are many ways to play the game
3) Really good mod community - Want nuclear reactors?  Harder enemies?  Scarier nights?  Planes?  Different kinds of ores?  Or just a new paint job for your train?  All there.
4) Devs that care about quality - fix bugs before features.  The game has always been solidly playable for me as long as I have had it.
5) Devs that think deeply and communicate often - it is good to see some computer science happening back there to make it efficient and work properly across different platforms.  I like computer science.
Never before has a game made me want to quit what I am doing and make my own game.  Or join theirs :-)
11/10 - Bravo, team Factorio!

I've been a fan of this game since it's free beta. It takes a great premise that takes inspiration from real life events that history buffs will enjoy and combines that with gameplay mechanics that seem simple at first that increases in difficulty. The multitasking makes the game challenging enough to keep you entertained, but isn't overwhelming.
The dark atmosphere and "ugliness" of the art style (I say ugly, but it's in a good way) makes the game stand out. The marching soundtrack fits the mood of the dystopian setting perfectly. All around, the style of the whole game truly makes you feel like an impoverished border control agent.
The choices you make throughout the game feel like they matter, and the multple endings are excellent.
This is one of my favorite games and worth every penny, but if you're doubtful, google the free beta and give it a try. The beta and finished product are very similar, save for a few upgrades and an extended story that make the full release well worth it, even if you play the beta all the way through.

Without any of the Add-Ons the game still feels whole however you are reminded that you haven't yet purchased those (in the customisation screen and at fast travel stations) by showing the locations and skins.
The player characters are a bunch of lovable mass murderers who don't contribute to the story but are sure entertaining to listen to commenting the combat.
Insanity rating of the playable characters (from sanest to insanest):
Maya, Axton, Zer0, Gaige, Salvador, Krieg.
The stories self proclaimed hero is Handsome Jack, a sarcastic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with no respect for human life whatsoever who makes you love and hate him at the same time.
The level design is fairly diverse, a glacier at the beginning and later tundra, desert, a bandit stronghold, highlands, an acidic cave, a city and  a volcanic wasteland.
The game also offers a plethora of enemies for you to shoot, stab, pummel, slash, burn, electrocute, corrode, blow up, overrun or accidentally kill while trying to make an exact cut right below the sternum in order to save 'em from Eridium poisoning (latter is possible only once every playthrough)*, namely being: Bandits, four-armed snow monkeys, mouth-defecating canine, more bandits shouting how they wanna buttrape you, midgets, land dwelling octopus-eels, bat-abominations, bat-abominationman,
egineers just trying to defend themselves, robots, flying robots, robots building other robots. I could go. I won't. But I could.
Hordes of unique bosses! I almost forgot to mention the hordes of unique bosses.
Additionally the game contains loads of pop-culture references/easter eggs with Top Gun, Game of Thrones and Dark Souls being just a short selection.
Attention: Do not play this game if you are easily offended it contains high doses of dark humour as well as a crapload of violence.
Few critic points I found:
-Inventory is a bit messy
-Game constantly reminds you of not yet bought DLC (although rather subtlety)

Taking ingredients from both of its predecessors, Demon's Souls and Dark Souls, this sequel refines many of the elements that made those two games special.
The open world remains from its immediate forbear, with added difficulty elements taken from the original game such as the depletion of maximum health and a focus on the central hub.
While it makes improvements in many areas, most notably the combat and the graphical quality of the PC version, it does seem as though compromises were made in the development and execution of the world. It feels disjointed, like a series of levels bound together by generic corridors, and although each level is great in its own right, the world feels inconsistent; this is wholly unlike Dark Souls, whose open world felt lived in and carefully crafted to be believeable as a single entity.
Despite this significant flaw, and some more specific problems with PVP and the prevalence of hacking online, this game comes highly recommended, especially if you are a fan of the first two games. Just don't expect it to be any easier.
If you want a real Challenge, this is the game for you.

Dishonored 2 as a whole is a fabulous expansion of the Dishonored series, and it magnifies the successes of the original game by promoting an array of choices and gameplay options. The boss level takedowns (non-lethally) are innovative and generally unique to the person being taken down such as zapping the mind of the Clockwork inventor Kirin Jindosh, or the disruption of occult powers as with Breanna Ashworth, or the switching of the Duke with his body double. These were unique viable options that were satisfying to the taking down the corrupt evil folks of Karnaca or those who were manipulated by unknown forces. However, in the case of the final boss battle with Delilah Copperspoon, the option to take her down nonlethally felt unsatisfying and tedious to discover and use to take her down. Furthermore, the true downside of DIshonored 2 is the overarching narrative to reach this point and the lack of emotion to drive someone to take the lethal path. In the first Dishonored, you witnessed your Empress get slaughtered before you, and you were thrown in jail for six months for a crime you did not commit, which led the evil doers to throw you under the bus. At the point of your release it felt reasonable to be angry and maybe take the lethal path the game offers to you; however, with Dishonored 2 it felt as if I hardly knew the villains/ people in need of saving (aside from the Duke, Aramis Stilton and Delilah), which is a shame because some of the antagonists were very interesting like Jindosh or Hypatia, whose missions felt like they came too soon or needed some build to them, or Ashworth whose character felt two dimensional. I suppose its difficult for me to phrase as the story in the original Dishonored was much more compelling, but in short the story just feels uninspired in comparison to the first.
Nonetheless, there were some notable characters like Aramis Stilton, who had a great tale and felt almost like one of the characters that was worth saving on every playthrough purely because of the insanity of what had happened to him. In addition, the Duke was another character that really had a personality as he made some of the most interesting speeches on the speakers throughout Karnaca. Also, it was nice to have bosses/targets/important figures, who at their core were not villains at all, like Stilton or Hypatia, who were both trying to do better by the people.   On that note the game had some fabulously crafted levels like the Clockwork Mansion that really forced some interesting choices, or the level about Aramis Stiltons' mansion "A Crack in the Slab", which introduced the concept of time travel that had impacts throughout the rest of the game. In all, I do recommend the game for it's ability to expand upon the lore of the first game and provide a truly unique gameplay experience with some levels that are truly a work of masterful level design; however, do not expect much from the main story to satisfy you as a whole because the ending feels rushed and less engaging than the original Dishonored's ending (though D2 does have a multitude of endings some more compelling but still lackluster) with villains that feel like they needed more expansion or an introduction to understand them.

It's only for that one mission, but it was just such a well-executed game mechanic. Looking forward to the next Dishonored if there will be one.

Sooo... Factorio....
Think of this game as... if Minecrafts Tekkit or Feed the Beast or Tech Mod Packs had a baby with OpenTTD.
Now put that baby on Steroids. You'll probably get something like Factorio.
If that doesn't tell you enough, i don't know what would, to be honest.

Do you like management games? But do you think that management games are too hard? Factorio is a good "in-between" game. Very easy to learn. You will learn the basics of the game within a couple hours. As well as this, the game is very intuitive, making it very easy to spot issues or improve your factory. However, this doesn't mean that you'll get bored once you've fininshed your first "mini-factory". Oh no. You are so wrong.
While this game might be easy to learn, it will take
of hours to master. In fact, you cannot master this game. Everything you build is unique to you. Everyone has their own way to do a specific task. And that is the beauty of it. While incredibly time-consuming (you *will* get very heavily addicted), you can design your factory exactly as you want it. There are a countless number of ways to approach some of the most simple of tasks. Because of this, you will find yourself constantly perfecting your base; constantly finding new and wonderful ways to lay out train stations; constantly discovering new ways to make your already efficient production line even more efficient and more conpact.
To top this all of, I'd just like to mention that the devs are fantastic. They are very active on the Factorio subreddit and do a very good job at banging out experiment update after experiment update. While we are still in the experimental phase of the latest major update, I can honestly say that I, only once, experienced a game-breaking bug. And it was solved
. Brilliant devs making a brilliant game. What more could you ask for.

If you like building, mining and logistics, then Factorio is for you. Upon landing on a human desolate planet, you are tasked with building the industry to conquer this planet.  Using a wide assortment of tools, buildings and science to fulfill you goals. But there is one small bug, the planet you are trying to conquer to feed your ravenous industry is populated by a hostile species of xenos. Thankfully with a little science and good bit of military industry, you can build the tanks and turrets to destroy all that stand in your path.

An amazing game about automation and managing the supply logistics of a futuristic factory on a hostile alien world. The true joy of this game is the sense of accomplishment one gets from setting up machines to build an otherwise complicated item in bulk, often in hundreds and thousands of units. Each step up is practically logarithmic, requiring many resources that get refined and folded back into themselves. It's strange to say, but the closest feeling to pulling this off is when you finally kill a difficult boss in Dark Souls- you are faced with a challenge that seems insurmountable until you chip away at it and figure out the quirks by trial and error, even if it isn't obvious at first.
You will go through 3 phases of thinking with each new challenge: What do I have to do, How do I do it, and How do I do it more better? Factorio will draw you in for hours as you make strides in automation and fix any shortages that crop up from your increased production.
The best TL;DR comes from a Reddit comment: "I have to expand my base to meet the needs of expanding my base".

What I thought I was going to do:
I bought 'Papers, Please' thinking that it was going to be, one of the games on my steam library that I would launch for maybe 30 minutes to get the feel of it, appreciate what they were trying to do, and then close out of it to never open it again.
What actually happened:
Upon opening the game you are greeted with the title bouncing up and down to what I can only assume, is the most communist sounding piece of music ever made by mankind. How this starts is with your character winning the labor lottery, yay? At the beginning of everyday you read the newspaper and depending on what is happening in the world, it will directly affect your game play. But, at the same time, you are an immigration inspector and your job is to control who gets to enter the country. So with rebels and recitalists teeming everywhere, your game play controls the future of the country, so what you do today in the game will heavily affect tomorrow. Aside from general mechanics though, the story is great and at times shocking. The characters have a sense of grit and feel real to the point where you will feel like the bad guy multiple times. And finally, believe it or not, the world is immersive. There are people from other countries and at that desk of yours, no matter whom they are, they are at their most venerable state. Buy this game; seriously, it’s an addictive experience you won’t regret it.
One last note:
This is NOT a point and click. Trust me, some people would like to call it that but there are too many other things going on, and with no clear goal because the game has 20 different endings most people are calling it an 'Adventure Game'.
Have fun!

Enslaved is a game that seems to achieved a status as a 'gem' in current video game culture. Just from reading from some current reviews you'll find descriptions of the game generally covered in positive vocabulary: "a must have", "a moving story", with "characters [...] gorgeous and so unique" and a "mindblowing ending". The game, though, apparently did not get to "make more of an impact" and is now seen as "underrated".
I disagree with every of those statements and in the following would like to briefly explain to you why.
While I don't regret to have played it---because it showed me what earlier works of Ninja Theory ("DMC", "Senua's Sacrifice") and Alex Garland ("Ex-Machina") looked like---I am in awe how the creators of this game turned the compelling set-up that they created in the first chapter further and further into a narrative mess reeking of tropes and clichés.
The story begins with our protagonists both escaping their slavers on an airship that is in the procress of crashlanding. You control 'Monkey' the game's white, bulky and hotheaded appropriation of a mythological chinese figure, and here focalizer of the game's story. In the first moments of the game, Monkey witnesses Trip (our other, more tech-savy protagonist) escape her prisoncell and start an escape from the airship. Monkey by circumstance becomes free shortly after and as the ship is starting to desintegrate and drift into a crashlanding, our male protagonist chases through the halls of the aircraft in search for an escape, always catching a glimpse of his future travelling companion. To establish Trip as another protagonist, we get to see Monkeys hotheaded screams and physical force from her point of view a few times, as the camera looks back from her onto him as her chaser, always seperated by a piece of soundproof glasswork. This ends with Monkey climbing ontop of the last escape pod of the airship that coincidentally Trip already is sitting in. He screams at her to let him climb in, but she again can only make out his gestures through the glass and decides to just eject the capsule, leaving the life of our angry and slightly misunderstood protagonist to fate. The first chapter ends and the next opens with our focalizer awakening alive but slightly groggy from the landing, right next to a silent but visually shaken up Trip. As Monkey is understandably♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at this almost committed manslaughter on his person, he approaches her to uh... express his emotions. She quickly stumbles out of his reach, while in return shouting a command at a headband that now crowns his head. Monkey is suddenly in a lot of pain and has to stop. Our scared but clever female lead had hacked a slaver-headband and put on top of him to protect herself and use Monkey as a tool to get herself home. If anything happens to her, the headband will take his life, a choice that Trip is still processing but for the moment sees as her best bet. Monkey on the other hand did not get a say in the matter, but quickly (and slightly grumpy) agrees to help her. The awkward duo then starts their journey to the west.
I'd say this is a setup that could easily make for a very interesting story about an unlike character duo in which a female protagonist controles a masculine brute and from there it could develop either into an personal exploration of slavery in which the two only half-heartedly work together or even grow to hate each other OR despite the enslavement-circumstances they befriend each other and develop their characters from there---Monkey gets in touch with his emotions and anger problem and Trip could work out the anxieties that lead them into this situation and redeem the sin of enslaving an individuals life for her own benefits.
The game, however, then decides to strip Trip completely from her agency. While she provides a goal for our duo's journey it is mostly Monkey that drives it. Our dude quickly establishes himself as the personification of 'hegemonic masculinity' as he commands her around in gameplay (you actually have an interface for giving her orders) and further shouts at her in most of the cutscenes, because she is emotional, afraid and  overwhelmed with the presence of the murder-robots the two encounter repeatedly. She just lets him walk all over herself, while she actually has the power to kill him or well... remind him of that to make him shut up and calm down. Trip is mostly there to provide Monkey with navigational data and open some pathways for him with her hacking skills. Monkey gets to do the manly stuff, like beating up robots and throwing her soft body around when she can't follow him in his super-human climbing tours. It is also established that Monkey is getting sick of her physical imperfections quickly. In one of the earlier levels he just commands her to hide in a trash container, while he climbs a tower which holds an objective. As he reaches the top she sees her stumbling over the ground at the bottom, to which his response is screaming at her. „Didn't I tell you to stay put?!” It is only shortly after that it is revealed that she is being followed by a giant robot. Monkey reacts by heroicly presenting himself as a target which makes the monster turn towards him and slips into a chasm as it attempts to climb the tower. After Monkey reunites with Trip she falls into his arms, shaken-up, telling him how horrible that experience was, all while the robot is climbing out of the chasm again. As they realize the danger is not yet overcome, protagonist-dude quickly throws his female companion onto his back and makes a run for it. Trip is just repeatedly screaming at him that the robot is chasing them.
This trope here, is just one of many gendered ones that are scattered throughout the story and it ruins any engagement a player might feel with the narrative of the two protagonists. The story becomes focused around Monkey, a character that has no real backstory aside from a few sentences that describe him as something of a lone wolf, drifting around whereever he can/wants to be. The game tries to develop him as a character, to actually feel some emotions towards his female companion, but all interactions between the two are awkward and undermined by the flat, stereotyped characterisations of them both. Because Trip certainly does not make up for her companions alienating bruteness. I have seen a few threads of reactions to her being an annoying and needy character and I got to agree with that - however, while those people aimed their anger at Trip, this is clearly a fault in the game's narrative. Someone wrote these two characters and had not given a second thought to the gendered roles they portray.
To keep the rest a bit shorter:
- All 3-4 other characters in this game are just as flat and underdelevoped as our protagonists.
- The game tries to make love a theme, but fails.
- Other themes like slavery, family, revenge, technology, the demise of the human race and the corresponding apocalypse are all critically underexplored.
- The game mid-way decides to focus on an over-arching narrative that does not get any real information until the epilogue - which is just a longer cutscene.
- Also, it is very bland and mostly leaves you with more questions
- The gameplay consists mostly of climbing (lots of repeated A-presses) and repetitive combat encounters
- You DO get an awesome hoverdisc, but only get to use it in certain restricted areas that narratively speaking does not make any sense whatsoever
I conclude:
Enslaved's story has not really moved me, aside from my emotional reactions to the bad writing.
The characters have terrible and underdeveloped personalities, though I have to admit that both are very attractive.
The end was not able to blow my mind, as I was already dulled by all the terrible writing that came before.
I would not say this game is a must have, though it might be an interesting text to study hegemonic masculinity.
It certainly is not underrated.
This was fun to play through, just don't expect a classic.

First off, lets start this review off by saying that this game caters to a certain "niche" of gamers, a very small one just by looking at all the reviews. My experience with theHunter in free to play mode was great; you start with a .270 hunting rifle w/optic, a "bleet" deer call, GPS, digital camera, binoculars, and the chance to take down as many mule deer as you want. To me this game is a true hunting simulator, you have to track down JUST the mule deer because that is the only tag you have. Just as in real life when you go hunting, you are not able to just walk around and shoot any animal you want. You have to track the specific species of animal for which your tag allows. It seems all the negative review users want is to be able to take every gun and run around shooting every living thing they see in the forest.. You are able to purchase tags for other animals with gm$ (game currency you get from completing missions) and em$ (real money). Tags are one of the few items in the game that are purchaseable with gm$ and em$ which is awesome because you dont need to spend real money to be able to hunt other species (temporarily). After playing 600+ hours of the souls trilogy on console and well on my way too 100+ on PC now, i'd say if you enjoy a game with a respectable challenge, good exploration, optional co-op, and PvP (Player versus Player) in a semi-medieval world... This is the game for you.
The story isn't really the main draw unfortunately, it has a story but a lot of it is left to player interpretation, and if you want to learn more about the story you have to listen to what most NPC's have to say which means hitting "talk" about 5 or more times, and reading a lot of item descriptions, which isn't a problem but if you don't want to put in a little effort to find out the story and just want it explained easily, then you're in for a poor experience.
For new players the game can be rather frustating to get the hang of although it is by far the easiest of the three souls games by a marginable note, mainly when it comes to combat.
That being said the combat in this game is... Unique, the combat in itself is great, I wouldn't say it's perfect because it certianly is not, a number of variables can ruin the combat experience a big one is latency (when it comes to PvP and some co-op that is), a little delay can go a long way in any PvP experience, and as per my experience about 40% of PvP fights, even if it's minor, have some degree of delay or lag that may not get you killed, but can sure be annoying.
The game is fairly long, if it's your first time playing the game and you want to try and grab as much of the items as you can if not all of them, it can take you anywhere from 15 hours if you get the hang of it right away and are breezing through it.
Or, it can take you an upwards of 30+ hours if your taking your time and exploring everywhere, trying out new weapons to find what works best for you, talking to all the NPC's, its by no means a short game. Sure you could do a speedrun but that doesnt determine the length of a game.
Dark souls 2 is also very flexible in what you are able to in terms of your character build, some people will say certain stats are useless and another will say that there are only a few good builds worth using if you want to do PvP or PvE but the honest truth is you can use whatever you want, you can use any weapon and armor matchup that YOU like to use.
So long as you have the skill and tactics you can beat anybody regardless of their build
You're stats aren't set in stone thanks to a new item that allows you to reallocate all your level's you've put into your character so if you find you're dual wield swordsman isn't working out for you, change you're stats to become a greatshield and greatsword wielding tank, or a mage.
My one and only disclaimer I can think of is if you do decide to buy this game, be full aware that you WILL wind up fighting other players online, unless you disconnect yourself from the internet and want to play all by yourself... You WILL be forcefully invaded by another player at some point in the game whether you like it or not, it is a part of the souls series, infact it's a very BIG part of the souls series so if you don't like PvP...
This likely isn't the game for you...
Also if you have a history of breaking your controllers/mice/keyboards/headsets in a rage you may want to stay away from this game as well. ;3
All that said this is my favorite game at this current moment in time, and the souls series is my favorite game series of all time, not for the story but soley for the gameplay. 10/10 but srsly FROM... who da fuq thought soul memory was a good idea for online connectivity... anybody else with me on that?

When I was a tiny child, all I could do was just play the original Homeworld, and I played it every day for hours on end. I finished the campaign maybe only twice, though. On account that I wasn't very good at strategy at the time. When I found out that they made a second game, I also quickly got that one, and played it just as much, although I was never able to finish it at the time. In time, I moved onto other games, and I have long since lost the disks for both of these games.
Every once in a while, I would check up on the status of the IP for the Homeworld series and would always be disappointed when I saw that it was tossed between companies, never to have a third game in the series. However, once I found out that it ended up with Gearbox and that they were going to be doing a remaster, I was ecstatic. At the time, many people were upset with the fact that Gearbox, who don't have a very good reputation with games, ended up with the franchise. I found no reason to doubt how good it would be, though. They would have actually TRIED to ruin a legitimate remaster in order to make it bad.
Once the game came out, I quickly pre-ordered, and discovered that it lived up to expectations. Some parts were lacking, including tactics and some balance issues with multiplayer (to be expected. it's still a beta!) but besides that, the rich story was all the same. It still holds the special place in my heart as my favorite game series ever, and I'm excited to see where Gearbox goes with this next (I'm so excited for Sands of Kharak.)
tl;dr: This game is very good. Please buy it. It's truly a classic and its story is incredibly rich and I recommend it to everyone!

If you liked Borderlands you surely would like this one as well.  Just like the first one it's all about shoot and loot. Literally.
Borderlands combines first person shooter with some rpg elements (upgrading skills). The developer likes to call it a role playing shooter and i think that pretty much covers the game. The art style might not appeal to everyone, as it is cellshaded. It looks a bit cartoony.  I have no problems with it myself, but i can imagine that some people might not like it. The gameplay however just does it. Normally shooters just have a shallow story, character ain't interesting and for most part you just shoot stuff. Borderlands 2 does have a pretty good story, though weird and the characters are interesting. The beginning of the game comes with a bang and you soon will fight your first boss, unlike the first borderlands. In my opinion Borderlands 2 is more difficult then the first one and there are more boss fights. The landscape contains now ice plains, especially at the very beginning. There are new monsters added and you will now find more loot. Some weapons will now drop more frequently, such as the jacobs. In the first borderlands jacobs weapons were somewhat rare. Also, bandit weapons are introduced now and a bandit ride. You can choose from 6 characters this time. 4 vault hunters by default, 2 more are added through dlc's.
It's not all positive though and the game does have it's downsides. The biggest one is the greed from the developer, as they released alot of dlc and tricked people who bought a season pass by releasing dlc that are not part of the pass. Later on they came with the game of the year edition, which contains all 4 dlc that were previously part of the season pass. Not cool from gearbox. Also, the mechromancer was made as seperate dlc, while with the release it was shipped as part of the premiere club dlc. I have a copy myself with the premiere club.
An other thing which i noticed is that bulletin boards this time ain't not much. I have the feeling you get less side missions. Catch a ride is also less frequent. Those are things i miss from the first Borderlands. I find claptrap this time also quite annoying, especially calling you his minion all the time. Too bad you can't shoot him.
Overall it's a good game. Lots to see, lots to loot and lots to shoot.

This game is surprisingly good. I remember hearing about it when it came out, but never tried it until I saw it on sale, and kinda wish I had paid full price. Since it's 7 years old at this point it has a lot of problems a game back then might have, like wonky controls, sketchy camera, and not to mention it's an extremely bad Xbox port. If you have an Xbox controller, play with that instead of the keyboard/mouse. But it's so late now it's hard to complain about those issues, and the story is really worth dealing with them for.
I also remember back in 2010 people would trash any game that was linear. Never did I think, even then, that I would miss extremely linear games with boss fights, a health bar, and chapter-by-chapter story telling. Some developers claim people don't want linear games anymore, but I have a feeling those developers mean people only want good linear games. Luckily this is one of them, and is way worth playing.

It was the best of times (cutscenes, characters, writing), it was the worst of times (bad console port/gameplay). Watching two thirds of the game's cutscenes on youtube was much more fun than anything I experienced in the game. While watching, I never once wanted to start the game and play through the parts between the cutscenes, but instead felt relieved that I could continue enjoying the good stuff without ever having to work for it.
I never want to use the word "work" when I'm talking about games, because games are supposed to be fun. They can be a learning experience and you might struggle with some parts, but they're not supposed to feel like chores. The basic gameplay here was so tedious that I quit 1/3 of the way.
The game was obviously not ported very well to PC - no rebindable keys, camera/controls a bit wonky, showing gamepad button prompts when using keyboard etc. I had to look up lots of info that should have been easily accessible in the game.
If the basic gameplay had at least been enjoyable I could have endured through it (yes, *endured*, not enjoyed), but I have better things to do with my spare time and much better games in my backlog.
If you look at some gameplay videos and see something you like, then perhaps this is a game for you. It was a much better movie than it ever was a game and that's about the worst thing I can say for something with so much effort put into it.

This game has had a pretty notorious reputation not long after it was announced in the early 2000's. It underwent numerous different designs, names, and builds before finally getting released in late 2007. Even then, some felt that the game was still a rushed beta, and honestly it was. It wasn't until several patches that the game was decently stable. However to many people, the game's now-trademark atmosphere, brutal gameplay and unforgiving gameplay environment were enough to leave the game permanently ingrained in gamer's minds across the globe.
Flash forward to 2013, and this game still has a devoted modding community who are regularly working on and releasing ambitious new total conversions, weapon packs, gameplay tweaks and even restorations of previously-cut content.
This game must be experienced first-hand. Even the base 2007 game is still good today, though the game truly shines once one ventures out and starts downloading various mods that make the game several orders of magnitude better. This reviewer here prefers 'Oblivion Lost 2.2', which is based on a previous version of the game -- it restores many gameplay concepts and features that were left out for reasons unknown. It adds in more weapons, more suits, creatures, improved graphics, smoother performance, vehicles, and even free-play. It also adds in complete A-Life, which is unlocked after a player beats the game with the best ending, where every STALKER in the Zone begins to operately totally freely, which can open up many unique scenarios which no two players will experience the same.
The story is fairly gripping, though players expecting constant cutscenes and characters who never shut up will be disappointed. The story is told primarily through notes left in PDA's and some interactions with other humans face-to-face, though the few cutscenes there are do a wonderful job of contributing to the haunting atmosphere the game promotes.
The gameplay is tough and unforgiving -- this game isn't for the noobs out there. You won't be charging at enemies doing 1080-degree backflips while going for no-scopes here. You have to pick your shots and battles carefully. Sometimes it's better to flee than fight, or use stealth to completely dodge enemies (or ambush them to take their loot!)
STALKER in essence is an FPSRPG. You've got the traditional first-person shooter gameplay, combined with an inventory system, a stats system for both weapons and equipment, the latter of which directly affects the player's endurance and performance, quests, NPC's to interact with, and a fully dynamic open world that is constantly alive.
The harsh environment, dubbed "The Zone", is as much a challenge as the humans and mutants you must deal with on a daily basis. Due to the events which took place prior to the game, the Zone has changed drastically, and there are mutant creatures and "anomalies" scattered everywhere. Careless players will go on raids without enough equipment, or foolishly walk through dark areas without watching their step, only to find themselves getting insta-gibbed by an anomaly.
The A.I. is nothing to snicker at either, and they get even tougher if you play with most mods. Don't be surprised to be in a firefight with someone, only to lose track of them and then have them sneak up behind you and offload half a magazine into the back of your skull.
Shadow of Chernobyl also boasts a pretty barebones multiplayer component, but in all honesty, this pales in comparison to the single-player experience, which is a shame. It can be fun for a little while, but several gameplay decisions quickly make it evident that it's easy to become overpowered against other players, making the experience very un-STALKER like.
All in all, this game is worth the asking price, even years later. Buy this damned game, it's worth it.

**EDIT**
Having played this a lot more now, I'm going to write a half decent review.
Firstly, I will go onto the base game. As you can see the game is officially licensed, and as such contains most if not all riders, teams, and tracks of the Motocross Grand Prix. Bike sounds (MX2 and MX1) and physics have been faithfully re-created (I'm playing with 'pro' physics enabled) as have the decals and gear etc. The game plays very well, and any fan of the late MX vs ATV games will feel right at home with this having had to deal with the goon riding of 'Alive' (Although Reflex was outstanding imo).
The career mode is basic yet very enjoyable. You begin your career as a wild card rider in MX2 for one of the lesser known teams, and compete in various GP's all over the world on the very well re-created tracks. By earning points and beating rival riders, you become more established and begin to attract fans and offers from various teams. Your team will set you goals of how many points you need to achieve, although failing to do so repeatedly apparently sees you losing your contract with that team (I've not had this yet). Bigger and better teams such as KTM/RedBull, Honda, Suzuki/Rockstar etc have more demanding goals than the smaller teams, and require you do maintain at least a top 3 position throughout the season. Doing well enough you can either transistion up to MX1 (Where the bikes are considerable more powerful and harder to handle) or choose to stay at MX2... The choice is all yours.
In terms of gameplay it plays very well. I'm currently running at max graphics and audio setting playing with a Windows Xbox 360 controller, and the game recognised it immedietly (no controller mapping required) so I can't comment on what a keyboard plays like. Rider animations are extremely diverse/dynamic and feel very life-like so it's all good in that department! The graphics are very good, although some people may notice a few crappy textures here and there, but rest assured the level of detail on the rider gear, bikes, tracks etc is more than pleasing. You can scrub too, nuff said.
The game did receive a few poor reviews which I think (upon actually playing the game) were very unfair. Most reviewers we're expecting an arcade style racer and based they're reviews upon that assumption. So don't knock this one MX fans, this is I think the most fun MX game I have played in recent years! (I've played most too). And to play on real tracksa with fully licensed bikes and sponsors is a nice treat too.
Now on to customisation, which is what most people like these days. You are free to choose the manufacturer of your bike, all the nice toys are there (Yamaha, Honda, KTM, Suzuki, Kawasaki, TMRacing). However, different teams use different bikes, so as offers come your way be sure to check the model of the bike before you decide what team you're going to sign with! (You get multiple chances to change anyway). You can choose from 12 (I think??) set helmets which come with preset goggles, your rider gear is determined by which team you are signed with. As far as boots go, I have no idea. The AI in the game sport boots by Alpinestars, Gearne, Fox etc so I'm not sure why the custom rider is stuck with Sidi boots! As usual you can pick a name and number, as long as that number isn't in use by one of the pro riders in the game. Most players will be pleased however, as there are a lot of teams to choose from all with unique gear so that should satisfy most players.
In terms of expansion, I see a lot of possibilities. I see most people asking for 2 Stroke bikes, but any real fan of the MXGP would know that they do not race 2 Stroke bikes in the MXGP, only 4 Stroke. Again, they're going for authenticity here guys. I would like to see more tracks added to the game, be they fictional or from other parts of the world (Glen Helen anyone?), or maybe even a track-editor so people can create and share tracks. Who knows.
Anyway, I hope this review helps. I'm overall very pleased with the game as I haven't had a decent MX game to play since I got insanely bored with Reflex (too many hours, lol) so this is a breathe of fresh air. Happy racing dudes!

I'm a big fan of survival horror games and i must say this game is absolutely amazing. The graphics are superb and the engine is very well optimized. The butter smooth framerates combined with this very highly detailed and dynamic world makes for a very immersive experience, which is crucial for games of this genre. The fully dynamic and volumetric lighting helps a lot to capture the atmosphere of the movie, too.
The game is very well ballanced in terms of switching between feeling powerful and powerless. At certain times during the game you are very powerless, and are forced to be clever and at other times you can feel safe in certain areas, where you can relax and take your time to solve puzzles or explore the world around you.
You are slowly introduced to new game mechanics throughout the game, in favor of having a "tutorial mission", which is a big plus in my book.
The A.I. in this game is extremely good. It's very satisfying to use the alien to your advantage in order to kill other enemies on your path. The A.I. feels very realistic and unpredictable. The Alien surprised me a LOT of times. Whenever you think you have found a brilliant safe-spot, the alien will eventually pull you out of there in a very well animated way... Any sound you or your motion detector make will be heard in one way or another, and will trigger a very realistic response depending on the enemy.
The crafting mechanics are simple, and i'm really glad that they are. I see other reviewers complain about it, but i actually really liked it's minimalism. I wouldn't want to spend too much time on crafting items anyway.
The game could really use some better facial animations. Not because they are bad, but because the rest of the game is ultra-realistic compared to the facial animations. The NPC's don't make proper eye contact with the player, and it makes conversations rather artificial and impersonal. The faces seem too static and unemotional. Animation in general is superb though.
The game was sometimes a bit unforgiving. Sometimes your death feels very unfair. The times when this occured, it didn't bother me all that much because i actually really enjoyed replaying certain parts of the game, as there are multiple ways to approach certain situations.
I have mixed feelings about the saving system. Part of me would really like to save the game at any given moment, but on the other hand i realize that would take away an important element in this game...
I rarely buy games at this high price point, but i must say this game is VERY well worth it... The price reflects the quality of this game very well. And the game is definetly long enough.
The Linux support was a big plus for me, as it is my main platform. I was worried performance would be bad on my GTX 670, as it doesn't meet the recommended specs on Linux, but it turned out to run very well. I feel like maybe the required specs for Linux/SteamOS are a bit overestimated.

3: Altough it's rare (and therefore merely a theory of my own): If you enter a room,it looks for you  in that room and doesn't find you. It memorises the layout of objects in that room. Note: I'm reviewing this game on patch 1.6. It has to be mentioned that this game had a very bad launch and it was the reason i haven't bought this game right after its release.
Creative Assembly shows once again that they are making best grand strategy games there are available on market. Despite Rome II not being a perfect product it introduces some of the best mechanics I have seen in this series so far.
Keeping the public order in the cities is finally done well. We have counter for order which shows a range form 100 to -100 and gives plenty of time to react before the riots start. Public order may drop at the rate of -50 as well as -1 and many variables determine the rate in which you will lose or gain public order.
Another cool mechanic are edicts. Cities in rome create provinces. Each province may have 2 to 4 cities including one big city and settlements. If you own all cities you may order a special edict in the province which gives you extra benefits like more food or lower cost of army.
The armies in rome have different movement types. You can move your army faster exposing yourself to enemy ambush or you can move slowly setting up defences whenever you stop. I think this mechanic needs a litle more corrections, like you should move faster than the enemy on your territory, but overall its another step forward.
In terms of combat the game is very good, offering you a good variety of units. In my opinion land combat is better than it was in shogun 2, where basic unit was a anti cavalry unit. Unfortunately naval combat in rome 2 is boring and comes down to ramming enemy ships. Too bad cause another interesting mechanic was introduced here, splitting the army into war ships and transporting ships depending on what army you are fighting with. NOTE: The combat is not well balanced. Some units like pikemen are totally overpowered which in my opinion is not that of a big issue. Historicaly some factions had better armies, however it could have been reflected in costs of those units especially in multiplayer.
Overall the game is another very good total war game which i definitely recommend. I hope that all of these new mechanics will be kept and further developed by Creative Assembly. In my opinion this game scores 8/10.

SC were absentee developers. In this sense, that's a good thing. Throughout playing any of the three Stalker games, it's difficult to feel like their attention is ever really on you. Instead it's on organising a hillside scuffle between the dog-things and those boar-things. Or orchestrating some skirmish between two gangs of Stalkers, or maybe some bandits. Or swirling up some horrendous, travelling anomaly, that will pull you into a whirlwind of radiation and wind, before flaying you alive. But it wasn't created for you - you just happened to be the dummy that walked into it. Idiot.
It's a world that exists despite you, rather than because of you. In an industry where a game like Skyrim has enough stuff for you to stumble across and trigger to distract you into thinking this is a living, breathing world, GSC actually managed to do it, for the most part. - Eurogamer.

Believe it or not, I used to actually be a fan of motocross sports. That said, I expected to enjoy this title, but it failed to impress. There's simply too many flaws for it to be enjoyable (mostly technical, however).
Don't get me wrong, the game has several good points, and the gameplay itself is rather fun, it just has far too many technical flaws. For one, the game's Vsync is broken. I have a 60Hz monitor, but the game chose to run at 30fps instead. I noticed that others had this problem and ended up disabling this Vsync, which led to framerates of ~200 and some very nice screen tearing. I did solve this by using AMD's control panel, but I shouldn't have had to take that extra step.
The game also had several sound issues. A lot of sounds weren't even implemented (really noticeable when your bike goes airborne) and the bikes sounds that were implemented just didn't sound right. I know what these bikes sound like and this just isn't it. Oh, and the game's online service? Broken. Tried three times over three days to play with a friend of mine and it couldn't hold a session for more than a minute. Very disappointing. At least the singleplayer is good?
Other than that, the game actually has some nice gameplay. The feedback and all is great and the bikes are easy to control (if you know how to). The game could have been much better had its flaws been fixed prior to release, however.

I've played a little of the remastered version, got it free with the preorder for the Desert of Kharak game coming in Jan 2016. It seems to remain true to the original game in as much as possible, however a few things of note.
It is fairly silly how easy things like standard corvettes are to capture, in the original, you would be very lucky to have captured even one standard corvette from the turanic raiders. But it is not directly limited to the raiders, any fast strikecraft can be captured without any trouble at all. i cleaned out the taiidan and or  turanic raiders entire supply of fighters and corvettes without any trouble at all with the exception to defenders and assault frigates in one place, that can chew up and spit out the corvettes without issue. other then that, i had mostly an alien line up of fighters and corvettes to play with in the early missions and then frigates, destroyers and a carrier later on.
On the return to Kharak, i noticed that the assault frigate capture had two problems with it in the remastered version; there are one too many frigates which means you can easily lose all the trays within minutes. and number two on the list is when you captured the first assault frigate from the taiidan, the rest that you captured do not show up, so it makes the effort to try completely worthless. in the original you had anything from 3 to 5 frigates by random attack the trays and you get to keep all but one of the frigates you captured.
I have yet to pass beyond the mission with the mothership passing through the asteroid belt, but i already know whats ahead because i used to play the original quite a bit.
Aside from the capture of ships which is very easy to do. the overall feel of the game is still very much in the remastered version and thats important because that was what made the original worth playing; the amount of time you spend between missions. The Graphics are a step up from the original and in the right direction, but the Kharak sequence could use another going over when the taiidan arrive during the cinematics.
The formation system doesn't work and there is no priority on targets, in the original you had scouts in x formation on aggressive, they all fired on the same target and got more shots in while being slow enough to destroy one target and then move to another, usually when enough targets were destroyed the scout wing could destroy the rest without needing to make another run at any of the others. in this version each scout has its own target and breaks formation. So in reality, tactics and formation do not mean anything like it used to in the original. I mean pounding away with a group of interceptors on sphere formation and defensive tactics on an enemy destroyer on the original was one of the games defining moments.
The audio is much better, lots of issues in the cinematics and such were cleared out, also noted a few additional voiced bits that were not in the original game.
initial first impressions are fairly good and so is the the recommendation, that could change later on when going through more of the game.
Edit 1: I have played upto The Graveyard, i have noted two fairly interesting things.
The AI could do with an inprovement to enemy detection and action taken. an example would be mission 12, an enemy carrier with a whole load of vettes and fighters and a few frigates, the AI don't even notice you on top of it until you fire, by then it is far too late for the AI when you can deploy a g-well, over a dozen assault frigates, and various cap ships and then later on strikecraft when the g'well has had it's moment.
Finally, when you capture ships from frigate size upward from the taiidan, the color scheme and decals change from mission to mission, one you could be in mission 10 where a captured HC is yellow and red with the usual taiidan white decal, next thing you notice on mission 11 is the standard kushan blue and while with kushan decal and then mission 12 with the black and white HC with red taiidan decal. there should be some uniform ship paint job and decal over the campaign.
Edit 2: The tactical map display on some of the later maps makes seeing things impossible especially with that yellow disc on it, for example super nova research station was fairly hard to find the dust passages and the mission before that, finding resources was impossible.
Second to final mission depends on the amount of stuff you have stolen over the duration of the game from the enemy and carried into mission 15, if you are like me and had full fighters, vettes, 145 frigates, 16 cap ships (4 HC, 9 destroyers, 3 carriers). the nemy will be deployed with hundres of fighters, vettes and frigates, with a handful of destroyers. The final mission could do with more time in QA, the design of the map with such numbers on your side makes actually trying to survive the engagement completely impossible. by the time i can get enough frigates together to try destroy the enemy frigate group coming up i would of already lost the mothership. with increasing numbers, it feels as if the taiidan frigate group should be further out, the same with the warp in group lead by a HC. in the original it was like that.
As it stands i am unable to complete the final mission. so just becareful of capturing great numbers of enemies for later missions.
Edit 3: After stating having to know what is coming before you, i had to roll back to mission 15 and do a few things differently which turned mission 16 on it's head, made it a lot more easier. it was completed.
Heading into Homeworld 2 RM and one issue is immediately apparent, repairing and rebuilding strike craft, it repairs the strikecraft but it does not add new fighters on a bomber wing or an inceptor wing or a gunship wing for example. it means that the forces you can use on your enemy could be significantly diminished if most of your fighter groups contain 1 or 2 fighters each.

I want to love and praise Alien: Isolation because it is one of few really good, innovative and well made licenced games. Unfortunately it really overstays it's welcome.
Exellent use of the Alien franchise is an awesome thing but at the same time it feels like a curse. It takes a long time to actually see the Alien but because of the movies you know from the beginning  who the enemy is, what it looks like and how it behaves. I felt like i have to see how the thing is animated and when i did, it was like "Nice! Well, now what?". The sci-fi world of alien with it's old looking "high-tech" machines, smoke and darkness on the other hand never gets old. Moving around in the dark halls knowing that the alien is in the wents lurking is when the game scares the crap out of you.
I liked how alien the alien is to the surroundings it is in. Sure it moves around with ease but it is totally it's own thing from the rest. This game would work with just human and android enemies. Or it would work with just the alien. When there are both enemies present it feels like playing two different sneaking games at the same time. "I have to avoid this enemy's line of sight but do so in a way that the other enemy doesn't hear me." Good stuff.
It is of course for the sake of it being a game and you playing the protagonist that the alien spends a lot of time around you. That does get really repetetive after a while especially since you know that Sevastopol is a large station and that there are other humans who are not staying nearly as silent as you are. Go bother someone else for a change!
After you meet the Alien and get killed a few times the actual scariness almost gone. First of all the alien moves in a bit weird fashion. It's like the AI is making calculations of what to do next but the animation cannot always adjust to it. Sometimes it just changes directions without any sense of weight or drops down from a vent and immediately climbs back up. It might also come so close to whatever closet you are hiding in that it's head comes through the door. The Alien is an amazing piece of AI, animation and art but the less you see of it the better. Playing is still extremely intense  because you can only save at savepoints which are far apart. The Alien is really unpredicable and so any extra noise, mistake or just randomness can erase 15 minutes worth of gameplay. The thought of that is scarier than actually getting killed since you can choose if you want to see the death or not: You can always hammer the esc key faster than the Alien can kill you.
Alien: Isolation is set up to do one thing in one specific universe and it succeeds almost flawlessly. Graphics, atmosphere, sound, and everything else is really good. Was it a good Alien experience? Yes! No other game even comes close.
Was it a good gameplay experience? I'm not so sure about that. Sneaking in a new area  for the first time is great but 2nd and 3rd attempts are really tedious. Much worse than any other sneaking game. It feels like you can't "earn" freedom from the Alien. No matter how sneaky you are or how close call you escaped, it will be back in two seconds. It will force you into same closet 4 times for no apparent reason before you get to another room and repeat. It doesn't take long to learn the noises it makes and think "Not this crap again".
If the Alien were a creature that tried to hunt, eat and survive and you only saw it few times then Alien: Isolation would be the best thing ever. Unfortunately it is a creature that tries to entertain and serve a plot and does so way too often. There is a mod that disables the Alien AI. Around the 5 hour mark you understand why someone made it.
In the end it comes to two questions. Are you the kind of person who doesn't mind leaving a game unfinished and is the price right for 3-4 hours of entertainment? If you say yes to both, then get Alien: Isolation! Those few hours will be awesome!

Dishonored 2 is an excellent 'Stealth-action immersive sim'; slightly better than its predecessor with regards to the overall open-ended gameplay, visuals (especially the lighting and that gorgeous water), and level design. The city of Karnaca is brought to life with impeccable attention to detail to the point where, like Dunwall in the first game, it feels like an actual character as apposed to being just a setting. Some may find that the art direction is not quite as good as the first game depending on personal preference; however it is undoubtedly brilliant in many places.
The game's story on the other hand, is a rather big let down. While it's predecessor's story was nothing particularly groundbreaking to begin with, I found that game's supporting cast of characters to be alot more interesting and the lore & world building seemed to lend a greater sense of mystery and intrigue that helped to enhance the story. The most interesting parts of the original's story were sometimes what you didn't see or what was rather suggestive or implied instead of being explicitly spelled out. While this still holds true to some degree in the sequel, it often relies too heavily on expository dialogue, which can be downright cringe-worthy. I think it may have been the writer's intention to capture a similar noir like feeling of "Knife of Dunwall" & "The Brigmore Witches" with regards to the much stronger dialogue of the character "Daud", voice acted by the wonderful Michael Madsen; but it is a big misstep in this sequel where more restraint should have been exercised.
The game is (or was) diminished further by Arkane's choice to use "VOID", a highly modified version of Bethesda's in-house Id Tech 5 engine notorious for performance related issues. While Arkane have released several patches which have 'mostly' rectified the poor performance I initially had, it's worth noting that to this day there are still some that continue to suffer relatively low FPS and frame pacing issues, even on high-end setups. I would urge some caution if you are thinking of purchasing the game for PC. Try the demo first and maybe do some research in relation to your own hardware configuration.
Overall I had a blast with Dishonored 2. Even with all its pitfalls, it is still leagues ahead of many so called AAA titles on the market with their insidous micro-transactions and glorified gambling in the form of loot-boxes. It's a worthwhile, if flawed, entry in the 'immersive sim' genre and definitely a must play for fans of first game.

(mini-review)
Call of Duty Advanced Warfare continues the Call of Duty series' decline into mediocrity. While most of the previous games in the CoD franchise have all had some sort of exceptional plot twist to validate the singleplayer campaign and gratify gamers, this title has no such blessing. When combined with a predictable villain, rote and obvious plot elements and poor characterization, CoD Advanced Warfare probably has one of the worst campaigns in franchise history. In exchange, gamers are provided with advanced doo dads that exceed the technology in BO II, including the much hyped exosuits. Unfortunately, the exosuits just comes across as a desperate attempt at milking Respawn Entertainment's Titanfall success. Not only does the exosuit fail to truly impact the game in the campaign, but it actually impairs the multiplayer, as most maps are built far too small and cramped to accommodate such tools. With a mediocre campaign and a comparatively weak multiplayer outing the game's only saving grace is its dramatically rebuilt graphics engine which produces fantastic visuals. Performance is also good with minimal crashes, glitches or errors.
Still, a prettier but more vapid CoD is a game that was asked for by no one, ever. The title is worth picking up on the cheap if you can but isn't worth more than 10-15 bucks.
***addendum*** While multiplayer was lively for about 1 year after the game's release, the online play is now effectively dead.  I can't really recommend a game that pushed a medicre campaign and staid, expiring multiplayer for over 60 dollars USD. ***
