Gameplay: you use weapons in both hands.  You can mix and match: shields, swords, chimes, staves; 2 hand: great weapons.  As you level up you gain about 10 different stats that effect a multitude of different attributes.
There are 2 mechanics called invading and summoning where other players can enter your game.  Invading allows you to invade others games to try to kill them and others can invade your game to try and kill you.  You can summon people to help you to fight off invaders or just fight the bosses.
The world is connected and as you explore you can teleport back to different areas via the bonfire.  The bonfire system is where you level up.  As you use a bonfire though all of your enemies (besides bosses) respawn.  The world is varied and has different locations that are great to explore.
There are a bunch of different covenants that expand the gameplay and allow you to go on a different paths.  You can join all of them.  There is a NG+ and ++++++++ if you want.

What's disappointing is that the game consists of many different 4 strokes, but not a single 2 stroke. Fair enough that during the 2013 MXGP season there weren't any 2 strokes competing, but you've still got to give people the option to ride one. Maybe during rider customisation there could be a choice to make your own bike, and that's where the 2 stroke could come in, but we don't even have the option for that. The game gives many hours of gameplay, online and offline, and there's many different tracks and bikes to choose from. TL:DR:  8/10
I pre-ordered Total War Rome II but only just started playing the game due to the amount of negative backlash levied at the game from launch. Now I have finally started to play the game and I have really enjoyed it - but I should note that I am not playing the purely "vanilla" version of Rome II. After much reading I decided to download Toons' "All in One Mod" for Rome II and it is really good. So please note that my subsequent comments are coloured by having played the mod.
Rome II does some things really well compared to previous Total War games (of which I have played most of them). I really like how the Auto Resolve for battles has been addressed, whereby it shows you the likelihood of victory based on the battle stance you take (aggressive, balanced, defensive) and also the percentage of troops you will have left for each choice.
The enemy AI is also well balanced and fights well in the field battles as well as on the diplomatic side of things. I really liked the addition of the Pros and Cons listed by each faction for why they like or dislike your nation. This made it much simpler to determine why they might reject an offer as opposed to past TW games where it was infuriating to be rejected and not understand why.
Having naval support during battles is a nice touch also and builds upon the naval warfare introduced in Empire, even if it's still quite clunky at times.
The Spies and Heroes/Champions are also much better designed in this game than the previous Rome and Empire. Now you can assign perks to the individual agents and level them up as you desire. I remember thinking in Empire "What is the point of the spy! His chances of assassinating someone is barely 20%!" Now I have used them to great effect in weakening cities, garrisons and travelling armies. A great improvement all round!
There is also much more opportunities to conduct war in the political arena with assassinations and securing promotions etc. This has been greatly expanded from Empire and the previous Rome and adds a broader dimension to the game.
One thing that I don't like so much is the way armies can be split and travel. It is impossible (as far as I can see) to transport troops from one army to another unless the General travels with them in tow. This may well be more thematic but I feel that it hinders the game play a bit.
I also completely disagree with CA's decision to make this such a DLC heavy title/franchise. Some additional campaigns and so on are fine as added DLC to me but adding a Blood and Gore mode and other minor aesthetic changes that were already in the game files and just required "activation" is ridiculous. Companies need to stop selling us half-completed games!
But all in all I thoroughly recommend Rome II - especially if you seek out a mod like I did.

I felt like i have to see how the thing is animated and when i did, it was like "Nice! Well, now what?". The sci-fi world of alien with it's old looking "high-tech" machines, smoke and darkness on the other hand never gets old. Moving around in the dark halls knowing that the alien is in the wents lurking is when the game scares the crap out of you.
I liked how alien the alien is to the surroundings it is in. Sure it moves around with ease but it is totally it's own thing from the rest. This game would work with just human and android enemies. Or it would work with just the alien. When there are both enemies present it feels like playing two different sneaking games at the same time. "I have to avoid this enemy's line of sight but do so in a way that the other enemy doesn't hear me." Good stuff.
It is of course for the sake of it being a game and you playing the protagonist that the alien spends a lot of time around you. That does get really repetetive after a while especially since you know that Sevastopol is a large station and that there are other humans who are not staying nearly as silent as you are. Go bother someone else for a change!
After you meet the Alien and get killed a few times the actual scariness almost gone. First of all the alien moves in a bit weird fashion. It's like the AI is making calculations of what to do next but the animation cannot always adjust to it. Sometimes it just changes directions without any sense of weight or drops down from a vent and immediately climbs back up. It might also come so close to whatever closet you are hiding in that it's head comes through the door. The Alien is an amazing piece of AI, animation and art but the less you see of it the better. Playing is still extremely intense  because you can only save at savepoints which are far apart. The Alien is really unpredicable and so any extra noise, mistake or just randomness can erase 15 minutes worth of gameplay. The thought of that is scarier than actually getting killed since you can choose if you want to see the death or not: You can always hammer the esc key faster than the Alien can kill you.
Alien: Isolation is set up to do one thing in one specific universe and it succeeds almost flawlessly. Graphics, atmosphere, sound, and everything else is really good. Was it a good Alien experience? Yes! No other game even comes close.
Was it a good gameplay experience? I'm not so sure about that. Sneaking in a new area  for the first time is great but 2nd and 3rd attempts are really tedious. Much worse than any other sneaking game. It feels like you can't "earn" freedom from the Alien. No matter how sneaky you are or how close call you escaped, it will be back in two seconds. It will force you into same closet 4 times for no apparent reason before you get to another room and repeat. It doesn't take long to learn the noises it makes and think "Not this crap again".
If the Alien were a creature that tried to hunt, eat and survive and you only saw it few times then Alien: Isolation would be the best thing ever. Unfortunately it is a creature that tries to entertain and serve a plot and does so way too often. There is a mod that disables the Alien AI. Around the 5 hour mark you understand why someone made it.
In the end it comes to two questions. Are you the kind of person who doesn't mind leaving a game unfinished and is the price right for 3-4 hours of entertainment? If you say yes to both, then get Alien: Isolation! Those few hours will be awesome!

If nothing scares you nor makes you flinch and you are in desperate need of a jumpscare at least once in your life, this is the game to play.
The second biggest fear for Humans next to death is the unknown. Not knowing how much the electric bill will cost during winter. Not knowing if you left your car lights on. Not knowing if someone is hiding in an alleyway with a knife. But in the case of horror games, the AI are predictable and thus not scary. Why be afraid if you're going to know what happens? Well you're in for a treat because the AI in this game is so advanced and so unpredictable that you won't be able to predict how many pares of underwear you're going to need if you decide to play this game.
For instance, when I start from a certain checkpoint and last a few minutes before being pulled up into a vent and eaten alive by the Alien, I respawn and learn from my mistakes, (appropriate behavior for a gamer). I then go about the level in a different manner, careful to avoid that dark hole in the ceiling where I last died. Then boom! the Alien comes out of a room behind me and chases me and then death. Respawn. Avoid hole in ceiling and look all around me while I try to survive. I get a little farther this time with no signs of the Alien anywhere. I enter a room and find a savepoint! Thank God! I go and begin to save my game (which takes about 7 seconds). But all of a sudden, while I am literally saving my game I hear a screech followed by charging footsteps and then I find my character being scewered from behind, still in the save screen. Yes, the Alien can kill you any second of the game. The ONLY way you are safe is if you pause the game, but that only pauses the game. You still have to go back and face that Alien again. The save was unsuccessful and everytime I respawned after that, no two deaths were the same. I had to have died 7 times before finally saving and everytime was unique and unpredictable.
This Alien is hunting you. He is not hindered by rules in the program. There are no boundaries to his search patterns. He will adapt to how you play. He will find new ways to mess with your head and new ways to kill you. You are now the prey. Prepare to be hunted.

If you're looking for a base-builder/survival game with a lot of potential, this game is great. Gorgeous graphics, active devs, and enough uniqueness to set it apart from other games of the genre, it's quite a bit of fun.
As it is two years old at this point, a lot of work has been put into it, and you can tell. It is very polished, with *plenty of content base-building wise*.
For example, you can upgrade most everything in the game. I found myself wishing the fingerless glove of death and destruction could be used to boost. I checked the upgrades, and sure enough, you could do that.
Speaking of the fingerless glove of death and destruction, it's amazing. 10/10 would juggle fish, use animals to knock down trees, and Mjölnir aliens into the ground with it again.
The game as is does "lack content", in the sense that if you're looking for a story, set objectives, or "endless hours of fun!", you will be disappointed. Your enjoyment of the game in it's current state is up to you. If you just want to build a base, explore, terrorise innocent animals, or just screw around, you'll probably have a blast. There isn't a "point" to the game, and that's fine. But if you want an experience similar to, say, The Forest, where there is an end goal, you're not gonna be happy with the current state of this game.
The graphics in the game are beautiful, kudos to the devs. I am able to run max graphics and a solid 60fps using a GeForce GTX1060. I haven't tried multiplayer yet, but it looks quite interesting with you being able to create different groups of colonists. I think it'd be quite a lot of fun to get a group of friends and battle it out.

Hello, world. It's the end of 2017 and one of my favorite games I played this year came out in 2010 (albeit this Steam version came out in 2013 and has the extremely fun Pigsy's Perfect 10 DLC).
Why? I'll skip my usual wall-of-text review form and just spell it out as simply as I can.
* The game is gorgeous. This version of the Unreal engine was already quite dated in 2010, but here it does work. Impressive draw distance, fluid movements, detailed models - especially the post apocalyptic New York is a sight for sore eyes.
* Impeccable voice acting. Andy Serkis really does work here.
* The story - it really shows it was the focus in this game (not that the gameplay is lacking). The characters' motivations are believable. The moment with the enslaving, when you realize what the stakes are - you have to play the game to really feel it, but it's all there. The ending leaves no loose ends and is EXTREMELY satisfying.
* The gameplay - combat + platforming all remind a lot of Uncharted. They're really well balanced and satisfying. Monkey feels like a really powerful main character and while the combat is pretty simplistic, it never stops being fun.
*The music - didn't really care for the really loud and bombastic moments, but the quiet and chilling moments were really impactful.
*The humor. It's really tasteful and the already mentioned professional voice acting delivery makes things feel really good. For example, passing through some run down truck full of boxes that say 3DTV, Trip asking "What are those?" and Monkey answering "Just some ancient redundant technology". I chuckled.
* It's quite easy. Don't play the game on Normal like me, play it on Hard. I'm not a great platformer player at all and I breezed through the game feeling kinda disappointed.
* The camera switching from "free form" to static at will can be disorienting and annoying, to say it lightly.
* Motion blur. Thank god there's an option to turn it off.
* The boss fights were all really boring and poorly designed. Thank god there weren't many of them, only 3 (
). The Rhino made me pull my hair out.
* Too many XP collectibles make the game feel like Pac-Man at times, and you can't really skip collecting as the upgrades are all quite useful.
As it can be seen, most of the negatives are quite minor. A must play by all means.

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a game that I had wanted to play since I was a teenager. Many years later that dream came true and I am thoroughly impressed that it has aged this well.
Enslaved: Odyssey to the West was probably the most underrated game of 2010. Hell maybe even the most underrated game of all time. But it does not come without its flaws. I always felt the need to finish the combat sections as fast as possible, though with the sneaking sections and having Trip to distract the turrets were mediocre. While repetitive and scripted, the platforming felt pretty good to me. But I loved the Cloud. Surfing through the area with it was great! I wish it was an open world game only for being able to travel around with the cloud. It would have been great.
As this is a reimagination of the story Journey to the West, I like the connection this game has with the Dragon Ball anime. There are many similarities, but the best one has to be the flying Nimbus. Monkey is able to fly on his own portable, electronic cloud that is a joy to control on screen as it hovers over water and land, plus allowing Monkey to travel at exceptional speed. The music throughout the game is well composed, and really sets the atmosphere of each chapter.
The graphics in this game still stand up to today’s standards very well. Whilst the levels have plenty of locations that buffers the next stage, textures and view distances are impressive, with the colourful art style placing plenty of detail in the junk and artefacts that lie around the maps. The mechs look brilliant and definitely appear scary with their humanoid limbs but fast to strike motions and gallops. Boss fights are well fought out, and for those that like collectibles, this game has plenty of those, with many achievements also available to unlock.
I recommend purchasing the game when it comes out on sale :)

If you enjoy motocross games, get MXGP.  That's as simple as I can say it.

But I played a few races with the assists off, and a few on harder levels...and it's pretty unforgiving.

Again, if you're a motocross game fan, stop reading, get the game.  (Well, okay...maybe wait for the Steam Spring Sale.  But if you like motocross you really can't go wrong here).

This is a really awesome game. It can appeal to those who really race and appreciate the physics of the realistic mode more, or those who just like to play a fun racing game. If you are wondering how this compares to other off road racing games, particularly MX vs ATV, this is how:
-MXGP has really good physics and is less arcady than MX vs ATV (especially when you are on the realistic mode)
-MXGP gives you option to set up your bike however you choose. This will probably appeal to those who really race or know a thing or two about it.
-MXGP has a more realistic career mode, letting you choose a team to sign with and wearing your endorsments on your jersey and bike.
-MXGP features all real brands, people, and tracks, unlike MX vs ATV (MX vs ATV only has KTM available as a real brand for dirt bikes)
Those are just a few of the ways MXGP beats MX vs ATV. As far as the graphics and sound go, I'd say both games are pretty good there. MXGP does have nice graphics, but the animation at the end of the race when you win is just... unnatural.
MX vs ATV give you more things to do, being a game that doesn't only focus on dirt bikes (even though that was probably their main focus).
MX vs ATV lets you drive a bunch of other different vehicles like an ATV, trophy truck, and more. MX vs ATV also features more types of racing. It features supercross, motocross, enduro, and has free ride available.
Things I wish were included in this game:
-Free ride
-Enduro
-Hard Enduro
-Multiplayer for each of those things
Overall, MXGP is a great game for motocross enthusiasts and your average gamer alike. As for which of the two games mentioned are better, that depends entirely on you and the features/style of offroad racing game you want. MX vs ATV supercross is planned and hopefully supercross isnt the only style of racing they include because that is one thing that I do love about Reflex (the amount of racing styles available).
Another thing is that MX vs ATV might beat MXGP with the real time ground deformation, but both games do it well.

This game has a lot going for it, but falls flat in some very important areas.  On the good side of things the career mode is killer, it’s a really cool idea that keeps things fun instead of just grinding away races for no reason.  Getting interests from teams and getting picked up for new contracts ect.
The game falls short with the actual riding. This is kind of what’s important here.  The in air controls are just horrible.  You can't use any gyro effects of the bike to pitch or throw cool whips.  If you try to do a whip it auto corrects you and you will always land, and you can't do a low scrub using the gyro of the bike.  The jumps all seem pre-determined it doesn’t seem to matter if you seat bounce, rail a corner and come in hot you almost always go the same distant.
The ruts develop after racing, but seem to have no mesh behind them, you just ride right past em, There is no getting cross rutted or railing a rut.  The extra lean with the right stick also doubles as the button that makes you auto scrub, so if you try to use your weight in the air to land in a rut you end up doing a scrub and falling. Also if you try to lean into a turn to rail it hard if you catch any air from a bump while railing a turn you start to scrub and fall.  It doesn't seem the right stick actually has any sensitivity it might as well be a button press.
There’s no clutch or starting gate, you just sit there holding the throttle and you go.  Makes getting a holeshot a tad easy. Also with no clutch it doesn’t let you keep traction railing through turns and resort to riding different ways to counteract it.

There are a lot of random bugs with the audio not working, the bike disappearing in your pits or the rider disappearing from the bike, the achievements don't work right, the list goes on; just go read the forums. Dark Souls has proven that even in an age when games tend to spoonfeed the player, a niche game can still attract a reasonable following. Its blend of simple yet engaging combat mechanics, fantastic visuals and unforgiving difficulty is a rarity in the industry nowadays that managed to wow players all over the globe, especially those longing for a challenge. Despite that, it was a bit rough around the edges - edges that the sequel smoothened out to some extent. Still, if you loved Dark Souls, you can't help but feel slightly disappointed about this one.
At its core, it's Dark Souls all over again: You roam bizarre fantasy environments, fight monsters and upgrade your gear in order to fight monsters more effectively, interrupted only by the occasional invader who is after your hard-earned souls. The differences are in the details.
Take the combat, for instance. Essentially, the mechanics remain unchanged, only now your character's moveset lacks Dark Souls' distinctive sluggishness. As a result, combat in Dark Souls 2 feels more fluid, slightly faster and more direct. Unfortunately, it also feels rather weightless. What I always liked about Dark Souls was that its sluggishness conveyed the feeling that the player character's gear actually weighed something. Watching the character struggle when swinging his greatsword gave the combat a certain grittiness - a grittiness that is mostly absent in the sequel.
The PC port of Dark Souls is notoriously bad and thankfully, From Software has taken steps to avoid another shoddy porting job. Dark Souls 2 features all the good stuff a spoiled PC gamer is used to. Still, the game manages to be somewhat underwhelming visually.
A lot of that comes from the inconsistent art design: Sometimes it's great, sometimes it's lackluster. And sometimes it's just plain awful. A giant castle decorated with spikes within a sea of lava? This is just a few steps above Super Mario World.
The environments in Dark Souls are wondrous places and mostly bizarre variations of established fantasy designs like "old castle" or "mysterious forest". And yet, they possess the quality of making the player stop whatever he's doing and simply enjoy the scenery for a moment. Dark Souls 2 has those environments as well, but they are more scarce.
Despite the higher resoultions, the texture work is surprisingly bland and makes repeating textures even more obvious. Many environments suffer from looking washed out and rather grayish. Better lighting and shadowing could have improved the atmosphere.
The enemies share a similar perceived blandness in design, in addition to some of them seeming like mere copy and paste jobs from the previous game.
Despite its unforgiving nature, Dark Souls rarely felt cheap. Now Dark Souls has turned into the posterboy for "the hardcore game" - something that even From Software acknowledges in their promotion material.
If you died, it was usually your fault for adapting poorly to the situation. However, much of the difficulty in Dark Souls 2 feels cheap and inflated. Most of the time, it seems that the team knew no other way of providing a challenge than pitting you against multiple enemies at the same time or turning enemies into damage sponges. This is especially painful considering that Dark Souls had quite imaginative and challenging boss fights. Not that the game wasn't guilty of taking a shortcut every now and then, but in Dark Souls 2 it's more of a bad habit.
Speaking of shortcuts: The areas aren't interconnected anymore, making Drangleic seem less of an "actual place" compared to Lordran. At the same time, it's getting rid of the sense of wonder when discovering a new route into a previously explored area.
All of this may sound pretty negative, but it's just nitpicking, really. Dark Souls 2 is weaker than its predecessor (even the soundtrack made by the same composer seems like a step back), but it's still a phenomenal game since the aspects that made the first one great are still present, although slightly fainter. In fact, you should have a blast with this game if PvP was your focus in the previous one. There are far more options that allow you to help other players, fight them or to flat-out turn the game into a glorified griefing engine.
Dark Souls 2 is an exceptional game and a good sequel, even though it's lacking in some areas that made the first one great.

TL;DR - (A) Area Design, (A) Combat, (B) Story - Endorses an overwhelming sense of personal achievement.
Dark Souls 2's learning curve is more like a brick wall, which after enough time bashing your head at it, will eventually break and you proceed not quite understanding why it took you so long to do so.
General rules that lead to this realisation are that fighting an enemy one on one, is always preferable unless you have giant swords. Bows are a great tool to achieving this goal as just like Skyrim, most enemies seem oblivious to arrows. A 100% physical protection shield is your best friend and rolling at the last second makes your character invincible because of Japanese programming techniques not working great for PC (see i-frame).
These reasons are precisely why this game is not easier than Dark Souls 1, it's wall simply takes less bashing as most people have already half broken it from the first game.
Pushing past difficulty, I don't believe graphics are a reason to judge this game, it is a console port from an old generation, by a company that has once admitted they have no clue about porting, however the beauty comes from some of the amazing areas this game has to offer. Ushered from lips come phrases engraved in all players memories, such as "Praise the sun" and "Amazing view", which is all they can say with the limited words on the messaging system but none the less, where these phrases are to be found, offer some of the most breathtaking visuals I have seen in gaming.
The map design, I will admit, is still really good, but it is in no way, as amazing as Dark Souls 1. The inter-connectivity that made players stumble over the words "Oh, I'm back here", is mostly lost, however replacing that feeling is some great level design. Areas all feel unique, each having there own linearity or maze-like progression, differing amounts of hazards, enemies, treasure and secrets, leading them to having their own personality achieved from a wide colour palette and excellent design.
So it's a hard game with good level design? Why do people love it so much? These are the questions most people ask around about now. This comes from the personal achievement found within. There is no handholding, no go this way, speak to this person, coupling this with the difficulty leaves this overwhelming feeling of satisfaction when you achieve a goal. Whether it be getting to the next bonfire, killing a boss that has been a thorn in your side, or helping someone achieve their own goals in co-op, right up until the end of the game you get the feeling of overwhelming achievement, its not a reward in the form of more powerful items etc, it's an entirely personal feeling, that keeps you playing, wanting to progress and do better than before.
So what happens when you finish? Well, the game does become noticeably easier with a new character, you have learned the ways, broke that wall and understand all areas, enemies and bosses. Oh wait, sorry, I nearly forgot (sarcasm). Dark Souls 2 knows it's strength is personal achievement, and offers "new game plus", an opportunity to start again. Same character, but entirely new enemies, new items and new boss mechanics. After new game plus it goes all the way to new game +7, however that is just more health and more damage from enemies, which is understandable given the timeframe the company had.
The story is left to be unravelled by the player in the form of item descriptions and dialogue, along with most areas notable features. An excellent youtuber called VaatiVidya provides what he believes to be the lore of characters and the game in general on his Youtube channel, which I highly recommend if you enjoy the game and want to understand it more.
Second to last, is the combat. There are generally three different paths a character can take. The sorcerer, relying on magic to overcome his foes, usually using a staff or chime depending on miracles, hexes or sorceries as the chosen school and a shield to protect himself. The duel wielding warrior, a powerhouse, powerstancing two weapons of the same type increases damage but is harder to wield, and leaves the user vulnerable to attacks, unless dodged appropriately. Then there is the standard warrior/magic hybrid, not enough points to go full warrior all the time, he rolls with a sword and shield, with some support magic or lightning spells and buffs. The types of combat actions characters can perform are light attacks; heavy attacks; jumping attacks; special attacks unique to weapons; powerstancing; blocking; shield breaking; shield bashing; parrying; riposting and dodging, leading to a fully fledged enjoyable and challenging combat system, ideal for PvE and PvP.
Performance wise, there will be no problems playing on the highest settings for any gaming PC. This time though, it has 60fps and the difference in smooth gameplay makes it much more preferable to it's predecessor. Gamepad is still required though.
Learn your playstyle, break that wall and enjoy the beauty of a game that is Dark Souls 2.

Many people will say, that DS1 was better due to better level design, or that it was more difficult and so on and so on. So here is my opinion: DS1 levels had entire environments ridden with more traps, hidden ambushes and generally, they gave you that sensation, that the ENTIRE world was against you, which also gave off the feeling that the game was more difficult and the environments more complex (which at some points of the game I agree that they were).
.....................................................................HOWEVER.....................................................................
I disagree with the opinion that DS1 is more difficult a game that DS2 since: DS2 has WAY more difficult bosses, many of which are virtually impossible to defeat without help like The Smelter Demon or Duke's Dear Freja, while in DS1 I personally as a gamer defeateed all the bosses (some more difficult that the others) alone, because back then i used to play on the xbox and i didn't have an xbox live membership. Also concerning the many traps of DS1, in DS2 they have simply been REPLACED with more NPCs not because of poor level design, but rather due to the lore. Also  let's not forget that NPCs in DS1 after NG+ -while still becoming stronger- they were not anywhere near as strong as how strong the player would become later in the game, effectively making them a LOT easier to deal with, something that is not true at all with DS2 since the enemies become gradually more and more powerful, not only individually, but in numbers as well since every NG+ in DS2 comes with more enemy NPCs, on top of which they are red phantoms as well, which are even stronger than their already stronger (due to the NG+) normal counterparts.
I don't think DS2 is in any way inferior to DS1, especially with the new DLC which were absolutely amazing imo. There are many more features of DS2, that i personally find superior compared to those of DS1 like: 1) a greater variety of weapons, shields, spells, armor etc etc 2) better graphics (which was expected as a newer game ofc but it's still worth mentioning imo) and 3) better pvp (once again, in my opinion) which for me was the most important aspect as a mainly pvp player.
I am not going to emphasize any more on the topic, as I believe everyone  has understood by now  what i'm trying to say so all I'm going to do is compliment this game on how great it is, and finally advise the people that don't like it to simply play something else, since obviously they don't like this one.

Never forget. A game you don't like, is not a game for you !

First some history: Eso caught my attention before launch thanks to some friends but they (and I) lost interest when more and more features weren't to our liking. Launch didn't improve my oppinion of the game and I decided not to purchase it though I did occasionally browse the reviews.
Time passed and one Tamriel was launched, a massive improvement in my books. But let's go to the good, the not so good and the rest.
The good!
ESO doesn't feel much like grinding through quests. I yet have to find any 'kills so many of these' quests. Most quests make you go to places where things happen.
Also very pleasant is that ESO reacts to your achievements to an extend. You see and hear things on your screen others may not while in the same area. For exemple ghost npc's may be hostile to one player and neutral to a second.
ESO looks really good. I love walking through a sunlit forest or stare out at sea from a cliff. Characters have a lot of detail as well and the range of emotes is enormous and varied. A city feels like a city in this world and not a collection of hovels and four NPC's doing nothing.
ESO is not pay to win. ESO has no subscription and while a monthly fee makes life a little smoother and easier you by no means need it to prosper.
The combat in ESO to me feels very intuitive. So far I don't have to ask veterans for help with about every decision I have to make. There are many skills you can specialise in, from woodcutting to Daedra summoning to wearing heavy armor. It starts quite simple and as you progress you get more and more skills and potential choices.
Level matters but not so much as it does in most mmo games. My level 12 sorceress contributed nicely in a dungeon run along with 3 much higher level (40+) and better equipped characters. Sure, she wasn't the best but she wasn't sidelined either nor killed by one enemy blow.
The not so good and not so bad:
ESO remains an MMO and unlike GW2 you don't (always) have your own loot on the map. Some highly covered loot like thief stashes may be rushed at by more then one player and tempers may well flare. Some camp near the spawn locations as well.
You have to pay to play an imperial. I am not sure how I feel about that myself. On the other hand, you can find many items from the crown (read pay) store also in the game.
The bad
Customer service. Seriously, you can't even register on the official forum without an invitation. Evidently buying their game doesn't warrant an invitation.
All in all it feels like a great game to me and as long as everything runs fine and you don't need to contact customer service you should have a great time. If you enjoy the same things as I do anyways!

TL:DR:  8/10
I pre-ordered Total War Rome II but only just started playing the game due to the amount of negative backlash levied at the game from launch. Now I have finally started to play the game and I have really enjoyed it - but I should note that I am not playing the purely "vanilla" version of Rome II. After much reading I decided to download Toons' "All in One Mod" for Rome II and it is really good. So please note that my subsequent comments are coloured by having played the mod.
Rome II does some things really well compared to previous Total War games (of which I have played most of them). I really like how the Auto Resolve for battles has been addressed, whereby it shows you the likelihood of victory based on the battle stance you take (aggressive, balanced, defensive) and also the percentage of troops you will have left for each choice.
The enemy AI is also well balanced and fights well in the field battles as well as on the diplomatic side of things. I really liked the addition of the Pros and Cons listed by each faction for why they like or dislike your nation. This made it much simpler to determine why they might reject an offer as opposed to past TW games where it was infuriating to be rejected and not understand why.
Having naval support during battles is a nice touch also and builds upon the naval warfare introduced in Empire, even if it's still quite clunky at times.
The Spies and Heroes/Champions are also much better designed in this game than the previous Rome and Empire. Now you can assign perks to the individual agents and level them up as you desire. I remember thinking in Empire "What is the point of the spy! His chances of assassinating someone is barely 20%!" Now I have used them to great effect in weakening cities, garrisons and travelling armies. A great improvement all round!
There is also much more opportunities to conduct war in the political arena with assassinations and securing promotions etc. This has been greatly expanded from Empire and the previous Rome and adds a broader dimension to the game.
One thing that I don't like so much is the way armies can be split and travel. It is impossible (as far as I can see) to transport troops from one army to another unless the General travels with them in tow. This may well be more thematic but I feel that it hinders the game play a bit.
I also completely disagree with CA's decision to make this such a DLC heavy title/franchise. Some additional campaigns and so on are fine as added DLC to me but adding a Blood and Gore mode and other minor aesthetic changes that were already in the game files and just required "activation" is ridiculous. Companies need to stop selling us half-completed games!
But all in all I thoroughly recommend Rome II - especially if you seek out a mod like I did.

If you liked Borderlands you surely would like this one as well.  Just like the first one it's all about shoot and loot. Literally.
Borderlands combines first person shooter with some rpg elements (upgrading skills). The developer likes to call it a role playing shooter and i think that pretty much covers the game. The art style might not appeal to everyone, as it is cellshaded. It looks a bit cartoony.  I have no problems with it myself, but i can imagine that some people might not like it. The gameplay however just does it. Normally shooters just have a shallow story, character ain't interesting and for most part you just shoot stuff. Borderlands 2 does have a pretty good story, though weird and the characters are interesting. The beginning of the game comes with a bang and you soon will fight your first boss, unlike the first borderlands. In my opinion Borderlands 2 is more difficult then the first one and there are more boss fights. The landscape contains now ice plains, especially at the very beginning. There are new monsters added and you will now find more loot. Some weapons will now drop more frequently, such as the jacobs. In the first borderlands jacobs weapons were somewhat rare. Also, bandit weapons are introduced now and a bandit ride. You can choose from 6 characters this time. 4 vault hunters by default, 2 more are added through dlc's.
It's not all positive though and the game does have it's downsides. The biggest one is the greed from the developer, as they released alot of dlc and tricked people who bought a season pass by releasing dlc that are not part of the pass. Later on they came with the game of the year edition, which contains all 4 dlc that were previously part of the season pass. Not cool from gearbox. Also, the mechromancer was made as seperate dlc, while with the release it was shipped as part of the premiere club dlc. I have a copy myself with the premiere club.
An other thing which i noticed is that bulletin boards this time ain't not much. I have the feeling you get less side missions. Catch a ride is also less frequent. Those are things i miss from the first Borderlands. I find claptrap this time also quite annoying, especially calling you his minion all the time. Too bad you can't shoot him.
Overall it's a good game. Lots to see, lots to loot and lots to shoot.

TL;DR summary - An enjoyable game with gorgeous graphics and art design, some replayability (probably twice as the two different playable characters), and interesting plot. The recent updates have fixed the PC porting issues, and performance is good throughout (although some mild framerate drops when using the Temporal Device). 8/10
Pros:
- Great plot, which follows on from the previous games
- Good to be able to choose between Emily Kaldwin and Corvo Attano, with suitably different 'powers' for each = replay at least twice
- Sumptuous graphics and art design
- Great sound design
- Good level design: the developers provided multiple ways to complete missions (that reward players who like to find alternative solutions over the direct 'brute force' approach)
- Fun and useful 'void powers' for stealthy and overt playstyles = more playthrough opportunities again
- Your actions affect future events in the game to some extent
- Just long enough
- Good price reduction ATM, or bundled with the new expandalone: Death of the Outsider
Cons:
- Still relatively linear overall (but that's what these games are - we're not in Witcher 3 Open World territory here)
- (minor niggle) initial screen loading times vary between two modes: ~10s (on a good day) or sometimes ~2mins, weird!
- Medium difficulty was too easy for me, so I would recommend playing on Hard if you like a challenge (rather than just enjoying the story and experience)
- No DLC; but then, a lot of DLC in games is rubbish and not worth the extra, so this isn't a big deal. That's apart from the lack of the 'special' package you get by buying the collector's edition (i.e. not Steam), which gives you access to two powerful bonecharms
About to play the next expandalone: Death of the Outsider... I hope it is an equally good experience!

First off, while this game is game focused on survival and defense, it leaves more to be desired. There are outposts you can explore, enemy encampments you can destroy, but it all begins to feel repetitive after 4 to 6 hours of gameplay.
I haven't explored the terrain all that much but it's very easy to learn where to expect what resources. You go the mountains for gold and silver, and you go to the valleys for almost everything else.
Secondly, and possibly the worst aspect of this game, is a lack of a soundtrack. I'm not immersed into a game unless I have music playing in the background that links to the environment. Imagine if iconic games like Halo or Skyrim didn't have their soundtracks to help draw you in? Would they have the same lasting impact?
Overall, this game is enjoyable. If building bases to protect against orange space aliens is your thing, this game is perfect. However, it lacks that drawing immersion some games need.

All I know is that I loaded this game five times, and I never managed to survive for more than three minutes. And if that were because I am horrible at it, then hey, fair enough. But when the game's framerate drops the moment enemies appear on screen, and you find you can't move or see around you, that's on the game. When I suddenly find myself clicking random stuff on my (thankfully very empty) desktop because the game didn't capture the mouse pointer properly in window mode, that's on the game. Once, while playing around with the settings, I managed to get into a mode where there was an offset between the mouse pointer and the on-screen UI, resulting in a situation where I could not start a new game or do much of anything.
There's no one big thing that breaks this game for me, but hundreds of tiny things. Any one of these would be expected in an early access game. But here, they combine in a way that just makes it impossible to play it. Maybe (very probably) that has something to do with my hardware or desktop resolution or whatever, and won't appear for anyone else. And maybe I could have gotten this game to work with enough online research about configuration files and the like, doing the developer's work for them. Maybe I just didn't have enough patience; you can see I played only three quarters of an hour. But each and every one of those forty-five minutes was sheer frustration, with only the vaguest hope that maybe I'd see something interesting. And I don't need a game for that. That's what I watch Doctor Who for.

Then the lights at the end of a big hall filled with baggage and rubble start flickering and not even a second before the lights go out, I catch a glimpse of a shadow quickly move across the space. If you like the first two movies of the Aliens series you will
enjoy Alien: Isolation.  It's basically a good game, with a lot of flaws.
The Good:
The plot is almost as good as the first two movies.
The graphics are great!  They look exactly like what you saw in the first two movies, only there is far more of it, and more variety.
The sound is also great!  The soundtrack, which seems to be wholly original, would be at home in the first two movies.  Many sound effects are taken from the first two movies, though new, fitting, ones are introduced.
The save points are reasonably distributed and implemented acceptably.
All the settings PC gamers expect are provided.
The Bad:
The reason the plot is almost
the first two movies is large swaths of it are
from the first two movies.  This game could have benefited greatly from more creative writing.
The reason the plot is
as good as the first two movies is it is too long and has too much filler.  When a movie in the Aliens series, or a video game, ends, it is usually on a note of success.  You never get that feeling of success in this game.  First you try Plan A, but that doesn't work…  Then you try Plan B, and that doesn't work either…  On and on until you run out of letters…  A good horror movie has at most 2 or 3 ‘plans’.  It's not that I wanted ‘less game’, it's that I want ‘more success per failure’.
Remember Amanda Ripley is supposed to be an engineer.  She should be rather intelligent.  The plot is very much ‘on rails’, and forces you (her) to do some really stupid things.  When Ripley encounters a barricade she never seems to question why it is there, or what could go wrong if she removes it.  She never constructs barricades (or anything but consumables) herself.  If these situations were going to arise in the game, it should have been for optional loot, and occasionally have had bad outcomes.
The plot also makes the opposite error.  Apparently Amanda Ripley is a master of all fields of study!  The game will tell you to <lingo> the <lingo>, and Ripley immediately understands this.  The poor player gets a circle on the map (which may be quite large, and refer to any floor), where they are expected to bumble around for an hour or three while being repeatedly killed by aliens before they understand what they are expected to do.  To further aggravate this problem, many interactive items are not obviously interactive.  For example, the first time you encounter a rats nest of blue pipes you will probably ignore it as more setting-appropriate clutter, especially since it has no gadgetry attached and doesn't highlight when you look directly at it, but no, that's interactive!
If you are at all technically-minded, you may be bothered by the fact that a lot of the setting makes no sense:
The ending is terrible.  It is both short and unsatisfying.
The designers went for cheap hits and jump scares, instead of the slower-building atmospheric horror of the movies on which this game is based.  The game is worse for that.  Playing it involves a lot of trial and error.
The aliens are too omnipresent.  They quickly change from being scary to
.  They frequently rapidly cycle through their patrol route, and the difficulty isn't in figuring out how to sneak past them, but doing it in the narrow time window you are given.  They also linger in the area they think you are in for ages, so you spend lots of time rolling your eyes and sighing in some locker, waiting for them to move on so you can make some progress.
The alien AI is too limited and mechanical.  This might have gone unnoticed if it were not a constant pest.  Soon the player learns that the alien is always in their local area, and will cycle through its patrol route unless it sees or hears them or a distraction.  When it sees or hears them or a distraction it will linger in that area until it sees or hears something else of interest, gets bored and returns to its patrol route, or finds the player.  It will only ever pass through ceiling vents unless it can see the player through a wall or floor vent opening.  Its attack always consists of running straight at the player, even if there is a lit flamethrower pointed at it.  At that point any feeling of being hunted is lost.  They should have made the aliens behave more organically, but kept it fair by having them telegraph their actions, making it possible to escape them after you have been spotted, and giving the player vantage points to observe them.
Apparently the designers think that if a decaying space station was infested with lethal alien parasites, 99% of the populace would turn into sociopathic idiots.  They will start shooting at you on sight while screaming, “It didn't have to be this way!”.  The game provides no way to interact with them.  You aren't allowed to say, “I've got no interest in your food or equipment, and gunfire will just attract the creature, so can I please just pass by you to use that elevator?”  Instead you either have to kill them yourself and attract the alien, or use a noisemaker to attract the alien to have it kill them for you.  In other words,
have to act like a sociopathic idiot.
The cleanroom suits some androids wear should not grant them the ridiculous protection it does.  It makes sense that it stops the stun baton, but it shouldn't do anything to protect them from a pipe bomb going off directly under their feet, or similar catastrophic damage.
It would have been more believable if adult aliens could be killed.  It
be difficult, and ammunition should remain limited.
There are many annoying quick time events in this game.  There is usually no time pressure, no decision to make, and no way to mess them up.  It just made the cinema scenes have awkward pauses and clutter over them, and felt like busywork.

While the setting is faithful to the original Alien movies, the gameplay is sadly not that great. The pattern the gameplay follows is this: get to some objective -> find out power is out -> turn power back on -> hack or turn on some other subsystems; it reminded me of Doorman: Absolution
This type of pattern is used at least on 5 occasions.
Other times the gameplay follows a style of: get to location A -> find out location A is not reachable via original path -> new objective is to find alternative path via B, all the while being chased by the Alien.
While it is fun for a few hours, this routine which makes up the entire gameplay, gets old after it is used time and time again.
Lastly, basic science accuracy is completely ignored - Sevastopol, the space station on which most of the gameplay takes place, has perfect Earth gravity, although it is in an orbit around a gas giant where there should be none. How this is possible is not properly explained throughout the game (and the station does not rotate to generate centrifugal force either). Even spacewalks feature Ripley stolling on metallic bridges without the least hint of trying to resist zero gravity. Even if you assume the space suit has some magnets in the boots that keeps it fixed to the metallic bridges during spacewalks, it still makes no sense aliens can walk around the outside like there's full gravity...
Completely unappealing for someone used to the kind of attention to detail as in Mass Effect
Final assessment 5/10 - weak story, and dull gameplay

As a small preface, I have played the game for over 100 hours (some offline), and have played through it three and a half times, plus most of the DLC.
Alien: Isolation, unlike it's brand predecessor Aliens: Colonial Marines, stays true to the title by retaining the core horror elements that made Alien so great, and less focus on the sci-fi action that made Aliens so great.
As Amanda Ripley you come to Sevastopol for the Nostromo flight recorder to learn what happened to your mother, Ellen Ripley. All hell has broken lose on Sevastopol and now you face danger and terror at every turn, and at the center of it all, the Xenomorph.
Alien Isolation looks long and hard at Alien, and decides what built up suspense for that film was not the terrifying action moments, it was the slow-burning tension, and this game perfectly replicates that. The game paces itself phenomenally, electing to not even show the Alien until potentially an hour and half into the game, letting you get on edge, excited, anxious even.
Then when it comes, you wish you could go back to before in a heartbeat. The Alien is a cunning creature, learning your behavioral patterns and adapting to your strategies. Just because you could distract it with a noisemaker one time, doesn't gurantee that it will fall for the trick again. The terror is very real, and you truly feel as though you are being relentlessly hunted, with the chase only given up at chance times. You carefully think out your every move, you wait for it to leave and ponder if it will quickly run back, you watch in horror as it stalks your room, creeping towards the closet you reside in. Any noise you make can be heard, and likewise with everyone else. Just because you're being careful doesn't mean someone else in the area is, and the Alien will gladly come for them, sweeping you up as a bonus. The AI that Creative Assembly has constructed in this game is one of the most intelligent and adaptive programs to date.
As you wander Sevastopol, you sometimes get glances out of windows, giving you unparalleled splendor to be seen in the wide, expansive views of space, brought together with the hand down, phenomenal lighting effects. While graphics are very servicable, the game truly shines visually with it's dynamic lighting. Swinging lights on the ceiling bounce back and forth, illuminating different locations, while shadows are crisp and fluid. The models themselves have great facial construction, and the Alien is the best we've seen in years.
The game has so many little details added for atmosphere, it truly feels like you're on the set for Alien. Little Drinking Birds sit on desks, common utilites are exactly like in the films, and there is an obvious 1979 Future feel to the world. Computers take time to boot up, save stations require you to wait for the activation lights, and small maintenance minigames look and feel exactly like the film.
The game, while mostly linear, has a sort of Metroidvania feel to it despite you getting everything in order. Most of the time, items you recieve start out weak, but you find upgrades to them, allowing you to access new places and find new secrets. Going off the beaten path can reward you with crafting parts, blueprints, audiologs, and logs from the Nostromo itself.
The game allows you total stealth freedom, giving you numerous craftable devices, different paths to an objective, and dynamic hostiles, which interact with eachother in different ways. You can craft different devices like noisemakers, EMPs, Molotovs, and Pipe bombs, and employ them how you see fit. Missions feel dynamic, and while most have a certain reach a point, activate a thing, return, layout to them, the game keeps it fresh with scripted events, new paths unveiling, and different enemies.
The Alien however, remains the star of the show, but finds himself put to the side for some time to allow for greater world building and pacing. The game isn't afraid of missions dedicated to immersion, with one putting you on LV-426, the planet from Alien and Aliens. It's a complete love letter to the fans, with audio logs recorded by all the original actors (Minus Ian Holm, but you wouldn't think listening to the impersonator). The game spends a period of time without the Alien, most have complained, but what it really does is desenstise you to danger, so when the Alien returns, you get to relive all that introductary fear again. So much attention to world detail really pays off, and objects/locations/style of construction are all near identical to what you see in the film.
All this tension is complemented by the fantastic and dynamic score, rising in excitement when you are spotted, flaring at moments of action, and incurring deep feelings of dread.
Everything in the game just works so well with eachother, the game truly feels like an authentic experience. This is an unbelieveably high reccomendation for any Alien fans, and horror fans will find themselves completely enthralled with the experience. People not into horror games as well will most certainly find plenty to love about the horror hit of 2014.
As a final note, major credit is due to Creative Assembly, who until this point made turn based warfare games, for absolutely nailing everything about the horror genre, first person genre, and Alien universe on their first try.

The game takes place in a post apocalyptic future. A world destroyed by war.
You start off on a slave ship. You and another slave named Trip escape.
But you're not free yet. Because Trip places a slave headband on you and asks (orders) you to help her get back home. The headband will kill Monkey if Trip dies.
He eventually develops Stockholm syndrome and follows her on his own accord.
As for the gameplay, the game is quite similar to ICO. With some similar mechanics. Although the puzzles and platforming are very dumbed-down. The game makes it clear enough where you have to go. So there isnt that sense of accomplishment like you get in ICO.
The camera sucks. Thats one of the things this game should not have copied from ICO.
Combat is button mashing for the most part. You have a light attack, heavy attack, charged attack, etc.
You do have to use different moves to get past the enemies' defenses though. You can shoot projectiles.
You can unlock/upgrade abilities by collecting orbs.
You can carry Trip on your back. You can throw her to hard to reach places. She can use distractions. You can use distractions. You even have a cloud you can use to hover around with. But you can only use it in places that are convenient to the game. Cant use it always.
The ending does have a twist that you probably wouldn't have expected. Philosophical. Although you dont get choices in the end.

This game is a combination of Action-Adventure, Hack & Slash, and a little bit Puzzle. In this game, the protagonist was taken by slavers, but then manage to escape on the middle of the way with "help" of a girl. And that girl turns you into her "slave" to make sure her safety to journey back home. Complicated, right?
Oh, this game is based on a novel, Journey to the West by Wu Cheng'en, but I haven't read it.
Gameplay:
This game basically is Action-adventure + Hack & Slash, all your enemy is robots, because why not? This game set in future. And you have a powerful staff as melee weapon and you can also shoot enemy with it. Some part of the game has puzzle where you need to solve some task to complete your mission.
This game feels like a co-op but with AI companion, first you have that "slaver" b- as your companion, then you get one more companion from her friend later, a 3 player co-op single player game.
Your role is to slash enemy, her role is to hack, and her friend, he is a sharpshooter. So this game is literally hack-and-slash-third-person-shooter game.
There is no manual save, and your progression automatically saved each checkpoints.
Graphic & Sound:
For a 2010 game, this game has an amazing graphic, nice detail, and good draw distance, the facial expression is good thanks to motion capture by great actors/actress. Voice acting is great too. But this game don't have or maybe have a poor anti-aliasing, but you could use ReShade. Sound effect and voice quality is good too, as some games from 2005-2010 tend to have a compressed audio files this game use all high quality audio.
Camera:
So this game is basically a ported console game, your mouse movement doesn't give accurate movement, instead read your mouse movement distance this game read your mouse axis, it maybe hard to explain, but moving your mouse faster doesn't make your camera move faster, it just like read the axis from joystick. You can't move your camera 45 degree quickly by moving your mouse fast.
And then, I am not a fan of isometric view, this game "cinematic" view has some part that camera is changed to isometric & side scrolling at some part. There is a couple times where camera placement is bad, like where you are from one room the camera is on right side and then changed to left side on next room and you could be looping if you are not careful enough, naturally you press right button to move forward if camera is placed on your character's right side, then the camera is changed to your left side and guess what happen next.
Story:
The story is pretty well done, from the beginning there is always interesting story goes on. Each chapter can be done in about 30-45 minutes.
But the ending seems like it done in a hurry. There is no actual boss-fight, as boss as the "villain" in game. Your robots enemy are just getting bigger and bigger. And instead put a gameplay to meet the "villain", you get a cutscene.
There is no open world, just a linear story line.
9/10 - I like this game, even those things I don't like that I write above, it's just a small part of the game, as a whole this game is great.

Everyone who shares responsibility for the creation and approval of this camera system deserves to blindfolded, spun until dizzy, then beaten with 20 heavy foam bats at once until the dizziness wears off then repeated a few dozen times.
It's a worthwhile game, but it would've been so much better with a normal (translation: not mounted on the head of a drunken monkey) camera. It's heavy on platforming and combat and both are all but ruined by the camera. So many times I've struggled to see where to go or what path to take through gunfire because the camera is locked in a particular direction. So many times I've been walking in one direction only for the camera to jump perspectives and I end up pressed against a wall/border or reversing back through the transition and having to do it over again because the new perspective changed what the stick direction is. So many times I've been blindsided in combat because the camera's so close to the character and usually facing any direction other than a helpful one. So many times I've tried to adjust the camera only for it spin madly around into any direction but where I want it like it's hanging from a twisted rope. Often I feel like my face is pressed up against the monitor and I find myself leaning back as if it would help.
It often feels too forced in how blatantly obvious they are in making situations to do the platforming and collaborative tasks and they can really go overboard with the handholding.
Despite all this, it's still enjoyable. The dialogue and acting are what save this and make it worth putting up with the other crap.

BE FOREWARNED, LIKELY CRASHES REQUIRING LOG OUT AT THE LEAST!
I give thumbs down, but it is in fact a pretty good game.  By far my biggest gripe is that when it crashes (which is too frequent) it blacks out the entire screen but keeps itself "on top", so even ctrl+alt+del to get task manager to kill it doesn't work because you can't actually get window focus on task manager.  The only recourse I've found with this is to sign out, which of course kills all programs the user, me, had running.  It also doesn't have a "windowed mode" option so I can't just use that.
As for the game itself, it's ok.  The combat is rather repetitive, you only have 4 primary moves in a single combo, then two variations on a stronger two-hit combo.  These harder hits are not "linked" with the 4 lesser hits, there's a definite pause between them, which makes combat seem a bit janky.  However, it's mixed up decently by having to dodge around, and a separate third charge attack that will stun opponents.  Still though, the bulk of combat is little more than mashing the two weak/strong attacks continuously.
The platforming is ok, but far too automatic.  Any platform segment, which are many, are more puzzle-like than any jumping difficulty.  In fact it's literally impossible to fall off a ledge or accidentally release from a hand-hold.  The only difficulty comes in trying to find your next hand-hold, which still isn't difficult at all since they all shine.  The main difficulty  results from...
Camera angles.  Boy, this game's a mixed bag with those.  For one, when it's free-360 views, the camera just feels sluggish, having nothing to do with horz/vert speed from the options (not even sure they're available come to think of it).  And far too often you don't have full-360 command of the camera, forcing you into particular perspectives.  They got way too "cute" with their camera management here.  The switches between fixed angles and 360 views are also anything but seamless, very jarring in fact.
A good game is apparent, but it's crowded by too many minor annoyances, and with the crashes and "always on top" aspect, a very major negative.
The primary thing to get from this game is the story, which is a new slant on "Journey to The West", of which many variations have been made over the years.  You'd probably be better off with a simple lets play of this one to get the story.

Heroes of Newerth was really my first MOBA. I've dabbled with DOTA, and League of Legends as well, during the very early stages of development for those games. I can't speak to the improvements made after I stopped playing, and although I enjoyed each of them respectively I have to admit that SMITE is the MOBA which stood out the most for me personally.
Until I played SMITE, I didn't really comprehend how to play MOBA's properly. SMITE helped in that regard, somehow making it easier to get involved in and learn the game play mechanics. I'm not sure what it was that made the process simpler, but I definitely connected more and became a better player than I was in previous MOBAs.
The familiarity with the God characters was also appealing, as I didn't have to really assume what that character would play like. It's pretty obvious if I pick Zeus that I'm going to be using some sort of lightning techniques, etc. I wasn't stumbling over learning how to play each God as much as in other MOBAs, and I was genuinely interested in seeing what other Gods they would include in the game.
Besides some dislikes about matchmaking features, and nitpicking things here and there, overall SMITE is the best game HiRez has ever delivered and they continue to support it with new content and features. The competitive scene for Smite has decent activity, and I can see this becoming a franchise game for HiRez in the future, hopefully.
I would definitely recommend this game to any gamer I know.

Recommending a game, or not, is a tricky thing sometimes. If you love something that most people don't, not because they haven't heard of it but because it's an odd niche title; do you tell them to stay away because you know they won't like it, despite your own feelings or tell them to try it and hope they're one of the few that agree?
Dark Souls II is the flip of that problem. Plenty of people love it, I don't but I also don't feel they're wrong for embracing it. I just think there are too many issues with it and, the very nature of a game where you're supposed to fail plenty, certainly wouldn't be for everyone. I likely wouldn't have played it myself if a friend hadn't insisted on going through it together, so this review comes late in the game's life. I may be somewhat biased as well, but none-the-less I'll try to give some objective points.
Style aside, I think most of the complaints are pretty well-covered at this point. The graphical quality is all over the map with little rhyme or reason to it. Your character looks decent, you won't be blown away by it but the textures are pretty solid. There are the typical little model hiccups like metal armour bending the same as cloth but that's awfully nit-picky. I sure do wish characters moved their mouths to talk though.
The world itself is a bit of a mishmash of high-quality terrain in one spot and then tiled, flat, repeating brickwork in another which looks extremely dated. The bonfires are a good example too - sometimes they'll cast a decent shadow off your character and in other places they seem to have forgot to turn that on. The view distance isn't something to write home about either and the sky-sphere is noticeable if you look for it. The only reasonable guess is that a lot of detail was cut to make it work on consoles and they couldn't, for some reason, stand the idea of letting PC's just look better. Maybe they fear it would make console players bitter they were getting a stripped version of the game.
There's not much music really, what's there isn't bad but you're going to be well and truly sick of it before too long, as well as much of the dialogue. You can skip it at least but I can't begin to guess how many times the blacksmith thought I must be dead or how often the Herald told me to seek larger souls. A few odd folly choices too but they might be part of the style they're trying for - or just don't want to annoy you too badly with more realistic sharp, jarring sounds.
Nothing so far is bad enough to write the game off of course, but then we get to game-play and things turn ugly. Again, this might be a slightly skewed opinion since I've played 95% of the game online with a friend but I'm sure I must not be the only one to have gone that route.
Lets start with PvP. It's not what I play the game for but it's also not something you can avoid if you're online. You WILL get invaded and you should not plan on it being a fair fight. NPC's wont attach the invader giving them free reign of the map and to attack with impunity regardless of your being in combat (there is an item you can get to change this but it's the default behaviour). Okay, it encourages some amazingly cowardly behaviour but I can mostly plan around that at least. What's hard to plan around is the lag. I don't have a terrible connection but actually hitting an invader is an amazing process of seeing your sword pass through them and do nothing. Nearly the only swings that have a chance of impacting are wide swings and, while I don't know if the situation is similar on their end, I do know I've been back-stabbed from the other side of a room more than once. If the netcode gets fixed (and the fact it hasn't been yet is an embarrassment to the developer as far as I'm concerned) then PvP might have a fun element to it.
PvE has, to a lesser extent, the same issues. There's been more than a few times where a blow which had the appearance of a clean miss has done damage. Now, being online, I don't really know if these calculations are being done locally or not. There's also some very odd AI behaviour on occasion - just standing there and taking it or getting oddly confused if I stand still. There's also a heavy element of BS which could practically be a paper in itself. People seem to be confused what 'difficulty' is. Grinding and taking hours to do something in a game is not difficult. An enemy that reacts flawlessly and is not bound by the same rules as you isn't difficult. Difficult is when it behaves with skill but bound by the same constraints as you. Is some cheating required to make an AI a threat to a player? Well, that's up for debate but this game certainly has no issues applying a different standard to PC and NPC units. If all they wanted was to induce frustration, well done, if they wanted a challenging fight that meant a bit more, the mark was missed.
There are certainly more points to cover but it's coming out quite negative and the game does have some promising points. The story is fed to you in subtle bits that keep you engaged. Though I don't understand why, out of the dozens of effigies I have, I can't save a couple of other people from hollow. Either I missed something or your character is a serious jerk. The combat, when you're in a fight that's stable and no special circumstances are being abused against you, is engaging enough and there's a good selection of options in how to kit out your character.
In the end though, the fun I'm having is from playing a game with a friend and I have no urge or interest to play it solo which I think speaks to the core experience I'm getting out of it. I'm certainly in the minority on this one, but I wouldn't recommend it.

Dark Souls 2 is a dark fantasy, adventure with rpg elements.
As an avid rpg lover, this has made me play NONSTOP from release, barely trying many other games out. I may take a break now and then as I did when playing WoW, but never a break over a week, it truly is addicting because of its massive amount of items and playstyles available, always making me come back for more especially after its predecessor.
Story - The story is not quite as good as the first game, but serves the gameplay. The main problem I have with the story is the final boss and ending cutscene, feeling not quite fleshed out and simply telling you nothing much else is going to happen after. This may change with the 3rd dlc I hope.
- 8/10
Graphics - The environment is amazing, but not quite interconnected as its predecessor was.
The quality of the weapons, armour and spells are definitely some of the best looking out of most rpgs, although many of the bosses and enemies you cannot get their weapon and/or armour, you usually have an item very similar in looks to these missing items (except the old dragonslayer).
It could do with a bit more variation in beast or demon-like monsters, but has very well thought out enemy design.
- 9/10
Audio - The audio is quite displaced in a lot of areas, however where it is placed correctly, will give you the ability to percieve where the next enemies or traps will be. Very defined sounds such as torches and the occasional arrow or two will let you simply see by feeling where it came from.
The mirror knight pre-patch had a certain attack which the sound is bugged, being able to hear it even if your sound was on 0 ingame.
- 6/10
Gameplay - This is arguably what makes the souls series of games, with big expectations because of its predecessors.
First off, powerstanced weapons feel very weak with the biggest trade-off being stamina, when weapons two-handed will provide the same damage with less stamina, bigger poise-breaking and ultra/great weapon class's ability to not be parried gives them almost no utility. There are certain weapons that rise above however, such as dual rapiers, great hammers, straight swords and the specialized weapon such as the Warped Sword or the Majestic Greatsword.
I did feel as though a lot of weapon classes such as maces, dual wield axes, great axes, claws, dual wield halberds and ESPECIALLY reapers have very boring movesets (both axes and greataxes not so much, but could do with more imagination still). Dual wield with all of these weapons also in account, they simply need to be more worthy in combat by simply having more reach, speed and differing movesets than how they are currently, there's a reason almost no one uses these weapons outside of "cosplay" (dressing as a character from the series or other series etc.).
There is a BIG problem to do with animations in PvP, with the enemy standing still on your screen, yet hitting you.
There is also weird bug/implementation to do with poise, if you hit someone at the end of their dodge roll, they will take the damage yet not be staggered in any way, which they then will use to their advantage to backstab you. On the subject of poise, some weapons such as katanas seem to stagger you quite often, no matter how much poise you have.
Certain enemies seem to have very weird AI. One such being the fire salamanders. which will lock onto your character and never lose sight of you while propelling fireballs making it very hard to combat them even when you're right in their face. The salamander will propel fireballs which have a 1-3 second delay not even giving you time to run/heal.
Outside of these problems however, is the best experience in PvP you can find through challenge and tactics based gameplay using spacing and environment knowledge, weapon knowledge, prediction and using items to your advantage.
- 8/10
Community - The community is very split, with 50% being people who will "gank" (multiple people fighting one person), hack and be generally nasty towards other players.
The other 50% are the kind ones who will see you using just your bare fists (no vanq seal or caestus)/ladle/broken weapon and join in using the same items. There are also the players who "cosplay" and those who will help you with fight against a gank (with one of us being summoned and the other invading) or those who kill a ganking host with a lifedrain patch, which is just beautiful.
- 7/10
Overall, a 8/10 (This is reviewed before the final dlc release which may change my opinion on the title)

The RBR of motocross:
I wasn't all that impressed with Milestone's WRC series, but having raced, collided and wiped out in real life, this one blew me away.
My pros:
-Bikes generate ruts, and the track changes during the race.
-Independent center of gravities for bike/rider and independent wheel physics...During a wheelie, you can push a wheel down on a high speed turning woop and turn slightly (great one at the start of Si Racha).
-Landing sideways or preloading the suspension on a slide will snap the bike back and forth to the point where the rider gets thrown over the bike (nice!).
-If you're scrapping to clear a double you can bunny hop some to help clear a gap.
-Track friction and berms make sense.
Cons:
-Takes a few hours to make the controls feel like a bike. It's just part of the deal though. Not really a complaint.
-Scenery a bit dull for today's graphics, but bikes look great.
-Scrubs felt a bit baked, but it's alright.
With a few tweaks, making an enduro/Dakar/Romaniacs out of this game would be fantastic (even if it was one race). A separate game for Trials would also be pretty cool. I think these guys could pull it off.
