Fun little Pixle Shooter with some minor short commings.
Broforce has you take the role of a random 80's action hero parody as you shoot and blow up lots of stuff while trying to rescue fellow hero's and make it to the exit in this 2-D side scrolling platformer shooter.
The barebones plot is basically there as a joke to Action movies of the 80's and the America ♥♥♥♥ Yeah additude of that era.  Your shooting terrorists for freedom and america.  Thats it.  Its very tounge in cheek and since its barely there it won't get in the way of the gameplay.
The game handles very similarly to super meat boy but with lots of shooting and explosions.   You can shoot through nearly every surface of the game allowing for some intresting ways of tackling levels.  Enemies will kill you in a single hit and there can be a lot of them so its a nice balance between tatical and reflex gaming.
The most intresting mechanic is the Bros themselves.  You start off as a rambo clone with a machine gun, greanades, and one life but its not long before you find a POW and upon saving them you switch to a new unlocked Bro with different weapons and a different playstyle and you get an extra life.  Every time you save a POW or die you switch to a random Bro and every few POWs you save unlocks a new Bro.  This will constantly force you to change up your tactics and you'll want to keep playing to see the next movie parody Bro unlocked.
Outside of Unlocking Bros There are an intresting variety of enemies and hazords and some really cool boss fights to keep you entertained as well as online drop in drop out co-op play.  The campain itself will last you 5-7 hours and it lets you play from the start with all you unlocked Bros which adds to the replay value.
My only gripes are that the jumping is very floaty which lead to a lot of cheap deaths and that some Bros are way more useful then others.  You'll scream when your trying to past a wave of bullets and the game keeps giving you melee characters when all you want is a gun.
Overall the game is simple and fun with lots of colorful characters and a very aware sense of humor.  Ideal to pick up and play for a couple of hours at a time.

Seeing how this game's price has completely crashed during the Autumn sale, I figured I would add in my own two cents.
My dad introduced me to the original Homeworld when I was about 7 years old. That was about 13 years ago, and even after playing every single spaceship-related game I could get my hands on, I never found anything which went into quite as much depth with story, lore and gameplay as Homeworld.
Now believe me I was just as hyped as the next person when Homeworld: Remastered was announced - in fact my dad would tell you I nearly brought the ceiling down with my enthusiasm, especially when I discovered that it was Gearbox, well-known for producing the Borderlands series (which I am also a HUGE fan of) was in charge of spearheading the project and bringing it to us. When it came out I didn't really see much of the shtick it got for myself, but after taking more time to play it since I have unearthed its little issues that the original game lacks. The good thing about this though is that you get the original games bundled with the remastered versions, so if the Remastered versions' issues become a bit much for you, you can easily revert to them to take a break. Now I'll give a breakdown of my own personal pros and cons, make of them what you will!
PROS -
- The game is, of course, remastered - graphically speaking, the game is stunning - the lighting is perfection, the backgrounds of matches are perfect, and the various ships look beautiful with their new models - the frigates even have moving turrets, which I think was lacking in the original game. There is not a single flaw in the graphical side of the remastering, at least in my opinion.
- The campaigns for both games have remained pretty much untouched - but a new GUI allows for easier interaction with the game world and better control over what comes into your mothership and what leaves it.
- The ship upgrade system located under the research section allows players to upgrade the stats of their various ships, including damage, defense, health and occasionally speed. They can also be used to teach some ships new abilities. In the campaign mode you are limited to when you get these upgrades however as many of them tie into the story in various ways.
- The addition of mod support, although often shaky at times, does allow for the addition of custom races, ship logos, maps and I think even gameplay modes. Some of these mods can even be used in online play, which I think is fantastic.
- While the original Homeworld soundtrack has been left untouched and rightly so, the Homeworld 2 soundtrack recieved a remastering which has drastically improved the sound of its music, which was in the original game something of a partial failure (Some of the songs sounded shoddy or rushed for example but these issues have been fixed in the remastered soundtrack).
- The lore is extensive and beautiful for this game, but many people are often unaware of this without having access to the original Homeworld manual, which was a hand-me-down from my dad which I still read regularly. The details contained within the manual are available on the Homeworld wikia for those who are curious about learning the extensive background of this universe, as much of it isn't actually mentioned in-game or at least not in a way that some people would really understand or remember.
CONS -
- The original game didn't have any bugs or glitches that I can remember. This one has a great deal of them, however - simple things like unresponsive ships, the occasional crash and other silly things you could perhaps expect from a game, but still annoying due to how flawless the original felt.
- Mods often deselect themselves and don't load after being used in-game for only one match. Sometimes mods don't work at all or crash the game, which is appearntly a very common occurrence.
- The patches do help but often don't fix the really important issues, such as common issues with multiplayer and mods.
- Some gameplay aspects that people really enjoyed were for some reason removed, such as the ability to Salvage (why they even bothered leaving the poor little Salvage Corvette in the game is beyond me, considering that in the main storyline of Homeworld 1 they are practically useless after the 3rd chapter now and just sit there collecting dust until destroyed by enemies) and also the need to refuel ships. While I actually think of this as a good thing, there have been complaints about it and I can imagine that for some people it must have taken some of the survivability element away from them.
- Although I have no solid proof at this time, I've heard that there are serious issues with multiplayer on occasion. Multiplayer also allows you to play as any of the races from the two games, which in some cases could be a little unfair as the races from Homeworld 2 have packs of Interceptors rather than one Interceptor per construction (just an example, I know there are others too), as well as having better ships overall.
Overall I'd say this game is worth its sale price, but maybe is only worth its true retail price to the hardcore fans who will appreciate it and can ignore its flaws indefinitely.
Also another tip: If you are one of the owners of the original CD of the game which came with the soundtrack on CD, you don't need to buy the Homeworld 1 Remastered Soundtrack. It's literally the same music. If your CD is still around or in good condition, use that instead and save your money :P However the Homeworld 2 Remastered Soundtrack is different from the original as stated above and is very much worth the money in my opinion.

Papers, Please is a game that has you play the role of a border agent. That translates into having absolutely no fun allowed, being paid a lousy wage, and having to deal with plenty of people relying on you to get them through, even if in vain. Largely influenced by Soviet/communist undertones, the opening theme is the Arstotzka national anthem – a boorish blare of brass, and your primary objective is to scrape what you can from your job to provide for your family.

The beginning of the game outlines the basics for you and lets you do your thing; but increasingly becomes more complicated and vigorous as the game progresses. You will need to finely inspect each document (and eventually, person) for inconsistencies or contraband in the six minutes they give you. You are paid 5 credits per person correctly admitted, and it’s quickly spent at the end of the day on utilities such as rent, food, and medicine.

The hand-holding in this game is minimal; after the rules are outlined for you, you are allowed to screw up twice a day without a penalty, After that, the penalty is 5 credits and goes up from there. With all these bills to pay, fighting the clock can be difficult. If you aren’t expeditious with processing each immigrant or expat, they’ll have to go without food and/or heat for the day.

Besides family business, the emotional impact the player receives from the game is extremely subjective. You could get all emotional and illegally allow a man’s wife across the border as easily as you can refuse her entry for having no valid passport. Apart from a few specific moments, there is no reprisal against you for following the rules against your own values.

In that regard, you are given a wide assortment of choices to make throughout the game, especially in the later days (levels). The legal option is not always the best choice, but neither is the humanitarian one. Everything beyond what has been spelled out in the rulebook is a gray area left for you to decide, and it’s often someone else’s problem. Above all else, you must provide for yourself and your family. Failure to do so results in a game over, but you’re always able to retry the same day again or start anew if you wish.

Sound and graphics aren’t necessarily given an emphasis in this game. It’s not necessarily a bad thing; the visuals are minimalist (similar to that of the early SNES era), and the audio for dialogue is composed of little more than a few unintelligible sound bytes, but they both serve their purpose in purporting a bland atmosphere for a game whose mood is purposefully bland.

Papers, Please is an anti-fun simulation of an occupation; somewhat like Hilton Ultimate Team Play. Your ability to be swift, accurate and conscientious is constantly tested, and your fate is ultimately decided upon these three attributes. You are bound to slip up one way or another on your first run through, but your ability to compensate for it and excel all depends on your willingness to do your job well. After all, there is no room for slackers in Arstotzka.

This game will destroy your life. Played it obsessively for months when I first bought it off their website. This is a true engineering game. If you like SpaceChem or Infinifactory this game is for you. I love the formerly-mentioned but Factorio actually gives you a reason to break your brain trying to make your fancy automations.
I would highly recommend NOT looking at guides for ideal conveyor belt setups for the first few dozen hours. The sense of accomplishment that comes with automating something in half the space as your last try is astounding. Don't be intimidated by the $20 price tag. A dollar per hour? Forget about it. Try pennies per hour played.

I was kind of surprised honestly, because I was expecting more or less just another 3rd person hack and slash with platforming elements which I might get bored of, and although it doesn't do anything new, it pulls off what it does have very well and kept me playing till the end.
In short, you find yourself in a post-apocalyptic world, having just escaped one of the mech ships where you were kept as a slave. The main character, Monkey, is incredibly agile and proficient at climbing stuff, in addition to wielding a staff with deadly skills to take down hostile mechs. He teams up with an attractive hacker girl, Trip, who keeps him under her control via a headband at first and later becomes more of an ally.
Perhaps the most alluring part of the gameplay are the constantly changing challenges and puzzles, most of which involve working together with your NPC ally. For example, some sections require you to tell Trip when to activate a decoy hologram in order to distract enemy turrets and allow you to get closer for a takedown. Then there are also sections where you use your staff as a shooting weapon to engage in long-range fights, and also sections where you use a hover pad called cloud to solve environmental puzzles or even fight a boss.
Although the overall game was fun, I do think the first half of it felt stronger and more focused. There was more variety of things in that, and also better looking environments in my opinion. A huge post-apocalyptic city taken over by plant life is just a more interesting place to explore than inside of enormous factories which comprise most of the second half of the game. At the very least the game didn't overstay its welcome and none of it felt padded.
Only one type of challenge irked me greatly, and that's those blasted landmines. Most of the time you die to them because the area of their blast effect is not clear, so you end up getting caught out when you're nowhere near the damn things. And it's insta-kill too. Gladly they're only in two parts of the game and hence only a minor irritation.
Visuals are really beautiful. Both as far as character designs and also most of the setting, environments, and style. Voice acting also great. And everything is rather straight-forward and intuitive, ranging from climbing and ending with combat. Getting a chance to level up some skills and attributes is also a nice addition.
All 3 of the main characters were quite interesting, and the story, although in the background most of the time, was good enough to keep things going along. Won't spoil anything, but the conclusion was rather surprising, almost out of the blue and unexpected, but I suppose it made the game end with a punch.
In general, an enjoyable game on all fronts and one of the better 3rd person action adventure games I've played. Well worth getting, especially if it's on sale. Highly advised to play with a gamepad.

Seriously though, ENSLAVED is a beautiful ride through amazing scenery with gameplay that reminds me of good old N64 and PS2 adventure games, but with a more adult approach. Even the subtle love story (or should I rather call it triangle?) is well placed and doesn't in any way conflict with the story and atmosphere.
Monkey is a durable protagonist and keeps up with the shenanigans Trip does to him, even though at first I just wanted to kill her ALL. THE. TIME. You will hate her and you will learn to love her.

A solid action adventure game based on tactical combat and environmental puzzles. The narrative is gripping, the characters compelling, and though the story is linear, it takes place in an immersive, beautifully realized world.
The voice acting is especially superb. Though there aren't many characters in the game, the actors make them feel rounded and real. Also astounding is the main character's animation: truly satisfying as he fluidly jumps and rolls and slinks up and down walls.
This is actually two games in one! In addition to the main story, there is an extra game based on one of the characters, offering a different style of stealth-based combat and a more lighthearted, humorous narrative. This extra game is surprisingly long and comprehensive.
Just to nitpick, I'll point out that ENSLAVED has a few minor weaknesses. Combat on “normal” difficulty can be too easy, and at times feels repetitive and grindy. There is a skill upgrade system based on collecting experience orbs, and though it's satisfying to gobble them up, there are just far too many in the game (sometimes you might feel like you're playing Pac-Man). Generally, the game could have been better with more variety: more characters, more types of enemies, more ways to earn skill points.
Also, controls can be a bit wonky. When you're just exploring an area and rolling around when you want to jump, it's annoying. But in the middle of combat it can be frustrating to die because your character didn't do what you thought it should do.
These problems are not very serious and did not keep me from thoroughly enjoying the game. I strongly recommend it for fans of action adventure!

The first thing I noticed on playing HW:RM was how the HW2 UI and seemed to be everywhere. It was as if the whole HW1 game had been transplanted into the HW2 engine... turned out I wasn't far off.
Unfortunately there are a few things that bring the quality of the remaster down as a whole - players aren't able to experience HW1 with it's Ballistics physics engine intact (shots fired could be evaded or go on to hit something else), instead shots fired by ships generally always hit (some RNG seems to be involved) the selected target as in HW2. This is a large part of what made HW1 stand out from other RTSes at the time (in fact most RTSes nowadays) and made certain manoeuvres such as doing increased damage to ships when attacking them from behind, etc, possible since damage resistance was also modelled as part of this engine. As far as I can recall this was not something that was taken through to the original HW2 or the Remaster. Pretty big deal in my opinion.
Formations in general are completely borked, meaning that a lot of the tactical (and at the time, genre defying) flavour of HW1 is completely absent; while I don't particularly miss the fiddly micromanagement and lack of context sensitive clicks, I do miss the extra depth of tactics that formations offered. If Gearbox ever start work on a Homeworld: Cataclysm remaster (the original HW:C = my favourite game of the series) they
to get this fixed. Good news is that a patch may be on it's way to restore formations to their intended form.
Overall I still enjoyed playing through the HW1:RM campaign, and ultimately found it more "playable" than the original (especially while using a Steam Controller). Basically I found the game easier and more accessible than it used to be, which for newcomers and busy old-schoolers like me is not a bad thing. I think it's a huge shame we never got to see the original ballistics physics etc on todays capable machines however.
Being completely honest I originally played Homeworld 2 the least of the games in the series, however I feel that the remaster did a solid job of restoring and enhancing the game for compatibility while staying pretty faithful to the original.
The remastered graphics
shine here, fleet battles are a thing of beauty. Seriously, pick a fight and soak in that goodness, JUST DO IT
Since the remaster has been so good to the game I have in effect enjoyed HW2 anew - I'd basically offer this collection as an instant recommendation for fans of the original. The only issues HW2 fans might have is that the voice actors from HW1 have been used instead of the ones they may remember from HW2, as well as a few other VA changes here and there (notably Makaan).
Gearbox have been patching things up slowly, with various bugs and issues like bad pathfinding (crashing into asteroids) being fixed. There are still issues like formations not working properly and friendly ships merrily continuing to pour heavy firepower on ships you are boarding/salvaging to add to your fleet, amongst other things.
Scoring based on faithfulness to the spirit of the originals;
Glorious hi-res Fleet battles and Furballs, gorgeously updated and retouched. The UI scales perfectly and there are sliders allowing you to adjust the scale of varying UI components manually.
Remastered audio (apparently; I can't tell I'm no audiophile), original voice actors (notably Fleet Command/ Mothership from HW1) brought back and re-recorded. HW Classic sound effects are particularly dated and low-def when compared to the remaster, so good job I guess.
In regards to HW1 the best I can say is some patching is definitely needed.
HW2 on the other hand is in a good place. If Gearbox attempt a remake of Homeworld: Cataclysm, I hope they get a better handle on what made these games great in the first place.
As a Remastered Collection It's a good update on the originals, however it's not perfect by a long shot. It's also a shame that some of the technical limitations that held the old games back have not really been challenged (in fact the opposite, much has been dumbed down). The unfulfilled potential is pretty crushing in my opinion.
Multiplayer is also a bit hit and miss, in that Gearbox are clearly putting a lot of work into the facilitation of mp matches, but the bugs/missing mechanics are keenly apparent at higher levels of play.
In any case I have to thank Gearbox for bringing back these games, and can only recommend this Collection as an essential for RTS fans, and those gamers who enjoy a good story alongside a challenge.

If faithfully capturing and recreating the first Alien movie's look and feel were enough to make a good game, this game would be no less than fantastic. Sadly, a game and a compelling story need more than that - interesting characters worth caring about, and six letters: PACING.
The formula "activate X, oh no, access to X is blocked by Y, you need to get a Z to get there, oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ the Z is supposed to be in the A, but someone took it to B and to get there you need to get rid of C" is compelling once or twice, but if the whole game consists of setbacks, it gets old and tedious. The same can be said for a Ripley crashing through the floor and losing progress / being diverted: For god's sakes, it can be done once, or twice, but do it more often and players become incredibly fatigued about something that is supposed to be HORROR.
About the gadgets: I very much liked the idea of plasma torches and Security Access Tuners. but to have actually three levels of them just becomes repetitive, as well as having to re-start generators and all that - all of the stuff looks great, but simply is used to often. Why? I don't know, perhaps to give the game some additional length? I honestly prefer playing a three-hour game that has my interest for the whole three hours, than having to push myself through a seven-hour-deal of repetition with little variety.
The worst thing however is this: A game that is so unforgiving for every little mistake should either auto-save on every corner or GIVE PLAYERS THE ABILITY TO SAVE ANYWHERE, ANYTIME. Yes, I understand that the concept of manual Quicksave is alien (hah) on console games, and their progresskeeping mechanics swap over to PC games as well nowadays, and yes I understand the argument that it would break the sense of risk and fear. But I really can't afford having to repeat 20 minutes of gameplay again and again just because there is no save point between here and there.
It simply all adds to the frustation with this game which could have been so much, but all the beauty it offers is swallowed up by all the repetition you have to suffer through for various reasons.
If you love the original Alien film like I do, this game is a must-play.

Dark Souls II (DaS 2) is the sequel to FROM Software's dungeon-crawling (2011) hit, DARK SOULS. True to the action adventure setting of the game, players will march their way through decayed prisons, toxic shrouded windmills, lava engulfed castles and other perilous environments. Much like the original game, DaS 2 features a high-level of difficulty. There's a reason why Namco uses the slogan "Prepare to Die" to advertise these games.
The combat itself can be described as tactical action-rpg, sort of like The Legend of Zelda with 100 time the depth. Unlike games like action RPGs like Torchlight (which are focused on killing hordes of enemies) Dark Souls is focused on dances between you and a few opponents. Spacing, dodging and timing are extremely important. Learning the attack patterns of your enemy is paramount to winning in this game--if you rush through encounters you will die, over and over and over and over again. If you poorly place a swing or are a bit too close to an opponent you will be
. Enemies hit for a large percentage of your health and will knock you down if you aren't heavily armored. If your target has buddies supporting him, expect them to take advantage of your mistake and eviscerate you.
While the combat is certainly the highlight of a Souls game, paying attention to the enviroment is just as important. Traps and ambushes are around many of this game's corners--taking things slow will be etched into your skull before you get a couple hours into this game. Most of the adventure comes from surviving and making it to the boss--puzzles and exploration, while present, aren't the main focus here.
Throughout Dark Souls 2, one will find dozens of unique weapons and magics that offer all sorts of ways to slaughter the grotesque creatures that you will be facing. What is really exciting is when you see an awe-inspiring weapon/armor set that an enemy is wielding. Most games would leave you fantasizing about what it would be like to use those armaments. In Dark Souls 2, those enemies will usually have a small chance to drop their various weapons, giving you weapons that have both unique statistical properties and (oftentimes) unique attack animations.
As expected from a FROM title, DaS 2 features a pitch-perfect art style that realizes the hopeless atmosphere of the game's world. Enemies are hideously deformed ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥izations of their original form, varying from the hollowed out decay of the undead soldiers to the grossly mutated denizens of some of the later locales.
That said, the game isn't without it's issues. Unlike Dark Souls 1 (which had a truly interesting story hidden in the subtext of the enviroment and item descriptions), Dark Souls 2's story isn't very entralling or all that coherent (I'll say it involves a lot of predestination for the sake of making it seem like Dark Souls 1). The online features have some baffling design choices (look up soul memory) and the netcode is truly awful for PvP. The game's world is less of a Metroidvania and more of a series of (bafflingly connected) corridors that occasionally branch out. The areas are still well-designed, but they feel like pieces designed by committee rather than the "home-made" locations in Dark Souls.
While it's not without it's issues, Dark Souls II offers a solid action adventure and anyone who is interested in high-difficulty, tactical action-RPGs should check this title out.

I bought this game on Day 1 and have seen it through all its permutations since.  I can personally confirm it was every bit as buggy and otherwise flawed as reviews stated.  That said, the version we now have is a very stable, engaging strategy game.  The DLCs and the Emperor Edition allow you to play in many different classical time periods and as one of the wide array of states operating in those eras, and there is enough variety between factions to support different styles of play.  Roman factions support the more stodgy, inexorable legions rolling slowly over everything with artillery and heavy infantry, while Eastern European and Middle Eastern factions support a hit-and-run, fast mover approach with lighter infantry and missile cavalry (absolutely infuriating to fight against as the former).
Fans of other TW games will notice significant differences in gameplay mechanics, particularly the Food system (buildings will generally trade off food for public order or vice versa) and in the inability to recruit armies or navies without generals.  The Families system, also, provides an internal threat and added challenge for the time when you become the scariest thing on the map and the worst possible thing you could face is your mirror image.  For those who find these and other systems lacking in some way, the game has been heavily supported by the TW modding community, offering everything from extra units to balance changes to complete overhauls.
The Pros (as of the time of writing)
+ Beautiful graphics on the campaign and battle maps
+ Stable game
+ Huge battles (typical TW)
+ Devilish agents, reminiscent of Shogun 2
+ Varied unit roster between factions
+ Naval battles are frantic and can morph into land battles
+ Reasonably well-balanced factions, where Rome can be given a run for its money
+ MP campaign is now stable.
+ Battle AI has improved in defensive battles for towns, where they will no longer sit still and get murdered by artillery (a fix Shogun 2 needed, also).
+ More complex than Civilization V
The Cons
- The AI are fine as trading partners, but as allies are useless at best and problem children at worst
-  Battle AI in the field uses fairly predictable tactics.
- The strategic resource system could be more in depth.  Few buildings or units require particular resources, so they are more or less interchangeable with each other.  It is not, however, the afterthough resources were in Shogun 2.
- Only one civil war can occur per game, allowing a player to go berserk after quelling it.
- Territories can't be traded.  I liked being able to buy regions peacefully in Empire and Napoleon, but here you have to fight for all of it.
- AI relies heavily on militia, making large but weak stacks
- In MP campaigns, what a player can and can't do on the off-turn can be frustrating (you can change technologies and tax settings, but can't even inspect diplomatic standing)
- It's not as complex as Europa Universalis IV
Most of these cons can be fixed with mods, however.  The underlying game is (now) a solid, enjoyable experience and I would recommend it to strategy game enthusiasts.

This game is nothing short of mechanical crack!
You start as a survivor of a spaceship crash on an alien world. You want off said rock, because the native bugs are none-too-friendly. So you begin by very simple mining, smelting, and assembly of increasingly high-tech components to survive, then industrialize. Most games would have you do this yourself, with your own inventory and crafting benches. Not this. You will need tens of thousands of units of coal, iron ore, and copper rolling into your facilities by automated railways and load/unload terminals before you even get close to accomplising what you need. You have to be the engineer building up what you need piece by piece from a huge array of low and high technology. Coal fired mining rigs, conveyors, splitters, inserters (robot arms to move things), flying logistical and construction robots are just a few of the many things you need to use to achieve your ulitmate goal - build a huge rocket and get off this rock before the natives get too restless for you to handle.
The trick is that the more you industrialize, the larger an area around your facilities you pollute. Bugs don't like pollution, and spawn attacks on you from each hive that falls within your pollution zone. Of course, you can build a truck, even a tank, fuel it up, load up on ammo, and go out and erase these hives to thin out the attacks if you like. You'd also be well advised to build walls and gun turrets to defend your far-flung mining complexes, because the maps get large. Thats why you'll be building diesel locomotives and laying rails to reach these resources deposits and meet your production needs.
As an aside the game can run on a potato, which is always a nice thing for gamers on a tight budget.
10/10 Would assemble mechanical crack again and again!
Definitely worth the $20. It's very addicting, so pay attention to how long you spend playing.

There is fun to be had here! Absolutely! When the level blow up in absolut madness and chaos, when you moaw your way through hordes of enemies as their guts fly around, the game can be absolutely enjoyable!
But after some playtime I realised the problems with this game, and they are not minor! I try to explain every negative point as well as I can, so you can (or maybe not) approve:
- Non free choosable charakters: Everytime you start a level or free a bro (get an extra life) you are transformed into a random bro. Well I read that some people like this idea. I don't. Why? Because it sometimes does not work!
What do you say? You are on one side of the map with 10 enemies on the other? Better don't get the flamethrower dude. Wups, dead.
Some charakteres like Chuck Norris and Mister T are basically just made for close combat. So if you find yourself in a situation where you need a charakter with a long range weapon you are basically ♥♥♥♥ed! Nothing you can do about it. Why don't they just let you cycle free through the charakters (at least the ones you have captures within the level)? Before you say, that this would destroy the mission flow, No! Dying because you got the wrong charakter causes the mission flow to be destroyed. It just is completely nervwrecking if you managed to get passed that one tricky situation and die because you get the wrong charakter with only 1 life left!
- Random damage system.
Bros die one hit, you get one free life with every bro you have rescued. That is okay. But actually damage taken by f.e. explosions seem to be completely randomised. Sometimes you die, sometimes you don't! The problem is, that you can not predict anything and basically always have to stop before you shoot those barrels because you don't know if, or if not the explosion will kill you.
- No up or down aiming. I am NOT speaking of 360° controlls here. I am speaking of the possibility to f.e. press "up" or "down" on the d-pad / keyboard to aim up or down. If you stand on or under a cage you can not simply fire it from beneath or above, you have to maneuver yourself next to it in order to shoot it. Even the old metal slugs had this "feature". Wtf? Sometimes those cages are at a cliffside, so instead of shooting it safely from above (WHILE YOUR ARE STANDING ON IT DAMNIT!), you have to carefully navigate yourself to its right side. This is plain stupid and a really missing feature!
- HORRIBLE SENSITIVE JUMPCONTROLLS!
This one is the biggest point of them all. Jump and Run is NOT fun! The floor seems to be buttered, because you always slide a bit. And the controlls are so sensitive, that the slightest and shortest press on that button will send you directly into your doom. If you have to be centimeter precise, the controlls just won't let you! Every Jump is a leap of faith. This is one of the most important and basic things in a 2D - Sidescroller. So why did they ♥♥♥♥ this up?
- Sometimes not responding controlls:
Yep that happened, I pressed a button and the charakter wouldn't act. After pressing the button again it worked. Absolutely satisfying in a game with one hit death!
Like i said earlier: There is a lot of fun here, but  for me it is just not recommandable in its current state! Controlls need a HUGE makeover, and the balancing needs some work aswell.
Everything is there for a great game! Visuals are great, the gameplay itself (if it is working) is satisfying, but that execution is just horrible.

If you don't like this review, let me know!

This was actually really fun! It's a straightforward AAA-style game as far as things go - linear level design, linear story, lots of fighting mooks and solving simple level puzzles. But everything is done to a nice degree of quality. The art is lovely - this is one of the best-looking post-apocalyptic settings I've seen, and what few characters there are are surprisingly well-animated with character and individuality (it helps there are really only three characters worth mentioning). The voice acting is generally good, the characters are likeable and their relationships generally believable (though a few things, like Pigsy's rivalry with Monkey, feel a bit rushed narratively speaking), the story is very basic but still solid, and the dialog writing is pretty natural and can actually get pretty funny sometimes.
Gameplay is really focused on two pillars, combat and puzzle-platforming. Combat is pretty straightforward, with a few possible moves and enemy types providing just enough variety in the enemies that combat doesn't get too repetitive. You've also got your companion Trip to coordinate with - she can setup decoys that distract enemy fire, or you can shout out to draw their attention and send her running around. Coordinating with her works well, and is a simple but nice way of reinforcing their narrative relationship through gameplay systems.
The level puzzles are generally simple, and the platforming is great fun - Monkey is the most hilariously athletic parkour athlete ever featured in video games. Seriously, he looks like 100 kg of solid muscle but this guy can fling himself ten meters in the air and do aerial backflips between bars across huge chasms. It's fun to watch, that's for sure.
It's not perfect, of course. Sometimes the camera can get a little wonky, though, switching angles suddenly or getting into awkward positions; and because movement is often screen-relative and not character-relative, this can throw you off and require a second to adjust how you're controlling the character. There's a hoverboard that's activated in a few sections, but controlling it is a bit awkward - it's both slippery and unresponsive, so it's easy to go flying off platforms or into walls. And the default settings for ranged weapon aiming sensitivity are just awful - go crank that stuff up to max.
There's a skill tree system, but to get the most out of it I think you really need to scour the levels thoroughly - I made a point to collect the XP I could see and only maxed out two of the four skill trees, with a couple of helpful skills from the remaining two, but achievements indicate it should be possible to unlock all the skills. The rest of that XP is probably hidden well out of sight.
But for the most part, I had a lot of fun with this. It's reasonably short, has a nice and simple action-adventure storyline, I liked both the protagonists as well as the world, and the gameplay was paced and varied out just enough that things never felt repetitive. Time and money well-spent, I say.

So a funny story about how I found this game and why it is a hidden gem to me. I took some bad advice from a friend who told me this was a really bad game way back when it first came out so I have never played it before. With the recent success of Ninja Theory's new game, Hellblade, I decided to see what other games the company has made and I came across this. Seeing as how, for obvious reasons, I am no longer friends with that person and remembering that everything he says is Bull$h!t, I decided to give this game a try. Man, I was not disappointed!
The story is great. A fantastic group of characters who do a good job on the acting front. The characters are likeable, funny, interesting, and are capable of depth. Also since this game came out awhile back, before all this SJW feminist garbage took over our society, they were able to introduce a vulnerable female character that wasnt afraid to admit when she was scared or needed help. It was very refreshing. The pacing did start to drag a bit toward the ending but all in all, it was very good. It also had a nice little twist at the end.
Gameplay was fun. It is basically a platformer with some combat. The platforming reminded me a bit of Prince of Persia (minus the wall running). It was fast paced, stylized, and fun. Game is also pretty linear. Some mild exploration in a few places but nothing major. Combat is also good. Nothing super special but it does the job. Kind of reminded me of a basic God of War. There is light and heavy attacks, blocking, dodging, a few finishing moves on certain enemies, and some cool slow motion effects when you kill the last enemy in a group. I enjoyed it for what it was.
The graphics really aren't all that great, but seeing as how this game was originally made back in 2010, it is forgivable and probably would have been decent for back then. However, there is one weird thing and that is the shadows on the character models during cutscenes. Not sure what is going on there but they are very odd. Like weird stripes that fade in and out, and it is just odd to describe. Overall nothing that is a gamebreaker though and is mostly fine.
The game runs really well. Almost any graphics card and processor will run this game no problem, doesn't take much. It also runs fine on Windows 7. No crashes, no glitches, butter smooth. This was back when games weren't coming out half baked all the time so it was good as to be expected. Also some people were complaining about camera issues however, I didn't seem to have any. I had no problem figuring out where to go or what to do.
Everything considered this was a really fun game. Can't believe this flew under my radar for so long and I'm glad I got the chance to play it. If you haven't ever had the chance I really recommend giving it a try, it is well worth it. Can't wait to see what Ninja Theory does next after Hellblade now.

Dishonored 2 is a game that I wish I could recommend. Despite lacking some of the polish of its predecessor, it does a lot of things correctly from a gameplay perspective. It took the system of powers and stealth that defined the original Dishonored, and gave them massive improvements (doubly so, thanks to Emily's appearence). In-particular, I am a huge fan of the option to turn powers off, turning an already moderately punishing experience into all-out madness. This is something that the original lacked, and Arkane's foresight to include this among other features deserves praise. The environments are extremely well-imagined, and its design is clever. It's a sequel that truly lives up to the original, which is something I don't say often,
So, why do I not recommend it then? For the same reason that a lot of other people don't. While the game might be pretty, my moderately beefy desktop runs like a toaster while playing this game. Using a NVIDIA GTX 1060 graphics card, 8 GB of RAM, and an Intel i5-4440 processor, I can barely squeak this game to acceptable frame rates. On some graphically intense levels, like the Conservatory, my PC just gives out under the massive load, forcing me to turn every option to the lowest setting possible and pray that it doesn't decide to graphically freeze for 30 seconds. These problems alone have turned me off from playing even a second time, and that's a damn shame because there's good stuff here. I had hoped for a patch a few months down the road that would improve performance, but that is starting to look like a pipe-dream now. If that patch is ever released, I will instantly change my review. This is a great game, and I'd love to play it again. I just physically can't for now. If you have an extra-beefy computer, consider buying. If you don't, but also play occasionally on consoles, consider buying (if on sale) for you PS4 or XBox One. After reading some reviews, I'd conclude that it's a much better, much more optimized game on consoles.
Overall, Dishonored 2 is a game that I'd love to recommend, but can't. I want to love this game for everything amazing it brings to the table, but I can't. It's major performance flaws shatter everything amazing about it, turning easily a 9.0/10 adventure into a 5.4/10. Buy if you have a beefy computer, or better yet, go for the console versions.

I don't remember exactly how old I was but at some point during my childhood, after much begging and pleading, I convinced my parents to let me watch the original Alien movie. I remember my mother telling me "If you have nightmares you still have to sleep in your own bed... understand?" and I agreed to these terms. I had no idea what I was getting myself into... no idea whatsoever.
To this day Alien and the sequel Aliens are two of the most intensely unsettling and scary films I've seen. "Great, so what does this have to do with Alien: Isolation?" you ask. There have been multiple attempts through the years to port the intensity of the Alien franchise into a viable video game but in my opinion all of them have fallen short - all of them except for this one. Alien: Isolation is the real deal. If you're a fan of xenomorphs, the low-fi technology of the future envisioned in the late 70s and early 80s, being scared out of your mind and the haunting solitude of space stop what you're doing right now and buy this game.

Great respect for the source material, setting, atmosphere, and audio are not enough to save Alien: Isolation from being a broken mess.
The controls are often unresponsive, the interface is mediocre (and obtrusive), the save system -- okay, wait. I actually like the idea behind it, but I had to replay the entirety of four different missions multiple times due to a loading loop error. Each time, I was able to get things back on track aside from the final level (mission 19) where the game inexplicably stuck a dead body at Ripley's feet. I would have had to replay mission 18 again to hopefully solve this problem, and it would've taken a lot of money for me to ever play that one again. Or mission 17. Or mission 16. Or...
If you're wondering how I racked up the final achievements despite being unable to move, I had to download someone else's save just so I could complete my game. Utter nonsense.
Oh how I wish this was the only bug in the game. It isn't. Not by a longshot. It merely is the most crippling and, literally, game-breaking of them all.
The pacing and actual gameplay have too much of a negative effect to recommend Alien: Isolation. Maybe if it was much shorter, tighter, had less to collect and, rather, had a stronger emphasis on weaving a compelling narrative, and... oh, yeah, it didn't keep eating my damn saves, I'd probably have enjoyed my experience.
If it wasn't for the save issue, I *may* have marked this as a recommended title (to be purchased only during a 75% sale), but honestly, watching Alien 10 times in a row would've been less tedious and monotonous than playing Alien: Isolation.
I guess there's a reason why this developer typically makes RTS games rather than these types. Stick to what you're good at, Creative Assembly. From what I've briefly experienced, you are quite good at strategy titles. Please leave Alien: Isolation II (Aliens: Isolation?) to another team.
I really wanted to love this game. I really did. Why else would I have spent 5-6 hours fiddling with saves, verifying files, replaying the same missions over again, and even resorting to other people's saves if I didn't? Unfortunately... well, you (possibly) read the review.
Hopefully you, if you choose to ignore my warnings, have better luck.

Like its predecessor, Dark Souls II adds meaning to its experience by having strict consequences. You cannot take enemies lightly. Even the easiest monster in the game remains a threat throughout. A dark corridor may bring swift death if you run in screaming “YOLO”. And yet in spite of seeming so rigid and punishing, Dark Souls II is fun.
At the start, you create a character from a selection of archetypes. You can be a spellcaster, or a swashbuckler, or someone that likes to hold giant swords in each hand. You could even go weaponless, there is much power in pugilism. You start off weak, with low values that represent the many aspects of your character, like how much health you have, how fast you are, how much equipment you can carry, and so on. As you explore and kill monsters, you’ll gain Souls: a precious commodity that is used to improve the stats of your choosing. But until you spend these Souls at a specific place, they’re at risk. If you get killed, you’ll respawn at the last bonfire you touched, but the Souls you’ve collected have dropped where you died. You’ll need to go fetch them without dying, or risk losing them. It sounds harsh, but it adds excitement. Do you press on, or play it safe and go back?
You’re not alone in Dark Souls II. If connected to the internet, you can occasionally see the ghosts of other players around you. Players can leave each other messages in the ground, helpful tips, inspiration, or deception. By placing special Summon Signs, you can be asked to assist another player in their copy of the world, or bring players to yours. You might even get invaded by another player who’s only goal is to kill you. There are a lot of complex systems at work governing this “ambient multiplayer”. Players can even join special Covenants that are worked into this system tightly. If you join the Blue Sentinels, you’ll be automatically summoned to aid a player who’s been invaded. Players looking to help others fight bosses can join Heirs of the Sun. More eclectic Covenants include the Bell Keepers, who exist only to hinder other players from ringing a bell in a specific area. Or the Rat King Covenant whose members guard a crypt full of traps.
If you’ve heard about the series’ alleged difficulty, it might sound strange to refer to it as “fun”. Often, those who tried the games and found them too hard, accuse those who do like them of being masochists. But that’s a shallow viewpoint. The Souls series became popular not only by being good, well-designed games. It’s just that, with much of the modern hand-holding in games, many have forgotten (or have yet to realize) that failing, challenge, and figuring things out is fun. Dark Souls II isn’t even that hard by classic game standards. There are some big franchises from the  PlayStation 2 era that can make a grown man cry. Dark Souls II, and its brethren, were made in spite of today’s push in gaming to make sure the player is having fun, long before giving them any challenge. While this tactic does work, especially with the easily amused, it devalues the experience somewhat. By contrast, Dark Souls II does not talk down to the player. It expects them to be intelligent, patient creatures that are interested yet cautious. There is an incredible thrill in exploring the unknown, of being afraid of what might lurk around the corner. But you need to experience that for yourself to feel it. You can be told what skydiving is like, but that will never be the same as actually jumping out of a plane. The only real barrier to having fun in Dark Souls II is impatience.
Even though it is conceptually more refined than the first game, Dark Souls II was released too soon it seems. It needed more time to cook in the oven. There are technical inconsistencies, like framerate issues, though nothing as bad as Blighttown from Dark Souls. There were cutbacks to the new game engine, specifically, the much-touted lighting system. The lore is also more fragmented in its presentation. The first game had a carefully constructed silent narrative that led the player through it, where the environment worked in concert with precious descriptions found in talking to NPCs and on items. Dark Souls II has all of this, but it just isn’t as cohesive. You can make a story of it all, eventually, but it will forever remain open to interpretation.
In spite of all this, it does improve on many of Dark Souls’ biggest flaws. The biggest single improvement being the “end game” of Dark Souls, which was rushed. The sequel has a better build up to its climax, with far more content after the first time the credits roll. This might be a bit of a spoiler, but it’s worth knowing. In the original, “New Game Plus” just upped the difficulty but in Dark Souls II, each successive New Game Plus remixes the game. It adds in new enemy placement, enemy types, and unlocks new weapons, gear and items to find. Combined with the Covenants being more in-depth and designed for long-term play, Dark Souls II has everything that matters where it counts. Even if the execution isn’t as good as it could have been.

I bought this game on Day 1 and have seen it through all its permutations since.  I can personally confirm it was every bit as buggy and otherwise flawed as reviews stated.  That said, the version we now have is a very stable, engaging strategy game.  The DLCs and the Emperor Edition allow you to play in many different classical time periods and as one of the wide array of states operating in those eras, and there is enough variety between factions to support different styles of play.  Roman factions support the more stodgy, inexorable legions rolling slowly over everything with artillery and heavy infantry, while Eastern European and Middle Eastern factions support a hit-and-run, fast mover approach with lighter infantry and missile cavalry (absolutely infuriating to fight against as the former).
Fans of other TW games will notice significant differences in gameplay mechanics, particularly the Food system (buildings will generally trade off food for public order or vice versa) and in the inability to recruit armies or navies without generals.  The Families system, also, provides an internal threat and added challenge for the time when you become the scariest thing on the map and the worst possible thing you could face is your mirror image.  For those who find these and other systems lacking in some way, the game has been heavily supported by the TW modding community, offering everything from extra units to balance changes to complete overhauls.
The Pros (as of the time of writing)
+ Beautiful graphics on the campaign and battle maps
+ Stable game
+ Huge battles (typical TW)
+ Devilish agents, reminiscent of Shogun 2
+ Varied unit roster between factions
+ Naval battles are frantic and can morph into land battles
+ Reasonably well-balanced factions, where Rome can be given a run for its money
+ MP campaign is now stable.
+ Battle AI has improved in defensive battles for towns, where they will no longer sit still and get murdered by artillery (a fix Shogun 2 needed, also).
+ More complex than Civilization V
The Cons
- The AI are fine as trading partners, but as allies are useless at best and problem children at worst
-  Battle AI in the field uses fairly predictable tactics.
- The strategic resource system could be more in depth.  Few buildings or units require particular resources, so they are more or less interchangeable with each other.  It is not, however, the afterthough resources were in Shogun 2.
- Only one civil war can occur per game, allowing a player to go berserk after quelling it.
- Territories can't be traded.  I liked being able to buy regions peacefully in Empire and Napoleon, but here you have to fight for all of it.
- AI relies heavily on militia, making large but weak stacks
- In MP campaigns, what a player can and can't do on the off-turn can be frustrating (you can change technologies and tax settings, but can't even inspect diplomatic standing)
- It's not as complex as Europa Universalis IV
Most of these cons can be fixed with mods, however.  The underlying game is (now) a solid, enjoyable experience and I would recommend it to strategy game enthusiasts.

Came to Rome 2 after Medieval 2, been playing TW for years. At first I was overwhelmed as Medieval 2 is pretty strait-forward, while here there are many subtle things to learn. Now the game is extremely deep, I'm just doing my first campaign as the Seleucids, and still discovering stuff.
Many great factions yet to explore in campaign, but the battles are the best in a TW game so far. Collision isn't perfect yes, but the blood, the sounds of soldiers speak, the graphics look good even though I'm on a laptop. The variety of units is staggering, and they are beautifull. Aside from the different uniforms and armour, you have female warriors (which are often better than their male counterparts), armored knights/cataphracts, arnored elephants, war dogs of various kinds, armored camels even. And I don't have every DLC out there with new units...
What do I miss from Medival II though? First the research system wasn't there, and I love that it's here but - It's overly complex. Too many techs, some just give bonuses and shouldn't be gateways to Temples or advanced barracks. Core tech aside and auxiliary tech aside. And if you do leave it there, make several tech's researchable together, one military one civilian let's say.
Secondly we do miss core stuff such as roads, where are they? Romans were famous for them, others built too, it should be in. Same for walls, built automaticlly as you advance your city and I can't configure them. What If I want an advanced city with wooden walls, because it's far away, and a small village with catapult towers, becuase that's where my food suplly is? And forts, castles of some sort, everyone did build them. No it's not a European invention.
Thirldy when doing a custom battle, why can't we have sunset or sunrise? Only day and night? On Medieval II it made for some really atmosperic battles.
Saved the best for the last, garrisons. Why on earth can't I determine my own garrison? Come automathiclly that's fine. But Hoplite (infantry) barracks giving you horses as garrison? A town with stables will have riders, a town with barracks soldiers and archery range gives archers, so on. Oh and just 'love' the smallish Icon that shows what garrison you have to defend with. How about, just make it trasparent and have the adviser tell you 'hot' 'getting hotter' oh just missed it...
Seriously CA...
So battle's are great (aside from the occasional axe stabbing the same way a sword would in the neck), campaign needs some perfection yet, but still it's an amazing game world. Have to mention the naval battles and landings here - really close to perfection. Best executed part of the game for me, but would like to determine which infantry unit should be used as marines. Anyways 8.5 out of 10. Enjoy!

By far the best in the series, STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl is an excellent, albeit buggy, game produced by GSC. It's an open-world game with a lot of freedom of movement, so one could in theory simply wander the Zone, soaking in the sights (and the radiation). If the bugs and dated graphics don't thrill you, download STALKER Complete 2009, or once it comes out, Complete 2012. Both of these mods bring the game up to current standards graphics-wise and fix many game-related issues, translation issues, etc.
However, if you like games with interesting lore and games that are challenging, atmospheric, and unique, STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl might just be what you're looking for.
Good hunting, Stalker.

Great respect for the source material, setting, atmosphere, and audio are not enough to save Alien: Isolation from being a broken mess.
The controls are often unresponsive, the interface is mediocre (and obtrusive), the save system -- okay, wait. I actually like the idea behind it, but I had to replay the entirety of four different missions multiple times due to a loading loop error. Each time, I was able to get things back on track aside from the final level (mission 19) where the game inexplicably stuck a dead body at Ripley's feet. I would have had to replay mission 18 again to hopefully solve this problem, and it would've taken a lot of money for me to ever play that one again. Or mission 17. Or mission 16. Or...
If you're wondering how I racked up the final achievements despite being unable to move, I had to download someone else's save just so I could complete my game. Utter nonsense.
Oh how I wish this was the only bug in the game. It isn't. Not by a longshot. It merely is the most crippling and, literally, game-breaking of them all.
The pacing and actual gameplay have too much of a negative effect to recommend Alien: Isolation. Maybe if it was much shorter, tighter, had less to collect and, rather, had a stronger emphasis on weaving a compelling narrative, and... oh, yeah, it didn't keep eating my damn saves, I'd probably have enjoyed my experience.
If it wasn't for the save issue, I *may* have marked this as a recommended title (to be purchased only during a 75% sale), but honestly, watching Alien 10 times in a row would've been less tedious and monotonous than playing Alien: Isolation.
I guess there's a reason why this developer typically makes RTS games rather than these types. Stick to what you're good at, Creative Assembly. From what I've briefly experienced, you are quite good at strategy titles. Please leave Alien: Isolation II (Aliens: Isolation?) to another team.
I really wanted to love this game. I really did. Why else would I have spent 5-6 hours fiddling with saves, verifying files, replaying the same missions over again, and even resorting to other people's saves if I didn't? Unfortunately... well, you (possibly) read the review.
Hopefully you, if you choose to ignore my warnings, have better luck.

An enjoyable game not without some flaws. I bought it on sale 66% off, a price which I would recommend to someone looking for a casual RPG time sink. This is a game that I did not feel too invested in, but I recalled having fun with it.
When I first considered this game, I was heavily swayed by its environmental design. It's always refreshing to see a beautiful and bright depiction of a post-apocalyptic world. I especially enjoyed the feel of nature taking the land back from man: broken bridges sunk across rivers, tree roots snaked around machines, vines crept across crumbling buildings, etc.
The story also seemed promising. It got kind of weird at the end, but it was acceptable because it had a good message that I could agree with. You play as Monkey, a guy who gets enslaved and breaks out of the slave transportation ship. You later come into contact with Tripitaka, a fellow enslaved runaway, who later enslaves YOU for survival. Talk about bad luck! I was interested in seeing what sort of writing and character development might come of that.
Sadly, the character development sucked. The general framework for the story borrowed from the Chinese fable "Jouney to the West", and it seemed like a cop out. Each main character was a caricature of their correlating inspiration. Monkey looks like a monkey, has blatant allusions to Wukong in his costume and weapon designs, but he sounds like an angry New Yorker from the 1980s. It's hard to reconcile his personality and design without some kind of explanation, but he is later revealed to have virtually no past.
Tripitaka (Trip) has an actual backstory, but her character fills the same role as the monk Xuanzang: She's naive, physically useless, and intellectual, so she's technologically savvy, a history bookworm, and a gifted hacker. She's basically the Sailor Mercury of the party.
Pigsy also literally looks like a pig and acts lecherous like his counterpart in literature. His lustful nature is used as a driving force to inform the player
Gameplay was fun and encouraged me to see this game to completion. Combat is simplistic but not completely boring because of skill leveling (incentivizing you to fight) and some variables in mechanics. Monkey's staff does a 4-hit basic attack combo chain, and there is a 2-hit heavy combo. Both are activated by two different buttons, but you hit the same button to execute their respective combo chains. In my experience, there was a method to the madness instead of simply spamming heavy attack. Since some enemy attacks cannot be interrupted, you need to factor in blocking or evading. I was happy with using basic attacks to weaken an enemy, culminating with a heavy combo or additional unlocked skill. Not to mention, Monkey's staff shoots 2 types of ammo, which become extremely useful from mid to late game.

I think it wouldn't be fair to judge ENSLAVED as a game. It's rather a piece of art that is trying to convey its story through the medium of a video game. Most game that try to do this end up as walking simulators or pretentious platformers, but I think ENSLAVED does an excellent job marrying a fantastic story with a gameplay that neither overshadows it nor feels underwhelming.
I don't want to spoil the story, so it's enough to say that it's about companionship, trust, hope, perseverance and vengeance. All of the characters (there are 3 in total) are so well-fleshed-out that you sometimes feel like this game is based on a true story, on real people. The story is really incredible; there are many heart-breaking moments as well as comic relief scenes. As long as you have some love for literature, you're going to love the story.
The game takes place in a post-apocalyptic setting. It's not very clear whether there was a Termimator-esque war between the Mechs and the Humans, or the humanity destroyed the world in a cataclysmic war where the Mechs were the main weapons. However it may have happened, the world of ENSLAVED is not a nice to place to be.
Most of the game is linear platforming; going off the rails simply gets you some extra credits or finding masks scattered throughout the game, which just shows you flashbacks of the world before the war (this might be a minus for you if you like collecting things to unlock extras). When you're not platforming, you are fighting Mechs (all throughout the game, you see almost no other human beings apart from our main trio).
The combat system is good enough for this game's purpose. Remember, this is a very-heavily story-focused game, so don't expect a revolutionary fighting system or incredible action scenes (though the game has lots of heart-pounding chase scenes). You can upgrade your character in 4 different areas to help you fight better and survive longer. My advice is fully upgrading your health and shield first, so that survival won't be a big problem for you later on.
The sound department did an outstanding job, I must say. The voice-acting is, simply-put, mind-blowing. The last time I heard such high-quality voice acting was in Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor. You really feel like you are watching a film every time a cutscene comes out. This is to be expected, of course, knowing that our protagonist (Monkey) is voiced by Andy Serkis (best known for his role in LOTR: Gollum), Trip is voiced by Lindsey Shaw (a professional actress) and Pigsy is voiced by Richard Ridings (who is one of the big names in voice-acting industry). These three actors also did the motion capture themselves, so the characters' lines and tones match perfectly with what they are doing during the cutscene. The soundtrack is also awesome. Whenever a song plays, it always fits the current mood of the game. I especially fell in love with the credits theme (No Death in Love).
The visuals are good enough - neither breath-taking nor terrible. Thanks to motion-capture, the face animations are really good. Apart from a few scenes, the characters' faces really convey their emotions. Coupled with the voice-acting, you get a cinematic experience.
For me, the game has two noticeable downsides. The first is that camera controls and angles are (most of the time) really bad. There were many times I didn't understand where to go, where to jump, where the enemies are, etc. because of the bad camera angles. They really should have tested the game more for this kind of problem before releasing it. As it is, the game sometimes feels like a bad PC-port. (By the way, I can't comment on movement and combat controls because I played the game with a Xbox controller, and as this is originally a console game, I didn't have any problems whatsoever. I don't have any idea how this game plays with a KB+M combo.)
The other negative is the extra story - Pigsy's Perfect 10. It doesn't really add to depth to Pigsy's character. Theoretically, it's fun to play, because it's non-stop fighting and skirmishing, and Pigsy has tons of cool gadgets and abilities. But in every chapter (there are 19 mini-chapters), the whole gameplay boils down to mowing down ranks upon ranks of Mechs. The story is okay and has an unexpectedly sad endingi but as I've said, it doesn't really give a more in-depth look at Pigsy's character. I suggest you play this story until a certain point (the part where Pigsy builds "something"). After that point, the story just drags on unnecessarily. What could've been a nice little 1-hour story ends up making you feel frustrated, thinking "just finish already."
All in all, this is one of the best games I've ever played in terms of story-telling and creating a meaningful, realistic setting to put that story in. It has its drawbacks, sure, but the positives far, far outweigh the game's shortcomings. With its cheap price during sales, it's a must-play for those who value story in their games.

You really feel like you're struggling to survive, and the stats are all gear based - this is NOT an RPG. There are also several excellent mods out, which fix bugs, add content, tweak settings, and generally just make it a whole new game.

While we mourn the passing of the studio that was making STALKER 2 and who made the original here, lets reflect on STALKER. It was a good game for it's time, it's controls are not the sort of finely honed FPS you have come to expect from TF2, COD, etc, but it works.
Also it has a System Shock inventory system, so you must manage your inventory weight, your status effects (poisoned, radiation sickness, etc) all whilst trying not to fire off your last few rounds to stop that horrible invisible mutant from murdering you hard.
I wouldn't go back to playing this game anytime soon, but I would consider playing it's prequel (Call of Pripyat) just because it is far more polished, and this is the real shame, that we might never see how good STALKER can be because of the studio closing. Worth buying, only for nostalgia's sake.

The dual protagonist set up is executed perfectly and doesn't take away from the game whatsoever. You can even choose to play without any powers at all on either character.
The gameplay is exactly like Dishonoured but with minute chnages to small things like the ability to hold your sword attack button to do a piercing attack. The vast majority of the powers are able to be used by both a stealy, loud, non-lethal or lethal run and New Game+ is a gift from the gods.
There are so many small features that make the experience so fresh each time you play without it coming off as tacky at all and play through it once or twice and you have the option to play as Emily with Corvo's powers and starting off with 100s of bonecharm traits and 64+runes, ofcourse this is completely optional.
I only had small issues, firstly the game is hard to run, not broken. It was very un-optimised on lanuch but now it is simply just a hard to run game like crysis 3 and about as optimised as crysis 3. The graphic options are numerous and there is a great deal of customisation, near perfect support for 21:9 except the hud is done for 16:9 and some loading screens however that is all and the rest functions perfectly. Other than that I can't really find any except that the first loading screen when the game is launched is a static image used in the marketing material. Come on Arkane, this isn't 2006.

Take Dishonoured, add a bit more purple colour to the powers and put the cool features on steriods. Also there is Granny Rags so instant 10/10.

I bought this at Walmart around a month ago (for a super cheap price you would never see on Steam from an Activision game which is interesting), and only just got around to playing it yesterday. My play time is entirely the campaign. I'm more of a single player person, but I'll casually check out multiplayer in games if it's there. I don't buy games for the multiplayer unless it's an MMO or something like that. I share this in hopes that it gives some perspective on how I play video games so it will help in understanding my critique of this game in particular.
I should also mention, while I tried many times over a couple days, I could not get into a single multiplayer match. I think no one is playing this game on PC anymore which is bizarre as usually Call of Duty games seem to have some amount of players even after they're new, but I guess this shows how these games should abosultely, under no circumstances, be bought at the ridiculous prices they are always listed at on Steam even a decade after they've come out.
So, I will mainly talk about the single player campaign. I mainly bought it because Kevin Spacey is awesome anyway. I will first say *don't do that*. Kevin Spacey *is* in this, and he gives an expected fantastic "Kevin Spacey is the political bad guy" performance. Unfortunately he isn't in it enough (he realy couldn't be if you consider that this is a video game and not a movie), and what else there is to the game is completely skippable like any Call of Duty game (expcept Black Ops which is a fantastic game and very unlike any other Call of Duty I have ever played).
Like always the story is a complete rip off. In this case it's a rip off of several things, which is mostly fine, but the end is entirely The Watchmen plotline. All it's missing is a giant space octopus.
The characters are actually really good- which surprised me. Maybe it shouldn't, but it did. Ilona and Gideon are fantastic companions and I really felt a comraderie with them. Troy Baker is always great and it was nice to hear he was in this as well (he played Mitchell, the guy you play).
The problems I have with this game, and most all Call of Duty games since Call of Duty was first a thing, is game play. There is very little of it. It would be shocking how well this series does if not for the fact that the majority of the people who buy these games do not care about single player games at all. I've known people like that so I know they do not care about story and they completely ignore everything that has to do with relating to other people, or laying out exposition or anything like that. They don't care about that stuff. They just want to shoot guys- and that's fine.
The game play in this is terrible. Sure shooting feels fine, but in this particular case I enjoyed it less because it's guns that both don't exist and are meant to be near futuristic so they are different than real guns and I just hate the way it feels. It's not satisfying to shoot guys in this game.
Anyway, the game play is dull as rocks. The missions are almost always "follow that person" until it ends, sometimes you don't do anything at all except hit e occasionally. If you're lucky (in maybe 2 or 3 missions) you actually get to walk around and shoot dudes until the game decides you cant anymore. How has no one made the comparison that these games are no different than non-games (that I still like but they aren't games) like Dear Esther? The only thing that makes this a game (unlike Dear Esther) is the shooting galleries you occasionally get to take part in.
Thankfully games like the new Doom, and Shadow Warrior exist. There are finally good first person shooters to play that are exciting again. That require strategy and quick thinking. Call of Duty can give a compelling experience (again, I thought Black Ops was fantastic, but that was years ago), but it doesn't have to because the majority of players don't give a stool about compelling narrative- which again I'm not mocking thse players. That's fine, but it means the developers can time and time again give a lack luster experience to those few who even care.
Anyway, there isn't really much else to say. the game is really bad unless you have 0 brain cells. You might like the characters, but the game play is so dull, and that's more important in a video game when you get down to it. Don't get it for multiplayer either because apparently no one is playing it.
The multiplayer is dead. Don't buy it.

This game is excellent.
Each and every one of us can vividly recall someone who at one point meant everything to us, but is now just a distant memory. Emily is Away recounts the tale of a young man who is transitioning beyond high school and moving onwards into college life. He feels a multitude of emotions - excitement about moving off to a brand new place and learning new things, happiness about getting into the school he desired and being able to start an awesome new adventure in his life, and lastly, a small, neverending tinge of sorrow deep within his heart when he thinks back to his former best friend from high school, Emily.
The game encompasses 5 years of this person's life, quintessentially, his entire college experience. As time progresses, people change. People move in and out of each other's lives every day. Someone you may have spoken to every day back in high school may be a distant memory now. In this game, you play the role of the young man described earlier and engage in multiple AIM-like chat conversations with your old friend Emily. These conversations are intermittent between each year, meaning that a lot of time passes in between each one, and therefore, both you and/or Emily may have changed a little during the time prior. This can be seen in the alterations in Emily's biography on the chat interface and her profile picture changes, as well as the stories she tells throughout the conversation while you catch up with one another's busy lives.
I won't get into too many details and will try to avoid spoiling anything for you, but I must say that the game does an excellent job of portraying the young and naive communications between a boy and a girl who may or may not have intertwined feelings for one another hidden within each keystroke. Whether or not this is the case is up to you and Emily. The dialogue choices you make throughout the game will effect what you learn throughout its course. I emphasize the word "learn" in this case because just like in real life, there may be thoughts or feelings that this person on the other side of the screen feels towards you which are not made clear - perhaps because you never ask them, or perhaps because they are too scared to tell you. Whether you seek to learn Emily's feelings about you or not is your choice. Every sentence spoken by both Emily and me felt like it was substantial and had some sort of consequence on our relationship (not a romantic relationship, just that between two people), and that is one of the many things that I just loved about this game.
Emily is Away is an impeccable embodiment of the human condition. Each of us has a special person like Emily in our life, someone who will remain in our thoughts and memories long after they have travelled hundreds or thousands of miles away. Someone who means a lot to you at this short moment in time always will. No matter how far apart you become from someone, your feelings of affection, respect, and love will always remain deep within your soul. Nevertheless, in reality, things do not always work out perfectly - and that's just how life is.
This game presented its message in a clear, precise, and stimulating manner, and I must say, every moment of it was great. I believe it took me around 30 minutes to complete it, and every single second was worth it. If you are looking for an exciting action game where you get to blow a ton of♥♥♥♥♥♥up and kill hundreds of terrorists, this is not the right game for you. But if you are looking for an intriguing, nostalgic, and intellectually stimulating experience which you will almost certainly be able to relate to and remember for quite some time, then you should try this game out.
All in all, this game is absolutely incredible. I highly recommend that you set aside a half hour of your weekend to enjoy this masterpiece and appreciate its wonderful story, message, and all the 00's nostalgia.
Final Rating: 10/10
