I downloaded this game because it peaked my interest from the videos and because it was "free". I have never really been interested in hunting, but  I was pleasantly surprised with how fun and relaxing it was for the first few hours. After I finally hunted down my first deer and killed it, I was really excited to go back to the store and see would I could purchase with the money I recieved from my hunt. It was then that I realized this is absolutely not a "free to play" game.
I understand that the developer has to make money, and I have no problem with them making the free to play members work hard for what they get, but it is literally impossible for free to play players to progress. The only thing you can really afford without paying is ammo, and it still takes a while to get the money for it. You don't even get money for harvesting your prey. You have to complete missions (which by the way, most require items that you have to buy in order to complete) to get the in game currency and the prices for the items that you are allowed to purchase with in game currency are astronomical. All of the weapons have to be purchased with real money. All outfits must be purchased with real money. The licenses' are available through in game currency, but it will take you a year of playing to get a 7 day license for one animal. The worst part is that the items in this game aren't even cheap. Almost everything is $3.00 and up, and that money will add up considering you have to buy basically each individual item (with the exception of some bundle packs).
Most free to play games offer premium and free to play. Usually, premium makes it a little easier to progress and adds more content to premium members. Not in this game. "Free to play" in this game is literally just a demo. You have to pay to play if you want to do anything other than hunt mule deer, keep the same weapon, stay on the same hunting ground, make your own game, and constantly get kicked from games after doing nothing wrong. So basically.. you have to pay if you want to do anything fun, and that's why I got this game to start. I would not recommend getting this game unless you plan on spending loads of money.
I also want to add a note to the developers. People will still spend money on this game if you make it more friendly towards free to play players. You are severely limiting the crowd of people playing your game by making it "pay to play". I know a bunch of people that have never had the slightest interest in hunting that would love to play this game. If you open up the game more, more people will come, and more people will be willing to support you and pay money. However, as of right now, I would not support this game because you have mislead me and many others that downloaded this game believing it was "free to play".
My review will change if the developers ever decide to remove the extreme restraints that they have placed on the players. If nothing changes, they need to list this as "demo" and put a price tag on the actual game, because the store page is very misleading.

text: Worst Souls game to date; improves on a few things, screws up the spirit and feel of the Souls games. Doesn't make it a bad game, though. If you haven't played a Souls game before, you'll have yourself a grand old time, but people who spent countless hours in the depths of Lordran or even Boletaria and experienced what this game is lacking tend to go back to Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition, from what I've seen.

"Prepare to die!"
A slogan which has become synonym with this series, and something that probably made me pass on the first game. Everything I read about the game was about the difficulty, how hard it is and some saying that it wasn't even "fun" at times, even though they still thought it was good. The difficulty seemed to be everything this game had to offer, as that's what most people talked about. Boy was I wrong in my interpretation of what this series is about...
After looking at some of the screenshots of Dark Souls II and being very impressed by the art direction of it, I bought the game and gave it a shot. 80+ hours later I'm as hooked as ever and never want it to end - and these 80 hours are the most I've spent on a game in years. Games rarely hook me nowadays, and even the ones that do I usually get tired of before even finishing them. And believe me, the difficulty of this game is far from the sole reason this game is so freaking good.
For one, the setting and great detail of the different environments is one of the best I've ever seen in a game. Whenever I play this game I'm glued to the screen and fully focused on whats ahead of me. It's not a rare thing for me (with this game) to just stop what I'm doing and stare in awe at the beautiful scenery. Like stated earlier, I've spent over 80 hours with the game and it never, ever drags. Every area feels like a work of art and carefully thought out.
Second, the combat. Oh the wonderful combat... This isn't an rpg that's all about stats. You can't level like crazy and just rush a group of enemies being insanely godlike and feeling like a superhero. Because you're not. You have to be strategic, and use your shield to block enemy attacks, or roll out of the way, or parry his attack, or ... the options are many. And the overall feel and flow of the combat is hands down the best I've seen in a modern rpg. Combat is just wonderful. Stats play a part but is not something you completely rely on.
And for number three I guess I'll talk about the difficulty for a bit. You have to with this game, right? Yes, this game is hard. Although, at least for me, very rarely frustrating. You'll die, yes - you WILL die. But you'll also prevail, become better at combat and learn enemy patterns and it brings a sense of satisfaction you hardly ever see in a game nowadays. Finding shortcuts that helps you progress through areas easier also brings satisfaction. The difficulty successfully make you more absorbed into the game as it demands your complete focus. This is difficulty done right and in all honesty, I think it would lose some of it's charm had it been much easier.

-If you want a game that will leave you speechless with amazing Story/Lore elements, insane boss design, memorable level design, interesting NPCs and a slightly clunky albeit charming style... Get Dark Souls 1.
-For those who don't necessarily care about the story or the lore, and I know there are many... Dark Souls II is the game you want. There are plenty of interesting places to invade and fight in. Absolutely loved Just Cause 2 and with the playtime that I've put into 3 you might think that I've at least enjoyed it enough to keep playing, right?  Wrong.  This game is only worth a couple hours at a time, otherwise it just gets way to repetitive.  For a $60 price tag plus another $30 for the extra DLC missions and content?  Not worth it.  At all.  $30 for the whole set would be fair and considering that I've had a hell of a time just trying to get it run smoothly without constant frame drops and random crashes as well?  Good lord.  How did we let it get this way?  What did we do wrong as consumers to let this sort of shoddy developement and overpriced half♥♥♥♥♥attempts at games start at AAA game prices?
You're looking at about a 15 hour main campaign and maybe 2 per DLC.  The rest of mine came from collectible hunting and upgrade points which was just tiresome to try and unlock a couple extra vehicles and weapons.  They try too hard to make you use the different tools for specific upgrades when it could be a whole lot more enjoyable to let me do it my own way. And add to that the fact that there's not even any sort of music playing other than the background is just inexcuseable when there's supposedly a radio station that makes announcements every time you take over a settlement..why can't we have a little music coming from there when travelling in vehicles?  I just don't know.  It makes the world feel so much more stagnant despite how open and really beautiful it is.
Saw this also being promoted, HEAVILY I might add, on different streams before release and surprise surpise it ran VERY WELL on those streams which is funny too considering the performance problems on release.
Just Cause 3?  Just a damn shame.  Wait for a sale, that's when I picked up the season pass for cheap.

So I completed the campaign for this and almost felt a sense of responsibility to post a review because of how under the radar this game is and because of how much I enjoyed it. There are many levels where large mechs and levels are emphasized and a big screen just makes all of this extremely immersive. 60fps looks great with all the big stuff happening.

-None

-Older title with somewhat dated graphics

Major Pros:
-Story (Based on a novel by the way)
-Characters (great chemistry and I really enjoyed the actors)
-Level ups are fun and not overly complicated. It makes it fun to find the orbs.
-Graphics are unique and sometimes impressive for the time, especially on a large screen.

-"Trip" is uhm.... ;-)

Alien: Isolation is best known for being one of the most pleasantly surprising titles of recent times. It thrusted itself out of ever-growing myriad of poor movie tie-in releases (many from the Alien franchise itself) and demonstrated exactly how survival horror should be done without being another Amnesia-esque clone. Short answer: I highly recommend. Not-So-Short answer? See below!
PROS:
1. Atmosphere: I hate to use the clichéd 'A'-word but the game's atmosphere really is amongst the most immersive I've ever played. Lighting and shadows are used to excellent effect and the soundscape is incredible. The number one tip I would give is "WEAR HEADPHONES". It's no fluke how Creative Assembly received a plethora of awards for its sound design. In moments of tension (of which there are bucketloads), your heightened senses mean you'll be picking out every little detail and will most likely end up being spooked by sliding doors and other mechanical sounds thinking they're enemy related.
2. Stealth and Survival: Without throwing too many spoilers out there, you encounter a Xenomorph early on in the game (crazy, I know) and the missions that followed gave me more hibbly-jibblies than anything I've played, watched or read thus far. It reminded me what I love about the genre across all mediums. It executes the whole run-and-hide-from-an-unstoppable-foe incredibly well, particularly in an early mission where you're working your way through a medical facility. You will spend a lot of time hiding in cupboards, lockers and under tables. You will spend a lot of time checking your motion tracker to see where the menacing and unpredictable Xeno is at, and...
3. Unforgiving: ...You will die. A LOT. Okay, maybe that in itself isn't exactly a 'pro'. As stated above, the A.I. is unpredictable. Many people have categorized this as a negative aspect, saying there should be a good level of predictability so that the player can learn enemy patterns and develop a sense of reward when the he/she eventually responds correctly. In my opinion, this unpredictability brings a truly organic feel to enemy behaviour seldom seen in stealth games and fully outweighs the above counterargument. Sure, it can be frustrating and at times feel like a lesson in trial-and-error, but I feel it manages to aid engagement more than it hinders, and the end rewards feel all the more gratifying.
4. Visuals: The art direction and visual narrative stays true to the original movies. Being on the Torrens and Sevastopol really does feel like you're in a 20th-century-conceived futuristic world in which the Nostromo existed (even including the quirky late 1970's/80's style low-res computer stations).
5. Environment: An impressive amount of detail is seen in all parts of the environment, in which you can get close to and read displays on the wall to or research documents on a worker's desk. Miscellaneous items such as mugs, documents, tools and other devices are placed on tables and shelves in a way that would seem naturally to anyone living, working or visiting there. On a wider scale, Sevastopol feels like it is assembled and linked together naturally. There's no "well why would this room be next to this room" or "how could someone possibly work here when there is a silly platformer sequence between here and there?" All of these elements help to bring a sense of the station's former glory and fills the environment with life even though there's a lot more death around.
==========
CONS:
Whilst there are many things Isolation does so right, there are several points that, for me, prevent it from becoming a masterpiece...
1. Mission Design, Lack of Variety & Pacing: I lost the amount of times I had to press buttons, pull levers, turn on generators, turn off breakers, find passcodes, disable lockdowns, find keycards. Numerous times you will have to execute several of these actions in a row just to get from one side of a door to the other. "Oh, there's a door with a passcode lock. OH! There's a computer 3 feet away. I wonder if that has the passcode! Well what do you know, it does! Ugh..." Simply put there is very limited variation in the types of set pieces and the way objectives are reached. It got to the point where I'd be going through the motions hoping for the alien to come back to try and kick me up the backside and raise the adrenaline again. I understand the laws of pacing, but you still have to keep the quieter bits interesting too.
2. Unfulfilled & Redundant Game Mechanics: There are a couple of game mechanics that end up becoming squandered potential, most notably the rewiring system. It could have been used to employ clever traps or simply block enemy progress. In the end it only gets used to turn off security cameras or unlock doors (some of which have to be unlocked to progress the mission anyway).
The other is the items and crafting system. You collect various components and combine them together along with scrap metal to produce items that aid you in your survival. Instead of having to carefully strategise the use of varying items, I barely used half of them. At no point did I ever use an EMP Mine, Pipe Bomb, Flashbang, Flare (apart from when the initial tutorial told me to) or Smoke bomb. Want to distract someone? Use a noisemaker. Want to use an offensive item? Just use a weapon. The flamethrower makes the molotov completely redundant as it's better in every department and, providing you loot adequately, never runs out of ammo.
Also, the game issues you with a flashlight early on and informs that it will need to be recharged with looted batteries. Despite being in a world where flashlights apparently last only 30 seconds (in the 22nd century no less), I drained the original battery to around 25% capacity and never had to recharge them the entire game. The arrival of the flamethrower does an adequate job of lighting up the surrounding space. Seriously, is there anything this flamethrower can't do?
3. Plot & Character Annoyances: I won't go into spoiler territory but there are occassions when the game tells us what our motive should be when it really doesn't deliver an adequate case for why we should empathize with it. Instead it ends up feeling like we're being taken for a ride on an errand-run by a lead character who seems all too accepting to be the only person getting any actual work done.
In addition, NPC's aren't given the opportunity for their characters to be built properly, having barely any development and ultimately lacking any real depth. And when it comes to their inevitable death scenes (minor spoiler, I guess? Come on, we all know NPC's die), I can only assume the game intends for us to be moved alongside Amanda's teary reactions. Instead, I just felt like saying "oh well, sucks to be them. Now, let's actually focus on getting ourselves out of this mess". Maybe I'm just a selfish, cold-hearted SOB. This player-character disonance reached boiling point at a critical stage in the game where an NPC decided to take a certain course of action that I personally agreed with, whilst Amanda decided against it. Sure enough, I had to do what Amanda wanted to do. It's schizophrenic mutiny* I tells ya!
And, even when you submit to the wills of the lead character and those around her, even after completing one of these arbitrarily convoluted errand-runs, the game manages to monumentally pull off one of the biggest slaps-to-the-face I have ever known in an interactive story. Most of you who've played it know which bit I'm talking about. If you're going to make a gamer take 50 steps forward and 500 steps back, motivate them to want to make up those 500 steps again.
==========
Alien: Isolation is undoubtably a game to experience and one I strongly recommend. However, whilst Its immersive atmosphere is second to none, its mechanical shortcomings and often-frustrating plot prevent it from reaching the level of 'masterpiece'.

It's so gratifying to find a game that goes back to the classic 8-bit style, especially one with a sense of humor.
Papers Please is a very addicting game, I can't help but enjoy the idea of deciding the fate of all those 8-bit saps waiting in line just so I can DECLINE their entry into the country XD.
But that said, don't be so eager to hit the DENIED stamp just yet.  The game's more memorable feature is it's attention to detail.  So when you're handed those papers, you need to make sure they ARE IN ORDER.  From photo ID, to nationality, the gender, height, weight, even the legitimacy of the documents themselves.    If you get even one item wrong, you will be penalized.
But the game isn't just about playing border patrol.  There are multiple stories implanted within the game from the start to the end.  Each one requires the player's personal choice of doing what is right or doing his job as the Inspector.  So you can either help the terrorists or make sure you stay in good standings with the Secret Police.
With so many different missions and subplots, it's not surprising too see why the game is addicting, since each choice decides one of twenty possible endings.
This is one of the better games on Steam. It's simple fun and quick to learn. This is a must have for anyone who enjoys a game with both a homage to the early days of gaming, a puzzle concentration and a concept that seems so out of the norm it's fun.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Despite what some people say, there are things about this game that are much better than previous Souls Titles. Its mechanical improvements are massive compared to the clunkyness of Dark Souls 1 and Demon's Souls.
Also, while the level design suffers in the Default Game... I can hardly believe the same people made Sunken King and Iron King that made Dark Souls II. If there was any reason to get this game, it would be the DLC.
As someone with 250+ hours in both Dark Souls 1 and Dark Souls II, I can say this for certain:
-If you want a game that will leave you speechless with amazing Story/Lore elements, insane boss design, memorable level design, interesting NPCs and a slightly clunky albeit charming style... Get Dark Souls 1.
-For those who don't necessarily care about the story or the lore, and I know there are many... Dark Souls II is the game you want. There are plenty of interesting places to invade and fight in. The combat is much more fluid and is not nearly the backstab-fetish pleaser that Dark Souls 1 PvP is. The game also looks amazing when you use GeDoSaTo.
P.S. I love both games a lot. The Souls series is my favorite set of video games ever. All this being said, they are both great games in their own rights. Some may like one more than others and everyone has their own opinion, which is fine. This is mine however. Enjoy!

Have you ever wanted to check passports at a strict communist like border checkpoint?
Me neither... However after playing this game I saw exactly what I was missing out on.
Your name is pulled in the labor lottery, you and your family are moved to a class-8 dwelling in East Grestin. You start your job by walking to work each morning, and then checking people's passports at the newly open boarder checkpoint in East Grestin.
The amount of required paperwork grows, as the needs of whats needed and what isn't needed always changes as the days go on. You have to be aware of fake passports, fake seals, fake names, drug smugglers, weapon smugglers, terrorists, and a lot more. You can choose who enters and who does not, who you arrest and who gets away.
However if you let the wrong someone through, it could mean the end of your home country of Arstotzka. Even worse you get fines for every mistake, these fines cut into your pay check and you may not be able to afford heat, rent, or food for your family.
This game takes a more serious tone then other games, and has its own unique style.
At this point all I have to say to you is this....
Papers, please.
*Stamps approved on your passport*
Cause no trouble...and GLORY TO ARSTOTZKA!
...NEXT!!!

It can be feeling quite depressing and desolate, as your family is starving and/or sick at home if you don't make enough money (for instance, letting people through that weren't supposed to go through will give you penalties). But it is fun in its own way. Glory to Arstotzka.

Of the horror games I've played, this is easily my favorite, there's an atmosphere of constant tension, the graphics are beautiful and very faithful to the original movie, the story and acting are generally spot-on, and the levels are well-designed for the most part. That said, the levels can be rather large and it's definitely possible to get lost if you aren't paying attention, and the save points can be spaced a good distance apart in some areas, meaning you could get bumped back 20 minutes if you get killed. If you want to see what it looks like when a team of people put their heads and hearts together for the purpose of lovingly crafting a game with precision and an admirably deep respect for the story universe in which they work, then Alien: Isolation is the game to play.  I can't think of another game that is so solidy built, and the level of detail and authenticy is so incredibly convincing that I really felt like I was experiencing what it would be like to live in the Alien universe.  Every decal and symbol, the shapes of the corridors, the bulkhead walls, the pipes and electrical conduits... more than I can list here.  It ALL looks
like it does in the films.  There are even discarded pieces of chewed gum stuck under some control consoles!  LOL  This game is a work of art, like few others (if any) can claim, and I was constantly stopping and wanting to take screenshots because everything looks so realistic.  The shadows, lighting, and shader effects had me shaking my head in amazement.  At one point, I was hiding under a medical table and noticed that  the specular map on the floor showed the faint swirl marks left by a mop.  That's just insane, but it's awesome!  It's that kind of little stuff that fills in all the realism "gaps" and makes you realize just how much care went into building this game.
Not only are the details and visuals fantastic, but the layout of the station makes sense and brilliantly conveys just how massive the place is.  But it doesn't just LOOK good, the sound in the game is also incredibly well done.  From the whiring of machinery, and the thudding of airlocks, the loud booms of explosions, the burst of flame from the flame thrower, to the subtle little beeps of control panels, the hissing of steam pipes, and the dripping of water... the station is alive with wonderfully immersive sounds!  I recommend headphones or better yet, a 5.1 or 7.1 sound system.  The positional audio with surround sound is sweet!  They also did a great job with sound occlusion, where walls and some larger objects will muffle sounds in varying degrees, which enhances not only the realism, but also the situational awareness.
The game play is fantastic as well, and sneaking around while the Alien, or other enemies, hunts you down, makes for some really intense moments.  Many times I crouched in the shadows behind a crate in a hallway, or under an examination table in a lab, or behind an executive desk, while the Alien pauses to scan the room only a few feet away, and I'm quietly saying, "Please don't see me, please don't see me..."  This game gave me goosebumps!  There are some combat elements against humans and androids, but it's worth noting that this game is a stealth game, not a first person "shooter".  Combat really should be a last resort, and in nearly every case, it can be avoided entirely if you're patient and skillful at sneaking around.  Exchaning gunfire can attract the Alien, so it's definitely not the wisest choice, although it's probably going to happen sooner or later.  (I won't get into the debate on why the Alien can't be damaged with gunfire... that's just how it is and it's fine.  Deal with it.)
I enjoyed the crafting system, which was not overly complicated and never tried to dominate the game.  It had just the right amount of balance where searching for components paid off with the ability to create useful items that you could use at your discretion.  In other words, some crafted items give you the option to solve situations in more than one way.  You can play the game without crafting anything, I believe, but it would have been more difficult.
The story is pretty good, and has very few cut scenes to pull you out of the action, but some people may prefer a bit more of a "movie" experience.  There's not a whole lot of deep character interaction, but I think it's more about you and your character, Amanda Ripley, and how she survives the ordeal.  That's not to say that I didn't learn to appreciate some of the NPC's for the roles that they play in the story.  The voice acting and motion capture is also extremely well done.
I do have a couple of gripes, however, though nothing game breaking or worth ranting about too much.  First, there are some sections of the game where the save points (beeping/flashing panels on the wall) are spread too far apart and I had to replay a handful of extremely difficult portions of the game repeatedly because I kept getting killed, and my closest available save point was not convenient, to say the least.  Maybe I was a bit careless, but one extra save point in the middle there somewhere would have been nice.
My second gripe is the length of the game.  Don't get me wrong, I love games that have plenty of play time, but the last few sections seemed like they dragged the story out longer than it really needed.  Every time I thought I had reached the final climactic moment of the game,.. nope, something else goes wrong and then I had to do yet
death defying task.  So, I complete that, thinking, "Okay,
am I at the end?"  Nope.  Something ELSE bad happens to poor Ripley, and now there's
problem I have to solve!  It's like this woman has the worst luck in the galaxy!  It just felt like the developers couldn't quite let go of the game... like they had to add just one more level... and then one more... and, umm, okay just
more, etc.
But, despite those "complaints", I had a blast playing Alien: Isolation and I very highly recommend it!

Homeworld is a very niche game. If you like space battles and want to see the absolute best there is on offer from any game to be frank, you'd want this game.
The actual game itself here is a bit of a rough diamond. The gameplay involves a spherical map where you can move your ships in basically any direction up or down as well as in the horizontal plane, which in theory would open up tactics and such. In practice, its mostly a minor annoyance, for all it is technically impressive. It is tactically useless, for the most part. You could the vast scope of the map, particularly its height to hide, but hiding is never practical to be honest - unless you're gimping yourself against the AI and carefully setting it up,  you're not making a battlestar galactica style comeback if you get smashed early on.
The gameplay boils down to who has the best fleet and the best target acquisition.  You select everything, and send it into the fray all at the same time and then click the enemy to death. The aesthetics are really down to your taste but personally I hate the design of the HW2 ships pretty much across the board while the Kushan in HW1 are in the same boat as looking awful (fighters look like flying ice cream tubs)  the Taidann look far more convincing and the only ships I really enjoy looking at. The NPC races in the campaign look pretty atmospheric and fitting as well.
The HW1 campaign is in the vein of traditional RTS games, where there are some missions with some absurd challenge that you need to try multiple times, which is a double edged sword but I think generally it works. It makes the game more interesting and about learning rather than turtling and then sending the biggest possible fleet at something. If you want the best experience, I'd never reload a save, (but you will spend hours waiting for resources to collect or fleets to build) and the reason for this is that with the gimmicky missions there's generally a key lesson that you'll learn or figure out on the first go, so the second attempt is really easy. In one mission, you'll find your small craft will almost always get wiped out due to overwhelming firepower. The solution is to just dock them in your carrier/mothership.
Units carry over between missions. In the original game, this meant that if you spent hours waiting to collect all resources before moving on, you'd have a significant advantage in the next mission. In remastered, you get all resources all over the map at the start of the next mission. There's a clear reason why Gearbox has made this change but it makes the last few levels♥♥♥♥♥♥easy.
The last 2-3 missions stop being unique like this and essentially become move and attack fests where you move your death fleet across the map and slowly destroy everything. The enemy fleets don't scale well to your own superfleet that is carried between missions and just about the most challenging large fleet action is in one later mission  where you effectively have to leave a small force of  capital ships behind to defend your mothership from flankers while you win the mission.
HW2's campaign is better designed such that a few of these problems are less significant or non-existent. The difficulty is more consistent throughout unlike in the first game where the difficulty is far worse at the beginning of the campaign. The story elements in both games aren't anything overwhelmingly special but are pretty decent and get the job done.
In terms of the remastered elements, Gearbox didn't totally screw it up, but they did do a pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job. If, like me, you have a fairly new AMD card with the latest drivers, you can't play either of the classic games as they will instantly CTD on launch. This issue has been around for several months and hasn't been fixed, and likely won't ever be fixed.  One graphical issue I've seen involves ships becoming completely see-through. This has been around since release and hasn't been fixed definitively, though there is a solution - its as overwhelming basic as changing the properties on the HW shortcut, so its pretty pathetic that its still around. In terms of campaign bugs, some missions or objectives fail to complete and particularly the infamous asteroid mission has artificial difficulty stemming from the stupidity of the pathfinding AI literally flying into rocks, and the long pause between being able to target split up asteroids.
One of the main reasons you may want to get it is because of the brilliant mods made for classic that are being ported to remastered (though extremely slowly - none of the major ones have yet made the transition) that literally serve to make Homeworld a platform for simulating any space warfare universe imaginable. There's Freespace 2, Halo, BSG, Star Wars, Star Trek, even Wing Commander amongst other things.
I'd say the game is still worth getting on sale, even despite all these faults. There is a net gain in enjoyment from playing this game, though be warned if you have an AMD card.
I'd give the game about a 7/10 on a scale where 5 is *the* average game, and not an "average game".

If you read the Steam reviews, as well as broader reviews in general, you will notice Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is generally critised on two fronts. 1) The graphics are not great on the pc port and 2) the platforming is linear and/or too easy.
Point 1) I really cannot fathom. This game has bright, colourful and expansive environments, distinct UE3 textures and particle effects, and some of the best acting and facial animation that I have ever seen in a game. I mean it's Andy Serkis for crying out loud! Sure you cannot tweak the graphics settings per se, but do some digging into the ini files and you can generally make the game look great on PC. If console ports were generally like this, we would not be doing too bad.
2) The platforming is easy for a reason. It places an emphasis on flow and story pacing rather than making you pause for long stretches at a time with an environmetal puzzle. If you are looking for more of a challenge, Tomb Raider and Prince of Persia are waiting for your visit. If you want something a little more flowy with an emphasis on character development give Enslaved a go.
Not a flawless game, but a great relief that it found its way to PC eventually.

ENSLAVED: Odyssey to the West is a game developed by Ninja Theory and published by NAMCO and BANDAI NAMCO Games

It's such a shame that this game didn't sell as well as it did and is hugely underrated because it really deserves to take a revisit back into ENSLAVED and it's Odyssey to the West

It's an MMO based on the Elder Scrolls universe, as a prequel. It tries to be "Skyrim with people" and it falls just short of it, mainly because an MMO does not work with the Skyrim format of "♥♥♥♥ around with the world," rather it keeps the player to a path and guides them through the story and up to the next region of the world like any other MMO.
The lore is as good as any other Elder Scrolls game though the lore books are relegated to just "lore bookcases" which may or may not give you a level in a skill.
The combat is Skyrim with a hotbar, and the leveling system is very robust, allowing you to wield and level up any weapon type as any class and do semi-decent with it.
The setting is as Elder Scrolls as ever, but it takes place so far in the past that, while you may recognize Riften or Anvil, they're not the same Riften or Anvil that you know from Skyrim or Oblivion. Those are at least a thousand years off into the future.
Overall, it's a bit bland as an MMO, and sort of awkward as an Elder Scrolls game, like that one awkward cousin at Thanksgiving who is probably gay but he tries so hard not to show it and all you wanna do is hug him and tell him "it's okay to be what you want to be." I just want to hug ESO and tell it "just be what you want to be, not this weird hybrid of a video game." I can only recommend it to diehard elder scrolls lore fans who want to see a good chunk of Tamriel that you haven't seen since Arena.

Have you ever wanted to check passports at a strict communist like border checkpoint?
Me neither... However after playing this game I saw exactly what I was missing out on.
Your name is pulled in the labor lottery, you and your family are moved to a class-8 dwelling in East Grestin. You start your job by walking to work each morning, and then checking people's passports at the newly open boarder checkpoint in East Grestin.
The amount of required paperwork grows, as the needs of whats needed and what isn't needed always changes as the days go on. You have to be aware of fake passports, fake seals, fake names, drug smugglers, weapon smugglers, terrorists, and a lot more. You can choose who enters and who does not, who you arrest and who gets away.
However if you let the wrong someone through, it could mean the end of your home country of Arstotzka. Even worse you get fines for every mistake, these fines cut into your pay check and you may not be able to afford heat, rent, or food for your family.

This game is weird. The only way I can describe it is a puzzle/RPG. But that doesnt do it justice.
You are a border guard in a fictional Iron Curtain-esque land. You have to look at people's documents to let them in your nation. Or not. The more people you process, the more money you make. But you will get cited if you let someone in with say an expired passport. Too many citations, and you get your salary penalized. And since youre a poor proletariat, you can barely afford to keep your family fed and housed as it is.
The interface is really intuitive. If you see a discrepancy IE an expired passport, click on "investigate discrepancy" then on the expired passport date, then on the clock/ calendar in the corner of your booth and then on your microphone to ask the person to explain.
At the end of every day, you see how much you made vs how much you spent taking care of your family and paying for rent, food, and heat(you dont have to pay for food and heat everyday). Over time you can also buy booth upgrades (keyboard shortcutrs that make it faster to process people) and maybe some medicine if a family member gets sick.
Alright, so whats the big deal? Well, theres an interesting story too. Each day as you go to work things change, security gets tighter or looser depending on international (there are a few other bordering nations) politics, terrorist attacks, spies showing up ect. So one day you might be asked to "search all people from a certain land" and then "check all work visas" the next day or whatever. Its gets slowly more complicated as the story progresses, and you have choices to make about who to let through/help. And your actions can affect outcomes or even the endings. Let someone through even though they dont have the correct info, and it might affect your interactions with another person later.
Its weird, unique and engrossing. I'm less than half way through the story (I think it goes for 31 days) and I'm already really interested in playing more to see what happens.

If you want to see what it looks like when a team of people put their heads and hearts together for the purpose of lovingly crafting a game with precision and an admirably deep respect for the story universe in which they work, then Alien: Isolation is the game to play.  I can't think of another game that is so solidy built, and the level of detail and authenticy is so incredibly convincing that I really felt like I was experiencing what it would be like to live in the Alien universe.  Every decal and symbol, the shapes of the corridors, the bulkhead walls, the pipes and electrical conduits... more than I can list here.  It ALL looks
like it does in the films.  There are even discarded pieces of chewed gum stuck under some control consoles!  LOL  This game is a work of art, like few others (if any) can claim, and I was constantly stopping and wanting to take screenshots because everything looks so realistic.  The shadows, lighting, and shader effects had me shaking my head in amazement.  At one point, I was hiding under a medical table and noticed that  the specular map on the floor showed the faint swirl marks left by a mop.  That's just insane, but it's awesome!  It's that kind of little stuff that fills in all the realism "gaps" and makes you realize just how much care went into building this game.
Not only are the details and visuals fantastic, but the layout of the station makes sense and brilliantly conveys just how massive the place is.  But it doesn't just LOOK good, the sound in the game is also incredibly well done.  From the whiring of machinery, and the thudding of airlocks, the loud booms of explosions, the burst of flame from the flame thrower, to the subtle little beeps of control panels, the hissing of steam pipes, and the dripping of water... the station is alive with wonderfully immersive sounds!  I recommend headphones or better yet, a 5.1 or 7.1 sound system.  The positional audio with surround sound is sweet!  They also did a great job with sound occlusion, where walls and some larger objects will muffle sounds in varying degrees, which enhances not only the realism, but also the situational awareness.
The game play is fantastic as well, and sneaking around while the Alien, or other enemies, hunts you down, makes for some really intense moments.  Many times I crouched in the shadows behind a crate in a hallway, or under an examination table in a lab, or behind an executive desk, while the Alien pauses to scan the room only a few feet away, and I'm quietly saying, "Please don't see me, please don't see me..."  This game gave me goosebumps!  There are some combat elements against humans and androids, but it's worth noting that this game is a stealth game, not a first person "shooter".  Combat really should be a last resort, and in nearly every case, it can be avoided entirely if you're patient and skillful at sneaking around.  Exchaning gunfire can attract the Alien, so it's definitely not the wisest choice, although it's probably going to happen sooner or later.  (I won't get into the debate on why the Alien can't be damaged with gunfire... that's just how it is and it's fine.  Deal with it.)
I enjoyed the crafting system, which was not overly complicated and never tried to dominate the game.  It had just the right amount of balance where searching for components paid off with the ability to create useful items that you could use at your discretion.  In other words, some crafted items give you the option to solve situations in more than one way.  You can play the game without crafting anything, I believe, but it would have been more difficult.
The story is pretty good, and has very few cut scenes to pull you out of the action, but some people may prefer a bit more of a "movie" experience.  There's not a whole lot of deep character interaction, but I think it's more about you and your character, Amanda Ripley, and how she survives the ordeal.  That's not to say that I didn't learn to appreciate some of the NPC's for the roles that they play in the story.  The voice acting and motion capture is also extremely well done.
I do have a couple of gripes, however, though nothing game breaking or worth ranting about too much.  First, there are some sections of the game where the save points (beeping/flashing panels on the wall) are spread too far apart and I had to replay a handful of extremely difficult portions of the game repeatedly because I kept getting killed, and my closest available save point was not convenient, to say the least.  Maybe I was a bit careless, but one extra save point in the middle there somewhere would have been nice.
My second gripe is the length of the game.  Don't get me wrong, I love games that have plenty of play time, but the last few sections seemed like they dragged the story out longer than it really needed.  Every time I thought I had reached the final climactic moment of the game,.. nope, something else goes wrong and then I had to do yet
death defying task.  So, I complete that, thinking, "Okay,
am I at the end?"  Nope.  Something ELSE bad happens to poor Ripley, and now there's
problem I have to solve!  It's like this woman has the worst luck in the galaxy!  It just felt like the developers couldn't quite let go of the game... like they had to add just one more level... and then one more... and, umm, okay just
more, etc.
But, despite those "complaints", I had a blast playing Alien: Isolation and I very highly recommend it!

I'm one of very few people who were crazy enough to play this on "nightmare" difficulty for the very first time. That means that my review is based on a single playthrough on "nightmare" difficulty.
- The game in general was good. It wasn't excellent but good.
- Technically it ran well on my 4790K @ 4,7GHz, 16GB RAM & 980 TI SLI rig using 5K NVIDIA DSR resolution.
- Horror aspect was scary for a while but later on it was mostly just fustraiting. Sometimes Alien manages to teleport himself right next to you even seconds ago he ran into totally different direction. Separating frendly and enemy humans was really difficult and in most cases I got shot then loaded the game and then avoided/killed them. Loading the game has some "lottery" algorithim because sometimes when you continued your game Alien was already in the same room with you and sometimes somewhere else. This killed me so many times before I realised that when you re-load enough times you will find that "not that difficult" version. Baby Aliens were silly because when you noticed one and tried to ran away (because of constantly pretty much 0 ammo) they jump on your face even you turn your back on them. :)
- Overrall the game was full of Hollywood clichés but I can understand that. Aliens if some old school scifi movies are the ones where they were used for very first times.
- Single player felt bit too long because at some point it started to repeat itself. "Get the tool, open the door, find the card, open the door, push the button, repeat." The game had potential to do much, much more.
- Sound was good in general and very well produced. Voice acting was good and you really could hear how much Amanda was scared. At some points I had to lower music's volume because I couldn't hear Alien's steps because of too loud music. (I'm using Sennheiser HD 650 cans wiht Audinst hud-MX1 DAC)
I can recommend this game to anyone who want to try something different from generic "pew, pew" FPS shootets and who are prepared to die... A LOT. :)

Enslaved is a fun adventure game with mostly great graphics that still hold up. The story itself is well acted, and in the least the duo is not annoying or superficial. They have been written to act like two normal people might in the same situation. Each has a good backstory that complements their design and voice acting.
As for gameplay this one has a decent amount in common with their previous game Heavenly Sword as far as aesthetics go, and yet this one still has good gameplay with a variety of upgrades and attacks that keep you interested in the overall flow. I was never really bored with this game. I played it over a bunch of smaller sessions and was always interested in what was coming next. They introduce new elements that give you more freedom as you continue your massacre of the robots.
Puzzle solving is good, and there are a decent amount of secrets. Trip and Monkey are forced to work together and the jank is kept to a minimum for the most part. Since you will be playing as Monkey it helps if you can identify with that character, but since Trip is huge part of the story you feel like you are playing her as well though you do not control her.
Overall, a competent and worthy story with sylish graphics that hold up alongside decent to good gameplay. Trip and Monkey are both likeable protagonists and its worth finding out what happens to them.

Enslave: Odyssey to the West is a typical puzzle and hack-n-slash game, which has interesting characters and an alright story.
Based on the chinese mythology about Sun Wukong, the games takes inspiration of the characters from its sources but doesn't take much else. The main character and the one the player controls, Monkey, has some obvious similarities to Son Wukong and.. well, a monkey.
The story takes place in a post-apocalyptic world where everything has been destroyed by war and now mech from that war roams the ruins while people struggle to survive in the wasteland. Slaveships run by "Pyramid" occationally picks up and kills any survivors they find, eventually also picked up Monkey and a girl named Trip, whom later on installs a slave-headband on Monkey to force him to help her get back home. As you progress through the game, they develop a strong friendship and help each other out during their journey.
If you're familiar with games such as Devil May Cry and Darksiders, you will not have problems getting into the combat, however, the combat can be quite simplified and maybe a little too much of the same for some people. Either way, it is easy to get the hand of and if you play with a controller, it is even easier. (I played with mouse and keyboard and I found the controls to be a bit funky, but it was still doable).
My biggest issue with the game is the pacing of the story. I spent 9½ hours playing this game, whereas maybe an hour or so is due to AFKing while having the game up, When I saw there was 14 chapters I thought the game would be much longer, but it felt like the game took its sweet time to get further into the story and once you actually finished the last chapter, it feels like they threw a lot of story into your face that explained some, but not all, of the "issues" in the world and whatnot. I felt it was a bit anticlimatic and not very satisfying, but then again, it also felt like they wanted to end the game sudden so that they could hype up for a sequel, which will probably never ever happen due to low sales when the game came out the first time.

Easily one of my new hero games, belonging to the same veins as my love for Beyond Good & Evil.
Enslaved was a classic that should have been more widely received but timing apparently nixed its reception among a bevy of AAA titles that hit simultaneously on its launch. I found it in 2017 and had never heard of it, but after playing it I'm really surprised a game this enjoyable went unnoticed in its day. It's like a time capsule of the best zeitgeist of it's year.
Enslaved is far more moving and good looking than I expected. The camera is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥- a result of there being a cinematographer on the design team - but the resulting cinematic experience is actually very smooth and very much contributes to the feeling you are playing a movie.
Normally playing a movie is an insult to a video game, but here it works. It left like a movie was being put together and then a really well made video game happened instead. The engine may be getting dated, and the watered down low-res textures won't stand the test of time -- but the character acting, and the expressions of the characters, just their little gestures and nods fit so well together with the voices that it is compelling enough to keep playing.
Combat is a cross between Beyond Good & Evil and the modern Batman: Arkham Knight or Mad Max style, but it is well put together and doesn't feel like it was taken out of your hands and contrived like those titles.  It does hijack the camera but not often. And the seamlessness of combat and dialogue doesn't get old. But Combat to me was largely a distraction from the lead characters getting to know each other while exploring beautiful places that look like they were made by an art team who cared about the details. Every detail of this game is polished and put together under layers of iteration. It's gorgeous to behold, even despite the small texture resolution.
The ending was abrupt and left me wanting a squeal - one that will never come - but it was good for its cause. it really did feel like I had just finished a 3 part film the lasted 10 hours.
I'll remember the characters and their little gestures. The same way I'll remember Beyond Good & Evil.
If you have a day or two to play a linear cinematic game that's fun, despite a few annoying issues that pop up in a few levels, play this. If you are looking forward to a fun but emotionally rich adventure game it wont disappoint you.

Where do I start when it comes to this game, I could go on and on about the countless hours I have spent in this game alone, I may only have one hundred hours on steam with this game, but I have been playing it for quite some time with out the steam version. All up, I would have put more then eight hundred hours into the game alone, only two hundred of those hours being without mods
Oh boy, I forgot about the mods for this game. The game is hard enough without mods when everything is set to difficult, all enemery spawns being huge and close to one another, but downloading a new mod such as the Bob's mob pack and then playing it on hard, is almost asking for the game to slaughter you at the start, yes it's possiable to win but. With every single crafting recipe becoming more difficult and requiring more compoments to craft. It's easy to get lost on what to make and when to make your next expension
The game is both rewarding and taxing at the same time for when you first start. Having to grind up for a few minutes while you get everything you need to get your self up on your feet. After that comes the hard part. Just how are you going to make your machine do your work. A simpe crate will do but, after a while. There is always a better way of doign it.
Building in this is very easy and striaght forward if you have a basic idea but don't let that catch you off guard. Making something basic is easy but it makes you think in the end when you are require to make something brand new or make a few adjustments to your buildings or even your construction line so you can make something new. Leaving you both confused and annoyed on just how you are going to over come the problem
As for the amount of threats that will come your way, it will be either a challenge or a cake walk, every playful being a little different from the last depending on where you spawn. A desert being harder due to the lack of wood and the amount of pollution you will make while a forest offering more wood and a slower pollution rise.
Overall, this game is well worth the money and time spent in it, the countless mods being made for this game as well as the amount of users putting hours into making both beautiful maps or even complex machines. It's breath taking and most importantly inspiring to look at.

Don't be fooled by the game time on Steam, this is my second ESO account since I picked it up on sale, I usually play via a Bethesda account only.
Premise:
I'm sure I don't have to introduce anyone here to Bethesda or the Elder Scrolls franchise. However, from the perspective of someone who hasn't finished a single Elder Scrolls game before hitting up their MMO offering and tried most MMOs from Europe to China (I am talking about the ones that aren't translated at all, too) and was always looking for an MMORPG to hold his interest (since starting Nostale when I was 12 years old, I was hooked on the concept), I can say that this is an absolute gem and no other exclusively online title has ever took me in so much.
Visuals: While this game is not too demanding hardware-wise, it looks totally stunning. From the sun rays to the textures, from the mounts to the small items that exist solely to be stolen, the graphic quality never fails to amaze me. This game does a lot with a little and while some quirks exist here and there, in general it's a sight to behold.
Audio design: Booming and semi-realistic. I consider this one of the strongest sound designs in any MMO. There is simply nothing that seems out of place. It makes me put on my headphones to truly enjoy it and neither me nor my guildmates listen to music instead of the ingame sound, which is rare.
Controls: This is what makes or breaks an MMO for me. Implement tab-targeting combat and I may get bored easily, depending on how dynamic combat feels. I dislike standing around and mashing my rotation. Luckily, you get none of that in The Elder Scrolls Online: Tamriel Unlimited. You have a free targeting system that soft locks when you face the enemy. You have a little margin of error, which makes some maneauvers easier - which is probably what was intended in order to implement the game on consoles. And here we come to the one big problem I see - the amount of skill slots. I would feel extremely limited if this game would work like other MMOs do. But fortunately, it does not. The amount of procs via passives, armor pieces or even pets (in the widest sense) provide you with a lot of flexibility.
PvE: Extremely rewarding and challening at times, while being very fair. There is very little RNG to speak of that would make the game more about luck than skill and equipment. A lot of the dungeon bosses have mechanics in place that require coordination which makes the combat feel even nicer.
PvP: A masterpiece when it comes to Cyrodiil, simply because it feels so epic. You have to attack or defend the strongholds currently held by your faction (Aldmeri Dominion/Ebonheart Pact/Daggerfall Covenant) and can use all kinds of siege engines to accomplish this. From pouring hot tar down the stairs to bashing the gates in, you will surely not be disappointed - unless you have a weak machine, that is. Cyrodiil is rather demanding and tends to be a lagfest, which can be combated up to a point using plugins.
Final verdict: It's on sale right now! BUY IT.
Even for the regular price it is absolutely worth it's money. However, you might find yourself wanting to buy the Gold Edition or subscribe to ESO Plus - both very viable options. Especially considering you get 1500 crowns/month of ESO Plus, this is a pretty clever move to get access to all of the DLC as long as your membership lasts.

As a kid, I remember asking my father about all the different ships as he was playing the original Homeworld. As soon as the Remastered version came out, I had to buy it.
Overall I'm very happy with the game. The remastered version is beautiful, and in my opinion one of the best things about it is that it has a great storyline behind it. While I understand that not everyone cares about that, for me it makes the game so much more. Homeworld offers a rather unique experience as a strategy game in a 3 dimensional enviornment which isn't really like anything else I've played.
Both HW and HW2 remastered versions seem to be optimized well, as I've never had any lag or framerate issues. I can't speak for the mods, as I haven't yet felt the need to utilize any - there hasn't been any that I've seen that have caught my eye as a "must have".
Some people have complained about scenarios being more or less difficult depending on how well you're doing throughout your campaign. Say you fail a mission, but you rememeber what's thrown at you and plan accordingly beforehand - the next time you start it stronger only to find there's even more enemy ships. Personally I kind of have mixed feelings about this aspect, it makes the game more unpredictible and more challenging, as you can't plan for everything the way you can with most other game's missions/scenarios.
As a negative, I have encountered a couple small glitches with scenarios, such as objectives not checking off as complete even though you've finished it, therefore making the scenario impossible to finish. I also don't particularly care for HW2, the storyline and ship variants just don't do it for me. In my opinion the first game is far superior but that's simply a matter of opinion. I can't say I have anyone to try Multiplayer with but I think it would be an excellent MP game with a few friends looking to out-strategize one another.
In conclusion, I recommend this game to anyone looking to try out a new type of strategy game in a 3D space enviornment, or anyone who gets their kicks out of a great back story like myself.

- The game in general was good. It wasn't excellent but good.
- Technically it ran well on my 4790K @ 4,7GHz, 16GB RAM & 980 TI SLI rig using 5K NVIDIA DSR resolution.
- Horror aspect was scary for a while but later on it was mostly just fustraiting. Sometimes Alien manages to teleport himself right next to you even seconds ago he ran into totally different direction. Separating frendly and enemy humans was really difficult and in most cases I got shot then loaded the game and then avoided/killed them. Loading the game has some "lottery" algorithim because sometimes when you continued your game Alien was already in the same room with you and sometimes somewhere else. This killed me so many times before I realised that when you re-load enough times you will find that "not that difficult" version. Baby Aliens were silly because when you noticed one and tried to ran away (because of constantly pretty much 0 ammo) they jump on your face even you turn your back on them. :)
- Overrall the game was full of Hollywood clichés but I can understand that. Aliens if some old school scifi movies are the ones where they were used for very first times.

- Sound was good in general and very well produced. Voice acting was good and you really could hear how much Amanda was scared. At some points I had to lower music's volume because I couldn't hear Alien's steps because of too loud music. (I'm using Sennheiser HD 650 cans wiht Audinst hud-MX1 DAC)

No more pre-battle rousing general speeches.
No more ''forward! - oi!'' unit responses.
No more the g*y green Brutii or the boisterous blue Scipii and, of course. the ravaging red Julii.
No more ''g e n i t a l?'' for ''general?''
No more universal, international mercenary convention regarding green uniforms.
No more the screeching women, Amazons in Estonia, falxmen, bastarnae.
Joke aside, although some of the above are really missed...
Now for the real fallacies:
Selling factions for ridiculous prices that should have been ingame.
IF YOU WANT TO SELL INDIVIDUAL FACTIONS, make the game cost 30 euros and every faction 1 euro. I would NEVER, ever play with, for example, the stinking Gauls, or the Parthians, so THAT would be a good move. But NOT paying 50 euros for a game with 10 factions and then selling 20 other factions at 6 euros per faction. No, no!
No more city swapping in diplomacy.
Still lvl 9999 armored hoplites and scythed chariots/elephants/entire cavalry divisions in risen slave armies and in bandit armies. SLAVES SHOULD HAVE INCREASED MORALE, MAKESHIFT SPEARS AND SOME SWORDS, SLINGS AND CLUBS, NOT ELEPHANTS AND GOLDEN HOPLITES. Bandits should be a tad little bit stronger than that.
Greedy DLC spamming with features that should have been in game already.
Sea battles decided by numbers.
Still the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ diplomacy.
Family system easily understandable by 5-year-olds (almost non-existent). Politics system ditto.
A 2000 legionnaires-strong unit is still called ''legion'' and is the largest tactical unit available.
A 160-men legionary unit is still called a ''cohort''.
The blood&gore DLC, although it costs mere eurocents, made me the most angry. Seriously? SELLING blood, wounds, animations for weapons dealing wounds, and blood-stained tunics and shields OUTSIDE THE STANDARD PRODUCT? With modern technology. graphic cards, graphic standards in games? EWW EWW EWW.   Virtual control stick.
What is this you ask?
Well, on the console, you have a stick, and you move it around to move the camera.
On the PC, you have a mouse, so you move that to move the camera, right?
Well, you would think so
And you would be wrong.
Instead, there is a virtual joystick, moving the mouse moves the virtual joystick, and moving the virtual joystick moves the camera.
What does this mean?
1) Camera control is laggy
2) There is no direct mapping from mouse input to camera movement
3) Camera movement rate is backwards
wait, what? what does #3 mean?
Well, lets move the mouse slowly, what happens?
It takes a while to move the mouse across the mousemat, and all the while, the virtual joystick is being pushed to the side, resulting in a lot of camera movement, when we want a slow continuous pan.
Now, lets move the mouse quickly, what happens?
The mouse reaches the other side of the mousemat rapidly.  The virtual joystick reaches the extent of it's range and almost immediately drops back to neutral.  The camera
in the direction I want it to go.
This is beyond broken... it's... well.  It's exactly like the port of Dead Space.   Only at least so far, I haven't come across physics glitches tied to the frame rate being released from it's 30fps console prison.  So at least it has that...
I'm going to go off now and find a controller I can use, to play this game like a console peasant, because some idiot can't implement actual control bindings.
Verdict - probably ok if you have a controller, avoid otherwise.

I want to love this game, I really do but this has to be the worst game I've ever played due to a lack of support, bugs, glitches and a very lacking game in general.
When I first started this game up I had no idea what to expect never having played a pirate themed game before. The first problem was the voice over's. Terrible.
I got into the game and found it rather basic but did enjoy it's subtle charm. I realise that the land missions were a bit dated but honestly the sailing around I had no problem with at all. Once I had the hedgehog (best ship in the game IMO) my enjoyment went up even more. Unfortunately this is the only good thing I'll be saying about this game.
When I hit the half way mark I realised some of the achievements were buggy and had not unlocked for things I had gone for. After multiple attempts some of them unlocked. I realise achievements aren't for everyone but if I can grab a couple while I'm playing and enjoying a game I see it as a "misc quest" of sorts.
Shortly after this issue I came across another. When I opened the menu in game and tried to save my game I would CTD. I played around with it for an hour trying to fix the issue by reloading, going to new areas, etc and nothing worked. I never needed to use the in game load option but that also bugged out and caused a CTD.
I discovered during my testing that at least the game auto saved when leaving land so I had an annoying way to at least progress to finish the game.
The I came to worst problem I've ever come across in a game ever. The final mission is broken. So badly that even if you get past the first bug or issue there are another 4 waiting for you. I re loaded and tried multiple things multiple times and nothing worked. Oh and this issue, it's been un answered and around since 2011. Everywhere I looked all I found was more people with the same issues and a lucky few, had issues beyond where I was up to in the final mission. All in all I found 5 different common game breaking bugs with the final mission. I cannot get past the second out of the five of them.
Overall I wanted to love this game, I forgave its poor design choices on the land maps, I got use to the terrible voice over's and surprisingly I even got use to having to use the auto save feature. The fact that the final mission is that much of a problem for so many people is unacceptable. Especially since nothing has been done about it for so long and the game is still available for purchase. 0/10

Definitely a thumbs up and maybe even more, a reference in the genre.
If you like Setllers and its chain of production, behold, this gets to the next level and the flexibility of the game is incredible.
Start with your hands, dig a bit of ressources, assemble them and start automating tasks after task.
Your map will slowly grow in a huge automated factory that you could watch for hours if only the resources were infinite, but nope... Everything you build will probably need to be reconfigured as other sources are needed or as your production steps up.
If you like the challenge, you'll compete against a quite aggressive species on the world that do not like at all the nasty fumes that come out of your big mess.
Turrets, more supplies and research become necessary.
One mistake ? Your base could be wiped out by the swarm that tries to break your wall now and then. Plan with caution, avoid cutting the electricity if you decided to electrify your base.
Build tanks or buggies or exoskeletons and explore the infinite world until you find more resources.
Relocation there or should you build a fast train that will crush the once peaceful aliens ?
Mor automation, circuits, traffic lights.
Keep researching until you can build the rocket and go back to space. Meanwhile, the aliens will gather, grow and surround you.
Call for help and let them join your game cause your brain will not be sufficient alone.
Fluids, conveyor belts, rails, chests, cranes, roads.
This game is just awesome and its replayability is almost infinite because there is always room for improvement in your designs and the mods that the community provide can add more depths or difficulty to the production chain or the aliens.
A must buy, honestly.

The only fun thing in this game is destruction and parachuting/gliding everything else is horrible.
- Graphics are fine, but have a lot of issues: flickering, no SLI support, poor performance compared to graphical fidelity.
- Worst driving I have ever experienced in a modern videogame. Every vehicle drives like a tank, you can´t make slight adjustments instead the vehicle violently dashes to the direction you are steering, rubbery impact makes you bounce off cars and objects without impacting proper damage to either vehicle even when crashing at top speed
- Story is very boring, lackluster and generic with uninteresting characters
- The world feels like it only exists as a facade for you to destroy. Killing innocents or even your own soldiers has zero impact on anything.
- Gunplay is very generic and boring. You can´t even aim down the sights with most weapons and you cannot properly take cover. Instead you just stand in the open, run around and gun down generic bad guys while shooting inaccurately from the hip.
- Character progression. You are forced to collect cogs from crappy minigames in order to unlock skills and fun gadgets. This would be fine but most of the minigames are very repetitive and boring and if you don´t do them you can´t get the "cool" stuff.
- It is purely a singleplayer game, but you have to be online inorder to play it. The only "multiplayer" feature it has are leaderboards about random things such as how many headsoths can you get in 30 seconds etc. The leaderboards have zero impact on the game, you don´t get any rewards or achivements or anything from being the first.
This game is fun for a while since you´ll get carried away blowing up enemy bases with tanks, helicopters, rpgs, car bombs and civilian suicide bombers. This fun doesen´t last for long though as you go to explore the other aspects the game has to offer and realize they are all crap. The game is a fun if you play it in short sessions and just blow things up. If you are looking a game to spend a lot of time on you shouldn´t waste your money on this.

STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl is a difficult game to start, but rewarding to finish. I enjoyed this game more and more as I played; loved it by the end. Fantastic atmosphere.
The game is very grim and challenging. It plays mostly like an RPG, because you're taking on missions and learning a story as you go. But there are no levels, no experience points, and no skill tree, so in that regard it's somewhat like an FPS. It's also scary, and resources are scarce, so it bears elements of the survival horror genre, too.
The ending is satisfying. Unlike many RPGs that cop out with a boss battle, STALKER gives you answers and a conclusion that makes sense.
A few tips if you play. 1) Find and use the "STALKER Complete" mod. It improves the graphics and the English translation, and fixes bugs. 2) It's OK to play on Novice -- you'll die plenty on any setting. 3) Use a game guide. It will help you with the weapons, and keep your story on track. I liked IGN's guide.

Since I have a decent amount of hours, I think I might be able to write a review about NMRIH. This game has got to be one of the best zombie games out there. It is a free co-op survival horror game where your ammo is scarce, you dont get to respawn so easily unlike any other type of game and has a deep strategy in it. Here are some of the pros:
- Its free
- Unlike L4D, its a much slower paced game
- The infection system is unique and challenging. Once you get bitten, you need to decide quickly if you take some pills to delay the symptoms or just throw yourself to death and wait for the next wave (or use a respawn token)
- Like any other type of game, NMRIH tries to be as realistic as possible, this is why the difficulty can be hard for new players but once you get the hang of it, its challenging and enthusiastic
- Its free
- Despite the fact that there are many official maps you can also play community maps, these can be a fresh air if you are getti tired of the same maps
- Over 90 achievements (some are relatively easy tbh) to bring you even more stuff to do since you can become bored after a couple of hours of the game
- Its free
- Ammo and medical supplies are rare so think before you throw yourself to a zombie orgy with a TNT or a Colt
- Like I said before, in this game everybody needs to work together in order to win, so if you like to be a lone-wolf in games you either carry your team to victory or you die on wave 2 to a kid zombie
- if you dont like to just hold positions on survival maps you can try objective maps, where your team has to rush through locations to be rescued. Its a mission type of map where you only have 1 life so try to not suck
- Did i mentioned its free? oh sorry about that
Now seriously, NMRIH is one of the best zombie games today and if you like challenges what are you waiting for?  Grab a friend or 2 and go kick some zombie♥♥♥♥♥

Ever imagined having to face a Xenomorph yourself, like Ripley? Well, you came to the right place! This game does an excellent job of immersing you into the world of Alien. It follows the movie extremely faithfully, as even the signs next to doors can be found in this game (Pro tip: By learning what those signs mean, you can predict what kind of room it is and what would be found inside before even entering the said room!). The game can get extremely tense as the alien's smart AI adapts to your behaviour, and constantly hunts you. The game encourages exploration (even though its quite risky) by the various terminals and logs litered around the place, which can give you some backstory to what was happening previously on the space station, give you codes to gain access to some extra loot, or even logs from the Nostromo itself, voice acted by the actors from the film. That's not to say that the game is perfect, however. The other enemies in the game are much less interesting than the alien (even quite annoying to deal with at times). Also, there are some sections that can drag on and become a little boring, especially towards the end of the game where you pretty much explored most if not all of the space station. Even though I'm not the biggest fan of survival horror (the only reason I bought this game was because it was an Alien game), I can safely say I had quite a lot of fun with this game, and I would definitely recommend it to other Alien fans.
You may want to have some spare underwear ready, by the way...

No, hunting takes patience and a little bit of skill to nail the big trophies, It feels rewarding to call in that big buck and smack him.
Now the ballistics in the game when shooting an animal could use some work, for instance when you shoot an animal it either dies and falls right over, or it gets hit and just runs, I have hunting experience and when a deer takes a bullet they dont take it like a champ and start running, they'll show you that they are hit I.E. they'll jump, flinch pretty bad or almost do a squat like move where they lower their whole body and then run. I use a .270 and the last time I shot a whitetail with it he flipped on his back and died almost instantly, of course his nerves still acted up and he'd kick his legs. That's what should be in the game, in that regard weapons feel weak and that there is no kinetic energy in the bullets.
The player movement could use some work but its really not that big of a deal.

As you start a campaign the first thing to smack you in the face is the horrific voice acting. If you choose Walker de Planc (side note, expect several puns of dad-quality throughout), you will get an immediate front-row seat to just how little the developers cared about who they hired to voice act. To his credit, I could tell he was trying to pull off an Irish accent. He's immediately joined by a forgettable side character that also made me want to pull my hair out. I barely made it out of the first ten minutes of gameplay.
With that out of the way, the rest of the game is actually pretty well done for what it is. PoBC is a silly little arcade game that never attempts to take itself seriously, and that's not necessarily a bad thing. Sea navigation/battles are compelling, though weather and day/night cycles are sorely missed. Land navigation/battles are unremarkable, but passable. A.I. leaves something to be desired, especially when one or two of your men somehow manage to get stuck behind a pillar, resulting in their death in the event of a retreat. The story is only as good as the voice actors sell it, so as things go, it's not great.
It's a below average game, but it's definitely a fun way to pass a few nights playing. Well worth the $2.49 I paid for it on a Steam sale.
