Arkane's hit sequel to the fantastic new IP from 2012 is now playable - after numerous patches.
Dishonored 2 was a mess upon release. Things are now better, but the framerate is still unstable at times. I played the game on a high-end gaming PC myself in 1440p everything on ultra, and the fps fluctuated from a rather stable 72 all the way up to 150. This was a non-issue for me, however, since the game itself is still a ton of fun.
In short, here are my pros and cons:
For:
+ The lifelike, handcrafted city of Karnaca teems with life and secrets to find, so be sure to search every nook and cranny
+ Two playable characters: Corvo and Emily, each with their own individual powers which can be upgraded to your liking
+ A new game plus mode
+ Experience Dishonored 2 in its entirety: there is a "Clean hands" achievement here too. I recommend playing the game once in high chaos and once in low chaos with stealth
+ Animations are gorgeous and fighting, especially, is visceral and even cathartic
Against:
- Variations in terms of missions is a hit or miss. Note that there are many types of missions and locales ranging from an impeccable clockwork mansion with mechanical soldiers to a dilapitated spa complex. Some may appeal to you more than others.
- The assassination targets are not as interesting or original this time around, which is a shame
- The story feels rushed and altogether to the point. This is not bad in and of itself, but the sense of urgency and injustice which surved as the fulcrum of the first Dishonored is not here. Emily sees her throne usurped from her by a returning character whose motives are not really explored. You as Corvo/Emily need to deal with this character and "her" inner circle while on the run.
- The game still suffers from bugs and glitches. During my 22 hours of gameplay the game also crashed to desktop few times.
There is a demo of Dishonored 2 available for everyone on Steam. Check it out before buying to see how the game runs on your rig.
Despite of all the issues mentioned before, I still wholeheartedly recommend Dishonored 2 for both the fans and newcomers.

Elder Scrolls Online holds true to the long running series. But this time, in an Open world MMO.

Although The Elder Scrolls Online suffered a very rocky launch it has done nothing but improve with each and every update. Both the PVE and PVP aspects of the game are well developed, there's plenty of content for those seeking group adventures as well as those determined to go it alone. While it may not be exactly like the last few Elder Scrolls games, some changes to crafting and leveling most notably, it does stand on its own quite well. Among the recent changes that I like best are the loot and enemy leveling to your current level as this allows you to explore the different regions of TESO's huge world in whatever order you want and on your own time-line instead of how the developers think you should. This also prevents the game from dumping a ton of worthless quest rewards on you if you missed a string of low-level quests and try to go back to them. The loot leveling to your level keeps those potentially "low-level" quests relevant and worth completing.
+The combat is a blast and instantly familiar to anyone who has played any of the 'Morrowind-Oblivion-Skyrim' Elder Scrolls games.
+ The graphics are amazing for a MMO and well optimized. My aging PC has no trouble with the graphics cranked up.
+ The attention to detail in the audio is also pretty impressive and really helps with the immersion.
+ Anything with a combat advantage is attainable in game without additional spending. The money they make (post-game-purchase) is through 'cosmetic' and 'convenience' items only.
+ The DLC's do cost extra, unless you get the TESO Gold Ed' , but the ones I do have are huge and feel like a good value.
- The 'cosmetic' and 'convenience' items are far too expensive for what you get, but that's kind of the standard. At least it keeps servers up and real development in the pipe-line.
In spite of a rough start this game has become one of my favorites.

I've played hundreds of games in my 24 years of gaming. This is one of the few titles that make my life as a gamer worth it. I'm far from finishing the title but the atmosphere of this game has pulled me in so far that i want to savor every moment. The graphics are absolutely amazing! I feel as if this game truly takes me to a time that should exist for everyone. A true fight for survival in this universe that we can never predict. One alien... is exactly how it should be. A thousand more could never match the fear of the one that lurks my nightmares. I feel the alien, and i feel the isolation in every step of this game!
They hit it out of the park with the atmosphere in this game. I really wasn't expecting how good it was. It's a little too long, but the first few hours are amazing.

Although Alien: Isolation is a fine horror game - nailing, especially on Nightmare mode with limited crafting and motion tracking, true survival horror, combined with the sheer terror of being hunted by a truly alien monstrosity - the greatest strength of this gem is in it's atmosphere and setting. Everything - from the font used, to the CRT monitors, to the use of the Semiotic standard - pulls you into the Sevastopol Station and the Alien universe. You really do feel like alone on what truly looks like an industrial, commercial and residential space station. More often than not, I had goosebumps not from the tension of being stalked - although that is ever present - but from seeing something that was just so well placed, like the vent system mirroring that in the original Alien film, or the condensation from the cooling towers later on in the game. The music, like all good video game music, just heightens that appreciation, and the ending credits theme especially is wonderful.
Of course, there are flaws, even in something which I rate as one of the best games of all time. The principal flaw is later game pacing - you go from area A to B to accomplish C, and then a catastrophe happens that necessitates a repeat of the cycle. There are points in the game where you think "Ok, surely that's it done", only for some new twist of fate to occur. Amanda is probably the unluckiest woman in the galaxy. This is not a critique of length - I enjoyed every second of the game. But at times it feels 'stilted' in structure. Another issue is that xenomorph AI can be be pretty poor at some times, and it does get a little frustrating on the later levels - particularly Chapter 17 where it can get a little silly. But for every slightly frustrating part, there's areas - like Chapter 14 - which make this game so memorable.
The DLCs are actually quite good, surprisingly. I'm not one to condone this sort of system, but scenarios such as Crew Lockdown, which place you on board the Nostromo, are great for fans of the original Alien film.
If you're a fan of immersive settings, science fiction, the first Alien film, or are a horror fan looking for a meaty challenge (Nightmare, in particular, can be rather brutal) with intensity and suspense, then Alien: Isolation will appeal to you. Enjoy one of the most captivating experiences in gaming.

To put it simply - Homeworld literally revolutionized the RTS genre when it was first released over 15 years ago. I bought the original game and throughout the years, it was always a deep regret that this great game was not available on Steam for everyone else to discover... until now! This remastered version is not just putting the original game on the Steam store - every part of the game has been improved and updated, surpassing all expectations for such a classic reborn. This digital collection is a great opportunity to experience what made Homeworld such an enduring game. The amazing fanbase which has kept this game alive all these years finally prompted the original developers to update and release it on Steam.
If you are a fan of the Star Wars movies or gigantic space battles with epic scenery, this is definitely something that you should check out. Homeworld is quite different and special compared to other RTS games - it has an original outlook on space combat with a game engine capitalizing on the beauty of combat in space, which has never been as successfully captured in any other games. The game is so beautiful that you could make movies from the gameplay footage if you wanted - in fact, there are several fan-made movies out there with Star Wars or Battlestar Galactica mods, simulating the original look of the various ships in their respective franchise.
The story and sound effects are very immersive, contributing to a chilling cinematic atmostphere where you can feel the loneliness of your civilization lost in space as you build your fleet while preparing for explorations and enemy encounters. The learning curve is easy compared to other strategy games so feel free to give it a try. It's worth it!

think I got it back in a Humble Bundle a while ago, and based on the ‘Very Positive’ review rating on Steam alongside many redditors constant appreciation of this game I was quiet eager to try it out. I’m about to finish the game on Hard. To be honest I’d struggle to say I have been enjoying my time with this game. I simply don’t think it’s a very good game. Whilst I can appreciate a good story, I hold gameplay first and foremost in importance, and this game simply doesn’t have good gameplay, it doesn’t feel nice to play. People really like this game so this is going to be long whilst I explain my reasons -
Starting off, the camera is atrocious, as in possibly the worst camera I’ve experienced in a third person game. It constantly is moving around and sits at strange angles. Many of the 3-second cut scenes where the game will focus on an enemy had me simply facing a wall the entire time. But that’s not an issue in terms of gameplay. The issue is that the game is a Batman-style fighting game, you need to be able to see all the enemies in the mob you’re currently fighting so you know when to evade, counter, who to prioritise etc. But the camera will only ever focus on really one enemy so you spend a lot of time guessing when the enemy behind you should be attacking.  Couple this with the constant changing to static cameras when you’re doing the climbing scenes and you’ll frequently have the controls switched on you which causes you to start running backwards opposed to forwards because the axis has changed. It just doesn’t feel good.
Back onto combat, this is probably where the game fails the most. The combat ¬– which comprises entirely of pressing X,X,X or Y,Y or Y,A  - is unbelievably repetitive, shallow and uninspired. As aforementioned it’s similar to the Batman: Arkham series, but done far worse (given Arkham only released a year before I’m sure they didn’t have time to learn from its combat). Pulling of a counter-attack is near impossible, the enemies (of which there is lucky to be over 4 different types) all seem to unleash a 3-hit combo which stun locks you and combining this with some pretty unbelievable tracking you’ll find yourself getting frustrated.
And it’s the same fights throughout the entire game.
This is the two scenarios that happen
-	You enter a new area, there is 3 guys, then another set will appear, and maybe if youre unlucky and didn’t kill and enemy before he summons more you’ll find another set.
-	You get momentarily split from Trip and need to trigger a stationary machine-gun type sequence.
That’s largely it and so many of the combat sequences had me going “are we seriously doing another wave… I don’t care, just let me go forward” and it feels like padding.  Unfortunately this doesn’t improve with the boss fights either as it’s largely the exact same boring fighting. I actually was shocked with the 2nd Boss the ‘Dog’, you spend like 3 chapters running from this thing so you are pretty excited to finally fight it, and the fight its literally you spam the Stun-laser, land a combo, Stun-Laser, combo, maybe have you’re combo power built up so use that – rinse and repeat. Then its stage two is initiated by you walking up to it and pressing B followed by the entire process again. In the cutscenes this thing was ♥♥♥♥ing terrifying. In the game it was literally easier that the normal trash mobs.
The rest of the game is you climbing stuff – essentially pressing A and holding the stick forward. Personally I’m not a fan of when games do this, I get that it’s a spectacle and people seem to like it, I just don’t think it is really engaging. Tomb Raider did it probably the best where you at least have some agency to where and how you move but for the most part they aren’t great or defining sections. Oh and you’ll spend a lot of the game collecting hundreds if not thousands of these little orbs you can upgrade your character with (it’s not really a skill tree, most just bonuses if you ever play the game I suggest going for the special combo move and HP first to make the combat less boring), once again this is not really a thing im a fan of. I understand collect-a-thons in games like Banjo-kazooie etc, but in this I just felt it took me out of the experience and harmed the story as it was hard to suggest we were in a rush if I had time to run into some far off corner to collect these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t orbs.
Regarding the story, it alongside and atmosphere of an overgrown dystopic new york were certainly well done or passable. I have my issues with how calm Monkey is with being forced to be a slave and how easily he seems to accept it… or shows no resentment to his captor – especially when the game is praised for its ”real” characters. The game has some nice colour to it, still has some gross browns that were common back in 2010 when it was released, but still overall the levels look nice. Though in my opinion they start to all feel pretty similar.
Overall I’d probably never recommend this game to someone, and to be honest I’m still having trouble with why the game is considered so underrated. To me it was rightfully forgotten. It does everything ok but nothing great and there really isn’t much to it. Maybe it’s a case where it didn’t age well as every similar-game since its release (and arguably before as Batman released beforehand) has done a far better job.

Wow, this game has not aged well at all. Do you remember what it was like to play an RTS back in 1999? It feels like this: very poor unit readability, a right-click that willfully misunderstands you, units that default to "ignore enemies", spellcasters with no auto-cast... this game is just full of weird awkward design. Sound fun? Here's what you'll be doing half the time: squinting at a screen of dots, frantically hovering over them to figure out which tiny dot is the dot that will do some small ineffectual ability, and then figuring out how to get that dot to target another dot out of 100 dots.
This is a golden age of real-time strategy. They have unparalleled accessibility and visibility, more than any other time in history... and this is an RTS about HUGE 3D SPACES that doesn't let you use WASD to navigate it? Yikes yikes yikes.
The Foss-inspired ship designs and Adagio for Strings are still there, and perfectly lovely.
But if you're honest with yourself, this game is surprisingly unpleasant to play. "Remastering" implies they've looked at RTS design within the last 15 years, and incorporated modern accessibility into the interface. They're hoping you're so nostalgic that you overlook their laziness. Maybe that's OK, maybe Gearbox really needed some quick revenue and this was a fairly sure bet, fair enough.
In doing so, they commit the worst crime in AAA -- they feel cheap.

I like this game! Its very colourful, its not meant to be a historical recreation of pirating & its addictively fun!
Your character starts off with a ship, a crew & a pirate base to sail from. The game is mostly quest-driven, the goal being to complete quests for the different factions in the game (there are three), which rewards you with gold & reputation with that respective faction. The ultimate goal is to unite the three factions in order to take on the dreaded Black Cove Pirates & then become the Pirate King. Your character gains experience & reputation along the way, which unlock new skills. Your ship can be upgraded to become ever more powerful & you can recruit a pirate army to help you plunder colonies around the Caribbean. I found that the game mechanics were quite intuitive & its not a game you need to spend hours poring over a manual or practicing detailed tutorials just to play.
Sea combat is very easy & basic, but I have found it to be less cumbersome than the mechanics in "Sid Meier's Pirates! Gold".  If this game were only about sailing around, fighting other ships & plundering gold from their wreckage, it would be a boring game. But it isn't. Its about questing, accomplishing missions, gaining rewards & experience, & following a storyline. That keeps it interesting & fun & not too serious, enough to hold the player's attention. There are loads of corny pirate jokes to be picked up in bottles floating in the sea so you might even get a laugh out of it. I think the developers have done a lot of work trying to make the game as least serious as possible, to make it a fun game to play rather than a simulation.
At the price that its being offered on Steam, in my opinion it is worth the money. Its becoming one of my most enjoyable games to play :)

A-Train holds a special place in my heart, as the 1992 version published by Maxis is the first video game I ever bought and I spent countless hours on it. I was a bit hesitant to purchase A-Train 8 as it looks dated, the GUI feels awkward and the reviews and overall player feedback seemed mostly negative. But I played the time-limited demo, and even if one hour is a bit short to get a good feel of the game, I ended up purchasing it.
The game has quite a learning curve, and trial and error is very expensive, so you’ll probably botch your first attempts. There isn’t much of a tutorial, the provided documentation is useful but minimal, and I found very little help on the web. The interface is functional once you get used to it, but not very intuitive and it doesn’t provide much feedback about what you can and cannot do. Finally, the track building is rather restrictive, as there is only one turn radius possible, and that’s a bit frustrating at times.
That being said, I am really happy with this game, and I am glad I bought it. The mechanics are simple (dispatching building materials and tweaking train schedules) but designing an efficient and profitable network is a challenging task. Watching the city grow and the numbers add up in response to your actions is very satisfying. The visuals are simple, but I like the style and it makes the game perfectly smooth on my mid-range video card, with everything maxed up on high resolutions, even when the screen is filled up with large buildings. I haven’t encountered any bug so far, and the game runs fine in windowed mode and allows unconstrained resizing.
It is a game that will not suit all tastes, and I think it takes time to start appreciating it. But if like me you are willing to bring back good memories from 1992, don’t hesitate.

A simple and intriguing game! The A-Train series has been published since 1985, and was the first game of its kind! It inspired Maxis to implement the isometric perspective in SimCity 2000! It has been a very long time since A-Train received a US release, since A-Train is developed by Artdink in Japan. The most well-known US release was published by Maxis in 1992. A-Train has a very large learning curve, but when you accomplish the basics through repetition. It can be a rewarding experience! As with any simulation management game, each one varies in difficulty and has to be approached with a clear mindset. No references can be made, or confusion is inevitable! A-Train 8 has simple mechanics in theory, but can have very complex behavior at times with certain situations.
First, you must build a simple passenger line from point A to point B. This system can be built anywhere on the map (unless you are trying to accomplish a scenario). Purchase a basic commuter train and place it at any section of track that is straight. Let the train make full stops at each station (which will be done automatically, unless you command it a specific route). When this occurs, the passenger line will attract people and businesses to your railroad.
Now that you have people swarming to you transportation services, they need materials to build houses and offices. Next, you will build a “materials factory” near your passenger line. You can choose the size of the factory, but larger the building does not produce any faster or better. Larger factories just have more lot space for storage. Materials factories produce “materials” which are used to build structures and houses for you town.
You can combine passenger and freight systems together on 1 rail system, but I see at times they are more efficient if you separate them (costs more money to build extra track though). Build a separate freight line to deliver the newly produced materials. Build another station next to the material factory and one of the passenger stations (for now, point A station we previously built), then build the new rail towards point B. At point B build a “materials depot” anywhere near the station. This is where the newly developed materials will be stored for you citizens to use.
Once all these basic systems are in place, your town will now start to developed and eventually turn into a giant metropolis! You can help further the growth and development of your city by purchasing company owned buildings and structures; when placed properly can earn you extra money. If you continually build more passenger stations around your small town, it will attract more and more people and businesses. Larger the rail system, the more volume of passengers it can handle.
And that is the basic mechanics of A-Train! If you need more information on how to play, I found a tutorial at their website:
Dated graphics, but not the worst. It accomplishes more in gameplay than visuals. Some mechanics need detailed explaining, but once you learn how they function then it makes sense. Map editor is a great addition, custom scenarios and maps make for endless replay value.

I'd recommend this game, it's fun, but it's fun despite itself, because it really does its best to ruin your enjoyment of it.
At core, you've got a relatively gripping "blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up"-simulator with funny quips from Rodriguez & Supporting Characters. This is satisfying! However, then you get saddled with a ton of equipment you'll never want to use and absolutely miserable controls for a lot of things(if I'm driving a tank and want to fire behind me while in a chase, it takes me half an hour to turn the turret, wingsuit controls are plain garbage, and why would I need something like SEVEN different control schemes? With the game not bothering to warn me when I bind the same key to two different things because I can't remember half the damn things I bound?), and crashing that seems to intensify the farther you get into the game. Which is ESPECIALLY annoying because mid-mission checkpoints are completely forgotten if the game crashes, in my experience, so have fun doing all that♥♥♥♥♥♥again if it crashes at the very end of a mission!
Also some general quirkiness with the grappling hook and physics at times.
I'm also having a hard time figure out if I like or hate the way the game lets you off easy. If an outpost is, against all expectations, giving you trouble, you can just run at it over and over, blowing up one chaos object at a time. Nothing gets reset or has to be done over, you can just slowly chip away at it. It makes getting killed feel more like an annoyance than anything else, the real reason not to die is just that having to get back to where you were is a chore at times.
On the other hand, considering that there are enemies with shotguns who can stunlock you(GREAT idea in a game where you're meant to be leaping everywhere like a monkey on meth), explosions that can ragdoll you, and that it's possible to get killed in one or two shots at times... maybe it's not so bad that the game is a bit forgiving. Though I'd rather they polished the combat than forgave you when it ruined you on accident.
Driving and shooting is also kind of a mess because most cars with mounted guns, you can't control while driving. You can only let an AI helper man it which is, ha ha, absolutely useless, so those guns are all worthless. Tanks and helicopters are the only things you'll ever really want to spawn. Also the issue that there's ZERO gun stabilizing while driving, flying or sailing, so in a game where your main defense is dodging, in order to have anything resembling accuracy... you need to stand stock still or move at a snail's pace.
But, aside from that... the game is somehow fun. It helps that it looks real pretty and that the music's perfect. Try it, especially if it's on sale. Also the DLC isn't bad(the stuff that has missions, at least, not the stuff that's just extra guns or vehicles), though it's kind of on the short side for the cost.

A great MOBA that separates itself from others in its own unique ways. Behind-the-character camera, body blocking, and a stronger reliance on aiming to hit with basic attacks gives it a more action-esque feel than many MOBAs with an overhead/RTS-style camera, The champions are gods all from mythologies of different cultures around the world (which is a plus for me, since I really enjoy mythology), and the design behind them is fairly well done. Many of the characters fit basic archetypes (with 5 classes and most characters having some form of dash/chase/escape), though there is enough diversity within and among classes to make things interesting and for each god to have their own playstyles, advantages, and disadvantages.
I definitely recommend the God Pack (unlocks all gods currently available and that will be available in the future, which is cheaper than the unlock systems for many MOBAs), though the gods are also available, similar to most MOBAs, on a rotating weekly schedule as well. There are multiple game modes (Conquest, which is a typical MOBA style; Arena, similar to team deathmatch; Assault, random 5v5 single-lane Conquest; 3v3 or 1v1 Duel; MOTD; etc.) which allow for some good variety and different playstyles to keep things fresh.
As far as cons go, there are issues from time to time with servers and lag, though that's nothing out of the ordinary, some minor balance issues when new gods are released (with a tendency to be overpowered which, alongside not knowing their counters well yet, can make for a number of frustrating matches for the two weeks or so it typically takes for them to start any sort of tweaking for balance), and that many of the "better" skins are only available through RNG chests (which cost on average $7 a roll for smaller chests, or are half the price but filled with many recolors/voicepacks/ward skins that you could otherwise earn just through playing). Of course, skins are only an accessory and don't change anything really, so that's a minor gripe, especially for a game that is available to play for free.
Again, I'd definitely recommend this game. Whether you're a fan of MOBAs or completely new to the genre, try downloading the game and give it a shot. I hope you enjoy it as much as I have.

Rome 2 was a horrible game when it released. It was full of game breaking bugs such as dead AI, turns taking more than 5 minutes to complete, huge FPS drops from doing something simple like clicking on a city and so many more. Now that it has received almost 20 patches and is finally fixed it is no longer one of the worst games ever released - it is merely the worst Total War game ever released.
What I like: The graphics
What I dislike: Literally everything else. The "politics system" is neither politics nor a system, it's a broken idea that doesn't do anything. You can go through an entire game without ever opening the politics tab and you won't notice. The music is bland and boring and doesn't bring the game to life like in Rome 1, Medieval 2 or Shogun 2. No family tree, making important people within your empire faceless, nameless and pointless. Generals and important people in your realm are non-entities. In previous Total War games losing a beloved faction leader or general could break your heart. In Rome 2 there are no beloved faction leaders or generals and when you do lose one they are instantly replaced by some other faceless non-entity.
The list of things this game got wrong is almost endless. I find it impossible to become immersed in its setting, I feel nothing when playing it. I've tried very hard to like it as I spent £34.99 on it and have been a fan of Total War since the days of Medieval 1, but I simply can't. It is truly horrible.

I'd recommend this game, it's fun, but it's fun despite itself, because it really does its best to ruin your enjoyment of it.
At core, you've got a relatively gripping "blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up"-simulator with funny quips from Rodriguez & Supporting Characters. This is satisfying! However, then you get saddled with a ton of equipment you'll never want to use and absolutely miserable controls for a lot of things(if I'm driving a tank and want to fire behind me while in a chase, it takes me half an hour to turn the turret, wingsuit controls are plain garbage, and why would I need something like SEVEN different control schemes? With the game not bothering to warn me when I bind the same key to two different things because I can't remember half the damn things I bound?), and crashing that seems to intensify the farther you get into the game. Which is ESPECIALLY annoying because mid-mission checkpoints are completely forgotten if the game crashes, in my experience, so have fun doing all that♥♥♥♥♥♥again if it crashes at the very end of a mission!
Also some general quirkiness with the grappling hook and physics at times.
I'm also having a hard time figure out if I like or hate the way the game lets you off easy. If an outpost is, against all expectations, giving you trouble, you can just run at it over and over, blowing up one chaos object at a time. Nothing gets reset or has to be done over, you can just slowly chip away at it. It makes getting killed feel more like an annoyance than anything else, the real reason not to die is just that having to get back to where you were is a chore at times.
On the other hand, considering that there are enemies with shotguns who can stunlock you(GREAT idea in a game where you're meant to be leaping everywhere like a monkey on meth), explosions that can ragdoll you, and that it's possible to get killed in one or two shots at times... maybe it's not so bad that the game is a bit forgiving. Though I'd rather they polished the combat than forgave you when it ruined you on accident.
Driving and shooting is also kind of a mess because most cars with mounted guns, you can't control while driving. You can only let an AI helper man it which is, ha ha, absolutely useless, so those guns are all worthless. Tanks and helicopters are the only things you'll ever really want to spawn. Also the issue that there's ZERO gun stabilizing while driving, flying or sailing, so in a game where your main defense is dodging, in order to have anything resembling accuracy... you need to stand stock still or move at a snail's pace.
But, aside from that... the game is somehow fun. It helps that it looks real pretty and that the music's perfect. Try it, especially if it's on sale. Also the DLC isn't bad(the stuff that has missions, at least, not the stuff that's just extra guns or vehicles), though it's kind of on the short side for the cost.

Well, for starters I can say this game has a pretty nice presentation: lush environments, a diverse and well-handled stereo soundscape, and fitting mechanics. Story is basically null, with missions in-game telling you "kill this with that" or "do these things with this animal", and that's good for the sim-feel of the game.
BUT, you will at most get 3 or 4 hours out of theHunter if you don't want to pay for every single thing (weapons/gear/licenses/sights/etc.) beyond your starting kit. Once you've performed the four missions revolving around the only animal you'll be hunting in free-mode (Mule Deer), there's not much left if you don't feel like paying 4,99 euros for the next animal's license (spoiler: there are well over ten species, and the price gets steeper at every one).
Sure you can wander around every reserve in the game (as a "guest" as you are referred to) and look at the gorgeous landscape, but you want to track and kill animals? Better haul out that wallet. My hope is that this gets a fixed price for the whole game, and unlockable weapons/gear as you progress in the missions. As it is now I can't recommend it, despite the hard work put into it.

A great MOBA that separates itself from others in its own unique ways. Behind-the-character camera, body blocking, and a stronger reliance on aiming to hit with basic attacks gives it a more action-esque feel than many MOBAs with an overhead/RTS-style camera, The champions are gods all from mythologies of different cultures around the world (which is a plus for me, since I really enjoy mythology), and the design behind them is fairly well done. Many of the characters fit basic archetypes (with 5 classes and most characters having some form of dash/chase/escape), though there is enough diversity within and among classes to make things interesting and for each god to have their own playstyles, advantages, and disadvantages.
I definitely recommend the God Pack (unlocks all gods currently available and that will be available in the future, which is cheaper than the unlock systems for many MOBAs), though the gods are also available, similar to most MOBAs, on a rotating weekly schedule as well. There are multiple game modes (Conquest, which is a typical MOBA style; Arena, similar to team deathmatch; Assault, random 5v5 single-lane Conquest; 3v3 or 1v1 Duel; MOTD; etc.) which allow for some good variety and different playstyles to keep things fresh.
As far as cons go, there are issues from time to time with servers and lag, though that's nothing out of the ordinary, some minor balance issues when new gods are released (with a tendency to be overpowered which, alongside not knowing their counters well yet, can make for a number of frustrating matches for the two weeks or so it typically takes for them to start any sort of tweaking for balance), and that many of the "better" skins are only available through RNG chests (which cost on average $7 a roll for smaller chests, or are half the price but filled with many recolors/voicepacks/ward skins that you could otherwise earn just through playing). Of course, skins are only an accessory and don't change anything really, so that's a minor gripe, especially for a game that is available to play for free.
Again, I'd definitely recommend this game. Whether you're a fan of MOBAs or completely new to the genre, try downloading the game and give it a shot. I hope you enjoy it as much as I have.

For me, NMRiH is such a fun experience. Just putting yourself, and a bunch of people together on one map, let it be mission or survival, with about hundreds of zombies around you, there's just no end to it.
With items spawning at different locations, and limited supplies, NMRiH always pits you into a struggle that even I won't even cope up with.
The combat seems just simple, but there is nothing wrong with that. It just feels so real. You have to check your mag, reserve some fuel and stamina, and you even have to tend to your wounds as well.
But what's seems so repetitive about this game is its mission maps. The game gives you different objectives every start of a game in order for it to feel even fresh, but as a person who played this game for a total of 23 hours, it all seems to come back at me, like I know how to do this at the back of my hand, but nethertheless, When the said objective requires a certain item you need that's around a crowd of zombies, it could get really intense.
The survival maps are really impressive. It pits you and your buddies in one map, with a random amount of waves of zombies, and with checkpoints for your group to defend. The barracade system is nice, with boards alike, but what if there were nails in the game? Would that add more immersion or will it just add struggle into the game? That is one question that I even ask myself.
The game comes with a small amount of weapons for you to choose from, and each has its own specific ammo to use. Sometimes, even more than one gun uses the same ammo type, so that adds room for decision either to go with an SMG or a Pistol.
The game interface is just like hardcore mode in CoD. There's no display on how much ammo you got, or how much ammo is in your clip, There's no aiming reticle, and there's no map. Only just your hands and a compass for you to guide yourself around the map.
The inventory system is just one thing, however. I find myself struggling to make room for my extra ammo, and also switching between weapons. One time, I tried switching from my sledgehammer to my shotgun, but I pulled out a bottle of pills instead.
The zombies themselves, well what to begin with them? There's the normal, slow walkers, the runners, even children, which is a bit disturbing, but realistic. They are everywhere, and no matter where I go, I always bring a flashlight to see if I have a zombie behind me, or worse, in front of me. I find the zombie AI simple. They walk around. If they see you, they'll come for you, and if you fire your weapon, they run after you. Basic zombie logic that is indeed good.
Since this game is just begginning to rise up from its shell, I would expect more from this game, probably even a single player survival mode, even. Where it puts you in one city, and you have no where to run. I would also expect the presentation of this game to improve more. I would like to see more things, but lets not push them too hard, huh?
I would recommend this game to any person that's a fan of the zombie survival horror genre, and I suggest playing it with friends, especially the ones who are new to the game. I could just tell you how much potential this game has, but for now, this is all I have to say, "I recommend playing this game. And it's for free, so no harm done playing it, right?"

I read a lot about how Rome II was bad and that it failed to capture the TWesque of previous games. I was very happy to find out that it was completely wrong. Rome II is the most immersive and driven TW game I remember. It is the first TW game that positively surprised me since I was spoilt by the first Rome.
If I had writen a list of all the things I wished to be improved in Shogun and previous TW games, Rome II would have met most of them:
Those alone make Rome II a big jump forward, but they are not the best new feature. That would be
. Provinces are the best new idea in TW ever. Not only do they make managing settlements both easier and more strategic, they actually serve as driving force for more conquest. When you have one settlement in a province, you are driven to get the rest for the advatages of having a province whole.
The last thing that I need to mention is how much of a difference
make in this game. Even though they barely changed anything, the fact that there are midterm goals now makes all the difference. TW games had always felt empty after the first quarter of a campaign. The new mission system doesn't entirely fix that, but it makes the campaign a lot more immersive and driven.
Rome II is not without faults.
But it is clear that we are reaching here. If they had done something to make generals more valuable and personal, this would have been the best TW game so far. Right now it is a tie for first place. The game is definitely worth buying, even if it not on sale (but do wait for one anyway :p)

Homeworld Remastered is a redone, from the ground up, version of Homeworld, released back in 1999 or thereabouts. Gearbox has nailed it, with the graphics and sound being truly immersive, and gameplay even better.
Once humanity discovers warp drives, and unknowingly breaks a millenia-old treaty with an intergalactic community, aliens are now tasked with erasing all of humanity with you being our only hope. You command the last human stronghold, a huge elliptical ship tasked with taking the fight back to them, and perhaps reign dominant or become at peace.
One of the greatest games ever created. Simply put. Worth the price. I am beyond excited that they remastered this classic!

I really thought I'll love this games when I saw the gameplay videos, the tactical options and the gfx. Sadly, I played about 10 hrs of Homeworld 1 remastered now and I am overly disappointed. The controls are the clumsiest ever, the whole game is buggy as hell (hey, try to reassign movent control keys..), and in the campaign I really did not get any feeling of a tactical gameplay. Since formations are broken, since the movement of squads and their behavior is neither well-controllable nor has any intelligent automatism, the whole tactic decisions come down to "the-more-the-better". In a battle you are often required to do sort of micromanagement with your fleet of fast-flying, hardly clickable ships, to tell them one-by one that they have to repair another ship, or have to do a special attack etc. Maybe I missed something, didn't play too long, but support-frigates that don't give any support/repair to the dozens of small crafts flying around them, without clicking each single one in action? Formations, the lowest, most basic tactical setting, simply do not work? And Gearbox talked themselves out of doing anything about that? I doubt I will buy any further Gearbox game next future.. Over 20€ for a game I really  dislike because it offers one frustrating moment after another is ways too much.
Having adored the original versions of the Homeworld games, the Remastered Collection is truly a labour of love in restoring these classic titles. I couldn't ask for more.

If you liked the first Dishonored, you'll like this. it's just as good as the first game, but with more choices.

+ Continues the beautiful, intricate level design and exploration gameplay of the first game.
+ Far greater variety of combat options, especially nonlethal options which the first game sorely lacked.
+ Ability to check the Stats page during a mission is a godsend as it allows you to see whether you're on track to get the Ghost and Merciful awards for a mission (the only way I play so far).
+ Improved visuals and, by now, solid performance on my midrange PC.
+ Great environmental and secondary storytelling (notes, overheard conversations, etc). I also really appreciated the attention to continuity; events from Dishonored 1 and the DLC are taken into consideration.
- Primary storytelling (cutscene dialog, facial animation, lipsync) is the same as the first game, which is to say fairly poor. You probably won't become too attached to these characters.
- It's nice to have the option to play as Corvo again but it was obviously added at the last minute. He simply has no character arc in this game while Emily does.

While my overall experience didn't change much, I feel like this is one of the first EA games to actually do it right. This game is being built from the ground up, which means it doesn't and shouldn't have content for the sake of content. Too many games shove in content to keep players playing, but because they're so focused on content the games are a buggy mess. This game does it right, so props to the devs. When things are added to the game they're polished and mostly bug-free. Every single mechanic they've added feels like a finished part of a game in development. Too many EA games feel like something that won't ever get finished. This game constantly improves and feels like it's actually making progress towards a release, rather than something that is going to be EA forever.
The amount of possibility right now is huge, this game can be more than just tower defense, more than just an action or open-world game. Depending on what's done this game could be something special. RNG loot, bosses, interesting and fun weapons, vehicles, different powers are all things that could be added to ultimately create an experience unlike any other I've seen and it excites me. Depending on what the devs decide to do this game could be truly huge.
Solid. Polished. Professional. These are all words I'd use to describe this game and the devs. No, it's not finished. No, it doesn't have the content of a finished game, but that's a good thing because I want quality over quantity every day of the week. I'm looking forward to what happens next with this game.
So far what I can say is: the combat is satisfying, the gathering doesn't feel like a chore and the building is fantastic. If you want to support some fantastic developers definitely give this game a try.

I tried during beta and I tried during this free weekend, but can't seem to get into ESO. I'm a MMO veteran with thousands of hours in WoW, LotRO, FFXIV, etc. Something those games have that this one doesn't seem to is that they make it obvious what sorts of things you have to look forward to if you keep playing. They have so many awesome new skills as you level up, it makes you want to keep playing to try them out.
ESO... well, there's just 4 classes, and each of them just has like 15 class skills across 3 trees, and you can only have 5 on your bar at a time. Meanwhile, each spec of each class in WoW probably has like 30+ skills to fill up however many hotbars you could possibly want.
Then there are weapon skills, which by the numbers sound weaker than the class skills, so I wonder why you would use those... and I'm sure the game is well-balanced and there are great reasons to level up the weapon skills, but it's not obvious by looking at the tooltips, and i don't want to have to be combing the forums as a level 10 newbie just to figure out how to play properly. Turning to the internet for min/maxing during the endgame is expected for an MMO, but should not be expected to learn the "right" way to play right from the start.
So anyway, that's my story. Maybe the endgame is awesome. But I can't find a reason to keep playing, knowing that I'm going to only be using 5 skills at a time, and all those skills across all 4 classes sound lackluster and samey.

The game has improved a lot from where it was in beta and at launch, and now sports a lot of content to consume and less grind. It feels like what it is, an Elder Scrolls game crossed with an MMO.
The business model is one that I prefer in modern MMOs, which is that you pay once for the game, and then pay for additional DLC or Expansions as you see fit. Most of the content in the in-game store is cosmetic, although there are some upgrades that I think should really be included in the base game at this point, like the any race / any alliance one. Not requiring a subscription means that you can come and go as you please, so you never feel like your wasting money if you aren't playing enough because some other new game came out you want to play through.

A great MOBA that separates itself from others in its own unique ways. Behind-the-character camera, body blocking, and a stronger reliance on aiming to hit with basic attacks gives it a more action-esque feel than many MOBAs with an overhead/RTS-style camera, The champions are gods all from mythologies of different cultures around the world (which is a plus for me, since I really enjoy mythology), and the design behind them is fairly well done. Many of the characters fit basic archetypes (with 5 classes and most characters having some form of dash/chase/escape), though there is enough diversity within and among classes to make things interesting and for each god to have their own playstyles, advantages, and disadvantages.
I definitely recommend the God Pack (unlocks all gods currently available and that will be available in the future, which is cheaper than the unlock systems for many MOBAs), though the gods are also available, similar to most MOBAs, on a rotating weekly schedule as well. There are multiple game modes (Conquest, which is a typical MOBA style; Arena, similar to team deathmatch; Assault, random 5v5 single-lane Conquest; 3v3 or 1v1 Duel; MOTD; etc.) which allow for some good variety and different playstyles to keep things fresh.
As far as cons go, there are issues from time to time with servers and lag, though that's nothing out of the ordinary, some minor balance issues when new gods are released (with a tendency to be overpowered which, alongside not knowing their counters well yet, can make for a number of frustrating matches for the two weeks or so it typically takes for them to start any sort of tweaking for balance), and that many of the "better" skins are only available through RNG chests (which cost on average $7 a roll for smaller chests, or are half the price but filled with many recolors/voicepacks/ward skins that you could otherwise earn just through playing). Of course, skins are only an accessory and don't change anything really, so that's a minor gripe, especially for a game that is available to play for free.
Again, I'd definitely recommend this game. Whether you're a fan of MOBAs or completely new to the genre, try downloading the game and give it a shot. I hope you enjoy it as much as I have.

SMITE is a very enjoyable MOBA. It isn't as hard to grasp as DOTA 2 can be, but it is a solid strategical game.
The third person aestetic is a refereshing change of pace in the genre. Only Paragon has done something similar. All the characters are based on gods, goddesses, and titans from various world mythologies, such as Greek, Roman, Norse, Chinese, and so on. I personally hope gods of African tribes and Native American tribes are added soon. Also, there are several different game modes to play on: Conquest (your standard MOBA fare), Clash (Conquest on a much smaller map), Joust (3v3), Arena (5v5 in a large circle in which players protect minions going through the opposite team's portal), Siege, and more. These game modes are really cool and different so the game doesn't get boring.
This is a game I highly recommend if you like games like DOTA 2, League of Legends, or Heroes of the Storm and want to try something different.

This is also one of the more challenging games out there as you eventually have to balance multiple different types of documents and search them for even more discrepencies with even more availiable tools. That being said, the main draw of this game is how unique it really is and how good the stories in such a simple game can be. I am a new fan to the Homeworld series, having still been playing with Legos when the original games came out. As such, my review is unbiased. That is not to say that I haven't played the originals at all, as they are both available along with the Remastered versions free of charge.
Pros: The game's graphics have been modernized in the best ways possible. That is not to say it'll kill your pc, as I run this game fairly well on my stock laptop at max graphics.
The interactions between objects looks great (resource collectors docking with flagships, units being launched from carriers, etc.)
The game has a great modding community that works hard to bring a new experience once you've decided you want to see more in the same game.
Cons: Many old fans will tell you this, and I am inclined to agree: Formations are broken. In the classics, units in formations would hold formation at all times, but the Remastered formations simply affect what your forces do before they meet an enemy unit. They break formation and act as if they never had one in the first place until they get a new move order. However, Gearbox is working on fixing that issue, and in the Remasters there are more formations, allowing for a more diverse screenshot at the moment. Hopefully we can see that fixed soon.
The multiplayer is still a beta, as it mixes both game's factions into the same game and thus has balance issues. Again, this is being worked on.

Dark Souls II - having finally reached endgame, I feel my thoughts on this tremendous sequel are validated.
Firstly, Dark Souls while being one of my favourite games of all time, is also one of the only games I own that I never completed. However, I still feel it is a superior experience to Dark Souls II for reasons that are not apparent at first.
Mechanically, and aesthetially, Dark Souls II is a marked improvement over the original, with gorgeous lighting (be sure to download Durante's GeDoSaTo to tweak the visuals) and wonderful animations. In terms of environmental design, Dark Souls II's strengths are also the source of the only drawback I could find. Let me explain.
Dark Souls II has an intriguing story with a huge world to explore. But that world lacks consistency. There is a moment wherein the player enters a windmill, fights a boss battle at the top only to take a lift up to a castle surrounded by lava. While the latter, the so-called Iron Keep is one of my favourite environments in the game, this makes absolutely no sense. Whether it was intentional, I think it is one of few missteps in the overall Dark Souls II package. However, the levels are largely diverse, changes in design not only visual, but mechanical as a wide array of enemy types are brought to the forefront of the gameplay experience. And in that respect, Dark Souls II is a worthy successor to the deep, complex skill-based RPG that is Dark Souls. To risk a torrent of hate, I also must mention one other moment where I felt the experience may have been misguided - The Shrine of Amana. This zone is a poorly designed puddle, with slowed character movement and Mages that have homing spells and can hit you from across the map, if they spot you. As a largely melee-focused build, my struggle here went beyond wonderfully challenging to completely abhorrent - the only way through was to spam arrows I scavenged on my travels from afar, a grindy and horrible experience. The boss of this area while interesting in terms of Lore and visual design, was so unimportant and wholly unimpressive in the larger scheme of the experience, making Shrine of Amana feel like a pit-stop of padding to extend the length of the already extensive game.
In terms of gameplay, hitboxes have been tightened, ragdoll physics are no longer immersion-breaking and the micromanagement of health items and armour/weapon durability are improvements over the more obtuse mechanics of Dark Souls. The level of difficulty is punishing, but rewards skill over grind, a very big plus, and the combat is tight, with none of the floatiness of many western RPGs (I'm looking at you, Skyrim).
The soundscape of Dark Souls II deserves special mention. It is superb. From the clanking of a heavily armoured golem as they prepare to flatten your avatar to the eerie quiet of a long lost mooring to the beautifully understated and largely atmospheric score, Dark Souls II is a sonic joy.
To say any more of this would be heresy, as it must be experienced first hand.
To sum up my feelings, Dark Souls while possibly superior to Dark Souls II also remains unfinished, sitting on my shelf.
Dark Souls II stands proudly among my favourite games of all time, all of which I've completed - while reviewing it, I failed to mention the only thing that anyone should take notice of.
Dark Souls II is fun

One of the major tennants of the Dark Souls franchise, I've noticed, is not feeding you information. Or at least feeding you enough information to whet your desire for more information. It doesn't hold your hand, telling you where to go, how to find items, or even what items are in the game. All the design philosophies about Dark Souls are 2 things, in my opinion:♥♥♥♥♥♥move, bro, and Make them want to learn. You learn what stats are good and how to utilize them. You learn what weapons are most effective. You learn where the illusory walls are, what boxes are mimics, what combination of Fire Resistance gets you through Iron Keeps molten lava areas. You learn all that stuff and you feel brilliant because of it. All those things happen to you as a player and to your character ingame. The game tries very hard to make sure you never feel like a God. You always feel like you have accomplished something when you win. It's not an achievement for completing a chapter or reading all the somethings. You try a boss a bunch of times, you summon some randoms or some friends, and then you finally beat it. And that feels amazing. Because you did it.
In the end, Dark Souls feels like it takes gaming back to it's roots, back to Explore and Learn about the world because we can't feed it all to you on this 8-bit cartridge and manual. It feels like it teaches you how to play through gameplay and ambience and visuals. And this is all in a good way.
You will hear people tell you it's hard, but there's a difference between being challenging and being hard. And this game is Challenging. You can figure it out, you can beat it, and when you do, as stated, you feel amazing. That's what makes this game so great for me. It has high replayability, good music, good hidden story elements.

If you liked the first Dishonored, you'll like this. it's just as good as the first game, but with more choices.

+ Continues the beautiful, intricate level design and exploration gameplay of the first game.
+ Far greater variety of combat options, especially nonlethal options which the first game sorely lacked.
+ Ability to check the Stats page during a mission is a godsend as it allows you to see whether you're on track to get the Ghost and Merciful awards for a mission (the only way I play so far).
+ Improved visuals and, by now, solid performance on my midrange PC.
+ Great environmental and secondary storytelling (notes, overheard conversations, etc). I also really appreciated the attention to continuity; events from Dishonored 1 and the DLC are taken into consideration.
- Primary storytelling (cutscene dialog, facial animation, lipsync) is the same as the first game, which is to say fairly poor. You probably won't become too attached to these characters.
- It's nice to have the option to play as Corvo again but it was obviously added at the last minute. He simply has no character arc in this game while Emily does.

Easily one of the most beautiful space-themed games I have ever played. Fidelity wise and atmosphere wise this game is one of the prettiest games available on PC. I haven't felt this immersed while playing a single player game in a long time. When you run into what i call the 'acid egg sac' in the middle of the woods because you couldn't see it through the amazing looking grass and it explodes on you is one of those 'OH SH-- WTF WAS THAT' moments in gaming that are actually enjoyable somehow.
The mechanic of dissassembling the enviornment for resources is very fun, with each piece of absorb having a chance to drop any one of a few resources instead of the usual guaranteed resource count from a node. The combat is challenging, almost a bit too challenging, but balance will come later in the process. Right now the scaling between the first few nights will take a few retries to get a good base build quickly.
The basebuilding is extensive as well as easy to use, with parts easily fitting into place and orientated without really needing to struggle like in most games with the mechanic. It's honestly a pleasure to base build especially when you can get your resources back by absorbing a piece of you misplace something. Most of these systems are a struggle to use, Eden Star plays like an absolute dream.
Probably the best part about this game is that the dev team is extremely responsive to feedback. I have bought at this point probably 100+ early access titles, and there are very few dev teams that respond like Flix Interactive does. I have watched the development of success stories like Prison Architect, and miserable failures like Blade Symphony, and Flix has that 'it' factor that really makes me believe they are going to go places. As a guy that watches game developers almost like some would watch a football team, I don't take such a positive evaluation lightly.
The only negatives of this game as far as I can see is you need a really decent system to run on high settings, the balance is a bit poor at the moment, and the UI needs some work. The good thing is that all of those issues will eventually be fixed or already are being fixed by the dev team.
Worth a buy, especially at the $20 USD price point. I've already gotten my moneys worth and I havent even made it an entire week in game yet.

Papers, Please is a masterful piece. You play as the lone border inspector at the only crossing of a secluded eastern european nation only just beginning to open to foreigners. It is amazingly deep and each day has something new, introducing game mechanics in the form of more stringent immigration policies, work permits, frauds, and even weaponry. I was hooked onto this game, and I love the dystopian setting. Even though the graphics are barely there in an aesthetic that harkens back to early PC gaming. it serves just enough to have purpose and I think it works perfectly.
There is also a surprising amount of choice to the game. From determining the fate of those seeking to gain entry without the proper papers to things much deeper, and perhaps more sinister. I've found myself playing a cold man following protocol, until certain events eventually led me to sacrifice nearly everything for the wellbeing of my nation. And guess what, that's maybe one out of 20 or so endings. One playthrough will probably get you a few hours, but in my opinion, the story mode is worth replaying for everything you might have missed, not to mention an 'endless mode'.
Additionally, it's not all easy. You must also use your meager income to pay rent and care for your family, which makes the idea of bribes and other incentives all the more appealing.
I heartily recommend this game, even if for the fact that it serves as a very good narrative of what the United States and other nations have done with their travel policies.

A great 3rd person adventure through a retelling of the old Chinese tale "Journey To The West" within a Sci-Fi post-apocalyptic world. I won't say much in terms of characters so here I go. Monkey is the brute while Trip is, as I like to call her, the gadget, Together they use each other strengths in the hopes of taking down mechs, the enemies of the game.
Now onto the pros and cons
Pros
- The characters are believable and enjoyable, this is aided by the dialogue which is written to not be too serious but enough to where you are able to care for the characters
- The game is beautiful, even by today's standards, even if some of the textures aren't highly detailed
- The pacing for this game is in my opinion imaculate, through every combat, jumping or puzzling stage the game pulls you through with its story and new areas
- An obvious one for me, but the collectibles in this game have reasons to be there. The "Tech Orbs" help you with your upgrades while the the other collectible adds to the overall story of the game.
- Boss battles feel like boss battles, they're not necessarily difficult compared to other games but they are always graduose in scale and always fresh due to the new mechanics that get introduced to defeat the bosses
Cons
- The gameplay can get rather tedious, it's a lot of button mashing and so on, on top of this many enemies can come at you all at once and since you only have a limited amount of blocking it can create some frustration
- The humour in the game cn be hit and miss depending on your comedic tastes
- The upgrade system is rather basic but does help you especially in the later stages
- A small one, but the cutscenes are unskipable for all I know. For example, I'l beat a chapter and then watch the cutscene leading to the next chapter, I'l then quit the game so I can play it later, when i play it again I have to watch the cutcscene again without being able to skip it.
There is a lot more to be said about this game but I will leave it up to you on whether or not you want to play it, Like all steam games, I'd recommend getting it on sale. The gameplay is nothing groundbreaking but the story, characters and visuals make it all worth playing till the end. 7.8/10

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a fairly average action adventure puzzle game which has a pretty decent story and quite an unpleasant mash of gameplay mechanic. It is a game which mixes third person beat em up, third person shooting, stealth and puzzle elements together and I felt that it was not combined well as you could be beating up enemies at one point for a short while and next you would be at a turret section shooting them. The fixed camera angle is also really horrible as it is very hard to see enemies when you beat them to a corner or at certain puzzle section you would feel difficulty maneuvering around platforms or obstacles.
The story is pretty decent and fairly lengthy as well, There are mainly only 3 characters which you would see for most of the game and that is Monkey, Pigsy and Trip. Trip is a really dislikable character at the start as you would find her annoying and useless but you might grow to like her more as the story progresses. Voice acting in this game is great as talents such as Andy Serkis is giving voice to Monkey.
The DLCs included in the Premium edition are skins for Trip and Monkey which looks pretty alright and can only be used upon completion of the Game as well as Pigsy perfect 10 which serves as a story prequel to the main game with pigsy as the main protagonist. Pigsy Gameplay is quite different from Monkey as you would be playing mostly a third person shooter with stealth elements. The story is pretty bland and boring, it does not add much to the main game lore-wise as well.
Overall, I would only recommend this game for the story as it is fairly lengthy and interesting (Main Game only not Pigsy Perfect 10 DLC), however be warned about the bad camera angles and generic gameplay elements. I would give this game a 5/10.

However if you're new to Homeworlds and are a big fan of space RTS's then get this, Technically for the price you are getting 4 games, and it's totally worth it.
I'm not usually a fan of remasters, as I don't see the point in touching up something that is already good. But in the case of these games Gearbox has done an amazing job, and really brough Homeworld into competing with modern games. The care that has gone into remastering this masterpiece, is beyond what you would expect.
The storyline is just as engaging as it was all those years ago, I'm not going to spoil anything, so you'll have to find out for yourselves.
I personally haven't tried the multiplayer yet, but I will in time, if it's anything like the original multiplayer (i.e. back in the days of linking 2 pc up in the same home, long before the days of himachi) or better, then it's going to be awesome.

I decided to play through both H1 and 2 before writing a review, just to make sure I had an accurate idea of what has been changed. I'm not going to say much about the original Homeworld releases - I'm sure there's years of reviews already, suffice to say you will already know if you like this kind of thing.
Without a doubt, this Remaster is one of the best examples of it's kind, applied to one of the best RTS games ever made. Graphically, it's sublime - the upgraded textures and effects make this look like some kind of blockbuster sci-fi movie, only you're playing it rather than watching it. The missions themselves have been tweaked slightly to make them a little less ridiculous - Gearbox are already posting fixes and further tweaks to the aspects of the missions that were less hard and more simply unfair (Radiation patches in missions being much easier to see, for example). The missions are still something of a challenge (including the fun Thaddis Sabah mission where the opposing Vaygr forces seemingly don't have a population cap) and both titles are still games of the early noughties.... i.e. you are expected to use your grey matter as much as your reflexes - but the core gameplay was so ahead of it's time that when attached to the new visuals, it looks like a brand new AAA title.
I believe they've updated the voice actors in H2 to use the same ones they used in H1, and the new UI is common to both versions. The resulting effect is that the games feel like different chapters of the same story rather than seperate games, and I'll be honest, the package works better for it.
There are a few negatives. The 'Collection' doesn't include the cleaned up, ultra-impressive remastered soundtracks, instead presented as DLCs. Personally I think they should have been given the 'all-inclusive' nature of the release, but meh. A minor nitpick that you can rectify in the next Steam sale.
Formations are a bit broken. Ships still assume them when ordered but break when they do something else, some of the time. I do have to admit that this was an aspect of the original games that I never really bothered with that much, and given Gearbox's track record for supporting this game it wouldn't surprise me if it's patched by the time you read this review. The games's (particularly H2) annoying habit of dragging your attention away mid-battle for a cutscene is still here, and it doesn't include Homeworld Cataclysm, on account of it's source code apparently being lost. It apparently crashes in MP often, but I don't do much MP so can't say that with any certainty.
It's not quite perfect.... but if you're into space games, RTS, or simply truly amazing gameplay, you will find this to be awfully near to it. The only people I wouldn't recommend this collection to are people who dislike sci-fi or fans of mediocrity.

Generally a good game which does an excellent job of managing tension via sound design. The game  is generally good; with excellent graphics and sound and no real bugs or glitches to get in the way.
The gameplay rewards exploration and every room feels like it has a valid place and function and is not just there to rush past. The early levels prior to your main encounters with the alien are the best - there's very little risk and the forced exploration to find resources fits well.
However - once the alien starts to show up, the risk of exploration is outweighed by the poor save game setup which unfortunately hinders rather than hightens the experience. There's many a time you have to drop back to a save five minutes earlier to do four minutes of tedious navigation / collecting only to reach the crisis point again, get caught and start again.
In the end this leads to avoiding the exploration and concentrating on getting through an area as quickly as possible - not the greatest of decisions however as many of your defenses against the alien and others later in the game rely on collecting these things.
We (by which i mean I)  end up in a vicious circle of having to replay large sections to collect scrap and components which i will need later on to get through parts but not getting anywhere as your exploration nearly always gets cut short by the appearance of the alien who seems intent on visiting every single  bit of the space station you are in at exactly the same time. This approach means that your options later in the game are hindered by not having blueprints or components to build things that would aid your progress.
Overall, I recommend the game.  As survival horror games go it does a grand job of recreating the atmosphere of the first film. However if you are the sort of person that likes to plough through a game and gets frustrated by having to replay large sections of essentially opening doors and collecting items from rooms to get back to the action,  then it might be worth avoiding or waiting until it plummets in a sale..

Great game! Creative Assembly weren't afraid to do things differently and take a few risks and it paid off brilliantly.
Don't go in expecting an experience like the second film. This game is designed as an accompaniment to the first film and the influences from Ridley Scott's classic are everywhere. It is all about recreating the suspense and terror of simply trying to survive while you're the prey. If you're fan of Alien, you'll appreciate so much of this game.
You rarely have the upper hand in any given situation and usually your options go as far as either run, hide or run and hide! Such a welcome change for a first person game.
If I had to give one complaint it would be that the game can become a little bit of a slog around the half-way to two-thirds point in the story but after that there's a pace change and you'll motor through the last few missions. (I know, complaining about too much content! Shouldn't really be a negative should it?)
Fantastic sound design and wonderful visuals make this one of the most immersive experiences to be had in a game.

There is no game that better captures the Alien Universe like Alien: Isolation. I wish I could have played it with its highest graphical settings, but my computer is too old to run them. Nevertheless, this game was brilliant. I will be playing the DLC and the other modes for the game as well, and then I'll edit this review once I've had enough fun with those.
PROS of the MAIN STORY:
-Story. LOVED the story. It was a little slow at some points, but for the most part it was very... captivating. Yes, that's the word.
-Fear Factor: For me, this was a near pants-crapping experience. I recommend playing it on "Hard".
-Atmosphere: Spooky enough to keep me on the edge of my seat most of the time. Very few horror games can do that to me. I'm a tough guy.
-Ambience/Soundtrack: Ambience was as spooky as the atmosphere of the game, and the soundtrack was absolutely brilliant - and in some cases nostalgic.
-To quote Markiplier: "SPAAAAAACE!"
CONS of the MAIN STORY:
-Cat and Mouse: This is the big one. There are numerous situations in which you will be playing Cat-and-Mouse with the Alien. Because there is no way to kill it, the only thing you can really do is hide from it and hope it doesn't find you. Even when you get the... um... certainly lovely weapon of mass destruction, you'll likely find yourself hiding from the Alien. It is vital that you watch how much of that weapon's ammo you use, because if you're not careful, you'll be left with no way to defend yourself - I learned this the hard way.
-Androids: Trust me, you'll wish they didn't exist for pretty much the entire game. There are WAY too many androids stalking the halls, and they NEVER leave you alone.
Overall, quite a wonderful game.
EDIT #1: Do NOT play this game on Mac just yet. There are some things that need fixing.

This game should be removed from Steam as "Free to Play", as it is a "Pay to Play" game.  The only aspect of it that is free for users is to hunt mule deer and cottontail rabbits, the latter of which will be a disqualified kill for using the wrong type of weapon.  Because free users are also only given one weapon, it is not possible to have a qualifiying kill for anything aside from whitetail deer.  There are missions, typically giving 100 or so "gm" (game money?).  For about 5,000 gm you can purchase another 10 rounds of ammunition, however keep in mind that you need to pay a fee to reset your missions if you go this route.  The sole currency which can be used for weapons and most everything else is "em" (electronic money?), which can also be earned for "free", on the condition that you take a survey, or download something, or sign up for something, or give your credit card information to someone, ect.  The entire experience is ruined upon learning that this is not a free to play game at all.  The free aspect of it is nothing more than a demo.
***Steam, please see the above and remove this game from your "Free to Play" category, this is a demo and/or "Pay to Play".
Now, on to the gameplay aspects.  Shot placement counts, there is some internal hitboxing for vital organs but they don't appear to serve a purpose (lung puncture does nothing to prevent respiration of the animal, only serving to make it bleed out faster).  You can't skin the animals you kill, or butcher them, or really do much of anything aside from walk up to corpse and click them to say you got it and show which parts of them you hit.  Because you can't get their fat or their skins, there are no hides to be tanned, this game is not interested in anything happening after the kill.  Do not expect to be able to strip trees of bark or cut them down, or pick any of the wild flowers you walk through.  If you find a mushroom you can click it, but they aren't more than a collectible.  Want to walk to the top of that mountain you see?  Too bad!  Want to swim out to that yonder peninsula?  Sucks to be you!
There are no lifetime memberships to purchase, it will be an ongoing payment structure.  They have completely missed the mark of what it means to be free to play, and another game will likely come in to fill this market that is more "complete" with their features.

This game is almost unplayable. The forced camera angles are frustrating and nasea inducing. Protip, always go opposite the direction the camera wants you to go. You shouldn't have to fight the controls to play the game, but the game can't consistently decide if you want to wide attack or dodge, if you want to move or stand there, and it appears to assume you only want to platform between the same two obstacles.

Turning the settings on max doesn't help at all. The cutscenes are rarely any better, and if you ever die or restart, they are unskippable, have fun with that. The execution animations get stale after the first time, and I'd rather they not be their at all. There are also annoying, repeated animations of the main character almost falling, which interupts the climbing, and is repeated over, and over, and over again. I get it, very dangerous, now let me play the game.
Speaking of glitches, I have had to reload multiple times due to trip not wanting to finish climbing the ladder, or getting stuck on a platform and not being able to get to the next clearly highlighted platform. I've had bullets or staff shots be blocked by thin pieces of rope, or thin air if the game decides you arbitrarily haven't earned that kill.
Long story short, this game fails to do the one thing anyone purchases games for: be FUN.
