Factorio is a spectacular 2d isometric survival game and I reccomend it 100%. The depth and polish of this game is unlike that of any other game on steam early access, and in my 40+ hours of playing this game I never expirienced a single crash or bug. The gameplay was fresh and rewarding, but also challenging and fairly balanced. The art style, despite being some what bland and unappealing, felt very fitting and complemented the game nicely. The multiplayer in this game is phenomenal. It doesn't impose any unneccessary rules or restrictions, both players can pause and are free to♥♥♥♥♥♥around as equals.
Now onto the cons, of which there are few. The circuit system leaves quite a bit to be desired, it felt over complicated and clunky. The aliens felt underdeveloped and shallow, the ai would just mindlessly shuffle around their nests until a player came into their range. I feel like this game would benefit greatly from a more developed ecosystem, where the enemy aliens had to hunt for food and drink water. I'd also like to see a wider variety of weapons and vehicles to keep the gameplay fresh, as well as more resources that force me to venture outside of my base.
Over all factorio is a brilliant game with infinite potential and I can't wait for more!

Pros:
-The gameplay is varied: you will be jumping between exploring, solving simple puzzles, having fights in melee, ranged, and mixed combat and you can ride on a hoverboard.
-Character interactions are rather fun, especially once Pigsy shows up, then the characters finally start to banter with one another.
-The animations and scenery; the game is rather old at this point but it’s still wonderful to watch Monkey climb about the animations on him are stellar as well as some of the vistas that are seen throughout the game are masterfully crafted so that they stand the test of time.
-Pigsy’s Perfect 10: Once you beat the game go into the extras menu and you’ll have unlocked Pigsy's Perfect 10. It is a short campaign where you play as Pigsy, and the game embraces its silly nature and has you going on a quest to create your best bud.
Neutral:
-The skill tree system isn’t too developed but it’s good enough for what the game presents you with, mostly stat boots with few combat abilities thrown in.
-There is a low variety of enemies probably less than ten if you include the bosses. Although the variety is small they make up for it by making you fight them under different conditions so it doesn't get too repetitive.
Cons:
-This game has many enemies but the worst one is the the camera, between jumping between static camera shots and it not being responsive enough to follow you during fights and or when just exploring is tedious and annoying.
-Although the story is clearly based on to the Journey to the West the plot of the main game average at best with an okay ending.
General Thoughts:
Enslaved is a fun game in the style of Uncharted with a lesser focus on gunplay and bigger focus on melee. It, like Uncharted, is more of a story based game where the fighting is just a means of getting you from point A to B so that you can see the amazing vistas and go through the events our heroes experience; which are rather enjoyable. It’s not an amazing game however it is a good one. It’s just odd enough for you to want to keep playing to see what’s around the next corner.

Eh. Not bad. Just played through the tutorial missions (an hour or two). Feels a lot like Sid Meier's Pirates, but a bit less... I dunno. Just a bit less. Almost feels like this was what somebody on Sid's team wanted to do with that game, but split off and did their own thing instead.
The big differences aa that there's no "battle map," (when you meet another ship, you just start shooting, you don't run into it and then get whisked away to the enconter grid) and you actually have to walk around town to do things, as opposed to just clicking around town to access the buildings. When you meet a ship on the ocean, you just start shooting.
If you've never played Sid Meier's Pirates, I recommend this game. If you HAVE played Sid's game, and wish it was just a little bit different, give this a try. Overall I'm disappointed that it's so much like SMP, but it's not a bad game; it's juts not worth playing this AND Pirates.

Generally a good game which does an excellent job of managing tension via sound design. The game  is generally good; with excellent graphics and sound and no real bugs or glitches to get in the way.
The gameplay rewards exploration and every room feels like it has a valid place and function and is not just there to rush past. The early levels prior to your main encounters with the alien are the best - there's very little risk and the forced exploration to find resources fits well.
However - once the alien starts to show up, the risk of exploration is outweighed by the poor save game setup which unfortunately hinders rather than hightens the experience. There's many a time you have to drop back to a save five minutes earlier to do four minutes of tedious navigation / collecting only to reach the crisis point again, get caught and start again.
In the end this leads to avoiding the exploration and concentrating on getting through an area as quickly as possible - not the greatest of decisions however as many of your defenses against the alien and others later in the game rely on collecting these things.
We (by which i mean I)  end up in a vicious circle of having to replay large sections to collect scrap and components which i will need later on to get through parts but not getting anywhere as your exploration nearly always gets cut short by the appearance of the alien who seems intent on visiting every single  bit of the space station you are in at exactly the same time. This approach means that your options later in the game are hindered by not having blueprints or components to build things that would aid your progress.
Overall, I recommend the game.  As survival horror games go it does a grand job of recreating the atmosphere of the first film. However if you are the sort of person that likes to plough through a game and gets frustrated by having to replay large sections of essentially opening doors and collecting items from rooms to get back to the action,  then it might be worth avoiding or waiting until it plummets in a sale..

Play as Emily, the game is clearly made for her with Corvo as a bonus. The story is made for her, and her powers fit the levels a bit more.
Pros:
- Graphics are nice and really set the environment well
- Level design is simple enough to let a player traverse easily (if you play as Emily) but not so easily it isn't fun (if you play as Emily).
- Some of the characters are neat.
- The player feels more connected to the plot (compared to the last one). Instead of somebody telling you "Go eliminate this guy because I decided he shouldn't be around without consulting you," it's "All of us are working for the same goal and together decided that this is the next target.
- Emily's powers can be used in really creative ways that let you have fun with it.
- Bloodflies are slightly less irritating than rats
- Most of the levels are designed simply enough that you can memorize the layout to your advantage, but not so simple that they are all easy.
-- Even the gimmick level (A Crack in the Slab) is awesome, just because of how seamless they handled it. It's so cool. I want to gush about my feelings about this map, but that ventures into spoilers.
- Non-lethal eliminations are creative as ever. The non-lethal ones are often even more satisfying than a lethal one!
- Bonecrafting is helpful, and it lets you customize how you play even more. You know, it helps you ghost clean hands better, because I doubt anyone plays this game loud and lethal.
- We learn more about The Outsider
- New game plus is a great feature so you can play as the other character without totally starting over.
Cons:
- Maps still are pretty linear. Point A to point B, you might find a rune or some bloodflies or something on the way.
- Game is stupid easy with Corvo's powers. Levels are built to give Emilys a challenge while keeping it fun, but a Corvo can sprint through the whole thing and still ghost and clean hands a level. I mean, the player can deliberatly take it slow, but at that point you're doing a chore, not having fun.
- You move locations so much that it is sometimes hard to keep up with the story and some characters.
- Enviornments look better, but characters still look downright weird. I don't think anyone has ears that look like that.
- Emily is not good at hiding her identity. she just covers her mouth. She's the Empress of all The Isles, Corvo mentions that she sneaks around and hides out almost daily, but her best way to disguise herself is to cover her mouth with a cloth? Still running around in the probably pretty fancy noble clothes she wore to a formal event as Empress?
- The final boss was a bit lame to ghost.
- The extent of most sidequests are "You can rob the black market." Which is in every level with a black market. That's about it if you don't count the ones that set you up for a non-lethal elimination.
- Corvo's existance in this game is purely for nostalgia for those who played the first game.
- It's downright illogical that Corvo can walk around with that terrifying mask and civilians don't care. I'd evacuate the neighborhood if I saw somebody in that.
- Just like the last game, you'll find two or three powers that suit your playstyle, a couple passives that don't hurt your playstyle, and you will then accidentally start a rune collection, because you'll still keep collecting them even though you have no use for them.
- What we learn about The Outsider doubles the questions we had about him.
- The boat-driver is impossible to like and puts complete shame on the angel that is Samuel and all other boat-related professionals. Her attitude is psychologically built to make you want to ruin your Clean Hands run.
- There is a plot twist, just like the first game, but it is neither as cool or as important as it was in the first game. Takes you totally of guard though, which was good.
- None of those stupid music boxes that take away your powers for no good reason.
- I played on hard, and it was not that difficult. Play one difficulty higher than you wanted to be
- Pretty sure Emily's hair is made of plastic, or that hard frosting you put on designer cakes.
Pretty good though. I haven't found a lot of replayability in this game or the previous one, but I think that's just me.

Better than the first one in every way. Actually, I liked The Knife of Dunwall more than Dishonored, and The Brigmore Witches were even better. With Dishonored 2, Arkane keeps on delivering and improved everything we love about immersive sims.
Level design? Aramis Stilton's mansion is one of the best missions I ever played. And, of course, each objective can be reached in several ways on all locations.
Visuals? From the overall level design to the smallest details - this game looks incredible (and after the patches runs @60 fps on ultra on i5 and GTX1070).
Characters? Damn, I didn't expect to find so many memorable NPCs (both old and new) in one game. Moreover, one of the character-related revelations in the end was kinda unexpected.
Story? Still predictable like in Dishonored, but with a few twists.
Items and abilities? The game has a lot of tools for both lethal and non-lethal approaches.
After 24 hours (my first walkthrough with Corvo and no abilities on hard and high chaos), I want to play as Emily right away and see what changes in the story, dialogues and locations on low chaos.
Bottom line: this is one of the best immersive sims ever created. Just go play it.
P.S. Prey is awesome too.

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is game about a man named Monkey and his battle with stockholm syndrome. Jokes aside, I really like this game. I played originally on Xbox 360 after a friend let me borrow it years ago, and when I saw it on sale for $4 I decided to get it again and see if it held up. I'm glad to say that it did. It's a heavily story focused, character driven game that has some flaws, but I think it makes up for them.
The story is that the main character Monkey has a headband put on him by Tripitaka that forces him to do whatever she says or it hurts of even kills him. Trip wants him to take her to her hometown and then she'll take the headband off. At first, Monkey is doing it because he doesn't want to die, but the game turns into a pretty good dynamic between the two characters and their world views as they start to like each other and open up more and more. Though their characters do seem to awkwardly become different at times. It's hard to tell if Monkey is supposed to be a savage who was raised in the wilds or if he's an intelligent sort of everyday man with the build of the average professional wrestler. They're still likeable, but I wish the characters were a little more consistant.
Combat is pretty simple and easy to get into. I've played the game on easy, and I'm not sure any enemy has actually managed to kill me yet. You can get a health regen ability pretty early on if you save up for it, and it makes the game pretty easy. I haven't beaten it on PC at time of writing, so maybe the final boss is more of a challenge, but I don't really remember it being that hard. I remember the ending being a little confusing and not very satisfying, but then again I played the game in like middle school.
All in all, I think this game is an overlooked gem that I wish got more people's attention. If you see it on sale, I'd definitely recommend giving it a try.

You are a S.T.A.L.K.E.R.
One of the many mercenaries throughout Chernobyl that hunt artifacts formed by radioactive anomalies that do impossible things. Such as absorbing radiation, increasing resistances, granting health generation, or giving you near infinite stamina.
These artifacts are sought out after by scientists and stalkers alike, and can fetch large quantities of money, making the zone a goldmine for anyone brave enough to traverse its dangerously unforgiving atmosphere.
The game feels much more RPG than FPS, because every time you wield a gun it feels like an inaccurate wet noodle with a crooked barrel, while all your stalker friends, neutrals, and enemies have perfect laser beam accuracy and can take a clip to the face and live, while you get pinned to the ground dead at mach 10 if a stray bullet so much as brushes past your cheek. Even the illusive sniper rifles are weirdly inaccurate, and yes I know what bullet falloff and spread is, but this is ridiculous.
If you can get used to the gunplay, it provides a satisfying experience once you consistently take down enemies, watch them flop to the ground, loot all their corpses, and waddle back to the shop to pawn it all.
So S.T.A.L.K.E.R, get questing, killing mutants, shooting dudes, collecting artifacts, exploring creepy corridors, and taking in the sights of the hazardous deathtrap that is the zone.
One of the greatest FPS of the past decade. the atmosphere is absolutely stunning, the gameplay is challenging but fun, and the story is solid.

First off, this game is actually amazing when playing with friends, the team comp [usually] works out when everyone is good at their specific role. Communication is a key factor with this game and you can not pick "goofy" gods and expect to beat a well balanced team with gods that they know how to play. It always drives me crazy when someone autolocks, or locks in as a role that is already filled because they wanted to play that god, instead of putting on their big boi pants, and contributing to the team. That is really the only bad thing about this game, people complain about CC [croud control] in season 3 being OP, false, there are a numerous amount of items that counter/deter CC effects in the game. Im not gonna lie to you, this game is not all that balanced sometimes, but Hi-rez has been addressing the problems and everypatch a god gets a nerf or a buff depending on community feedback. This game has a great casual community, unless you run into the very few salty tryhards, the competetive is even better with everyone working together in order to acheive an ultimate goal. Whatever you do, do not pick this game up and expect to get what you want all the time, playing as only 1 god is a little frowned upon because sometimes you end up screwing over your team. Additionally, dont be salty if one of your teamates is down in the dumps on the leaderboards, we all have good and bad games. This game is great for getting into mobas if you are unsure if you enjoy them, the learning curve is not steep. If you enjoy this game you could get into even more like dota 2 or LOL. I will admit, I enjoyed season 2 more than season 3, but I guarentee there are people that enjoy season 3 and its progressive nature. The game is constantly adding new gods, items, and occasionally updating the maps to bring a fresh feel to the old.

For the record, there was a time when I loved this game. I have been playing since before the steam version  came out, with around 100 hours on it. To a new player this game is very refreshing, engaging, and interesting. Playing as gods from mythology really sets Smite apart from its competitors. The third person camera is also appealing to those who may not necessarily enjoy the typical movement system of a MOBA game. The game was a blast to play, UNTIL
You learn everything there is to know, and nothing is new anymore. Sure, you could purchase cosmetic items with microtransactions inputted into the game. (I personally Hate microtransactions, have a friend that spent $3500 on this game, yeah no joke.) The game becomes very addicting, and by the time you have found nothing left to accomplish, you find yourself addicted and have hours like mine.
Another main reason I cannot reccomend this game is because of how poorly the developers (Hi-RezStudios) have balanced the game. There is clearly unbalance with some of the characters, and the meta(Way the game is meant to be played) revolves less around skill but more around whoever has the most Crowd Control (Stuns, roots, mez, etc.) Is going to win. I find myself always being frustrated because whenever I try a goofy character I am always swept away at the sweaty people that pick these types of characters. Crowd Control is a vital part of a moba, but when you have it this bad with a very bad counter might I mention, what you have is a greatly themed game with interesting characters and a terrible core gameplay mechanic (Crowd Control).
For my final Verdicts:
Graphics: 6/10 - The game looks okay, but when compared with its competition, it definitely could look better than it already does. (Devs are attempting to update the graphics engine, however.)
Gameplay: 6/10 - I would have placed this higher, like an 8 or 9, but due to the poor choices of balance made by the devs, this game isn't as fun for me personally.
Sound: 9/10 - The sound is excellent in this game. Every character has its own unique abilities with unique sound and effects.
My Personal Enjoyment: Then: 9/10 Now: 5/10
Overall I would not recommend this game soley because of how addicting like drugs it is, and the poor balancing. You're more than welcome to try it, as Smite is friendly towards new players, but be warned: You may never wish to quit.

A great sequel to a true classic.
Dishonored 2 casually sports two of the greatest video game levels in the last decade and gives player a new set of skills to apply to the beautiful world it let's you play in.

Better than the first one in every way. Actually, I liked The Knife of Dunwall more than Dishonored, and The Brigmore Witches were even better. With Dishonored 2, Arkane keeps on delivering and improved everything we love about immersive sims.
Level design? Aramis Stilton's mansion is one of the best missions I ever played. And, of course, each objective can be reached in several ways on all locations.
Visuals? From the overall level design to the smallest details - this game looks incredible (and after the patches runs @60 fps on ultra on i5 and GTX1070).
Characters? Damn, I didn't expect to find so many memorable NPCs (both old and new) in one game. Moreover, one of the character-related revelations in the end was kinda unexpected.
Story? Still predictable like in Dishonored, but with a few twists.
Items and abilities? The game has a lot of tools for both lethal and non-lethal approaches.
After 24 hours (my first walkthrough with Corvo and no abilities on hard and high chaos), I want to play as Emily right away and see what changes in the story, dialogues and locations on low chaos.
Bottom line: this is one of the best immersive sims ever created. Just go play it.
P.S. Prey is awesome too.
P.P.S. I am not an Arkane studios fanboy :)

If you have a console I would advise purchasing Dark Souls II for it rather than PC. Keyboard & mouse controls are useless and using a 360 controller doesn't improve play much. All hints and tutorials, what few there are, reference 360 buttons rather than keyboard and mouse controls regardless of whether you are using one or not. Some moves such as jumping attack or guard break are next to impossible on either control scheme without the use of outside modifcations.
Gameplay wise it is challenging in a trial-and-error fashion. You have to study your enemies moves, looking for clear opportunities to attack and then taking advantage of openings. Works okay most of the time as long as the clunky mechanics and poor control scheme don't screw you over. Other times is is frustrating and tedious. Finally overcoming a challenging encounter provides a temporary sense of achievement until you reach the next where you will spend more time banging your head against the wall until you break through like a medieval Kool-Aid man weilding a greatsword.
Graphics are okay but certainly nothing special. The soundtrack and ambiance does justice to the despairing and lonely environment. There isn't much story to speak of and the characters are forgettable. The PvP is abhorrent in that the poor mechanics are exacerbated by lag or hackers. Some areas such as Belfry Luna are recommended by the community to be played offline to avoid such issues which is a strange recourse. I cannot think of any other game that I have recently played that provided a better experience by shutting out the rest of the gaming community.
The progression system involves collecting souls to spend on attribute points. It is a decent enough method and provides a clear picture of how increasing each stat improves your character. If anything I would say it is a bit bloated; perhaps some stats could be combined to prevent inefficiencies in character build. If you are just starting out, as others have said, try using a shield until you get the mechincs and systems down, then try your hand at your desired playstyle. It is almost baffling how effective using a shield can be in this game.
Overall it is a mediocre game but I wouldn't recommend it on PC. Despite all its good and could be better points, I cannot help but feel it was a rushed port to cash-in on PC gamer demand for a challenging RPG. Perhaps with more time and polish it could have been better. For a somewhat decent and challening RPG without the hassle of poor controls, try Divinity: Original Sin.

I'll start by saying that I love this game. It took a long time to beat, but half of the fun is accomplishing small goals that you set for yourself ( Kill a mastodon with no armor on, pvp with only a dagger...) and the other half comes from the feeling of accomplishing those goals. Whether it's beating the game, beating a boss, or just doing something awesome, there's this feeling of satisfaction.
While the story is not very clearly stated, it's still a very good one. Once you're in the community, you watch videos about it and feel amazed and inspired. Whether a character's story is tear-jerking, laugh-inducing, or anger-filling, you'll come to find out that the world that you were, admittedly, blindly tromping through was actually filled with interesting little tales.
Gameplay is the defining factor of any Souls game, and Dark Souls II delivers. It can be quick and panicky, or slow, methodical, and exact. This, of course, depends on your personal preference, but either way is perfectly viable. The endless amounts of builds, weapon combinations, and battle strategies keeps PvE and PvP exciting and fun, and there's no feeling in the world quite like parrying and getting a huge dagger crit.
The art style is quite monotone, I'll admit. There aren't a lot if deviations on the stock "castle/forest" locals that Dark Souls II puts you through, with the exceptions of the DLC, which are, so far, aesthetically beautiful. Drangleic Castle is probably one of my favorite areas so far, the reason being that the first time I saw it, even after having seen videos of it before, left me speechless. The massive, colossal towers and cramped rooms filled with new enemies was fun, exciting, and difficult.
Co-op is a blessing during some parts of the game. Being able to summon helpers for the first boss in Drangleic Castle and throughout the gutter is a huge help, especially if that helper is a higher level than you. PvP I haven't gotten tired of so far, because everyone tries different combinations of spells, swords, and shields and it makes you really have to think on your feet if you want to win.
My only cons with the game are it's lack of direction. I'm not talking about the level design, which is fine, I'm talking more about NPCs and hidden areas. To activate crucial events you have to cycle through dialogue, which isn't always apparent. And some areas are quite tucked away, leading me to try looking all throughout an area trying to find out how to progress.
My final verdict is a 9/10, because it's a really good, solid, difficult RPG adventure game. It has an enormous amount of replayability due to its immense internal reward for getting really good at a boss or area, it's breathtaking at points, it's ton of unique equipment, fun online, and challenging progression. My only problem with it is the lack of clear story and difficulties with NPCs. I hope you enjoyed this review and found it helpful, and thanks for reading!

I use the hell out of this software. I've gotten GOOD at this software. It has given me many opportunities I would have lacked with other solutions for building D&D style maps for my campaign.
The DLC is many and varied, and to my shame I purchased a few of them early in the life cycle of this product. The problem is that so far it has been ALL DLC.
One's capability to create beautiful maps in this is tied directly to their patience and probably an aptitude for 3D design/CAD software principles, with that DLC at a distant runner-up. The potential is there, I've slogged through this software for my players' sake, and to a degree it's been worth it, but at this point I'm more willing to just take whatever I can get from Roll20 instead. It may not be as dynamic, but the core design is far more robust than VBM.
There are many core issues that the product has that I and others have voiced on the discussion forums:
- Closing the software is instant and gives no confirmation prompt.
- To save a map, you enter a filename and click save, or click on an existing file name. IF YOU CLICK ON A FILENAME IT IS INSTANTLY OVERWRITTEN WITH ZERO CONFIRMATION.
- There is an undo function but it cannot undo a delete operation.
- Mousewheel scrolling over the objects list or category list navigates those incredibly slowly, but also zooms the main view in and out, as it never loses focus.
- Clicking on a new object in the object list with another object already selected places the previous object on the grid, as it never loses focus.
- Objects cannot be copied and pasted once placed.
- Snap-to-grid for position, rotation, and scaling is relative to a start position, not an absolute, making it difficult and time-consuming to arrange rows of similar objects.
- There is no tile/fill function.
- There is no copy/paste function.
- You cannot expand the objects menu.
- Objects are not identified or identifiable after being placed; if you use curiously_similar_wall_1 and want another, you have no way of identifying it among its cousins, curiously_similar_wall_2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. You must place each of these and compare visually if you want an exact match. They have no visible object names in the objects menu.
The problem is that every response from the developer has been "{We're adding it to|We've added it to|It's on} our list ;)". A month after this response, new DLC is up for sale. We got space and modern DLC before we got simple bug fixes.
If MWMDragon addresses this at some point in our natural lifespan, I'll reconsider. But I cannot abide recommending this software in its present state; it's simply not worth it.

I wasn't really sure whether I should write a review for this software or not - especially after I've initially struggled with using it and at first, found it largely un-intuitive. BUT... a recent campaign which I am going to run for our D6 based Star Wars virtual tabletop group has inspired me to give Virtual Battlemap another try, and so here I am ... attempting to do just that and give the program an unbiased review.
First off, this is a settings builder. It is a software that can help you as a GM (or a 3d visual artist) build a variety of places that make great visual aids in depicting fantasy role-playing scenarios. Now that I've had several hours to tinker with it, I can see that it is a lot like online LEGO - and like LEGO, it comes with a variety of DLCs or 'sets' that you can apply in creating a stunning visual of your game or adventure setting.
True to its description, VB is a program that will help you build tabletop rpg maps in virtual space and then export them as high quality images for live gaming purposes (whether tabletop or online play.) Exporting these maps for either of the aforementioned purposes can utilize high quality resolution, although I have only had the chance to test the online option, so far (given that our group only does virtual tabletop gaming, we do not have much use for the hard copy print outs).
I have to say that I was very pleased with the results; the lighting module which can change the ambiance of your setting in a flash - was especially stunning - specifically when building maps that were meant to project a particular type of ambiance, or mood. The amount of objects accessible so far, via various DLCs - is satisfactory and suitable for my purposes as a GM - the only area it is currently lacking in, is more science fiction components. I am patient however, and hope that more such relevant DLCs will be released in the near future.
Second, the controls. After having seen (at long last), the beginner's tutorial video (available both on YouTube and on the Developer's website), I finally gained a solid understanding of how to become more efficient with the program's mechanics.  I recommend this video to anyone who finds the software intimidating - you will find that as concise as it is, it gives you all the tools you need, to get going - and fast, too. (I am myself a visually impaired person, and I have to say even I find these controls to be easy to learn and manipulate.) All it took, was a little bit of patience.
Third, lets talk Price - and I mean, the whole price - including the DLCs. Sure, at $30 it is not considered 'inexpensive', and with the DLC's averaging at around half the price of the software, you will quickly spend a $100 without thinking about it. Yet, when you consider how much the basic LEGO set is, and then try to buy 5 or 6 *themed* sets to accompany it, you will spend quite a bit more. Basically, the way I see it, is this: What is the utility provided by this software, worth - to YOU? Is it worth what the developer asking for? Do you believe he has put in enough (or more than enough) effort, to warrant the price tag?
It definitely, is - to me.
As a Game Master who has spent years utilizing PDFs and crappy images of things found online (which more often than not, were grossly inadequate), I find Virtual Battlemap to be a breath of fresh air. YES, it will take time to build things with this software. YES, it will take a lot of patience on the user's part. YES, it will cost you some money if you wish to invest in it to the point where you can do everything and anything the software is capable of building. (I chose to forego going to Subway once a week to get myself a DLC. After a few months, I had all the DLCs I needed.) Yet in return, you will have a ton of fun, creating your own custom map which your players will appreciate and be awed by - as a Game Master, that is all the reward I need. :)
Thus, for the time being - I give it a 9/10 - with room for growth.
Highly Recommended - for patient, imaginative, open-minded Game Masters

I am really on the fence about whether to give this a positive or a negative. I would like to give it a solid "neutral" and so I will give it a thumbs down FOR NOW until they fix some usability issues. While I am patient and persevere through them, or find work arounds, I shouldn't have to be since they are pretty simple things.
Pros:
Great textures
Great Ideas for it
Can make beautiful lighting on the maps.
Cons:
Expensive as hell (creators justify it, but whether you agree or not, it's still damn expensive)
Tedious to the max! I don't mean like "oh, you gotta get things right", I mean like "oh, the things dont stick to each other, don't line up with the tiles, and often clip or create odd angles" because the actual placement of the objects needs a lot of thought and work (one simple improvement: allow floors to "stick" into the grid).
Further, the UI is abominable. They REALLY need to think about usability here. The ideas are great, but they need to think about how people actually use programs. This would require more explanation than a simple steam review, but suffice to say, the UI is tedious and nearly unusable.

In all honesty, this is one of those products you either have a use for or you don't, so the only questions beyond that are quality and value.
Does this product do what it promises to do? Yes it does. I've gotten some very nice results out of it. Suffice it to say, though, it's also one of those propositions where there's not that much you can do with the basic package, and need to splash out on no end of DLC to exploit the product's full potential. Which brings us to the question of value.
Here's where the negatives come in. The developers seem hell-bent on only putting the basic product on sale, and even then never for more than 20% off, despite it being released a year ago. The DLC? Never, ever seems to go on sale. I've even commented upon this in forums - something I only rarely do - to which the devs responded with an official party line about their prices being "compatible with the current market", or words to similar effect.
This attitude may, unfortunately, have some bearing upon how relatively few reviews of the product have been written, which I can only presume has resulted in similarly disappointing sales. It is, of course, the prerogative of the devs to sell their product at any price they damn well please, but unfortunately this is Steam, which is ultimately a bit of a "sales" culture.
Anyone who looks at this Store page right now will see the main product at a sale price, and a whopping great swag of DLC for nothing but full price. Even the DLC which was released almost a year ago. You don't have to be a psychologist to realise that most punters will see this as a good reason to promptly move on, and find something else to buy with their hard-earned sales moolah.
Which is a shame, really, because it's a good - if limited - product beyond that. I personally have been hanging out for some DLC goodies for some time now, but always find myself waiting for that elusive 10 or 20% off. And I don't kid myself: I'm not THAT unique, so if I'm doing this, so are others. Maybe I'll crumble some day, or perhaps the devs will crumble first.
My advice to those who are still interested is to chuck this in your wishlist, then wait for the prices to come down. Unless you have bucketloads of money, of course, in which case you may as well just buy the whole ♥♥♥♥ing lot right now. Good for some, eh?
Verdict: 7.5/10.

500 HOURS INTO THIS GAME.....almost.........Let's do a review thing. SMITE is an over the shoulder 3rd person MOBA. One of the special things about this game is that every character is a real mythological god, with beautiful designs and abilities to match their Lore. Every god is very unique in the way they play, even if you take 2 gods from the same class they will still be quite diffrent.  We are currently clocked in on 77 gods to play as and still rising. SMITE is alot better to look at in game since you're over the shoulder of the god and not just on the top looking over a board. Gameplay is alot more immersive, since everything is a pure skill shot, including basic attacks. Abilities are also super good to look at. You can have a fat drunk man (Bacchus, god of wine) breaking his wine bottle, wine flying everywhere intoxicating all enemies. Or how about we have a tiny, cute little girl, SUDDENLY REVEAL THAT SHE'S A GIANT MONSTER (Scylla, Horror of the sea) AND SMASH HER ENEMIES WITH HER 4 BEAST HEADS! This game alos has tons of game modes for all types of people. You got your classic 3 lane, 1 big jungle map (Conquest). Your single lane and small jungle (Joust). 2 far apart lanes with a huge jungle in the middle where you can summon siege monsters that you can teleport to and will attack tower, phoenixs, and the enemy titan (Siege). A singular circle with no towers, phoenixs, or titans where the goal is to lower the enemy ticket count by killing enough enemy minions/gods. (Arena). SMITE a huge game that I never get tired if playing. Immersive gameplay, multiple game modes, tons of gods, It's my legitimate favorite game of all time. Plus, it's completely free. Sure, you don't get all the characters if you play for free, but you can get alot of favor at the start to buy a few gods to start with, and move on up. Please, if you are interested in this game atall, play it. It  might take awhile to get  used to it,  but it's amazing.

I bought Call of Duty – Advanced Warfare on special, and for the price that I paid it was worth the entertainment that I got out of it. For the first time in a long while the gameplay mechanics in this year’s Call of Duty game were overhauled and it felt fresh again.
Set 40 years in the future, you play a soldier that fights wars in an exo-suit that grants you bursts of superhuman speed and strength. This alone opens up gameplay to some interesting tactical approaches that were not possible in past iterations of this FPS. Every level gives you slightly different exo-suit abilities that you can use for that level only, and the campaign serves as a tutorial to what you can do in multiplayer. You do things like control a high-tech drone to cover troops, to using a cloaking exo-suit to clear a base, to jumping from car to car in a freeway chase scene. The whole this is delivered in that classic cinematic Call of Duty style which is always entertaining.
The story is decent and made interesting with the villain played by the remarkable Kevin Spacey. He owns every cutscene that he is in, and he is very comfortable as a commander-in-chief style villain.
Overall, if you can get this for cheap, the campaign will definitely give you around 7 hours of entertainment. Don’t expect to get much more depth than that, but it’s defiantly a fun ride.
Pros
- Overhauled exo-suit mechanics makes the game feel fresh
- Interesting single player campaign story
- Cool futuristic weapons and exo-suit abilities to play with
Cons
- Like all Call of Duty games, it plays it very safe and doesn’t do anything THAT different from the last
- Main character looks like he has a rat face in cutscenes

This is only a technical review of Feral Interactive's SteamOS/Linux port of Alien Isolation. For information about game content or other platforms, please consult other reviews.
First and foremost,  Alien Isolation is a fantastic game.
The graphics are the same as the Windows version, but it runs at about 80% the framerate using NVidia proprietary graphics (expect worse on mesa).  However, the game isn't terribly heavy, and runs well on my outdated Q9400 and GTX 760.  With all the straight lines in the artwork, there is some serious shader-level aliasing that can't be eliminated, but this is present on all platforms.
Tragically, Feral's Linux/SteamOS port is missing surround sound. Given the outstanding quality of the audio in the Windows version, this is a huge disappointment. If you have a good sound system, seriously, play it on any other platform.  The Windows, XBox, Playstation, even MacOS versions of this game all support surround.
When I contacted Feral support about the audio issue, their response was that they had simply never tested it.  *sigh*.
In the end, If you play on headphones, you won't notice the difference.  But if you have a good audio system, Feral's port of Alien Isolation is a big letdown.

Dishonored 2 is one of the best games of all time in one of the best series of all time.
So why are there so many bad reviews? One word: optimization.
The easiest way to fix this is by turning shadows all the way down to low, but even that won't stop the occasional performance issues.
Now is the game as good as Dishonored 1? Yes and no. Dishonored 2 heavily improves on the gameplay of Dishonored 1, creating a lot more of a dynamic and smooth combat and stealth experience. This is coupled with the New Game+ option, which makes the game a lot more replayable.
However, Dishonored 2 lacks the immersive atmosphere and story that Dishonored 1 had. Maybe it simply had to do with the rat plague. Maybe it was the subtle details that changed based on your chaos level. Maybe it was just the fact that Dishonored 1 was the introduction to the Dishonored universe. Regardless of what it is, Dishonored 2 does not have nearly as memorable of a story as its predecessor.
Death of the Outsider could very well decide the fate of the series. It offers the best chance at expanding on the story of Dishonored 2, turning a reskinned Dishonored 1 story into something more.
Regardless, the game is worth picking up if you have the money. It is one of the few games in the immersive sim genre that offers such an expansive sandbox stealth/combat experience. For anyone new to the DIshonored series, however, the first game is far more memorable.

Enslaved is a sadly overlooked action adventure game inspired by the famous Journey to the West tale of Chinese legend (Any of you who have seen the TV show Monkey will know the story, even if you don't recognise Journey to the West). While the inspiration is very lose, it's still solid enough that I felt a connection.
Enslaved uproots the story and places it in a post apocalyptic future where civilization has been destroyed in a long ago war. The ruins of man have been taken over by nature, with overgrowth slowly reclaiming our buildings and cities. The game begins with Monkey a prisoner on a massive slave ship. During the process of escaping he is enslaved by a fellow escapee, Tripitaka (Trip), who wants Monkey to help her get safely to her home far to the west, after which she promises to release him.
The ruined world is overrun with hostile mechs, remenants of the old war, and Monkey will have to either fight or sneak his way around them, all the while making sure Trip survives. If Trip dies, the band on Monkey's forehead will give him a lethal shock, so it's in his own best interest to do so. Trip is not entirely helpless, if she gets caught, she can unleash an EMP blast that will stun enemies, hopefully long enough until Monkey can get there to save her. She can also create a hologram to distract enemies so that Monkey can sneak in close.
The combat is reasonable, though perhaps a little simplitic. Monkey fights with a staff that can deal light or hard blows, by mixing things up he can create combos to do more damage. The staff can also shoot blasts that can either stun an enemy or damage them, though these require ammo and the ammo is often scarse. Scattered around the world are tech orbs that Monkey can collect and these effectively act as experience, allowing monkey to buy or ugrade skills from a skill tree. The tree is not hugely expansive but, like the combat, it does the job.
The main draw of the game is the wonderfully vivid game world that is a lot of fun to explore. The graphics aren't hugely detailed, as to be expected from a game from 2010, but the art design is very evocative and I found the whole experience really very pleasing. The story is also quite good, coupled with the art desing, this is the main reason to play. The relationship between Trip and Monkey building slowly from resentment and anger to actual genuine friendship. It is well acted and convincing. Andy Serkis provides the voice and the motion capture for Monkey and he turns in a great performance.
This edition also includes a spin off Pigsy story that takes place before the events of the main game. I don't want to say too much about this as it really was a pleasant surprise. Pigsy has none of Monkey's melee ability and is quite fragile if enemies spot him, so the gameplay for this DLC is entirely different, relying on stealth and getting to a good position so that Pigsy can bring his sniper rifle to bear. As I said, this one really took me by surprise, I wasn't expecting much but it was a lot of fun and the story itself is both funny and touching.
Between the main story and the DLC, this is a great package and I wish the game had done better, as it really deserves to be more widely played.

At first glace, this game doesnt seem that fun.
"Wowie, you're a guy working as a border patrol agent. How can this be a good game?"
But it's so much more than that. Set in a foriegn European country, you are set with the task of approving and rejecting people into your homeland of Arstotzka. You get paid per correct citizen you allow in, and you get penalized for every mistake you make. The rules and regulations the country gives you makes the game more and more challenging.
At the end of each day, (level) you are given your pay, but you also have bills. The food, heat, and rent expenses pile up. Often leaving you to not pay for one, leaving your child, wife, and uncle either cold or hungry. Or both.
This game challenges your morals. Do you let the young wife into Arstotzka to be with her husband? Or do you reject her becuase of a missing work permit and follow orders?

I was really excited when I found this program, as I had been mulling over the idea of using a TV to display environments for my players in our D&D sessions. I had looked into other programs like Campaign Cartographer or Dunjini, but since those programs are about 10 years old, and at least $50+ each for the basic programs, I tried to find alternatives and found this. After I had spent some time with it, however, my optimism quickly faded.
The amount of time it took to make anything meaningful was atrocious. In the two hours of play time I had before I asked for a refund, I didn't really have anything to show for it except for a handful of really small rooms, and they weren't even that impressive. All of the tiles in the game had to be placed one at a time, including floors and walls. There wasn't any features akin to clicking and dragging while placing a floor tile to create a 10x10 room, for example. While the effects are neat (like the dust, wind, water, and torchlight), when you export your creations they are no longer animated.
On that note, your exports are just a screenshot of the game. If your camera is off center, or not zoomed in or out all the way, what you see is literally what you get. It made for some really low quality pictures when zoomed in on my TV, and since the environments were in 3D, there was a sort of blossoming out effect with the top-down view. The camera was also a pain to maneuver.
Lastly, the core game leaves a lot to be desired. The amount of assets included feel minimal, and samey, and with multiple add-ons with an asking price of $15 each bring the "true cost" of this program up to $100. Otherwise, you cannot make anything interior, nature, or cave themed, which are pretty frequent environments players seem to find themselves in, and we all know it.

The assets/dlc work very well with each other, and it exports an insanely fine picture at humongous dimensions- like 6400 x 3000 pixels- well over enough to provide a sharp and clear printed image. At the risk of sounding over the top- this package and its dlcs gave me a feeling of something like god-mode level creativity.  Thanks for this program- for me it's worth every penny I paid and then some.

I was really excited when this program was first announced and I saw the preview, being an avid roleplayer and a DM. However, I have to say, even after a few minutes of messing around with it, I was disappointed.
My computer isn't the greatest, but it's run other 3D games fine. This software lagged even on the fastest settings. Exporting is slow, which wouldn't be as much of a problem if it at least displayed a progress bar. I thought the program had crashed! (which it did a few times anyway)
Not only that, the interface is incredibly clunky and hard to use. Maybe it's just me, but I had a hell of a time with the camera controls. I'd try to reorient the camera with the right mouse button, and my view would fly around the map uncontrollably. Meanwhile, if I tried to navigate around the map with WASD, I felt like I was crawling at a snail's pace.
There didn't seem to be an obvious duplicate or copy-paste command (maybe I just didn't find it), which seems like one of the first things you'd want in a dungeon builder. Furthermore, there didn't appear to be a way to make parts snap to each other (they did snap to the building grid, at least). What was also a bit confusing was that the parts models were partly transparent if you looked at them from the wrong angle.
Overall, I must say I was expecting more for this price. The graphics look great, but the program is just too hard to use. It would be faster for me to just drag tiles around in Photoshop.

Keep in mind, I dont usually write a lot of reviews but SMITE is an acception. I am a former League of Legends player, and if you are too you would know that the community is terrible and toxic and the game is unbalanced as of now. If you are a long time veternan of that game and you see how much its fallen, you need to find other MOBA games that were released at a max of 2 years ago. SMITE is that game you need to look into.
First of all, the third person view. SMITE is the first ever MOBA style game to pull this off. So to former MOBA players this is an exciting and eccentric way to play MOBAS. In my opinion it makes the game 10x better. You really get better at shooting skill shot attacks in SMITE, because if your enemy jumps and runs in difficult to read patterns its harder to hit them. It is good training especially if you still play other MOBAS.
The Gods. This game is well known for its heros. They are actual gods, meaning that this game can grow in a limitless way when it comes to releasing new gods. There are so many! In the game, on the main hub they have a Gods tab. This tab shows you all of the selections and even the mythology they come from. In the about tab it tells you all about their history and how they came to be.
The Gamemodes. If you're like me, in MOBAS the gamemodes are what make the game alive. Well every SINGLE DAY, is a new gamemode for you to try out. There are a ton of gamemodes and they rotate everyday. Not just that there are permanent modes too that make the game fun. I usually dont play Conquest, (which is the 5v5 normal map) I usually play Arena (It's a 5v5 map where each team starts with 500 tickets, whoever gets to 0 first loses the match. A circular arena where both teams are constantly in battle action). The normal, permanent modes consist of: Arena, Joust, Conquest, Clash, Assault and Siege, and all have their unique way of play style.
The Mastery System. When you play normal online matches of any kind you get mastery points of that god you play. You level them up level 1-10 and can get exclusive skins every 5 levels. So at level 1 you can get a gold skin. (It's like Blue and Gold). Then at level 5 you get a Legendary Skin. (It's Black and Gold) and then at level 10 you get a diamond skin ( Which is full out Diamond). Keep in mind though, if youre a goal setter like myself you want to master them all. However it's not easy. Plan on having hundreds maybe even thousands of hours into this game if you want all those skins.
The game keeps track of LITERALLY EVERYTHING. On your profile page, you can go to accolades and it shows you literally everything you have done in any (online) game you have ever played. It keeps track of kills, minions killed, assists, first bloods, number of towers taken down, number of jungle camps taken in any game mode, etc, etc, etc. The list goes on.
In all, SMITE is such an addictive game, which I recommend playing. Be warned if you get into it you will have no life left. Kiss that girlfriend of yours bye, not gonna be answering her texts anytime soon. Me, I only have 50 hours. When I started with SMITE I would always forget my login. So id make seperate accounts when my friends wanted to play. So at the end of that I ended with like 30 hours. But then I actually thought I should try and remember my account and try going hard at it and in 1 day that 30 hours went to 50.
PLAY THE GAME AND GET GOOD AT IT CAUSE IT'S FUN AS HELL!!!!
(P.S. The Ultimate God Pack is worth the buy if you want to focus on mastering the champions)

Pretty good RPG, recommended for everyone that loves the genre and who loved the Souls series. Even though at the beggining it can be difficult or confusing, later on it will be really enjoyable both pvp and pve

I'll start by saying that I love this game. It took a long time to beat, but half of the fun is accomplishing small goals that you set for yourself ( Kill a mastodon with no armor on, pvp with only a dagger...) and the other half comes from the feeling of accomplishing those goals. Whether it's beating the game, beating a boss, or just doing something awesome, there's this feeling of satisfaction.
While the story is not very clearly stated, it's still a very good one. Once you're in the community, you watch videos about it and feel amazed and inspired. Whether a character's story is tear-jerking, laugh-inducing, or anger-filling, you'll come to find out that the world that you were, admittedly, blindly tromping through was actually filled with interesting little tales.
Gameplay is the defining factor of any Souls game, and Dark Souls II delivers. It can be quick and panicky, or slow, methodical, and exact. This, of course, depends on your personal preference, but either way is perfectly viable. The endless amounts of builds, weapon combinations, and battle strategies keeps PvE and PvP exciting and fun, and there's no feeling in the world quite like parrying and getting a huge dagger crit.
The art style is quite monotone, I'll admit. There aren't a lot if deviations on the stock "castle/forest" locals that Dark Souls II puts you through, with the exceptions of the DLC, which are, so far, aesthetically beautiful. Drangleic Castle is probably one of my favorite areas so far, the reason being that the first time I saw it, even after having seen videos of it before, left me speechless. The massive, colossal towers and cramped rooms filled with new enemies was fun, exciting, and difficult.
Co-op is a blessing during some parts of the game. Being able to summon helpers for the first boss in Drangleic Castle and throughout the gutter is a huge help, especially if that helper is a higher level than you. PvP I haven't gotten tired of so far, because everyone tries different combinations of spells, swords, and shields and it makes you really have to think on your feet if you want to win.
My only cons with the game are it's lack of direction. I'm not talking about the level design, which is fine, I'm talking more about NPCs and hidden areas. To activate crucial events you have to cycle through dialogue, which isn't always apparent. And some areas are quite tucked away, leading me to try looking all throughout an area trying to find out how to progress.
My final verdict is a 9/10, because it's a really good, solid, difficult RPG adventure game. It has an enormous amount of replayability due to its immense internal reward for getting really good at a boss or area, it's breathtaking at points, it's ton of unique equipment, fun online, and challenging progression. My only problem with it is the lack of clear story and difficulties with NPCs. I hope you enjoyed this review and found it helpful, and thanks for reading!

A game with a lot of potential, currently still early in its development cycle... and it shows at times.
THE UPSIDE:
I was really drawn to the sort of 'mass effect' feel in a survival game.  Even the tool you use to mine, craft, build or fight reminded me of an 'omni-tool', as do the weapons.  Survival games are so frequently based around the sword and board ages or... gah... zombies, this game presented a much welcomed alternative to those flavors.
The game looks beautiful and the mechanics seem well polished and in fairly good working order, particularly when you take the development point of the game into account.
THE DOWNSIDE:
There are two major problems with the game right now and both are likely to change as development continues... i hope.
The first as i see it, the game is extremely shallow.  While everything you can do works well and looks pretty good, you can do just about all of it within a few hours of play.  You can always make your base larger and more elaborate and you can always farm for more materials, but beyond that survival is never really an issue after the first few turrets are placed down.  That isn't to say there isn't something enjoyable about building elaborate structures and seeing just how difficult you can make it for another player to get into your base, but right now you are pretty limited by type/number of things you can build.
The second major flaw in the system right now, and really i can't stress this enough, the server system is an exercise in pure frustration.  As it stands right now, you join a server and maybe you even took the time to visit the forums and find out which servers are "most reliable".  Even among these your doing well if your server is up more than two or three days in a row without disappearing for that at least that long.  You can switch servers of course and restart your base again... and then you can do it again when this server vanishes... and again... and honestly if you do it again you kind of deserve what you get.
Largely for this reason multiplayer is a pretty lonely existence.  Rarely more than 2-3 people are ever on the supposedly "most reliable" servers.  And its fairly easy to understand why.
One confusing mechanic was that while all servers are listed as PVE, they are most certainly not.  By accident my friends and I had found our way into another base and were shocked to find we were able to access their resources.  We actually were somewhat pleased at this revelation because while i'm not sure its intended it meant the game had radically new meaning.  We had to rebuild our base to defend against players!  And we were going to gear up and venture out and see what other bases we could crack.  This was quite a lot of fun, but then enter the extreme unreliability of the servers, to say nothing of the general confusion as to the PVE/PVP status of those servers.
THE LOWDOWN:  6.0/10  *with a lot of potential
For someone who doesn't usually look twice at survival games this one really caught my attention.  It has a lot going for it and i really hope the development process continues along the very promising lines it seems to be.  If your truly are looking for a single player survival experiences (WHY?) then a lot of the issues i have with the game really don't impact you, however, if your looking for a multiplayer experience or to play with friends, the game right now is just not ready.  Its one i will most certainly be keeping an eye on and very hopeful that i'll feel i can rightly flip this review.

EDEN STAR is what you get when Rust/H1Z1/survival games have a beautiful baby with gems such as Lost Planet 2, Titanfall, and more.
There are so many wonderful ideas. From base construction, crafting, to automated defenses and a meaningful day/night cycle. But it doesn't stop there. Wall running parkour, grappling/riding enemies, unique abilities, and they are working on automatons to help you fight entire wars against other player factions.
The game is pre-alpha, but I would buy it again. The dev team posts updates practically weekly, and provide a level of transparency that is on par with or beyond even the famously open Star Citizen. They speak to us, and they have a personal relationship with the community. Unlike so many big corporations that follow strict PR guidelines, this is a group of people that know their audience, people who have soul, and most of all dedication: this is obviously a project of passion for everyone involved.
That really does meaning something, because gamers as consumers really care about the brands they play. They do have a more personal relationship with the creators and company than other consumers do. A game isn't like flour: I don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the flour or who supplies it, so long as it isn't wood pulp and it's reasonably priced. But games are something I may spend hundreds to thousands of hours on. They are something people care about and grow to love. That's why gamers are notoriously fickle: because they're passionate. They want to see a game be everything that it can be, and they see the company and developers as *partners* in that endeavor. But most game companies have not caught on to this, and still treat it like any other customer-business relationship
But not Flix Interactive. They understand the nature of their relationship with us. To have a game company actually listening and communicating is a breath of fresh air. There is no silence to make you nervous, there are no worries about if you're being heard or what's going on. You know. And they don't just talk to you. They listen. They take player feedback. For instance, players wanted to build huge bases, even cities. This was never planned for or intended. Do you know what they did? They began optimizing the game for accomodate large structures as best as they could. The idea for drones and fighting robots arose from this, and it's why they're developing it; it all came back to the players wanting large settlements, and those settlements needed defenders.
With all that said, the game is a pre-alpha. Performance is not exceptional, though over the last patch it has improved immensely in my opinion. The movement is janky at times, the UI is kinda buggy now and then, and it has its mechanical problems. But that's how it goes with a pre-alpha.
But as a cynical consumer, skeptical and disillusioned with a distant game industry stuffed with the same recycled material, this is a game that stands apart. This surely sounds like a contradiction, as the market is being flooded with survival games. Is this a survival game? Yes, absolutely. But it is not confined by that genre: it builds on it with great ideas. This is a game I can love with a dev team I can believe in.
If you are something of a gaming philanthrophist, then let me say now: if there was ever a game that deserved your money, it is this one. If for whatever reason, you don't want to spend money on it in its current state, that's fair. But be sure to check back every few months. I don't think you'll be disappointed.
If you want to see the future plans, what is being worked on at present, and what has been added, take a look at the trello board here:
Players can vote on what they'd like to see added next, provide feedback, and provide ideas. The devs are also active on steam, and have a subreddit which at the moment is practically just updates and patch notes.

Absolutely love this game. I am a huge fan of the first Dishonored and stealth based games in general, and this game improves on it's predecessors flaws in almost every way. Gameplay feels very fluid and smooth, and the scenery for each mission is unique and memorable.
Difficultywise the game is lacking, especially if you go for a high chaos approach with powers, but the flesh and steel mode combined with a low chaos/ghost style of playing does pose a challenge and makes for an overall very satisfying experience.
Concerning the story, i have to say that Delilah as an Antagonist just doesn't live up to her role. Her motivations seem childish, her endgame is a big joke, and her reaction to her allies dissapearing one by one should probably be something else except, well, basically doing nothing and screaming mean threats from time to time. That being said, i really enjoyed Emily's growth as a character during the course of the game and the dynamic between her and Megan is well written. Also seeing Sokolov aboard this creaking whaling ship and just the feel of Karnaca in general is nicely done, and the athmosphere is definitely there during the missions.
All in all a really good game that probably doesnt beat it's predecessor storywise, but definitely gameplaywise.
If you like stealth this is a game for you, if you liked Dishonored 1 this is definitely a game for you.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. SOC is like no other FPS out there. The degree of freedom that the player has roaming around the Zone is like that of an RPG, but it still retains an intense combat system that will make you rely on your wits to get out of alive on the upper difficulty levels. There are odd jobs the player can do to earn extra cash so he can buy better equipment. Throughout the zone are multiple factions, some looking to control the zone, and others who are just trying to strike at rich. The Zone is a very brutal, dangerous, and terrifying place (especially in X-16 I think it's called) that will press the player to push on through. Overall, the Zone feels like a living entity, and it provides a fantastic atmosphere of sheer suspense and worry all while still having a nice combat system.
Pros
-Fully open world!
-Intense combat
-Nice variety of actual guns (though I think all of them have been renamed)
-Interesting story
-Atmosphere so suspenseful that even Alfred Hitchcock would be proud
Cons
-Glitchy, glitchy, glitchy, glitchy,glitchy!!!
-Graphics are outdated even for when it was released
-There are "game-breakers" i.e. you may kill an character that you required to complete the game, or you POed the wrong faction! (get used to quicksaving)
Even for its flaws, I still highly recommend this game. It may interest those of you considering buying this game that there is a mod called Stalker Shadow of Chernobyl Complete which will eliminate all of the above cons!
Do yourself a favor, and experience of of the best FPS since the 90s.

As a scholar of East Asian culture and Journey to the West, I was eager to see how this game adapted the classic novel. It was nothing like I expected. Instead of ancient, it was futuristic, and instead of animal companions, everyone looked human and modern. It's similar to how Akira Toriyama handled his own adaptation of Journey to the West in Dragon Ball, where Xuanzang is a woman who uses technology instead of a man who uses faith. So if you're familiar with the source material, then it's a great game from that perspective.
What weighs Enslaved down is the repetitive game design. Once you've finished the first level, you've experienced about 90% of the game. That is to say, running, jumping, climbing, and attacking robots. This rinse and repeat process wears you down and will make you want to stop playing after a couple of hours. As a result, you play it like you would a book: reading a couple chapters and stopping.
The reason you pick it up again is because the story is so compelling. What saves this game and makes it worth playing is the writing, voice acting, graphics, music, and few stellar moments of memorable gameplay. Push through the countless robots and you'll find it was a positive experience.
The DLC is much longer and polished than I expected it to be, and almost rivals the main game.
I hope the creative team behind Enslaved make a sequel or a new series in a simlar style.

This is a sequel, and had a lot to live up to but it just couldn't make that happen.
True it's had a graphical downgrade and I can understand the game has to be playable but there was no warning of this before release.
I myself have played Demon's Souls, which was a PS3 exclusive, and got Dark Souls on all 3 platforms. But with Dark Souls II... I got it for PS3 and could only really play it on PC.
Well firstly, Dark Souls II DOES in fact fix a lot of issues.
Positives I could find within the game-
1) Combat feels more involved. Swinging weapons feels like it has some weight to it and heavier weapons tend to deal more damage but are normally slower... By a bit at least.
2) Parrying isn't as forgiving as in Dark Souls 1, and it takes some skill to pull off.
3) Many weapons have had improvements, both in use and in strength. Something like a fist weapon with strength scaling makes sense considering the more strength you have, the harder you can punch.
4) Dual wielding has meaning! In The previous games, it was almost impossible to dual wield weapons. However, this game has a feature that depending on how you level, you can dual wield most of your weapons and they each can work properly, plus if you level your character properly, Dual wielding can be even more interesting, plus depending on what two weapons your using your dual wielding abilities change as well
5) Magic... Magic is REALLY difficult to implement within almost any game if you ask me. To try and keep it from being too overpowered but most magic has been properly made to not be too strong but not too weak either. Magic feels a bit more balanced that way.
Negatives that I found within the game-
1) The game focuses WAY to heavilly on difficulty. Now hear me out on this one because I can explain this. The souls Series was infamous for it's difficulty, and was the common thing to be acknowledged. However, In the Souls Games, Difficulty was never the point. Like the original overseer of the previous two games said "Difficulty was never the point. The spikes in difficulty were a way to immerse the player within the world." Which means the game felt challenging, but fair.
Let me give you an example for how difficulty felt wrong in this game: You can reach an area within the game where you come across a door. However once you go near the door, it suddenly breaks down and without any indication or warning, a troll creature barrels through the door and eats you. Okay, did that sound fair? No... there was no indication or warning you were going to die there. There wasn't even an animation of the wall cracking first just like the beta showed. It just popped out and instant killed you.
There seems to be a lot of things within the game made to insta-kill you without any warning. Plus... The difficulty feels like the only times it was hard was when I was outnumbered by heavilly armored enemies.
2) Things eventually stop respawning. Why was this implemented? Theres a thing where resting at a bonfire respawns all the enemies, this is true. BUT if you do this enough times, you'll apparently cause genocide. Everything will eventually stop respawning. So if you're farming for something, you'd better hope and pray you'll get that object. There's now no way to make yourself stronger after for playing so long. And all the experience you get from enemies? If you die, they're all gone and there's now no way to get them back because enemies stop respawning. This is basically a giant middle finger to all item farmers and exp grinders everywhere.
3) ARMOR IS USELESS! Why does the game have so much heavy armor and yet it's all worthless? Some armor can give some significant changes to defense yet but all that is worthless in the long run. Heavier armor is supposed to give you a stat called "poise" which means "Balance" or within the game, it's "How much of a beating you can take before staggering" Well, no matter how much poise you have, it's all worthless. Poise just does not work. How can a guy with a dagger keep staggering me if I'm wearing armor like a tank? So what would you rather have? A slow moving character, wearing armor too heavy that slows him down and is worthless? Or a guy wearing an old pair of pants that can swiftly dodge damage all together?
4) Soul Memory is broken. It's a system where whenever you gain experience, you'll be able to invade or be summoned to those whom have gained near the same experience as you obtained. This is in no way tied to your lvl, so let me give you an example of why it's broken. How would you feel if someone who is lvl 200 invade you when you're only lvl 30? This system was implemented to keep that sort of thing from happening but it simply made the entire situation worse. Plus matchmaking with friends wont work at all either because if you want to play with a friend, you have to hope they have been playing exactly the same way you did. You could say this game wasn't made to simply play with friends, then why is there a ring made specifically to make co-op easier? Plus, Invasions and co-op is all made completely rare because the net code for online play is junk, and theres no way to easilly join like within the previous games.
5) covenants are broken. Within the game you can join specific groups called covenants. These were made to give rewards when you completed a specific task for that covenent. However, the rewards are near useless, and you can just leave whenever you want without penalty and join again later.
Sun Covenant - Why is this here..? Just why? It doesn't need to be here. Oh wait... Because it's merely the most talked about covenant ever is why.
Rat covenant - BROKEN! It's nothing but a lvl grind. Why would I want to be summoned to a world, treading through water that restricts my movement, against a giant armored enemy whicch squashes me, and an enemy that toxics me? Then be suddenlt kicked through another loading screen?
Abyss Traveler covenent - arguably the best covenant, but still flawed...
Blood Covenant - A covenant made to invade players, HOWEVER you get very limited invasion tools and not that many, plus they break upon use so there's no continuous way to invade. And to rank up within the covenant? You need to win 300 invasions. YOU CAN BARELY MAKE 10 HAPPEN IF YOU'RE LUCKY!
Blue sentinel covenant - Made to be summoned to another person's world to kill an invader. I've tried this... You're never summoned PERIOD.
Bell covenant - Where you invade a specific area to kill a player within that area. Action packed if you want to PVP but that's it really.
That's the covenants I can name from the top of my head...
6) The areas feel generic and uninteresting. Plus they don't flow together correctly. In Dark Souls 1, All the areas seemingly connected just right. The landscape was interesting and immersive, plus areas are placed in sensible spots. Dark Souls II however... Makes no sense with it's areas. Here's just one of many examples as to why. You're in a poison wasteland in a castle, the sky is green and you suddenly take an elevator GOING UP. Now you're in a lava wasteland with another castle in it, plus the sky is now red. But in the poisoned wasteland, there was no indication of lava anywhere in the sky. Basically... The lava part is above the castle you were just taking an elevator UP with.

I just finished the game as Corvo and half of the time I was trying to figure out why the game was constantly crashing to desktop (Steam).
I have a fully updated game, updated Windows 7 Pro 64 bit, functional Intel Core i7-3930K, error free 64 GB of RAM, error free SSDs, non-overclocked GTX 1080 with the latest driver, latest DirectX, and verified integrity of Steam game files.
I suspect the issue was mainly graphics related since I was only able to pass certain areas in the game by lowering the visuals of the game - at worst to very low. Funny since the default setting set by the game based on my graphics card was Ultra. Also, several times the game crashed when I tried to possess someone.
I haven't had this problem with other games I've played on my system on highest visual settings, and I can't remember any game crashing as often as this one since I played my first computer game on a Commodore 64 in 1987. It surprises me I didn't loose my sanity during these innumerable Dishonored 2 crashes, but unfortunately I will not replay this game as I did with Dishonored 1, or play it on Game Plus, or as Emily.
I liked the story and gameplay though. I hope you're not as unlucky as I was.
