Another hidden gem, found while rooting trough my library searching for something to play, while I don't have enough money for Nier.
I have actually been having this game on my radar for years, ever since I saw it on the cover of a danish free gaming magazine. I never really looked into what it was, and was solely interested in it because of the few screenshots/art I saw. I heard about it again when it was ported to PC, and then again when it was in the Bandai Namco Humble Bundle, where I bought it, but I didn't actually play until now. Fun fact: I started playing it because I was playing around with In Home Streaming, and have been playing this game from start to end via that service.
This I feel is this games strongpoint, although I'd say it's not enterly lacking in all other points. Its some years old now, and it defenitly shows, but I really enjoyed the concepts of the world, from how the mechs took on this very mechanical look with giant cogs, to how characters and the environment is designed. If you are interested in post-post-apocalypse this game doesn't do a bad jobof building a nice world, and designing some cool characters and enemies to inhabit it. With that said, I feel like the standard mechs, were a little out of place, looking slightly too round and designed, but that is entirely my opinion.
The gameplay is pretty decent character action, which I'm normally not fond of, because I suck major balls at it, but combat felt nice and fun, with (mostly) interesting enemies, and a few button combos. If character action is your jam, this game does a good job. Personally I think enemy variation was very sparse, and could have benefitted by doubling the amount of standard enemies, or at least creating varying looks for them.
Here comes one of the worse points about this game in my opinion. I really liked Monkey's character, though he's the mandatory gruff-guy lead, but he was at least believeable and sensible, also probs to the voice actor he did a great job. Trip on the other hand I found to be a boring onesided stereotypical woman character. As a gameplay element she was cool, but her character was only "shes the weak woman, also shes smart but we just think shes silly". I expected her character to evolve more trough the story but I found she stayed pretty much in the same role.
Now, Pigsy I really didn't like. He was designed to be comical relief, but was just unfunny, and whole thing with him liking Trip and being jelous at Monkey was cringeworthy at best, and just made him come off as creepy.
The story was pretty okay, nothing great, and I certainly dont expect to remeber it as something great I experienced. I'm glad I played trough the game, but if you are in it to experience a great story, then take a pass, I would recommend playing Bioshock or Half Life 2 for something simillar (typical I know).
I saw some people complaining about the end, and I can see where they are coming from, I didn't mind it, but that was only because it was as mediocre as the rest of the story.
I don't remeber the music, which probably means it was merely passable, to say something intlligent about it, I'd need to go back and play again, but I can't be arsed.
I enjoyed the game, it didn't outstay it's welcome, and it defenitly wasn't bad. The gameplay is very competent, and the story is fine, didn't care for the characters much though. If you are looking for cheap-ish character action you wouldn't go wrong with Enslaved. Also if you are looking for cool designs and a nicely designed post-post-apocalyptic world, Enslaved has it for you as well.
TL;DR: Competent Character-Action, bland story, bland characters, buy for gameplay.
If I were to give it a score I'd give it a very solid 6/10.

Well, well.. This one a tricky subject and controversial franchise in todays standards. There is so wide gap between those who still enjoy COD and those who absolutely despise or are tired to the bone with it. I personally have played the first 3 COD games and then some MW2 and MW3 and now this, so I'm definitely not a fanatic or have tired myself out with these games. I did prefer the first 2 games most at the time and never was a huge fan of the MW franchise but liked those too. The cinematic storytelling I quite like but don't like the direction it's taken with all these qte cutscenes that hardly lend anything to a gameplay experience. I would rather just watch a cinematic unfold than do tedious button mashing that's supposed to immerse myself into something I really have no meaningful interaction with in reality. The only exception to that sort of gameplay I found to be appealing in indigo prophecy made by same crew that did heavy rain. There they made it fit the game somehow. However I must say this COD action wise seems frantic and visceral, production values are high and I feel the immersion in combat. The story might not be groundbreaking or the qte sequences really doing much for the game, but when in combat I must say the excellent audio and extremely hectic battles do suck me right into the action. As I'm not a competetive COD player it could be just that I have not bored myself to tedium with the franchise and thus am able to enjoy this iteration from a ground up level. Visually the game is quite stunning and while the engine is not up to par with latest engines it certainly looks very good with the shaders implemented here for postprocessing. The one gripe I have with these is the quite lackluster storytelling (read Michael Bay style) And the static environments. It's quite funny to see tons of particle effects on screen but when you shoot a bucket with a shotgun it stays glued to the ground and does not even receive damage other than some default decals. That kind of ruins the immersion for me but then again the action is so frantic you hardly have time to notice that at all. I like it, so maybe give a cautious try if you like COD but have not worn yourself out with every single iteration of the franchise :) The zombie modes are fun too imho. Totally turning the tables on the campaign to show a picture from the 'other side' Some of the best character models and realism to any action game on the market here too, which helps feel part of the albeit lackluster story. I have'nt mentioned the futuristic exo weaponry for purpose here. That is due to their limited use in the game which is a let down for me. You only get to use certain gear on certain levels, meaning you won't be able to enjoy the touted abilities or gameplay as it seemed in the trailers. You feel restricted by the developers in the singleplayer campaign. I suppose this was done to keep the story tight and to blend in with level design but it still is a let down when this was supposed to revolutionize the combat mechanics. On the other hand, in multiplayer you DO get to use all your gear so your multiplayer games are not limited by your abilities or gear.

NMRIH is not your conventional zombie survival game, where you have a seemingly infinite supply of ammo, plentiful weapons and are the human manifestation of a sponge.
NMRIH is a very realistic game with factors that would actually play out on a zombie apocolypse, for starters, weapons are very finite, guns even more-so, you find very little ammo through out the game and if you do you usually can't keep all of it.Decent melee weapons are in scarce supply.
Secondly, the zombies, the zombies in NMRIH are quite realistic, the zombies are not too spongey where you simply can't kill them, yet aren't too weak to the point that you and your freinds/randomers can't steamroll through the various levels added with the fact that zombies can actually infect you leads to a enviroment of tactical play, you need to go at a managable pace, killing zombie one-by-one, and you need to stick toghether while traversing the levels.
This game is especialy dark and really represents what a real apocalypse would be like, this is represented with the suicide option, yep thats right, suicide option, you press K with a loaded weapom and ypu put it up to your head, then you Left Click and Boom! This feature is mainly useful if infected and you need to sacrifice your life, for your teams'
In conclusion this game is a fun multiplayer, zombie survival game that so truly captures the darkness of the apocalypse they added a suicide feature

About the game:
All I wanted was a new Rome 1 with better grafics but I got a Rome 2 which lost its soul of Rome Total War. I am missing the micormanagement of evolving my cities, getting in conflict with my neighbours and inventing new technologies to improve my armies. Rome II is much more easier than Rome I because some features are missing, e.g. to get in contact with other civilizations I just have to "see" their borders or an unit of them (in Rome I you had to send diplomats).
The grafics are okay without impressing me very much. I am able to play Rome II with extrem settings but the battles are not very immersive. The new feature, the unit camera in battles, is nice to have but absolutly unneccessary.
Like in any other Total War the AI is not the best. CA improved it but all in all the AI is not a tactical genious. In battles they try to flank you with riders but if you handle them you win. Without mods the AI spams tons of agents that is just annoying.
I enjoyed the game. Really. I like the ancient setting very much, that's the reason I played this game. But I do not recommend to buy this game (especially outside any sale) because without the expensive DLC it's unfinished. You are able to double its content by buying DLC - so you pay twice as much for a complete game. That's not fair!

March 12, 2016 - Pre-Alpha
+Beautiful Environment
+Smooth, flexible character mobility
+Simple gathering system
+Build a base, defend at night
-Combat feels unsatisfying
-Extremely limited base building options
-No sense of progression (resources / monsters)
While the simplicity of it all is satisfying at first, you'll soon wonder what on earth you'll do next to keep things interesting.
After over a year in Early Access, I expected more.
I played the game for an hour, built everything there was to build, and tasted a few nights of combat. Some people are giggly wiggly over the fact that you can grab the monsters from afar and toss them around; I feel that overall, combat just isn't satisfying. Your weapons feel like crap; when you hit something, it'd be nice to have some feedback / recoil / monster recoiling / Something! Even the meelee doesn't work so well; half the time, you will automatically target a dead monster instead of the live one right next to it. What irks me even more is that monsters have no loot, in a world full of things to be looted.
Indeed, if combat isn't so great, this type of game often falls back on creativity via building stuff, and exploration. I found however, that I could build everything right away! The resources aren't hard to find, or challenging to get; there's no sense of progression. I can't venture to a more dangerous area to retrieve a rare material to build a cooler turret to defend against a stronger monster. I can't discover more advanced tools or machines for my base, to fill it up with; I can just build a bigger base to fill up with a maximum of 3 types of turrets - and there isn't even an explanation of what differentiates them from one another.
I really wanted to love this game, and was excited to play it, but after an hour, all that's left to do is build more iron foundations and walls, more of the 1 model power generator, more eden kits, more of the same 3 turrets, and watch it all take down more monsters at night. Inevitably, I will fall off another cliff along the way, or die inexplicably outside my front door, and lose all my gathered materials again.
Perhaps in another year the game will be more fleshed out and start to resemble a final product; for now, all that can be done is play around with the mechanics.

I have played the original Homeworld & Homeworld 2 since years back and I am really happy that they made a remaster of both of the games. I recently finished the Homeworld & Homeworld 2 remastered campaign and it was absolutely brilliant. Imagine your greatest gaming moments returned to life with better graphics and smoother gameplay.
The nostalgia may play a big part in why I like this game, but I'll try my best to tell you the about the remastered version and the differences between the remastered versions and classic versions.
+ The three dimensional movement & combat is astonishing to look at and easy to control.
+ The story is great and really gives the game an amazing atmosphere around it while you play it.
+ The updated Homeworld 2 UI (which is used in both remastered version of the game) is easy to understand and use.
+ They captured the emptiness of space perfectly and it really sets the mood while you are playing the game.
+ The multiplayer has also been updated. You are able to play as Taiidan, Vaygr, Kushan and Hiigaran on restored maps with new bonuses and game modes that I've had loads of fun with after the campaign.
+ The game is slower paced than games like Starcraft, which means, you don't have to have super fast micro managing skills to be able to play well.
+ The game is easy to mod and uses steam workshop.
-+ The fuel system has been removed from the remastered versions (This was a system that could be seen as annoying or just another gameplay element depending on what the player thinks. The reason that the gameplay element was removed was probably because of the annoyance of having your ships becoming completely static in the middle of combat.)
- *FIXED* The Homeworld & Homeworld 2 races are a bit unbalanced against eachother in multiplayer (Keep in mind that the multiplayer is still development).
- *FIXED* The Resource collecting can be a bit buggy sometimes (when recource collecters want to collect debris from shipwrecks for example)
- *FIXED* Some cool and useful attack patterns and strategies have been changed since the both remastered versions are runing on an updated Homeworld 2 engine.
Overall, this game is truly a RTS masterpiece and is, AT LEAST, a must try for those who enjoy RTS.

I'm extremely disappointed. I purchased this software the first day it became available on Steam. As a builder, I was very excited to get my hands on this tool. I went into this purchase knowing full well that this was an Alpha release, that there may be bugs, and that it would be an unfinished product. I accepted that, and looked forward to seeing this software reach completion. So, why am I not recommending this? It would seem Dragom's business practices are a bit on the shady, selfish, and unethical side. Allow me to elucidate:
When you pay for a video game which is still in Alpha, do you expect to have to pay more for the content that was intended to be in the final release? No. As an example, I've logged HUNDREDS of hours into Ark: Survival Evolved since its initial release. The have added a plethora of new content to their game at no additional charge. That's how Alpha is intended to work.
The initial release of Virtual Battlemap offered a fair amount of (incomplete, IMHO) "classic" dungeon tile sets. Adequate enough to build basic dungeon rooms. By no means were these tiles flawless or even remotely complete. Within a couple of weeks the released their first official DLC pack at HALF THE COST OF THE CORE SOFTWARE!!! Pay DLC for an Alpha product with bugs and incomplete tile sets. If you bother scrutinizing the core tiles you will notice many of the models are incomplete. Walls and other terrain features are often missing a side, making them less useful if you try to creatively manipulate them. So, why should we be paying for what is likely to be more partialy completed assets?
I am very sorry to be one of the folks who backed this product for Steam Greenlight. I now regret having given Dragom any of my money. This is not a breakthrough in map building software. There is nothing special about this software that anyone with a modest level of competence could not learn to create with Unity (yes, this uses Unity). It is not unreasonable to want to profit off your time and effort. It is unreasonable to expect people to pay extra to fill in the gaps on your unfinished project.
Do not even consider buying this product until it is out of Alpha and is getting daily positive reviews again.

The real problem with the software are the business decisions behind it. $30 for the intiial buy in is pretty good. I would have paid $40. However it comes with assets only for the more classic dungeons. Clearly the model is to sell lots of DLC to flesh out the capabilities of the program. The problem here is that the first DLC (published a week into "early-access" mode and before a number of basic functionalities like I mentioned above are incldued), is $15. If you need only the base software to do what you want then this is probably worth the cost. But if you are looking for a map-making software to invest in for the long-haul then Multiply that $15 out by 10-15-20 over time as you buy all the DLC. The cost is high, and the developer response has been to say "tough luck".
Ultimately I would say for SURE wait until this software is out of "early access" As it may provide you with a better view of what their DLC roadmap looks like. Right now it's dismaying. I suspect that once it is out of early access it might be worth buying a big pack of DLC if sufficiently discounted, but either way you will have a better idea of what costs your opting into.

Enslaved is a prime example of a very interesting concept that is bogged down by a somewhat lackluster execution. First off, the game on PC has an innumerable amount of graphical issues such as excessive screen tearing, janky textures that pop in and out at seemingly random times, and character models in cutscenes that glitch out on occasion. I was able to fix some of these issues by messing around with the vsync settings, but ultimately over the course of the entire game it was something I just had to get used to and deal with. In terms of design, the environments all look very lush and beautiful with tons of color palette going on, unlike the typical brown and bloom ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that we are so often subjected to in modern gaming. But even with all of these lush environments, the gameplay is undoubtedly linear, with most of it revolving around moving in a semi-straight line going from point A to point B with little variation. Not to mention the Assassin's Creed style platforming, which is insultingly easy and nigh impossible to fail at unless you were specifically trying to get yourself killed. The puzzles were rather simplistic as well, even coming from the point of view of someone who despises puzzle games and wouldn't be able to complete one without a walk through if my life depended on it. From a combat perspective, it's rather middle of the road, your typical button masher that allows for a few fun combos and I will admit that Monkey's staff is rather fun and satisfying to use. Now I know that so far it just sounds as if I'm endlessly bashing the game despite the respectable rating I gave it, and that's because fundamentally it really is not a horrible experience at all. The story does a good job at keeping the player invested and I found myself being very much on edge finding out where our two characters would end up, or what kinds of peril they would find themselves in next. The chemistry between Trip and Monkey is very well done, even if slightly predictable by the end, and as I've stated before, traveling through the various decaying and post apocalyptic environments made me want to keep forging on in this journey. A lot of emotional moments that thankfully don't fully indulge in sappy melodrama, and an ending that was highly ambiguous and an absolute mind♥♥♥♥. So I think at the end of the day, this is one of the rare examples of story and environments over gameplay, because let's face it, you won't remember this game for the gameplay whatsoever, but the atmosphere, characters, and world building you most certainly will.

I'm a big fan of this style of game, and I really want to like it, but there are so many little annoyances and disappointments that keep it from being a really gratifying firefighting game.
Pros:
-It's good looking -- I think the graphical style is great.
-Laying hoses is super-cool, I remember playing older games like Fire Captain and Emergency Fire Response and wishing they would show hoses laid down instead of just abstracting it.  In Rescue 2, you have hoses going everywhere, and stuff connected to other stuff, and it's really neat.
-You can issue orders while paused!
Cons:
-You'll become annoyed with pathfinding at times, as well as the specific spots your firefighters sometimes insist on standing to extinguish a specific flame.
-You'll become annoyed when you notice that connecting your fire engine to a water source does not refill its internal water tank, it just remains empty until the mission is over.
-You'll grow tired of issuing the exact same orders to different firefighters when you want two dudes to move someplace together, because there does not seem to be a way to issue group orders, nor does there seem to be a way to even group-select units.
-Speaking of issuing orders, you cannot enqueue orders at all, so you will sometimes be hyper-focused on a single unit as they go through the sometimes-lengthly animations triggered by following your commands.
-You will laugh at how hilariously disinterested in saving people Paramedics seem, because half the things they do are at walking speed.
-The missions get repetitive pretty quickly.
-Right Mouse Button drag-scrolling around the map gets old really fast.
-It feels a little dorky when, at the end of a mission, after you've extinguished all the fire, there are still people standing around, panicking, until you have a firefighter walk over to them, pick them up, carry them like 20 feet out the door of the giant, empty, never-was-on-fire room, and set them down.
-You would think certain vehicles, like the Water Carrier, for example, would be equipped with all the valves and flanges and doodads necessary to allow more than one fire engine to connect to it at once, but no, you would be wrong.  Same with every water source, actually, only one thing can connect to it, and then only one thing can connect to that.

So guys, this is my "early" review of Dishonored 2 after having played it for roughly 10 hours.
It's obviously not going to count as a full review yet but judging from where this game is going i will happily finish it.
And by saying happily, i mean it because this game to me personally is great fun.
The graphics look great, the sound and music are great, the combat etc is great (it's all great).
The story missions are great fun, and there are plenty of those (there are even side missions)..
You can choose to be a Rambo type of player, a stealthy assassin, or a mixture of both and then some.. There's a ton of exploring, solving, reading and of course MURDERING to do.
You'll be rewarded with lots and lots of perks that you can use as you please, and there's even rune crafting involved so it's a bit like playing God.. Err, well a rather wrathful kind of God to be more precise, but that's all i'm saying... Whew, i almost said too much there guys.. Anywho,..
There are always alternative ways to reach your goals so that makes the game quite replayable too.
I know and i respect people having thumbed it down because of performance issues during it's launch etc, so i feel bad for them because personally as for me this game runs as smooth as butter.. I bought the game around one year after it got released during the sales. I still wonder if it's been patched up so well that we can finally all enjoy the game now?
I'm not going to say anything about the games story etc, not because i'm a lazy bustard or anything, no it's just because i don't like spoilers myself except for when they're on a car or something more useful.
I think the story is great too, i am not going to spoil it here so just pay and play the game and most of you'll say the same as i do..
So guys, that's all for this short review. If are a fan of the game or the franchise in general, i guess you'll gladly agree to saying this is a great game. And in case you don't like it, it's fine you can ingnore/refund it or give it a thumbs down for all i care.
I'm liking it anyway, regardless of what's been said or done.
Have a good one,

As for the game itself, this is perhaps the most underrated game of 2016. It improves on everything from the first game, mechanics, graphics, story and lore.
*Minor spoilers about the level design, but do read*
The game is designed similarly to Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, in that you can play exactly how you want. Whether it's charging head on, shooting everything, or going full stealth through hidden passages, roof tops and so on. This is a game that heavily rewards exploration into every room, hidden or not, with new blueprints for weapons, runes for your skills (if you choose to use them), bonecharms for buffs, and generally money, paintings, books, letters and audiographs, which all builds on the lore, story and general world building. Do yourself a favour and explore. That is the strength of this game.
Sadly the game was based on ID software's useless old graphics engine from their game
. This engine was written for the even more useless  graphics API called OpenGL, which is pretty much dead now. As such, the game engine was heavily modified to suit the needs of the game and support DirectX 11 instead, and renamed VOID engine. However, the problems with ID Engine 5 remained, such as slowly loading textures that pop in, mostly during the loading of a saved game.
Performance tanks in "A cracked slab", but this is due to the world having to be rendered twice in 2 different versions at once. There's just no getting around a massive performance decrease in such a situation. Same reason games don't have mirrors, and the few that do only exist in tiny rooms.
If you liked the first game, you will love the second game. The performance is good enough to not be an issue. Worst case, just unfold the special item in "A cracked slab", if it becomes an issue, and you're good.
Definitely one of the best games from 2016, and highly recommended. The sales figures are all due to early performance issues mostly solved now, so don't let that affect your purchase decision.

Hoo boy this is going to be a long one!  I played the first one back when I must have been around 13 years old, AND LOVED IT! Played the second one a while later and liked it but it didn't quite do it like the first one did. That bias is probably never going to go away but I'll do my best.
Gearbox has been nice enough to package the originals in case:
A) Your computer can't run the remasters
B) You are a HW1 Purist
C) You liked a bunch of HW2 Mods that haven't made the jump to Remaster yet
Because of this, this is going to be THREE seperate reviews (HW1 Classic, HW1 R, HW2/Remaster), since HWR, HW2, and HW2R use the same engine.
Lets Talk HW1 Classic first.
Homeworld 1 Came out in 1998 and blew minds for being an RTS that allowed for Full 3D control and you could effectivley re-enact the Battle of Endor from Return of the Jedi.
My take? It's a legend, for good reason. Granted age has taken it's toll on this (Notably low-ish framerate, and some poor UI decisions that do make things harder to execute at times), but it is still a brilliant, Micro-oriented RTS with emphasis on Unit composition and formation management.
Essentially all ships have a set amount of manuverability, and some ships have better turret coverage than others, while other ships (Fighters, excluding defenders and Taiidan Defense fighters, and Ion cannon frigates) can only fire forward, in a normal RTS this may be a nightmare to properly set up, except for one single mechanic, formations. Formations allow you to take full advantage of your fleet by arranging them in a pattern. Be it the claw formation which is a great offensive formation for fighters and corvettes as they envelop their prey, sphere for defending your resourcing operations, or an imposing wall of Capital ships to focus down other ships in quick succession. Knowing what you have and adapting your formation tactics is key to winning fights in HW1. Granted unit composition does a lot of heavy lifting too, but it does play a signifigant factor in combat.
It also has what I feel how story SHOULD be handled in gaming. Most of the story happens to you, and conveyed through in-game scenarios. The worldbuilding is fan-freakin tastic, with some genuinley unsettling set pieces, beautiful use of Adiago for strings (I still tear up every time it's played), and of course, THE GALAXY ACTUALLY FEELS LIKE IT'S TRYING TO KILL YOU! It's not a terribly complicated story, but it'll hit you in the feels, not to mention the writing is top notch.
Also you have a persistent fleet, meaning your resources, tech, and surviving ships carry over into the next mission. It's a neat concept and fits nicely into the story they were telling. Plus Salvage corvettes, those things are awesome.
Speaking of, the interim mission cenematics are quite stylish, basicaly animated concept art with some voice over in the background, it's a style relic will be known for (Company of Heroes comes to mind).
Also special mention to the tutorial, it doesn't progress until you get the mechanics and are ready to advance, then throws you into a small battle just to make sure.
Of course it has some issues that got worse with age. For one, in many missions (especailly a lot of the earlier ones) the strategy is to abuse triggers so you builld a strong enough fleet to take on the fleet you know is coming (Since they ambush you the first time), and then activate the trigger. This also kills quite a bit of the pacing, since construction takes FOREVER when you are building a fleet (not to mention the sluggish post-mission resource gathering).
That said, there are plenty of missions that don't follow this, and the best ones are those where you have to think outside the box, or are thrown immediatley into a battle.
Secondly the UI isn't that great. It's servicable, but it's got issues. Mainly due to the fact that to access anything pertaining to construction, research, or docking, you HAVE to go to a different screen. It wouldn't be nearly as bad if Homeworld wasn't so dang micro-oriented, to the point you are constantly monitoring somewhere between three to nine different control groups, depending on how you set things up. Plus selection I find can be a bit finnicky, as well as issuing orders if you aren't careful.
Now with that out of the way let's Talk HW2/HW2R
On the upside, HW2's engine vastly improved the UI. There are sidebar tabs, that allow you to access anything that at first took you to a different screen. Plus Issuing orders is stupid simple now. Albiet a little too easy as you can click on game objects and the ships will move towards them, so you still need to take some care where you click.
Also the pacing in the single-player campaign is better. You are typically always on the move, and resources are automatically gathered at the end of each mission, however, missions now end automatically, so you won't have much time to prepare for the next mission.
That said, the story is considerably weaker, it ignores some established canon (Three great hyperspace cores never sat well with me), and there's this very generic "Save the homeworld!" story going on. That said the Vagyr do put up a great fight, they are an interesting faction rather than a mirror faction, and the guy who did Makaan couldn't have done a better job with his acting. Just...the Vagyr don't hold up to the Beast or the Taiidan Empire (or anyone else you fight in HW1 for that matter) in terms of a villan you'll remember.
Not to mention formation management is mostly gone (except for fighters, which change formation depending on tactic, which was seperate in the first, Remastered 2.0 Fixes this, see the HWR section) which is a bummer, though admittedly it is more fun watching squads of fighters come out than single file.
So let's talk HW:R, It uses HW2's engine but with HW1's campaign.
So you get the better UI and pacing (you actually Auto-collect resources, AND can build a fleet to your desire before you hyperspace out) not to mention Gearbox's art team made both HW1R and HW2R Drop dead gorgeous.
Fuel management is also out of here like it was in HW2, so you don't need to constantly dock your strike craft (fighters and corvettes). I welcome this change actually, as it removes downtime from your fighters which were kinda underpowered in the first game regardless, and gets rid of some, honestly, needless micro.
EDIT 6/8/16: THEY FIXED FORMATIONS! Though they work differently from the base game. Now when you select formations the game auto selects ships and groups them up and splits the selected ships in several "Combat groups" that use said formations. So far I like it but I am dissapointed in losing something like a Giant sphere of Strike craft protecting my resource controllers. For the Record HW2 fleets works like this too, except they still retain the "Squadron" mechanic.
I'm not going to talk too much about Multiplayer since A) I only played one match and B) it's in beta hence, still in active development. Other than it's really neat to see HW1 fleets fight HW2 fleets, even if HW 2 fleets overpower HW1 fleets for the most part.
Last thing I'll dive into is Mod support, It's fantastic, My personal favorites are the Halo-themed "Homefront" and "Tactical fleet simulator" which is a balance overhaul mod that makes pretty much every ship useful in some way (and they add a whole bunch more). Albiet most of the mods are old HW2 mods re-uploaded onto steam, and the creators are still waiting on some updates so they can properly port the HW2 mods to HW2R, and it's glorious high-res coat of paint.
Also as an aside, I found it quite difficult to find tutorials, which is a shame, I kinda wanted to mess around with it. Though a knowledge of LUA is required.
So yeah I reccomend it, it's a great deal at 35 bucks, I honestly think Gearbox did the best they could, given the engine conversion from HW1 to 2.

I cannot remember the last time I played a game that impressed me as much as this one.  As a life long Alien fan I had high expectations, despite all of the previous video game iterations that were huge let downs.  These developers absolutely nailed it.  The atmosphere is the real winner here.  The music, sound effects and general feel of the game world are as close to the source as one could hope with todays technology.  I was skeptical about the fact that the gameplay consists of hiding from and out witting the alien rather than fighting and killing it but this mechanic turned out to add to the experience.  The sneaking and peaking actions made it more immersive by making you feel scared and helpless.  There were countless times where I was genuinely jump scared while creeping through a tunnel or room thinking I was safe only to have the alien run up and kill me.  I really can't think of another game besides the original Resident Evil that gave me that kind of scare.  Highly recommended.  I hope these devs make another one.

There is nothing inherently bad about this game, there just isn't anything particularly good either. Everything that is in the game works well, the units and equipment works intuitively, and I had no problems handling any of the missions. This is where the problems start though.
At no point did the game feel challenging. A dispatch gets logged, I have more than enough time to wait for each of my units to arrive at the scene before starting the mission. I couldn't see any reason to start missions when the first vehicle arrived rather then waiting for everyone to be there, the fire always started at the exact same point regardless. Once at the scene, some small fire would start and my crew would have all the time in the world to setup, grab any civilians and casually extinguish the fires. This only gets worse once you unlock access to the water/foam/powder tenders as they can mop up any outdoor fire all by themselves in seconds.
It may be harsh to judge the game based on this, as I supose it is a more accurate depiction of what actual firecrews face, more chip pan fires than multi-story infernos, however the story missions should have pushed the boat out brought in some terrifying scenarios but instead they all just felt a little limp.
It is a shame, I did want to like this game to be amazing, and it's shortcomings could perhaps be forgiven if this was a first attempt, but from what I read about the previous game, it seems a large number of interesting features and mechanics have actually been removed. Which makes it hard not to see this as a rushed cash grab.

I've been a fan of the Homeworld series since I was a kid, purchased the Game of the Year edition, still sitting proudly on my bookshelf with its Silver Clans Description & story books, along with its sequels. Hearing about the remastered edition, I nearly screamed in excitement because the game is long overdue for a refreshment, and I'm happy that I bought it.
(JUST THE REVIEW OF THE REMASTERED HOMEWORLD CLASSIC, NOT 2)
Okay, details now:
What I like about the Remastered Edition of Homeworld (aside from its obvious graphics) is the new UI. It's much cleaner and is easily accessible all on one screen without actually visiting the 'Build', 'Rearch' & 'Launch' pages, which are now converted to panels. Having said that there are some downsides to it: I cannot click the 'B' key to quickly close my 'Build' panel, likewise with the 'Launch' panel, but only works with the 'Research' panel. It's not a huge problem, but it gave me a feeling that the remastering was rushed, rather than tested.
Secondly, I don't like the unit ships display on the lower left corner, that in itself is more appropriate for Homeworld 2. I much rather have the Unit Ships of the Homeworld Classic, originally displayed on the top right corner for easily monitoring how many ships I have left in the game. It doesn't matter where it's displayed, I could care less, but having Homeworld 2's UI for Unit Ship Display in a Homeworld Classic where it's Build Per Ship, not Build Per Group of Ships, is annoying. All I see are just colorful outlines of  random ships in a non-scrollable display, with my assumption to myself, "even though I built 30 Interceptors.... maybe I have 25 left? Less? Idk?"
Sound can be glitchy, where ship chatter is close to non-existent, or I'm dealing with persistent ship engine noise all game, even when I pan far far far away, and docking is the only option left for me to get rid of that painful white-noise.
And now, capturing ships with Salvage Corvettes doesn't intern them into my ships, they get recycled, and now I'm stuck with more minutes into each stage of the game just rebuilding them, because if you know anything about Homeworld, it's this: SALVAGE SALVAGE SALVAGE = BIGGER ARMY.
So there are more Cons than Pros on the Remastered Collection, however that being said, I'm still a proud supporter of the game and the series, I just wished that the Remastering did some more gameplay testing before launching. Now I'm just sitting back and hoping that there will be updates to the game.

One mission has you dodging and destroying asteroids before they can hit your mothership, and if you decide to use your bombers to take them out about half of your bombers will kamikaze(which is a seperate action you can order them to do) by accident into each asteroid. This game is not without its bugs, but as of my review it seems that the majority of them are patched.
Needless to say the AI is a little underwhelming, and some missions poorly executed. Planning to capture enemy capitol ships and succeeding can be rewarding. Overall, thanks to the story and acknowledging that this is an older game with only a graphics touch up it stands up well today. Worth the sale price. 7.5/10

This is a game about automation. And part America Simulator 2015/2016
You put obtain wood, stone, coal, iron ore and copper ore. You setup your first furnace setup to automate copper and iron production.
You start to explore into electricity. You build steam engines, boilers, pipes and pumps. You start connecting coal suply lines to your boilers.
You discover research and start researching automation and logistics. You increase your mining production and build more smelters which are then used to produce resources for research.
Expanding more and more, your need for more resources increase. As does your production.
And then it hits you, there are sirens blaring, caution signs popping up in the map, you run over as fast as you can and are swarmed by bugs. The bugs kill you and half your base while your trying to produce weapons and ammo to fight back but it isnt enought, the bugs have already eaten your electricity production.
Your iron, coal and copper production soon follow in flames. You say ♥♥♥♥ it and turn the game off. That night while your trying to sleep, your mind is racing with what you did wrong, new smelting setups, more efficient power setups, new factory lines and automation designs.
The next day you spend as much time as you can trying to make your production as efficient as possible. You are attacked by bugs again, but this time, you dont quit. You start a new world, as soon as you have researched the bare essentials you research turrets.
You line your base with turrets and stock them with ammo. But then, a new type of bug emerges, one that can fire from range, they break into your base once again, but you have enough perimeter turrets to kill any scavengers. You then make a double layer of turrets around your base aided by layers of stone walls. You start mass producing ammo, and mass producing turrets. You then proceed to give the bugs the♥♥♥♥♥♥kicking they deserve.
This is a game that will test your limits, but make you keep coming back for more, make you recommend it to your mates. You will discover new things about this game every time you play, you will experiment with new technologies you have found, ♥♥♥♥ around with cars, tanks, flamethrowers, shotguns, rocket launchers.
You then discover how oil works, you discover a new fuel source, and go give them buggers freedom in exchange for their oil. You become the America of this alien world.
15/10 would become a yank again.
Factorio developer/s, congrats for your arrival on steam, you guys deserve it.

Enslaved's story is set in a future where most of humanity has been destroyed.

You play as Monkey. After being captured by a group of slavers, Monkey is freed in the midst of another prisoner's escape.

Monkey's fate is tied to Trip's. If her heart stops, he dies. And their journey begins.
In the post-post-apocalypse, there are massive obstacles that Trip and Monkey encounter in their travels, and it's typically up to Monkey to get them past it.
Monkey is capable of deft acrobatic feats, jumping from handhold to pole to ledge and back again, kill enemies with his energy-charged staff and something called cloud.
Whether through beatiful cutscene or incidental dialogue as Monkey and Trip navigate from place to place, Enslaved builds its characters as they struggle to survive and understand each other.

What an odd yet wonderful little gem of a game is.  Modeled after the Chinese folk tale Journey to the West, this adaptation of the story takes place in a post apocalyptic America and tells the story of a woman and her enslaved companion as they search for home and all the trouble they run into along the way.   The game itself never tells you too much about the setting (which I can appreciate as it isn't terribly essential to the story and allows the player to fill in the blanks as they see fit).  The world within the game is lush and beautiful and the models are extremely well done for a game released in 2010.  One thing I absolutely have to say is this game has some of the best voice acting I've ever heard.    The conversations actually feel like real conversations.  Combine these elements with some fun gameplay and you'll find yourself finishing it in one sitting because of how well the game flows.  One last thing - the ending.  Obviously I won't go into detail but it was such an odd and curious thing- and I loved it.  If you're looking for a short and linear adventure with phenominal voice acting and writing and a philosophical ending, look no further.

This game is an interesting one. The whole thing revolves around a basic tower defense principal, where you build and protect your Eden Kit from hostile native species, because you're the invading alien and they don't like you. Beyond the possibility of some shoehorned social-political commentary or some such, this game is actually pretty good.
The combat system is responsive and fun and you have to pay attention to pretty much every enemy so you don’t get pinned into a corner. The parkour system helps with this, allowing you to do a bit of guerilla warfare by running up with your Gauss Cannon, hitting a hive for a few seconds, before running back off into the trees and away from the hordes of enemies. You can and will augment your personal arsenal of firearms and energy weapons with turrets placed around your base to keep away the night time raids. The turrets are fairly basic, as there’s currently only 3 types, missile, auto (machine gun), and laser. You also have to manage power levels in your base, each turret takes some power, and each generator adds some power to the pool. I’m not terribly far in this game yet, so I’m not sure if there’s a practical limit on turrets.
A big part of this game is the building system. As far as I know, your structures won’t collapse in Red factions style if you build them poorly (I hope that gets added in at some point) but if you’re not careful, you’ll eventually get a message telling you that you cannot place XYZ at that location because your structure is weak. This can get a bit annoying when trying to build a bridge, but I appreciate the realism. In order to build structures, you’ll need to strap on your big boy pants and venture out into the wilderness to collect resources. Each structure, as far as I know, can be built out of different base materials, depending on what you have or what you need. For example, an Ironite base is the strongest, but Ironite can be a bit annoying to come by, especially early in game if you don’t know where to look. So, instead of Ironite, you can build with Bridgmanite (no idea if I spelled that right) and take a slight dip in health to stock up on Ironite. Or, you may have a small Ironite structure protecting your Eden Kit, with a larger Bridgmenite fortification. Most weapons and modules can also be built from 2 or 3 base materials, which allows you to ration supplies more effectively.
Storage is a big problem in this game. If there’s a storage container that isn’t your Eden Kit, I haven’t found it. The Eden Kit has 5 material storage slots, and each of those can hold a stack of 300 of one material. This is fine at first, until you’re going out and coming back with your inventory full, because you didn’t use all your bullets the previous night. Your character has an inventory of 10 slots, each able to hold a max of 300 of one raw material, much like the Eden Kit, the place where this gets a bit iffy, is that ammo only stacks to a certain amount, I think around 144 per slot (which sounds like a lot until you get mobbed by 20 enemies and you begin to fire wildly into the crowd).
The last thing I want to say is just little things I like about the game. The physics in this game are amazing. Pretty much any material node can be deconstructed into physics particles (except for large boulders, which just fuzz out of existence if you try to cut them into smaller pieces). As you mine, collectable materials will spawn and then despawn as you absorb them. PSA though, don’t stand on top of what you’re mining, because there’s a rare chance that the game will flip its♥♥♥♥♥♥with the physics objects and launch you into the air. The environments, are beautiful, with each biome having different resource nodes that give you different materials. As far as I know, and I haven’t done any extensive exploration, the basic biomes are: Desert, Forest, and Swamp, with a nice blending where they border each other. Each biome will have its own sort of special resource nodes that will give you a specific material, so you’ll eventually need to branch out and explore to get a decent stockpile.
So yeah, this game is pretty good so far, pretty solid gunplay, a decent parkour system, and it seems to have a lot of polish for an early access game. There isn’t a lot of depth to it yet, but I think I can see where they’ve left room to add that later, with time and more updates.

So, I saw this last year and thought: "That looks amazing, it can't be that good" Well, I ate my words, here are some thoughts I've had about the game and the (amazing) company.
Pros:
1) Extremely involved and attentive development team - Not only do they communicate with the players, they ARE players themselves, they play the game and share many of the same interests as the community. They're friendly, polite and I'd love to join them in game some time.
2) Even in alpha this game has very few bugs that I have found, and the developers find bugs I never knew existed and fix them quickly. In addition to this they give patch notes that explain in english any gamer can understand without being overwhelming.
3) A well-planned development map that so far they have followed. The developers give frequent updates on the status of their work and share teaser screenshots. The development map is updated often with ideas that players and devs alike want. They don't seem to hear a new idea and go "Oh we can't do that, that would require work!"
4) Graphically pleasing, this game is gorgeous and performs well on even my 3-year old GPU and 5-6 year old motherboard/processor.
Cons:
1) Being alpha, this game does not have quite as much content as I would like. However, see my comment about the development map and keep in mind they update frequently.
So, in closing, would I recommend this game? Yes, I would. If you are patient and interested, help the devs out and join the pre-alpha. You'll have content to last you for quite a while and they're constantly adding more. If you aren't into early access? That's alright too, keep up with the development map and don't forget Eden Star: this game is going to be even more amazing than it is now.
Cheers to the devs and anyone who made it this far

On top of this you have to make enough money to support your family and survive yourself. Will you follow the rules or turn to taking bribes to make ends meet? What new can I possibly write about Homeworld and its sequel? Unique in time of their original releases, both games still hold up well, after all those years, and prove that design is everything when it comes to creating memorable gaming experiences. Despite somewhat dated appearance both are still very much playable, though I personally have much trouble getting both old versions to run properly on my modern hardware. Thus comes the Remastered Collection, allowing me to again experience both games.
You see, I never played Homeworld games specifically for their mechanics, but rather – for one-of-a-kind atmosphere, fantastically designed universe and somewhat mystical approach to space travel. For me, those two games were just wonderful, interactive stories, and strategic gameplay was only a package in which they were delivered. This is probably what makes me oblivious to all the mechanical alterations, and maybe even flaws, that Gearbox has introduced in this remaster. As for the stories themselves I will not say a word – they are to be experienced personally.
Mechanically, Homeworld is an RTS in 3D space, to put it bluntly. You collect resources, build units, attack enemies and win missions either by destruction, timer, capture or any combination of those. Sounds pretty standard, right? Well, it is, sort of. Third dimension adds a new element to unit positioning, and in this game it really matters which units attack which targets, in which order and how they are set up in space. You need to apply formations effective in each situation, change unit tactics and generally move around the battlefield a lot more than in a standard RTS. More often than not games also ask for quite a degree of multitasking – luckily in singleplayer active pause comes in handy, allowing to place orders and think out the situation before acting.
As I mentioned, not everything works as it should in Homeworld Remastered. Especially in the first campaign it is evident that a lot of things broke when transplanted onto the new game engine. Omission of refuelling mechanic drastically changes the way strike craft operates and renders some ships almost useless.
Conversely, in Homeworld 2 Remastered formations seem largely broken. There are more things behaving differently from original, so purists and hardcore game fans will be put off, but I – for reasons I mentioned above – enjoyed both campaigns to the fullest. Sure, sometimes I had to put more clickwork to make things fly around as intended, however none of the issues would break the game for me.
I have not tested the multiplayer component yet, though I am not much of an online gamer so I might never do that actually. Keep in mind that my review is from single player standpoint only. Also I’d like to point out that the lack of Cataclysm in the remaster is a bit disappointing, but maybe, just maybe, some day they will be able to release that too.
From a visual standpoint, the game is the definition of what a “remaster” should be. Every model in the game has been reworked from ground up and even the smallest fighters are now more detailed than largest capital ships in the original Homeworld. Great texturework is accompanied by a set of subtle effects like volumetric lighting, multiple-source dynamic shadows and lighting, depth of field and of course high resolution support. Animatics between missions have been re-drawn in high definition and compressed with quality in mind. Homeworld Remastered Collection is simply gorgeous. Stunning visuals are accompanied by great voiceover and absolutely stunning soundtrack, which is as far as I’m concerned absolutely unique in games world, combining ethnic and symphonic themes into one. The game simply feels majestic at times. Audio has been, of course, cleaned up since the original.
Overall, there is really no reason one should not get Homeworld Remastered Collection. It is a great re-release of two great real time strategy games, providing many hours of gameplay even in single player mode, though I'll state this again - for me most important here are the epic story and atmosphere. There is already extensive mod support too, meaning that fans of altering the game will be able to find something for themselves, and purists should be able to ‘fix’ the game soon enough. In terms of presentation it’s flawless. If it was flawless mechanically, we’d have an absolute remaster benchmark on our hands. As it is, it’s just great.

It seems unfair to write a (negative) review with just a few hours spent, but the game simply doesn't impress me. This goes for the remastered versions, I haven't tried the classics yet.
+ Beautiful. Nice settings, nice backgrounds, nice ships. All good.
+ Sound/music. Some people might argue that there shouldn't be any explosions or sounds in space but...not me.
+ User interface. Very easy to handle, gives you all the information you need. Very intuitive.
+ Real 3D space battles. This is the one aspect that I still have a lot to learn of.
+ There's a limited amount of resources on each map and you carry your surplus with you to the next mission.
- Each battle feels like I just mass my ships and plunge them in there. No thrill, no excitement, no fun. Maybe I'm a natural at composing fleets that'll crush all opposition, but I don't know... The missions I've played so far has just been me waiting for my fleets to destroy the enemy and retreating damaged ships for repairs. And carrying tens of thousands of resources from each map means that I can build 2-3 new fleets if I should get my fleet wiped out.
In conclusion, the game looks great and feels great but just doesn't give you a proper challenge. I would recommend the game if you are unfamiliar to the genre.

Eden Star is one of those few early access titles that I've bought into. I generally stay away from them, apart from a few exceptions, and Eden Star is one of them. It caught my eye as a survival game with more of a base-building/tower defence focus, in which you gather resources and build your base and defences during the day, and defend it during the night.
You start off with an Eden Kit and some resources, and you have until night to find a decent spot for your base. The base-building is quite versatile, and as long as you have the resources, you can create the base that you want to properly defend your Eden Kit.
The Eden Kit is what protects you from this planet's toxic night air. If you go outside it's protective shield (which can be upgraded to increase it's radius) at night time, you start taking damage, and will eventually die. This makes defending it a top priority, and since the creatures that inhabit this world have taken a personal offence to your giant shield, defend it you must, as they will attack in swarms at night.
This of course means combat, and it starts off as fairly standard, with a variety of guns and a melee weapon in case you run out of ammo. However, some upgrades to your MATA tool (essentially it's what allows you to harvest, build, etc), and you can basically become a jedi with an energy sword, and the ability to push and grab enemies and hurl them at whatever you want (this can also be chained, provided you don't hurl them outside grabbing range).
Now, they may be cool to watch and everything, but they're just a gimmick right? Just shooting enemies is surely a lot easier? Well, in short, no. First off, the grab ability (the most useful and fun to watch) is tied in with your MATA tool's harvesting, so you don't have to bother switching to your gun. So depending on what you're pointing the reticle at, you can either harvest or kill. It's more of a convenience thing, but one I like. The second (and more important) benefit is that it saves on inventory space. Ammo for guns takes up inventory slots, so the more ammo you bring along for your trip, the less space you have to carry the resources you need.
This means the non-gun options actually provide a tangible benefit to using them, since they don't require the ammo that guns do (although the push does require energy, but that is something completely separate and doesn't take up inventory space). And apart from all that, it's hilarious to grab an enemy, smash him into a rock, then fling him up into the sky.
Right now, it is fairly light on content, and as you'd expect of an early access game, there are some bugs, glitches and crashes (although I personally haven't had a single crash), and I can always tell when a horde of enemies is about to attack my base at night, since the framerate dips fairly noticeably.
However, I do have to say, the devs are doing a fantastic job with this game. They're passionate and dedicated, and I have no doubt they'll make this game the best they possibly can. They're incredibly transparent, regularly posting updates on what they're working on, and the vast majority of forum posts are answered by them personally. Ultimately, this is what convinced me to buy Eden Star, and if you like the concept and the direction of this game, you should too.

tells us the story of a two adventurous heroes who fight to survive, but mostly, fight for freedom... each, at his own way.
On a world collapsed by war, where robots and mech freaks rule the land, it takes muscle and heart to overcome the dangerous traps that destiny has planed.
Monkey grew up alone in the wild, knows the danger around every corner, but was caught by the slavers. Trip grew up in a colony, with her father and loyal friends. When both escape, they begin a journey to find out what it really means to be free.
With an amazing color palette,
got me from the very first minute. Just by looking at the images, everyone can tell it's a beautiful world, filled with detail, amazing character development and a cool concept. The entire game is exactly like that, with amazing levels, from forests, to swamp areas with mech fuel as lakes, abandon buildings covered with trees and vegetation, and even a huge titan mech.
It's impossible not to enjoy the view and the casual humour that goes around sometimes.
As gameplay goes, I appreciate the simplicity of the combat
. With combos as simple as a handful of moves, the player doesn't have much diversity, but then again, there are only a handful of enemies, so I guess it's even.
It's a good thing, because with an uncomfortable camera implanted in
, even simple combat can be challenging. I have no idea what led the creators to sit in their offices and accept this decision, but the camera is awful... It self arranges in weird positions, it's fixed at some points, and moves well at other times. It's a conflict mix that works, of course, and even if it's the only bad thing I have to say about this great game, I still had to point out. Bad camera make terrible combat moments, and I'm happy combat it's as basic as it can get.
But
is not all about action, platforming makes a major impact, and the level design takes a huge bonus on how good it is to jump around with Monkey.
Boss fights do a cool appearance, with a great concept, and not exaggerating which is always nice!
The gameplay is solid, especially at 60fps, where the fluid movement compensates for the bad camera. Although this was a console port, this game was made to run at 60fps!

Tl;DR: Immersion due to the beautiful graphics and getting the hang of province/army management will keep you well entertained for 100-200 hours, longer if you care for the single battles more than the overall challenge of the campaign.
Full review:
I have played the TW series since Medieval Total War (1). The game is an expected continuation of the series, in both good and bad ways as well as the general direction of what the game is about.
Good ways: Every sequel since MTW (1) added new features of the game, better graphics, more units, more awe at how beautiful it is.
Bad ways: Only every other sequel makes for a truly challenging game (but never as much as the first ones), because the AI development just can't keep up with the increased depth. And the long waiting times after ending turns and loading battles can make games tedious.
General direction: For winning a campaign, the importance of battles and managing them yourself declines, while the importance of province management increases.
In MTW (1), there was very rudimentary play on the abstract, gameboard-like campaign map.
In Rome 1, that map became meaningful, with moving armies instead of game-pieces. You could use the terrain, build forts, lay sieges. Unfortunately, the AI did not do any of those, so you had a huge advantage even before a battle began.
In MTW 2, harder units and bigger armies made the game challenging again, at least until the middle-phase. You could get big, meaningful battles - sometimes.
Empire: Total War was the worst part of the series. Naval warfare was introduced and it could have been beautiful if it wasn't for the impotent campaign AI that didn't even manage to assemble fleets. The campaign was just an exercise in building construction and you rarely even had an own town attacked. The expansion N:TW is not worth mentioning.
Shogun 2 was a good game again, finally challenging, and beautifully done.
Rome 2 seems to be mostly about managing provinces and moving around armies. I have played the campaigns Rome, Athens (Wrath of Sparta) and now Markomannia (Augustus). Playing battles actually seems to have become optional and you only do it because it's Total War and you want to see your units in action sometimes. But most of the time, the prediction for the outcome is very precise, and it's rarely so that you won't clearly win or lose, so there is little motivation in it.
As usual in Total War, about 90% of the time of the campaign is when you already know you will win. Playing through is to complete it, and to maybe see some battles with high-end units.
Here's the twist, though: That sounds rather bad, but surprisingly, it isn't. Even after 10 years of playing the game, I still can play whole campaigns purely for the joy of occasionally playing a battle just to see the army I have lead for many turns triumph or lose, even if it means nothing for the campaign. They just get the immersion element of the game right, and I guess that's the beauty of TW.  :)

Story
Homeworld is a masterpiece. The stories still give me the chills years after playing them for the first time, particularly Homeworld 1. The voice acting was updated, along with sound effects which add to the updated 3D models of the game. These updates give the feeling of actually controlling a fleet in space, which adds to the atmosphere of this beautiful game.
Gameplay
The gameplay was unique when it was first released, and it is still one of the few games to do 3D RTS correctly. AI is great as well, and makes for a challenging experience. The 2.0 patch released in June 2015 changed the game for the better, making it so that formations were viable and usable across all races that you control. Gearbox has worked long and hard to alter the Homeworld 2 engine function in a way which Homeworld 1 and Homeworld 2 units could compete with each other.
Bottom line
I recommend this game series for anyone who enjoys a great space opera narratives, as well as any Science Fiction fan. Real Time Strategy gamers will also find something here that doesn't exist in most RTS titles.

For those of you who played Homeworld or Homeworld 2...you know why you should buy this.
For those of you who have never had the priveledge...this game is still considered by many experts of the RTS genre to be the defining RTS experience.  One of the most polished, best story-driven RTS games ever made, AND the sequel.

It is...the most beautiful RTS I have ever seen.   Even before the remaster, I would've said so.  Now...it is updated in every way one could hope for, without ANY changes to the core mechanics.
The story is the same, but the voice acting is all-new, from the same actors who voiced the original.  The graphics are modernized, and the game feels...fresh.  It feels as it should;  essentially unchanged, but better than ever before!
I recommend this game to anyone who seriously wishes to give the RTS genre a genuine try.   If you don't like this, you probably won't like many other RTS games. On the other hand; If you like RTS games, this will likely be the jewel of your collection.

I've had my eye on this game ever since it had been first revealed. Like, in its first Alpha. Eventually, when it was available for free, I gave a go with the free Beta 5- and I had been just as pleased with the limited WiP content of that as I was with the videos of watching the game. If you want a basic feel of the game, I suggest you play the Beta 5 first (It can be found on GameJolt). But with that being said, here are my Pros, Cons, and Thoughts on common arguements against the game.
PROS:
> Steelraven7 is the ONLY developer for the game- and as of right now, they still are. That alone should show dedication to making agreat game. And if that isn't enough, Steelraven allows for players to upload their own maps and weapons onto the Steam Workshop for all to use, and I'm sure they are on their way to extending that to vehicles and whatnot.
> The game graphics are lovely- at least, from what I see on Youtube and when I run them on high quality. However, my laptop is literally an office-grade tablet-laptop, so I can't exactly run the super good stuff. But even with signifigantly lower settings, I still find myself mesmerized by the design and appearance of the game.
> The gameplay is... well hell, it's great! This has been a fantasy of mine since I first came into FPS; massive team-based gunfights. And Ravenfield fits just that. You can run how ever many bots as you please, balancing them however you please, and then killing them or getting killed by them to your hearts desire. Which brings me to another point- even on Normal difficulty, the enemies of the game are tough; there is no form of damage reductioin whatsoever to ANYONE in the game, player or AI, and damage is always the same in terms of difficulty (EX: A shot that does 23 damage on Easy still does 23 on Hard.). Damages are realistic, and where you think you'll survive you'll die, while where you think you'll kill an enemy they may survive. Going back to difficulty, the different levels merely affect the overally intellect of the AI- meaning all a player needs to adapt to when stepping up a difficulty level is better AI tactics. Youcan chose to play God on the battlefield or be pinned down and struggle to find the moment to strike.
> The guns feel great and the majority of sound effects are... sexy. Yeah I know that sounds weird- but believe me, some of the weapon sounds WILL turn you on. The guns also have nice designs, and there is fairly decent variety amongst the base game selection.
> The maps are nice- the variety amongst the themes makes for great fun, and in some maps there are obvious advantages one team may have, making the game more challenging in the sense that a player will have to really push themselves and their army to take a point.
> The vehicles are fun- not gonna lie, I suck at using the airplanes and they are tricky to get the hang of. But if you watch gameplay on Youtube, the planes are very fun to use and appear to be well worth the time to learn using.
There are some other things I'd like to list in the Pro's but let's face it you probably stopped reading this after the first 2 lines so time to get to the CONS:
> Although the previously mentioned 'map advantages' can provide a fun challenge, they can just as easily be annoying or even infuriating. I remember spending 10 minutes pushing one point and finally taking it, only to immediately lose another point to not 30, not 40- but 2 enemies. And by the time I got there, 40 had already begun to defend it.
> The AI on the enemy team appears to be smarter than the AI on your team; they actually split up between defending and attacking, prioritze deployment based on contestment, spread out evenly, and attack in masses. The AI on your team for the most part seems to be a massive jumble that merely appears to replicate the formulated battle plan. Still- the friendly AI still has it's moments.
As much as it pains me to say, there are still problems with the game I either can't recall or just aren't willing to mention. And now moving on to discussing some common complaints:
"The game isn't multiplayer! This sucks!"
Well YEAH it's not multiplayer- Steelraven7 explicitly told us that it wouldn't be and look at it like this- are you really going to enjoy playing with like 39-119+ OTHER people? Who's gonna run that? What's the chat gonna look like? It'd be utter CHAOS. If you want large-scale battles online, go to Battlefield- Ravenfield is meant to allow you to enjoy even larger battles, and the only way that can be made enjoyable is through sacrificing online play. And don't get me wrong, I LOVE online FPS; but in a game like Ravenfield, I'd just come to hate it.
"The game has too many bugs! It crashes too much!"
1) Early Access 2) I run this on one of the least-qualified laptops for gaming; and it runs NICELY; it cannot be Steelravens fault that you have a bad PC, run the wrong settings, or have bad processing. The only crashes I experience are car crashes and when I try to run game settings on a Workshop map that doesn't support them. And neither of those are Steelraven's fault.
"It's too expensive!"
Well, personally, I think this game is a perfect price when you compare it to those big shooters like Call of Duty; I mean, what does Call of Duty provide? A 6 v 6 small-scale online fight. That's the simplest way to put it. For like 60 bucks. And if ANYONE has bad internet, it can affect the entire game. Ravenfield, for $15, provides large-scale Player+Ai v Ai gunfights with the cap at whatever a computer can handle. That's the simplest way to put it. For 4x the price you get 6v6 online play subject to internet connection versus adjustable team size singleplayer FPS action. Not to mention the maps are bigger, you don't recieve absurd killstreaks (I loved BO2 with all my heart- but a damn assault chopper in a 6v6 firefight!?!?!) and instead select 3 points worth of gear, ranging from ammo or health bags to grenades and bazookas. If you had no problem spending around 60 bucks on WWII, a game that has very contreversial reviews,comes from a dying market, and is 90% the same as previous CoD games, then I don't see why you'd complain about Ravenfield, even if it doesn't interest you.
Overally, the game is a solid 9.7/10 from me, and if it grows the same way it has been since I first found it, then it damn well may become my first 10/10.

After playing the beta for more than 20 hours I finally decided to spring for the real deal. Here are a few things that I believe make the game- 1. Bullet time, even though bullet time is my favorite game mechanic ever, though there are some games that add it for no good reason (such as CoD WW II). I have had the time of my life nailing six shots from a .357 straight through the head of red soldiers in the middle of the desert whilst Dirty Harry plays in my head. 2. Mods, while there may no be too many at the moment, I still have to respect the developers for putting mods into the game. 3. Ragdoll, this and the graphics are what's keeping this game from becoming just a standard FPS with no charm. It is very funny to see the enemy (or teammate) fly up into the air after a straight head shot from a sniper rifle or grenade. 4. Developers, the Developers of the game constantly update it with buffs, nerfs, bugs, or vehicle improvements. 5. battle planning, when you first start a game you can choose how to attach, from which bases to take to what forts to defend. This is a very nice addition to the already great strategical feel of the game.
That's all the main things I have to say about the game, now I know this game is in early access (and I'll be happy to update this review when it comes out of early access) but there still are some problems with it, problems I hope are the first thing on the developer's mind. 1. AI, probably the most notorious aspects of the game, your teammates constantly run into walls and run over each other with vehicles, the enemy will sometimes just stand there and wait for their pixelated brains to get blown out. 2. Weapons, the weapons need some work, similar to any game with guns they're not perfect. I hope that more guns get made, I'd love to see more snipers, shotguns, pistols, and stealth guns. A few weapons feel like you're using a watergun with recoil while some feel like you're firing a handcannon (not talking about the actual handcannon in the game). 3. Maps, this is more of a neutral thanks to mods, but that still doesn't excuse the absent of maps, though every map could count for two because you can switch between Eagle and Raven forces.4. Vehicles, thankfully this is only ever really a problem with the helicopter and the assult planes, the controls on all of these needs some work at very least, or maybe a tutorial. Those are my main issues with the game and the ones I feel like the SteelRaven7 (Now that I think about it that sounds like an xbox 360 username back in the days) needs to work on.
