I'm gonna go with a YEAH - OH HELL YEAH - on this one.
As a guy who was spoon-fed the old-school cartoon version of The Monkey King as a child, (the one that was too ugly to be called anime,) I was somewhat skeptical on this reboot. And, though I will grant that the whole post-apocalypse-robots-wasteland-deal took a while to grow on me, I must confess, in the end: The story, (it took forever after the opening Action Sequence too get REALLY interesting,) quite simply DRAGS you into it, (kicking and screaming if it has to,) and if you have ANY knowledge of the original story I mentioned earlier, you can't help but contemplate the complexity of the concept, once you've finished the game. (noooooo WAKE UP... Not Even One spoiler! - Once you've finished the game y'all might even get that joke.)
Right, so... The game itself - (I'll leave the story with you for evaluation.) The controls are actually so easy you have to make an effort to get it wrong, (granted it'll take you a while to learn to trust that fact.) Other games could learn something from these Devs. I'm not saying this platform of control or key configuration is the best ever, cause it's not. It's just that the controls are SO responsive that you actually have to be CAREFUL not to jump the gun. (You'll understand soon enough. Half of the game IS a 3D-Platformer, after all...)
The Graphics are utterly beautiful, spectacular and fantastic. (Granted, there are a few "gaps," where you go WTF because the beauty goes right out the window. But it's not that big a deal. The Game never really loses touch with it's background scene, so it works even without the sparkles on it.)
The extras are... - extra. I don't really know how else to put it. You don't really need it. You don't really need to go through the game again with a new "mod" turned on, but if you wanna replay, and re-experience the stunning story with a completely "weird" or "ridiculous" outfit or other mods, you can. I personally didn't. (But then, I spent a good long week, after completing the game, reasoning out all the story-lines shout-outs to the Original Story; the philosophy; the multitude of morals implied in the game; and how absurdly many White Rabbits there are sprinkled around the entire storyline.)
Combat System: Oh for the love of pete... - I know I said the controls are fabulous, (cause they are, repsonse-wise) but the combat/shooting system is REALLY flawed. Multi-target tracking is TOO DAMNED SLOW. (You'll get why later on in the game, when multiple enemies begin to become a stable fixture.)
Puzzles - Well, they're not Mensa-Crackers but they WILL annoy you, if nothing else, because they take time to complete. - (You WILL be happy once you're finished with one, and curse the Devs whenever you find the next one...) But that's the way with puzzles in a 3D platform game, isn't it?
Funfactor... - Meh...! It's fun the first time. But It's kind of an adrenaline-based thing. Run over here. Move this. Up, down, right, bla bla bla. Kill this, hack that, hurry, move this way - OOPS blocked, find another way. All the while, usually with a "hurry or your companion will die!" kind of thing hanging over you. It works, once. I found it hard to engage properly during the second playthrough, but I'm thinking it was just too soon. I've since left the game on the shelf a while to age a bit. I'm thinking when I dust it off again and play it once more, it'll be fun again.
So Overall?
Pros 7/10 - Good Game; Great Story;  Interesting Characters (they actually grow with the story! thumbs up for the writers!)  ; Great Graphics, SOOOO MUCH Better Than Average Controls, everythings explained, everythings understandable and generally doable, (just mind your timing,) ; the multiphasing platforming (and that's as far as I'll go towards spoilers,) works very well, even if it's a little confusing at first; Great, Scenic, Rich 3D Environments for a Platformer! - I DO hope that other Devs are taking notes. Depth Matters!
Cons 3/10 - The Combat/Shooting System (see above) is without a doubt the most frustrating problem in the entire game. I died more times during "that" phase than I did in the rest of the entire game; Replayabillity; I love your game, Devs and I love your effort, but it's a little heavy to pick up a second time in short order, when you know the score and how it all plays out - (F-Y-I, a couple of mods won't change that. I WILL play again, but it won't be because of the mods.) ; Finally - Not enough FUN-Factor. The game, while certainly a great re-boot of the Monkey King lore, a great take on the 3D-multi-Platformer, a gorgeous piece of art, graphics-wise - it's all good, really - but there's a lack of good clean fun. (Oh I DID laugh quite a bit during the development of the story and the characters, but it was all soooo serious. I get it, I do, The Monkey King was big on High Drama. But it was funny too. So if you're gonna revamp it, why not do the funny as well? I'm not asking for Crash Bandicoot fall on your bum Fun, or witty one-two-or-three-liners. Just give us a reason to like PLAYING the game, besides getting it out the way so we can get to the next cut-scene?)
So... - Good game. Very Pretty. Great Story. Fun, but not tons of it. I'd reccomend it to Story-Lovers, whether they know or like The Monkey King saga, or not. Oh yeah, and just so you know, (I like this, but I'm guessing some people don't,) from a gamer's point of view, this game is LOOOOOOOONG! So bring patience, lean back, and enjoy.

Alien: Isolation is the most tense game I've ever played, and the best Alien game I've ever played.
Everything about the game's sound, lighting and level design perfectly suits the feel of the original movie: Air vents hiss, corridor lighting systems noisily sputter to life when you enter them, and a generator's start-up routine makes *far* too much noise when you're trying to hide yourself from the terrifying creature that's audibly prowling it's way through the next room seeking you! When everything inevitably starts going to hell, the atmosphere only ramps up with some great atmospheric effects, (smoke, fire, space debris "dinking" against your helmet whilst outside the silence of space surrounds you)
I can't recall the last time a game genuinely made me fear for the life of it's main character, and usually I'm pretty blasé about whether they get to live or die. In some games I'll even seek death out as a lazy alternative to quick loading. It's testament to this game's designers and the main character's voice actress that almost every death (whether it was at the hands of the alien or something else) was something I'd desperately tried to avoid.
Another brilliantly immersive thing about the design is the fact that you're playing as an engineer / civillian, not some gung-ho Space Marine, so plenty of effort is made to make you *feel* like a fish out of water when it comes to combat and the exploration of an unfamiliar and old fashioned station: Shotgun shells (when you *get* a shotgun) need to be reloaded one at a time, there's no "jump" button. (The spacebar instead brings up the all important motion tracker which again, is perfectly transposed from the movies.), the bolt gun requires a good 3-4 seconds to charge up before it'll aim straight, and even the task of opening certain doors can involve pressing two mouse buttons at once followed by a key combination.
Being forced to wait, to take time doing or building things, (even saving the game!) and carrying out finger gymnastics to open doors actually adds to the immersion. Nothing comes easy, everything *feels* like you're fighting against the odds, and it masterfully manages to keep everything about the game balanced on a knife-edge.
Pretty long. It took me about 22 hours to complete the 18 chapters, though the nature of the game's hazards means a lot of time is spent playing hide and seek with the alien and the other denizens of Sevastapol Station. Also you *know* that every plan concocted by the crew you're in radio contact with is going to go awry in some way whilst the game contrives to turn what should be simple tasks into matters of life-and-death.
Get it if you love Alien, Survival Horror, or just brilliantly crafted videogames.

For those of you who played Homeworld or Homeworld 2...you know why you should buy this.
For those of you who have never had the priveledge...this game is still considered by many experts of the RTS genre to be the defining RTS experience.  One of the most polished, best story-driven RTS games ever made, AND the sequel.

The story is the same, but the voice acting is all-new, from the same actors who voiced the original.  The graphics are modernized, and the game feels...fresh.  It feels as it should;  essentially unchanged, but better than ever before!
I recommend this game to anyone who seriously wishes to give the RTS genre a genuine try.   If you don't like this, you probably won't like many other RTS games. On the other hand; If you like RTS games, this will likely be the jewel of your collection.

Homeworld Remastered looks great, but I wouldn't call it a polished (or even finished) product. If you're reading this review, you're doing more due diligence than I did. I saw "User Reviews: Very Positive" and "$17.49," and went for it. Ten hours of playtime later, my refund request has been denied and my local content has been deleted. I never played the original Homeworld 2, but apparently in converting HW1 to the HW2 engine, lots of unit behavior changed (or just went away), and unit balance is totally different. Strike craft are nearly useless now. You can't select-box-repair with a support frigate. Formations are more of a suggestion than an order. But the number one show-stopper for me is that resource harvesters will just ... stop. For no reason. This is unacceptable. I might come back to this game if Gearbox releases a comprehensive bug fix patch.

I never played the originals (back then) but i heard so much about them, tried to play the 1999 version and i simply couldnt, when i heard they were making a remake i followed the news until release when i patiently waited for a good discount before jumping in, my experiences are as follows:
Homeworld 1 Remastered
The game
Play the tutorial, dont jump in recklessly. 3D movement is iffy, formations are useless-ish. The game looks beautiful and the intro missions really encourage you to continue on your quest. The balance of this game is off, leaning towards a mass of ion cannon frigates, destroyers and heavy cruisers. Hard counters are not hard enough, specially when facing a mass of fighters in one of the missions or several ion cannon frigates in another mission. It boils down to "can i outgun you before you destroy me?" with ion cannon frigates. The automatic balance worked very strangely during my run, giving me two very easy final missions. The AI can be wonky ni your favor or against you, some units may stay put, some will follow a single probe to infinity and beyond or sometime you may be relentlessly attacked, also movement in this game and the next takes time and theres no time compression. All in all if you played old time RTS like command and conquer (the first one) you should be fine with the interface and controls.
Story and sound
The story has a good start a sluggish middle chapter and a fantastic resolution even thou the final battle itself is not that epic, i was enthralled at the start almost quit playing at mission 10 when a game breaking bug ocurred but pushed on to Mission 11 where stuff happens and it was one wild ride to the end. The voice acting is monotonous as it was on the first original game, i feel some of the "feels" were lost when no emotions are shown by the different voice actors with the exception of the mothership which is a "machine". Finally the soundtrack that really grabbed me in the entire game was the Homeworld version of Adagio for Strings that really enhances the scenes it is played on.
Conclusion for Homeworld 1 Remastered
Bear with the mechanics, enjoy the story, bask in the glow of ion cannons! Also someone needs to slow down those support frigates....
Homeworld 2 Remastered
The game
If you played the first then the second uses the exact same mechanics but balances out some of the problems of the first game, small crafts comes in squadrons and fighters and bombers remain viable to the end game (mostly fighters). Ion cannon frigates are now for the most past useless-ish unless you can hide them properly behind destroyers and battleships. Formations are still broken, you need to macro manage your ship classes to prevent your corvettes or frigates form making contact with the enemy before your bigger ships which would result in the complete anhilation of your smaller craft. 3D movement is still wonky and the AI can be..how can i put this?...dense, for example in one of the missions you are tasked with destroying a ship, in the map theres another ship reinforcing or producing more units but these units stayed put until i destroyed the objetive and won the mission, so i felt no pressue. I did enjoy the tactical aspect more as i had to carefully position my ships to pull and counter the attacks during several missions. Small cradt counters work better now and capital ships can take move hits unlike Homeworld 1 were a few ion cannon frigates would melt a heavy cruiser or destroyer in seconds. In the end the balanced reamained in the capital ships and fighters craft to defend them.
Story and sound
The story is much better told and presented, the soundtrack introduced songs with different rhythms like the one during the "boss" fights. The voice acting remains monotonous but the cast is more diverse this time around, still some of the "feels" are lost due to the voices.
Conclusion for Homeworld 2 Remastered
Bear with the interface (again), enjoy the story, enjoy the music, enjoy using tactics to engage some enemies.

So to start of. For a pre-alpha game it's very impressive.
Concept: The concept is very interesting. At times feels like a fps
with some satisfying weapons (currently pistol, SMG, Rifle, Sniper, Baton, Energy Baton)
and then feels like a 3D mine craft.
The build system is very similar to fallout 4 in terms of snapping objects etc..
but atm, as it is pre-alpha, doesnt have content (basic structural components, 3 types of turret and a few utilities, power gen etc..)
FPS: FPS wise it's pretty solid having been built with Unreal Engine 4.
Weapons have satisfying models and sounds and the enemies are varied enough to
require different tactics not just spamming rifle. You can also upgrade you
mining tool to project kinetic blasts for knock back and through upgrades
add furhter knock-back, damage, projected laser etc.. to make combat much
more varied. Feels sort of like a fantasy RPS with both guns and magicks.
Enemies: There are a select few differnt types of enemies that spawn at certain sites,
destroying the hive while enemies attack is challanging and rewarding (rare ore telirium?)
On a night they attack your base and if you don't take care of the hive the attacks
become worse, sustaining damage to walls,defenses and your EDEN kit.
Movement: I really like the parkour in this game. Very satisfying to be acble to scale rock faces with
the ability to actually reach ledges significatly higher than you.
Mining: Mining is cool. Holding the right mouse strips ore deposits and
trees with a nice context menu telling u the compisition of different minearls.
THe mining can also be upgraded to either be faster, reach futher or enhance combat by paralysing enemies and
then throwing them etc..
Graphics: Very nice graphics as expected form unreal engine 4. Lighting is a bit
odd for me (could just be me) but the light and dark areas can be too high contrast at times.
However as pre-alpha this isn't something I would hold against the DEVS.
Mulitplayer: Not done multiplayer yet but the devs have some pretty good looking guides for
setting up a server.
Upgrading and construction: The upgrades and construction require certain minerals/ores
as a base cost and some allow you to choose the aditional ore/mineral. This allows
you to play stategically in what ores/minerals you have to spare etc..
basic structures like walls etc. can be made using a select few, some way more common than others
but the rarer minerals/ores add bonuses / debuffs to HP heat resistance etc... which is a nice
touch. Equipment wise upgrades for your mining tool, kinetic force, repair tools requires both specific minerals/ores
and additional. Ammo is made at the Eden Kit so you have to work for your ammo, again a nice touch.
Development: The devs seem very pasionate about this game and what they've promised
to include looks like this game could become very popular.
Future prospects: Once more content is added, simple structures, utilties, defenses etc and more upgrades
I think this game could be a real hit. I can forsee large multiplayer servers with factions etc..
in a PVE environment. Differnt builds such as Heavy hitters, expert miners, expert navigators etc, crowd controllers..
Bosses should be an interesting feature in terms of reward etc..
Here are some of the features in dev at the time of this review:
16km island, should be very interesting
Boss like enemies
Explosive weapons - will like to see how much the ammo drains ur resources
More buildables
Creature creation - should be fun
Vehicles - Yes please!
and some features planned:
more melee - would be cool to see upgrades
upgradeable armour - very nice, shield upgrades? regen, damage etc...
More utilities - not just power generators
caves - would be awesome builing in a cave with a heavly fortified front
robotic allies - customisable would be awesome
My thoughts: Been a space age open world builder, I would like to see some advance structures and
the ability to change fine details etc.. no doubt someone will try and build a death star. Things like teleport stations so u can set up microbases in distant locations.
Jump pads to cross chasms, surveying tools, maybe bots that go out to survey where good
sources of minerals are.
Storage boxes are needed.
More upgrade trees that allow characters to focus on one aspect. such as enhancing the fps elemnt,
enhancing the "magic" elements, enhancing the melee elements. This could make boss battles
similar to MMOs where each class can have a differnt input that complents others.
Armour upgrades trees that can favor sotrage, defense, speed, parkour etc..
Large muliplayer servers not just private ones (64 player+ ?)
More trees etc...
Game music etc..
More minerals/ore types.
Also with a game like this you need some way of keeping people interested. If I build everything why do I keep playing?
By defeating bosses can I get new upgrades? Super rare ores to allow new upgrades?
Prehaps require minerals/ores for a power source. Have a constant drain on the bae to encourage
stocking more / upgrading eficieny.
Overall I feel this game has real potential, based on what is already in this build.
By buying pre-alpha you put money into something and the reward could be huge.
p.s. wrote this article in a notepad editor and my spell check was giving me jip. Expect mistakes.

To say that there are a fair number of "crafting survival" games these days would be a dramatic understatement. It seems like nary a week goes by without a handful more hitting Steam, let alone other platforms. And yet, Eden Star is proof positive that there is still a lot of room for different, novel ideas to take root in a genre becoming increasingly crowded.
It's highly likely that you've played this kind of game a thousand times before now. Start with nothing. Forage stuff. Build stuff. Survive the night. Forage better stuff. Survive the increasingly difficult nights. And so on. The basic gameplay loop hasn't fundamentally changed from what Minecraft established years ago.
Where Eden Star differentiates itself is two fold: one, its sci fi skin actually proves to be pretty compelling, as both the bases, defences, and weaponry you have at your disposal genuinely feel rewarding. There's inklings of Mass Effect and Deus Ex here in everything from the weapon design to the way the "magic" feels. The core gameplay here is rock solid.
More importantly, though, Eden Star differentiates itself by way of its developers. Early access games are hard to get right, and Eden Star is helmed by a crew who is deadset on staying active in the community. The Trello Board is updated frequently, and the communicativeness of their planning and execution makes this one Early Access title you shouldn't be afraid of.
Plus, having just patched in an entire multiplayer mode right before the holidays, it's clear the crew is dedicated to their game.
Ultimately, though, both of these differentiating factors wouldn't matter if the game wasn't fun to play, and it is. More content will only help Eden Star become an even better, more widely adopted and successful game than it already is.
Here's to that future success.

With almost every game there are a long list of pros and cons but I think you will find TheElderScrollsOnline's list of pros to outweigh the cons. The MMORPG you end up playing always ends up being a choice of preference rather than choosing a "better" game. With the MMORPG genre being oversaturated as it is the ones that stand out are the ones that have unique features to them that are also implemented well, and ESO does just that.
With a unique combat system (a compromise between classic [out-dated, in my opinion] tab-targeting and the newer action combat) that weaves auto-attacks into the common spell-casting norms we are all used to in MMORGPs. If you play this game like any other game, trying to obliterate enemies with only spells or abilities, you will find yourself in trouble quite fast. The Skill system and hybrid class-classless system is unique in where you can choose from 4 classes and then build them however you want (tank, dps, healer). All classes can do them all, they can all be magicka users or stamina users; and any class, and any build can where any armor (light, medium, heavy) or use any weapon, and you can switch them out whenever you want. Play a stamina FireStaff weilding 'nightblade' for 2 weeks, then switch to a magicka dual-wielding swords 'nightblade' for just a few in-game gold if you need to reset your skill points. Obviously all things don't work as well as the other, and you will see the classic Min/Maxers but a unique build or style is definitely viable. It is truely a fantastic combat/skill system.
The PvE is great as well, decent combat and the questing is also very enjoyable. With nearly every quest being voice-acted and the overall coheciveness of each quest if you are looking for an enjoyable story this is it! The Main-Story is only 1 so multiple characters will have to endure repeated story (unlike the best Main-Story MMORPG I've played, SWTOR with it's 8 Main unique Stories). However the amount of quests all tied together with compelling and interesting content is so large that at least while leveling my first character I was completely taken in by the content.
PvP in ESO is an epic cluster-fish* of spells and death. With no open world combat and 1 MASSIVE Faction vs Faction vs Faction zone that has capturable and destructable keeps the PvP is EPIC and not for everyone. Tactical play as you could imagine of a sword and magic wielding age is mostly non-existent, with "zerging" (hoards of players hoping to just outnumber the enemy in swarms) being the most effective and common tactic seen.
TLDR:
Overall ESO is a unique MMORPG that differs from the cookie-cutter WoW format. I highly suggest picking it up during a sale for ~ $10-$15, give it a try, and see if it is for you. The PvP will either be a hit or miss for you as well as the combat but I'm sure any MMORPG player will appreciate the Questing/Content as well as the class/skill system. ESO is not my perfect MMORPG by far but it is my Go-To after playing MANY different ones.  8/10 I SUGGEST!

Minuses:
-No server-wide auction house.
-The game relies on addon to make the UI actually useful or even usable.

While I can't comment on the endgame yet, the enjoyment I got from this title was already worth the sale price (25€ for the Gold Edition).

Too bad the storyline is messy and shamefully chooses to provide cheesy explanations for what worked much better as a mystery. Too bad the endgame is truly dreadful, switching from free roaming exploration to frustratingly hard, corridor based shooting. There is still greatness in Stalker, even if there isn’t perfection. Just Cause 2 set an impossibly high bar; I remember back in high school, talking with friends about how years from now, Just Cause 3 would be, like, the most fantastic game in existence if it ever happened. Imagine JC2 with even better hardware, and physics, and detail! Who'd ever need another game at that point?
Alas, it wasn't to be. This isn't terrible, by any means, but I'm just kinda shocked I can't really recommend it. The gigantic map full of towns, cities, gas stations, and other such destructible things is now replaced with one that has lush, gorgeous greenery and beautiful coastlines... and huge empty spaces full of nothing. There's much, much less to destroy, which in a game expressly about destroying, is pretty damn sucky.
The game's new additions are primarily locked behind boring, padding challenges that are best played by immediately ignoring their rules somehow. For instance, a challenge that sees you destroying an enemy harbor with a boat is most easily solved by setting up a ton of tethers and explosives, setting them all off at once, and, uh... never getting in or near the boat. Some of these are pretty fun, like the wingsuit challenges, but making them more mandatory than JC2's mostly decorative challenges made them
less enjoyable. It feels like busywork.
The physics are phenomenal. This game is a magnificent tech demo. No pre-rendered destruction like before; every little piece crumbles apart. Water towers no longer simply burst in a convenient shower that masks the tower having its model replaced with a broken version, but now can be wrecked from any angle, including prying apart the individual supports until it topples to the ground. This level of detail is absolutely magnificent and I highly appreciate it. However, it feels like the game map is made so much more barren to compensate for this. When you're on a roll bringing down a base, you'll feel like an absolute badass like you should, and it takes skill and finesse now to pick everything apart during a firefight. Handily, those little extra pieces towards the end that are hard to find now get marked on your map.
But despite so much of this feeling right, it feels like... I dunno. It feels like a tiny fraction of what Just Cause 2 was. Like it's not done. I have none of the DLC and that's really felt. You really aren't just, like, a tiny superhero in a massive playground of destruction. You're forced through a long degree of story missions, despite much of my praise for JC2 being, well, not bothering with that crap. Most of the game is story instead of sandbox, structured missions instead of whatever you want to do, exact sets of collectibles instead of general boosts. It's a game design step in the complete wrong direction from its magnificent predecessor.
(And this is personal opinion, but I find the game's constant, agonizing insistence of Rico being a beloved hero that does no wrong ever to tug on my suspension of disbelief way, way harder than just accepting that blowing everything up is okay normally. You're telling me that the base I just nuked from orbit, wiping out an entire mountain, was only staffed with evil military dudes, AND there's a convenient repair crew that'll undo all the damage I cause, AND the police station I am very clearly walking into with a rocket launcher and killing everyone in is conveniently replaced by armed men expressly chosen by the general I'm up against, AND I can intentionally run people down on the street and nobody will even care... I have a much easier time believing Gamera is a friend to all children and nobody in Townsville dies.)
I mean, there's a hell of a lot that's a positive about this game, but it's just structured badly and takes itself far too seriously, when its predecessor had neither issue. I would almost recommend it just to kill an afternoon or two, but the most damning thing here is that when I finish a game I enjoy, I tend to replay it again and again. I finished Just Cause 3 several months ago. I have not booted it up at all since. It's just not worth the time. Just Cause 3 had an impossibly high bar to live up to, and apparently it really was impossible, because it's this good and still just not good enough.

I have just finished the game, and I am really annoyed at the bullcrap ending, so before I do the negatives I want to run quickly through the positives. This is a beautiful game with amazing modeling, animation, visual effects, sound effects, and to a certain extent story and level design; they are all state of the art, and the people who made them should be proud of the work they did. In the end, however, the game suffers from massive gameplay issues. Weapon selection is a mess, compounded by the decision to have real time pass when you're on the weapon/build menu. Look-at-and-select objects trigger inconsistently, and are often grouped too close together. Quick time events are constantly pulling the player out of immersion, and frequently lock the player into lengthy animations that get them wounded or killed despite no rationale to justify the player being stuck (especially welding and using computers or rewire boxes). The player has no jump button, yet gets stuck on foot-tall ledges or bodies because they are not marked as climbable. There are also several general bugs; characters that wouldn't acknowledge my presence, doors that got stuck in their open position when closed and could not be passed or interacted with, etc. Then there is the ending: you can't win, you can only proceed until the gameplay stops and the credits roll. It was an odd choice, and I'm assuming there is going to be some sort of DLC to resolve this. The biggest problem is that, aside from how amazing this game looks, actually playing it is a stressful chore. I found myself saving obsessively just so I wouldn't have to play a minute longer than I had to to get it done, which pretty much invalidates the reason for buying most of the existing DLC. I give this game 7 out of 10, and I do recommend buying it, but wait until it drops below $30. It took me about 29 hours to finish the game, although I like to explore; this is a pretty good length for a game of this type.

But, this game had little holding power. This beautiful experience was just that, an experience, you only do those a few times then you move on. I love this game too, that's what makes this kind of sad. The community is already quite dead, the mods are slowly coming out but nobody is playing them, and the multiplayer is somehow STILL in Beta. Also, the devs didn't take advantage of the hype to introduce more for the community that grew up with this game and the new fans that came to it because of the remaster. They made a boring top down kind of RTS instead of more of what made HomeWorld great.
HomeWorld is about a 3d environment, it's about a story that is actually pretty intrigueing for a strategy game, it's about cool fights in space and feeling like you are acheiving something important. The spin off had none of that and now this will very likely be the last iteration of HomeWorld we get. The glorious story and risch universe of dying civilizations and the rebirth of your species ancient empire. The struggle to survive of your whole species on board a starship that YOU command. This was and is awesome!
I can only hope that this isn't the end of this franchise, or at least the universe of Lore it has built, There are oppurtunities to explore it's lore that haven't been tapped, there are stories to be told, and I hope they are told.

indepth review
Graphics. 4.5/5
Incredible graphics while i do have a gaming pc its not the most powerfull and didnt want to take my chances playing on high graphics but even on medium the game looks outstanding, stunning scenery in the newyork level looks breathtaking in both beauty and shock. amazing job with monkey to look like the monkey king ( as he should) but also at times can look like an actual monkey with a slightly sloped posture and bare feet and slight jutting of the lower jaw.  Motion capture and voice for monkey being done by andy serkis ( gollum and ceasar)  so you know you're in for a treat there but i honestly couldnt tell it was him i was getting the vibe of a differnt actor with how he looks  a more Sean Pertwee ( lestrad in elementary) and another vide with the voice acting cant quite place my finger on it.
Story 4/5
Post apocalyptic retelling of the chinese classice journy to the west while ive not read or seen the original i certainly will be after this. While i was already familiar with the persona of the monkey king from other media i quickly picked up on who monkey was meant to be right around the time he got his staff ( big give away to be honest). The story is great a couple of moments that honestly seems meh in my opinion but overall has been keeping my interest im only up to chapter 11 but im loving every bit of it and looking forward to delving deeper in to this post apocalyptic world
Gameplay 4.5/5
Now this is what ive got the most to talk about. Like i said in the short review if you have played any of the batman arkham series you will quickly get to grips with the controls as the movement and combat system work very similar to them including some of the cons such as if you get caught on the very edge of a corner/barricade it can be awkward moving around it.
The free running is amazing While it can feel slightly unresponsive sometimes but i chalk this up to me trying to rush it too fast. it is very fluid and incredibly fun, I got a slight simpler version of assasins creed feel going at the free running climbing moments the slight glow to the objects you can climb make it a lot easier to see them in the dense enviroment but not so much as to be glareingly obviouse.
The combat. Oh boy now i can imagine a lot of people who have a problem with this game might be with the combat as you can very easily get overwhelmed by the mechs youfight and have your health dropped very quickly as well as it feel like you have to struggle with every fight. and honestly while for most other games this could be a problem i found it worked very well for Enslaved due to the story and what you are fighting every fight feels like you are facing something that can easily kill you but not to a dark souls point just enough to give you the feel of having to pay attention to what you're doing or at least be aware as to where all the mechs are.
That being said once you upgrade your stun attack fights quickly become much easier to deal with. But the combat always felt very satifying to do, I would of liked to see more combos and special moves you could unlock/upgrade to spice things up a little more.
over all this game is a very solid 4/5  and while i got this from the recent bandai namco humble bundle now that ive paid it i would gladly say £15 is a fair price for such a well made game

Before I continue, please note that this game still has immense performance issues. The demo falsely represents the performance of the rest of the game. Please buy this game at your own risk.
Aside from the port problems, Dishonored 2 is a fantastic sequel. It builds upon the previous game in every way.
The level design is more interesting, prettier, and grant more gameplay options. There are breathtakingly grand and beautiful maps with their own tones and mechanics. The university is a disgusting, gritty area with infestations and traps strewn about with clever solutions to traversing it. The mansion is ominous and grand, with levers everywhere throughout the map to change the entire layout of a room to your advantage. Every area has its own charm, and set of secrets.
There are more powers and gadgets, with more fun applications in the gameplay. You can fling items and enemies with Far Reach. You can use rats, fish, bloodbugs, and even guards to navigate through the level with Posession. Domino allows you to link the souls of living things together like voodoo dolls: if one dies, they all die. Bend Time turns the game into its head by allowing you to set up clever chains of events by flipping bullets, killing everyone in the vicinity without their knowledge, and flat out walking through Walls of Light. You get the idea.
This gameplay is complemented by a great story, and juicier lore. Books and notes provide insight into the world of Dishonored, as well as creative clues about the current map and objective.
My only complaint about the game itself so far is that the voiced protagonists are sort of a con for me. In my current playthrough, I am going for high chaos and no detections as Emily. I drop down from a rooftop with my knife landing through one of my guards' jugular, set a springrazor trap on his torso, throw it into a croud and shred 4 guards and 5 civillians, then use a grenade to dismember the witnesses. Emily suddenly pipes in and says something about the Duke of Serkonos not caring about his people. It's very ironic, and kinda funny.
Overall, Dishonored 2 is more than worth it if you can run it, especially on sale.

Dishonored 2 is a game that can be finished fairly quickly, but shouldn't be. It is an incredibly rich game with many stories to tell. Despite the fact there is a set sequence to 'levels', the game allows you a lot of freedom in the way you solve each level. Each nook and cranny is worth exploring because there is always something worthwhile to find, with many clever details that are easily overlooked if you rush through. Combat, whether lethal or non-lethal, is smooth and makes sense. A clever touch is that it matters where you hide the bodies: leave an unconscious body too close too serious health hazards and you will have a dead body eventually. Don't save without a good look at your stats first! The game very helpfully tells you how many you have killed and how often you were spotted. Invaluable information if you want to be a merciful ghost.

Great game, but have a hard time recommending it in it's current state. It's the risk of early access, I suppose, but still.
- The premise:
You're an advanced colonial super ninja type engineer cyborg dude in some sweet♥♥♥♥♥futuristic battle garments. Your left arm has a powerful piston powered baton spear thing (that would make a mean plot device in some weird Japanese sex game, but I digress) and your right arm has some device that can eat trees and rocks.
There's currently no story, but the context more or less lets you know that you crashed landed on a strange environment, from an espace pad. The environment is abundant and has alien fauna and flora. You use the right hand device to deconstruct and "consume" and store elements from those objects. Different objects offer different elements.
Those elements can be used to construct an "Eden Star" which is some sort of colonization kit that is the heart of your base. Around this base, there's a wide array of componets to build with. Basic things like foundation blocks, walls, doors, panels, but also turrets, laser fences, etc. Building anything use a block-like system where you snap-and-click different componenets together.
Here's why I like this game so much: it takes the free-roam, sandbox games and gives you a clear purpose: gather, build and DEFEND. I love sandbox games, but their achilles heel is that they tend to be pointless: you gather, build and... then what?
Eden Star on the other hand, offers a very solid narrative in that there's a day-night cycle. During the day, local alien goons are fairly inactive and will only pursue you if you get too close to their hives (ie.: destructable spawn points). During the night, however, they get the alien munchies and somehow have a taste for your Eden Kit. In other words, in a true open-world fashion they will flock to your base in numbers and it's up to you to defend it.
This causes you to explore, harvest and build during the day, so you can defend your base at night. At some points, you're really minding the clock so you can manage your time in harvesting, building and defending.
You, the player, can craft weapons and items that can be equipped, or you can upgrade your gear. For example, the right hand tool that is used to deconstruct the local fauna and flora, can be upgraded to become a gravity type weapon: lock on to a baddy, grab it in a gravity type field and just launch it into space, smash it against and object or my favorite: fling it at another alien. It's oddly satisfying.
The Eden Kit can also be upgraded with a better shield and offers a few neat little tricks itself.
- Gameplay:
It's pretty nice. The mechanics are easy to use, the harvesting, combat and building aspect felt solid and fluid to me. The harvesting is fairly balanced, in that it does NOT get grindy. You do not need to take down an entire forest worth of trees to build a single block. Inventory management is also easy and hassle-free. You can focus on building, crafting, exploring, adventuring and defending. Going through the different categories and building materials can be a tad confusing.
Game offers a solid single player experience and has added a multiplayer aspect not too long ago. Multiplayer needs some work, griefing is there but it's just not that easy to run up to another player's base and not get torn to shreds. Thus far, the player community has been helpful and non intrusive. Sure, I've been chased around by some random dude who really wanted to fist me with his left-hand-piston-power-spear-baton♥♥♥♥♥♥♥contraption, but I've also set up bases with random strangers I encountered.
- Graphics:
Noting extraordinairy, but nothing poor either. Everything feels well executed. Performance is also agreeable, game loads fast. Level design is actually pretty cool. The setting is no planet, but a series of giant, floating rocks. The terrain is diverse. Monsters currently feel a bit silly and stiff. Nothing at all threatening, as you can just bolt out of there with your infinite stamina colonial cyborg ninja. Did I mention you look pretty sweet? You look pretty ♥♥♥♥ing sweet.
- Sound:
A bit lacking as of yet. Nothing that really garners your attention. Currently, there are no missing sound clips and I suppose the devs are focussing on the core game.
- Stability:
Alas, this is my biggest gripe with Eden Star: Single player crashes to desktop one too many times. Multiplayer offers dedicated servers that appear and disappear at the blink of an eyes. Especially frustrating if you chanced upon a helpful stranger and were setting up a base... only to be dc'ed and can no longer find the server. I hope the devs take their time to increase this.
At the moment, I've stopped playing Eden Star, because there is no point in investing any time in a single or multiplay session, your work is lost all too easily.
A damn shame, because I honestly, believe this game really deserves a lot more credit.
- The devs:
These guys are really going for it. If you follow their updates, you cannot dislike them. They're very enthusiastic and they seem to listen to their community. I haven't been all that involved myself, so I might be off. The only thing I do want to say, is that I like seeing information on updates - ACTUAL GAME UPDATES.
Never thought I'd say this about an indie dev, but these guys overdeliver on information. They share updates on... updates. That are to be released weeks later. It's fun, guys and I dig the spirit, but maybe you should keep those posts on the forum or something.
Anyway, I'll be checking in on those game more often.
- The conclusion:
Buy it, try it, support the devs, enjoy a refreshing take on open-world sandbox games that offer a DECENT narrative and a goal and if your fancy is tickled by tower defense games, this game is the perfect hybrid.
Be wary about stability, though. Both single player and multiplayer are NOT crash free.

Currently, Eden Star is a game with some incredibly amusing concepts, great visuals and suprising amounts of polish considering its an Early Access tittle still being in early alpha. Currently, the main aspect of the game is building and protecting a base in a tower defense esque setting. Starting out, you will spawn in a pretty small world of floating isles, having the ability to collect resources trying to set up a small base before the first night. You do so using a system reminiscent of Rust or Ark: Survival Evolved which is quite well implemented in this game. You will be able to roam the world using the suprisingly competent parkour movement, avoiding being mauled by enemies roaming the world. On your travels you will be able to harvest resources that can be used to build up your base and craft new gear for your character. Af it stands, the content that is there is fairly solid and is quite well implemented with some nice modeling and animations on your enemies, very simple to understand buildign and material mechanics and simplified crafting systems making the mechanic a fun method of progressing rather than a tedious bore.
This is however where the good things about the game end as the amount of content currently avaiable is rather slim. Yes, there is a fairly nice variety of resources and structures you can build to defend your self from the incoming enemies, however you will find that the enemy variety it self is limited to a few monsters. The amount of things to do simply seems too small for the amount of time the game expects you to spend preparing for enemy attacks. Yes you can build up your defences, however I found that the amount of enemies that attack you at night is not big enough to pose a threat and while it might increase slowly over time, I found that its too slow allowing you to greatly outmatch the upcoming waves removing challenge from the equation.
To summarise, while the amount of content is fairly small, the quality of the content that is there is mostly outstanding. This game has a lot of potential, with the quality of the content thats there, I am having no doubpts about this game becoming something great. If you don't mind the lack of features, I'd say give it a go and see if you enjoy it your self.

My first review! May contain inaccuracy. If there's anything I can do to improve it, please let me know!
Rescue 2: Everyday Heroes is an Emergency firefighting strategy game in the city of Belvitsia in which you control a large variety of different vehicles and personnel. This is the sequel to
.
- New fire types. You now have many different fire types posing different hazards and will definitely be more challenging.
Interactable map. You can view the whole city in 3D as well as your fire department, the location of the incident, and much more.
New art style. Changing from very realistic and highly detailed, while quite a risky move, actually changed to a slightly more cartoonish style, while in general still very realistic.
CARDS! Yep, the game now has Steam cards! This will definitely be helpful to make badges, trade with other people or get a bit of money on the market. However, with 15 cards to collect, this will be a difficult task. Are you up for it?
More vehicles. You can now take control of many more vehicles, including the ladder. Now you can access second or third floors quickly instead of taking the stairway.
The controls are a little more difficult and may take a bit to get used to. There is a lot less "Click this, then click that". You click a lot more buttons on the HUD, compared to how minimal it was in the first game. It should not really take long to get used to, which will not be an issue as you start with really simple missions and you are bound to get good control as you get into the harder missions later on. Controls are really no big issue as well, since after all, it is a Point & Click game.
The graphics are definitely much better compared to the first. It is so different, they even gave it a little extra cartoonish style, which definitely gets my interest. Shading and reflections are incredible and definitely beats the first game. The only problem is that on average computers, VSync, Bloom and Water reflection are large creators of lag. This drops the framerate down a bit, but if you are fine with just small amounts of jittering, this should be no issue.
There are many options you can choose from.
There are many quality options and you have the choice to choose between Full Screen and Windowed. You can even have Fullscreen with or without a border. You can also go advanced and choose to disable or enable VSync, Anti-Aliasing, Bloom and more.
You also get options to turn on or off the music, the SFX or the voice, or set your own volume for them. You also have many speaker modes, ranging from Raw to Stereo, even 5.0 to Prologic.
In general, you can adjust scroll speed and even disable the HUD if you want to. The best part is that you can even switch between over Six differerent languages!
The gameplay is of course the most important part. The gameplay differs completely to the first game, with a new way to dispatch, play missions and your station management. In the first game, you are able to customise your own fire station with props to make it look as you want it to be. In this game, thet feature was removed, but you are able to own 3 different fire departments. Dispatching units to missions is also different; In the first game, you can click a button to set yourself to alert phase and a mission will come up, whereas here, 2-3 random missions will appear on the map. Sending vehicles is quite the same, but sending personnel is different. In the first game, in the dispatch screen, you are able to choose which units go into which vehicles. In this sequel, you have to assign your units to a vehicle first inside a fire station before dispatching the vehicle itself. (More detail on dispatching units is explained further below)
The Fire Station is a lot less interactable as the feature to add furniture to decorate your station has been removed. However, there is more to do. From here, you can manage your team and their "Talents", which give them extra abilities to do in a mission, such as longer survivability, faster use of of tools and equipment (like hoses), etc.You can also purchase equipment to use and to place in your vehicles. There are also many more vehicles to use, and the most noticeable feature is the addition of a ladder truck. Another great thing is that you can paint your vehicles from a large variety of colours with no need to buy them. The one bonus feature that stood out the most for me is the addition of
Dispatching a unit have changed completely. As the game is now more in a "Freeplay" mode, random fires will generate, maybe even two at a time. You have a full 3 minutes to send all your units to the fire and to begin the mission. Before dispatching your units, you can manage them in your stations, which will pause the time. You also cannot do two missions at a time, so while you do one, the time is also paused. While you can send
units at a time, you cannot dispatch them while managing the crew at the same time. You will have to first go to your station to assign personnel to the vehicle. This will be problematic for lazy gamers who prefer to get everything over and done with.
Missions will randomly generate all over Belvitsia, sometimes having to deal with
at a time. Over time, you may encounter "Story" missions which are important to be able to unlock more vehicles, equipment and more missions. For the first hour or two of the game, you may get bored of having to play the same missions repeatedly, which is unfortunately important if you wish to keep your
high. When you have no more reputation with the city, it will be
You will have to start the entire game all over again. As you complete these missions, you will gain higher reputation as well as quite a large sum of money. As you complete story missions, the repetitive side of things will eventually fade as you have a larger variety of missions to play. Though, there are only very few missions so as you start to progress towards the end, you will quickly get the feeling of repetition again. Story missions can only be completed once
and there are many interesting story missions, including a large fire on the top floor of an office and even a competition against a rival fire department against the clock.
Overall, there are very few problems with this game. This is a huge improvement from the first game. There are so many great new features and even when you finish the game, you just want more. You might feel like you want to come back and play the game again some more. Yes, it gets highly repetitive, but there are many different ways you can complete some missions.
I give this game a 7/10 as long as you get it on a sale. I find it very enjoyable and challenging, though quickly repetitive. Worth getting for a couple dozen hours of playing, though way overpriced for the amount of content you get. (I bought this game when it was $25, but I would recommend $10, maybe $15 at the most)
If you feel there is something that has been overlooked or is missing from this review, please let me know!

With almost every game there are a long list of pros and cons but I think you will find TheElderScrollsOnline's list of pros to outweigh the cons. The MMORPG you end up playing always ends up being a choice of preference rather than choosing a "better" game. With the MMORPG genre being oversaturated as it is the ones that stand out are the ones that have unique features to them that are also implemented well, and ESO does just that.
With a unique combat system (a compromise between classic [out-dated, in my opinion] tab-targeting and the newer action combat) that weaves auto-attacks into the common spell-casting norms we are all used to in MMORGPs. If you play this game like any other game, trying to obliterate enemies with only spells or abilities, you will find yourself in trouble quite fast. The Skill system and hybrid class-classless system is unique in where you can choose from 4 classes and then build them however you want (tank, dps, healer). All classes can do them all, they can all be magicka users or stamina users; and any class, and any build can where any armor (light, medium, heavy) or use any weapon, and you can switch them out whenever you want. Play a stamina FireStaff weilding 'nightblade' for 2 weeks, then switch to a magicka dual-wielding swords 'nightblade' for just a few in-game gold if you need to reset your skill points. Obviously all things don't work as well as the other, and you will see the classic Min/Maxers but a unique build or style is definitely viable. It is truely a fantastic combat/skill system.
The PvE is great as well, decent combat and the questing is also very enjoyable. With nearly every quest being voice-acted and the overall coheciveness of each quest if you are looking for an enjoyable story this is it! The Main-Story is only 1 so multiple characters will have to endure repeated story (unlike the best Main-Story MMORPG I've played, SWTOR with it's 8 Main unique Stories). However the amount of quests all tied together with compelling and interesting content is so large that at least while leveling my first character I was completely taken in by the content.
PvP in ESO is an epic cluster-fish* of spells and death. With no open world combat and 1 MASSIVE Faction vs Faction vs Faction zone that has capturable and destructable keeps the PvP is EPIC and not for everyone. Tactical play as you could imagine of a sword and magic wielding age is mostly non-existent, with "zerging" (hoards of players hoping to just outnumber the enemy in swarms) being the most effective and common tactic seen.
TLDR:
Overall ESO is a unique MMORPG that differs from the cookie-cutter WoW format. I highly suggest picking it up during a sale for ~ $10-$15, give it a try, and see if it is for you. The PvP will either be a hit or miss for you as well as the combat but I'm sure any MMORPG player will appreciate the Questing/Content as well as the class/skill system. ESO is not my perfect MMORPG by far but it is my Go-To after playing MANY different ones.  8/10 I SUGGEST!

Dark Souls II is the (worthy?) successor to the game that was known for not holding anyone's hand and spit at your face at the same time when you ♥♥♥♥ed up, each death was your very own fault after all.
So how much did change? Is it an upgrade to its predecessor? Did it remain challenging after so many people were complaining about its difficulty? Let's see.
First of all a relief to all souls veterans among us, yes Dark Souls II did retain the difficulty of its predeceessor. The developers did exactly what they have promised, they made the game more accessible while maintaining its well-known artificial difficulty.
Players that were new to the souls series had a hard time in Dark Souls as there were no hints where one should proceed and there was merely a 33% chance to pick the right (and only) path that wouldn't screw you over from the beginning on, many mechanics of the game were a mystery until one searched the wiki for information - All of this isn't the case in Dark Souls II anymore.
People who aren't completely new to games should be able to make perfect sense of the mechanics present in Dark Souls II within their first few hours of playtime.
So what does make Dark Souls II an upgrade to its predecessor?
Just one word, functionality. People who "tried" to play the multiplayer part of Dark Souls will know what I mean by that, for those who didn't, the multiplayer part of Dark Souls was barely playable. If you were lucky you would connect to a random player in 1 out of 15 cases, connecting to friends was basically impossible without using the proper mods, and even by using them it still felt a lot like gambling.
In Dark Souls II everything works as it was intended, summoning other players works in 99% of the time, also the developers added a specific ring to the game which makes playing with your friends a lot more simple.
So functionality is a big plus in Dark Souls II in direct comparison to Dark Souls, but are there any downsides?
Yes, unfortunately. Everyone who has played Dark Souls will remeber bosses like Smough & Ornstein and The Four Kings known for their high difficulty and uniqueness, also most people will remember the complex and fascinating level design from Dark Souls. Sadly none of these aspects made it to Dark Souls II.
As a matter of fact, most bosses in this game look rather boring and unoriginal compared to the bosses in Dark Souls. Same goes for the level design, don't expect the same magnificent level design from Dark Souls, you won't find it here. Also the way of how some areas are connected to each other just gives me the headache, it feels like they were designed seperate from each other, and then just "somehow connected" when they were done. Best example for this being the transition from Earthen Peak to Iron Keep. Seriously, what the ♥♥♥♥ From Software? Even with that elevator it's still completely absurd.
Okay, so which game is better?
Well, none really. In my personal opinion I would say that Dark Souls is better in terms of level and enemy design, while Dark Souls II is the more functional game. Does that make one game better than the other? Not at all.
Both games are amazing and people who enjoyed Dark Souls simply can't go wrong with Dark Souls II. I had 700 hours of playtime in Dark Souls and +200 hours in Dark Souls II (still going) at the time I wrote this review, for those who care.

With hindsight I kinda like AW, although my CoD gameplay is generally at least +90% multiplayer. In the earlier games I played the SP first, but starting with BO2 I've ignored SP and only played SP as an afterthought. That's a shame because SP is still a big part of a CoD title - rightly so.
So back to AW - I am 4hrs into the SP and 50hrs in MP, which means this is my least played CoD - I've even racked up more hours in Ghost (+100hrs). So with low mileage came BO3 and AW was left to wither away...
But as I was testing my latest GPU, I tried a little AW SP - which was good, if I ignore the future element, and I tried even some more MP which was even better, although I missed the wall hugging - I realized that AW was a pretty decent CoD.
I'm boycotting CoD map dlcs, because they are fragmenting the player base and not a good return of investment, but any CoD vanilla game is still a fun if you enjoy an epic sp and fast mp experience. That's also the case with AW.
Imho Activision has now added a third trend that effects CoD in a negative way:
1. Map dlcs that fragment the player base
2. Too much future warfare
3. Fast replacement cycle
They even effect each other
Not only is the player base fragmented by dlcs, by the time the last dlc is released most players go to the next game...
So with the constant pressure to innovate and a fast replacement cycle you'll soon run out of ideas, so what is left after going into space, going fantasy WW1 (again) like the competition?
CoD is CoD that's not a bad thing, but by going on a three developer one game a year combined with full paid dlc program, you can outlive your welcome with even your most dedicated fans.
I'll probably keep buying and playing CoD games as long as they tickle my inner beast, the one that loves the fast paced mp shooters (hardcore) experience that CoD offers, but I am also glad that there are games that offer a far better battlefield experience to balance the playing field.
Countdown to Infinity...
EDIT: now passed 100hr mp mark, unfortunately only standard TDM, not much else going on in the vanilla lobby. Glad I did not buy the dlcs. No longer willing to pay for a fragmented community that gets smaller with every map dlc released.

Make no mistake, this game is NOT a free to play title.  It will not fall along your expected lines of Free To Play like PlanetSide 2, World of Tanks, Team Fortress 2 etc.  The game is escentially a payment hub to acquire the full game.  Free players can hunt Mule Deer, and use a gun...one, singular, one animal, one gun.  It's upsetting to see this title handled like this, when the actually quality of the full experience in actually not that bad earning between a 6.5 and 7.5 in my opinion  With decent visuals, expansive map, a good selection of animals, guns and hunting tools, make it a surprisingly decent hunting simulator compared to its competitors......but, and it's a big BUT, the cost associated with the full experience is pretty ridiculous.  Subscriptions, starter packs, and micro transactions gate off pretty much all of this game's content behind a rather dauntingly high pay wall for the average player.  This game would be better served as a one time payment game of maybe $20-$30 where you could experience all the content.  With poor optimization, almost all content locked, multiplayer restrictions, and some serious but not game breaking gameplay flaws throughout, this title has absolutely no god damn right to ask for the amount of money you'd need to spend to experience it.  A decent hunting simulator, ruined so it can be exploited as a cash grab.

Graphics and Audio are stunning, but gameplay (yes I know it's a Hunting Simulator) is impossibly long. Without membership and buying equipment, it's completely impossible to get anywhere. You tend to spend about 2 hours tracking just for the deer to spot you 100m off and flee. (probably to encourage player to buy membership/equipment as rabbits are free to shoot, but against hunting rules to kill with starting gun, and Deer are far to impossible to shoot without better stealth)

A game that may have been state of the art ten years ago, 99% of content locked away behind very restrictive paywalls. Want to shoot some other kind of deer? 10 bucks. Want to shoot a rabbit? Sorry your starter rifle isn't permitted, how about a shotgun with birdshot for 5 bucks? There is an ingame currency that you can earn doing "missions" but that is only usable to buy limited use lures and ammunition. Weapons? Real money. Clothing? Bags? Scopes? Your credit card please. And it's not just nickel and dime stuff, weapons are 5-10 a pop and scopes start around 4.
One of the few developers that hasn't figured out how to do a proper f2p model in tyool 2014. If the game didn't nag and badger you to fork over your money every five minutes and let you actually do and earn currency it would be a whole lot better and attract more customers.
But before you go, even if you have terrible spending habits and don't care about throwing money away: The game isn't very good. The graphics are extremly dated, there is a hard render limit of a few hundred feet after which animals are invisible, the animations and sounds are sloppy, gunplay mediocre at best, small selection of weapons and ammo and it is missing many key features of other games such as being able to rest your weapon on anything (how can you not have this in a hunting game?!), bullet cams, whatever you could hope for.
Don't waste your precious time with this unless you have some autistic need to crouch through blurry forests for hours and shoot at pixelated deer and too much disposable income. No wait, buy yourself a real hunting license for 20 bucks and go outside.

Before I continue, please note that this game still has immense performance issues. The demo falsely represents the performance of the rest of the game. Please buy this game at your own risk.
Aside from the port problems, Dishonored 2 is a fantastic sequel. It builds upon the previous game in every way.
The level design is more interesting, prettier, and grant more gameplay options. There are breathtakingly grand and beautiful maps with their own tones and mechanics. The university is a disgusting, gritty area with infestations and traps strewn about with clever solutions to traversing it. The mansion is ominous and grand, with levers everywhere throughout the map to change the entire layout of a room to your advantage. Every area has its own charm, and set of secrets.
There are more powers and gadgets, with more fun applications in the gameplay. You can fling items and enemies with Far Reach. You can use rats, fish, bloodbugs, and even guards to navigate through the level with Posession. Domino allows you to link the souls of living things together like voodoo dolls: if one dies, they all die. Bend Time turns the game into its head by allowing you to set up clever chains of events by flipping bullets, killing everyone in the vicinity without their knowledge, and flat out walking through Walls of Light. You get the idea.
This gameplay is complemented by a great story, and juicier lore. Books and notes provide insight into the world of Dishonored, as well as creative clues about the current map and objective.
My only complaint about the game itself so far is that the voiced protagonists are sort of a con for me. In my current playthrough, I am going for high chaos and no detections as Emily. I drop down from a rooftop with my knife landing through one of my guards' jugular, set a springrazor trap on his torso, throw it into a croud and shred 4 guards and 5 civillians, then use a grenade to dismember the witnesses. Emily suddenly pipes in and says something about the Duke of Serkonos not caring about his people. It's very ironic, and kinda funny.
Overall, Dishonored 2 is more than worth it if you can run it, especially on sale.

Dishonored 2 is a game that can be finished fairly quickly, but shouldn't be. It is an incredibly rich game with many stories to tell. Despite the fact there is a set sequence to 'levels', the game allows you a lot of freedom in the way you solve each level. Each nook and cranny is worth exploring because there is always something worthwhile to find, with many clever details that are easily overlooked if you rush through. Combat, whether lethal or non-lethal, is smooth and makes sense. A clever touch is that it matters where you hide the bodies: leave an unconscious body too close too serious health hazards and you will have a dead body eventually. Don't save without a good look at your stats first! The game very helpfully tells you how many you have killed and how often you were spotted. Invaluable information if you want to be a merciful ghost.

This is one of those flawed games that you can play and wonder about how a few little things could have made it better. Controls aren't good, it's very picky about the place where you can jump from, and when you are climbing you must point the stick in the direction of the next spot but it isn't always where it seems to be onscreen (also keyboard configuration is atrocious and onscreen all cues are displayed showing gamepad buttons). The story is not great either, but the dialogs and face expressions are good (also short, no exposition) and convey what the characters are feeling (largely unused in video games: telling with facial expressions).
The combat becomes tedious and some aspects of it exist but are almost useless unless you upgraded them, like the shield, for instance. It is weak, too weak when you start, but if you upgraded a couple times it becomes useful. So you must pick if you want to hit harder or to be harder to kill, because in one playthrough you won't be able to get all the upgrades. But if you play the chapters again you play with all your upgrades from the previous playthrough, so you start overpowered even if you move from Medium to Hard difficulty.
It is about 12 hours long and you have the premium version you can also play Pigsy Perfect 10 (check the Extras menu), it is more focused on platforming and gadgets than in melee combat and gives you another 3 hours of gameplay. It's also a stand alone story, not related with the main game's.
Nowadays, with all the sales, you can buy it for cheap, and if you have time to spare it'll give you a decent time.

JC3, like JC2 before it is one of the most indulgently fun games I've played in a long, long while.  Freedom, beauty, and curiosity run rampant through this game experience.  Everywhere you look there's some vista to appreciate, some distant target to explore, some military base to attack, or some wacky challenge event to participate in.  It's everywhere and the size of the world is so vast that it will take you a long, long time before you've fully exhausted what's on offer.  More on that in a moment...
Since JC3 is a single-player experience it's nice that the cast of characters are expanded upon both in number and in depth.  Seeing Rico walk about and chatting it up is so much more entertaining than before and lightyears beyond a mute Gordon Freeman just receiving dialogue from other characters.  There's a tremendous amount of fun in listening to the banter between characters and the sly nod-and-a-wink to the more outlandish aspects of the gameplay.  If I had a gripe about the characters and storytelling it's that there's often a tonal clash between the gravitas implied in the mission and liberation scenarios and the utterly ridiculous ways in which you dispatch the opposition.  Nobody bats an eye if you load up a cargo plan with tether attached cars and explosive barrels and crash it into the enemy base, or hook-shot your friendly militia soldiers and throw them into other explosive chaos objects (the game scores you on distance even!) and when the dust settles an encouraging radio broadcast from your revolucion compadre announces that the People's Will is UNLEASHED and a GLORIOUS NEW DAY APPROACHES!
One of the greatest clashes occured when I freed an entire province and then discovered one of the missions took place there.  SUDDENLY(!!!) there was a terrible conflict erupting and the might of Señor Bad Guy was out to harm the rebels.  The cinematic scenes dutifully showed military power in grand form waging battle with my people... and THEN BATTLE WAS JOINED and... I just floated along from a little skirmish here and there mopping up puddles and strolling past the patrol posts and fortresses I'd already vanquished.  Huh.  I guess he's not so tough after all.
And there you go, that's the #1 thing I have to get across: there's no challenge for this game.  You are ludicrously powerful and nothing even closely comes to match your devastating potential.  It's rare that I ran out of ammunition for the basic weapons but even when I did it was dirt simple to re-arm from dropped weapons or storage racks.  All vehicles have unlimited ammunition and tanks are armored enough that you can kill a whole base easily.  Even if you DO face some challenge from sheer number and die you come back into the game with those previously accomplished objectives still credited, so you can just whittle away at your pleasure.  As you progress you gain access to some weapons that kill anything instantly, and you can nuke things from orbit just to be sure.  Take a helicopter with rockets overhead and at a distance and then enemy won't even see you as you lob high explosives on everything of value.
You will have to invent your own challenges for this game if you want it in combat.  The game makes up for the lack of combat difficulty with the sheer AMOUNT of opportunities for combat.
There are other side-challenges you can engage in to beef up your awesomeness and those are fun time-wasters, though the rewards are somewhat dubious:  who needs auto-tracking grenades when I can call on a portable nuclear rocket launcher with more ammunition?  Why do I need turbo boost on a car when it's so much more fun to fly with the wingsuit?
OOH, the wingsuit.  That's a nifty thing.  The wingsuit addresses my chief complaint with Just Cause 2 which was that the infinity parachute and parachute thrusters were so useful and necessary that you'd never want any other combat vehicle, but it made for slow traveling if you really wanted to get around.  The wingsuit lets you ballistically travel all over with the force of gravity on your side and it's a beautiful thing to hurl yourself through the air and then gracelessly faceplant in front of your rebellion bro-hards.
The DLC add-ons are fun, but kind of light-beer experiences.  There's very little explanation for what this Black Hand Army is and the fact they don't have a presence in the general storyline makes their DLC presence seem haphazard and random, like some sort of training opponent rather than some genuine foe you can understand.  The payoffs for the DLC missions are the toys you unlock: the super battle-boat, the jetpack wingsuit upgrade, and the floaty mech-tank.  Unfortunately while it's fun to use those toys they don't have much use in the long run.  The shooty-boat is left to be forgotten because so little of the game takes place on water, the mech is terrifically powerful but not really any more so than a tank or helicopter you can easily get access to normally.  The jetpack wingsuit is GOLD however and once you equip yourself with that you never really need another vehicle again.  I did like that the DLC shook up the gameplay with mech and sea combat, and the aerial fortress was probably the most interesting diversion.
I tell ya though, if you go after the DLC missions early enough in the main game then your massive overkill potential increases even further and you just slam-dunk the opposition effortlessly.
So what do I say ultimately in review?  It's incredibly fun to be an unstoppable vengeful (flying) spanish god and I would have liked the game to stop talking to me like I'm an above-average mortal soldier.  I do think the gameplay wears out it's sense of majestic freedom long before it's run out of things for you to do.  Paying $60 for the game + expansion packs will let you feel like you're getting your money's worth and any price below $30 for everything will surely be a bargain.

Many have heard of him, but his location is relatively unknown. In order to find this man, you must journey through a post-apocalyptic Chernobyl, filled with mutated creatures, deadly radiation, and the lowest dregs society has to offer within an area known simply as "The Zone". You are immediately thrust into this world with nothing but a pistol and your wits to save you. In order to make it to the top, you're going to have to survive...and in The Zone, that is no easy task. Bandits, murderers, thugs, assassins, and any number of mutated, hostile creatures are in your way.
