Writer's note: This review is kinda rambly and unhelpful. Tl;Dr: Bad optimization, bad controls, bad powers, bad story, bad characters, bad voice acting. Bad game. Really sad.
It breaks my heart to give this game a negative review. The first Dishonored was my favorite game of all time. This game... did not meet expectations. Ignoring all of the issues at launch, even now it's terribly optimized. I have a pretty nice PC, and it's always stuttery or dropping frames. And it actually runs better for me on Ultra than on Low, whatever that means, even though everything looks fairly identical. Ultra gets me 60-80 fps, low gets me 20 fps.
The biggest issue is the way the mouse feels. It's always sluggish. Even at 100% sensitivity, it's slow and unpleasant feeling. On top of that, for some ungodly reason, your mouse sensitivity is tied to your fps. The higher your fps, the lower your mouse sensitivity. That means when you happen to look in a direction where you gain some frames, your mouse sensitivity will drop like a brick until you look back in a graphics-heavy direction. That said, even at 7 FPS with 100% mouse sensitivity, it's still painful.
The story is also lacking. All of the love is gone from the production. Emily is a cardboard character. She wanders the world, her annoying inner monologue Whining in your ears, "Ooooooh... I just don't know if I want to be [Low Chaos] or [High Chaos]... I just don't know who I am," in the most thinly veiled attempt to make the different endings more unique I've ever seen. Corvo has a voice now as well, and it's super annoying. It's the nasal guy who voiced Mercer Frey in Skyrim, who doesnt fit the bill for Corvo in the slightest. Corvo's inner monologue is just as uninteresting and shallow as Emily's. The Outsider's voice actor has been replaced too, despite the original actor being open and wlling to participate, and even in the trailer. He said in a Reddit AMA that Bethesda totally ghosted him after the trailer, and he didn't know why. The new guy is awful. In the original game, the Outsider was meant to be an impartial god just messing with the world out of boredom, completely apathetic to the outcomes of his meddling. This new guy is always way too eager to interact with his good ol' buddy corvo.
Emilies powers are unpleasant. To be fair, I couldn't play more than a few minutes of Emily, because of her awful writing and useless mobility power. While Corvo has Blink, Emily has a strange arcing tetacle that lands... somewhere. Usually offscreen. You'd think that it would reach out and pull you towards whatever surface you look at, right? Well no. It's hard to explain.  The gist of it is that your tentacle only has a certain reach and maximum and Y trajectory of the arc, but it doesn't play well with the 360 degree actual point of view of the player. so you can usually see the high point of the arc, but not where it lands. Every jump is a crapshoot.

Optimization issues NOT FIXED. Even on the lowest settings. The frame rate tanks when looking at light sources, anything from candles to streetlights to reflections. God help you if you come close to a dust cloud near a light source like a dimly lit dusty room and an open window. The game thinks I should be able to run it at high/medium settings at 1050p, cannot even do it at the lowest settings. Refunded.
Storywise, inaccurate.But still lots of fun especially if you play with a mate, either in competitive or co-op mode is good.

There have been many times where I wanted to recreate certain battles or enjoy large scale wars like what one would see in movies like Lord of the Rings or Gladiator. I enjoy RPG games for that reason. Command vast armies and watch as your forces and another faction duke it out from a bird's eye view...what's not to like? Unfortunately, so few games get it right. Not naming names or titles, but a few games I had hoped would offer these epic battles fell short of my hopes, either because of micromanagement being to essential, resource gathering being a long process that cuts into the game play, or the characters interact in a way that would take away from how an actual battle might play out because of animation issues or such.
Rome 2, however, gets it right for the most part. No excessive micromanagement that makes one late for the unfolding action or long going resource gathering that interferes with one's battles. No problems in how characters interact with eachother that could be conisdered problematic (at least in my opinion). And best of all, a player can see the battle from above, zoom in to get up close, or get right in there with the cinematic camera (a rather underutilized tool methinks).
Is it perfect? Of course not. Rome 2, like any other game, has its own flaws and limitations. Is it for everyone? No, most certainly not. Go online and search for other reviews or check youtube for numerous gamers' rants about how they praise or condemn the game, claiming it either a successful product or an expensive failure and waste of time. Keep in mind, though, that opinions are simply that...opinions. Look up play through videos of actual gameplay and determine for yourself if you might like to try it as much as I did.
For me, the elements, the pros, that earned my favor were the animations, the graphics, the mechanics, and the--while somewhat pricey--the dlc's. But the most significant factor was the history behind it all and the effort put into reearching the past and history behind these civilizations and peoples. These were wht enticed me to try the game out for myself. For people interested in these elements, I do highly recommend this game. For other people, you might find something more suited to your tastes elswhere. All the same...
Happy hunting, my fellow gamers.

A movie license game that's actually very good, as triple-A no less? Sega finally managing to get someone do the franchise justice? The world can still pleasantly surprise us, it seems.
This is a brilliant game based on the first Alien film and when I say based, I mean it brilliantly pays homage to it. While it doesn't take place on the Nostromo, in fact it takes place 15 years after the destruction of the ship, it recreates the look of that late 70's/early 80's sci-fi technology perfectly with the lovingly crafted enviroments that are joy to explore. That game also succeeds in making the Alien horrifying, at least for the initial encounters. As the game progressed, I found myself becoming increasingly jaded and less scared. However, it almost seems like that the developers anticipated this reaction and fit it into the narrative. You are given ways to deal with the creature and other threats futher into the game, so you will have more straightforward options than just hiding. It's like you follow the main character's, Amanda's growth as she learns to deal with the problems instead of running from them. The story is fairly well paced. It spends time to build suspense, as a proper horror story should. After a particularly terrifying section you are usually given few more peaceful sections to calm down before it amps up the horror again. The familiar tropes of the Alien films are respected. It felt like it dragged on at some parts, but in the hindsight I don't think it was too long. Took me about 15 hours to finish it on hard.
The controls are pretty good. Slight clunkiness maybe, but it fits the horror theme as well as the zeerust look of the enviroment. Amanda is no space marine trained to fast draw and aim her weapon in an instant. One minor annoyance is that sometimes the things you are supposed to interact with can be hard to find. It may be the kind of keyboard or screen that was part of the scenery in the previous areas and now is an object to interact with. Our game conditioned brains have trouble dealing with that especially when simultaneously trying to hide from the black horror of our nightmares that will instantly kill us if it sees us.

So, my feelings on this game are mostly positive but there are some pretty big caveats.  Let's start with the good: even older, this game's design from a visual standpoint still holds up.  The levels are varied with some interesting twists, the enemies are mostly the same design but still look good, bosses are simple, but still look good.  The aesthetic still holds up well and does something different than the usual post-apocalyptic thing (closest I've seen recently would be trailers for Horizon: Zero Dawn).  The voice acting is superb, especially between the two primary characters.  The combat feels good - impact feels nice and heavy, and while there isn't a lot of depth, it still feels satisfactory.  Bonus, my steam controller worked immediately with only tweaking needed, so I was happy with that.
On the downside, the camera SUCKS.  Easily the worst camera on a third person game that I've played in a long, long time.  You'll die from things off screen, you'll get hit in combat from not being able to move the camera fast enough to see the enemies - it is REALLY frustrating.  Thankfully, the in-game checkpoints are plentiful, so there's never more than a couple minutes to move through again.  The other gripe I have is that the story is phenomenal, but it doesn't really end - there's no setup for a sequel; the story just kind of ends without any real feeling of finality or closure.  It doesn't take away from the rest of the journey, so to speak - but it does kind of sour some satisfaction with it.
Still, worth five bucks on sale.  If you're looking for an adventure beat'em up, it's not bad at all.  Also good for people getting used to a Steam Controller.

Enslaved has a decent story, interesting characters and fun dialog. It's overall a game worth of playing just for the characters and dialog. Especially for Pig and his dirty mind. In terms of gameplay, well, that's an another story.
The gameplay is repetitive and often bad. Combat is rather braindead hack-slash and gear upgrades are nearly useless.
The game itself is platforming heavy. The platforming sucks. You cannot actually do any platforming. You just press an action button and your character automatically moves to another platform. The puzzles are also spoonfed easy.
The controls are weak. You often do just random dodges instead of moving to another platform due the same binding. Your placement before the action is often finicky. Especially in the DLC, you start to refer to the controlls with the words cluster and duck with an F. You move with wasd, you change to bomb with arrow keys, then you press mouse 3 to aim, shift to confirm this action and mouse 1 to perform the action. It is really overly comblicated and awkward. Behind a million button presses even if rebinding.
The camera angles are static. Meaning it changes often based to the current screen. This also effects your mouse sensitivity in every different screen. Another annoying problem is stun effect which turns the came 180 degrees around 50% of the time.
The game is also cutscene heavy. You cannot pause during the cutscenes. The game is around 8 hours long with 2 hours of cutscenes. One would expect more control over the cutscenes. Way too many of them can't be skipped either. Due to the save points always being before cutscenes, sometimes you have to watch unskipable cutscenes over and over if you happen to die.
One more thing I have to compain about is the turrets and their overuse in the DLC. It ruins the flow of the game as well as kills all the fun. Overall the DLC was a disappointment due to the crazy amount of enemies and forced sneak combat which the character really was not suitable for since the progress was wave based mob killing.. and sneak... with guns. Yes, it doesn't really work.
Overall I will recommend this game for the humor and characters despite the flaws and lacking gameplay.

Let me tell you, I have been looking forward to this game for a while now. It's just such an original concept. In Papers, Please you play a border control agent, going to work everyday deciding who goes through the border, who doesn't, and who gets arrested.
The gameplay of Papers, Please is very basic, it's basically "Tell me what's wrong with this picture?" Each person who comes through gives you their immigration papers and it's up to you to check them and make sure the information is correct in a certain amount of time, things like the expiration date, the photo, the weight of the person. While it may sound boring to some people, I found it very addicting.
Papers, Please also follows through on it's promise of a thrilling story. There are several moments where♥♥♥♥♥♥really hits the fan and your job, your country, and your family are put in jeopardy. The story reminded me of alot of different movies and books, especially "V for Vendetta." There's a secret organization that requires your help much like the one in "V for Vendetta." This game also has multiple endings, 20 in total. And there not all cookie-cutter, you get a good ending if you made good choices and a bad ending if you made bad choices. Sometimes a good deed in this game does go punished.
The game also has an endless mode, you can unlock if you just want to see how accurate you are.
Rarely do games try and have a political point to make, and when they do they are usually very forced and sometimes conflict with other events of the game. But Papers, Please gets it right. It shows how extremely tight border security might end up doing more harm than good. I feel this game hit incredibly close to home, living in Texas, a border state, and having a grandmother who immigrated to the US from Mexico. I remember there was actually an immigrant in the game that oddly resembled her...
I can't recommend Papers, Please enough. It's got great messages, a great story, it's original. If you have doubts about whether you'll like this game or not. Play the beta version on the developer's website,

Updated Review 2/28/2016
Now-  serious part of the review. (MANY MANY run on sentences)
Seeing as, I don't have so many hours in this game - That doesn't make someone bad whatsoever. Eden-Star is that type of game where you arent judged by how good you are in hours put into the game, The game is relativley very easy to pick up, where the hours would only mean how large someones base could possibly be. In four hours, I have achieved most things (Some things i dont like to unlock) - this is not including weapons. This game is very free-to-do on your own basis, as in it has no meta.
I'll break it down with some points on how free you are from many things.
Combat System -
With the combat system, in most games that involve survival, you'd have to use a "main" tier of weapon, primarily relying on a gun, or some sort of other system. In Eden-Star, you can obtain the Energy Blade relativley early (Basically a superbuffed version of a wrist baton) ; with the addon of automatic aim for melee, you have the capability of charging air enemies, and in basic, warp jumping and smashing them out of the sky (It's not a one hit kill most of the time). Including, you cant just sweep and expect to kill everything, the melee system is Voxel-Physics based, If i were to hit something they could possibly tumble and slightly damage other enemies around them, the blade slicing from the main enemy into the next one besides it. Not only this, due to the physics/voxel way of the game, you have the capability of shoving things down hills or off cliffs.
(A quick note) RMD Modules -
Laser hand! Be Iron-man!
Use the force to litteraly smash explosive cysts onto your enemies, or smash them into walls, other enemies, throw them in the sky, etc! (Some enemies explode on death, though they have a start up timer to that, you can throw corpses away or into other enemies!)
Gauss cannon! Because whatevers in your face is going to die.
With guns, The different types of weapons you have in Eden-Star have the capability of using any of them as a main weapon, as they are all realistically powerful; though are able to be played for people with different playstyles, riflemen, bullet spazzing-smg players, or snipers.
Building -
Since the world is voxel based, If you play Space Engineers you can get a feel for how it all works. Though with that, you can mesh things together (Like in Medieval Engineers) ; If you play Ark Survival Evolved, you may also get this concept. If you place one foundation, you can place walls on all four sides, then on the outer part of those walls, and below into the floor covering the foundation itself (Sometimes you cant, as it runs into voxels which balances it; though for the most part you have very free basis to add even more armor to foundations with this feature). In short, if that confused you, One foundation can hold 12 walls (Which is very cheap) - leaving bases able to be very cheap to create. The game also has a bit of 'structural integrity', platforms only go so far without having a support beam under them (Which can be covered with eight walls on one platform) - as real physics dictates, if that beam breaks, you can be sure whatever ontop of it will go down with it - sadly you wont get the resources from whatever broke. Turrets are automated and for the stages of this game, GREATLY work. They cover a bit of angles, and don't fire directly into your base, or try to fire if somethings inside, breaking your own stuff. Not only this, Since the game is voxel based, you could have turrets wherever you want, they are not limited to platforms, or foundations. You can have half walls out on the fields as well, not limiting it to just platforms/foundations.
- The only thing with building is that it can only get a certain extent from your EDEN-Kit (3x3 Square Core you need to protect, loosing this does not end the game) ; This ONLY applies to what i know, solid big mass buildings, you can freely place other foundations/EDEN Kits and whatnot inside/around your EDEN-Kit's bubble (Expandable). Not only this - Buildings, are VERY. VERY. Tough. (Since i use Ironite, very common)

Eden Star is a fantastic game, and the direction it is being taken in is one I can whole-heartedly support. I've backed numerous Survival EA games, and this one by far is the best one I've backed so far.
You're dropped in an escape pod onto an alien planet, where the nights become so toxic they can kill you. The aliens on the planet do not like your being there, and attack you. You have your MATA-Tool on your hand to gather materials and build, but that's the extent of what you have in the beginning.
You get an Eden Kit, which provides power and a shield to keep you safe at night. The aliens do not like the Eden Kit, and will attack it, becoming more aggressive as time goes on. Collecting materials, you have to craft with them to build your base to keep you and your Eden Kit safe from hostilities. You can craft a multitude of different blocks, turrets with different attributes, and utilities like doors and generators.
You can also use what you have gathered to upgrade your suit, make weapons (assault rifle, pistol, sniper rifle, submachine gun) and to craft ammo, of which you can make different types.
There are three biomes, with more planned. They are hand-crafted and well detailed, with different advantages and disadvantages.
The aliens you encounter will all be different, from little splintermites crawling around like pests to a bird that likes to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off and steal the materials you're working on gathering.
They recently introduced multiplayer, which is basic for now, but has a colony system to allow people to group together.
The game runs on Unreal Engine 4, and the graphics are fantastic compared to other EA titles I've seen in the Survival genre.
The developers also release consistent blog development updates about the game, what they are working on, what they are fixing, and each individual person working on the game gives a short snippet of what they are currently focused on.
All in all it's a great game, great concept, great execution, all done by a great and vocal development team.

The game features a pre designed world with multiple biomes fill with neutral and aggressive creatures. You need to build a base to survive the night, because during night, the atmosphere turns toxic and you are only protected from the toxicitity by your base. During day time you can gather materials and use it to build floors and walls, defence turrents, generators, or use it to craft upgrades, weapons, and ammo. The world is huge, but generic, which is disappointing, but never the less, still great.
There are some crucial problems though - motion sickness. For a survival base-building game, it is a killer problem to have motion sickness, and although motion sickness may not apply to everyone, from my experience, it hurts my brain. In a survival base-building game, you expect players to grind and run all around the place for a long duration, and so motion sickness will accumulate and just hurt the player physically, which is just terrible. A suggestion from me will be adjust the audio, and also make sure when gathering materials, the debris don't fly into the camera. Soften the colorful effects for material gathering, the bright color flashing around hurts the eye.

JC3, like JC2 before it is one of the most indulgently fun games I've played in a long, long while.  Freedom, beauty, and curiosity run rampant through this game experience.  Everywhere you look there's some vista to appreciate, some distant target to explore, some military base to attack, or some wacky challenge event to participate in.  It's everywhere and the size of the world is so vast that it will take you a long, long time before you've fully exhausted what's on offer.  More on that in a moment...
Since JC3 is a single-player experience it's nice that the cast of characters are expanded upon both in number and in depth.  Seeing Rico walk about and chatting it up is so much more entertaining than before and lightyears beyond a mute Gordon Freeman just receiving dialogue from other characters.  There's a tremendous amount of fun in listening to the banter between characters and the sly nod-and-a-wink to the more outlandish aspects of the gameplay.  If I had a gripe about the characters and storytelling it's that there's often a tonal clash between the gravitas implied in the mission and liberation scenarios and the utterly ridiculous ways in which you dispatch the opposition.  Nobody bats an eye if you load up a cargo plan with tether attached cars and explosive barrels and crash it into the enemy base, or hook-shot your friendly militia soldiers and throw them into other explosive chaos objects (the game scores you on distance even!) and when the dust settles an encouraging radio broadcast from your revolucion compadre announces that the People's Will is UNLEASHED and a GLORIOUS NEW DAY APPROACHES!
One of the greatest clashes occured when I freed an entire province and then discovered one of the missions took place there.  SUDDENLY(!!!) there was a terrible conflict erupting and the might of Señor Bad Guy was out to harm the rebels.  The cinematic scenes dutifully showed military power in grand form waging battle with my people... and THEN BATTLE WAS JOINED and... I just floated along from a little skirmish here and there mopping up puddles and strolling past the patrol posts and fortresses I'd already vanquished.  Huh.  I guess he's not so tough after all.
And there you go, that's the #1 thing I have to get across: there's no challenge for this game.  You are ludicrously powerful and nothing even closely comes to match your devastating potential.  It's rare that I ran out of ammunition for the basic weapons but even when I did it was dirt simple to re-arm from dropped weapons or storage racks.  All vehicles have unlimited ammunition and tanks are armored enough that you can kill a whole base easily.  Even if you DO face some challenge from sheer number and die you come back into the game with those previously accomplished objectives still credited, so you can just whittle away at your pleasure.  As you progress you gain access to some weapons that kill anything instantly, and you can nuke things from orbit just to be sure.  Take a helicopter with rockets overhead and at a distance and then enemy won't even see you as you lob high explosives on everything of value.
You will have to invent your own challenges for this game if you want it in combat.  The game makes up for the lack of combat difficulty with the sheer AMOUNT of opportunities for combat.
There are other side-challenges you can engage in to beef up your awesomeness and those are fun time-wasters, though the rewards are somewhat dubious:  who needs auto-tracking grenades when I can call on a portable nuclear rocket launcher with more ammunition?  Why do I need turbo boost on a car when it's so much more fun to fly with the wingsuit?
OOH, the wingsuit.  That's a nifty thing.  The wingsuit addresses my chief complaint with Just Cause 2 which was that the infinity parachute and parachute thrusters were so useful and necessary that you'd never want any other combat vehicle, but it made for slow traveling if you really wanted to get around.  The wingsuit lets you ballistically travel all over with the force of gravity on your side and it's a beautiful thing to hurl yourself through the air and then gracelessly faceplant in front of your rebellion bro-hards.
The DLC add-ons are fun, but kind of light-beer experiences.  There's very little explanation for what this Black Hand Army is and the fact they don't have a presence in the general storyline makes their DLC presence seem haphazard and random, like some sort of training opponent rather than some genuine foe you can understand.  The payoffs for the DLC missions are the toys you unlock: the super battle-boat, the jetpack wingsuit upgrade, and the floaty mech-tank.  Unfortunately while it's fun to use those toys they don't have much use in the long run.  The shooty-boat is left to be forgotten because so little of the game takes place on water, the mech is terrifically powerful but not really any more so than a tank or helicopter you can easily get access to normally.  The jetpack wingsuit is GOLD however and once you equip yourself with that you never really need another vehicle again.  I did like that the DLC shook up the gameplay with mech and sea combat, and the aerial fortress was probably the most interesting diversion.
I tell ya though, if you go after the DLC missions early enough in the main game then your massive overkill potential increases even further and you just slam-dunk the opposition effortlessly.
So what do I say ultimately in review?  It's incredibly fun to be an unstoppable vengeful (flying) spanish god and I would have liked the game to stop talking to me like I'm an above-average mortal soldier.  I do think the gameplay wears out it's sense of majestic freedom long before it's run out of things for you to do.  Paying $60 for the game + expansion packs will let you feel like you're getting your money's worth and any price below $30 for everything will surely be a bargain.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. puts you in the role of the Marked One, a S.T.A.L.K.E.R. who was found, presumed to be dead. He has no memory of who he is, or why he was "dead" only minutes ago. The only clue to his past is a simple message: Kill Strelok. Your job is fairly obvious, to find this Strelok, and kill him. Why? You don't know, and no one else in the world seems to know either. Many have heard of him, but his location is relatively unknown. In order to find this man, you must journey through a post-apocalyptic Chernobyl, filled with mutated creatures, deadly radiation, and the lowest dregs society has to offer within an area known simply as "The Zone". You are immediately thrust into this world with nothing but a pistol and your wits to save you. In order to make it to the top, you're going to have to survive...and in The Zone, that is no easy task. Bandits, murderers, thugs, assassins, and any number of mutated, hostile creatures are in your way.
Good hunting, Stalker.

1: The hit-detection has been replaced with RNG and it's annoying and doesn't feel right
2: Tactics no longer affect formations- units break formation when in combat regardless of tactic
3: Captial class ships too tanky and ion beams are overpowered compared to the original game- fighters used to be viable against capital-class ships, this is no longer the case.
4: Selection boxes are bigger than the model, this is lazy and the original game handled it perfectly
VERDICT: Get the original from Ebay, it's better and cheaper. AND you get a physical box. Not to mention that the original boxed versions still have multiplayer (unlike classic in the remastred collection)

As you go through the station, you encounter others who will probably fight you, killer sinthetics said to never hurt humans, and of course the alien. The only downside of this game is the other humans you need to go through. They are always really annoying and don't add much to the horror of survival horror.
If you don't like a story, the devs poured a lot of money into a Survivor Mode. Basically you are given one objective and a few side objectives. It's the arcade mode of horror games. You only have to run from the alien, and its AI is more advenced in this mode. It will investigate noise, look into open portholes you crawl through, and adapt to your strageties, making you change tactics. It's a good mode aside from the story, but it feels too hard. Then again, surviving the perfect organism was never easy!

This game is simply incredible. It's everything Dishonored was, with a more realistic graphics/art style, bigger levels, more freedom, more non-lethal options (including combat takedowns and drop knockdowns as an alternative to drop assasinations), even smoother and more violent combat, more complex and varied power system, etc.
It feels that they experimented with some ideas in the Daud DLCs for Dishonored (think about the expansive final levels of each DLC), then took the things that worked there and just went crazy. Some of the setpieces at the start are incredible, the open spaces are bigger, more populated, with a lot more verticality and hidden spots for hiding or looting. Imagine Dunwall, with buildings twice as tall, streets twice as wide and twice the options to get from one place to the other. If in Dishonored you pretty much had 3 "layers" to most open spaces (one sewer level, one street level, one air conditioning/balconies/rooftops level), in Dishonored 2 there tends to be an expansion of the vertical play to split rooftops, balconies and air conditioning vents into separate layers. The level design so far blew me away, it's a lot more intricate, less predictable and with far fewer safe spots - guards are crawling everywhere, even on the vertical levels of the map, where you would usually feel safe in Dishonored.
And when you get from the open spaces of Karnaka's streets to the various buildings where your assassination targets are, the level design is even more impressive. I personally found 3 of the levels in the game to be amazing and unlike anything I've ever seen in a FPS. I don't want to spoil anything and actually I advise you to stop reading about the game and just go play it, the effect is even more powerful when you don't know what to expect.
There are some bugs, glitches and optimization issues (there are still wild FPS drops in the more demanding areas of the game), but I didn't find anything really annoying so far. Sometimes the way the guards detect you or fallen bodies is not very consistent - they might notice things out the corner of their eye, or they might fail to get alerted by a body on the ground, because there's a piece of geometry in front of it, even if it's not completely covering the body. Combat *feels* a bit easier, but I can't quite put my finger on why that is (I think blocking is more effective and easier to pull off?maybe?). It might be because the game is also built with the "no powers" playthroughs in mind. But playing on higher difficulties fixes everything and keeps the game challenging, since there are a lot of guards and two-three sword strikes will kill you.
Corvo has a voice now, which you might or might not appreciate, depending on how much you are attached to the idea of a non-speaking main character. I personally find it interesting and it gives me some strong Thief: The Dark Project flashbacks whenever Corvo comments on the various things that you witness in the game.
The story is, again, not incredibly inventive, but just like in Dishonored 1, it starts off slow and then adds a lot of lore and detail through books/notes/journal entries, that you start feeling very immersed in the universe.
All in all the graphics, level design and gameplay simply blew me away. Playing on a higher difficulty level with objective markers off and having to explore each one of the huge levels is an incredible experience.

Eden star is one of the best survival games out there. It has the best dev team I have ever seen, they are very active in thier community and will answer any question you have. Keep in mind that this is still early access and that the devs are working hard to improve it. there is already lots to do in this game, from slaming hostile aliens into wall, trees. and rocks (this alone is reason enough to buy it), to building  a fortress full of rocket turrets to defend you in the night, to taking the fight to the aliens and destroying thier hives. This game is a very good investment if you like sci-fi survivals, and is more than worth it at only $20.

The game has a ton of potential. I'm really looking forward to them adding more content and enemies. Adding multiplayer is nice and all but there's not much to do in singleplayer, let alone multiplayer.
The build system/UI in this game is light years ahead of other survival games that I've played. It's really streamlined and non-invasive. Only issue, however, is that you can basically build everything right from the get go. Not much researching needs to be done. Just need to find the materials.
The combat system, both with guns and the MATA Tool, is great. Looking forward to more weapons and enemies! They should add melee weapons that can be weilded at all times like the guns.
The movement system is also great. I love the parkour aspects of it. Being able to climb up walls/run across walls makes the entire experience more enjoyable.
The only issue is there's no content to keep you coming back. Surviving isn't that difficult. Set up a few turrets and the game basically plays itself.
I'm recommending it because I want them to get more funding to keep the project going, but don't expect to spend hours upon hours playing the game just yet.

Not sure if I've made a review for this yet... And I'm not exactly sure doing this at 6 in the morning, with no sleep at all, is the brightest of choices, but here I go.
What's a good way of describing Eden Star? Well... It's good. Like, really good. How it works is much different than any others like it. In fact, it confused me at first... Instead of knowing about wall running, and taking that first path towards the Eden kit, I went a long way around, and leaped off a cliff to get to it. Can something like minecraft, or the countless other Survival games do that? Maybe. But it more than likely won't make you seem like such a bad-a** while doing so.
Aside from that, there's no terrain deformation. All there is, is the ability to cut down trees, dig into various above-surface ore deposits (Which regenerate over time... Somehting that could be seen as unnerving), and go at the various "Hives" around the game area, in order to get the lovely rare as all hell resource that you use to respawn, upgrade equipment, and so on.
Where am I going with this? Not exactly sure, but I'm guessing that I'm doing pretty good so far. Anyways, the combat system is very unique... It's rare for a game to go "Here. Have fun." and give you access to an item that lets you throw things around like rag dolls. Sure, the targeting is a bit off... Making it hard to actually hit things that are close to you... But it's a fun and unique part of the game that adds that much more charm to it all.
And on the topic of charm... The design of the map is beautiful. And with the ability to run up and along walls for short distances makes it that much better. I can't tell you how long I spent climbing a single mountain, to "save some time", while exploring. Spoiler warning: It didn't. And I was attacked about halfway up. Without a gun. Fun, right?
But yeah, I haven't played the game lately, as... Even with all its charm, I have to admit, it can get a bit old after a while, in the stage it was at. But I would play this game over any other, any day of the week. Because really, it's fun, and I enjoy how different it is compared to other games. Sure, there are people out there who could play "Call of duty advanced Z nuke strike" and call it innovative in its rinse-wash-repeat design, and good on them. They found a game they like. But I'm thinking that they wouldn't enjoy this game too much... It'll just be too complicated for them. But yeah, you may like this game, or you may not. This is just my opinion on it, and if you don't like it, leave.

Still my favorite PC game I've ever played as of this writing (and 4th favorite game of all time!), Shadow of Chernobyl crafts a world where terror and violence lurks in the irradiated grasslands and the seemingly-empty shells of civilization that make up the Exclusion Zone. With its consistently bleak atmosphere, minimalist sound design, fantastic gunplay, and horrifying monsters, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.:SoC has given me more lasting nightmares and sudden screams than other games that actually try really hard to scare you. Players who persevere through the initially high learning curve and generally bug-riddled nature of Eastern European games will find that SoC isn’t a mere FPS with RPG elements, but a whole new experience in its own right.

Easily one of my all-time favorite games (when fully patched... with either the AMK or Complete 2009 mod), STALKER places you in the middle of "The Zone," an area near the Chernobyl power plant which, due to high amounts of radiation and forces unknown, has become a major site of scientific study, a battleground of rapidly evolving creatures and abominations of nature (pockets of flamable air, pockets of air which will tear a man in two, etc). Though officially the property of a few Scandinavian governments, "The Zone" is, in spite of its dangers, one of the most compeling discoveries in human history and all of the countries of the world want in. This is where the stalker comes in, opportunits whom have broken through the government barriers around "The Zone" and attempt to smuggle out artifacts to sell on the black market to the highest bidders. There's some linearity to the game, but all in all you're left to do what you will. The atmosphere's great. Harshly realistic weapon damage.

There are very few if any RTS's that stand the test of time like Homeworld does. The work that Gearbox have done to this timeless masterpiece is fantastic the graphics have been updated beautifully, the control system still feels the same 95% of the time there is the odd glitches here and there with certain fleet formations and occasionally having to redo a mission due to an event not triggering. But considering they’ve been working with code that is roughly 15 years old I can forgive all that. The missions are still challenging as ever, which seems to be lacking these days with quite a few AAA titles. Gearbox had a lot to live up to with this and from what I’ve read they’ve done the most intelligent thing any company can do with reviving a franchise they engaged with the community continually and took on board their comments and suggestions and still post release.

This game was amazing in its own way.  I'm used to games where you have to run around and blow things up, this is the exact opposite, so it was abit frustrating to get into, but once you learn the basics and don't mind your heart racing as you try and hide from the alien it's awesome.
There are a few cons that I found while playing the game:
1) The alien was ALWAYS nearby.  You could be on a large level, crawling everywhere to keep your noise to a minimum, but the alien just kept patrolling a short distance from your location, back tracking like crazy instead of exploring the entire area for you.
2) The cyborgs on certain missions are almost impossible to get around, one mission in particular I had to lower the difficulty to even scrape by.
3) DON'T blow through your flamethrower in the nest, you'll regret having little fuel left in the last few missions and may have to go back and redo it to make sure you have enough moving forward. Flamethrower = Survival
Beyond those few things the game was great, keeping me on my toes, my heart was beating like I was running the entire time and I always jumped even when I knew it was going to happen when the alien got me.

The alien enemy AI is way to random.  You can't plan an effective strategy because you have absolute no way of predicting what enemies do, especially teh alien AI.  It will ALWAYS be hovering right around where you need to go, or hover outside a room you just entered keeping you trapped for long periods of time before it moves.  Other times when it's moving it will move in random directions.  It will start to move away from you and then suddenly turn around and move right toward you (or maybe this is cheating AI from the programmers).  Either way moving through anywhere is 100% trial and error because of this sensless randomness.  Also, this is a HUGE station with other people on it yet the alien is ALWAYS roaming the halls of where you are.  Kinda convenient it always knows what area you are in.  Toward teh end the alien AI isn't random enough, the dev go into "minefield mode" placing the alien encounters at specific points making it more like learning where not to step on the mines by trial and error.
There are lots of bugs as well.  Items don't always work as they should.  EMPS sometimes don't disable androids, molotovs won't burn people, people can still target and shoot you through smoke bombs. The hacking device sometimes goes invisible when trying to hack meaning you can't see the information needed to complete the hacking mini-game.  This is especially annoying when you have to complete the hack before being discovered by a roaming android.
Also, when did shotgus stop having a wide area of effect?  So many games now shotgus need to be just as accurate on aiming as any single shot weapon.  If your shotgun crosshair isn't exactly on what you're shooting at you will miss.  Facehugger coming at you?  Even if your only slightly to the left of it and fire you WILL miss.  Hey devs, shotguns are SCATTER weapons, they should EVERYTHING in front of you if you're close to point-blank range.  Stupid morons.
The save system is the worst ever.  There is an auto save, but only when you complete broad sections of the game, meaning that auto saves are far and few in between.  There are manual save stations but they too are far and few in between and have a cooldown before you can use them again.   You generally have to complete an entire area before you get to save again and with how random the alien is not only will you be dying over and over again but sometimes you will find yourself unable to save for 20 minutes or more and if you die you have to do everything over again.  This is especially stupid once you've completed puzzles or mission objectives.  They could have at least granted you an auto save when you complete an objective.  I was forced to do one annoying puzzle 4 times because I kept dying before getting back to a save and the puzzle itself took about 2 minutes to solve and changed each time.  On the off that chance that you have something easy to do the devs when out of their way to make sure it takes for freakin ever to get it done. This game is also a boring typical broken down space station you have to repair; stuff you've seen in a million games before.  You need to get to A, but the door is seasled and you have to go all the way over to B to activate the power or get the code or use the unlock terminal so that you can get through the door.   Basically all the same stuff you did in every other space station game or old factory game.  Turn power on here, get key card there, rinse, repeat.  <YAWN>  In fact, sometimes it gets so bad that you will be in one area to get something, have to go all the way around to another area to continue, and once you get there something will happen forcing you to go all the way back to where you just were to fix whatever broke and then go all the way back again to continue.  These idiots have no god damn concept of game design.  They are a bunch of morons.

Alien: Isolation delivers a great game in every aspect and I do not regret my purchase or playthrough. However I do not recommend it and it took a lot of thought not to.
The story of Alien: Isolation is cliche throughout the entire game, but this is exactly what I expected and wanted as an Alien fan. You play as Amanda Ripley, Ellen's daughter to find out what exactly happened to your mother 15 years ago. She was promised that she would see her on her 11th birthday and never saw her again. And so your journey begins. The rest you should find and figure out.
Like a lot of people will tell you, it's best to have a good sound system or headphones. The sounds are top notch and it gets your adrenaline pumping hearing even the softest hisses from doors opening and closing to the hissing and thumping of the dreaded Xenomorph. The lighting is some of the best I've ever seen in any game and pops out more than anything else (other than the smoke).
The Xenomorph AI is one of the most impressive AI systems I've ever seen. No two encounters are ever the same. Sometimes she's relentless, sometimes you won't even see her in an area. Sometimes she's loud and sloppy, sometimes she gets you before you even know what the hell happened. This isn't like any horror game you've played where it's obvious if you've been seen or not. The AI is smart enough to make it vague at times, pretending it didn't see you or pretending it did to make you panic. The alien is very unpredictable and makes for one hell of a ride. Survivors are just downright broken. Unless you're behind clear cover, they do not miss. Last time I checked, fear makes you inaccurate at long range. Working Joes are nothing but irritating, nearly impossible to melee and you'll be seeing and fighting them more than the Xenomorph and survivors combined. Or that's how it felt for me.
Alien: Isolation is worth the purchase and for the first 5 hours or so you will be awed by its morbid beauty. After that, it's a very tedious mess of running back and forth restarting generators, hacking (which is actually fun) trying to find ways to open doors and hiding anywhere you can for 5-15 minutes at a time. Wow... this game...
I don't think any other piece of fiction in history has so accurately portrayed the slow, sad decay of a friendship over time. As the years go on, the messages between you and Emily become less enthusiastic, more formal, more detached. The fun and excitement of the earlier years slowly fades, and fades. She moves on, and despite you trying to as well, you just can't; you always keep coming back to the same small hope that you and her can have the same thing that you did in the past years. Nostalgia is an unbelievably strong and human thing, and it's also something you can't wish away whenever you want. You'll always yearn for the better times of the past. No other game has effected me on an emotional level like Emily is Away has, and that's because I've experienced exactly what occurs in this game in real life, over almost the same amount of years and with a person in almost the exact same situation. The final chapter ends on an absolutely haunting note - you just can't let her go, and then when you finally realize you have to, the only thing you can say is goodbye, and that's the end of your life with her.
I finished this game in thirty minutes, but it made me feel years worth of emotion.
10/10.

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a post-apocalyptic action adventure with high production values but boring and stale gameplay.
The graphics hold up quite well and many of the environments are gorgeous. There are a few low resolution textures and graphics glitches here and there, but overall the game still looks great. Animations and voice acting are very high quality too.
Unfortunately the gameplay is rather stale and boring. The game is extremely linear and the combat is rather simple and fairly easy even on hard difficulty. This kind of melee combat against waves of enemies has been done way too many times before and often much better than here. The camera controls can be rather annoying at times too, especially when the game switches to a more "cinematic" (i.e. terrible) camera angle.
The platforming sections are even more disappointing than the combat. It's pretty much impossible to mess up jumps and as a consequence the platforming is so trivially easy that even a trained monkey could do it.
The story and the writing are more of a mixed bag. The core story is a decent enough (if very loose) retelling of the famous Chinese novel Journey to the West. Unfortunately the characters themselves are not particularly interesting and often feel like walking cliches. Trip in particular is rather cringeworthy and having to rescue her all the time gets old fast.
Overall I found Enslaved: Odyssey to the West a very mediocre game. Not really recommended, although if you can get it cheap it's certainly not a terrible way to spend your time.

Boy oh boy, where to start with this game...
Ever since I tried this masterful work back when it first released, I was immediately hooked to it, Great combat, nice quick puzzles that don't make you annoyed, AMAZING scenery, and let me just say the storyline is one you would get sucked into pretty quickly.
Lets start off with the pro's~
The combat: With each mech I come across, I just feel the need to smash them to bits, because the combat in this game? Lets just say every. Single. Hit, feels so damn satisfying, I can't really explain my joy for it, the staff you use makes you feel like you have weight to it in a way. This might be a con for some people because unless you upgrade a bit, the combat may tend to get a bit, er, repetitive.
The characters: I won't spoil much, but the character you control is a huge buff man who goes by the name of "Monkey" (kinda silly, I know...) who just so happens to have ended up "enslaved" by another... er... "main" character named Trip, who actually isn't that annoying for technically being an escort character. Both of them have likeable personalities and grow good chemistry with eachother later on when you get farther into the game. Like I said, I won't spoil much, so I'll just leave that be.
The Graphics: The beginning few chapters of this game will make you want to explore every inch of this pathway you either fight through or climb through (yes, i said "pathway", more on that later) the scenery just looks so gorgeous.
Gameplay besides combat: This game has exploration moments that would be somewhat if not more similar to, say Uncharted, and Prince of Persia, basically having you climbing walls, swinging from poles, etc. Its nothing to actually get mad over though (atleast I don't think) because previously mentioned scenery makes you want to keep exploring here and there.
The pacing: nothing really to go into detail about this. Not too fast, not too short, it keeps a steady pace all the way through with its story~
Now onto the mixed reveiws of this game...
Camera: the camera tends to be tightly controlled... that is, to a fault. I had to raise the mouse sensitivity up a bit before getting comfortable moving the camera with the mouse, it was very slow to turn upon starting the game, so I had to go through the settings a few times to select just the right speed for it, after that small problem, the camera seems to collide with walls and such, but its nothing gamebreaking... so thats good.
The glitches: This here isn't too bad, but it could be fixed up just a tad, but just like the camera, It's nothing to keep you from progressing more into the game. I've never really run into any serious glitches like some reviews are saying, but I probably have yet to...
Last and VERY least, the cons
Tech orbs: I've seen nobody address this, so I'm just assuming I'm the only one annoyed with this, Tech orbs are these spherical red orbs that are scattered around each chapter you have to collect, my problem with them being? There is an achievement that states you indeed have to collect every last one of them, their purpose is simple, to upgrade your abilities, which is nice, yes, but... alot of the time they're so damn hard to even spot because of how small they are, and when you're a guy like me that feels the need to 100% everything, its so damn tedious...
The achievements: SOME of these achievements like the previously mentioned tech orb one, make you slowly want to rip your hair out, like not getting hit a single time in a chapter? That's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, luckily, they're only achievements, but I say again, if you're a guy like me, you want to 100% everything.
Overall, this is a pretty swell game, I definitely recommend anyone who has read through this review to buy it, experience it for yourself, trust me, you WILL have fun~

Eden Star is another open world, survival and crafting game available in early access on Steam. But what separates it from the all the rest that are vying for your hard-earned money are some nice twists, a unique combat system, and a futurisitc sci-fi setting. (okay, GRAV has that last one but BitMonster,Inc really dropped the ball with their futuristic survival game)
It’s worth noting at this point that Eden Star is in a very early alpha state and that there is a LOT of content that needs to be added. At the moment I’d say that there’s about 2-4 hours worth of gameplay (depending how much you like base building). But even in its current state it's good fun, it has a solid gameplay foundation, and has a vast amount of potential. Moreover, the devs seem genuinely passionate about their creation, are continually keeping us updated with their plans and their progress, and are very good at replying to comments in the forums.
So, Eden Star has a unique combat system that involves grabbing enemies with your telekinetic device and then throwing them in a chosen direction. This brings no end of fun, as you can launch them soaring up high into the air only to have them plummet and splat back onto the ground several moments later (okay, the devs haven’t added a nice squishy “splat” yet). After grabbing you can also quickly turn around and cast individual aliens off a cliff and watch them disappear down into the misty abyss below, or (and my personal favourite) you can grab one alien bug and use it to smash another one in a truly delightful process that hasn’t ceased to amuse me.
In addition to the grab and smash approach, your equipment has an energy blast weapon that does exactly what it says to the alien creatures. This can be upgraded through unlocks to increase the power and duration of the blast so that it becomes a concentrated beam of searing energy. Thus adding another unique feature to this genre.
The final part of (the current) combat are the more traditional weapons (currently just a pistol and an assault rifle), which help to complete the FPS aspect of the game. (There’s a rather nice looking sniper rifle on the Eden Star drawing board, and there are plans for grenades too)
Harvesting resources is an essential part of the survival genre, and here Eden Star provides another variation on the theme. Instead of hacking away at rocks and trees with hammers and axes you use your energy harness tool to disintegrate and extract materials from their surroundings. Large rock formations slowly fall to pieces as the “tractor beam” wrenches them out of place and into your inventory.
It’s actually quite satisfying to watch a tree crumble under gravity and disintegrate in front of you as you harvest the materials and energy from it with your high-tech resource gathering tool. What makes this even greater is that you can upgrade this, as well, to make harvesting faster and also to allow you to perform it from a greater distance from the target material. I really do love the unlockable and upgradeable features they’ve included so far.
An interesting twist to the genre appears upon nightfall. Whereas Savage Lands brings a terribly bitter cold that forces you to seek shelter and huddle around a campfire to which you cling for dear life, and The Forest plunges you into true pitch black conditions in a hostile woodland, Eden Star brings something new to the table. As well as an increase in enemy activity (this is when you’ll be doing the most of your tower defence of your base) night time brings a potentially lethal exposure to radiation that compels you to withdraw and find refuge under the protective umbrella of your base’s energy shield. Keep an eye on the planet’s local time because you will need to get back to safety before you become fatally irradiated and/or before the hostile indigenous life rips your base to shreds.
Very briefly, the base building is excellent so far and seems to be a futuristic version of Rust. Eden Star allows you to build floors, walls, and ceilings separately so that you can construct your base exactly how you want it. No prefabricated rooms or buildings that constrict your creative freedom here!
Obviously, because this is still very early access I will be updating this review in the future after the devs have released significant updates. But for the time being I’m giving Eden Star a definite thumbs up!
Things I would like/need to see developed for the final game include:
- More action. Many more hostile life forms that are more threatening, thus deepening the FPS and tower defence aspects of the game to develop it into a true survival experience. The world is a little tame at the moment.
- More types of defence towers and the addition of traps to defend your base during the night time attacks.
- More fauna. Hostile, neutral, and friendly to enhance the feeling of the environment and the immersive atmosphere.
- More geological feature. E.g. caves, water systems, impassable cliffs, geothermal pits, volcanoes - again to improve the environment further and to provide some unique locations for exploration.
- Some sort of story and quests (i.e. an end game scenario). E.g. destroy all enemy life to make the planet habitable for your race to colonise. Or survive long enough to build a shuttle to escape from the hostile world on which you’ve been stranded. These are just my ideas.
*** 21st December 2015 Update ***
- A new energy blade melee weapon (that's rather reminiscent of Star War's light sabres). This is really good fun to use, it sounds absolutely fantastic (although quite a few ingame sounds are still buggy), and it really adds to the futuristic setting of Eden Star.
- Two new enemies, the best of which is a particularly agressive flying creature that will suicide bomb attack your eden kit if you're not careful. It'll also dive attack you as well, knocking you back quite a distance. This can easily push you outside the shield of your eden kit thereby exposing you to the lethal night time radiation, or even worse, can propel you off a cliff to instant death. Be careful how you fight them!
- Multiplayer!!! Both coop and PvP!
For more information on current progress and future plans, check out what the devs post on
, and as always leave questions here and I'll get back to you.
Happy surviving, and remember: if you do die, be sure to clean up the mess please.

Feels like a good game being hijacked by Wall Street.
1. It's a demo, not a F2P game by any regard. There's no logical way to progress without paying.
2. It's subscription-based despite being mainly a singleplayer game with token multiplayer.
3. Even if you subscribe, there are semi-arbitrary limitations on what guns can be used on what animal, forcing you to A. Buy two more guns B. Buy a shotgun and then continuously buy special ammo. C. Buy a bow, which is far harder to use than any other weapon. Either way, you either pay more or pay some and gimp yourself.
4. Even if you buy the subscription and then guns you've only made the game passable. Forget about accessing any other guns, utilities or clothing without paying even more. So be prepared for about $18 just to get the very basics, and at only a 3-month lease to boot.
5. The retail version of the game right now is about $16, for which you get 7 weapons, 6 months subscription and assorted goodies. The 'Starter Pack' closest to that one is $32 for 4 weapons, 6 months subscription and assorted goodies. Here's a hint. The first one is a decent price. The second one is deliberate milking of its customers for even less content.
So yes, the game itself is something I'd definitely see myself playing, but even after subscribing I can't motivate myself to throw more and more money at it to get anywhere. It's a nice enough game, with well-made environments and soundscape, but without a campaign of any kind or more elaborate multiplayer experience it's more of a 'pick it up every now and then to relax' type of game. Which is fine, but completely hampered by the constant money grabbing - as a one-off I'd happily pay $25-40 for it, but for that kind of money now you'd barely get 10% of the full game and a subscription ending
to watch out for.
[edit] Turns out that even if you have the licensing and the appropriate gun, you need to shell out more cash for hunting some species (e.g. mallards) for decoys and whatnot, or get shafted. Neat.

Easily one of my all-time favorite games (when fully patched... with either the AMK or Complete 2009 mod), STALKER places you in the middle of "The Zone," an area near the Chernobyl power plant which, due to high amounts of radiation and forces unknown, has become a major site of scientific study, a battleground of rapidly evolving creatures and abominations of nature (pockets of flamable air, pockets of air which will tear a man in two, etc). Though officially the property of a few Scandinavian governments, "The Zone" is, in spite of its dangers, one of the most compeling discoveries in human history and all of the countries of the world want in. This is where the stalker comes in, opportunits whom have broken through the government barriers around "The Zone" and attempt to smuggle out artifacts to sell on the black market to the highest bidders. There's some linearity to the game, but all in all you're left to do what you will. The atmosphere's great. Harshly realistic weapon damage.

And all this is present in an Eastern European game that still assumes that we have brains to understand such things as battle tactics, changing surroundings, and philosophical dilemas.

Overall, this has been one of my favorite games to play that has came out in recent years. It has quite a bit of replay value, if mostly due to the sandbox format and being able to do basically the same thing over again, but in creative ways. Once they released the first DLC (Air), the game was almost like new again. That bavarium wingsuit was awesome. It made a person feel like they were IronMan with the way they could take off and fly.
I must say though, for all the fun the game is, what kept it from being one of my favorites ever, is the constant crashes and other issues that exist even to my review date (9-16-2016) after all 3 DLC's have been released. I rarely ever sit down to game, play until I am done, and exit the game. 99% of the time, it crashes and I don't feel like waiting for the long reload times so I stop for the night. Crashes are annoying enough, but when you have some record streak going on and it crashes, it doesn't save the progress of course so you lose it. Another huge thing is my favorite mission in the game is the flying fortress and you cannot replay it. They repeatedly have said that was an oversight and they were fixing it and would be released by the time the next DLC is released. Now the other two DLC's are out and the issue still remains. I kept my save file so I have went back and played it a few times, but lose all your gear, records, and such by doing so.
I am normally not much of a multiplayer, but this is one of those games where co-op multiplayer would be absolutely awesome! Personally, if you aren't going to give us multiplayer, then remove the leaderboard.
There is also a lot of things a person should be able to customize that you can't, mostly in the ways of controls. Also views and such. I will paste a running suggestion/bug report I kept on JC3 at the end of this review. Below the dashes...
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Bugs or issues:
Ridiculous long load times, particularly the intro
No SLI support. It is such a beautiful game but even with a GTX980, I have to turn some of the settings down to run it at 4k
Game crashes often. I did find that while EVGA Precision X itself doesn't cause the game to crash, with its resident "Server" application running, it does happen more often. If you disable that, but leave the Precision X running it helps dramatically, but in no way do the crashes ever stop completely (the Precision X doesn't cause any issues in ANY other game that I play).
Gameplay:
Allow us to adjust difficulty. Could be as simple as adjustments causing the AI to give (or take away) xx number of enemy personel or vehicles for every xx% you adjust it.
Give us a way to turn off damn leaderboard completely (currently, I just go offline completely so I don't get interrupted). The server drops have been reduced drastically, but I don't want to see it (don't care what other people do in their game). If this were truly multiplayer, then maybe... It seems when you go offline, it doesn't keep records however.
Allow a way to "re-oppress all settlements" or "re-oppress all MILITARY settlements" at once
Option to re-oppress the two SkyFortress DLC bases - we were told via official sources that this was going to happen by the time of the "Land DLC" but now it and Sea DLC's have been released and that still is not fixed.
Option to "re-oppress" without fast travel. Particularly this would be nice when going after things like "time spent wingsuiting" as it resets it if you "re-oppress and fast travel"
Have a way to reset the game and not have to find all the cars, shrines, etc. after you have completed the game once (may not be as important if "re-oppress all settlements" option is available. Same with the challenges. I spent a LOT of time on it the first play-thru and didn't realize it would reset it when I started over. Thankfully it didn't take away the steam achievements for it.
Sometimes when you try to place a waypoint marker it makes a sound and won't do it for no apparent reason
toggle on/off seeing the summary after liberating every settlement; it gets old
Make "auto-aim" an option under each mode (wingsuit, helicopter, parachute, ground, etc) instead of just globally
After the 1st DLC, if you destroy a SAM, the second you convert the base, it will occasionally fire on you a time or two. The base right next to where you meet Mario when he was in the boat by the minefield, does this almost every time.
make it to where you don't have to hit enter after completing a base
AAA guns - once you destroy them, they shouldn't come back; at the very least not while you are in the area.
Trains need nerfed. Firing 6 missles at once is a bit much. Their "reaction time" is way too fast. YOu can approach a train with no HEAT, get very close, and fire but before one could even change directions, it accurately fired 6 missles at me in a split second killing me. All this while the train was derailing and going going over a cliff.
GE-64 explosives: Since you can equip and drop from the air, why do you have to be looking straight down to plant them while on the ground? It would be great to be able to run and drop them as you go.
After the base commander at Porto Tridente is killed, his red triangle to kill him remains. Thankfully, it at least registers the kill and allows you to liberate the base.
Trains won't trigger proximity bombs
Clearing a base makes drone go away
Certain elements can be inconsistent, particularly wingsuiting, or transitioning from another form TO the wingsuit.
Exiting a vehicle takes a LOT longer than it did in JC2.
Wing Suit:
Bavarium Wingsuit auto-target will fire on your own hacked (converted) SAM's. It also prioritizes explosive barrels instead of combatants or military assets for some stupid reason.
Make a way to disable camera auto-center while wingsuiting (when I am looking around at targets while flying, it works as long as I am steadily moving the camera, but if I pause, it centers the camera again).
Make a way to either disable, or re-key the tether retract while wingsuiting after DLC bavarium upgrade. I remapped the rocket key to right-click which works, as long as I am not too close to anything or it will retract me right into whatever I just fired at.
Not sure if this is even possible, but it would be nice to be able to map a single key to do the boost/brake turn. Hitting shift and ctrl is extremely difficult to do reliably on a keyboard.
Inconstistency with SAM's and trains. Sometimes you can destroy an entire base and a SAM will never fire, other times they fire seemingly way beyond their range. I would suggest reducing the base SAM's range slightly so there is a chance of taking them on one at a time if approached from the right angle. This promotes using tactics.
Some sequence of keys (haven't figured out what exactly) when done just before you stall in the wingsuit, makes it turn into freefall instead; also breaking flight suiting time records. I have the option to close the wingsuit when slowing turned off...

This game was amazing in its own way.  I'm used to games where you have to run around and blow things up, this is the exact opposite, so it was abit frustrating to get into, but once you learn the basics and don't mind your heart racing as you try and hide from the alien it's awesome.
There are a few cons that I found while playing the game:
1) The alien was ALWAYS nearby.  You could be on a large level, crawling everywhere to keep your noise to a minimum, but the alien just kept patrolling a short distance from your location, back tracking like crazy instead of exploring the entire area for you.
2) The cyborgs on certain missions are almost impossible to get around, one mission in particular I had to lower the difficulty to even scrape by.
3) DON'T blow through your flamethrower in the nest, you'll regret having little fuel left in the last few missions and may have to go back and redo it to make sure you have enough moving forward. Flamethrower = Survival
Beyond those few things the game was great, keeping me on my toes, my heart was beating like I was running the entire time and I always jumped even when I knew it was going to happen when the alien got me.

Space Station Repair Simulator:  Hide & Seek Championship Edition
The alien enemy AI is way to random.  You can't plan an effective strategy because you have absolute no way of predicting what enemies do, especially teh alien AI.  It will ALWAYS be hovering right around where you need to go, or hover outside a room you just entered keeping you trapped for long periods of time before it moves.  Other times when it's moving it will move in random directions.  It will start to move away from you and then suddenly turn around and move right toward you (or maybe this is cheating AI from the programmers).  Either way moving through anywhere is 100% trial and error because of this sensless randomness.  Also, this is a HUGE station with other people on it yet the alien is ALWAYS roaming the halls of where you are.  Kinda convenient it always knows what area you are in.  Toward teh end the alien AI isn't random enough, the dev go into "minefield mode" placing the alien encounters at specific points making it more like learning where not to step on the mines by trial and error.
There are lots of bugs as well.  Items don't always work as they should.  EMPS sometimes don't disable androids, molotovs won't burn people, people can still target and shoot you through smoke bombs. The hacking device sometimes goes invisible when trying to hack meaning you can't see the information needed to complete the hacking mini-game.  This is especially annoying when you have to complete the hack before being discovered by a roaming android.
Also, when did shotgus stop having a wide area of effect?  So many games now shotgus need to be just as accurate on aiming as any single shot weapon.  If your shotgun crosshair isn't exactly on what you're shooting at you will miss.  Facehugger coming at you?  Even if your only slightly to the left of it and fire you WILL miss.  Hey devs, shotguns are SCATTER weapons, they should EVERYTHING in front of you if you're close to point-blank range.  Stupid morons.
The save system is the worst ever.  There is an auto save, but only when you complete broad sections of the game, meaning that auto saves are far and few in between.  There are manual save stations but they too are far and few in between and have a cooldown before you can use them again.   You generally have to complete an entire area before you get to save again and with how random the alien is not only will you be dying over and over again but sometimes you will find yourself unable to save for 20 minutes or more and if you die you have to do everything over again.  This is especially stupid once you've completed puzzles or mission objectives.  They could have at least granted you an auto save when you complete an objective.  I was forced to do one annoying puzzle 4 times because I kept dying before getting back to a save and the puzzle itself took about 2 minutes to solve and changed each time.  On the off that chance that you have something easy to do the devs when out of their way to make sure it takes for freakin ever to get it done.  Slow♥♥♥♥♥spacewalk on one of the longest platforms in gaming anyone?
This game is also a boring typical broken down space station you have to repair; stuff you've seen in a million games before.  You need to get to A, but the door is seasled and you have to go all the way over to B to activate the power or get the code or use the unlock terminal so that you can get through the door.   Basically all the same stuff you did in every other space station game or old factory game.  Turn power on here, get key card there, rinse, repeat.  <YAWN>  In fact, sometimes it gets so bad that you will be in one area to get something, have to go all the way around to another area to continue, and once you get there something will happen forcing you to go all the way back to where you just were to fix whatever broke and then go all the way back again to continue.  These idiots have no god damn concept of game design.  They are a bunch of morons.
The selection cursor is iffy.  There are several things I tried to interact with and you sometimes have to be very precise in your aim to get the interact option to show up.
Graphically the game looks great.  The station looks nice, lighting and effects are very well done. For the most part character models are good except the alien.  Other than a few special encounters with the alien it just looks too plain as it tromps up and down the halls like a utility robot.  Other than the disappointing alien this game looks really good.  There are some incredible environments too.
On the audio end the voice acting is better than average and the music is standard fare, but man they need to adjust volume levels, or let you adjust ALL volume output.  I turned the music way down and it STILL drowns out voices.  Ripley practically whispers through the whole ame and half the time it's either music or environmental sound that drowns her out.  You are god damned forced into using subtitles because you won't be able to hear half of what anyone says.
All in all this a great looking game with horrible game design.  If the game isn't annoying you with it's sensless AI and bugs then it's boring you with over used tropes, stock character personalities, similar environments and lots and lots of backtracking.
ADDENDUM:  The two story based DLC: Crew Expendable and Last Survivor are short and mostly pointless.  Though it was kinda nice to see a a young Sigourney Weaver again as I've always fancied her.  I did not play any of the survivor or salvage modes as those types of play styles don't interest me.

Wow... this game...
I don't think any other piece of fiction in history has so accurately portrayed the slow, sad decay of a friendship over time. As the years go on, the messages between you and Emily become less enthusiastic, more formal, more detached. The fun and excitement of the earlier years slowly fades, and fades. She moves on, and despite you trying to as well, you just can't; you always keep coming back to the same small hope that you and her can have the same thing that you did in the past years. Nostalgia is an unbelievably strong and human thing, and it's also something you can't wish away whenever you want. You'll always yearn for the better times of the past. No other game has effected me on an emotional level like Emily is Away has, and that's because I've experienced exactly what occurs in this game in real life, over almost the same amount of years and with a person in almost the exact same situation. The final chapter ends on an absolutely haunting note - you just can't let her go, and then when you finally realize you have to, the only thing you can say is goodbye, and that's the end of your life with her.
I finished this game in thirty minutes, but it made me feel years worth of emotion.
10/10.
